lessons.n: Permutations and combinations

it.q: In how many ways can 5 runners finish first through fifth?
it.h: Multiply 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1.

it.q: In how many ways can a president, vice president and secretary be chosen from 8 club members?
it.h: Order matters: 8 x 7 x 6.

it.q: In how many ways can a team of 4 players be chosen from 9 players?
it.h: Order does not matter. Use 9C4 = 9! / (4! x 5!).

it.q: A lock code uses 3 digits from 0 to 9, and digits may repeat. How many codes are possible?
it.h: Each position has 10 choices.

it.q: How many different arrangements are there of the letters in the word LEVEL?
it.h: Divide by the number of ways to arrange the repeated letters.

it.q: Explain whether choosing 3 toppings for a pizza from 10 toppings is a permutation or a combination, and find the number of ways.
it.ans: It is a combination because the order of the toppings does not matter. 10C3 = 120.

lessons.u: Series, probability and statistics
lessons.n: Probability rules: unions, independence and conditional probability

it.q: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.1. What is P(A or B)?
it.h: Use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).

it.q: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of getting 3 heads?
it.h: The flips are independent, so multiply.

it.q: In a class of 30 students, 18 play a sport, 12 are in band and 6 do both. What is the probability that a student is in band, given that the student plays a sport?
it.h: Only look at the students who play a sport.

it.q: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.3. Are A and B independent?
it.h: Check whether P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

it.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
it.h: After one red marble is drawn, 3 of the 9 marbles left are red.

it.q: In a survey of 40 people, 25 like tea, and 10 of those also like coffee. Of the 15 who do not like tea, 9 like coffee. Explain how to find P(coffee given tea) and P(tea given coffee).
it.ans: P(coffee given tea) = 10/25 = 0.4. In all, 10 + 9 = 19 people like coffee, so P(tea given coffee) = 10/19, about 0.53. The two are different because they divide by different groups.

lessons.u: Series, probability and statistics
lessons.n: Normal distributions and z-scores

it.q: Test scores have a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8. What is the z-score of a score of 86?
it.h: z = (value - mean) / standard deviation.

it.q: In a normal distribution, about what percent of the data lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
it.h: Use the 68-95-99.7 rule.

it.q: Plant heights are normally distributed with a mean of 30 cm and a standard deviation of 4 cm. What height in cm has a z-score of -1.5?
it.h: Value = mean + z x standard deviation.

it.q: In a normal distribution, what percent of the data is above the mean?
it.h: A normal curve is symmetric about the mean.

it.q: Battery lifetimes are normally distributed with a mean of 500 hours and a standard deviation of 50 hours. About what percent last between 450 and 550 hours?
it.h: How many standard deviations from the mean are 450 and 550?

it.q: Ana scored 82 on a test with mean 74 and standard deviation 4. Ben scored 88 on a test with mean 80 and standard deviation 8. Explain who did better compared with their own class.
it.ans: Ana's z-score is (82 - 74)/4 = 2 and Ben's is (88 - 80)/8 = 1. Ana did better compared with her class because her score is more standard deviations above the mean.

lessons.u: Series, probability and statistics
lessons.n: Sampling, experiments and margin of error

it.q: A study randomly assigns patients to take a new medicine or a placebo. What kind of study is it?
it.h: Did the researchers assign a treatment?

it.q: A radio host asks listeners to call in with their opinion on a new law. Why might the results be biased?
ch: Only people who choose to call in are counted
Everyone in the city is counted
it.h: Who decides whether to be part of the sample?

it.q: In a random sample of 200 students, 130 prefer later school start times. What percent of the sample prefers later start times?
it.h: Divide 130 by 200 and write the result as a percent.

it.q: A survey estimates 48% support with a margin of error of 3%. Which interval is the likely range for the whole population?
it.h: Subtract and add the margin of error.

it.q: A margin of error is often estimated as 1 divided by the square root of n, where n is the sample size. What is this estimate, as a percent, for n = 400?
it.h: The square root of 400 is 20.

it.q: Explain the difference between an observational study and an experiment, and why only an experiment can show cause and effect.
it.ans: In an observational study researchers watch and record without changing anything. In an experiment they randomly assign treatments. Random assignment makes the groups alike except for the treatment, so a difference in results can be credited to the treatment.

lessons.u: Series, probability and statistics
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: What is the sum of the first 8 terms of 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ...?
it.h: Find the 8th term, then use n(a_1 + a_n)/2.

it.q: In how many ways can 3 students be chosen from 6 for a project team?
it.h: Order does not matter.

it.q: A fair coin is flipped and a fair number cube is rolled. What is the probability of heads and a 6?
it.h: The events are independent, so multiply.

it.q: Scores are normally distributed with a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 5. About what percent are between 70 and 90?
it.h: How many standard deviations from the mean are 70 and 90?

it.q: Which sample is most likely to represent all adults in a city?
ch: 300 adults chosen at random from city records
300 people who answer an online poll
300 people who live on one street
it.h: Every adult should have the same chance of being picked.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Limits from graphs and tables, and one-sided limits

it.q: A table shows f(1.9) = 4.8, f(1.99) = 4.98, f(2.01) = 5.02 and f(2.1) = 5.2. What does the limit of f(x) as x approaches 2 appear to be?
it.h: Look at what the outputs approach from both sides.

it.q: The left-hand limit of f at x = 3 is 7 and the right-hand limit is 7, but f(3) = 2. What is the limit of f(x) as x approaches 3?
it.h: A limit depends on values near 3, not the value at 3.

it.q: f(x) = 1 for x < 0 and f(x) = -1 for x > 0. What is the limit of f(x) as x approaches 0?
it.h: Compare the two one-sided limits.

it.q: f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = 3x - 1 for x >= 2. What is the limit of f(x) as x approaches 2 from the left?
it.h: Use the piece for x < 2.

it.q: g(x) = abs(x - 4)/(x - 4). What is the limit of g(x) as x approaches 4 from the right?
it.h: For x > 4, abs(x - 4) = x - 4.

it.q: Explain why a table of values can suggest a limit but cannot prove it.
it.ans: A table shows only a few inputs near the point. The function could behave differently between or closer than those inputs, so a table suggests the limit, but a graph or algebra argument is needed to be sure.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Evaluating limits algebraically

it.q: What is the limit of (x^2 - 3x + 2) as x approaches 4?
it.h: Polynomials are continuous, so substitute.

it.q: What is the limit of (x^2 - 16)/(x - 4) as x approaches 4?
it.h: Factor the numerator and cancel.

it.q: What is the limit of (x^2 + 5x + 6)/(x + 2) as x approaches -2?
it.h: Substituting gives 0/0, so factor first.

it.q: What is the limit of (the square root of x - 3)/(x - 9) as x approaches 9?
it.h: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by (the square root of x + 3).

it.q: What is the limit of ((5 + h)^2 - 25)/h as h approaches 0?
it.h: Expand and simplify before letting h approach 0.

it.q: Explain why substituting x = 1 into (x^3 - 1)/(x - 1) does not give the limit directly, and find the limit.
it.ans: Substituting gives 0/0, which tells us nothing yet. Factor: x^3 - 1 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1). Cancel (x - 1) and substitute: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Limits at infinity and horizontal asymptotes

it.q: What is the limit of 5/x^2 as x approaches infinity?
it.h: The denominator grows without bound.

it.q: What is the limit of (4x + 1)/(2x - 3) as x approaches infinity?
it.h: Divide the numerator and denominator by x.

it.q: What is the limit of (x + 7)/(x^2 + 1) as x approaches infinity?
it.h: The denominator has the higher degree.

it.q: What is the limit of (x^3 - 2)/(5x^2 + x) as x approaches infinity?
it.h: Compare the degrees of the numerator and denominator.

it.q: f(x) = (6x^2 - x)/(3x^2 + 2) has the horizontal asymptote y = c. What is c?
it.h: When the degrees are equal, divide the leading coefficients.

it.q: Explain how to find the limit of (7x^2 + 3x)/(2x^2 - 5) as x approaches infinity.
it.ans: Divide every term by x^2: (7 + 3/x)/(2 - 5/x^2). As x approaches infinity, 3/x and 5/x^2 approach 0, so the limit is 7/2.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes

it.q: What is the limit of 1/x^2 as x approaches 0?
it.h: 1/x^2 is positive and gets larger as x gets close to 0.

it.q: What is the limit of 1/(x - 3) as x approaches 3 from the right?
it.h: For x slightly greater than 3, x - 3 is a small positive number.

it.q: What is the limit of 1/(x - 3) as x approaches 3 from the left?
it.h: For x slightly less than 3, x - 3 is a small negative number.

it.q: f(x) = (x + 4)/(x^2 - 9) has two vertical asymptotes. What is the negative one? Give the x-value.
it.h: Set the denominator equal to 0 and check that the numerator is not 0 there.

it.q: Which function has a vertical asymptote, not a hole, at x = 1?
it.h: A hole happens when the factor cancels.

it.q: Explain how to tell whether a zero of the denominator of a rational function gives a vertical asymptote or a hole.
it.ans: Factor and cancel common factors. If the factor that makes the denominator 0 cancels completely, there is a hole. If that factor is still in the denominator after canceling, there is a vertical asymptote.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Continuity and types of discontinuity

it.q: What type of discontinuity does f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) have at x = 2?
it.h: Does the factor (x - 2) cancel?

it.q: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x + 3 for x >= 2. What type of discontinuity does f have at x = 2?
it.h: Compare the one-sided limits.

it.q: f(x) = (x^2 - 1)/(x + 1) for x not equal to -1. What value should f(-1) have to make f continuous at -1?
it.h: Find the limit as x approaches -1.

it.q: f(x) = kx + 1 for x < 3 and f(x) = x^2 - 2 for x >= 3. What value of k makes f continuous?
it.h: Make the two pieces equal at x = 3.

it.q: On which interval is f(x) = 1/(x - 4) continuous?
it.h: Find where the function is undefined.

it.q: Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to explain why f(x) = x^3 - x - 1 has a zero between x = 1 and x = 2.
it.ans: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous. f(1) = -1 < 0 and f(2) = 5 > 0. A continuous function that goes from a negative value to a positive value must pass through 0, so there is a zero between 1 and 2.

lessons.u: Limits and continuity
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: What is the limit of (x^2 - 49)/(x - 7) as x approaches 7?
it.h: Factor the numerator.

it.q: What is the limit of (5x^2 - 3)/(x^2 + 2x) as x approaches infinity?
it.h: Compare the leading terms.

it.q: What type of discontinuity does f(x) = 1/(x - 6) have at x = 6?
it.h: Does the function approach a finite value near 6?

it.q: f(x) = x^2 for x < 1 and f(x) = 2x + c for x >= 1. What value of c makes f continuous?
it.h: Make both pieces equal at x = 1.

it.q: What is the limit of 4/(x + 1)^2 as x approaches -1?
it.h: Near x = -1 the denominator is a small positive number.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: Average and instantaneous rate of change

it.q: f(x) = x^2 + 3. What is the average rate of change of f from x = 1 to x = 4?
A car is 30 miles from home at 1:00 pm and 150 miles from home at 3:00 pm. What is its average speed in miles per hour?
it.h: Divide the change in distance by the change in time.

it.q: The instantaneous rate of change of f at x = a is
ch: the slope of the tangent line at x = a
the slope of the secant line from 0 to a
the average of f(0) and f(a)
it.h: Think of a secant line whose second point slides toward the first.

it.q: s(t) = 4t^2 is a position in meters after t seconds. Which expression is the average velocity from t = 2 to t = 2 + h?
it.h: Average velocity is change in position over change in time.

it.q: s(t) = 4t^2 is a position in meters after t seconds. The average velocity from t = 2 to t = 2 + h simplifies to 16 + 4h. What is the instantaneous velocity at t = 2, in m/s?
it.h: Let h approach 0.

it.q: Explain the difference between average velocity and instantaneous velocity.
it.ans: Average velocity is the change in position divided by the time over an interval. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one moment: the limit of average velocities over shorter and shorter intervals, which is the derivative of position.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: The definition of the derivative and differentiability

it.q: Which expression is the definition of f'(x)?
ch: the limit as h approaches 0 of (f(x + h) - f(x))/h
the limit as h approaches 0 of f(x + h)
it.h: It is the limit of a difference quotient.

it.q: Use the definition of the derivative to find f'(2) for f(x) = 3x^2.
it.h: (3(2 + h)^2 - 12)/h simplifies to 12 + 3h.

it.q: Use the definition of the derivative to find f'(x) for f(x) = 5x - 1.
it.h: Everything cancels except 5h in the numerator.

it.q: Where is f(x) = abs(x) not differentiable?
it.h: Look for a sharp corner.

it.q: Use the definition of the derivative for f(x) = x^2 + 4x, then evaluate f'(1).
it.h: The difference quotient simplifies to 2x + h + 4.

it.q: Explain how a function can be continuous at a point but not differentiable there, with an example.
it.ans: A graph can have no break but still have a sharp corner, cusp or vertical tangent. abs(x) is continuous at 0, but its slope is -1 on the left and 1 on the right, so there is no single tangent slope and no derivative at 0.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: The power rule and derivatives of polynomials

it.q: What is the derivative of x^8?
it.h: Bring the exponent down and subtract 1 from it.

it.q: What is the derivative of 4x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 9?
it.h: Differentiate each term. The derivative of a constant is 0.

it.q: What is the derivative of the square root of x, written x^(1/2)?
ch: 1/(2 times the square root of x)
2 times the square root of x
it.h: Use the power rule with n = 1/2.

it.q: f(x) = 3/x, which is 3x^(-1). What is f'(1)?
it.h: The power rule works for negative exponents too.

it.q: What is the slope of the tangent line to y = x^4 - 2x at x = 1?
it.h: Find dy/dx and substitute 1.

it.q: Find the equation of the tangent line to y = x^3 - 2x at x = 2.
it.ans: y(2) = 8 - 4 = 4. y' = 3x^2 - 2, so the slope at x = 2 is 12 - 2 = 10. The tangent line is y - 4 = 10(x - 2), or y = 10x - 16.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: The product and quotient rules

it.q: Use the product rule to find the derivative of x^3(x + 1).
it.h: (fg)' = f'g + fg'.

it.q: Use the quotient rule to find the derivative of x/(x + 1).

it.h: Use the product rule, or multiply out first.

it.q: What is the derivative of x e^x?
it.h: Use the product rule with f = x and g = e^x.

it.q: g(x) = (x^2 + 1)/x. What is g'(1)?
it.h: You can divide first: (x^2 + 1)/x = x + 1/x.

it.q: Explain why the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives, using f(x) = x and g(x) = x.
it.ans: fg = x^2, whose derivative is 2x. But f' times g' = 1 x 1 = 1, which is not 2x. The product rule, f'g + fg' = x + x = 2x, gives the correct answer.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: The chain rule

it.q: What is the derivative of (3x - 2)^4?
it.h: Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

it.q: What is the derivative of (x^2 + 1)^5?
it.h: The inside function is x^2 + 1.

it.q: What is the derivative of the square root of (4x + 1)?
it.h: Write it as (4x + 1)^(1/2).
Use the chain rule, then substitute 2.

it.q: y = (x^2 - 3)^2. What is dy/dx at x = 2?
it.h: The outer function is u^2 and the inner function is x^2 - 3.

it.q: Explain the chain rule using the example y = (5x + 2)^3.
it.ans: y is a function of u = 5x + 2, and u is a function of x. dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx = 3u^2 x 5 = 15(5x + 2)^2. The two rates of change multiply.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: Derivatives of exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions

it.q: What is the derivative of cos x?
it.h: Think about the slope of the cosine graph at x = pi/2.

it.q: What is the derivative of ln x?
it.h: ln x is the inverse of e^x.

it.q: What is the derivative of e^(x^2)?
it.h: Use the chain rule with the inside function x^2.

it.q: f(x) = sin(3x). What is f'(0)?
it.h: The derivative of sin(u) is cos(u) times u'.

it.q: f(x) = ln(x^2 + 1). What is f'(1)?
it.h: The derivative of ln(u) is u'/u.

it.q: Explain, using the graph, what it means that the derivative of e^x is e^x.
it.ans: At every point on y = e^x, the slope of the tangent line equals the height of the graph. The function is its own rate of change, which is what makes e special.

lessons.u: Derivatives
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: What is the derivative of 3x^4 - x^2 + 7?
it.h: Use the power rule on each term.

it.q: f(x) = x^2(x + 1). What is f'(1)?
it.h: Multiply out first, or use the product rule.

it.q: What is the derivative of (4x + 3)^2?
it.h: Use the chain rule.

it.q: f(x) = 2 cos x. What is f'(0)?
it.h: The derivative of cos x is -sin x.

it.q: What is the average rate of change of f(x) = x^2 from x = 2 to x = 6?

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Increasing, decreasing and the first derivative test

it.q: f'(x) < 0 on an interval. What does that tell you about f there?
it.h: The derivative gives the slope.

it.q: f(x) = x^2 - 8x + 1. At what x is there a critical point?
it.h: Solve f'(x) = 0.

it.q: On which intervals is f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 increasing?
it.h: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2). Where is it positive?

it.q: f'(x) changes from positive to negative at x = 5. What does f have at x = 5?
it.h: The function rises and then falls.

it.q: f(x) = 2x^3 - 6x + 1 has a relative minimum at a positive x. What is that x?
it.h: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6. Check where the sign changes from negative to positive.

it.q: Use the first derivative test to classify the critical point of f(x) = x^4.
it.ans: f'(x) = 4x^3 = 0 at x = 0. f' is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0, so f decreases then increases, and x = 0 is a relative minimum.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Concavity, inflection points and the second derivative

it.q: f''(x) > 0 on an interval. What is true about the graph of f there?
it.h: A positive second derivative means the slope is increasing.

it.q: f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 4. At what x is there an inflection point?
it.h: Solve f''(x) = 0 and check that the concavity changes.

it.q: On which interval is f(x) = x^3 - 3x concave down?
f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) = -4. What does f have at x = 3?
it.h: The graph is concave down at a horizontal tangent.

it.q: f(x) = 2x^4 - x. What is f''(1)?
it.h: Differentiate twice.

it.q: Explain what an inflection point is and how to find one.
it.ans: An inflection point is where the graph changes concavity, from concave up to concave down or the reverse. Find where f''(x) = 0 or is undefined, then check that f'' changes sign there.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Absolute extrema on closed intervals

it.q: What is the absolute maximum of f(x) = 3x + 2 on [0, 4]?
it.h: A line has its greatest and least values at the endpoints.

it.q: What is the absolute minimum of f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7 on [0, 5]?
it.h: Check the critical point and both endpoints.

it.q: What is the absolute maximum of f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [0, 3]?
it.h: Compare f at x = 0, at the critical point x = 1 and at x = 3.

it.q: What does the Extreme Value Theorem say?
ch: A continuous function on a closed interval has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there
Every differentiable function has a critical point
A function on an open interval has a maximum
it.h: It needs two conditions: continuity and a closed interval.

it.q: What is the absolute minimum of f(x) = x^3 - 12x on [0, 3]?
it.h: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12. Only one critical point is in the interval.

it.q: Describe the closed interval method for finding absolute extrema.
it.ans: Find the critical points inside the interval. Evaluate f at those points and at both endpoints. The largest value is the absolute maximum and the smallest value is the absolute minimum.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Optimization problems

it.q: Two positive numbers add to 30. What is the largest possible value of their product?
it.h: Write the product as x(30 - x) and find where its derivative is 0.

it.q: A rectangle has an area of 64 square meters. What is its smallest possible perimeter in meters?
it.h: Write P = 2x + 128/x and set P' = 0.

it.q: A farmer fences a rectangular field beside a river with 600 m of fence and uses no fence along the river. Which dimensions give the greatest area?
ch: 150 m by 300 m, with the 300 m side along the river
it.h: If x is each side perpendicular to the river, the side along the river is 600 - 2x.

it.q: In an optimization problem, what should you do right after drawing and labeling a picture?
ch: Write the quantity to optimize as a function of one variable
Guess an answer and check it
it.h: You need a single function of one variable to differentiate.

it.q: An open box is made from a 12 cm by 12 cm square of cardboard by cutting a square of side x from each corner. Its volume is V = x(12 - 2x)^2. What x gives the greatest volume?
it.h: V' = (12 - 2x)(12 - 6x). Which zero is between 0 and 6?

it.q: Find two positive numbers whose product is 100 and whose sum is as small as possible, and explain.
it.ans: Let the numbers be x and 100/x. S = x + 100/x and S' = 1 - 100/x^2 = 0 at x = 10. S'' = 200/x^3 > 0, so this is a minimum. Both numbers are 10.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Motion: position, velocity and acceleration

it.q: s(t) is an object's position. What is s'(t)?
it.h: Velocity is the rate of change of position.

it.q: s(t) = t^2 - 6t + 4 meters after t seconds. At what time in seconds is the object at rest?
it.h: Set the velocity s'(t) equal to 0.

it.q: s(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t meters after t seconds. What is the acceleration at t = 2, in m/s^2?
it.h: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

it.q: An object's velocity is v(t) = t^2 - 4 m/s. For t >= 0, when is it moving in the negative direction?
it.h: Find where v(t) < 0.

it.q: At t = 3, an object's velocity is -5 m/s and its acceleration is 2 m/s^2. What is happening at that moment?
ch: It is moving in the positive direction
it.h: Compare the signs of the velocity and the acceleration.

it.q: A ball's height is h(t) = -16t^2 + 64t feet after t seconds. Explain how to find when it reaches its highest point and how high it gets.
it.ans: The velocity is h'(t) = -32t + 64, which is 0 at t = 2. The velocity changes from positive to negative there, so the ball peaks at t = 2 s, at a height of h(2) = -64 + 128 = 64 feet.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Related rates

it.q: The side of a square grows at 3 cm/s. How fast is its area growing when the side is 10 cm?
it.h: A = s^2, so dA/dt = 2s ds/dt.

it.q: A cube's edge grows at 1 cm/s. How fast is its volume growing when the edge is 4 cm, in cubic cm per second?
it.h: V = s^3, so dV/dt = 3s^2 ds/dt.

it.q: A 10-ft ladder slides down a wall, and its base moves away from the wall at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the base is 6 ft from the wall?
it.h: Use x^2 + y^2 = 100, differentiate with respect to t, and find y when x = 6.

it.q: In a related rates problem, when should you substitute the values given for one moment?
it.h: Quantities that change must stay variables until after you differentiate.

it.q: Two cars leave the same point at the same time. One drives north at 30 mph and the other drives east at 40 mph. How fast is the distance between them growing, in mph?
it.h: The distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 30t and 40t.

it.q: Oil spreads in a circle whose radius grows at 0.5 m/s. Explain how to find how fast the area is growing when the radius is 4 m, and give the rate in terms of pi.
it.ans: A = pi r^2, so dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt = 2 pi (4)(0.5) = 4 pi square meters per second.

lessons.u: Applications of derivatives
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: f(x) = x^2 - 10x + 3. At what x does f have its minimum?
it.h: Set f'(x) = 0.

it.q: f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2. Where is its inflection point?
it.h: Solve f''(x) = 0.

it.q: s(t) = t^2 - 10t meters after t seconds. What is the velocity at t = 2, in m/s?
it.h: Differentiate the position function.

it.q: What is the absolute maximum of f(x) = 4x - x^2 on [0, 3]?
it.h: Check the critical point and the endpoints.

it.q: A circle's radius grows at 1 cm/s. How fast is its area growing when r = 10 cm?
it.h: dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt.

lessons.u: Integrals and accumulation
lessons.n: Riemann sums and approximating area

it.q: Use a right Riemann sum with 4 rectangles of width 1 to estimate the area under f(x) = x^2 from x = 0 to x = 4.
it.h: Use the heights f(1), f(2), f(3) and f(4).

it.q: Use a left Riemann sum with 4 rectangles of width 1 to estimate the area under f(x) = x^2 from x = 0 to x = 4.
it.h: Use the heights f(0), f(1), f(2) and f(3).

it.q: f is increasing. How does a left Riemann sum compare with the exact area under f?
it.h: Sketch the rectangles. Where are their tops compared with the curve?

it.q: A car's speed is 10, 14, 18 and 20 m/s at t = 0, 2, 4 and 6 seconds. Using a left Riemann sum with intervals of 2 seconds, estimate the distance traveled from t = 0 to t = 6, in meters.
it.h: Each rectangle has a width of 2 seconds and uses the speed at its left end.

it.q: f(0) = 3 and f(2) = 7. What is the estimate of the area under f from 0 to 2 using one trapezoid?
it.h: The area of a trapezoid is the width times the average of the two heights.

it.q: Explain why Riemann sums get closer to the exact area as the number of rectangles increases.
it.ans: Thinner rectangles follow the curve more closely, so the gaps and overlaps between the rectangles and the curve shrink. In the limit, the sum equals the exact area, the definite integral.

lessons.u: Integrals and accumulation
lessons.n: Antiderivatives and indefinite integrals

it.q: What is an antiderivative of 4x^3?
it.h: Increase the exponent by 1 and divide by the new exponent.

it.q: What is the integral of (6x - 5) dx?
it.h: Integrate each term and add C.

it.q: What is the integral of x^(-2) dx?
it.h: Use the reverse power rule with n = -2.

it.q: What is the integral of cos x dx?
it.h: Which function has derivative cos x?

it.q: F'(x) = 2x and F(0) = 5. What is F(3)?
it.h: F(x) = x^2 + C. Use F(0) = 5 to find C.

it.q: Explain why we add + C to an indefinite integral.
it.ans: Many functions have the same derivative, because the derivative of any constant is 0. For example, x^2, x^2 + 3 and x^2 - 7 all have derivative 2x, so the antiderivative of 2x is x^2 + C.

lessons.u: Integrals and accumulation
lessons.n: Definite integrals and their properties

it.q: What is the integral of 4 dx from 1 to 6?
it.h: The region is a rectangle.

it.q: Using geometry, what is the integral of x dx from 0 to 6?
it.h: The region is a triangle with base 6 and height 6.

it.q: The integral of f from 0 to 3 is 7 and the integral of f from 3 to 5 is 2. What is the integral of f from 0 to 5?
it.h: Integrals over intervals that meet end to end add.

it.q: The integral of f from 2 to 6 is 10. What is the integral of f from 6 to 2?
it.h: Switching the limits changes the sign.

it.q: The integral of f from 1 to 4 is 5. What is the integral of 3f(x) from 1 to 4?
it.h: A constant factor can be moved outside the integral.

it.q: Using geometry, explain how to find the integral of the square root of (9 - x^2) dx from -3 to 3.
it.ans: The graph of y = the square root of (9 - x^2) is the top half of a circle of radius 3. The integral is the area of that half circle: (1/2) pi (3)^2 = 9pi/2.

it.h: The derivative of an accumulation function is the integrand evaluated at x.

it.q: Evaluate the integral of (1/x) dx from 1 to e.
it.h: An antiderivative of 1/x is ln x.

it.q: Water flows into a tank at r(t) liters per minute. Use the Fundamental Theorem to explain what the integral of r(t) from 0 to 10 means.
it.ans: It is the total change in the amount of water, in liters, from t = 0 to t = 10 minutes. By the Fundamental Theorem, integrating a rate of change gives the net change in the quantity.

lessons.u: Integrals and accumulation

it.q: What is the integral of 2x(x^2 + 1)^3 dx?
it.h: Let u = x^2 + 1, so du = 2x dx.

it.q: What is the integral of cos(5x) dx?
it.h: Let u = 5x, so dx = du/5.

it.q: What is the integral of e^(3x) dx?
it.h: Let u = 3x.

it.q: Evaluate the integral of 2x(x^2 + 1) dx from 0 to 1.
it.h: With u = x^2 + 1, the limits become u = 1 and u = 2.

it.q: Which substitution works best for the integral of x/(x^2 + 4) dx?
it.h: Look for an inside function whose derivative also appears, up to a constant.

it.q: Use substitution to find the integral of x^2(x^3 - 1)^4 dx, and explain each step.
it.ans: Let u = x^3 - 1, so du = 3x^2 dx and x^2 dx = du/3. The integral becomes (1/3) times the integral of u^4 du = u^5/15 + C = (x^3 - 1)^5/15 + C.

lessons.u: Integrals and accumulation
lessons.n: Area between curves and accumulation in context

it.q: What is the area of the region between y = 4 (on top) and y = x^2 from x = -2 to x = 2?
it.h: Integrate (top - bottom) = 4 - x^2.

it.q: Which integral gives the area between y = x + 2 (on top) and y = x^2 from x = -1 to x = 2?
ch: the integral of (x + 2 - x^2) dx from -1 to 2
the integral of (x^2 - x - 2) dx from -1 to 2
the integral of (x + 2 + x^2) dx from -1 to 2
the integral of (x + 2) dx from -1 to 2
it.h: Subtract the bottom curve from the top curve.

it.q: What is the area between y = x + 2 and y = x^2 from x = -1 to x = 2?
it.h: An antiderivative of x + 2 - x^2 is x^2/2 + 2x - x^3/3.

it.q: A population of 1,000 grows at r(t) = 200 + 30t people per year. Which expression gives the population after 5 years?
ch: 1000 + the integral of (200 + 30t) dt from 0 to 5
the integral of (200 + 30t) dt from 0 to 5
it.h: Final amount = starting amount + accumulated change.

it.q: A population starts at 1,000 people and grows at r(t) = 200 + 30t people per year. How many people are there after 5 years?
it.h: Integrate the rate from 0 to 5 and add the starting amount.

it.q: Explain why the integral of a velocity function can differ from the total distance traveled.
it.ans: The integral of velocity gives displacement, which subtracts movement in the negative direction. Total distance adds up the absolute value of velocity, so whenever the object moves backward the two answers differ.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Friends and Neighbors (narrative writing)
lessons.n: How characters respond to events

it.q: Read: "Ben dropped his ice cream. His lip shook, and a tear rolled down his cheek." How does Ben feel?
it.h: Look at what Ben's face does. What do people do when they feel this way?

it.q: Read: "When the new girl sat alone at lunch, Kenji picked up his tray and sat next to her." What does Kenji's action show about him?
it.h: Think about why someone would choose to sit next to a person who is alone.

it.q: Read: "A loud crash came from next door. Mia ran to the window to see what happened." What event does Mia respond to?
ch: a knock at her front door
a phone ringing in the kitchen
it.h: Find what happened first. Mia's action comes after it.

it.q: Read: "Mr. Patel's car would not start. Lucia's mom grabbed her jumper cables and walked over." How does Lucia's mom respond to Mr. Patel's problem?
ch: She goes over to help start his car.
She calls a tow truck to take his car away.
She waits inside until Mr. Patel leaves.
She asks Lucia to lend him her bike.
it.h: What did she grab, and where did she go?

it.q: Who is the main character in a story?
ch: the person or animal the story is mostly about
the person who wrote the story
the place where the story happens
the last person who talks in the story
it.h: Think of the character you read about the most.

it.q: Read: "Dev's kite got stuck in Mrs. Wong's tree. Mrs. Wong brought out her tall ladder." What problem happens, and how does a character respond?
it.ans: The problem is that Dev's kite is stuck in the tree. Mrs. Wong responds by bringing out her tall ladder so she can help get the kite down.
it.h: First tell what went wrong. Then tell what someone did about it.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Friends and Neighbors (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Main topic and key details in informational text

it.q: What does a heading in an informational text tell you?
ch: what one section is mostly about
how many pages the book has
it.h: Headings are like small titles inside a text.

it.q: Read: "Firefighters do more than put out fires. They teach families about fire safety. They also help people who are hurt." What is the main topic?
it.h: Which idea do all three sentences tell about?

it.q: Read: "Firefighters do more than put out fires. They teach families about fire safety. They also help people who are hurt." Which detail from these sentences tells one job firefighters do?
ch: They teach families about fire safety.
They drive the fastest cars in town.
it.h: Go back to the paragraph and find the detail that is really there.

it.q: A text has two headings: "Where Mail Carriers Work" and "Tools Mail Carriers Use." What is the whole text about?
it.h: What word do both headings share?

it.q: Which question does a text called "How Do Bus Drivers Keep Riders Safe?" answer?
ch: how bus drivers keep riders safe
where buses are parked at night
how much a bus ride costs
it.h: The title of this text is already a question.

it.q: Read: "Crossing guards wear bright vests. They hold up stop signs. They help children cross the street safely." Write the main topic and one key detail.
it.ans: The main topic is crossing guards. One key detail is that they hold up stop signs (or wear bright vests, or help children cross safely).
it.h: The main topic is who or what the paragraph is about. A key detail tells more about it.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Friends and Neighbors (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Short and long vowels; nouns and collective nouns

it.q: Which word has a long a sound?
it.h: A long a says its own name. A silent e at the end of a word can make the vowel long.

it.q: Which word has a short i sound?
it.h: Say each word. Which one sounds like the middle of "sit"?

it.q: Add a silent e to the end of "hop." What new word do you make?
it.h: The silent e makes the o say its name.

it.q: Which collective noun names a group of birds?
it.h: A collective noun names a group. Which group word goes with birds that fly together?

it.q: Which word in the sentence "The happy dog barked loudly" is a noun?
it.h: A noun names a person, place, animal or thing.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses the collective noun "family."
it.ans: My family eats dinner together every night.
it.h: "Family" names a group of people. Use it as one group in your sentence.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Friends and Neighbors (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Story structure: beginning, middle and end in a neighborhood story

it.q: What usually happens at the beginning of a story?
ch: The characters and setting are introduced.
it.h: Think about what a reader needs to know first.

it.q: Read: "On Saturday morning, Jamal and his grandma walked to the corner bakery on Elm Street." Which part of a story does this sentence most likely come from?
it.h: Does this sentence tell who and where, or does it wrap things up?

it.q: Read: "Finally, the lost puppy was back home, curled up in its bed." Which part of a story does this sentence most likely come from?
it.h: Look for a word that shows something is finished.

it.q: What does the ending of a story usually tell?
Read: "Ms. Ellis's cat climbed to the top of the tall oak tree and would not come down." What part of the story structure does this sentence show?
it.h: Is something going wrong, or is something being fixed?

it.q: Write a beginning sentence for a story about two neighbors. Tell who and where.
it.ans: "One sunny afternoon, Ana and her neighbor Mr. Cho sat on the front steps of their apartment building."
it.h: A good beginning names the characters and the setting.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Friends and Neighbors (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing: Complete sentences, time-order words and details in a narrative

it.q: Which is a complete sentence?
it.h: A complete sentence tells who or what and what they do.

it.q: Which time-order word best begins the last event in a narrative?
it.h: Which word tells the reader the story is wrapping up?

it.q: Which sentence adds the best detail to "Theo helped his neighbor"?
ch: Theo carried three heavy grocery bags up the stairs for Mrs. Ruiz.
it.h: Details tell exactly what happened.

it.q: Which sentence fixes this fragment: "Walked the dog after school"?
ch: Ana walked the dog after school.
Walked the dog after school with.
it.h: The fragment is missing who did the action.

it.q: Which pair of sentences can be joined with "and" to make a compound sentence?
Rewrite these sentences using time-order words: "We found a lost cat. We read its tag. We called the owner."
it.ans: "First, we found a lost cat. Next, we read its tag. Finally, we called the owner."
it.h: Put a time-order word at the start of each sentence.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Through the Seasons (informative writing)
lessons.n: Rhythm, rhyme and sensory words in poems

it.q: Which two words rhyme?
it.h: Rhyming words end with the same sound. Say each pair out loud.

it.q: Read: "Splash, splash, splash in the puddle!" What do the repeated words help you hear?
it.h: Say "splash" out loud. What makes that sound?

it.q: Read: "The snow is a soft white blanket on the hills." What does the poet compare the snow to?
it.h: Look for the thing the snow "is" in the sentence.

it.q: Read these lines: "Thunder rumbles, thunder roars, / Raindrops drum on all the doors." Which word tells the sound the thunder makes?
it.h: Which word tells what you would hear?

it.q: What is a group of lines in a poem called?
it.h: Stories have paragraphs. Poems have a different word for a group of lines.

it.q: Write one line of a poem about wind that uses a sound word, such as whoosh or howl.
it.ans: The wind went whoosh around the corner of my house.
it.h: Close your eyes and think about what the wind sounds like.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Through the Seasons (informative writing)
lessons.n: Text features and science words in informational text

it.q: What is a glossary?
ch: a list of words and their meanings at the back of a book
a picture with labels that name its parts
a list of chapters at the front of a book
a short note about the person who wrote it
it.h: Think of a small dictionary that comes with a book.

it.q: A photo of a tornado has words under it: "A tornado is a spinning column of air." What are these words called?
it.h: These words explain a picture.

it.q: Read: "Fog is a cloud that forms close to the ground." What is fog, according to the sentence?
it.h: The sentence tells you exactly what fog is. Look after the word "is."

it.q: In a book about weather, you want to find the page about hail. Where should you look?
ch: the first page of chapter one
it.h: Which part of a book lists topics in ABC order with page numbers?

it.q: Read: "When warm, wet air rises, it cools. Tiny drops of water then form clouds." What happens to warm, wet air when it rises?
it.h: Find the words "when warm, wet air rises." What comes right after?

it.q: Why do authors put some words in bold print?
it.ans: Bold print shows readers that a word is important. Bold words are often explained in the text or in the glossary.
it.h: Think about which words stand out on the page and why.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Through the Seasons (informative writing)
lessons.n: Vowel teams and synonyms

it.q: Which word has the vowel team "ai"?
it.h: A vowel team is two letters that work together to make one vowel sound.

it.q: Which word has the same long o sound as "snow"?
it.h: Say "snow" slowly. Listen for the o that says its name.

it.q: Which word is a synonym for "chilly"?
it.h: Synonyms are words that mean almost the same thing.

it.q: Which word means almost the same as "damp"?
it.h: Think of a towel after someone uses it.

it.q: Which word is spelled correctly in this sentence? "We had to ___ for the bus in the rain."
it.h: The long a sound in the middle of a word is often spelled ai.

it.q: Write a sentence about weather that uses two words with vowel teams. Name the vowel teams.
it.ans: The rain soaked the road. Rain has ai, and soaked and road have oa.
it.h: Look for pairs like ai, ay, ee, ea, oa and ow.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Through the Seasons (informative writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two texts about tornadoes

it.q: What does it mean to compare two texts?
ch: to tell how they are alike and different
to read only the first one
to draw a picture of them
it.h: Comparing means looking at two things side by side.

it.q: Text A says, "Hurricanes form over warm ocean water." Text B says, "Warm ocean water gives hurricanes their energy." What do both texts say?
ch: Hurricanes are connected to warm ocean water.
it.h: Find the words that appear in both sentences.

it.q: Read: "Because the air was very cold, the rain froze and fell as sleet." What caused the sleet?
it.h: Look at the part after "Because."

it.q: A text has a bold word, "blizzard," and a glossary. Where can you find what "blizzard" means?
Read: "Fog forms when tiny drops of water float in the air close to the ground." What is fog?
ch: tiny drops of water floating near the ground

it.q: Two texts are about hail. One tells how hail forms. The other tells how to protect a car from hail. Explain how the main topics are different.
it.ans: The first text explains how hail is made in storm clouds, and the second text tells what people can do to keep their cars safe from hail.
it.h: Ask, "What is each text mostly about?"

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Through the Seasons (informative writing)
lessons.n: Words and writing: Antonyms, compound weather words and an informative paragraph

it.q: Which word is an antonym (opposite) of "freezing"?
it.h: An antonym means the opposite.

it.q: Which compound word is made from "rain" and "coat"?
it.h: Put the two small words together in order.

it.q: What does "snowfall" mean?
ch: snow that falls from the sky
it.h: Think about what each small word means.

it.q: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about rainbows?
ch: Rainbows form when sunlight shines through raindrops.
it.h: A topic sentence tells what the whole paragraph will explain.

it.q: Which word is an antonym of "calm" when talking about weather?
Write a concluding sentence for a paragraph about why people should wear sunscreen in summer.
it.ans: "Wearing sunscreen in summer keeps your skin healthy and safe from sunburn."
it.h: A conclusion sums up the main idea.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Fables and Folktales (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Fables and their central message

it.q: What is a fable?
ch: a short story that teaches a lesson, often with animal characters
a true story about a real person's life
a list of facts about real wild animals
a poem about the four seasons of the year
it.h: Think about the stories that end with a lesson, like "Slow and steady wins the race."

it.q: Read: "Goat shared her shade with Lizard on a hot day. Later, Lizard warned Goat about a snake in the grass." What lesson does this teach?
it.h: Goat did something kind first. What did Lizard do later?

it.q: Read: "Turtle tried to carry all his food at once, and it spilled everywhere. The next day he carried a little at a time and got it all home." What is the central message?
ch: Doing a job step by step works better than rushing.
Turtles are very slow animals that walk a lot.
Some food is much too heavy to carry home.
Spilling things everywhere can be fun to do.
it.h: Compare what happened the first day with what happened the next day.

it.q: Where is the moral of a fable often found?
ch: at the end of the story
it.h: The lesson usually comes after the characters learn something.

it.q: Read: "Crow laughed when Beetle fell off the branch. A moment later, Crow slipped on the same branch." What does this part of the fable show?
ch: Making fun of others can come back to you.
Crows can fly very high above the trees.
Tree branches are always slippery when wet.
Beetles are better climbers than crows.
it.h: What happened to Crow right after he laughed?

it.q: Think of a fable you know. Write its moral in your own words and tell one event from the fable that teaches it.
it.ans: In "The Tortoise and the Hare," the moral is that steady work pays off. The hare takes a nap during the race, and the slow tortoise keeps going and wins.
it.h: First write the lesson. Then tell what a character did that taught it.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Fables and Folktales (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Learning about folktales from informational text

it.q: What is usually the author's purpose when a text explains how something works?
it.h: Texts that explain give readers facts.

it.q: Read: "Puppet shows have been used to tell stories for a very long time. Puppets can be made of cloth, wood or paper." What is this paragraph mostly about?
ch: how to sew cloth to make puppet clothes
why paper is thin and easy to tear
where to buy wood for building things
it.h: What do both sentences tell about?

it.q: A book is titled "How Do Storytellers Remember Long Tales?" What will the book most likely answer?
ch: the ways storytellers remember long tales
the places where famous storytellers were born
how to draw pictures for a long tale
which tales are the shortest to remember
it.h: The title asks a question. The book will answer it.

it.q: Read: "Some storytellers repeat words and lines. This helps listeners remember the story." Why do some storytellers repeat words?
it.h: Look for the word "helps" in the second sentence.

it.q: Which sentence would best fit in a text about folktales?
ch: Many folktales begin with words like "Long ago."
My bike has a flat tire after school today.
Rain falls from clouds when they get heavy.
Pizza is a popular food at birthday parties.
it.h: Pick the sentence that stays on the topic of folktales.

it.q: Read: "Libraries often hold story hours. Children listen to tales read aloud, and sometimes they act them out." Write the main topic and one key detail.
it.ans: The main topic is story hours at libraries. One key detail is that children listen to tales read aloud (or that they sometimes act the tales out).
it.h: Ask yourself: what are these sentences mostly about?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Fables and Folktales (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Irregular plural nouns

it.q: What is the plural of "foot"?
it.h: This word does not add -s. Its vowels change instead.

it.q: What is the plural of "mouse"?
it.h: Think of the story "Three Blind ___."

it.q: Which sentence uses the correct plural?
ch: Two geese swam in the pond.
Two gooses swam in the pond.
Two geeses swam in the pond.
Two goose swam in the pond.
it.h: One goose, two ___. The plural does not end in s.

it.q: What is the plural of "leaf"?
it.h: For many words that end in f, change the f to v and add -es.

it.q: Which word stays the same when it means more than one?
it.h: You can say "one ___" and "ten ___" with the same word.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses the plural of "child."
it.ans: The children ran to the swings at recess.
it.h: The plural of "child" does not just add -s. What do we call a group of kids?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Fables and Folktales (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two versions of a fable

it.q: Which best describes a fable?
ch: a short story that teaches a lesson, often with animal characters
a true story about a famous person
it.h: Think about the stories with talking animals and a moral at the end.

it.q: Two stories both teach "Slow and steady wins the race." What do the two stories share?
it.h: "Slow and steady wins the race" is a lesson.

it.q: Read: "In one version, the clever bird drops stones into the jug. In another, the clever bird uses a straw." How are the versions different?
ch: how the bird reaches the water
it.h: Look at what the bird does in each version.

it.q: Why might the same fable have different versions?
ch: People in different places retold it in their own way.
The first version was lost forever.
Authors are not allowed to use the same title.

it.q: Read: "The lion let the little mouse go. Later, the mouse chewed through the net to free the lion." What is the lesson?
ch: Even small friends can be a big help.
it.h: Who helped whom in the end?

it.q: Explain what readers should look for when they compare two versions of a story.
it.ans: The characters, the setting, the events, how the problem is solved and the lesson; then tell how each is alike and different.
it.h: Think about the parts of a story.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Fables and Folktales (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Opinion writing: Reasons and linking words

it.q: Which sentence states an opinion?
ch: Fables are the best kind of story to read.
A fable is a short story.
it.h: An opinion tells what someone thinks or feels. Others may disagree.

it.q: Which linking word best connects an opinion and a reason?
it.h: Which word answers the question "Why?"

it.q: Which reason best supports the opinion "Everyone should read fables"?
ch: Fables teach lessons that help us make good choices.

it.q: Which linking word adds a second reason?
it.h: Which word means "and one more thing"?

it.q: Which sentence is the best conclusion for an opinion piece about fables?
ch: That is why I think fables are worth reading.
Once upon a time, there was a fox.
Fables were first told long ago.

it.q: Write an opinion about your favorite fable character and give one reason with "because."
it.ans: "I think the tortoise is the best character because he never gives up."
it.h: Start with "I think" and add "because."

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Story structure: beginnings and endings

it.q: What does the beginning of a story usually do?
ch: tells how the problem is solved
gives the moral at the end
it.h: Think about what a reader needs to know first.

it.q: Read the end of a story: "At last, the pumpkin was big enough for the fair. Nina hugged it and smiled." How does Nina feel at the end?
it.h: What do Nina's actions tell you?

it.q: Read: "The wind knocked over Jin's tomato plant. Jin tied it to a stick so it could stand up again." How does Jin respond to the problem?
ch: He ties the plant to a stick.
He leaves it on the ground.
it.h: Find the problem first. Then find what Jin did next.

it.q: Which sentence would most likely come at the end of a story about planting a garden?
ch: Finally, the family ate a salad made from their own vegetables.
One sunny morning, the Garcias bought some seeds.
First, they dug up the hard dirt in the yard.
"Let's plant a garden this spring!" said Papa.
it.h: An ending tells how things turned out.

it.q: A story begins with Lia finding an acorn. In the middle, she plants it and waters it for years. Which sentence would best fit the ending?
ch: Lia sits in the shade of a tall oak tree.
Lia finds another acorn under a bush.
Lia buys a brand-new watering can.
Lia wakes up early and gets dressed.
it.h: What does an acorn grow into after many years?

it.q: What usually happens in the middle of a story?
it.ans: In the middle of a story, the characters face a problem and try to solve it.
it.h: Think of the part between meeting the characters and the ending.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Steps in a process and diagrams

it.q: Which words help show the order of steps?
it.h: Which words tell what to do and when?

it.q: Read: "First, fill a pot with soil. Next, poke a hole with your finger. Then, drop in a seed." What do you do right after filling the pot?
ch: poke a hole with your finger
drop in a seed and cover it
buy a bag of soil at the store
it.h: Find the step that starts with "Next."

it.q: A diagram of a flower has labels for the petals, stem and leaves. What is the diagram's purpose?
ch: to show the parts of a flower
to tell a story about a flower
to list the steps for planting
to give the price of flowers
it.h: Labels name the parts of something.

it.q: Read: "Bees visit flowers to drink nectar. As they move from flower to flower, they carry pollen. This helps plants make seeds." How do bees help plants?
ch: They carry pollen that helps plants make seeds.
They eat the plant's leaves and stems.
They carry water to dry flowers.
They dig holes in the soil for seeds.
it.h: Read the last two sentences again.

it.q: Read: "Some seeds travel on the wind. Dandelion seeds have fluffy tops that float like tiny parachutes." What helps dandelion seeds travel?
it.h: What part of the seed is like a parachute?

it.q: Write three steps you would follow to plant a seed. Use order words.
it.ans: First, I fill a cup with soil. Next, I push the seed into the soil. Then, I water it and put it in a sunny spot.
it.h: Use words like first, next and then.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Compound words and the prefixes un- and re-

it.q: Which word is a compound word?
it.h: A compound word is made of two smaller words put together.

it.q: What two words make up "raindrop"?
it.h: Find a whole word at the start and a whole word at the end.

it.q: What does "replant" mean?
it.h: The prefix re- means again.

it.q: What does "unhappy" mean?
it.h: The prefix un- means not.

it.q: Use the meaning of the two smaller words. What is a "seedpod"?
ch: a seed that is very large
it.h: Put the meanings of "seed" and "pod" together.

it.q: Write a sentence using a word with the prefix re-. Tell what the word means.
it.ans: I had to rewrite my spelling words. Rewrite means to write again.
it.h: Add re- to a verb you know, like read, fill or build.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: How bees and other pollinators help flowers

it.q: Read: "Pollen is a yellow powder made by flowers." What is pollen?
ch: a yellow powder made by flowers
it.h: The sentence tells you exactly what pollen is.

it.q: Read: "Because the soil was dry, the seeds did not sprout." Why did the seeds not sprout?
it.h: Look at the part after "Because."

it.q: Read: "The tiny plant inside the seed is called an embryo." What is an embryo?
ch: the tiny plant inside a seed
the hard cover of a seed

it.q: Why would an author write a text called "How to Plant Bean Seeds"?
ch: to explain how to do something
to get you to buy beans
it.h: What will the reader be able to do after reading?

it.q: Read: "Some seeds need light to germinate, or start to grow." What does "germinate" mean?
it.h: Look at the words right after "or."

it.q: Read: "First, the seed soaks up water. Then the seed coat splits. Next, a root grows down." Explain what happens after the seed soaks up water.
it.ans: The seed coat splits, and then a root grows down into the soil.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Words: Context clues and glossary words; writing about how a plant grows

it.q: What is a glossary?
ch: a list of words and their meanings at the back of a book
a list of chapters at the front
it.h: Where would you look to find what a bold word means?

it.q: Read: "The sprout was so fragile that a light touch could break it." What does "fragile" mean?
it.h: What happens with a light touch?

it.q: Read: "Cacti can survive in arid places where it hardly ever rains." What does "arid" mean?
it.h: Look at the words after "where."

it.q: In a dictionary, which word comes first in ABC order?
Which sentence would best begin an informative paragraph about how a bean plant grows?
ch: A bean plant grows in several steps, from seed to sprout to plant.

it.q: Read: "Soak the seeds overnight so they absorb water and soften." Explain how the words around "absorb" help you know what it means.
it.ans: "Soak," "water" and "soften" show that the seeds take in water, so "absorb" means to soak up or take in.
it.h: Look at the words just before and after "absorb."

lessons.u: Unit 4: Plants and Seeds (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: A biography of a plant scientist, George Washington Carver

it.q: What is a biography?
ch: a true story about a real person's life
a made-up story with talking animals
it.h: Think about books that tell about real people.

it.q: Read: "After many years of growing cotton, the soil became worn out, so crops grew poorly." What caused the crops to grow poorly?
it.h: Look at the part before "so."

it.q: Read: "He was curious about plants, so he asked questions and tested ideas." What does "curious" mean?
ch: wanting to learn or know more

it.q: Which words help readers follow events in a biography in order?
ch: as a boy, later, then, finally
it.h: Look for words that tell when.

it.q: Read: "Some plants, like peanuts, can help put nutrients back into the soil." Why might a farmer plant peanuts?
ch: to help make the soil healthy again

it.q: Read: "As a girl, Rosa loved flowers. Later, she studied plants in college. Now she helps farmers grow healthy crops." Tell how Rosa's childhood connects to her job today.
it.ans: Rosa loved flowers as a girl, so she studied plants in college, and now her job is helping farmers grow healthy crops. Her childhood love of plants led to her job.
it.h: Connect what she loved as a child to what she does now.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Characters' points of view

it.q: What does a character's point of view mean?
ch: how a character thinks or feels about something
where and when the story takes place
the title the author gave the story
the very last event in the story
it.h: Think about what the character believes or likes.

it.q: Read: "'Night is the best time to hunt!' said Owl. Robin yawned. 'Night is for sleeping,' she said." How do Owl and Robin feel differently about night?
ch: Owl likes being awake at night, but Robin wants to sleep.
Both birds want to sleep at night.
Robin likes the night, but Owl does not.
Neither bird likes the night at all.
it.h: Read what each bird says. Do they agree?

it.q: Read: "'Snow again!' cheered Penguin. 'Snow again,' groaned Camel." Who is happy about the snow?
it.h: Look at the words "cheered" and "groaned."

it.q: Read: "The little fish thought the shark was scary. The shark thought the little fish looked like lunch." Which character feels afraid?
it.h: Who thinks the other one is scary?

it.q: How can a reader show different points of view when reading a story aloud?
ch: use a different voice for each character
skip the words in quotation marks
it.h: Think about how you read when two characters are talking.

it.q: Read: "Mole loved his dark, quiet tunnel. Bird wanted to fly out of it and into the sunshine." Explain how Mole and Bird feel differently about the tunnel.
it.ans: Mole likes the tunnel because it is dark and quiet, but Bird does not like it and wants to get out into the sunshine.
it.h: Tell what each animal wants.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Points and reasons in informational text

it.q: What is a habitat?
ch: the place where an animal lives and finds what it needs
a kind of food that an animal eats
a baby animal that lives with its mother
a group of plants that grow together
it.h: Think about where an animal gets food, water and shelter.

it.q: Read: "Camels can go many days without drinking water. This helps them live in the desert." What point does the author make?
ch: Camels are able to live in the desert.
Camels drink lots of water every day.
Deserts have many lakes and rivers.
Camels live best in cold, snowy places.
it.h: The second sentence tells the big idea.

it.q: Read: "Ducks have webbed feet. The webbing pushes against the water and helps them swim." What reason does the author give for why ducks swim well?
ch: Their webbed feet push against the water.
They have long necks for reaching.
They eat plants that grow in water.
They can fly very high and far.
it.h: Look for the word "helps."

it.q: One book about frogs says frogs lay eggs in water. Another book shows tadpoles swimming in a pond. What point do both books share?
ch: Young frogs begin life in water.
Frogs live mostly in dry deserts.
it.h: What do the eggs and the tadpoles have in common?

it.q: Read: "An owl can turn its head very far to look behind it." What can an owl's body do, according to this sentence?
it.h: Read only this sentence. What does it say the owl can do?

it.q: Read: "Ducks have oily feathers. The oil keeps water from soaking in." Explain how oily feathers help a duck.
it.ans: The oil keeps water from soaking into the duck's feathers, so the duck stays dry and can float.
it.h: What would happen if water soaked into the feathers?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Contractions and possessives

it.q: What is the contraction for "do not"?
it.h: The apostrophe takes the place of the letter o in "not."

it.q: What two words make the contraction "we're"?
it.h: The apostrophe replaces the letter a.

it.q: Which sentence uses an apostrophe to show that something belongs to someone?
it.h: An apostrophe and s after a noun can show that something belongs to it.

it.q: Which contraction correctly completes the sentence? "Frogs ___ live in the desert."
it.h: "Can not" becomes one word, and the apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters.

it.q: What is the contraction for "I am"?
it.h: Which letter is left out? Put the apostrophe there.

it.q: Write a sentence about an animal that uses the contraction "isn't." Then write the two words it stands for.
it.ans: A whale isn't a fish. Isn't stands for is not.
it.h: Isn't is made from two words. The second word is "not."

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Comparing habitats: coral reef and rainforest

it.q: What does the word "habitat" mean?
ch: the place where an animal or plant lives
it.h: Think about an animal's home and the area around it.

it.q: Read: "The Arctic is very cold. Polar bears have thick fur and a layer of fat to stay warm." How are polar bears suited to the Arctic?
ch: Thick fur and fat keep them warm.
Big ears help them cool down.
it.h: What keeps the polar bear warm?

it.q: A text has the subheadings "Plants of the Pond" and "Animals of the Pond." Under which subheading would you find facts about frogs?
Read: "Monkeys have long arms and tails that help them swing from branch to branch." Which habitat is a monkey suited for?
it.h: Where would swinging from branches help?

it.q: Text A says frogs need wet places. Text B says frogs lay eggs in ponds. What do both texts show?
Explain why a fish could not live in a desert habitat.
it.ans: A fish needs water to breathe and swim, and a desert has very little water.
it.h: Think about what a fish needs to live.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Words and writing: Precise verbs and a habitat report

it.q: Which verb best describes how a snake moves?
it.h: Think about a snake moving without legs.

it.q: Which word describes a faster way to move than "walk"?
it.h: Which word means to run as fast as you can?

it.q: Which verb is the most precise in "The owl ___ down and grabbed a mouse"?
it.h: A precise verb shows exactly how the action happened.

it.q: Which question would be a good research question for a report about sea otters?
Where is the best place to find facts for a report on frogs?
ch: a fairy tale about a frog prince
it.h: Which one tells true information?

it.q: Write a sentence about an animal using a precise verb instead of "moves."
it.ans: "The kangaroo bounds across the grassland."

lessons.u: Unit 5: Animal Habitats (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: Wetlands, a habitat between land and water

it.q: Read: "A marsh is a wetland where grasses and reeds grow in shallow water." What is a marsh?
ch: a wetland where grasses and reeds grow in shallow water
it.h: The sentence tells you what a marsh is.

it.q: Read: "Herons have long legs, so they can wade in water without getting their feathers wet." Why are long legs helpful to herons?
ch: They can wade in water and keep their feathers dry.
They can run fast in the desert.
it.h: Look at the part after "so."

it.q: An author writes, "Wetlands are important. They give homes to many animals, and they help stop floods." How many reasons does the author give?
it.h: Count the reasons after "Wetlands are important."

it.q: Read: "The roots of marsh plants trap mud and dirt, so the water flowing out is cleaner." What is the effect of the roots trapping mud?
ch: The water flowing out is cleaner.

it.q: Read: "A wetland acts like a sponge." What does this comparison tell you?
ch: A wetland is yellow and soft.
A wetland is used for washing dishes.

it.q: Read: "Ducks build nests in tall marsh grass, where foxes cannot easily see them." Explain how the marsh helps ducks.
it.ans: The tall marsh grass hides the ducks' nests, so foxes cannot easily find the eggs and babies.
it.h: Think about why hiding a nest matters.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Asking and answering questions about a story

it.q: Read: "On Saturday, Mateo built a birdhouse in his garage." When did Mateo build the birdhouse?
it.h: A "when" question asks about time.

it.q: Read: "On Saturday, Mateo built a birdhouse in his garage." Where did Mateo build the birdhouse?
it.h: A "where" question asks about a place.

it.q: Read: "Priya's robot kept falling over, so she made its feet wider." Why did Priya make the robot's feet wider?
ch: so it would stop falling over
so it could fit in a box
it.h: Look for the word "so." It tells the reason.

it.q: A picture shows a boy smiling and holding up a paper airplane with a blue ribbon on it. What does the picture help you understand?
ch: He won a prize and feels proud.
He is sad about his airplane.
He is about to throw the plane away.
He is lost at the park.
it.h: What does a blue ribbon usually mean? What does his face show?

it.q: Read: "Sam's kite would not fly. He added a long tail, and the kite rose into the sky." How did Sam solve his problem?
ch: He gave up and went home.
it.h: Find what Sam did right after the problem.

it.q: Read: "Mira wanted to reach the top shelf, so she stacked two boxes and stood on them carefully." Write a "why" question about this sentence and answer it.
it.ans: Why did Mira stack two boxes? She stacked them so she could reach the top shelf.
it.h: Start your question with "Why did Mira...?"

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Connecting events in a biography

it.q: What does a biography tell about?
ch: the life of a real person
it.h: "Bio" means life.

it.q: Read: "Before light bulbs were common, many people used candles and oil lamps at night." What does this sentence tell about?
ch: how people lit their homes before light bulbs
how candles are made from wax
why people went to sleep very early
where the oil for lamps comes from
it.h: Look at the word "before."

it.q: Read: "Ice melted fast in summer, so people kept food cold in iceboxes. Later, electric refrigerators took the place of iceboxes." What came first?
it.h: The word "later" tells you which came second.

it.q: Read: "The first bicycles had no pedals. Riders pushed with their feet. Pedals were added later so riders could go faster." Why were pedals added?
ch: so riders could push with their feet
it.h: Look for the word "so" in the last sentence.

it.q: What is the author's purpose in a text titled "How to Build a Paper Helicopter"?
ch: to explain the steps to make something
to tell a story about a pilot
to describe a real helicopter ride
it.h: The title begins with "How to."

it.q: Read: "Inventors often test an idea many times. Each test shows what works and what needs to change." Explain why inventors test an idea more than once.
it.ans: Each test shows the inventor what works and what needs to change, so testing many times helps them make the idea better.
it.h: What does each test show?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Irregular past tense verbs

it.q: What is the past tense of "make"?
it.h: Say "Today I make. Yesterday I ___."

it.q: What is the past tense of "go"?
it.h: Irregular verbs do not add -ed. "Yesterday I ___ to the park."

it.q: Which sentence uses the correct past tense verb?
it.h: Draw is irregular. It does not take -ed.

it.q: Choose the verb that completes the sentence: "Yesterday, Ben ___ a new kite."
it.h: The word "yesterday" tells you to use the past tense.

it.q: What is the past tense of "think"?
it.h: Say "Last night I ___ about my invention."

it.q: Write a sentence about something you made or did yesterday. Use an irregular past tense verb and underline it.
it.ans: Yesterday I made a card for my aunt. (made)
it.h: Try verbs like make, take, build, draw or write.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: How an invention works: diagrams and text features

it.q: What does a caption tell?
ch: information about a picture or diagram
it.h: Captions are the words near a picture.

it.q: A diagram of a bicycle has labels: "pedal," "chain," "wheel." What do the labels help you do?
ch: name the parts of the bicycle

it.q: Read: "When you push the pedals, the chain turns, and the back wheel spins." What makes the chain turn?
it.h: Which action comes first in the sentence?

it.q: Which text feature would show the steps for building an invention in order?
it.h: Which feature uses 1, 2, 3?

it.q: Read: "Before the zipper, people closed clothes with buttons or hooks." What does this sentence compare?
ch: how clothes closed before and after the zipper

it.q: Explain how a diagram can help a reader understand how an invention works.
it.ans: A diagram shows the parts with labels, so a reader can see each part and how the parts connect, which makes the words easier to understand.
it.h: Think about what a diagram shows that words alone cannot.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Words: Prefixes dis-, pre- and re-; an opinion about an invention

it.q: What does the prefix "re-" mean in "rebuild"?
it.h: Think of "redo" and "retell."

it.q: What does "preheat" mean?
it.h: "Pre-" means before.

it.q: What does "disconnect" mean?
Which word means "to not agree"?
it.h: Which prefix means "not" or "the opposite of"?

it.q: Which sentence states an opinion about an invention?
ch: The bicycle is the most useful invention ever.
People ride bicycles in many countries.

it.q: Write a sentence using a word with "re-." Tell what the word means.
it.ans: "I had to rewrite my report." Rewrite means to write again.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Inventors and Inventions (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading: A young inventor solves a problem

it.q: In a story, what is the problem?
ch: something that goes wrong that a character must fix
the place where the story happens
it.h: The problem is what the character is trying to fix.

it.q: Read: "Every afternoon, Jun's little sister tripped over the shoes piled by the door." What is the problem?
ch: The shoes by the door make his sister trip.

it.q: Read: "Jun's first shoe rack fell over. He frowned, then added a wider base." How does Jun respond to his first try failing?
ch: He changes his design and tries again.
it.h: What does Jun do after he frowns?

it.q: Read: "Ayla taped a mirror to a stick so she could see the ball stuck under the couch." Which word best describes Ayla?
Which part of a story usually tells how the problem is solved?

Read: "The plant on the windowsill kept drying out while the family was away. Lena filled a bottle with water, poked a hole in the cap and stuck it upside down in the soil." Explain how Lena solved the problem.
it.ans: The plant was drying out, so Lena made a bottle that slowly drips water into the soil to keep the plant watered while the family is away.
it.h: Tell the problem, then tell what Lena built.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Tales that explain nature

it.q: A pourquoi tale is a story that
ch: explains why something in nature is the way it is
gives true facts about science and nature
tells about the author's own real life
lists the steps for making something new
it.h: "Pourquoi" is a French word that means "why."

it.q: Read: "Long ago, Zebra was all white. One hot day she napped under a roof of reeds, and the sun painted dark stripes on her wherever the shade fell. That is why zebras have stripes." What does this tale explain?
it.h: Look for the words "That is why."

it.q: Read: "Ant was the smallest animal in the valley. When a pebble blocked the spring, only Ant could crawl into the crack and wiggle it loose." What lesson might this tale teach?
ch: Even small creatures can do important things.
Big animals always win in the end.
Springs never get blocked by pebbles.
Pebbles are too heavy for ants to move.
it.h: Why was Ant the only one who could help?

it.q: Read: "Thunder and Rain argued about who was stronger. Thunder boomed and shook the sky, but nothing grew. Rain fell softly, and flowers bloomed everywhere." What is the central message?
ch: Gentle actions can be stronger than loud ones.
Thunder is louder than any other sound.
Flowers need lots of sun to grow tall.
Arguing about who is stronger is fun.
it.h: Which one made something good happen?

it.q: In a pourquoi tale, where do you usually learn the reason something in nature began?
ch: near the end of the tale
it.h: The "why" is usually explained after the events of the story.

it.q: Write a title for a pourquoi tale about something in nature. Tell what the tale would explain.
it.ans: "Why the Moon Changes Shape" would explain why the moon looks different on different nights.
it.h: Start your title with "Why" or "How."

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Cause and effect in science texts

it.q: Read: "Because it rained all night, the river rose." What is the cause?
it.h: The cause is what made something happen. Look after the word "because."

it.q: Read: "Waves crash against the cliff every day. Little by little, the cliff wears away." What is the effect of the waves?
it.h: The effect is what happens because of the waves.

it.q: Read: "Wind blew sand against the rock for thousands of years, so the rock now has smooth curves." Why does the rock have smooth curves?
ch: Sand blown by the wind wore it smooth.
Someone carved it with sharp tools.
Rain painted curves on it over time.
It was always that same shape.
it.h: Find the word "so." What came before it?

it.q: Read: "A glacier is a huge, slow-moving river of ice." What is a glacier?
ch: a huge, slow-moving river of ice
a deep hole in the ground
it.h: The sentence tells you the meaning right after "is."

it.q: Which word means the opposite of "sudden"?
it.h: A sudden change happens all at once.

it.q: Read: "After a fire burned the plants on the hill, heavy rain washed the soil down the slope." Name a cause and its effect.
it.ans: Cause: a fire burned the plants, and then heavy rain fell. Effect: the soil washed down the slope because no plants were holding it.
it.h: What happened first? What happened because of it?

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Adjectives and adverbs

it.q: Which word is an adjective in "The tall mountain was covered in snow"?
it.h: An adjective describes a noun. Which word tells what the mountain is like?

it.q: Which word is an adverb in "The river flowed quickly"?
it.h: An adverb tells how, when or where. Many adverbs end in -ly.

it.q: Which adjective best describes lava?
it.h: Lava is melted rock.

it.q: Choose the word that completes the sentence: "The rocks fell ___ down the hill."
it.h: The missing word tells how the rocks fell.

it.q: Which sentence uses an adjective to describe a noun?
ch: The gray rock sat by the river.
The rock sat there by the river.
The river flowed past the rock.
It rolled away into the water.
it.h: Look for a word that tells what something looks like.

it.q: Write a sentence about a river. Use one adjective and one adverb, and label each.
it.ans: The muddy river rushed loudly past the rocks. Adjective: muddy. Adverb: loudly.
it.h: Use an adjective before "river" and an adverb after the verb.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Fast changes: floods and landslides

it.q: Which is an example of a fast change to Earth's land?
ch: a river slowly carving a canyon
wind slowly wearing down a rock
a glacier sliding over many years
it.h: Which change could happen in minutes?

it.q: Read: "Heavy rain soaked the hill, so the mud slid down onto the road." What caused the mudslide?
it.h: Look at the part before "so."

it.q: Read: "A landslide can happen in minutes, but erosion by wind can take thousands of years." What does this sentence compare?
In a science text, words in bold print usually
ch: are important words that may be in the glossary
are the names of the authors
it.h: Why would an author make a word stand out?

it.q: Read: "The river overflowed its banks and spread across the fields." What does "overflowed" mean?
it.h: Break the word into "over" and "flowed."

it.q: Read: "After the flood, a thick layer of mud covered the farm. Some fences were knocked down." Tell two effects of the flood.
it.ans: Mud covered the farm, and some fences were knocked down.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Words: Compound words, dictionaries and writing about erosion

it.q: Which is a compound word?
it.h: A compound word is made of two smaller words.

it.q: What does "riverbank" mean?
ch: the land along the side of a river
a bank where rivers keep money
it.h: Think about the two small words.

it.q: Which word would be on a dictionary page with the guide words "earth" and "erupt"?
it.h: The word must come after "earth" and before "erupt" in ABC order.

it.q: Read: "Erosion happens when wind or water carries soil and rock away little by little." What does "erosion" mean?
ch: the carrying away of soil and rock by wind or water

it.q: Which sentence would best end an informative paragraph about erosion?
ch: Erosion slowly changes the shape of the land.

it.q: Write two compound words that name things in nature and use one in a sentence.
it.ans: sandstone, waterfall; "The waterfall splashed over the rocks."

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Slow changes: how glaciers shape the land

it.q: Which change to the land happens very slowly?
it.h: Which change takes many, many years?

it.q: Read: "Snow piled up year after year until it pressed into thick ice." What caused the thick ice to form?
ch: Snow piled up year after year and pressed together.

it.q: Read: "The glacier crept down the mountain, moving only a few inches a day." What does "crept" mean?
it.h: Look at the clue "only a few inches a day."
