it.q: Why might an author write a text called "How Glaciers Move"?
Read: "As the glacier melted, it left behind piles of rocks it had carried." What is the effect of the glacier melting?
ch: It left behind piles of rocks.

it.q: Read: "Long ago, glaciers covered parts of North America. As they moved, they scraped the land and dug out holes. Later the holes filled with water and became lakes." Explain how some lakes formed.
it.ans: Glaciers scraped the land and dug out holes as they moved; later the holes filled with water and became lakes.
it.h: Put the events in order.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Earth Changes Fast and Slow (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: How people protect land from erosion

it.q: What is erosion?
ch: wind or water carrying soil and rock away
it.h: Think about what moves the soil away.

it.q: Read: "Farmers plant grass between rows of crops so rain does not wash the soil away." Why do farmers plant grass between rows?
ch: to keep rain from washing the soil away
it.h: Look at the part after "so."

it.q: An author writes, "Planting trees on hills is a smart idea. Tree roots hold soil, and leaves soften falling rain." Which sentence gives the author's point?
ch: Planting trees on hills is a smart idea.

it.q: Read: "Some beach towns build fences from sticks to trap blowing sand." What problem do the fences solve?
Read: "Terraces are flat steps cut into a hillside." What are terraces?
ch: flat steps cut into a hillside
it.h: The sentence tells you exactly.

it.q: Read: "Without plants, the hillside soil washed away in every storm. After volunteers planted bushes, the soil stayed in place." Explain what caused the change.
it.ans: The bushes' roots held the soil, so storms no longer washed it away.
it.h: What was different after the volunteers came?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: How characters make a difference

it.q: Read: "When Tia saw trash on the playground, she picked it up and threw it away." What did Tia do?
it.h: Find the action word right after "she."

it.q: Read: "The library needed books for its little reading room. Sota gave five of his favorite books." What does Sota's action show about him?
it.h: Think about what it means to give away something you love.

it.q: Read: "Grace was nervous about reading her poem at the assembly, but she took a deep breath and began." How does Grace respond to feeling nervous?
ch: She takes a deep breath and reads anyway.
She asks a friend to read for her.
it.h: Look at what Grace does after the word "but."

it.q: Read: "Every Saturday, Mr. Lee's class picked up litter at the beach. By June, the sand was much cleaner." What happened because of the class's work?
it.h: What was different by June?

it.q: Which detail would best show that a character is brave?
ch: She walks into the dark gym to find the lost puppy.
She eats a sandwich at lunch with friends.
She wears a red jacket to school.
She likes to read books about dogs.
it.h: Brave people do something even when it is scary.

it.q: Think of a character from a story who helped someone. Describe what the character did and what it shows about them.
it.ans: In "The Sharing Shelf," Rosa set up a shelf so neighbors could share food. It shows she is creative and cares about her neighbors.
it.h: Tell the action first. Then tell what kind of person would do that.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Connecting events in the life of a community leader

it.q: What is a citizen?
ch: a member of a community or country
a kind of building in a city
a type of vote in an election
a holiday for a whole country
it.h: Think about the people who live in a town or country.

it.q: Read: "Firefighter Ana Ruiz visits schools every month. She teaches students how to make a fire escape plan." What is the main idea?
ch: Ana Ruiz teaches students about fire safety.
Fires are very hot and dangerous.
Students like going on field trips.
Schools have many rooms and halls.
it.h: What is the paragraph mostly about?

it.q: Read: "In 1955, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus. Her action helped start a protest that changed unfair laws." What happened because of Rosa Parks's action?
ch: It helped start a protest that changed unfair laws.
She got a brand-new bus to ride.
Buses stopped running in the city forever.
She became a bus driver for the city.
it.h: Look for the words "helped start."

it.q: A text has a timeline: 1930, born; 1962, started a group; 2012, received a medal. What does a timeline show?
ch: important events in order by date
it.h: Look at the numbers. What do they stand for?

it.q: What is usually the author's purpose in a biography about a community helper?
ch: to tell about the person's life and work
to tell a made-up story with animals
to give directions to a nearby park
to sell a book about firefighters
it.h: A biography is about a real person.

it.q: Read: "Because the park had no trash cans, people left wrappers on the grass. Neighbors asked the city for trash cans, and the park became cleaner." Explain how these events are connected.
it.ans: The park had no trash cans, so people left wrappers on the grass. That made the neighbors ask the city for trash cans, and once the cans were there, the park became cleaner.
it.h: Use the words "because" or "so" to connect what happened.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Synonyms and shades of meaning

it.q: Which word is a synonym for "help"?
it.h: A synonym means almost the same thing.

it.q: Which word means the angriest?
it.h: Picture each feeling. Which one is the biggest?

it.q: Which word means to walk slowly and quietly?
it.h: Think about how you walk when a baby is sleeping.

it.q: Read: "Benji was nervous before his speech." Which word means almost the same as "nervous"?
it.h: How might you feel just before a big speech?

it.q: Which word means to throw something very hard?
it.h: Toss and hurl both mean throw. Which one is stronger?

it.q: Write one sentence using "toss" and one sentence using "hurl." Explain how their meanings are different.
it.ans: I will toss the ball gently to my baby sister. The pitcher can hurl the ball across the field. Toss means to throw lightly, and hurl means to throw very hard.
it.h: Think about how hard each kind of throw is.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two texts about a young citizen; author's purpose

it.q: What is an author's purpose?
ch: the reason the author wrote the text
it.h: Ask, "Why did the author write this?"

it.q: A text says, "Volunteer at the food bank! Your help can feed families." What is the author's main purpose?
ch: to describe the food bank building
it.h: Is the author trying to get readers to do something?

it.q: A text says, "A food bank collects food and gives it to families who need it." What is the author's main purpose?
ch: to explain what a food bank does
to persuade readers to buy food
to tell about the author's dog

it.q: Two texts tell about the same park cleanup. One is a news article and one is a diary entry. How might they be different?
ch: The diary tells the writer's feelings, and the article tells facts.
The diary has headings and a glossary.

it.q: Read: "Picking up litter keeps parks safe for animals. Broken glass and plastic can hurt them." Which reason does the author give?
Explain why it helps to read two texts about the same topic.
it.ans: Each text may give different facts or points of view, so reading both gives a fuller picture of the topic.
it.h: What might one text tell that the other does not?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing: An opinion letter with commas and linking words

it.q: Which greeting in a letter is written correctly?
it.h: Use capital letters for the name and a comma at the end.

it.q: Which closing is written correctly?
Which sentence states an opinion for a letter to a principal?
ch: I think our school should have a garden.
The principal's name is Mrs. Diaz.
it.h: An opinion tells what the writer thinks should happen.

it.q: Which linking word best joins these ideas: "We need more trash cans. The park will stay clean."?
Which date is written correctly?
it.h: Put a comma between the day and the year.

it.q: Write the greeting and the first sentence of a letter to your principal asking for something that would help your school.
it.ans: "Dear Principal Gomez, I think our school should have a buddy bench so no one feels left out at recess."

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Characters, events and illustrations

it.q: What does an illustration in a story do?
ch: helps show the characters, setting or events
it.h: Think about the pictures in a storybook.

it.q: An illustration shows a girl in a heavy coat and mittens while snow falls. What can you learn about the setting?
it.h: What do the girl's clothes tell you about the weather?

it.q: Read: "Leo's ice cream cone dripped onto his fingers. 'Hurry, eat it fast!' said his sister." What is happening to the ice cream?
it.h: Why would ice cream drip?

it.q: Read: "In the morning there was a puddle on the sidewalk. By afternoon, only a dry spot was left." What most likely happened?
ch: The sun dried up the water.
it.h: Think about what the sun does to water.

it.q: An illustration shows a character smiling and holding a mug with steam rising from it. How does the character most likely feel?
it.h: Look at the face and think about what is in the mug.

it.q: Imagine an illustration of a snowman on a hot, sunny day. Write two details an illustrator might draw to show what is happening.
it.ans: The illustrator might draw water dripping off the snowman and a puddle around its base. The snowman's stick arms might be drooping, and the sun would be shining brightly.
it.h: Think about what happens to snow in the heat.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Following steps in a how-to text

it.q: In a how-to text, what does a materials list tell you?
ch: what you need before you begin
the steps you follow in order
it.h: Materials are the things you use.

it.q: Read: "1. Fill a glass with ice. 2. Leave it on the table. 3. Check it after one hour." What do you do after leaving the glass on the table?
it.h: Look at the number after 2.

it.q: Read: "Melted chocolate is a liquid. When it cools, it becomes a solid again." What happens when melted chocolate cools?
it.h: Find the word "cools" and read what comes next.

it.q: Read: "A gas spreads out to fill any container. The air inside a balloon is a gas." What happens to air when you blow up a balloon?
ch: It spreads out to fill the balloon.
It turns into a solid inside.
It sinks to the bottom of it.
It becomes a liquid like water.
it.h: What does the first sentence say a gas does?

it.q: Why do some how-to texts include a note such as "Ask a grown-up for help"?
it.h: Think about steps that might be hard or unsafe for a child.

it.q: Write two steps for making a glass of chocolate milk. Use numbers or order words.
it.ans: First, pour cold milk into a glass. Next, stir in two spoons of chocolate syrup until it is mixed.
it.h: Think about what you do first and what you do next.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Suffixes and reflexive pronouns

it.q: What does "helpful" mean?
it.h: The suffix -ful means full of.

it.q: What does "careless" mean?
it.h: The suffix -less means without.

it.q: Which word completes the sentence? "Pip hurt ___ when he fell off the truck."
it.h: Pip is a "he." Which word goes with he?

it.q: Which word means "one who teaches"?
it.h: The suffix -er can mean a person who does something.

it.q: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
ch: We made the ice pops ourselves.
We made the ice pops ourself.
We made the ice pops ourselfs.
We made the ice pops themselves.
it.h: "We" goes with a word that ends in -selves.

it.q: Add a suffix to "slow" to make a word that tells how something moves. Use the new word in a sentence.
it.ans: Slowly. The ice cube melted slowly on the warm plate.
it.h: Which suffix often tells how something is done?

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: Changes you can undo and changes you cannot

it.q: Which is a liquid?
it.h: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

it.q: Read: "When you put water in the freezer, it turns into ice." What causes the water to turn into ice?
Read: "Chocolate melts in the sun. When it cools, it becomes hard again." Can this change be undone?
ch: yes, cooling makes it hard again
no, it can never be hard again
only if you freeze it for a year
it.h: Look at what happens after it cools.

it.q: Which signal word often shows cause and effect?
Read: "When you bake cake batter, it turns into a fluffy cake. You cannot turn the cake back into batter." What kind of change is baking?
ch: a change that cannot be undone
a change that can be undone
a change from gas to liquid
it.h: Can the cake become batter again?

it.q: Read: "Water vapor in the air cools when it touches a cold glass, so drops of water form on the glass." Tell the cause and the effect.
it.ans: Cause: water vapor cools when it touches the cold glass. Effect: drops of water form on the glass.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Grammar: Adjectives for describing matter and compound sentences

it.q: Which adjective describes how a rock feels?
it.h: Think about touching a rock.

it.q: Which adjective best describes honey?
Which sentence is a compound sentence?
ch: Ice is a solid, and water is a liquid.
it.h: A compound sentence joins two complete sentences.

it.q: Which word best completes the sentence? "The juice was cold, ___ the soup was hot."
it.h: The two ideas are opposites.

it.q: Which word is an adverb that tells how?
Write a compound sentence that describes a solid and a liquid. Use "and" or "but."
it.ans: "A brick is hard, but milk is runny."

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: The water cycle

it.q: Read: "When water evaporates, it changes from a liquid into a gas called water vapor." What is water vapor?
it.h: The sentence tells you what water vapor is.

it.q: Read: "Because the air high in the sky is cold, water vapor cools and forms tiny drops." Why does water vapor form drops high in the sky?
A science text shows a diagram with arrows going in a circle from the ocean to the clouds to the rain and back to the ocean. What does the diagram show?
ch: that water moves in a cycle
how to make a cloud in a jar
it.h: What shape do the arrows make?

it.q: Read: "Precipitation is water that falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail." Which is a kind of precipitation?
Read: "Water that soaks into the ground is called groundwater." Where is groundwater found?
Read: "The sun warms a lake. Some of the water evaporates. Later, it falls as rain." Explain how the water from the lake ends up as rain.
it.ans: The sun warms the lake, so some water evaporates into the air as vapor; the vapor cools and forms clouds, and later the water falls as rain.
it.h: Follow the water step by step.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Solids, Liquids and Gases (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading: Choosing the best material for the job

it.q: What does it mean if a material is waterproof?
it.h: Think about a raincoat.

it.q: Read: "Cooking pots are made of metal because metal gets hot quickly and does not melt on the stove." Why are pots made of metal?
ch: Metal gets hot quickly and does not melt on the stove.
it.h: Look at the part after "because."

it.q: Read: "Windows are made of glass so light can shine through." Which property of glass makes it good for windows?
Which material would be best for a sponge?
Read: "Tires are made of rubber. Rubber is flexible and grips the road." What does "flexible" mean?
it.h: Think about how a rubber band acts.

it.q: Read: "Builders use bricks for walls because bricks are hard and strong." Explain why a builder would not make walls out of paper.
it.ans: Paper is soft and weak and would tear or get wet, so it could not hold up a building like hard, strong bricks.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Long Ago and Today (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two versions of the same story

it.q: What does it mean when two stories are versions of the same tale?
ch: They tell the same basic story in different ways.
They are about two different topics.
They are written by the same person.
They do not have any characters.
it.h: Think about two people telling the same story in their own way.

it.q: In one version of a tale, a wolf chases three pigs. In another version, a coyote chases three javelinas. What is different?
it.h: Compare who is in each story.

it.q: Two versions of a trickster tale both end with the trickster getting caught. What is alike in the two versions?
it.h: Which part of the story happens last?

it.q: One version of a fairy tale happens in a castle. Another version happens in a modern city. What changed?
it.h: Where and when a story happens is called the setting.

it.q: Why might storytellers in different places change a tale?
ch: to fit their own places, animals and ways of life
because they forgot the rest of the story
only to make the story much shorter
so nobody else could understand it
it.h: Think about what is familiar to the people listening.

it.q: Imagine telling "The Tortoise and the Hare" in your own neighborhood. Name one thing that would stay the same and one thing that could change.
it.ans: The lesson, that slow and steady wins, would stay the same. The setting could change to a race around my school's track.
it.h: The lesson usually stays. The characters or setting can change.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Long Ago and Today (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Then and now in informational text

it.q: What does "long ago" mean in a history text?
ch: a time in the past, many years before today
a time next week or next month
a time far in the future
it.h: Think about when your great-grandparents were children.

it.q: Read: "Long ago, people washed clothes by hand on a washboard. Today, most families use washing machines." What changed?
ch: the kind of soap people use
it.h: Compare the first sentence with the second sentence.

it.q: Read: "Before cars were common, many families traveled in wagons pulled by horses. The trips took a long time." Why did trips take a long time?
ch: Wagons pulled by horses moved slowly.
The roads were too smooth and slippery.
Families liked to take long trips.
it.h: How fast can a horse pull a heavy wagon?

it.q: A photo in a text has this caption: "A family cooks dinner on a wood stove in 1900." What does the caption tell you?
ch: what the photo shows and when it was taken
the steps for following a recipe
the name of the person who wrote the text
the meaning of a hard word in the text
it.h: Captions explain pictures.

it.q: Read: "Long ago, children played with toys made of wood and cloth. Today, many toys are made of plastic." What is being compared?
ch: toys long ago and toys today
it.h: Look for the words "long ago" and "today."

it.q: Read: "Long ago, many families got water from a well. Today, most families turn on a faucet." Write one sentence that compares then and now.
it.ans: Long ago, families had to pull water up from a well, but today most families just turn on a faucet.
it.h: Use a word like "but" to show the difference.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Long Ago and Today (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Capital letters and commas in letters

it.q: Which holiday is written correctly?
it.h: Names of holidays begin with a capital letter.

it.q: Which place name is capitalized correctly?
it.h: The names of cities and states both need capital letters.

it.q: Which greeting of a letter uses a comma correctly?
it.h: The comma goes after the name of the person you are writing to.

it.q: Which closing of a letter is written correctly?
it.h: The closing starts with a capital letter, and a comma comes right after the closing word.

it.q: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
ch: My family visits the Pacific Ocean in July.
my family visits the pacific ocean in july.
My family visits the pacific Ocean in july.
My Family visits the Pacific ocean in July.
it.h: Capitalize the first word, the name of the ocean and the month.

it.q: Write the greeting and the closing of a letter to someone in your family. Use capital letters and commas correctly.
it.ans: Dear Aunt Lupe, ... Your nephew, Marco
it.h: Start with "Dear" and end with a closing like "Love," or "Your friend,".

lessons.u: Unit 10: Long Ago and Today (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Point of view and theme in a story told by a grandparent

it.q: What does "point of view" mean in a story?
ch: how a character sees and feels about events
the place where the story happens
it.h: Think about how two characters might feel differently about the same thing.

it.q: Read: "'I am so tired of this rain,' grumbled Owl. 'I love the rain!' croaked Frog." How do Owl and Frog see the rain differently?
ch: Owl dislikes it, but Frog loves it.
Owl loves it, but Frog dislikes it.
it.h: Look at the words each character says.

it.q: Which clue shows that a character is speaking?
When readers read aloud, how should they show different characters' points of view?
ch: use a different voice for each character
read every part in the same flat voice
it.h: Think about how a storyteller makes characters sound different.

it.q: What is the theme of a story?
Read: "Grandpa said, 'When I was your age, we had no TV. We played games outside until dark.' Lucas thought, 'That sounds fun, but I would miss my shows.'" Compare how Grandpa and Lucas feel.
it.ans: Grandpa remembers playing outside happily; Lucas thinks it sounds fun but would miss his TV shows.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Long Ago and Today (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing: Narratives with dialogue; contractions and possessives

it.q: What are quotation marks used for?
ch: to show the exact words a character says
it.h: Look for them around talking in a story.

it.q: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
ch: "Let's go to the museum," said Dad.
"Let's go to the museum, said Dad."
Let's go to the "museum," said Dad.
"Let's go" to the museum, said Dad.
it.h: The quotation marks go around only the words Dad says.

it.q: Which contraction means "I will"?
Which word is spelled correctly in "Grandpa was ___ the fence"?
Which sentence adds dialogue to a narrative about visiting a farm long ago?
ch: "Look at the cows!" shouted my brother.
it.h: Dialogue is what characters say out loud.

it.q: Write a sentence with dialogue that shows a character's feelings about a trip to a history museum.
it.ans: "This old train is amazing!" gasped Tara.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
lessons.n: Character traits, motivations and actions

it.q: Read: "Devon held the door for a man carrying boxes, even though Devon was running late." What trait does Devon show?
it.h: Think about why someone would stop to help when they are in a hurry.

it.q: What is the difference between a character trait and a feeling?
ch: A trait is part of who someone is, but a feeling can change quickly.
A trait changes every minute, but a feeling never changes.
Traits and feelings mean exactly the same thing.
it.h: Brave, honest and kind describe a person most of the time. Happy or scared can change in a moment.

it.q: Read: "Ruby practiced the violin every evening because she wanted to play at her cousin's wedding." What is Ruby's motivation?
it.h: A motivation is the reason a character does something. Look after the word "because."

it.q: Read: "Because Jae forgot to close the gate, the goats wandered into the garden." How did Jae's action affect the events?
ch: It let the goats get into the garden.
It kept the goats safe in their pen.
It helped the garden grow faster.
It made the goats fall asleep.
it.h: What happened as a result of the open gate?

it.q: Read: "'I'll never be good at this,' Lila muttered, tossing the paintbrush down." How does Lila feel?
it.h: Look at what she says and what she does with the brush.

it.q: Read: "Owen saw that the new student was standing alone at recess. He walked over and asked her to join the kickball game." Name a trait Owen shows and explain which action shows it.
it.ans: Owen is friendly (or kind). He shows it when he walks over to the new student who is alone and asks her to join the kickball game.
it.h: Name the trait first. Then point to what Owen did.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
lessons.n: Main idea, key details and text features

it.q: Which text feature lists topics in ABC order with page numbers?
it.h: You find it at the back of a book, and it tells you where to look.

it.q: Read: "Crossing guards help children cross busy streets. They wear bright vests so drivers can see them. They hold up stop signs to stop traffic." What is the main idea?
ch: Crossing guards help keep children safe near streets.
Drivers should always drive slowly near schools.
Bright vests are a popular kind of clothing.
Stop signs are red, white and easy to see.
it.h: Which idea do all three sentences support?

it.q: You want to find out what "volunteer" means in a book about your city. Where should you look first?
it.h: Which part of a book gives meanings of words used in that book?

it.q: On a website, what does a hyperlink do?
ch: It takes you to another page with more information.
It prints a copy of the page you are reading.
It closes the website and turns off the screen.
It shows how old the author of the page is.
it.h: Hyperlinks are usually underlined or a different color.

it.q: Read: "Food banks collect food and give it to families in need. Many grocery stores donate extra food. Volunteers sort cans and boxes." Which detail tells how food banks get food?
ch: Many grocery stores donate extra food.
it.h: Look for the sentence that tells where the food comes from.

it.q: Read: "Our city's recycling center keeps trash out of landfills. Workers sort paper, plastic and metal. The sorted materials are made into new products." Write the main idea and two key details.
it.ans: Main idea: the recycling center keeps trash out of landfills by recycling it. Details: workers sort paper, plastic and metal, and the sorted materials are made into new products.
it.h: The main idea is what the whole paragraph is about. Key details tell more about it.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
lessons.n: Nouns, plurals and parts of speech

it.q: Which word is an abstract noun?
it.h: An abstract noun names an idea or feeling that you cannot touch.

it.q: What is the plural of "city"?
it.h: When a word ends in a consonant and y, change the y to i and add -es.

it.q: Which word is a proper noun?
it.h: A proper noun names a specific person, place or thing and begins with a capital letter.

it.q: What part of speech is "quickly" in "Marisol walked quickly to the market"?
it.h: Which kind of word tells how an action is done?

it.q: What is the plural of "woman"?
it.h: This is an irregular plural. Think of "man" and "men."

it.q: Write a sentence that uses the abstract noun "friendship."
it.ans: Our friendship grew stronger when we worked on the garden together.
it.h: Friendship is an idea. You cannot hold it, but you can describe it.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
lessons.n: Writing a personal narrative: order of events, details and feelings

it.q: Who is the narrator of a personal narrative?
ch: the writer, telling about something that really happened to them
a reporter telling facts about a city
it.h: Think about whose experience a personal narrative tells.

it.q: Which word best tells the reader that one event comes after another?
it.h: Look for a time-order word.

it.q: Which sentence uses a detail to help the reader picture the moment?
ch: The bus hissed to a stop, and the doors folded open with a squeak.
Things happened on the way to school.
it.h: Which sentence lets you hear or see what is happening?

it.q: A writer wants to show that she felt proud. Which sentence shows it best?
ch: I stood up tall and could not stop smiling.
it.h: How does a proud person look or act?

it.q: Which sentence would make the best ending for a personal narrative about learning to ride a bike?
ch: Now, whenever I ride past that hill, I remember that falling is part of learning.
Bikes have two wheels and pedals.
My friend has a red bike.
it.h: A good ending tells what the writer learned or how they feel now.

it.q: Write a first sentence for a personal narrative about a time you helped a neighbor. Make it grab the reader's attention.
it.ans: The day Mrs. Ortiz's cat got stuck on the roof was the day I became the bravest kid on our street.
it.h: Start in the middle of the action or with a surprising detail.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Community Connections (personal narrative)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: asking and answering questions about a community garden

it.q: Which question word asks about a place?
it.h: Which word could you answer with "in the park"?

it.q: Read: "Volunteers at the shelter walk the dogs twice a day." Which question does this sentence answer?
ch: How often are the dogs walked?
it.h: "Twice a day" tells how often.

it.q: Read: "The fire station holds an open house every May. Families can climb into a fire truck and meet the firefighters." What is the main idea?
ch: Families can visit the fire station at an open house.
Fire trucks are red and loud.
it.h: What are both sentences about?

it.q: Which question can be answered by looking back at a text, instead of guessing?
ch: What does the text say the volunteers do?
What is the author's favorite color?
it.h: The answer should be written in the text.

it.q: Read: "Our school started a reading buddy program. Fifth graders read with kindergartners on Fridays." Who reads with the kindergartners?
it.h: Look for the word that names the people.

it.q: Read: "The city painted bike lanes on Grant Street. Now more people ride bikes to work." Write one question about these sentences and answer it with words from those sentences.
it.ans: Question: What did the city paint on Grant Street? Answer: The city painted bike lanes on Grant Street.
it.h: Start your question with Who, What, Where, When, Why or How.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
lessons.n: Recounting stories and finding the central message

it.q: What is the central message of a story?
ch: the big lesson the author wants readers to learn
the name of the main character
the place and time of the story
it.h: Think about what the story teaches, not just what happens.

it.q: Read: "Every day, the little ant carried one seed to her nest. When winter came, her nest was full while the other ants went hungry." What lesson does this teach?
ch: Small efforts every day add up.
Ants do not like the winter.
Seeds are too heavy to carry.
it.h: What did the ant do every day, and what happened because of it?

it.q: Which event would best support the message "Patience brings rewards"?
ch: A girl waits months for her tree to bloom, and at last it does.
A boy runs as fast as he can to catch the bus.
A dog barks every morning at the mail carrier.
A girl grabs a quick snack before soccer practice.
it.h: Look for a character who waits for something good.

it.q: Read: "The tadpole wished for legs. 'Wait,' said the frog. Weeks later, the tadpole hopped onto a lily pad." What happens at the end?
ch: The tadpole has grown legs and hops.
The tadpole gives up and swims away.
The frog swims off and leaves.
The lily pad sinks into the pond.
it.h: What can the tadpole do in the last sentence that it could not do before?

it.q: When you recount a story, what should you include?
ch: the most important events in order
every single detail from every page
only what happens at the very end
the parts with your favorite pictures
it.h: Recounting means retelling the key parts.

it.q: Read: "Every morning, Arjun fed the hen and kept her nest clean. Weeks later, three fluffy chicks peeped beside her." Write the central message and the detail that supports it.
it.ans: The message is that taking good care of something brings rewards. Arjun fed the hen and cleaned her nest every morning, and weeks later three chicks hatched.
it.h: What did Arjun do, and what good thing happened?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
lessons.n: Sequence and cause and effect in science texts

it.q: Which word signals time order?
it.h: Which word tells when something happens?

it.q: Read: "Because the pond dried up in summer, the frogs moved to a nearby stream." What is the effect?
ch: The frogs moved to a nearby stream.
it.h: The effect is what happened as a result.

it.q: Read: "First, a ladybug lays eggs on a leaf. Next, larvae hatch and eat tiny insects. Then each larva forms a pupa. Finally, an adult ladybug comes out." Which stage comes right before the adult?
it.h: Find the step that begins with "Then."

it.q: Read: "A frog's skin is smooth and wet. A toad's skin is bumpy and dry." How are these two sentences connected?
ch: They explain a cause and an effect.
They tell part of a story.
it.h: Are the sentences showing how things are alike or different?

it.q: Read: "Chickens hatch from eggs after about 21 days." What does "hatch" mean?
it.h: What happens to a chick on day 21?

it.q: Read: "Salmon hatch in rivers, swim to the ocean to grow, and then return to the river where they were born to lay eggs." Explain the steps in order using sequence words.
it.ans: First, salmon hatch in a river. Next, they swim to the ocean to grow. Then they return to the river where they were born. Finally, they lay their own eggs there.
it.h: Use first, next, then and finally.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
lessons.n: Verbs and simple verb tenses

it.q: Which word is the verb in "The tadpole swims in the pond"?
it.h: The verb tells what the subject does.

it.q: Which sentence is in the future tense?
ch: The eggs will hatch next week.
The eggs are in the nest.
it.h: Future tense often uses the helping verb "will."

it.q: What is the past tense of "grow"?
it.h: Grow is irregular. Say "Last year, the puppy ___ bigger."

it.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Yesterday, the butterfly ___ out of its chrysalis."
it.h: "Yesterday" tells you the action already happened.

it.q: Which sentence is in the present tense?
ch: The frog will catch a fly.
The frog had caught a fly.
it.h: Present tense tells what happens now or usually.

it.q: Write three short sentences about a chick: one in the past tense, one in the present tense and one in the future tense.
it.ans: Yesterday the chick hatched. Today the chick eats seeds. Tomorrow the chick will explore the yard.
it.h: Use words like yesterday, today and tomorrow to help.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative paragraph: topic sentence, facts and linking words

it.q: What does a topic sentence do?
ch: It tells what the whole paragraph is about.
It ends the paragraph with a joke.
It lists every fact in the paragraph.
it.h: It is usually the first sentence of an informative paragraph.

it.q: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about how ladybugs grow?
ch: A ladybug goes through four stages as it grows.
it.h: The best topic sentence names the topic and what the paragraph will explain.

it.q: Which linking word adds another fact?
it.h: Which word means "and one more thing"?

it.q: Which sentence is a fact, not an opinion?
ch: A baby kangaroo is called a joey.
it.h: A fact can be checked in a book.

it.q: Which sentence gives a definition?
ch: A larva is the young, wormlike stage of an insect.
I found a larva in the garden.
it.h: A definition tells what a word means.

it.q: Write a concluding sentence for a paragraph about how sea turtles hatch on the beach and crawl to the ocean.
it.ans: The journey from nest to ocean is the first big challenge in a sea turtle's long life.
it.h: A concluding sentence sums up the topic in a new way.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Animal Life Cycles (informative writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two texts on the same topic: frog life cycles

it.q: When you compare two texts, you look for
it.h: Compare means find ways things are the same.

it.q: When you contrast two texts, you look for
it.h: Contrast is the opposite of compare.

it.q: Text A says frogs lay eggs in water. Text B says frogs lay eggs in jelly-like clumps in ponds. How are the texts alike?
ch: Both say frogs lay eggs in water.
Both say frogs lay eggs in trees.
Both say frogs do not lay eggs.
Both say eggs are hard like a chicken's.
it.h: Find the fact that appears in both texts.

it.q: Text A tells about frogs. Text B tells about butterflies. Which important idea could both texts share?
ch: Some animals change their body shape as they grow.
it.h: Think about tadpoles and caterpillars.

it.q: Read: "The tadpole's tail gets shorter and shorter until it disappears." What does "disappears" mean?
it.h: The prefix dis- means "not" or "the opposite of."

it.q: Name one way a frog's life cycle and a butterfly's life cycle are alike and one way they are different.
it.ans: Alike: both start as eggs and change shape a lot before they are adults. Different: a tadpole lives in water and breathes with gills, but a caterpillar lives on land and makes a chrysalis.
it.h: Think about where each young animal lives and how it changes.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Narrator's point of view and my point of view

it.q: What is a narrator?
ch: the person or character who tells the story
the person who draws the pictures
the last character in the story
it.h: Ask yourself: whose voice is telling what happens?

it.q: Read: "I hated the heat wave. The sidewalk burned my feet." Who is telling this part of the story?
ch: a character in the story who uses "I"
an outside narrator who is not in the story
it.h: Look at the word "I."

it.q: Read: "I think snow days are boring. There is nothing to do inside." Which reader would most likely disagree with the narrator?
ch: a reader who loves playing in the snow
a reader who wants to stay indoors
a reader who thinks snow days are dull
a reader who dislikes cold weather
it.h: Find the reader whose opinion is the opposite of the narrator's.

it.q: Read: "'Wind is my favorite weather,' said Kai, as his kite soared." What is Kai's point of view about wind?
it.h: What does Kai call wind?

it.q: Why is it helpful to know a narrator's point of view?
ch: It helps you understand why events are described in a certain way.
It tells you how many pages the story has.
It proves that every event in the story is true.
It tells you who drew the pictures in the book.
it.h: A narrator's feelings shape the way they tell the story.

it.q: Read: "I love thunderstorms. The booming makes me feel like I'm in an adventure movie." Write the narrator's point of view about thunderstorms and then your own point of view.
it.ans: The narrator loves thunderstorms because the booming sound feels exciting. My point of view is different: I do not like thunderstorms, because the loud booms make it hard to sleep.
it.h: First tell what the narrator thinks. Then say whether you agree.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Main idea, connections and maps in informational text

it.q: What does a map key, or legend, tell you?
ch: what the colors and symbols on a map mean
the title of the book the map is in
the name of the person who drew it
today's date and the time of day
it.h: It is usually in a box in the corner of a map.

it.q: Read: "Fog forms when warm, wet air moves over cold water. The air cools, and tiny water drops form near the ground." What causes fog to form?
ch: warm, wet air moving over cold water
cold air moving over hot sand
it.h: Look at the first sentence. What has to happen first?

it.q: Read: "Some places get a lot of rain. For example, parts of the Pacific Northwest get rain on many days of the year." What does "for example" signal?
ch: The next part gives an example of the first idea.
The author is changing to a new topic.
The text is about to end.
The sentences are steps in a process.
it.h: Think about what usually comes after the words "for example."

it.q: A weather map shows a blue line with triangles on it. Where should a reader look to find out what this symbol means?
it.h: Which part of a map explains its symbols?

it.q: Read: "Hurricanes form over warm ocean water. They bring strong winds and heavy rain." What is the main idea?
ch: Hurricanes form over warm oceans and bring wind and rain.
Ocean water is always warm all over the world.
Heavy rain is wet and falls from dark clouds.
Strong winds can blow trees over in a storm.
it.h: Put the two sentences together into one big idea.

it.q: Read: "In the desert, days are often hot, but nights can be cold. This is because dry air and clear skies let heat escape quickly after sunset." Explain the cause and effect in these sentences.
it.ans: The cause is that dry air and clear skies let heat escape quickly after sunset. The effect is that desert nights can be cold even though the days are hot.
it.h: The word "because" points to the cause.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Subject-verb agreement and the suffixes -ful, -less and -y

it.q: Which verb agrees with the subject? "The clouds ___ dark."
it.h: "Clouds" means more than one. Which verb goes with a plural subject?

it.q: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
it.h: A singular subject usually takes a verb that ends in -s.

it.q: What does "cloudless" mean?
it.h: The suffix -less means without.

it.q: Which word means "full of hope"?
it.h: The suffix -ful means full of.

it.q: When you add the suffix -y to "wind," what does "windy" describe?
ch: weather with a lot of wind
a person who winds a clock
weather with no wind at all
it.h: The suffix -y can mean "having a lot of," as in rainy or snowy.

it.q: Write one sentence about weather with a singular subject and one with a plural subject. Make sure each verb agrees with its subject.
it.ans: The storm brings heavy rain. The storms bring heavy rain.
it.h: Try the same sentence with "storm" and then "storms."

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative report about weather: grouping facts under headings

it.q: What is a heading in a report?
ch: a title for a section that tells what it is about
the last sentence of the report
it.h: Headings are like small titles inside a longer piece.

it.q: A report about storms has the headings "Thunderstorms," "Tornadoes" and "Hurricanes." Under which heading does this fact belong? "A spinning column of air reaches down from a cloud to the ground."
it.h: Which storm is a spinning column of air that touches the ground?

it.q: Which fact belongs in a section called "How to Measure Rain"?
ch: A rain gauge collects rain so you can see how much fell.
Wind can blow leaves off trees.
it.h: Which fact tells about a tool for rain?

it.q: Which is the best introduction for a report about fog?
ch: Have you ever woken up to find your street hidden in a gray cloud? That cloud is called fog.
I am going to write about fog now.
it.h: A good introduction gets readers interested and names the topic.

it.q: Which source would be the most trustworthy for facts about weather?
ch: a website from a national weather service
a comic book about a talking cloud
it.h: Which source is written by weather experts?

it.q: Write two facts you could group under the heading "Staying Cool on a Hot Day."
it.ans: Drink plenty of water. Stay in the shade or indoors during the hottest part of the afternoon.
it.h: Both facts should be about the heading.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: thunderstorm and lightning safety

it.q: What causes the sound of thunder?
it.h: Thunder always comes with a bright flash.

it.q: Read: "When you see lightning, go inside a building. A car with a hard metal roof is also a safe place." What is the main idea?
ch: There are safe places to go during lightning.
it.h: What do both sentences tell you?

it.q: Read: "Because tall objects are more likely to be struck by lightning, never stand under a lone tree in a storm." Which is the cause?
ch: Tall objects are more likely to be struck by lightning.
it.h: The cause comes right after the word "because."

it.q: Read: "The storm was severe, with hail the size of marbles and winds that knocked down fences." What does "severe" mean?
it.h: What would hail like marbles and wind that knocks down fences be like?

it.q: Which sentence is the best summary of a text that tells people to check the weather, have a flashlight ready and stay away from windows during storms?
ch: People can take steps to stay safe in storms.
it.h: A summary tells the most important idea in a few words.

it.q: Read: "Lightning can strike more than 10 miles away from a storm. That is why experts say, 'When thunder roars, go indoors.'" Explain how the first sentence connects to the second.
it.ans: The first sentence gives the reason for the rule in the second. Because lightning can strike far from a storm, you should go inside as soon as you hear thunder.
it.h: Does the first sentence give a cause or reason?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather and Climate (informative writing)
lessons.n: Compound words and weather vocabulary with a glossary

it.q: Which word is a compound word?
it.h: A compound word is made of two smaller words put together.

it.q: What two words make up "thunderstorm"?
it.h: Look for two whole words you already know.

it.q: Read: "A downpour soaked the field in minutes." Use the two smaller words to figure out what "downpour" means.
it.h: Think about "down" and "pour" together.

it.q: In a glossary, which word comes first in ABC order?
it.h: Look at the first letter of each word.

it.q: Which compound word names a tool that shows which way the wind blows?
it.h: Which word is made of two words, one of which is a piece of clothing?

it.q: Make a compound word with "snow" and explain what it means.
it.ans: Snowflake: a single flake, or small piece, of snow.
it.h: Put "snow" together with another whole word.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Folktales and Storytellers (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Folktales: central message and character actions

it.q: A folktale is a story that
ch: was first passed down by people telling it aloud
was written by a scientist to give facts
always takes place in outer space
it.h: "Folk" means people. Think about how stories were shared before books.

it.q: Read: "The rich man laughed at the poor farmer's small gift. But the king smiled and said the farmer's gift was the most generous of all, because it was all he had." What lesson does this teach?
ch: The value of a gift comes from the heart.
Rich people always give the best gifts.
Kings like to laugh at people.
it.h: Why did the king think the small gift was the most generous?

it.q: In many folktales, characters face three tests or tries. Why might storytellers repeat events three times?
ch: It builds suspense and helps listeners remember.
It makes the story end more quickly.
It shows the storyteller forgot the story.
It adds more facts to the story.
it.h: Think about how it feels to wait for the third try.

it.q: Read: "Each time Fox tried to trick the hens, Rooster warned them. At last, Fox gave up and slunk away." How did Rooster's actions affect the story?
ch: They kept Fox from tricking the hens.
They helped Fox catch the hens.
They made the hens leave the farm.
They made Fox and Rooster friends.
it.h: What happened to Fox in the end because of Rooster?

it.q: Which is usually true about the ending of a folktale?
ch: It shows a lesson through what happens to the characters.
It gives a list of facts about real animals.
It does not have a clear ending at all.
It brings in many new characters at once.
it.h: Think about how the characters are rewarded or punished.

it.q: Think of a folktale you know. Name its central message and one key detail that shows it.
it.ans: In "The Tortoise and the Hare," the message is that slow, steady work can win. The hare naps during the race, but the tortoise keeps going and crosses the finish line first.
it.h: Tell the lesson, then tell what a character did that teaches it.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Folktales and Storytellers (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Learning about storytellers from informational text

it.q: What is usually the author's purpose in a text that explains how storytellers once used picture cards to tell tales?
ch: to get readers to buy cards
it.h: Does the text teach, entertain or persuade?

it.q: Read: "Puppet shows are popular in many countries. In Indonesia, shadow puppets made of leather are moved behind a lit screen." What does the second sentence do?
it.h: The first sentence makes a general point. What does the second sentence add?

it.q: Read: "Storytellers often begin with special words. Some English tales begin with 'Once upon a time.'" What is the main idea?
ch: Storytellers often begin tales with special words.
English tales are the oldest tales in the world.
Time is the most important part of any story.
All stories begin and end in exactly the same way.
it.h: Which sentence is the big idea, and which is the example?

it.q: Read: "Before printing presses, books were copied by hand, so they were rare and expensive." Why were books rare long ago?
ch: They had to be copied by hand.
People did not like to read.
Books were too heavy to carry.
it.h: Look at what comes before the word "so."

it.q: In a text, the word "oral" is in bold. The glossary says it means "spoken, not written." What is oral storytelling?
it.h: Use the glossary meaning.

it.q: Read: "Quilts can tell stories, too. Some families sew pictures of important events into their quilts and pass them down to their children." Write the main idea and one supporting detail.
it.ans: The main idea is that quilts can tell stories. One detail is that some families sew pictures of important events into quilts and pass them down.
it.h: The main idea is often in the first sentence.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Folktales and Storytellers (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Antonyms and context clues

it.q: Which word is an antonym of "generous"?
it.h: An antonym means the opposite.

it.q: Which word is an antonym of "ancient"?
it.h: Ancient means very, very old. What is the opposite?

it.q: Read: "The path was narrow, not wide like the road." What does "narrow" mean?
it.h: The words "not wide" are a clue.

it.q: Read: "The weaver was patient. She did not rush, even when the work was slow." Which words help you understand "patient"?
it.h: Look for words that tell how a patient person acts.

it.q: Which pair of words are antonyms?
it.h: Look for two words with opposite meanings.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses a hard word and gives a context clue to its meaning. Underline the clue.
it.ans: The soup was scalding, so hot that it burned my tongue. (Clue: so hot that it burned my tongue)
it.h: Add a few words that explain or give an example of the hard word.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Folktales and Storytellers (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: characters, dialogue and a clear ending

it.q: What is the problem in a story?
ch: the trouble or challenge the characters must face
it.h: Most stories have something that goes wrong.

it.q: Which sentence punctuates dialogue correctly?
it.h: The quotation marks go around only the words the character says.

it.q: Which beginning introduces a character and a problem?
ch: Tortoise wanted to cross the river, but he could not swim.
it.h: Look for a who and a trouble.

it.q: Which sentence shows what a character is like through her actions?
ch: Mei shared the last of her rice with the hungry crane.
it.h: What a character does tells us what she is like.

it.q: Which ending solves the problem "Fox could not reach the berries on the high branch"?
ch: Fox asked Bear for a boost, and together they shared the berries.
it.h: The ending should tell how the problem is fixed.

it.q: Write two lines of dialogue between a rabbit and a turtle who disagree about who should go first across a bridge. Punctuate them correctly.
it.ans: "I am faster, so I should go first," said Rabbit. Turtle smiled and replied, "Then you can wait for me at the other side."
it.h: Each speaker's words go inside quotation marks, with a comma before the closing mark.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Folktales and Storytellers (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Fables and their morals

it.q: What is a moral?
ch: a lesson that a story teaches
the name of the main character
it.h: Fables often end by telling what we should learn.

it.q: Which is a common feature of fables?
ch: animal characters that talk and act like people
it.h: Think about stories with a talking fox or tortoise.

it.q: A fox tricks a crow into dropping her cheese by praising her singing. What lesson does this teach?
ch: Be careful of people who flatter you to get something.
it.h: What did the crow lose by listening to the fox's praise?

it.q: In a fable, a lazy grasshopper plays all summer while ants store food. In winter, the grasshopper is hungry. How do the grasshopper's actions lead to the ending?
ch: Because he did not prepare, he has no food in winter.
Because he worked hard, he has plenty of food.
Because the ants were lazy, they are hungry.
Because it snowed, the ants left.
it.h: Connect what he did in summer to what happens in winter.

it.q: Which moral fits a story where many small birds together lift a net that one bird could not lift alone?
it.h: What did the birds do that one bird could not?

it.q: Explain how a fable's moral is different from its events.
it.ans: The events are what happens in the story, like the tortoise winning a race. The moral is the lesson we learn from those events, like "slow and steady wins the race."
it.h: One is what happens. The other is what we learn.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Parts of plays, poems and stories

it.q: What is a scene in a play?
ch: a part of the play that happens in one place and time
the list of characters at the beginning of the play
a line of dialogue that rhymes with another line
the name of the person who wrote the play
it.h: A play can be divided into parts, like chapters in a book.

it.q: What do we call a group of lines in a poem?
it.h: Plays have scenes. Books have chapters. Poems have ___.

it.q: In a play, what is the list at the beginning that names the characters called?
it.h: It tells you who will be in the play.

it.q: How does a chapter in a book usually build on the chapter before it?
ch: It continues the events from the earlier chapter.
It always starts a brand-new story with new people.
It repeats the same events from the last chapter.
It only lists all of the characters again.
it.h: Think about reading a chapter book over several days.

it.q: Read this part of a play: "MAYA: (whispering) Shh! The baby is sleeping." How should the actor say Maya's line?
it.h: Look at the words in parentheses.

it.q: Explain one way a play is different from a story.
it.ans: A play is written mostly as dialogue, with each character's name before their lines and stage directions in parentheses. A story uses paragraphs and a narrator who tells what happens.
it.h: Think about how the words look on the page.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Connecting events in an inventor's life

it.q: Which group of words signals time order in a text?
it.h: Look for words that tell when something happened.

it.q: Read: "Thomas Edison's team tested thousands of materials. Finally, they found one that let a light bulb glow for many hours." What happened after the team tested thousands of materials?
ch: They found a material that glowed for hours.
They gave up on the light bulb idea.
They failed one more time and stopped.
They sold their first light bulb in a store.
it.h: Look for the word "Finally."

it.q: Read: "Before the refrigerator, people kept food cold with blocks of ice. Ice melted quickly, so food often spoiled." What was the effect of ice melting quickly?
it.h: The word "so" comes right before the effect.

it.q: Read: "The first telephones had no dials or buttons. A caller had to ask an operator to connect the call." How did people make calls on the first telephones?
ch: They asked an operator to connect them.
They turned a round dial on the phone.
They sent a text message instead.
it.h: Read the second sentence again.

it.q: Which question would a biography of an inventor most likely answer?
ch: What problem did the inventor try to solve?
What is the reader's favorite color?
it.h: A biography tells about a real person's life and work.

it.q: Read: "Josephine Cochrane was tired of her fine dishes getting chipped when they were washed by hand. In 1886, she patented a dishwasher that cleaned dishes with water pressure." Explain the connection between the problem and the invention.
it.ans: Cochrane's dishes kept getting chipped when they were washed by hand. Because of this problem, she invented a machine that used water pressure to clean dishes without handling them roughly.
it.h: Tell the problem first, then tell how the invention solved it.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Prefixes and comparing with adjectives and adverbs

it.q: What does the prefix dis- mean in "disagree"?
it.h: If you disagree, you do the opposite of agree.

it.q: What does "preheat" mean?
it.h: The prefix pre- means before.

it.q: Which word means "spelled wrong"?
it.h: The prefix mis- means wrongly.

it.q: Which word completes the sentence? "Rosa's backpack is ___ than Dev's."
it.h: Use -er to compare two things. Change the y to i first.

it.q: Which word completes the sentence? "That was the ___ invention at the fair."
it.h: "Good" is irregular: good, better, ___.

it.q: Write three sentences about cars or bikes using "fast," "faster" and "fastest."
it.ans: My bike is fast. My sister's bike is faster than mine. Our neighbor's racing bike is the fastest on the street.
it.h: Use "faster" to compare two things and "fastest" to compare three or more.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion piece: reasons, linking words and a conclusion

it.q: What does an opinion piece tell?
ch: what the writer thinks and why
it.h: An opinion is what someone believes.

it.q: Which is the best opinion statement for a piece about inventions?
ch: The bicycle is the most useful invention for kids.
it.h: An opinion statement says what the writer believes clearly.

it.q: Which linking words introduce a reason?
it.h: Which word tells why?

it.q: Which reason best supports the opinion "Every classroom should have a pencil sharpener"?
ch: Students waste less time when they can sharpen pencils quickly.
it.h: A good reason explains why the opinion makes sense.

it.q: Which linking phrase is best to begin the last sentence of an opinion piece?
it.h: The last sentence sums up the opinion.

it.q: Write an opinion sentence about which invention you could not live without, and give one reason using "because."
it.ans: I could not live without the refrigerator because it keeps our food fresh and safe to eat.
it.h: State your opinion, then explain why.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Text structure: sequence in the history of the bicycle

it.q: What does a sequence text structure show?
ch: events or steps in time order
it.h: Think about "first, next, then, last."

it.q: Which words signal sequence?
it.h: Which words tell when?

it.q: Read: "Long ago, people wrote everything by hand. Later, the typewriter made writing faster. Today, many people type on computers." What changed over time?
ch: the tools people used to write
it.h: Look at what each sentence describes.

it.q: Read: "Because early phones needed wires, people could only call from home. When cell phones were invented, people could call from almost anywhere." What caused the change?
it.h: What new thing let people call from anywhere?

it.q: Which question would a timeline answer best?
ch: What is the author's favorite invention?
How many pages long is the book?
it.h: A timeline shows dates in order.

it.q: Read: "First, the inventor drew a plan. Next, she built a model. Then she tested it and fixed the problems." Retell the steps in your own words using sequence words.
it.ans: First, the inventor planned on paper. After that, she made a model. Last, she tried it out and fixed what did not work.
it.h: Use words like first, after that and last.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: a play about an inventor's mistakes

it.q: In a play, what are stage directions?
ch: words that tell actors how to move or speak
it.h: They are often written in parentheses.

it.q: How is a play different from a story?
ch: A play is mostly dialogue and is meant to be acted out.
A play never has a problem.
it.h: Think about how you would read a play with friends.

it.q: Read: "MILO: (throwing down his tools) This robot will never work!" What do the stage directions show?
it.h: How does a person act when he throws down his tools?

it.q: In a play, what is a scene?
ch: a part of the play that happens in one time and place
a single word in the play
it.h: Plays are divided into parts, like chapters.

it.q: What is the cast of characters?
ch: a list of the characters at the start of a play
it.h: It comes before the first scene.

it.q: Write one line for a play, with stage directions, that shows a character is excited about an invention.
it.ans: ZARA: (jumping up and down) It works! The lamp turned on all by itself!
it.h: Put the actions in parentheses and the words after the character's name.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Inventions That Changed Our Lives (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Research: gathering facts about an inventor and taking notes

it.q: What is the first step of a short research project?
it.h: You need to know what you are looking for.

it.q: Which question is best for a short report about an inventor?
ch: What problem did Garrett Morgan's traffic signal help solve?
Who are all the inventors in history?
it.h: A good research question is focused on one thing.

it.q: Which keyword search would best help you learn about the inventor of a type of traffic signal?
it.h: Use names and specific words.

it.q: Which part of a book helps you find the page about a certain inventor quickly?
ch: the back of the title page
it.h: It lists topics in ABC order with page numbers.

it.q: Which note is the best example of putting facts in your own words?
ch: Morgan - signal with warning position - helped cars stop safely
it.h: Notes are short and use your own words.

it.q: Why is it important to use more than one source when you research?
it.ans: Using more than one source helps you check that facts are correct and find more information.
it.h: What if one source has a mistake?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Comparing stories about the same characters

it.q: When you compare two stories by the same author, what can you look at?
ch: the themes, settings, plots and characters
only the page numbers in each book
only the titles printed on the covers
the prices of the two books
it.h: Think about the parts of a story.

it.q: In one book, Kai learns to swim. In another book about Kai, he learns to ride a bike. What is alike about the plots?
ch: Kai learns a new skill in both books.
Kai goes to the beach in both books.
Kai is afraid of water in both books.
Kai rides a bike in both books.
it.h: Look past the details. What does Kai do in each book?

it.q: One story by an author takes place on a farm, and another story by the same author takes place in a big city. What is different?
it.h: Where and when a story happens is its setting.

it.q: In two different stories, a character learns that honesty is important. What do the stories share?
it.h: A theme is the big lesson of a story.

it.q: Why might an author write several stories about the same characters?
ch: so readers can follow the characters through new adventures
because the author forgot the first story
so each story can have a different author
so readers never learn much about the characters
it.h: Think about why readers enjoy book series.

it.q: Think of two books in a series you know. Name one way the stories are alike and one way they are different.
it.ans: In two books about Frog and Toad, the characters are always best friends who help each other. They are different because in one story they look for a lost button and in another they fly a kite.
it.h: Compare the characters, setting, plot or lesson.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: How local government works

it.q: What is a government?
ch: a group of people who make rules and decisions for a community
a type of school where adults take classes
a kind of store that sells things to a town
a large park where a community can play
it.h: Think about who decides on laws.

it.q: Read: "The city council voted to build a new library. Construction will begin in June." What happened first?
it.h: Which event had to happen before the building could start?

it.q: Read: "I believe every city should have a youth council so that kids can share ideas with leaders." What is the author's point of view?
ch: Kids should have a way to share ideas with city leaders.
Kids should not be allowed to talk to city leaders.
Cities should not have any councils at all.
Only kids should be allowed to be city leaders.
it.h: Look at the words after "I believe."

it.q: A diagram shows three boxes with arrows: "City" points to "County," and "County" points to "State." What does the diagram show?
ch: how each level is part of a larger one
the steps for voting in an election
who sits where at a council meeting
it.h: Think about which is the smallest area and which is the largest.

it.q: Read: "Rules at school keep students safe. Laws in a community do the same thing for everyone." How are these two sentences connected?
ch: They compare school rules with community laws.
They tell the steps of a process in order.
They tell a short story about a school.
They list two problems that need solving.
it.h: The words "the same thing" are a clue.

it.q: Read: "Because many families complained about speeding cars, the city put speed bumps on Elm Street." Explain the cause and the effect.
it.ans: The cause is that many families complained about cars speeding. The effect is that the city put speed bumps on Elm Street to slow the cars down.
it.h: The cause comes after the word "because."

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Conjunctions and compound and complex sentences

it.q: Which word is a coordinating conjunction?
it.h: Coordinating conjunctions include and, but, or and so.

it.q: Which word best joins these sentences? "Lena was nervous. She gave her speech anyway."
it.h: The second idea is a surprise after the first. Which word shows a contrast?

it.q: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
ch: Lena spoke, and the class listened.
it.h: A compound sentence has two complete sentences joined by a comma and a conjunction.

it.q: Which conjunction completes the sentence? "We stayed inside ___ it was raining."
it.h: The second part tells why.

it.q: Which sentence is a complex sentence?
ch: When the bell rang, the meeting began.
The bell rang, and the meeting began.
it.h: A complex sentence uses a word like when, because, if or although to join a part that cannot stand alone.

it.q: Combine these two sentences into one, using a conjunction: "The city fixed the road. Drivers were happy."
it.ans: The city fixed the road, so drivers were happy. (Also correct: Drivers were happy because the city fixed the road.)
it.h: Think about whether the second idea is a result of the first.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion letter to a community leader

it.q: Which part of a letter comes first?
it.h: Think about the top right of a letter.

it.q: Which greeting is written correctly?
it.h: Use capital letters for names and a comma after the greeting.

it.q: Which closing is written correctly?
it.h: Only the first word is capitalized, and a comma follows.

it.q: Which sentence clearly states an opinion for a letter to the city council?
ch: Our town needs a crosswalk in front of Lincoln School.
it.h: Which sentence tells what the writer wants and believes?

it.q: Which is the most polite way to ask a leader to act?
ch: Please consider adding a stop sign on Pine Street.
You have to put a stop sign there now!
it.h: Respectful words help readers listen.

it.q: Write one reason, with a fact or example, that could support a letter asking for more trash cans at a park.
it.ans: There is trash on the grass every weekend because the two trash cans near the playground are always full.
it.h: Give a reason the leader could check or see.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: a story about citizens solving a problem

it.q: What is a character's point of view?
ch: what the character thinks or feels about something
it.h: Two characters can feel differently about the same thing.

it.q: Read: "Lena thought the new park rule was unfair. Her brother thought it would keep everyone safe." How are their points of view different?
ch: Lena dislikes the rule, but her brother thinks it is helpful.
it.h: Compare what each one thinks.

it.q: Read: "Kofi counted the cars that zoomed past the school and wrote the numbers in his notebook." Why might Kofi do this?
ch: to gather facts about the traffic
it.h: What could numbers help him show?

it.q: Which detail would show a character is determined?
ch: She kept asking for signatures, even after many people said no.
it.h: Determined means not giving up.

it.q: A story character says, "One voice is small, but many voices are loud." What does she mean?
ch: People working together are more likely to be heard.
it.h: Think about what happens when many people ask for the same thing.

it.q: Do you agree with this idea: "Kids can help make their community better"? Give one reason.
it.ans: Yes, because kids can notice problems, like trash at the park, and ask leaders or neighbors to help fix them.
it.h: Tell your own point of view and explain why.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: why communities have rules and laws

it.q: What is a law?
ch: a rule that everyone in a community, state or country must follow
it.h: Laws are made by governments.

it.q: Read: "A town has a law that dogs must be on a leash in parks. This keeps people and other dogs safe." What is the reason for the law?
ch: to keep people and dogs safe
it.h: Look at the second sentence.

it.q: Which is a rule at home or school, not a law made by a government?
ch: Raise your hand before speaking in class.
Drivers must stop at red lights.
Children must ride in car seats.
it.h: Which one would a teacher make?

it.q: Read: "Speed limits are lower near schools. As a result, drivers have more time to stop if a child steps into the street." Which is the effect?
ch: Drivers have more time to stop.
Speed limits are lower near schools.
it.h: "As a result" comes right before the effect.

it.q: Who usually makes the laws for a city?
it.h: Think about the group of leaders who meet to vote for a city.

it.q: Name one rule or law and explain how it helps people.
it.ans: Wearing a helmet when riding a bike is a law for kids in California. It helps protect your head if you fall.
it.h: Tell the rule, then tell the reason.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Government and Citizenship (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Capital letters and commas in letters, dates and places

it.q: Which word should always begin with a capital letter?
it.h: Names of specific places are proper nouns.

it.q: Where does the comma go in a date?
ch: between the day and the year
between the month and the day
it.h: Look at "July 4, 1776."

it.q: Which city and state are written correctly?
it.h: Use capitals and put a comma between the city and the state.

it.q: Which street address is written correctly?
it.h: Capitalize each word of the street name.

it.q: Which holiday name is capitalized correctly?
it.h: Capitalize each important word in a holiday's name.

it.q: Write the date and city line you would put at the top of a letter written in your town today. Use correct capitals and commas.
it.ans: Sacramento, California, May 12, 2025 (any real city with comma before state and a correct date)
it.h: Put commas between city and state and between day and year.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Traits and Adaptations (informative writing)
lessons.n: Asking questions and using illustrations

it.q: When you answer a question about a story, what should you use?
it.h: Good answers point back to the words in the story.

it.q: Read: "Kofi's sneakers squeaked on the wet gym floor as he raced to catch the ball." Which question can be answered from this sentence?
it.h: Which answer is actually in the sentence?

it.q: An illustration shows a girl hugging a puppy while tears roll down her cheeks, and she is smiling. What does the illustration add to the story?
ch: It shows she is so happy that she is crying.
It shows she has been hurt and is in pain.
It shows the puppy is lost and she is worried.
It shows it is raining hard outside.
it.h: Look at both the tears and the smile.

it.q: Read: "Ellie peered over the edge of the diving board, her toes curled tight." What can you infer about how Ellie feels?
it.h: Why would someone curl their toes on a diving board?

it.q: Which question asks about a character's motivation?
ch: Why did the character decide to enter the contest?
What color is the character's house on the hill?
How many pages are in the whole book?
Who drew the pictures for this story?
it.h: Motivation is the reason a character does something.

it.q: Read: "Tomas grabbed his umbrella, then looked at the sky and put it back." Write a question about this sentence and answer it with a detail.
it.ans: Why did Tomas put his umbrella back? He looked at the sky and probably saw that it was not going to rain.
it.h: Start your question with Why, What or How.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Traits and Adaptations (informative writing)
lessons.n: Adaptations and science words

it.q: What is an environment?
ch: the surroundings where a living thing lives
a type of wild animal that lives alone
a kind of food that animals eat
a report about the weather today
it.h: Think about everything around an animal, like water, plants and weather.

it.q: Read: "Camouflage is coloring that helps an animal blend in with its surroundings." Which animal is using camouflage?
ch: a brown moth resting on brown tree bark
a red bird sitting on white snow
a yellow fish in blue water
a black cat on a white rug
it.h: Which animal would be hardest to see?

it.q: Read: "Some animals hibernate, or go into a deep sleep, during the winter." What does "hibernate" mean?
ch: go into a deep sleep in winter
it.h: The words after "or" explain the meaning.

it.q: Read: "Desert foxes have large ears that release body heat." Which question does this sentence answer?
ch: How do desert foxes stay cool?
How fast do desert foxes run?
it.h: What does releasing body heat help with?

it.q: Read: "Porcupines are covered with sharp quills. When attacked, a porcupine raises its quills." Why does a porcupine raise its quills?
ch: to stay warm on cold nights
to help it find its food
it.h: Look at the words "When attacked."

it.q: Read: "Many birds migrate, or travel long distances, to warmer places in winter." Explain how migrating helps birds survive.
it.ans: Migrating helps birds survive because they travel to warmer places where it is not too cold and they can still find food during the winter.
it.h: Think about what winter is like and what birds need.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Traits and Adaptations (informative writing)
lessons.n: Pronouns and possessive nouns

it.q: Which pronoun completes the sentence? "The otter cracked a shell on ___ chest."
it.h: One otter. Which word shows that something belongs to "it"?

it.q: Which word completes the sentence about one otter? "The ___ fur is thick."
it.h: To show that something belongs to one animal, add an apostrophe and s.

it.q: Which pronoun completes the sentence? "Sea otters wrap ___ in kelp."
it.h: The subject "sea otters" is plural.

it.q: Which phrase shows toys that belong to more than one dog?
it.h: For a plural noun that ends in s, add only an apostrophe.

it.q: Which pronoun could replace "Aiyana and her grandmother" in "Aiyana and her grandmother looked at photos"?
it.h: The pronoun must stand for two people and be the subject.

it.q: Write one sentence with a singular possessive noun and one with a plural possessive noun.
it.ans: The bird's nest was in the oak tree. The girls' bikes were parked by the fence.
it.h: Singular: 's. Plural ending in s: s'.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Traits and Adaptations (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text from research notes on an animal adaptation

it.q: What are research notes?
ch: short words or phrases about important facts from a source
a whole story copied word for word
it.h: Notes help you remember facts in your own words.

it.q: Which note is written in the student's own words?
ch: camels - store fat in hump - use it for energy
"The camel's hump stores fat that the animal can use for energy when food is scarce."
it.h: Notes are short and do not copy whole sentences.

it.q: A student is researching how polar bears stay warm. Which fact belongs in the notes?
ch: thick fat layer under the skin
it.h: Which fact answers the research question?

it.q: Which source would give the most accurate facts about owls?
ch: a science book about birds from the library
a cartoon about a talking owl
it.h: Which one is written to give true information?

it.q: Why should a writer list the sources used?
ch: so readers know where the facts came from
so no one reads the report
so the writer can copy it
it.h: Think about checking facts.

it.q: Turn this note into a complete sentence: "cactus - thick stem - stores water."
it.ans: A cactus has a thick stem that stores water so it can survive in the dry desert.
it.h: Add a subject and verb, and explain why it matters.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Traits and Adaptations (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: camouflage, hiding in plain sight

it.q: What is camouflage?
ch: coloring or shape that helps a living thing blend in with its surroundings
a loud call to warn others
it.h: Think about an animal you might not see until it moves.

it.q: Read: "A green katydid sits on a leaf. Its wings look like leaves, with lines like leaf veins." How does this help the katydid?
ch: Predators may not notice it among the leaves.
It helps the katydid fly faster.
it.h: What would a bird see when it looks at the leaf?

it.q: Read: "Some animals use mimicry. They look like a dangerous animal even though they are harmless." What does "mimicry" mean?
it.h: The next sentence explains the word.
