it.q: Text A tells how a snowshoe hare turns white in winter. Text B tells how a flounder's colors match the sea floor. What main idea do the texts share?
ch: Animals' colors can help them hide.
it.h: What is the same about the hare and the flounder?

it.q: Which detail best supports the main idea "Camouflage helps predators, too"?
ch: A tiger's stripes help it hide in tall grass while it sneaks up on prey.
A deer runs away from danger.
it.h: A predator hunts other animals.

it.q: Explain why an animal with brown fur would be hard to see in a forest in autumn.
it.ans: In autumn the forest floor is covered with brown leaves and dirt, so brown fur blends in and makes the animal hard to spot.
it.h: Think about the colors around the animal.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Myths that explain the natural world

it.q: What is a myth?
ch: a traditional story that often explains something in nature
a true science report about the stars
a set of directions for playing a game
a list of facts about the planets
it.h: Myths were told long ago to answer "why" questions.

it.q: Read: "Long ago, Moon was jealous of Sun's bright light, so each month she hid behind the clouds until only a thin sliver showed." What might this myth try to explain?
ch: why the Moon seems to change shape
why the Sun is so hot in the summer
why clouds look white during the day
why people need to sleep at night
it.h: What happens to the Moon in the story each month?

it.q: Read: "Each of the three brothers tried to lift the heavy stone. Only the youngest, who asked the river for help, succeeded." What lesson might this teach?
ch: Asking for help can be wise.
The oldest is always the strongest.
it.h: What did the youngest brother do differently?

it.q: Which event would best support the message "Working together is stronger than working alone"?
ch: Many ants together carry a leaf that one ant could not lift.
An ant walks home alone after a long day.
An ant finds a crumb under the picnic table.
An ant sleeps through the long, cold winter.
it.h: Look for many characters helping each other.

it.q: When you retell a myth, which events should you include?
ch: the key events that lead to the explanation at the end
every small detail from every part of the story
only the title and the name of the author
only the first sentence of the myth
it.h: Retell the parts that explain how something came to be.

it.q: Make up an idea for a myth that explains something about the sky. Write one sentence that tells what happens and what it explains.
it.ans: A brave turtle climbs a rainbow every night to hang the Moon in the sky, which explains why the Moon rises each evening.
it.h: Pick something real, like the Moon, a rainbow or the stars, and invent a reason for it.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Science words and text features about space

it.q: Which text feature would help you find the page about Mars in a book about planets?
it.h: Which feature lists topics with page numbers?

it.q: Read: "A telescope is a tool that makes faraway objects look closer." What is a telescope?
ch: a tool that makes faraway objects look closer
it.h: The sentence gives the definition.

it.q: Read: "Earth spins like a top. It takes about 24 hours to spin around once. This is why we have day and night." What causes day and night?
ch: Earth spinning around about every 24 hours
the Moon moving all the way around Earth
the Sun turning off every single night
clouds moving in to block the Sun
it.h: Look for the words "This is why."

it.q: You want to learn about Saturn's rings on the internet. Which key words would work best?
ch: planets that are red and dusty
how to bake a cake shaped like a planet
it.h: Choose words that name your exact topic.

it.q: Read: "Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun. Neptune is the planet farthest from the Sun." How are these sentences connected?
ch: They tell a cause and effect.
it.h: Closest and farthest are opposites.

it.q: A sidebar in a book about space says, "Did you know? Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth." Why might an author include a sidebar like this?
it.ans: An author includes a sidebar to give an extra, interesting fact that connects to the topic without interrupting the main text.
it.h: Think about what a sidebar adds to the page.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Multisyllable words and spelling with suffixes

it.q: How many syllables are in the word "astronaut"?
it.h: Clap as you say it slowly: as-tro-naut.

it.q: Which shows "planet" divided into syllables correctly?
it.h: Each syllable has one vowel sound.

it.q: Which word shows "shine" with -ing added correctly?
it.h: When a word ends in a silent e, drop the e before adding -ing.

it.q: Which shows "orbit" with -ed added correctly?
it.h: The last syllable of "orbit" is not stressed, so you do not double the t.

it.q: Which word has the same vowel spelling pattern as "moon"?
it.h: Look for the same two letters making the same sound.

it.q: Divide "telescope" into syllables. Tell how many syllables it has.
it.ans: tel-e-scope. It has three syllables.
it.h: Clap the word and count the vowel sounds.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative piece about the moon: introduction, facts and conclusion

it.q: What should the introduction of an informative piece do?
ch: name the topic and get readers interested
it.h: The introduction comes first.

it.q: Which fact about the moon is correct?
ch: The moon does not make its own light.
The moon is bigger than Earth.
The moon is closer than the clouds.
it.h: Where does moonlight really come from?

it.q: Which linking words help a writer give more information?
it.h: Which words add one more idea?

it.q: Which sentence uses a comparison to help readers understand a fact?
ch: The moon is about one-fourth as wide as Earth, so about four moons could fit across Earth.
The moon is nice to look at.
it.h: A comparison helps readers picture size.

it.q: Which title would best fit an informative piece about the moon?
it.h: The title should match the topic.

it.q: Write an introduction of two sentences for an informative piece about stars.
it.ans: When you look at the night sky, you can see thousands of tiny lights. Those lights are stars, giant balls of hot, glowing gas very far away.
it.h: Start with something that makes readers curious, then name the topic.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: the phases of the moon

it.q: What lights up the moon?
it.h: The moon reflects light like a mirror.

it.q: A diagram shows the moon's shapes in a circle, with arrows going from one to the next. What does the diagram help explain?
ch: how the moon's shape seems to change in order
it.h: Arrows in a circle show a repeating order.

it.q: Read: "When the lit part of the moon is growing, the moon is waxing. When it is shrinking, the moon is waning." What does "waning" mean?
it.h: Look at the sentence that uses "waning."

it.q: What do we call the phase when we see the whole bright side of the moon?
it.h: Think about a round, bright moon.

it.q: Which text feature would help a reader find the word "gibbous" defined?
it.h: Which feature lists word meanings?

it.q: Explain why the moon seems to change shape even though it is always round.
it.ans: The sun always lights half the moon. As the moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of the lit half, so its shape seems to change.
it.h: Think about which part of the moon faces us.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth, Moon and Stars (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word parts in space words: tele-, astro- and -scope

it.q: The word part "tele-" means "far." What does a telescope help you do?
ch: see things that are far away
it.h: Put "far" together with "see."

it.q: The word part "astro-" means "star." What does an astronaut do?
it.h: Astronauts travel toward the stars.

it.q: The word part "-scope" means "a tool for looking." Which word names a tool for looking at very tiny things?
it.h: "Micro-" means "small."

it.q: If "graph" means "write," what is an autograph?
it.h: "Auto-" means "self."

it.q: Which word has the same word part as "telescope"?
it.h: Look for "tele-."

it.q: Explain how knowing "tele-" means "far" helps you understand "telephone."
it.ans: "Phone" means sound, so a telephone is something that lets you hear sound from far away.
it.h: Put the meanings of both parts together.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Literal and nonliteral language in stories

it.q: What is literal language?
ch: words that mean exactly what they say
words that compare using like or as
it.h: Literal means "just as it is."

it.q: What does "It's raining cats and dogs" mean?
ch: Pets are falling from the sky.
Animals are playing in the rain.
it.h: This is an idiom. It does not mean what the words say.

it.q: Read: "The classroom was a zoo after the fire drill." What does this sentence mean?
ch: The classroom was noisy and wild.
There were animals in the classroom.
The class went on a zoo field trip.
it.h: Think about what a zoo is like, then compare it to a classroom.

it.q: Which sentence uses a simile?
ch: The puppy was as quiet as a mouse.
The puppy is small and brown.
it.h: A simile compares two things using "like" or "as."

it.q: Read: "Dad said, 'Hold your horses! We're not ready to leave.'" What does Dad mean?
it.h: Look at the second sentence for a clue.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses the idiom "break the ice," and explain what it means.
it.ans: At the party, Leo told a funny joke to break the ice. "Break the ice" means to do something that helps people feel comfortable and start talking.
it.h: Think about the first time you meet new people.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Forces and connections in science text

it.q: Read: "The magnet pulled the paper clip toward it." Is the magnet's force a push or a pull?
it.h: Look at the verb in the sentence.

it.q: Read: "Because the hill was steep, the wagon rolled faster and faster." What is the cause?
it.h: The cause comes right after "because."

it.q: Read: "First, Ana pushed the swing gently. Then she pushed harder, and the swing went higher." What happened when Ana pushed harder?
it.h: Look at the second sentence.

it.q: Which example shows friction slowing something down?
ch: A bike's brakes rub the wheel, and the bike stops.
A balloon floats up high into the sky.
A magnet sticks to the front of the refrigerator.
A ball falls off the edge of a table.
it.h: Friction happens when two surfaces rub together.

it.q: Read: "Magnets can push or pull some metal objects without touching them." What does this tell you about magnets?
ch: Their force can act without touching.
They only work when they touch something.
it.h: Look at the last three words of the sentence.

it.q: Read: "Sneakers have bumpy rubber soles, so runners do not slip on the track." Explain how this connects to friction.
it.ans: The bumpy rubber soles rub against the track and make more friction. The friction helps the sneakers grip the ground so runners do not slip.
it.h: Do bumpy surfaces make more or less friction?

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Idioms and shades of meaning

it.q: What does "a piece of cake" mean in "The spelling test was a piece of cake"?
it.h: Would a test really be made of cake?

it.q: Which word shows the slowest movement?
it.h: Picture each way of moving.

it.q: Which word describes the strongest feeling of being tired?
it.h: Which one means "completely worn out"?

it.q: What does "on cloud nine" mean in "Ella was on cloud nine after the concert"?
it.h: Think about how Ella felt after a great concert.

it.q: Which word shows that a person is the most certain about something?
it.h: Which word means there is no doubt at all?

it.q: Put these words in order from least hot to most hot: boiling, warm, hot. Then use the strongest word in a sentence.
it.ans: warm, hot, boiling. The water in the pot was boiling, so Mom added the pasta.
it.h: Think about bath water, a sunny sidewalk and a pot on the stove.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative with time-order words and a problem to solve

it.q: Which word tells that an event happened at the same time as another?
it.h: Which word means "while this was happening"?

it.q: Which sentence best introduces a problem in a story about a wagon race?
ch: The morning of the race, Tomas noticed his wagon's front wheel wobbling loose.
it.h: A problem is something that goes wrong.

it.q: Which sentence uses a strong verb to show motion?
ch: The wagon rocketed down the hill.
The wagon went down the hill.
The wagon was on the hill.
it.h: Which verb helps you picture speed?

it.q: Which time-order word fits best? "___ the whistle blew, the racers took off."
it.h: Which phrase means "right when"?

it.q: Which is the best way to solve the problem "The kite would not fly because there was no wind"?
ch: Jada waited until a breeze picked up in the afternoon, and the kite soared.
Jada went home and the story ended.
it.h: The solution should connect to the problem.

it.q: Write two sentences about a ball rolling down a hill. Use one time-order word and one strong verb.
it.ans: At first, the ball inched slowly over the top of the hill. Then it zoomed faster and faster until it bounced off a fence.
it.h: Use a word like first, then or suddenly, and a verb that shows motion.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how magnets push and pull

it.q: What is a force?
it.h: Think about moving a door open or closed.

it.q: Read: "When two north poles of magnets face each other, they push apart." What is this push called?
it.h: Repel means to push away.

it.q: Which object would a magnet most likely attract?
it.h: Magnets pull on objects that contain iron, like steel.

it.q: Read: "A magnet can pull a paper clip through a sheet of paper." What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force can act through some materials without touching.
it.h: The magnet and paper clip are not touching.

it.q: Read: "Because the north pole of one magnet faces the south pole of another, they snap together." Which is the effect?
ch: A north pole faces a south pole.
it.h: The effect is what happens.

it.q: Explain one way people use magnets in everyday life.
it.ans: People use magnets to hold notes on a refrigerator door, because the magnet pulls on the steel in the door.
it.h: Think about your kitchen or a cabinet that clicks shut.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Forces and Motion (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: plot, problem and solution in a race-day story

it.q: What is the plot of a story?
ch: the events that happen from beginning to end
it.h: Plot means what happens.

it.q: Which event is usually near the end of a story?
it.h: Stories end when the trouble is fixed.

it.q: Read: "Ana's cart kept veering left. She checked the wheels and found one was bent." What is the problem?
ch: A bent wheel made the cart go left.
Ana did not want to race.
it.h: What made the cart go the wrong way?

it.q: Read: "Dev added a heavy bag of sand to the back of his cart, and it zoomed faster down the ramp." How did Dev's action affect the events?
ch: It helped his cart go faster.
It made him lose the race.
it.h: What happened after he added the sand?

it.q: Which detail shows a character is a good sport?
ch: She shook the winner's hand and said, "Great race!"
it.h: How does a good sport act after losing?

it.q: Read: "Kai's kite crashed. He added a longer tail, and the next time it flew high." Name the problem and the solution.
it.ans: Problem: Kai's kite crashed. Solution: he added a longer tail, and it flew high.
it.h: First tell what went wrong, then how it was fixed.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Poems, Poets and Family Stories (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading poems: lines, rhythm and images

it.q: What is a line in a poem?
ch: one row of words in the poem
it.h: Poems are written in rows instead of paragraphs.

it.q: Read: "The wind is a wolf that howls at the door." What is the wind compared to?
it.h: Look at what the wind "is" in the line.

it.q: Read: "Buzz, hum, the bees have come." Which words imitate sounds?
it.h: Which words sound like what they name?

it.q: How is a poem usually different from a story?
ch: It is written in lines and often uses rhythm and rhyme.
It always has chapters with titles.
It never describes the poet's feelings.
It has a cast of characters and scenes.
it.h: Think about how a poem looks and sounds.

it.q: Read: "The moon rolled over the rooftops, a silver coin on the sky's blue sleeve." What is the moon compared to?
it.h: Find the words right after the comma.

it.q: Write two lines of a poem about rain that rhyme.
it.ans: Rain taps softly on my door, then dances quickly on the floor.
it.h: Choose rhyming words first, like door and floor or play and gray.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Poems, Poets and Family Stories (narrative writing)
lessons.n: A poet's life and an author's point of view

it.q: What is an author's point of view?
ch: what the author thinks or feels about a topic
the place where the author lives
the number of pages in a book
the picture on the book's cover
it.h: Look for words like I think, should or best.

it.q: Read: "Poetry is the best way to share feelings, and every student should write poems." What is the author's point of view?
ch: Poetry is a great way to share feelings, and students should write it.
Poetry is boring and very hard to understand.
Only adults should be allowed to write poems.
Feelings should always be kept secret.
it.h: What does the author say students should do?

it.q: Read: "In 1950, the author moved to Chicago. Two years later, she published her first book." In what year did she publish her first book?
it.h: Add two years to 1950.

it.q: Read: "Maya Angelou worked many jobs before becoming a famous writer. She was a dancer, a cook and even one of the first Black women to work as a streetcar conductor in San Francisco." What is the main idea?
ch: Maya Angelou worked many jobs before becoming a writer.
Maya Angelou worked as a cook in a restaurant.
San Francisco has streetcars that carry people.
Dancing is hard work for anyone who tries it.
it.h: Which sentence do the other details support?

it.q: An author writes, "Poems should always rhyme." Which reason could a reader use to disagree?
ch: Many poems use rhythm and images without rhyming.
Rhyming poems are easy to remember.
Most songs that people sing rhyme.
it.h: Look for a reason that goes against the author's idea.

it.q: Read: "Every family has stories worth saving. Ask your grandparents about their childhood before those memories are lost." Tell the author's point of view and whether you agree. Give a reason.
it.ans: The author thinks family stories are important to save before they are forgotten. I agree, because my grandmother's stories about growing up teach me things I could never learn from a book.
it.h: First tell what the author believes. Then tell what you believe and why.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Poems, Poets and Family Stories (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Dialogue, addresses and titles

it.q: Which sentence uses quotation marks correctly?
ch: Let's write a poem," said Ava.
it.h: Quotation marks go around the exact words a person says. A comma comes before the closing quotation mark.

it.q: Which address is written correctly?
it.h: Put a comma after the street and after the city. Capitalize the names.

it.q: Which book title is capitalized correctly?
ch: The Night Before the Big Game
The night before the big game
the Night Before The Big Game
The Night before the Big game
it.h: Capitalize the first word and the important words. Small words like "the" in the middle can stay lowercase.

it.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
it.h: When the speaker comes first, put a comma before the quotation. The question mark goes inside.

it.q: Which shows a city and state written correctly?
it.h: Both names need capitals, with a comma between them.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence with correct punctuation: I love Saturdays said Lila
it.ans: "I love Saturdays," said Lila.
it.h: Which words did Lila say? Put those inside quotation marks.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Poems, Poets and Family Stories (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a family story: beginning, middle and ending with dialogue

it.q: What is a family story?
ch: a true story about something that happened in a family
it.h: Families pass these stories down.

it.q: Which beginning best starts a family story?
ch: My grandfather still laughs about the day he drove our family's goat to the market in his tiny car.
it.h: Which one makes you want to keep reading?

it.q: Which sentence punctuates dialogue with a question correctly?
ch: "Do you remember the flood?" asked Grandma.
"Do you remember the flood"? asked Grandma.
"Do you remember the flood," asked Grandma?
Do you remember the flood? "asked Grandma."
it.h: The question mark goes inside the quotation marks.

it.q: Which detail best helps a reader picture the setting of a family story?
ch: The kitchen smelled of cardamom, and steam fogged the window over the sink.
It happened a long time ago.
it.h: Use your senses.

it.q: Which middle event fits a story about a family's first day in a new country?
ch: At the airport, Papa showed our papers while I held my baby sister's hand.
it.h: The middle tells what happened.

it.q: Write the last sentence of a family story about a lost-and-found dog. Show how the family feels.
it.ans: When Pepper came bounding up the driveway, we all ran outside, laughing and crying at the same time.
it.h: Show feelings with actions.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Poems, Poets and Family Stories (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: family stories and their central message

it.q: What is the central message of a story?
ch: the big idea or lesson the author wants readers to understand
the name of the main character
it.h: Ask yourself, "What did the character learn?"

it.q: Read: "Grandma kept every button from every coat she had ever owned. 'Each one holds a memory,' she said." What does this show about Grandma?
it.h: Why would someone keep old buttons?

it.q: In a story, a boy is embarrassed by his father's accent. Later, he hears his father give a kind speech at a meeting and feels proud. What is a likely central message?
ch: Learn to value people for who they are.
it.h: How do the boy's feelings change, and why?

it.q: Which detail would a reader use to explain a character's motivation?
ch: the reason the character does something
the color of the character's shirt
it.h: Motivation means "why."

it.q: An illustration shows a girl and her grandfather smiling as they cook together. What mood does it add to a story?
it.h: Look at the faces in the picture.

it.q: Read: "Ever since Mom taught me to make dumplings, I have taught my little brother, too." What message might this sentence suggest?
it.ans: It suggests that family traditions and skills are passed down from one person to the next.
it.h: Think about who teaches whom.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: describing a character with text evidence

it.q: Which word best describes Lucia in "The Bench on Alder Street"?
it.h: Think about what Lucia does after Mateo says she cannot change the city's decision.

p.x: Every morning, Mr. Okafor sat on the green bench outside the Alder Street library and fed bread crumbs to the sparrows. Every morning, Lucia Herrera waved to him on her way to school. So on the first Monday in October, when Lucia saw a sign taped to the empty bench, she stopped. // "BENCH TO BE REMOVED OCTOBER 20," the sign said. "Damaged. City Parks Department." // Lucia looked closer. One of the wooden slats was cracked, and a bolt had rusted through. Mr. Okafor was nowhere in sight. // At dinner she told her older brother, Mateo. "Where will Mr. Okafor sit? He walks with a cane, and the next bench is three blocks away." // Mateo shrugged. "It's the city's bench. You can't change what the city decides." // Lucia was not so sure. That night she wrote a letter to the Parks Department. She explained that the bench was the only place to rest between the bus stop and the senior apartments. She counted the people she saw using it on her walk home: eleven in one afternoon. She asked whether the bench could be repaired instead of removed. Then she made copies of the letter and asked her neighbors to sign them. // By Friday she had forty-two signatures. Her hand ached, and her shoes were dusty from climbing apartment stairs. Mr. Okafor signed twice by accident and laughed at himself. // Two weeks later, a city truck parked on Alder Street. Lucia held her breath. Two workers unloaded new boards, a can of green paint and a toolbox. By the afternoon, the bench looked better than ever. // The next morning, a small metal plate shone on the back of the bench. It read, "Repaired at the request of the neighbors of Alder Street." Mr. Okafor tapped it with his cane and grinned at Lucia. "The neighbors," he said, "had a very good letter writer."

it.q: Why does Lucia worry when she reads the sign on the bench?
ch: Mr. Okafor walks with a cane and needs a place to rest
She wants the bench for herself
She thinks the library will close
She is afraid of the sparrows
it.h: Reread what Lucia tells Mateo at dinner.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: main idea, reasons and evidence

it.q: What is the main idea of "Speaking Up at City Hall"?
ch: Young people can take part in local government by speaking up and sharing ideas.
The Brown Act was written by a city council.
Public comment always lasts three minutes.
it.h: Which choice covers the whole article, not just one paragraph?

p.x: Many people think only adults can make a difference in their city. In fact, young people can play an important part in local government. // Most California cities are run by a city council, a group of people elected by the voters. The council decides things like where to build parks, how to fix roads and when the library will be open. Council meetings are public, which means anyone may attend. A California law called the Brown Act requires these meetings to be open and gives members of the public a chance to speak. // This time to speak is called public comment. A speaker usually fills out a card, waits for their name to be called and then talks for a short time, often two or three minutes. Because the time is short, good speakers plan ahead. They state their request clearly, give one or two strong reasons and support each reason with facts. // Facts matter because council members must make choices for the whole city. Saying "Our park is dangerous" may not be enough. Saying "Three swings at Oak Park have been broken for six months" gives the council a clear picture of the problem. // Young people can also share ideas in other ways. They can write letters or emails to council members, join a youth commission if their city has one, or collect signatures from neighbors who agree with them. // Local government works best when people take part. A student who shows up, speaks clearly and brings evidence is practicing one of the most important jobs in a democracy: being an active citizen.

it.q: According to the article, what kinds of things does a city council decide?
ch: where to build parks and how to fix roads
which laws the state will pass
it.h: Look in the second paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: prefixes, complete sentences and capital letters

it.q: The prefix "re-" means "again." What does "rebuild" mean?
it.h: Put the meaning of the prefix together with the base word.

it.q: Which group of words is a complete sentence?
ch: After the long meeting at city hall.
it.h: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought.

it.q: Which is the best way to fix this run-on? "Lucia wrote a letter her neighbors signed it."
ch: Lucia wrote a letter, and her neighbors signed it.
Lucia wrote a letter her, neighbors signed it.
Lucia wrote, a letter her neighbors signed it.
Lucia wrote a letter her neighbors, signed it.
it.h: A run-on joins two complete thoughts with nothing between them. Where does the first thought end?

it.q: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
ch: Last June, Mayor Chen visited Lincoln Park in Fresno.
Last june, mayor Chen visited Lincoln park in Fresno.
last June, Mayor chen visited lincoln Park in fresno.
Last June, mayor chen visited Lincoln Park in fresno.
it.h: Months, titles before names, and names of places are capitalized.

it.q: Read: "The old bench was unsafe, so the city closed it." What does "unsafe" mean?
it.h: The prefix "un-" changes the meaning of the base word.

it.q: Rewrite this fragment as a complete sentence: "Collected forty-two signatures."
it.ans: Lucia collected forty-two signatures.
it.h: Who collected them? Add a subject.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion: reasons supported by facts and details

it.q: In an opinion essay, what is a reason?
ch: an idea that explains why the writer holds the opinion
a fact that has nothing to do with the topic
the last word of the essay
it.h: A reason answers the question "Why?"

it.q: Which opinion statement is clearest?
ch: Our school should start a student recycling team.
Recycling is a thing people do.
Some people recycle and some do not.
I am going to write about recycling.
it.h: A clear opinion tells exactly what the writer thinks should happen.

it.q: Opinion: "Kids should volunteer in their community." Which detail best supports the reason "Volunteering teaches responsibility"?
ch: When students care for shelter animals, they must show up on time and follow every step of the feeding schedule.
it.h: Which detail shows responsibility in action?

it.q: Which linking phrase best connects an opinion to a specific example?
it.h: Which phrase introduces an example?

it.q: Which sentence is a fragment that needs to be fixed in an opinion essay?
ch: Students can help because they care.
Every student can help in some way.
it.h: A fragment cannot stand alone as a complete thought.

it.q: Write one reason and one supporting fact for this opinion: "Our town should build a skate park."
it.ans: Reason: kids need safe places to be active. Fact: right now, many kids skate in parking lots, where cars drive through.
it.h: Give a reason, then a fact or example that backs it up.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Citizens Who Make a Difference (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: a biography of Dolores Huerta

it.q: What is a biography?
ch: a true story of a person's life written by someone else
a made-up story about a hero
a story a person writes about their own life
a poem about a famous person
it.h: The prefix "bio-" means life.

it.q: Biographies are often organized in chronological order. What does chronological mean?
ch: in the order that events happened
it.h: "Chrono-" relates to time.

it.q: Read: "After seeing children come to school hungry, the teacher decided she could do more to help their families." What caused the teacher's decision?
ch: seeing children come to school hungry
it.h: Look at what happened first.

it.q: Which detail would best support the central idea that a person worked hard for others?
ch: She spent decades organizing workers and speaking up for fair treatment.
She was born in the spring.
it.h: Which detail shows work for other people?

it.q: An author writes, "Her words became a rallying cry for millions." What does "rallying cry" mean?
ch: words that inspire people to work together
it.h: Think about what a team does at a rally.

it.q: Explain why an author might start a biography with an important moment from the middle of a person's life instead of the day the person was born.
it.ans: To grab readers' interest right away and show why the person matters before going back to tell the earlier events.
it.h: Think about what makes readers want to keep going.

lessons.u: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: setting and theme

it.q: How does Tomas feel about the desert at the beginning of "The Desert Wakes Up"?
it.h: Reread what Tomas says in the car.

p.x: Tomas pressed his forehead against the car window. Outside, the desert stretched flat and brown in every direction, dotted with gray bushes and a few spiny plants that looked like bundles of dead sticks. // "There's nothing here, Abuela," he said. // His grandmother smiled and kept driving. "Wait," she said. // Abuela had lived in Borrego Springs for forty years. She said the desert was like a person who doesn't talk much: you have to pay attention to hear what it is saying. Tomas thought the desert wasn't saying anything at all. He had only agreed to visit because his cousins had gone to the beach without him. // That night it rained. Tomas woke to the sound of drops drumming on the tin roof of the porch and the sharp, clean smell of wet creosote bushes drifting through the window. // A few days later, Abuela shook him awake before sunrise. "Come," she whispered. // They walked out into the cool gray light. Tomas stopped. The dead sticks were not dead after all. The tall, spiny stems of the ocotillo had sprouted tiny green leaves along every branch, and their tips glowed with flame-red flowers. At his feet, patches of yellow and purple flowers had opened where there had been only sand. A hummingbird zipped past his ear toward the red blossoms. // "Where did all this come from?" Tomas asked. // "It was here the whole time," Abuela said. "The seeds wait in the ground, sometimes for years, until there is enough rain. The desert is patient." // Tomas knelt and touched a tiny yellow petal. He thought about his cousins at the beach, splashing in the waves. For the first time all week, he did not wish he were with them. // "Abuela," he said, "can we come out again tomorrow?"

it.q: What event causes the desert to change in the story?
it.h: What happens the night before the flowers appear?

Abuela had lived in Borrego Springs for forty years.

lessons.u: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: main idea and how events are connected

it.q: What is the main idea of "Four Regions, One State"?
ch: California has four regions with different land and climate that are connected to one another.
The Central Valley is the best region in California.
Mount Whitney is the tallest mountain in the lower 48 states.
it.h: Read the first and last paragraphs. What idea do they share?

p.x: California is a big state with many kinds of land. Geographers often divide it into four regions: the coast, the mountains, the Central Valley and the desert. Each region has its own landforms and climate, and each has shaped the way people live there. // The coast region stretches more than 800 miles along the Pacific Ocean. Because the ocean changes temperature slowly, coastal towns tend to have mild weather, cool in summer and rarely freezing in winter. Ports such as Los Angeles, Long Beach and Oakland ship goods around the world. // The mountain region includes the Sierra Nevada, a long range along the state's eastern side. Mount Whitney, the tallest peak in the lower 48 states, rises more than 14,000 feet in the Sierra Nevada. In winter, heavy snow piles up in these mountains. When it melts in spring and summer, it flows into rivers and reservoirs that supply water to cities and farms far away. // The Central Valley lies between the coastal mountains and the Sierra Nevada. It is about 450 miles long and very flat, with deep, rich soil. Water from the mountains and a long, sunny growing season make it one of the most productive farming areas in the world. Farmers there grow almonds, grapes, tomatoes, rice and hundreds of other crops. // The desert region covers much of southeastern California. Deserts get very little rain, and summer days can be extremely hot. Death Valley holds the lowest point in North America, about 282 feet below sea level. Even so, plants and animals have adapted to survive there, and people visit the desert parks to hike and see the stars. // From foggy beaches to snowy peaks, California's regions are connected. Snow in the mountains waters the valley, and the valley's crops feed people on the coast and far beyond.

it.q: According to the article, why do coastal towns have mild weather?
ch: The soil is deep and rich.
it.h: Find the sentence that begins with "Because."

Snow keeps the valley cool in summer.

it.h: Follow what happens to the snow in spring and summer.

Ports ship goods around the world.

it.ans: The Central Valley depends on the mountain region. Snow piles up in the Sierra Nevada in winter, and when it melts it flows into rivers and reservoirs that water the valley's farms. Without that water, farmers could not grow so many crops.

lessons.u: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: suffixes, relative pronouns and relative adverbs

it.q: The suffix "-less" means "without." What does "fearless" mean?
it.h: Put "without" together with the base word.

it.q: Which word means "full of color"?
it.h: Which suffix means "full of"?

it.q: Which relative pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The ranger ___ led our hike knew every plant."
it.h: Use "who" for people and "which" for things.

it.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Borrego Springs is the town ___ my grandmother lives."
it.h: The missing word tells about a place.

it.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Spring is the season ___ the desert blooms."
it.h: The missing word tells about a time.

it.q: Combine these two sentences using "which": "The tomol was a plank canoe. The tomol crossed the channel."
it.ans: The tomol, which crossed the channel, was a plank canoe. (Also correct: The tomol was a plank canoe, which crossed the channel.)
it.h: Use "which" to add the second idea about the tomol.

lessons.u: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text: organizing facts about a region with headings

it.q: What should an informative essay's introduction include?
ch: a hook and the main topic
it.h: The introduction tells readers what the essay is about and makes them want to read.

it.q: A report on California's regions has the headings "Coast," "Mountains," "Central Valley" and "Desert." Which fact belongs under "Desert"?
ch: Some areas receive only a few inches of rain each year.
Fog often rolls in from the ocean.
Snow piles up on high peaks.
Farms grow many crops on flat land.
it.h: Which fact describes a very dry place?

it.q: Which linking phrase best signals a comparison between two regions?
it.h: Which word shows two things are alike?

it.q: Which sentence uses a domain-specific word and defines it?
ch: The Central Valley's fertile soil, which is rich in nutrients, helps crops grow.
it.h: Look for a science or geography word followed by its meaning.

it.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
it.h: Check each letter carefully.

it.q: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about California's coastal region.
it.ans: California's coastal region stretches along the Pacific Ocean, where cool fog and ocean breezes shape the land and the way people live.
it.h: Name the region and the main idea of the paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 2: California's Regions and First Peoples (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: acorns and California Indian food traditions

it.q: What is a staple food?
ch: a main food that people eat often
a snack eaten once a year
food that is only for parties
it.h: Think about a food a community depends on.

it.q: Read: "Acorns contain tannins, which make them taste bitter. People rinsed the ground acorn meal with water to wash the tannins away." Why did people rinse the acorn meal?
it.h: What did the tannins do?

it.q: Read: "Families gathered acorns in the fall and stored them in raised granaries." What is a granary most likely?
ch: a kind of basket for fishing
it.h: Families stored the acorns in it.

it.q: Which text structure describes the steps for preparing a food in order?
it.h: The steps happen one after another.

it.q: Which detail best supports the idea that oak trees were important to many California Indian peoples?
ch: Acorns were a main food that could be stored for many months.
Some oak trees grow near rivers.
it.h: Why would people value a tree?

it.q: Explain why being able to store a food for a long time would be helpful to a community.
it.ans: Stored food could feed people in winter or in years when other foods were hard to find.
it.h: Think about seasons when plants do not grow.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)

it.q: What are Isabel and Rafi trying to do in "The Pizza Box Oven"?
ch: make s'mores using the sun's energy
it.h: Look at the first paragraph.

p.x: Isabel had promised her little brother, Rafi, that they would make s'mores without a campfire. Now, standing in the backyard with an empty pizza box, a roll of foil and a library book, she was starting to worry. // "Step one," she read aloud. "Cut a flap in the lid." She cut three sides of a square with Mom's scissors and folded it back. They glued foil to the inside of the flap, shiny side out. They taped plastic wrap tightly over the hole in the lid, making a little window. Then they set a graham cracker, a square of chocolate and a marshmallow inside, closed the lid and waited. // Twenty minutes later, Rafi peeked. The marshmallow looked exactly the same. // "It's broken," Rafi said. "Your oven doesn't work." // Isabel's face felt hot, and not from the sun. She wanted to stuff the box in the recycling bin. Instead, she sat down on the patio and opened the book again. She read the instructions slowly, the way her teacher said to read a hard math problem. // "We skipped two things," she said at last. "We were supposed to put black paper on the bottom, because black soaks up heat. And the flap has to point the sunlight into the box. Ours is pointing at the fence." // They found black construction paper in the craft drawer. Rafi held the flap while Isabel propped it up with a ruler until a bright patch of light fell right across the marshmallow. They waited again. // This time, when Rafi peeked, the chocolate had turned glossy and soft, and the marshmallow had puffed up like a tiny pillow. Rafi squashed his s'more together and grinned with chocolate on his chin. // "Your oven works," he said. // "Our oven," said Isabel. "And it only works because the first one didn't."

it.q: Why does the first oven fail?
ch: They skipped the black paper and did not aim the flap at the sun.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: explaining scientific ideas and using text features

it.q: What is the main idea of "Energy on the Move"?
ch: Energy moves from place to place and changes from one form to another.
Brakes get hot when a car stops.
it.h: Look for the idea that every paragraph explains.

p.x: Energy is the ability to make things move or change. You cannot hold energy in your hand, but you can see what it does. Energy also has a remarkable habit: it moves from place to place and changes from one form to another. // Think about a game of marbles. When you flick a marble, your finger gives it energy of motion. The faster the marble rolls, the more energy it has. If it crashes into a second marble, some of its energy moves into that marble, which starts rolling. Some of the energy also turns into sound, which is why you hear a click. A tiny bit becomes heat, warming the marbles just slightly. // Energy can travel in other ways, too. Light carries energy from the sun across millions of miles of space to Earth. Heat moves from warmer objects to cooler ones, so a spoon in a cup of hot cocoa soon feels warm. Sound carries energy through the air as vibrations. If you stand near a big drum, you can sometimes feel the sound in your chest. // Electricity is another way energy moves. An electric current carries energy through wires from a power plant to your home. When you switch on a lamp, the electric energy changes into light and heat. When you plug in a fan, it changes into motion. // Scientists say that energy is never used up; it only changes form or moves somewhere else. When a car brakes to a stop, its energy of motion does not disappear. Much of it turns into heat in the brakes. // Next time you turn on a light or kick a ball, look for the energy. Where does it come from, and where does it go?

it.q: According to the article, what happens when one marble crashes into another?
ch: Some energy moves into the second marble, and some becomes sound and heat.
Both marbles lose all their energy.
it.h: Reread the second paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: Greek roots and progressive verb tenses

it.q: The Greek root "therm" means "heat," and "meter" means "measure." Which word names a tool that measures heat?
it.h: Look for both "therm" and "meter."

it.q: The root "photo" means "light," and "graph" means "write or draw." What is a photograph, word by word?
ch: a sound that is written down
it.h: Put the meanings of the two roots together.

it.q: The Greek root "hydro" means "water." Which word names electricity made by moving water?
it.h: Find the word that begins with the root for water.

it.q: Which sentence uses the present progressive tense?
ch: The blades are spinning in the wind.
The blades spun in the wind.
The blades spin in the wind.
The blades will spin in the wind.
it.h: The present progressive uses "am," "is" or "are" plus a verb ending in -ing.

it.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Yesterday at noon, Isabel ___ the solar oven."
it.h: "Yesterday at noon" tells you the action was happening in the past.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence in the future progressive tense: "The turbines spin all night."
it.ans: The turbines will be spinning all night.
it.h: The future progressive uses "will be" plus a verb ending in -ing.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text: explaining an energy process with precise words

it.q: What does a writer do when explaining a process?
ch: tells the steps or stages in order so readers understand how something works
gives an opinion about the topic
it.h: A process happens in steps.

it.q: Which transition best shows the next stage of a process?
it.h: Which phrase signals time order?

it.q: Which sentence uses the most precise language?
ch: The solar panel changes sunlight into electricity.
The thing makes power out of stuff.
The panel does something with the sun.
it.h: Precise words name exactly what happens.

it.q: Which definition would best help readers understand "renewable energy"?
ch: energy from sources that are naturally replaced, such as sunlight and wind
energy that is used only at night
it.h: "Renew" means to make new again.

it.q: Which detail best fits a paragraph explaining how a wind turbine works?
ch: Wind pushes the blades, which spin a shaft connected to a generator.
Wind turbines are tall and white.
Some people think turbines are pretty.
it.h: Which detail explains the steps?

it.q: Rewrite this vague sentence with precise words: "The stove made the stuff hot."
it.ans: The burner on the stove heated the water in the pot until it boiled.
it.h: Replace "made," "stuff" and "hot" with exact words.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: energy from the sun and wind

it.q: What is a renewable energy source?
ch: a source that is naturally replaced, like sunlight
a source that will run out forever
a source found only in batteries
it.h: "Renew" means to make new again.

it.q: Read: "Fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years. Once they are used, they cannot be replaced quickly." Why are fossil fuels called nonrenewable?
ch: They cannot be replaced quickly after being used.
They come from the sun each day.
it.h: How long did they take to form?

it.q: A text has the heading "Advantages and Disadvantages of Wind Power." Which structure will it most likely use?
ch: a timeline of a person's life
it.h: It will look at good points and problems.

it.q: A chart shows that a home's solar panels made more electricity in June than in December. What does the chart suggest?
ch: There is more sunlight in June than in December.
People use less power in June.
it.h: What do solar panels need?

it.q: Read: "One disadvantage of solar power is that panels make little electricity at night." What does "disadvantage" mean?
it.h: The prefix "dis-" means not.

it.q: Name one advantage and one disadvantage of wind power.
it.ans: Advantage: wind is renewable and does not pollute the air when it makes electricity. Disadvantage: when the wind is calm, turbines do not make electricity.
it.h: Think about what happens on a calm day.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Energy All Around Us (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: theme and inference in a power-outage story

it.q: What is an inference?
ch: a conclusion reached using text clues and what you already know
a fact copied word for word
it.h: Inferences go beyond what is stated directly.

it.q: Read: "When the lights went out, Grandpa smiled and reached for the box of candles he kept under the sink." What can you infer about Grandpa?
ch: He has been through power outages before and is prepared.
He is afraid of the dark.
He has never seen a candle.
He is angry about the outage.
it.h: Why would someone keep candles ready?

it.q: Which statement is a theme, not just a topic?
ch: Sometimes losing something helps us notice what really matters.
it.h: A theme is a full sentence about life.

it.q: Read: "Without the TV humming, Maya could hear the rain tapping on the roof for the first time in months." What does this detail suggest?
ch: Maya is noticing things she usually ignores.
Maya is angry at the rain.
it.h: What changed when the TV went off?

it.q: Which detail would best support a theme about family connection?
ch: The family played cards by flashlight, laughing until midnight.
The clock on the stove blinked.
it.h: Which detail shows the family together?

it.q: Read: "Leo groaned. 'No video games for a whole night?' But by bedtime, he was asking Dad for one more story." Explain how Leo changes and what caused the change.
it.ans: Leo goes from upset about losing his games to enjoying the night. Dad's stories made the evening fun, so he wanted more.
it.h: Compare the beginning and the end.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: myths, folktales and their themes

it.q: What is Arachne's special talent?
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.x: In ancient Greece, there lived a young woman named Arachne who could weave more beautifully than anyone in the land. Her cloth was so fine that people traveled from distant villages just to watch her work. Her thread seemed to flow like water through her fingers, and the pictures she wove looked almost alive. // "Surely," said the visitors, "the goddess Athena herself must have taught you." // Arachne tossed her head. "No one taught me," she said. "My skill is my own. I am a better weaver than Athena, and I would prove it if she dared to compete with me." // Athena, the goddess of wisdom and of weaving, heard these words. She disguised herself as an old woman and came to Arachne's door. "Child," she said, "be proud of your gift, but do not compare yourself to the gods. Ask Athena's forgiveness, and she may be kind." // Arachne only laughed. "Let Athena come herself, if she is not afraid." // At once the old woman threw off her disguise and stood tall and shining before her. The visitors fell to their knees, but Arachne, though her face went pale, did not back down. The contest began. // Athena wove a tapestry showing the gods in all their glory, and in its corners she wove small scenes of people who had been punished for their pride, as a warning. Arachne wove scenes making fun of the gods' mistakes. Her work was flawless; even Athena could find no error in it. But its message was disrespectful, and the goddess's anger flared. // Athena touched Arachne with her weaving shuttle. Arachne began to shrink. Her arms and legs grew thin and long, and she became the first spider. // "Weave, then," said Athena, "you and all your children, forever." // And that is why, the ancient Greeks said, spiders are always spinning their beautiful webs. Even today, scientists call spiders and their relatives "arachnids," a word that comes from her name.

it.q: Which word best describes Arachne's character?
it.h: Think about what she says when visitors ask whether Athena taught her.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: words from myths and stories in the sky

it.q: What is the main idea of "Ancient Myths, Modern Words"?
ch: Many English words come from ancient Greek and Roman myths.
it.h: Read the first and last paragraphs.

p.x: Thousands of years ago, the people of ancient Greece and Rome told stories about gods, goddesses and heroes. These stories, called myths, tried to explain things people wondered about, such as why the seasons change or where thunder comes from. The ancient Greek and Roman worlds are long gone, but their myths live on in a surprising place: the words we use every day. // Have you ever heard someone call a hard job a "Herculean task"? In Greek myths, the hero Heracles, whom the Romans called Hercules, was famous for his great strength. As a punishment, he had to complete twelve nearly impossible labors, such as capturing a fierce lion and cleaning enormous stables in a single day. Today, a Herculean task is any job that takes enormous effort. // Another hero, Achilles, was said to be impossible to hurt, except in one spot. When he was a baby, his mother dipped him in a magic river to protect him, but she held him by the heel, so the water never touched that spot. Today, a person's "Achilles' heel" is their one weakness. // Some words come from myths about nature. The nymph Echo was cursed so that she could only repeat the last words other people said. Now an echo is a sound that bounces back to us. The god Pan, who watched over shepherds and wild places, was said to fill travelers with sudden fear. From his name we get the word "panic." // Even breakfast has a myth inside it. Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain and harvests, and her name gave us the word "cereal." // When you meet one of these words, you are hearing an echo, so to speak, of stories told long ago. Knowing the myth behind a word can help you understand what it means.

it.q: Your friend says that cleaning out the garage was a "Herculean task." What does your friend mean?
it.h: What was Hercules famous for?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: words from mythology and modal auxiliaries

it.q: In a Greek myth, King Midas wished that everything he touched would turn to gold. What does it mean to say someone has "the Midas touch"?
ch: Everything they try is successful and makes money.
it.h: Think about what happened to everything Midas touched.

it.q: Nike was the Greek goddess of victory. Why might a sports company choose this name?
it.h: What does "victory" mean?

it.q: Which modal verb shows that something is required? "Students ___ wear closed shoes in the science lab."
it.h: Which word means there is no choice?

it.q: Which modal verb shows that something is possible but not certain? "It ___ rain tomorrow, so bring a jacket."
it.h: Which word shows a maybe?

it.q: Which sentence uses "may" to ask permission?
ch: May I borrow your book about myths?
You may be right about that.
it.h: Asking permission means asking whether you are allowed.

it.q: In a Greek myth, a weaver named Arachne boasts that she is better than the goddess Athena. Write a sentence using "should" to give Arachne advice.
it.ans: Arachne, you should apologize to Athena before she gets angry.
it.h: "Should" tells what someone ought to do.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: sensory details and vivid descriptions

it.q: What are sensory details?
ch: words that describe what you see, hear, smell, taste or touch
it.h: Think about the five senses.

it.q: Which sentence uses the sense of sound?
ch: Thunder cracked like a giant whip across the sky.
it.h: Which sentence tells what you would hear?

it.q: Which sentence shows, rather than tells, that a giant is huge?
ch: Each of the giant's footsteps shook the ground and rattled the windows of the village.
The giant was huge and tall.
it.h: Show what happens because the giant is so big.

it.q: Which word is the most precise verb for a snake's movement?
it.h: Which verb helps you picture exactly how it moved?

it.q: Which sentence best describes the setting of a myth?
ch: High on Mount Olympus, golden halls glittered above the clouds.
it.h: Choose details that help you picture the place.

it.q: Write a sentence that describes a forest at night using at least two senses.
it.ans: Owls hooted overhead, and the cold air smelled of pine and wet earth.
it.h: Include what you hear and what you smell or feel.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Myths and Tales from Many Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Pourquoi tales: stories that explain why

it.q: What is a pourquoi tale?
ch: a story that explains why something in nature is the way it is
a true story about a scientist
it.h: "Pourquoi" is the French word for "why."

it.q: Which title most likely belongs to a pourquoi tale?
ch: Why the Bat Flies at Night
it.h: Which title asks or answers "why"?

it.q: In many pourquoi tales, a character's action causes a change that lasts forever. Which is an example?
ch: Because Turtle boasted, his shell cracked into the pattern turtles still have today.
Turtle walked to the pond and swam.
Turtle liked to sleep in the sun.
Turtle had a friend named Duck.
it.h: Look for a change that explains something in nature.

it.q: Two pourquoi tales from different cultures both explain why the moon changes shape. How are they alike?
ch: They explain the same thing in nature.
They have exactly the same characters.
They were written by the same author.
They happen in the same country.
it.h: Think about the topic they explain.

it.q: Which theme is common in pourquoi tales about proud animals?
it.h: What usually happens to boastful characters?

it.q: Think of something in nature, such as why the zebra has stripes. Write one sentence telling what event in a pourquoi tale could explain it.
it.ans: Long ago, Zebra rolled too close to a fire, and the burned grass left dark stripes on his white coat forever.
it.h: Make a character's action cause a lasting change.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: describing events and making inferences

it.q: What is the first sign of the earthquake that Leilani notices?
ch: The water in the fish tank sloshes.
it.h: Reread the first two sentences.

p.x: The first thing Leilani noticed was the fish tank. The water in it began to slosh from side to side, as if an invisible hand were stirring it. Then the windows rattled, and a low rumble, like a truck passing too close, filled Room 9. // "Earthquake!" someone shouted. // For one frozen second, Leilani could not move. Pencils rolled off desks. The map on the wall swung on its hook. Then Ms. Ortiz's calm voice cut through the noise: "Drop, cover and hold on!" // Leilani's body remembered what to do before her brain did. She dropped to her knees, crawled under her desk and grabbed one of its metal legs with both hands. The desk shook against her palms. Across the aisle, Dylan, the new boy who had just moved from Ohio, was standing in the middle of the room with his mouth open. // "Dylan!" Leilani called. "Get under your desk! Hold the leg!" // Dylan blinked, then dove under his desk. // The shaking lasted only about ten seconds, but it felt like ten minutes. Then, as suddenly as it had started, it stopped. The fish tank sloshed a few more times and went still. Somewhere down the hall, a little kid was crying. // Ms. Ortiz counted heads. Everyone was fine. A few books had fallen, and the class's tomato plant had tipped over, spilling dirt across the windowsill. // On the way outside to the field, Dylan walked next to Leilani. His face was pale. "We never had one in my town in Ohio," he said. "I didn't know what to do." // "Nobody knows the first time," Leilani said. She didn't tell him that her own hands were still shaking. "That's why we practice. Next time, you'll know." // Dylan nodded. Then he almost smiled. "Thanks for yelling at me." // "Anytime," said Leilani.

it.q: Which detail best helps the reader understand how the earthquake sounded?
ch: a low rumble, like a truck passing too close
The map on the wall swung on its hook.
it.h: Look for a comparison to a sound.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: cause and effect

it.q: What is the main idea of "Slow Changes, Big Results"?
ch: Weathering and erosion slowly change Earth's surface and can create huge landforms.
The Grand Canyon is in Arizona.
it.h: Which choice tells about the whole article?

p.x: Some changes to Earth's surface happen in seconds, like an earthquake. Others happen so slowly that you would never notice them in a lifetime. Yet these slow changes, called weathering and erosion, have carved some of the most famous landforms on the planet. // Weathering is the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces. One cause of weathering is ice. When rain trickles into a crack in a rock and then freezes, the water expands, pushing the crack a little wider. After the ice melts and refreezes again and again, the rock can split apart. Plant roots cause weathering, too. A tree root growing into a crack can slowly pry a boulder open. // Erosion is what happens next. Erosion is the moving of broken rock and soil from one place to another. Moving water is the most powerful cause of erosion. Rivers carry sand and pebbles downstream, and as the pebbles tumble along, they scrape the riverbed deeper. Wind blows sand across deserts, and ocean waves wear away cliffs along the shore. // Glaciers, huge slow-moving rivers of ice, cause erosion as well. As a glacier creeps downhill, it picks up rocks and drags them along, grinding the land beneath it. Long ago, glaciers helped shape California's Yosemite Valley, scraping it into a wide U shape with steep granite walls. // Given enough time, weathering and erosion can create enormous landforms. The Grand Canyon in Arizona was carved mainly by the Colorado River over millions of years. Layer by layer, the river cut down through the rock until the canyon was more than a mile deep. // The rock you stand on today may seem permanent. But water, ice, wind and plants are always at work on it, slowly changing the shape of the land.

ch: the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces
the moving of soil to a new place
it.h: Look for the definition in the second paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: Latin roots, adjective order and prepositional phrases

it.q: The Latin root "rupt" means "break." What does "erupt" mean?
ch: to break out or burst out
it.h: The prefix "e-" means "out."

it.q: The Latin root "terra" means "earth" or "land." Which word means "the type of land in an area"?
it.h: Look for the word that contains "terr."

it.q: Which phrase about a volcano puts the adjectives in the correct order?
it.h: The usual order is size, then age, then color.

it.q: Which phrase about a flower puts the adjectives in the correct order?
it.h: Opinion words like "beautiful" come first.

it.q: Which group of words in this sentence is a prepositional phrase? "The fern grew between two rocks."
it.h: A prepositional phrase begins with a word like in, on, under or between and ends with a noun.

it.q: Add a prepositional phrase to this sentence to tell where: "Leilani crawled."
it.ans: Leilani crawled under her desk.
it.h: Use a word such as under, behind or into.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text about weathering and erosion

it.q: In earth science, what does the word "weathering" mean?
ch: the breaking down of rock into smaller pieces
the moving of rock and soil to a new place
the melting of rock deep underground
it.h: Weathering breaks; erosion moves.

it.q: What is erosion?
ch: the moving of rock and soil from one place to another by wind, water or ice
the breaking of rock into pieces in place
it.h: Erosion carries pieces away.

it.q: Which sentence correctly uses the word "deposition"?
ch: When the river slowed down, deposition left a layer of sand at its mouth.
Deposition broke the rock into pieces.
Deposition is a kind of rainstorm.
The deposition flew into the sky.
it.h: Deposition means dropping or laying down sediment.

it.q: Which detail best supports the topic sentence "Water is a powerful force of erosion"?
ch: Over millions of years, the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon.
it.h: Which detail shows water moving rock?

it.q: Which transition best introduces an example?
it.h: Which phrase signals an example is coming?

it.q: Write a sentence that explains the difference between weathering and erosion.
it.ans: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, while erosion carries those pieces away to a new place.
it.h: Use "while" or "but" to show the difference.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: what causes earthquakes

it.q: What is a fault?
ch: a crack in Earth's crust where rocks move
it.h: Earthquakes happen along these cracks.

it.q: Read: "Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces called plates. When plates slide past each other, stress builds up." What happens when that stress is suddenly released?
it.h: Think about what shakes the ground.

it.q: Read: "Seismologists use instruments called seismometers to measure ground shaking." What is a seismologist?
it.h: The word "seismometer" gives a clue.

it.q: Which text structure would best explain why earthquakes happen?
it.h: Earthquakes have causes and results.

it.q: Which is the best safety action during an earthquake, according to safety experts?
ch: Stand in a doorway near glass.
it.h: Many California schools practice this in drills.

it.q: Explain why California has many earthquakes.
it.ans: California lies where two of Earth's plates meet and slide past each other along faults such as the San Andreas Fault, so stress builds up and is released as earthquakes.
it.h: Think about plates and faults.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Changing Surface (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading diagrams and charts in texts about landforms

it.q: What does a diagram usually show?
ch: the parts of something or how a process works
it.h: Diagrams use pictures and labels.

it.q: A diagram has arrows going from a mountain, down a river, to a delta at the ocean. What do the arrows most likely show?
it.h: Arrows show movement.

it.q: A bar graph shows that a beach lost 2 meters of sand in 2021, 3 meters in 2022 and 5 meters in 2023. What trend does it show?
ch: The beach lost more sand each year.
The beach gained sand each year.
The beach lost less sand each year.
it.h: Compare the numbers from year to year.

it.q: What is the purpose of a caption under a photo of a canyon?
ch: to explain what the photo shows
it.h: Captions are short explanations.

it.q: A cross-section diagram of a volcano shows a magma chamber, a vent and layers of ash and lava. What does a cross-section show?
ch: the inside of something as if it were cut open
it.h: "Cross-section" means a slice.

it.q: A table shows that sand dunes in a desert moved 4 meters in January and 10 meters in March, a windier month. What can you conclude from the table?
it.ans: Stronger winds move sand dunes farther, so the dunes moved more in windy March.
it.h: Connect the wind to the distance.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Animal Survival and Adaptations (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: character change and inference

it.q: What problem does Marisol's family have in "The Owl Box"?
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.x: The gophers were winning. Every morning, Marisol's father walked the rows of the family's vineyard near Lodi and found new mounds of fresh dirt and another young grapevine wilting where its roots had been chewed away. // "Poison would be quicker," said Mr. Alvarez from the farm next door, leaning on the fence. // Papa shook his head. "Poison can hurt the hawks and owls that eat the gophers, and the neighbors' cats too. I want a helper, not a poison." // That weekend, Papa and Marisol built the helper's house: a wooden box about the size of a suitcase, with a round hole in the front. They bolted it to the top of a tall pole at the edge of the vineyard. // "Who's going to live there?" Marisol asked. // "Barn owls, if we're lucky," Papa said. "A family of barn owls can eat hundreds of gophers and mice in a year." // For weeks, the box stayed empty. Marisol checked it every afternoon after school. Mr. Alvarez chuckled every time he saw her looking up. "Still waiting for your tenants?" he called. // Then, one evening in March, Marisol was carrying the trash out when a pale shape drifted over her head without a sound. It was white underneath, with a heart-shaped face that glowed in the dusk. It swooped low over the vines, dropped into the grass and rose again with something small and wriggling in its talons. Then it flew straight into the box. // Marisol ran inside so fast she forgot to close the door. "Papa! An owl! It moved in!" // By summer, there were five fuzzy owlets peering out of the box, hissing like tiny teakettles whenever their parents brought food. The new gopher mounds grew fewer and fewer. // One evening, Mr. Alvarez stood at the fence watching the owls hunt. He was quiet for a long time. Then he turned to Marisol. // "So," he said, rubbing his chin, "how big did you say that box was?"

ch: Poison could hurt hawks, owls and cats.
Mr. Alvarez told him not to.
Poison does not work on gophers.
it.h: Find what Papa says to Mr. Alvarez.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Animal Survival and Adaptations (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how authors use reasons and evidence

it.q: What is the main idea of "The Kangaroo Rat: A Desert Survivor"?
ch: The kangaroo rat has adaptations that help it survive in the harsh desert.
Kangaroo rats are related to kangaroos.
Owls hunt kangaroo rats at night.
it.h: Find the sentence in the first paragraph that tells what the article will explain.

p.t: The Kangaroo Rat: A Desert Survivor
p.x: In the deserts of Southern California, summer days can be blistering hot, and months may pass without rain. Most animals would not last long there without water. Yet one small rodent, the kangaroo rat, thrives in these harsh places. It has several adaptations, or special features and behaviors, that help it survive. // First, the kangaroo rat can live its whole life without drinking water. It eats dry seeds, and its body makes water as it breaks the seeds down for energy. This may sound impossible, but it works because the kangaroo rat is also very good at saving water. Its kidneys are so efficient that very little water leaves its body. // Second, the kangaroo rat avoids the heat. During the day, it stays in a cool burrow underground, often plugging the entrance with soil to keep out the hot, dry air. It comes out to look for seeds at night, when the desert is cooler. Inside the burrow, it stores seeds it has gathered, so it can stay hidden for long periods. // Third, the kangaroo rat's body helps it escape from predators such as owls, snakes and coyotes. It has huge back legs and a long tail with a tuft at the end. Like a kangaroo, it hops on its back legs, and it can leap several feet in a single bound, changing direction in midair. Its tail helps it balance. Its large eyes and sharp hearing help it notice danger in the dark. // Each of these adaptations helps the kangaroo rat survive where water is scarce and danger is everywhere. Scientists study kangaroo rats to learn how animals save water, a lesson that matters more and more as California faces dry years. This tiny desert hopper proves that you do not have to be big to be tough.

ch: Its body makes water as it breaks down dry seeds.
It drinks from desert pools at night.
It stores water in its tail.

it.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The owls raised ___ owlets in the box."
it.h: Which word shows that something belongs to them?

it.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The kangaroo rat stays in ___ burrow all day."
it.h: "It's" always means "it is."

it.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "We walked ___ the grove to count butterflies."
it.h: Which word shows direction?

it.q: Which word is a synonym for "scarce" in "where water is scarce"?
it.h: A synonym means the same or almost the same.

it.h: An antonym means the opposite.

it.q: Write one sentence that uses "their," "there" and "they're" correctly.
it.ans: "They're watching the owls over there in their box."

lessons.u: Unit 6: Animal Survival and Adaptations (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion using evidence from informational texts

it.q: What is text evidence?
ch: facts, details or quotations from a text that support an idea
the page number of a book
it.h: Evidence comes from what you read.

it.q: Which sentence correctly introduces a quotation as evidence?
ch: According to the article, "Sea otters eat sea urchins that would otherwise destroy kelp forests."
it.h: Name the source, then give its exact words in quotation marks.

it.q: Opinion: "People should protect wetlands." Which piece of evidence best supports it?
ch: Wetlands provide homes for many birds, fish and insects and help soak up floodwater.
it.h: Which evidence shows why wetlands matter?

it.q: After giving evidence, a writer should
ch: explain how the evidence supports the opinion
repeat the evidence word for word
it.h: Readers need to know why the evidence matters.

it.q: Which linking phrase best introduces evidence?
it.h: Which phrase points to what a text says?

it.q: Read this fact: "Bees pollinate many of the fruits and vegetables people eat." Write a sentence that uses this fact to support the opinion "We should plant flowers that help bees."
it.ans: We should plant flowers that help bees because bees pollinate many of the fruits and vegetables people eat, so helping bees helps our food supply.
it.h: Connect the fact to the opinion with "because" or "so."

lessons.u: Unit 6: Animal Survival and Adaptations (opinion writing)

it.q: What is migration?
ch: the regular movement of animals from one place to another, often with the seasons
the way animals hide using color
the sleep some animals take in winter
it.h: Think about birds flying south in fall.

it.q: Read: "Many animals migrate to find food, warmer weather or safe places to raise their young." What is the main idea?
ch: All animals stay in one place.
it.h: The sentence lists several reasons.

it.q: Read: "In winter, monarch butterflies cluster together on trees along the California coast." What does "cluster" mean?
it.h: Think about grapes growing in a bunch.

it.q: Which text structure would best explain why animals migrate?
it.h: Migration happens because of something.

it.q: Read: "Gray whales travel south to warm lagoons in Mexico to give birth. Then they swim north to cold Arctic waters to feed." Why do gray whales swim north?
it.h: Look at the second sentence.

it.q: Explain why migration can be dangerous for animals.
it.ans: Migrating animals travel long distances, so they can run out of energy, face storms or predators and lose places to rest or feed along the way.
it.h: Think about what could happen on a very long trip.

it.q: Who is the speaker in "Saturday at the Night Market"?
ch: a child who helps at the family's food stall
it.h: Look for the words "I" and "my."

p.x: When the sun slips down behind the hills / and the parking lot turns blue, / my father strings the paper lamps / and the market wakes up new. // The grills begin their hissing song, / the smoke curls up like thread, / and Auntie Lin is folding dumplings / as soft as pillows on a bed. // I stack the cups and count the change, / I wipe the counter clean; / my little brother hands out napkins, / the proudest worker ever seen. // The crowd moves in, a river of people, / it rushes and it bends, / with grandmas pushing shopping carts / and teenagers with friends. // A drummer taps on plastic buckets, / a baby laughs nearby, / the mango slices glow like sunsets / stacked up three feet high. // The air is thick with garlic, ginger, / with sugar, salt and lime; / I'd know this smell with my eyes shut / in any place or time. // "Two skewers, please!" "Extra spicy!" / "Do you have any more?" / My father's hands are quick as sparrows; / he's done this all before. // By midnight all the lamps are dimming, / the grills are cooling down, / the river of people trickles home / across the sleepy town. // My feet are sore, my apron's sticky, / my eyes are full of sand, / but my father squeezes my shoulder / with his warm and smoky hand. // "Good work," he says. Two words. That's all. / But I carry them like gold / the whole way home, beneath the stars, / through the night so clear and cold.

ch: a group of lines in a poem, like a paragraph in a story
