it.q: Where was Juan Felipe Herrera born?
it.h: Look at the first sentence.

p.t: Juan Felipe Herrera: A Poet from the Fields
p.x: Juan Felipe Herrera was born in 1948 in Fowler, California, a small farm town in the Central Valley. His parents were farmworkers who had come from Mexico, and the family moved often, following the crops from harvest to harvest. Sometimes they lived in a trailer; sometimes they lived in a tent by the side of the road. // Moving so much was hard. Juan Felipe changed schools many times. When he started school, he spoke mostly Spanish, and he felt shy and unsure of his English. But his mother loved words. She sang songs, recited poems and told stories about her childhood in Mexico. From her, Juan Felipe learned that language could be beautiful and full of feeling. // A turning point came in third grade. His teacher asked him to sing a song in front of the class. Nervously, he sang. When he finished, his teacher told him he had a beautiful voice. Herrera later said those few kind words gave him the courage to believe in himself. // As he grew up, Herrera wrote poems about the people and places he knew: farmworkers, families, city streets and the colorful mix of cultures in California. He often wrote in both English and Spanish. He went to college, became a teacher and wrote many books for adults and children, including picture books about his own childhood in the fields. // In 2012, Herrera was named California's Poet Laureate, an honored poet chosen to share poetry with the people of the state. Then, in 2015, he became the Poet Laureate of the United States, the first Latino poet to hold that honor. He used the role to invite people of all ages to write poems together. // Herrera's life shows that a voice that begins quietly can grow strong enough to be heard across a whole nation.

it.q: Why did Herrera's family move often when he was a child?
ch: They followed the crops from harvest to harvest.
His father was in the army.
They wanted to live near the ocean.
They were looking for a bigger house.
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.t: Juan Felipe Herrera: A Poet from the Fields
p.x: Juan Felipe Herrera was born in 1948 in Fowler, California, a small farm town in the Central Valley. His parents were farmworkers who had come from Mexico, and the family moved often, following the crops from harvest to harvest. Sometimes they lived in a trailer; sometimes they lived in a tent by the side of the road. // Moving so much was hard. Juan Felipe changed schools many times. When he started school, he spoke mostly Spanish, and he felt shy and unsure of his English. But his mother loved words. She sang songs, recited poems and told stories about her childhood in Mexico. From her, Juan Felipe learned that language could be beautiful and full of feeling. // A turning point came in third grade. His teacher asked him to sing a song in front of the class. Nervously, he sang. When he finished, his teacher told him he had a beautiful voice. Herrera later said those few kind words gave him the courage to believe in himself. // As he grew up, Herrera wrote poems about the people and places he knew: farmworkers, families, city streets and the colorful mix of cultures in California. He often wrote in both English and Spanish. He went to college, became a teacher and wrote many books for adults and children, including picture books about his own childhood in the fields. // In 2012, Herrera was named California's Poet Laureate, an honored poet chosen to share poetry with the people of the state. Then, in 2015, he became the Poet Laureate of the United States, the first Latino poet to hold that honor. He used the role to invite people of all ages to write poems together. // Herrera's life shows that a voice that begins quietly can grow strong enough to be heard across a whole nation.

it.q: How did Herrera's mother influence him?
ch: She showed him that language could be beautiful through songs, poems and stories.
She taught him to play soccer.
She moved the family to a city.
She told him to stop speaking Spanish.
it.h: Find the paragraph about his mother.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: similes, metaphors, idioms and punctuation for effect

it.q: Which sentence contains a simile?
ch: The baby's cheeks were as round as peaches.
The baby's cheeks were two peaches.
it.h: A simile uses "like" or "as" to compare.

it.q: "My little brother is a tornado when he cleans his room." What does this metaphor mean?
ch: He moves fast and makes a mess.
it.h: What is a tornado like?

it.q: What does the idiom "It's raining cats and dogs" mean?
ch: Pets are falling from the sky.
The animals want to go outside.
it.h: An idiom means something different from what its words say.

it.q: What does the idiom "a piece of cake" mean in "The spelling test was a piece of cake"?
it.h: Would a test that is "a piece of cake" feel hard or easy?

it.q: Which punctuation mark best shows strong feeling in this sentence? "Watch out for the puddle__"
it.h: Which mark shows excitement or a warning?

it.q: Write a simile and a metaphor that describe a busy place. Label each one.
it.ans: Simile: "The lanterns glowed like tiny moons." Metaphor: "The parking lot was a beehive of shoppers."
it.h: A simile uses like or as; a metaphor says one thing is another.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative from a character's point of view

it.q: Which pronouns does a first-person narrator use to talk about himself or herself?
it.h: The narrator is a character in the story.

it.q: Which sentence is written in third person?
ch: Kenji climbed the tree and looked out over the orchard.
I climbed the tree and looked out.
it.h: Look for a name or "he" or "she" instead of "I."

it.q: A story is told by the family dog. What point of view is it most likely written in?
ch: first person, with the dog as narrator
third person, with an outside narrator
it.h: The dog tells its own story.

it.q: Which sentence shows a first-person narrator's thoughts?
ch: I wondered whether the old bridge would hold my weight.
it.h: Look for the narrator's own wondering.

it.q: How would a story change if it were told by a different character?
ch: Readers would learn that character's thoughts and see events differently.
The events would have to be different.
The story would have no setting.
it.h: Every character notices different things.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence from first person to third person: "I tripped on the stairs and dropped my lunch."
it.ans: Ava tripped on the stairs and dropped her lunch.
it.h: Use a name or "he" or "she" instead of "I," and change "my."

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Point of view: comparing first- and third-person narration

it.q: In first-person narration, who tells the story?
it.h: First-person narrators use "I."

it.q: What is an advantage of first-person narration?
ch: Readers know the narrator's thoughts and feelings closely.
Readers get no information about feelings.
it.h: Think about how close you feel to an "I" narrator.

it.q: What is a limit of first-person narration?
ch: Readers know only what the narrator knows or notices.
Readers know too many characters' thoughts.
it.h: Can the narrator read minds?

it.q: Read: "Sami thought the test was easy. Across the room, Tess was sure she had failed." What point of view is used?
ch: third person, sharing more than one character's thoughts
it.h: Whose thoughts are shared?

it.q: Read: "I was sure Dad was angry, because he did not say a word on the drive home." Why might a reader question the narrator's idea?
ch: The narrator is guessing; Dad might be quiet for another reason.
The narrator knows exactly what Dad is thinking.
The narrator is not in the car.
it.h: Does the narrator really know Dad's thoughts?

it.q: Explain how the same event, a broken vase, might be described differently by the child who broke it and by the parent who finds it.
it.ans: The child might describe feeling scared and trying to hide the pieces, while the parent might describe surprise at finding the mess and wondering what happened.
it.h: Think about what each person knows and feels.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: historical fiction about the Gold Rush

it.q: Why did Clara's father come to California in "The Pie Wagon"?
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.x: In the spring of 1850, Clara Mendes and her mother arrived in the mining camp at Coloma with two trunks, a small iron stove and one sack of dried apples. Clara's father had come to California a year earlier to dig for gold. In his letters he had written that he would soon be rich. Instead, his last letter said he had found only enough gold to buy beans. // Clara looked around at the tents flapping in the wind, the muddy street and the men in torn shirts hurrying toward the river with picks and pans. "Where's all the gold?" she asked. // "In the river, mostly," said her father. "And in the pockets of anyone smart enough to sell the miners what they need." // Mama was already rolling up her sleeves. That night she baked six apple pies in the little stove. In the morning, Clara carried them through camp on a wooden board, calling, "Fresh pies! Apple pies!" // The miners stared as if they had seen a ghost. Most of them had not tasted pie since they left home. One man with a gray beard bought a whole pie and ate it standing in the street, his eyes closed. Another paid her with a pinch of gold dust from a leather pouch. By noon, all six pies were gone. // Every day after that, Mama baked more pies, and Clara sold them. Flour was expensive, and eggs sometimes cost a dollar each, but the miners paid gladly. By the end of the summer, the Mendes family had saved more gold from pies than Papa had found in a whole year at the river. // One evening, Papa sat on an overturned bucket and laughed until he wiped his eyes. "I came all this way to dig for gold," he said, "and it was in your mother's kitchen the whole time." // Clara grinned. She was thinking that the real treasure might be something else: the three of them, together, at the end of a long day.

it.q: What does Papa mean when he says the gold is also "in the pockets of anyone smart enough to sell the miners what they need"?
ch: People can make money by selling goods to miners.
Miners keep gold in their pockets.
Clara should take gold from the miners.
Gold is only found in pockets.
it.h: Think about what the family does next.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: firsthand and secondhand accounts

it.q: Which account in "Two Accounts of the Discovery" is a firsthand account?
ch: Account 1, because Marshall describes what he saw himself
Account 2, because it gives exact dates
Account 2, because it was written later
both, because they are about the same event
it.h: A firsthand account is told by someone who was there.

p.x: ACCOUNT 1: THE DISCOVERER REMEMBERS // In January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for John Sutter on the American River at Coloma. Years later, he described the moment he found gold. This is adapted from his own account, published in 1857: // "One morning in January, it was a clear, cold morning, I shall never forget that morning, as I was taking my usual walk along the race after shutting off the water, my eye was caught with the glimpse of something shining in the bottom of the ditch. There was about a foot of water running then. I reached my hand down and picked it up; it made my heart thump, for I was certain it was gold. The piece was about half the size and of the shape of a pea." // ACCOUNT 2: A HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERY // On January 24, 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall noticed shiny flakes in the channel of water, called a tailrace, below the sawmill he was building at Coloma. Marshall and the workers tested the flakes. They bit them, hammered them flat and boiled one in lye soap. The metal did not break or darken, so they believed it was gold. // Sutter wanted to keep the discovery a secret so his workers would not leave to dig for gold. But news spread. In May 1848, a San Francisco merchant named Sam Brannan walked through the streets holding up a bottle of gold dust and shouting about gold on the American River. Soon thousands of people were heading for the hills. By 1849, people from around the world were rushing to California. They became known as the forty-niners. Neither Marshall nor Sutter became rich from the gold rush.

it.q: According to Marshall, how big was the first piece of gold he found?
ch: about half the size of a pea
as small as a grain of sand
it.h: Look at the end of Marshall's words.

There was about a foot of water running then. I reached my hand down and picked it up; it made my heart thump, for I was certain it was gold. The piece was about half the size and of the shape of a pea." // ACCOUNT 2: A HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERY // On January 24, 1848, a carpenter named James Marshall noticed shiny flakes in the channel of water, called a tailrace, below the sawmill he was building at Coloma. Marshall and the workers tested the flakes. They bit them, hammered them flat and boiled one in lye soap. The metal did not break or darken, so they believed it was gold. // Sutter wanted to keep the discovery a secret so his workers would not leave to dig for gold. But news spread. Soon thousands of people were heading for the hills. By 1849, people from around the world were rushing to California. They became known as the forty-niners. Neither Marshall nor Sutter became rich from the gold rush.

ch: If the metal did not break or darken, it was likely gold.
Soap made the gold shine for selling.
Boiling turned the metal into gold.
it.h: Read the sentence after the list of tests.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: commas and quotation marks

it.q: Which sentence about Clara punctuates dialogue correctly?
it.h: The question mark goes inside the quotation marks.

it.q: Which sentence about Papa punctuates dialogue correctly?
ch: Papa said, "The gold is in the river."
Papa said "The gold is in the river."
Papa said, "The gold is in the river".
Papa said, The gold is in the river.
it.h: Put a comma before the quotation and the period inside the closing quotation mark.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly with a coordinating conjunction?
ch: The miners worked all day, but they found little gold.
The miners worked all day but, they found little gold.
The miners, worked all day but they found little gold.
The miners worked, all day but they found little gold.
it.h: Put the comma before "and," "but" or "or" when it joins two complete sentences.

it.q: Which sentence needs a comma before "and"?
ch: Mama baked the pies and Clara sold them.
The pies were warm and sweet.
it.h: Does "and" join two complete sentences, each with its own subject and verb?

it.q: Which sentence correctly punctuates words quoted from a text?
ch: Marshall wrote that the gold "made my heart thump."
Marshall wrote that the gold made my heart thump.
Marshall wrote that the gold, "made my heart thump".
Marshall wrote, that the gold made "my heart thump.
it.h: Put quotation marks around the exact words the writer used.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence with correct punctuation: Wing said I will come home next year
it.ans: Wing said, "I will come home next year."
it.h: Add a comma, quotation marks and end punctuation.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion about a historical question: the Gold Rush

it.q: What should an opinion essay about history include?
ch: a clear opinion supported by historical facts and evidence
a list of dates with no opinion
it.h: Opinions about history still need facts.

it.q: Which is the clearest opinion statement for an essay about the Gold Rush?
ch: The Gold Rush changed California more than any other event in the 1800s.
it.h: Which statement takes a position someone could argue?

it.q: Which fact best supports the opinion "Shopkeepers often did better in the Gold Rush than miners"?
ch: Many merchants earned steady money selling supplies at high prices to miners.
it.h: Which fact shows shopkeepers making money?

it.q: Which linking phrase best introduces a second reason?
it.h: Which phrase adds a new reason?

it.q: An opinion essay about the Gold Rush should also consider other viewpoints. Whose experiences should a fair essay include?
ch: California Indians, immigrant miners and newcomers from the eastern states
it.h: Many groups were affected in different ways.

it.q: Write one reason, with a supporting fact, for this opinion: "Life in a mining camp was difficult."
it.ans: Mining camps were difficult places to live because food and supplies were scarce, so prices were very high and many miners spent most of what they found.
it.h: Give a reason and then a fact that shows it.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: life in the gold fields

it.q: What were the people who rushed to California in 1849 often called?
it.h: The nickname comes from the year.

it.q: Read: "Because thousands of miners needed food and tools, and supplies were scarce, prices in mining towns soared." What caused high prices?
it.h: Look at what comes after "Because."

it.q: Read: "Miners swirled water and gravel in a shallow pan. The heavy gold sank to the bottom." Why did gold stay in the pan?
ch: Gold is heavier than gravel and sinks.
it.h: What does "heavy" tell you?

it.q: What does "boomtown" most likely mean?
ch: a town that grows very quickly
it.h: Think about something that booms, or grows suddenly.

it.q: Which detail would support the idea that mining was hard work?
ch: Miners stood in icy rivers for hours, shoveling and sifting gravel.
it.h: Which detail describes the work itself?

it.q: Explain why many shopkeepers in mining towns earned more money than miners.
it.ans: Miners needed food, tools and clothing, and supplies were scarce, so shopkeepers could charge very high prices and earn steady money, while most miners found little gold.
it.h: Think about who needed to buy things every day.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: a Gold Rush journey in diary entries

it.q: What is a diary entry?
ch: a dated piece of writing where a person records events, thoughts and feelings
it.h: People often write diary entries each day.

it.q: Historical fiction is
ch: a made-up story set in a real time and place in the past
a story set in the future
it.h: The characters may be invented, but the setting is real.

it.q: Read a diary line: "Oct. 3 - Another week of rain. My boots have not been dry since Tuesday." What can you infer about the writer's life?
ch: The writer lives in a desert.
The writer just bought new boots.
it.h: Think about how wet boots feel for a week.

it.q: Why might an author tell historical fiction through diary entries?
ch: to let readers see events through one person's thoughts day by day
to give a list of dates only
it.h: Diaries are personal.

it.q: Read: "I have found three small flakes today. Mr. Wu, who sells beans, says it will not buy a week of supper." What does this suggest?
ch: Prices were high and the writer found little gold.
it.h: Three flakes are not enough for a week of food.

it.q: Read: "May 12 - I promised Mama I would come home rich. Now I would settle for coming home." What does this entry show about how the writer has changed?
it.ans: At first the writer hoped to get rich, but now hardships have made the writer just want to return home safely.
it.h: Compare "rich" with "coming home."

lessons.u: Unit 8: The California Gold Rush (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Research: taking notes from firsthand and secondhand sources about the Gold Rush

it.q: What is a firsthand (primary) account?
ch: a description by someone who was there
a description written much later by someone who was not there
it.h: "First" hand means the writer saw or did it.

it.q: Which is a secondhand account of the Gold Rush?
ch: a diary kept by a cook in a mining camp
a photograph taken in a camp in 1852
it.h: Which one was written by someone who was not there?

it.q: What is paraphrasing?
ch: restating an author's ideas in your own words
it.h: "Para" means beside; you write beside the original in new words.

it.q: Which note best paraphrases this sentence: "Supplies had to be shipped from far away, so prices in the camps were extremely high"?
ch: camps - very high prices - supplies came from far
"Supplies had to be shipped from far away"
it.h: Use short phrases in your own words.

it.q: Why should a researcher use both firsthand and secondhand sources?
ch: Firsthand sources give personal details, while secondhand sources give the bigger picture.
Secondhand sources are always more exciting.
It does not matter which source is used.
it.h: Each kind of source offers something different.

it.q: Name one thing a miner's letter could tell you that a textbook might not, and one thing a textbook could tell you that a letter might not.
it.ans: A letter could tell how one miner felt and what his daily life was like. A textbook could tell the overall causes and effects of the Gold Rush and facts about many groups.
it.h: Think about personal details versus the big picture.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: drama, stage directions and character

it.q: In "The Bridge Challenge," which part of the play tells where and when the scene takes place?
it.h: Look near the top of the play.

p.x: A play in one scene. // CAST: ROSA, a fourth grader; DEV, her teammate; MR. KIM, their teacher // SETTING: A classroom on the day of the bridge-building challenge. Two desks are pushed together. On them sits a bridge made of craft sticks and glue. // (MR. KIM places a small bucket on a table at the front of the room.) // MR. KIM: Each team's bridge must hold this bucket while I add pennies, one cup at a time. The bridge that holds the most wins. Rosa and Dev, you're first. // DEV: (whispering) Our bridge is going to be amazing. I can feel it. // ROSA: (nervously) I hope the glue dried. // (MR. KIM hangs the bucket from the middle of their bridge and pours in one cup of pennies. The bridge creaks. He pours in a second cup. With a loud CRACK, the bridge snaps in half. Pennies spill across the floor.) // DEV: (groaning and covering his face) Noooo! Two weeks of work! // ROSA: (kneeling to look at the broken pieces) Wait. Look where it broke, Dev. Right in the middle. // DEV: So? It broke. That's all that matters. // ROSA: No, it matters where. The middle is the weakest part. It had nothing underneath to hold it up. // MR. KIM: (smiling) That's exactly what engineers do, Rosa. They study failures to find out why something didn't work. // DEV: (slowly lowering his hands) So... if we added triangles under the middle, like on that bridge we saw in the book... // ROSA: (excited, grabbing a pencil) Triangles! They don't bend out of shape. We could build a truss! // MR. KIM: Teams who want to rebuild have until Friday. // DEV: (picking up a craft stick and grinning) Friday? We'll be ready by Thursday. // ROSA: (laughing) Let's let the glue dry overnight this time. // (They bend over the desks together, sketching. Lights fade.)

it.q: What is the purpose of the words in parentheses, such as "(nervously)" and "(kneeling to look at the broken pieces)"?
ch: They are stage directions that tell how characters speak and move.
They are lines the actors say aloud.
it.h: Would an actor say these words or act them out?

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: explaining a process and an inventor's life

it.q: According to "How Engineers Solve Problems," what is a prototype?
ch: an early model used to test an idea
the final product sold in stores
it.h: Look at Step 3.

p.x: An engineer is a person who uses science and math to design solutions to problems. Engineers build bridges, design phones, invent medical tools and much more. Although their projects are very different, most engineers follow a similar set of steps called the engineering design process. // Step 1: Define the problem. Engineers start by asking questions. What exactly is the problem? Who has it? What would a good solution need to do? They also list the limits, called constraints, such as how much money they can spend, what materials they can use and how much time they have. // Step 2: Brainstorm and research. Next, engineers gather information and come up with as many ideas as possible. At this stage, no idea is too wild. Often a strange idea leads to a great one. // Step 3: Plan and build a prototype. A prototype is an early model used to test an idea. It does not have to be pretty. Many prototypes are made of cardboard, tape or clay. // Step 4: Test it. Engineers test the prototype to see whether it solves the problem. They measure results and look carefully at what goes wrong. A failure is not the end. It is information. // Step 5: Improve and repeat. Using what they learned, engineers change the design and test again. Most successful inventions go through this cycle many times. That is why the process is often drawn as a circle instead of a straight line. // Think of a team designing a better lunchbox. They might find that the problem is soggy sandwiches. They might try a box with a separate cold section, build one from a shoe box, test it with a real sandwich and discover that the ice pack leaks. Then they would fix the leak and test again. Step by step, the design gets better.

it.q: Which of these is an example of a constraint?
ch: The team can spend only twenty dollars.
The team has a great idea.
it.h: Constraints are limits.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: Greek and Latin roots, precise words and spelling

it.q: The Greek root "tele" means "far," and "scope" means "look at." What does a telescope help you do?
ch: see things that are far away
it.h: Put the two word parts together.

it.q: The Latin root "aud" means "hear." Which word means "able to be heard"?
it.h: Find the word with "aud" in it.

it.q: The Latin root "spect" means "look." What does a spectator do at a game?
it.h: What does a person who looks do?

it.q: Which word is the most precise choice? "The bridge ___ under the weight of the pennies."
it.h: Which word tells exactly what happened?

it.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
it.h: Many nouns that name things people make end with -tion.

it.q: The Latin root "scrib" or "script" means "write." Explain what "describe" and "manuscript" mean.
it.ans: To describe something is to tell or write about it in detail. A manuscript is a book or paper written by hand or typed before it is printed.
it.h: Think about how each word is connected to writing.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text: explaining how an invention works

it.q: When explaining how an invention works, a writer should
ch: describe its parts and the steps in which they work together
give an opinion about its color
it.h: Readers want to understand the process.

it.q: Which sentence best introduces an explanation of how a can opener works?
ch: A hand-held can opener uses a sharp wheel and a gear to cut a lid open in just a few turns.
it.h: Which introduction names the topic and the main idea?

it.q: Which transition shows that two parts work at the same time?
it.h: Which phrase means "simultaneously"?

it.q: Which sentence uses a precise verb?
ch: The gear grips the rim of the can.
The gear is on the can.
it.h: Which verb shows exactly what happens?

it.q: Which feature would help readers understand the parts of a pencil sharpener?
it.h: A picture with labels shows parts.

it.q: Write two sentences explaining how a zipper closes, using a transition word.
it.ans: First, the slider pulls the two rows of teeth toward each other. Then the teeth lock together, closing the zipper.
it.h: Use "first," "then" or "as."

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: the engineering design process

it.q: What is the first step in the engineering design process?
it.h: Engineers must know what they are solving.

it.q: What is a prototype?
ch: an early model built to test an idea
the final product sold in stores
it.h: "Proto-" means first.

it.q: Read: "The team's first bridge sagged in the middle, so they added a triangle-shaped support and tested it again." What step of the design process does this show?
it.h: What did they do after the test showed a problem?

it.q: What are constraints in an engineering problem?
ch: limits, such as cost, time or materials
the parts that make it look nice
it.h: Constraints are things the design must work within.

it.q: Which text structure best describes the engineering design process?
ch: sequence, often repeating in a cycle
it.h: The steps happen in an order and may repeat.

it.q: Why do engineers often test their designs more than once?
it.ans: Each test can show problems, so engineers improve the design and test again until it works well.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Inventors and Problem Solvers (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: theme in a story about a young inventor

it.q: How can readers find a story's theme?
ch: by thinking about what the main character learns and how they change
by looking at the page numbers
it.h: Themes often come from a character's lesson.

it.q: Read: "Every time her robot fell over, Nadia wrote down what went wrong." What trait does this show?
it.h: She keeps trying and learning.

it.q: Which statement is a theme?
ch: Failure can teach us how to succeed.
it.h: A theme is a lesson in a complete sentence.

it.q: Read: "Grandpa watched Jun's tangled wires and said nothing. He simply handed Jun a notebook." What can you infer about Grandpa?
ch: He wants Jun to figure things out and keep track of his ideas.
He does not care about Jun.
He wants Jun to stop inventing.
He is angry about the mess.
it.h: Why give a notebook instead of an answer?

it.q: Which detail would best support the theme "Great ideas often come from noticing others' problems"?
ch: Mai saw her grandmother struggle to open jars and designed a gripping tool.
it.h: Which detail connects an idea to someone else's problem?

it.q: Explain the difference between a story's topic and its theme. Give an example.
it.ans: A topic is what the story is about, like inventing. A theme is the lesson about life, like "Mistakes are part of learning."
it.h: One is a word or phrase; the other is a message.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: comparing themes in tales from different cultures

it.q: Why can't the crow drink at first in "The Crow and the Pitcher"?
ch: The water is at the bottom of a narrow pitcher, and her beak cannot reach it.
it.h: Reread what the crow sees when she peers inside.

p.t: Two Tales of Drops and Pebbles
p.x: TALE 1: THE CROW AND THE PITCHER (a fable from ancient Greece, retold) // On a hot summer day, a crow was so thirsty that her wings drooped. At last she spotted a tall clay pitcher in a farmyard. She flew down and peered inside. There was water at the bottom, but the pitcher was narrow and deep, and her beak could not reach it. // The crow tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy. She pecked at its side, but the clay was too hard. Many birds would have given up and flown away. Instead, the crow looked around and thought. // Then she picked up a pebble and dropped it into the pitcher. Plop. She dropped in another, and another. With each pebble, the water rose a tiny bit. The crow worked all afternoon, one pebble at a time, until at last the water rose high enough for her to drink. // Little by little does the trick. // TALE 2: THE HUMMINGBIRD (a story told in South America, retold) // One day, a fire broke out in a great forest. The animals fled to the edge of the trees and watched in horror as the flames spread. The jaguar, the bear and the tapir stood frozen. "It is hopeless," they said. "The fire is too big." // But a tiny hummingbird flew to the river, scooped up a single drop of water in her beak and flew back to drop it on the flames. Then she did it again, and again. // The bigger animals laughed at her. "What do you think you are doing? You are too small. Your drops will never stop this fire!" // Without stopping, the hummingbird answered, "I am doing the best I can." // The Kenyan environmental leader Wangari Maathai, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004, often told this story. She said it reminded her that everyone can do something to help, no matter how small.

it.q: How does the crow finally reach the water?
ch: She drops in pebbles one at a time until the water rises.
She breaks the pitcher with her beak.
it.h: Reread the third paragraph of the first tale.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: reasons, evidence and solutions

it.q: What is the main idea of "California's Water Puzzle"?
ch: California faces several water challenges, and people are working on many solutions.
Drip irrigation is the only solution.
it.h: Read the first and last paragraphs.

p.x: California has some of the richest farmland and biggest cities in the country. It also has a water puzzle that is hard to solve. // The first piece of the puzzle is that California's rain and snow are unpredictable. Some winters bring huge storms that flood rivers. Others bring so little rain that the state falls into drought, a long period of dry weather. From 2012 to 2016, California suffered one of the worst droughts in its history. In April 2015, the Sierra Nevada snowpack measured only about 5 percent of its usual amount. That year, for the first time, the governor ordered cities and towns across the state to cut their water use by 25 percent. // The second piece is groundwater, the water stored underground in layers of soil and rock. During droughts, farmers and towns pump more groundwater to make up for the missing rain. But when too much water is pumped out, the ground above can actually sink. In parts of the San Joaquin Valley, the land has sunk by many feet over the past century, damaging roads, bridges and canals. In 2014, California passed a law requiring local areas to manage their groundwater so that it is not used up. // The third piece is the large number of people. Almost 40 million people live in California, and all of them need water for drinking, cooking and washing. Farms, businesses and wildlife need water, too. // People are working on many solutions. Some cities clean and reuse wastewater. Some capture storm water so it soaks back into the ground. Farmers are switching to drip irrigation, which delivers water straight to plant roots. And families are replacing thirsty lawns with native plants that need little water. // No single answer will solve California's water puzzle. But each piece of the solution helps the pieces fit together.

Others bring so little rain that the state falls into drought, a long period of dry weather. From 2012 to 2016, California suffered one of the worst droughts in its history. In April 2015, the Sierra Nevada snowpack measured only about 5 percent of its usual amount. That year, for the first time, the governor ordered cities and towns across the state to cut their water use by 25 percent. // The second piece is groundwater, the water stored underground in layers of soil and rock. During droughts, farmers and towns pump more groundwater to make up for the missing rain. But when too much water is pumped out, the ground above can actually sink. In parts of the San Joaquin Valley, the land has sunk by many feet over the past century, damaging roads, bridges and canals. In 2014, California passed a law requiring local areas to manage their groundwater so that it is not used up. // The third piece is the large number of people. Almost 40 million people live in California, and all of them need water for drinking, cooking and washing. Farms, businesses and wildlife need water, too. // People are working on many solutions. Some cities clean and reuse wastewater. Some capture storm water so it soaks back into the ground. Farmers are switching to drip irrigation, which delivers water straight to plant roots. And families are replacing thirsty lawns with native plants that need little water. // No single answer will solve California's water puzzle. But each piece of the solution helps the pieces fit together.

it.q: Choose one solution from "California's Water Puzzle" and explain how it helps solve part of the problem.
it.ans: Drip irrigation delivers water straight to plant roots, so farmers waste less water and need to pump less groundwater, which helps keep the land from sinking.
it.h: Connect the solution to one of the problems.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: proverbs, formal and informal English, and reference materials

it.q: What does the proverb "Don't count your chickens before they hatch" mean?
ch: Don't plan on something good before it actually happens.
it.h: Think about what might happen if some eggs never hatch.

it.q: A crow drops pebbles into a pitcher one at a time until the water rises high enough to drink. Which saying best fits the crow?
ch: Slow and steady wins the race.
Two heads are better than one.
The early bird catches the worm.
it.h: Which saying is about patient, steady work?

it.q: Which sentence uses formal English, the kind used in a letter to a city council?
ch: I am writing to ask the council to build a community garden.
Hey, you guys should totally build a garden.
it.h: Formal English uses complete sentences and polite words.

it.q: Which situation calls for informal English?
ch: texting a friend about a soccer game
giving a report to the class
writing a letter to the mayor
it.h: Informal English is for relaxed talk with people you know well.

it.q: A dictionary entry says: "con-serve (verb) 1. to protect from loss or waste. 2. to keep fruit with sugar." Which meaning fits "We must conserve water"?
ch: to protect from loss or waste
it.h: Which meaning makes sense with water?

it.q: Rewrite this informal sentence in formal English: "Our lawn is, like, super thirsty and it's kinda wasting water."
it.ans: Our lawn needs a great deal of water, and it wastes much of the water we use.
it.h: Remove the slang and use complete, polite language.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion using evidence from two texts about water

it.q: When writing an opinion from two texts, a writer should
ch: use evidence from both texts to support reasons
use only one text and ignore the other
copy both texts word for word
it.h: Strong writers combine information.

it.q: Text A says showers use less water than baths. Text B says fixing leaky faucets saves water. Which opinion could both texts support?
ch: Families can save water with small changes at home.
it.h: What do both texts suggest about saving water?

it.q: Which sentence correctly gives credit to a source?
ch: In "Every Drop Counts," the author explains that a dripping faucet can waste many gallons a week.
Faucets drip a lot, I guess.
it.h: Name the text, then give the information.

it.q: Which linking phrase best connects evidence from a second text?
ch: Similarly, the second article states that
it.h: Which phrase shows the second text agrees?

it.q: Which sentence explains evidence instead of only repeating it?
ch: This means that small changes by many families can add up to a big difference.
it.h: Explanation tells why the evidence matters.

it.q: Write a sentence combining these two facts to support the opinion "Schools should save water": Fact 1, "Low-flow faucets use less water." Fact 2, "Schools use water in many sinks every day."
it.ans: Because schools use water in many sinks every day, switching to low-flow faucets, which use less water, could save a large amount.
it.h: Show how the two facts connect.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: where California's water comes from

it.q: What is snowpack?
ch: layers of snow that build up in the mountains during winter
a kind of glacier in the desert
it.h: Think about snow piling up high in the mountains.

it.q: What is an aqueduct?
ch: a channel or pipe that carries water a long distance
it.h: "Aqua" means water.

it.q: What is a reservoir?
ch: a lake, often made by a dam, where water is stored
it.h: It stores water for later.

it.q: A map shows most of California's rain and snow falls in the north, but many people live in the south. What problem does this create?
ch: Water must be moved long distances from north to south.
The south has too much rain.
No one needs water in the south.
it.h: Compare where the water is with where the people are.

it.q: What is groundwater?
ch: water stored underground in soil and rock
it.h: Wells pump it up.

it.q: Explain why a winter with little snow in the Sierra Nevada can cause problems the next summer.
it.ans: Melting snow fills rivers and reservoirs in spring and summer, so with little snow, there is less water for people and farms during the dry months.
it.h: Think about when the snow melts.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Comparing two texts with different views on solving water shortages

it.q: When two texts on the same topic disagree, a careful reader should
ch: compare the reasons and evidence each author gives
it.h: Look at how well each author supports the point.

it.q: Author A writes, "New reservoirs will store more water for dry years." What is Author A's point?
ch: Building reservoirs is a good solution.
Saving water is the best solution.
it.h: What does Author A want?

it.q: Which is evidence, not just an opinion?
ch: A study found that homes with new water-saving toilets used less water each year.
Saving water is the right thing to do.
it.h: Evidence can be checked.

it.q: Author B says saving water is cheaper than building reservoirs. Which detail would best support this?
ch: Cost reports comparing water-saving programs with the price of building a dam
it.h: Which detail compares costs?

it.q: Two articles both describe a drought. One is by a farmer, and one is by a city water planner. Why might their points of view differ?
ch: They have different needs and experiences with water.
One of them is always wrong.
it.h: Think about how each person uses water.

it.q: Explain why it is helpful to read more than one text about a problem before forming an opinion.
it.ans: Different texts give different reasons and evidence, so reading several helps you understand the whole problem and make a fair, well-supported opinion.
it.h: Think about seeing a problem from more than one side.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Water in California: Making Choices (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Presenting an opinion: speaking clearly with evidence and formal language

it.q: What is formal English?
ch: careful, polite language used in school reports and presentations
it.h: Think about how you would speak to a city council.

it.q: Which sentence for a presentation to the principal is the most formal?
ch: I recommend that our school install water bottle refill stations.
We gotta get those water things.
it.h: Which sentence avoids slang?

it.q: Which action makes a presentation easier to understand?
ch: speaking clearly at an understandable pace
reading very fast in a quiet voice
it.h: Listeners need time to understand.

it.q: Why should a speaker include facts in an opinion presentation?
ch: Facts make the opinion more convincing.
Facts are not allowed in speeches.
it.h: Audiences want reasons they can trust.

it.q: Which is the best way to end a presentation?
ch: restate the opinion and the main reasons
it.h: The ending reminds listeners of your point.

it.q: Rewrite this informal sentence in formal English for a presentation: "Leaky sprinklers waste a ton of water, so somebody's gotta fix 'em."
it.ans: Leaky sprinklers waste a great deal of water, so they should be repaired.
it.h: Replace slang with exact words.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Facing Challenges (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: theme and how characters respond to challenges

it.q: Why did Malia quit the ocean swim last summer in "Count the Strokes"?
ch: A wave hit her face, and she panicked.
She got a cramp in her leg.
Her uncle told her to stop.
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.x: Last summer, Malia had quit the junior lifeguard tryout two hundred yards into the ocean swim. A wave had slapped her in the face, salt water had burned her throat, and she had panicked and waved for the rescue board. She still remembered the long, embarrassing walk up the sand while the other kids cheered for the finishers. // This year, she was going to finish. // Every morning at six, before school, Uncle Keoni drove her to the community pool. The water was cold enough to make her gasp. She swam laps until her shoulders burned, and Uncle Keoni sat on the bleachers with a stopwatch and a thermos of coffee. // "You're thinking too far ahead," he told her one morning, when she stopped at the wall, panting. "You keep thinking, 'Five hundred yards. Five hundred yards.' That's too big to swim. Count your strokes instead. One, two, three, breathe. Just swim the stroke you're on." // Malia rolled her eyes. It sounded too simple. But the next day she tried it, and somehow the laps went faster. // On tryout day, the ocean was gray and choppy. A flag snapped on the lifeguard tower. Malia stood at the edge of the water with forty other kids, her heart pounding so hard she could feel it in her ears. // The whistle blew. She ran into the waves and dove. // The first wave hit her just as it had last year. Salt water stung her nose. For one terrible second, she felt the old panic rising in her chest, and her arms wanted to stop. // One, she thought. Two. Three. Breathe. // She swam the stroke she was on. Then the next one. She did not look at the buoy or think about how far away the beach was. She counted, and breathed, and counted again. When she finally rounded the last buoy and saw the shore, she was surprised. She had stopped counting yards so long ago that she had forgotten to be afraid. // When her feet touched sand, Uncle Keoni was standing at the water's edge, his coffee forgotten in the sand. // "Well?" he asked. // Malia was too out of breath to talk. She held up one finger, then two, then three, and grinned.

it.q: Which quotation best shows how much last year's failure still bothers Malia?
ch: "She still remembered the long, embarrassing walk up the sand while the other kids cheered for the finishers."
"The water was cold enough to make her gasp."
"A flag snapped on the lifeguard tower."
it.h: Look for a feeling that lasted a whole year.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Facing Challenges (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: two main ideas and summarizing

it.q: What are the two main ideas of "Ellen Ochoa: Reaching for Space"?
ch: the power of education and the importance of trying again after hearing no
her flute music and her trips to Houston
the space shuttle and Earth's atmosphere
her childhood home and her school friends
it.h: The author states them in the first paragraph.

p.x: When Ellen Ochoa was growing up in La Mesa, California, in the 1960s and 1970s, there were no women astronauts. Today she is known as the first Hispanic woman to go to space. Her story shows two important ideas: the power of education and the importance of trying again after hearing "no." // Ochoa's mother raised five children mostly on her own. Even so, she took college classes for many years, a few at a time, because she believed learning never had to stop. Ochoa later said that watching her mother study showed her how much education mattered. Ochoa did well in school, especially in math and science, and she was also a talented flute player. In college she studied physics, and then she earned advanced degrees in electrical engineering from Stanford University. As a researcher, she helped invent optical systems, ways of using light to inspect objects and process images, and she received patents for her work. // The second idea in Ochoa's story is persistence. While she was studying at Stanford, she learned that NASA was choosing new astronauts and that some of them would be scientists. She applied. She was not chosen. She kept working, earned her pilot's license and applied again. Finally, in 1990, NASA selected her. // In April 1993, Ochoa flew aboard the space shuttle Discovery on a mission to study Earth's atmosphere. She brought her flute and played it while orbiting the planet. Over the next several years, she flew three more missions, spending nearly 1,000 hours in space. Later she became director of NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she led the people who train astronauts and run missions. // Ochoa often visits schools to talk with students. Her message is simple: study hard, find what you love and do not give up the first time someone says no.

it.q: Which detail supports the main idea about education?
ch: Ochoa's mother took college classes for many years while raising five children.
She played her flute in space.
it.h: Which detail is about learning?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Facing Challenges (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: conjunctions, prepositions, interjections and context clues

it.q: Which word in this sentence is an interjection? "Wow, the swimmer reached the buoy!"
it.h: An interjection shows sudden feeling.

it.q: Which word in this sentence is a conjunction? "Hana was scared, but she kept climbing."
it.h: A conjunction joins words or ideas.

it.q: Which word in this sentence is a preposition? "Malia swam toward the buoy."
it.h: A preposition shows how a noun relates to other words, often by location or direction.

it.q: Which conjunction best completes the sentence? "Ochoa was not chosen the first time, ___ she worked harder and applied again."
it.h: The second idea is a result of the first.

it.q: Read: "The 1901 glider was a disappointment; it rose far less than the brothers had hoped." What does "disappointment" mean?
ch: something that does not meet your hopes
it.h: Use the words after the semicolon.

it.q: Write a sentence about a challenge that uses an interjection, a conjunction and a preposition. Label each one.
it.ans: "Oops, I fell off my bike, but I got back on at the park." Interjection: Oops. Conjunction: but. Preposition: at.
it.h: Start with a word such as "Oh" or "Whew."

lessons.u: Unit 1: Facing Challenges (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: pacing, dialogue and transitions

it.q: What does pacing mean in a narrative?
ch: how quickly or slowly the events are told
the order of the characters' names
it.h: Writers speed up some parts and slow down others.

it.q: A writer wants to slow down the moment a character steps onto a stage. Which sentence does that best?
ch: Her shoes squeaked on the boards, the lights burned her eyes, and a thousand faces blurred together as she took one breath, then another.
it.h: More detail stretches out a moment.

it.q: Which transition best signals a change in time?
it.h: Which phrase tells when?

it.q: Which line of dialogue reveals a character's worry?
ch: "What if the rope snaps?" Elias asked, his voice cracking.
it.h: Look for words and actions that show worry.

it.q: Which sentence correctly uses an interjection?
ch: Wow, the view from the top was incredible!
Wow the view, from the top was incredible.
The view wow from the top.
The view from the top was wow incredible!
it.h: An interjection is followed by a comma or an exclamation point.

it.q: Write a sentence that speeds up the pace of a story by summarizing a long period of time.
it.ans: For the next three weeks, Nora practiced every afternoon until the song felt as natural as breathing.
it.h: Cover a lot of time in a few words.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Facing Challenges (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: how a narrator's perspective shapes a challenge story

it.q: What is a narrator's perspective?
ch: the narrator's attitude and feelings about the events
the time of day the story happens
it.h: Two narrators might describe the same event very differently.

it.q: Read: "The new coach made us run laps for no reason. I could tell she didn't like any of us." How might the narrator's perspective affect the description?
ch: The narrator may be unfair, because the coach might have reasons the narrator does not see.
The narrator knows exactly what the coach thinks.
it.h: Can the narrator know what the coach thinks?

it.q: Which detail shows a narrator's perspective changing?
ch: "By the end of the season, I understood why she made us run."
it.h: Look for a new understanding.

it.q: A story about a hard hike is told by a narrator who loves the outdoors. How might it differ if told by a narrator who hates hiking?
ch: The second narrator might focus on blisters and complaints instead of the views.
The events would be completely different.
Both would describe it the same way.
it.h: Perspective shapes what details a narrator notices.

it.q: Which statement is a theme about challenges?
ch: Facing a hard task can show us strengths we did not know we had.
it.h: A theme is a lesson in a full sentence.

it.q: Read: "Everyone said the math test was easy. Of course they did; they weren't the ones who had missed a week of school." Describe the narrator's perspective.
it.ans: The narrator feels frustrated and a bit resentful, because missing a week of school made the test hard for them even though others found it easy.
it.h: How does the narrator feel compared with everyone else?

it.q: What are Marco and Lucia arguing about in "The Case of the Vanishing Sugar"?
ch: whether sugar disappears when it is stirred into lemonade
it.h: Reread the opening lines.

p.t: The Case of the Vanishing Sugar
p.x: It started with an argument over lemonade. // "The sugar disappears," said Marco, stirring the pitcher until the last white grains swirled out of sight. "Poof. Gone. That's why you can't see it." // His cousin Lucia shook her head. "It can't just disappear. Then why does the lemonade taste sweet?" // "Because it disappeared into sweetness," Marco said, as if that settled it. // Lucia did not think it settled anything. Marco liked to decide things quickly and loudly. Lucia liked to check. Their grandmother, who was slicing lemons at the counter, smiled the way she did when she knew something they didn't. // "Why don't you test it?" Abuela said. "My kitchen scale is in the drawer." // Lucia pulled out the scale and a clean glass. She poured in water and wrote down the mass: 250 grams. Then she measured 30 grams of sugar into a small dish. // "If the sugar disappears," she said, "then when I mix them, the glass will still weigh 250 grams." // "Obviously," said Marco. // Lucia poured in the sugar and stirred until the water was clear again. She set the glass back on the scale. Marco leaned so close his nose almost touched the display. // 280 grams. // Marco frowned. "The scale is broken." // "Then let's test the scale," said Lucia. She weighed a can of beans, which the label said held 425 grams. The scale read 425. // Marco was quiet for a long moment. "So the sugar is still in there," he said slowly. "We just can't see it." // "The pieces got too small to see," Abuela said. "They spread out all through the water. But nothing was lost. Matter doesn't vanish just because our eyes give up looking for it." // Marco grabbed a second glass. "Okay, but what about salt? Does salt do the same thing? And what if we use hot water?" // Lucia laughed and handed him the notebook. "Now you're thinking like a scientist." // "No," Marco said, already reaching for the salt, "now I'm thinking like you."

ch: "Marco liked to decide things quickly and loudly. Lucia liked to check."
"Lucia pulled out the scale and a clean glass."
"Their grandmother, who was slicing lemons at the counter, smiled."
it.h: Look for a sentence that describes both cousins.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Properties of Matter (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: explaining relationships between scientific ideas

it.q: What are two main ideas of "Too Small to See"?
ch: Matter is made of tiny particles, and the way the particles move explains the states of matter.
Basketballs need air, and bread smells good.
Ice is cold, and water is wet.
Microscopes are useful, and puddles dry quickly.
it.h: Look for ideas that are explained across several paragraphs.

p.x: Everything around you, from the air you breathe to the chair you sit on, is made of matter. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. But here is a surprising fact: all matter is made of particles far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope. // You can't see these particles, but you can find evidence that they exist. Think about what happens when you inflate a basketball. You pump in air, which you cannot see, and the ball becomes firm. The air particles push against the inside of the ball from every direction. Or think about the smell of baking bread spreading through a house. Tiny particles from the bread travel through the air until some reach your nose. // The way particles are arranged and how they move explain the three common states of matter. In a solid, such as an ice cube, the particles are packed tightly and can only vibrate in place. That is why a solid keeps its own shape. In a liquid, such as water, the particles are close together but can slide past one another, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. In a gas, such as water vapor, the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, so a gas spreads out to fill any container. // When matter changes state, the particles themselves do not change. Ice, liquid water and water vapor are all made of the same water particles. Heating makes the particles move faster and spread apart; cooling makes them slow down and move closer together. // Scientists have also found that when matter changes state or is mixed, the total mass stays the same. If you melt a 10-gram ice cube in a sealed bag, you will have 10 grams of water. The particles are all still there. They have only moved. // So the next time something seems to disappear, such as a puddle drying in the sun, remember: the particles have not vanished. They have simply spread out where your eyes can't follow.

it.q: How does the example of a basketball give evidence that particles exist?
ch: Air we cannot see makes the ball firm by pushing against it.
it.h: Reread the second paragraph.

Think about what happens when you inflate a basketball. You pump in air, which you cannot see, and the ball becomes firm. The air particles push against the inside of the ball from every direction. Or think about the smell of baking bread spreading through a house. Tiny particles from the bread travel through the air until some reach your nose. // The way particles are arranged and how they move explain the three common states of matter. In a solid, such as an ice cube, the particles are packed tightly and can only vibrate in place. That is why a solid keeps its own shape. In a liquid, such as water, the particles are close together but can slide past one another, so a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. In a gas, such as water vapor, the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions, so a gas spreads out to fill any container. // When matter changes state, the particles themselves do not change. Ice, liquid water and water vapor are all made of the same water particles. Heating makes the particles move faster and spread apart; cooling makes them slow down and move closer together. // Scientists have also found that when matter changes state or is mixed, the total mass stays the same. If you melt a 10-gram ice cube in a sealed bag, you will have 10 grams of water. The particles are all still there. They have only moved. // So the next time something seems to disappear, such as a puddle drying in the sun, remember: the particles have not vanished. They have simply spread out where your eyes can't follow.

it.q: Use "Too Small to See" to explain what happens to a puddle that "dries up" in the sun.
it.ans: The sun's heat makes the water particles move faster and spread apart until the liquid water becomes water vapor, a gas. The particles have not vanished; they have spread into the air where we cannot see them.
it.h: Use what the article says about heating and gases.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Properties of Matter (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: perfect verb tenses and Greek and Latin affixes

it.q: Which sentence uses the present perfect tense?
it.h: The present perfect uses "has" or "have" plus a past participle.

it.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense?
ch: The ice had melted before the bell rang.
The ice melts before the bell rings.
it.h: The past perfect uses "had" plus a past participle.

it.q: Which sentence uses the future perfect tense?
ch: By noon, the puddle will have evaporated.
By noon, the puddle has evaporated.
By noon, the puddle had evaporated.
it.h: The future perfect uses "will have" plus a past participle.

it.q: The suffix "-able" means "able to be." What does "breakable" mean?
it.h: Combine the meaning of the suffix with the base word.

it.q: The prefix "trans-" means "across" or "through." What does "transparent" describe?
ch: something light can pass through, so you can see through it
it.h: Think about what light does with a clear window.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence in the past perfect tense: "The cousins tested the scale." Then explain what the past perfect shows.
it.ans: "The cousins had tested the scale." The past perfect shows that an action was finished before another past action or time.
it.h: Use "had" plus the past participle.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Properties of Matter (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text: explaining a science investigation

it.q: What does a hypothesis state?
ch: a testable prediction about what will happen in an investigation
it.h: It often uses "If... then..."

it.q: Which hypothesis is testable?
ch: If salt is added to water, then the water will freeze at a lower temperature.
it.h: Can it be checked by an experiment?

it.q: Which transition best introduces the results of an investigation?
ch: On the other hand, I feel
it.h: Results tell what happened.

it.q: Which sentence uses precise, domain-specific language?
ch: The sugar dissolved completely in the warm water within two minutes.
The sugar went away in the water.
it.h: Look for exact science words and numbers.

it.q: What is a variable in an investigation?
ch: a factor that can change or be changed
it.h: Scientists change one thing at a time.

it.q: Write a conclusion sentence for this investigation: "Ice cubes in sunlight melted in 12 minutes. Ice cubes in shade melted in 25 minutes."
it.ans: The investigation showed that sunlight makes ice melt faster, because the cubes in sunlight melted in less than half the time of those in shade.
it.h: State what the data shows and use the numbers.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Properties of Matter (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: physical and chemical changes

it.q: What is a physical change?
ch: a change in size, shape or state that does not make a new substance
a change that creates a new substance
a change in a person's mood
it.h: Melting ice is still water.

it.q: Which is a chemical change?
it.h: Which change makes a new substance?

it.q: Read: "When baking soda and vinegar mix, bubbles of gas form. The gas is a new substance." What kind of change is this?
it.h: A new substance formed.

it.q: Which clue usually signals a chemical change?
ch: a new color, gas, light or heat that was not there before
it.h: Think about what you observe when something burns.

it.q: Read: "The ice cube melted, but its mass stayed the same." What does this show?
ch: Matter is not lost in a physical change.
Ice gains mass when it melts.
it.h: The mass stayed the same.

it.q: Explain why toasting bread is a chemical change, but slicing bread is a physical change.
it.ans: Toasting changes the bread into new substances, shown by browning and a new smell. Slicing only changes its shape; it is still the same bread.
it.h: Ask whether a new substance forms.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Properties of Matter (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading data in a science text: mixtures and solutions

it.q: What is a mixture?
ch: two or more substances combined that keep their own properties
it.h: Trail mix is a good example.

it.q: What is a solution?
ch: a mixture in which one substance dissolves evenly into another
a mixture you can easily pick apart
a new substance formed by burning
it.h: Salt water is an example.

it.q: Which tool would best separate iron filings from sand?
it.h: Iron is attracted to magnets.

it.q: A table shows: water at 20 degrees C dissolved 36 grams of salt; water at 80 degrees C dissolved 38 grams of salt. What does the data show?
ch: Temperature had only a small effect on how much salt dissolved.
Salt does not dissolve in water.
it.h: Compare 36 and 38.

it.q: How could you separate salt from salt water?
ch: pour it through a coffee filter
freeze the salt out with ice cubes
it.h: What is left behind when water dries up?

it.q: Explain why a salad is a mixture but not a solution.
it.ans: The salad's ingredients keep their own properties and can be picked apart, and nothing dissolves evenly, so it is a mixture but not a solution.
it.h: Can you see and separate the parts?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ecosystems and Food Webs (informative writing)

it.q: What does Nora find at the beginning of "Tracks in the Snow"?
ch: large wolf tracks beside the creek
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.x: Nora found the tracks on the last day of winter break, pressed into the snow beside the creek behind her grandfather's ranch in northeastern California. Each print was bigger than her whole hand, with four toe pads and claw marks in front. // She ran to get Grandpa Walt. He crouched beside the tracks for a long time without saying anything. Then he took off his hat and rubbed his head. // "Wolf," he said. // Nora's heart jumped. She had read about gray wolves. They had been gone from California for most of a century, hunted and trapped until none were left. Now a few had wandered back from Oregon. She had never imagined one would walk past her own creek. // "That's amazing," she whispered. // Grandpa did not look amazed. He looked worried. "We've got forty head of cattle and six new calves in the lower pasture," he said. "Your great-grandfather used to say a wolf can wipe out a rancher's year in one night." // At dinner, the argument started. Nora's older cousin Jesse, who was studying wildlife biology in college, said wolves keep deer and elk herds healthy by hunting weak and sick animals. Grandpa said that was easy to say for someone who didn't have to pay for a dead calf. Nora's mother said there were programs that helped ranchers protect their herds. Nora mostly listened. // The next morning, Jesse showed up with a roll of bright red flags on a long rope. "It's called fladry," he said. "Wolves are cautious about new things. Hang this around the calving pasture, and they'll usually stay away. Not forever, but it helps." // Grandpa frowned at the flags flapping in the wind. "Looks like a used-car lot," he grumbled. But he helped string it up anyway, and he moved the calves closer to the barn at night. // Weeks went by. The calves grew. The tracks came back twice, circling the edge of the flagged pasture and then heading up into the hills. // One evening in March, Nora and Grandpa stood on the porch and heard it: a long, low howl rolling down from the ridge. Nora held her breath. // Grandpa listened until the sound faded. "Well," he said finally, "I suppose there's room for both of us. As long as he minds his manners." // Nora smiled. It was the closest thing to a welcome she had ever heard him give.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ecosystems and Food Webs (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: text structures and relationships in ecosystems

it.q: According to "Following the Energy," where does the energy in almost every ecosystem begin?
it.h: Read the first paragraph.

p.x: Every living thing needs energy to grow, move and stay alive. In almost every ecosystem on Earth, that energy begins with the sun. // Plants, algae and some bacteria are called producers because they make their own food. Using energy from sunlight, along with water and carbon dioxide from the air, they produce sugars that store energy. A blade of grass, an oak tree and the tiny green algae floating in a pond are all producers. // Animals cannot make their own food, so they are called consumers. They get energy by eating other living things. A grasshopper that munches on grass is a primary consumer because it eats producers. A frog that eats the grasshopper is a secondary consumer. A hawk that eats the frog may be a third-level consumer. // Scientists show these feeding relationships with diagrams. A food chain is a single path: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then hawk. Arrows point from the living thing that is eaten to the living thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy moves. But most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real ecosystems look more like a food web, many food chains linked together. In a web, a hawk might eat frogs, mice and snakes, and a mouse might eat seeds and insects. // At each step along a chain, most of the energy is used up. Animals use energy to move, breathe and keep warm, and much of it escapes as heat. Only about a tenth of the energy at one level is passed on to the next. That is why there are far more plants than plant eaters in an ecosystem, and far more plant eaters than top predators. // Finally, decomposers such as fungi, worms and bacteria break down dead plants and animals. They return nutrients to the soil, where producers can use them again. Without decomposers, dead material would pile up, and the soil would run out of the nutrients plants need.

it.q: Why are plants called producers?
ch: They make their own food using energy from sunlight.
They are at the top of the food chain.
it.h: Look at the second paragraph.

it.q: How is the paragraph about primary, secondary and third-level consumers mainly structured?
ch: in sequence, following energy from one living thing to the next
as a story told by a frog

p.x: Every living thing needs energy to grow, move and stay alive. In almost every ecosystem on Earth, that energy begins with the sun. // Plants, algae and some bacteria are called producers because they make their own food. Using energy from sunlight, along with water and carbon dioxide from the air, they produce sugars that store energy. A blade of grass, an oak tree and the tiny green algae floating in a pond are all producers. // Animals cannot make their own food, so they are called consumers. They get energy by eating other living things. A grasshopper that munches on grass is a primary consumer because it eats producers. A frog that eats the grasshopper is a secondary consumer. A hawk that eats the frog may be a third-level consumer. // Scientists show these feeding relationships with diagrams. A food chain is a single path: grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then hawk. Arrows point from the living thing that is eaten to the living thing that eats it, showing the direction the energy moves. But most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real ecosystems look more like a food web, many food chains linked together. In a web, a hawk might eat frogs, mice and snakes, and a mouse might eat seeds and insects. // At each step along a chain, most of the energy is used up. Animals use energy to move, breathe and keep warm, and much of it escapes as heat. Only about a tenth of the energy at one level is passed on to the next. That is why there are far more plants than plant eaters in an ecosystem, and far more plant eaters than top predators. // Finally, decomposers such as fungi, worms and bacteria break down dead plants and animals. lessons.u: Unit 3: Ecosystems and Food Webs (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: verb tenses for time and sequence, tense shifts and word relationships

it.q: Which sentence correctly keeps the verb tense the same?
ch: The hawk circled the field and dove at a mouse.
The hawk circled the field and dives at a mouse.
The hawk circles the field and dove at a mouse.
The hawk will circle the field and dove at a mouse.
it.h: Both actions happened in the past.

it.q: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in verb tense?
ch: Nora finds the tracks and ran to get Grandpa.
Nora found the tracks and ran to get Grandpa.
Nora finds the tracks and runs to get Grandpa.
Nora will find the tracks and run to get Grandpa.
it.h: Look for a sentence that mixes present and past for no reason.

it.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "If the urchins ___ the kelp, the fish will lose their shelter."
it.h: The second part uses "will," so the "if" part uses the present tense.

it.q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "By next summer, the kelp ___ back on the cleared reefs."
it.h: The action will be finished before a time in the future.

it.q: Which pair of words is related as producer and consumer?
it.h: One makes its own food; the other eats it.

it.q: Correct the inappropriate shift in tense: "Hollis stopped hunting, and the mice multiply quickly." Explain your change.
it.ans: "Hollis stopped hunting, and the mice multiplied quickly." Both actions happened in the past, so both verbs should be in the past tense.
it.h: Make both verbs show the same time.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ecosystems and Food Webs (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text about a food web with precise vocabulary

it.q: What is a producer in a food web?
ch: a living thing that makes its own food, usually from sunlight
an animal that eats only meat
a living thing that breaks down dead matter
it.h: Plants are producers.

it.q: Which sentence correctly uses the word "consumer"?
ch: A rabbit is a consumer because it eats plants for energy.
Grass is a consumer of sunlight.
it.h: Consumers eat other living things.

it.q: Which transition best shows the flow of energy from one organism to the next?
it.h: Which phrase means "next in a chain"?

it.q: Which sentence explains an idea with a cause and effect?
ch: If the number of mice drops, the owls that eat them may go hungry.
it.h: Look for "if... then" thinking.

it.q: Which is the best definition of "decomposer" to include in a report?
ch: an organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks down dead plants and animals
a predator that hunts at night
it.h: Decomposers recycle nutrients.

it.q: Write a sentence that explains how energy moves from the sun to a hawk.
it.ans: Energy from the sun is captured by grass, which is eaten by a grasshopper, which is eaten by a snake, which is eaten by a hawk.

ch: break down dead plants and animals
it.h: They are nature's cleanup crew.

it.h: Fungi are decomposers.

it.q: Where can readers find clues to a story's theme?
ch: in what characters learn, how they change and what the conflict reveals
it.h: Themes grow from the whole story.

it.q: Read: "At first, Omar thought one person picking up trash could not matter. Then he saw ten neighbors join him." What theme is suggested?
ch: Small actions can inspire others and grow into big change.
it.h: What did Omar learn?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Voyages and Encounters (opinion writing)

it.q: What does Kalani believe about her grandfather's stories at the beginning of "The Navigator's Granddaughter"?
ch: She thinks they are just stories.
She thinks they are completely true.
She thinks they are about the mall.
it.h: Reread the first two paragraphs.

p.x: Kalani had always thought her grandfather's stories were just stories. He told them on the porch after dinner: tales of canoes that crossed thousands of miles of open ocean, guided by nothing but stars, waves and birds. "No compass," he would say, tapping his chest. "No map. Everything you need is here, and up there." // Kalani, who used a phone to find her way to the mall, did not believe it. // Then, the summer she turned eleven, Grandpa took her out on a small sailing canoe with his old friend Uncle Moku. They sailed past the reef, beyond sight of land. Kalani clutched the side as the canoe rose and fell. Without the island behind her, every direction looked the same: blue, blue and more blue. // "Which way is home?" Grandpa asked. // Kalani turned in a circle. Her stomach tightened. "I don't know." // "Close your eyes," he said. "Feel the canoe." // She closed them. At first she felt only the rocking. Then she noticed a pattern. Long, slow swells came from one side, lifting the canoe gently, like a breath. Smaller, choppier waves came from another direction. // "The big swells come from far away, from storms we cannot see," Grandpa said. "They are steady, like old friends. If you know where they come from, you know which way you are facing." // That evening, as the sun sank, he showed her how it set in a particular place on the horizon. When the stars came out, he pointed to one rising low in the east. "Each star rises in its own house on the horizon," he said. "Learn the houses, and the sky becomes a compass." // A seabird flew low over the water, heading toward the dark edge of the sky. "Noio," said Uncle Moku. "In the evening they fly home to land." // Kalani watched the bird, then felt the long swell lift the canoe, then looked at the rising star. Three clues, all pointing the same way. // "Home is that way," she said, pointing. // Grandpa smiled so widely that his eyes almost disappeared. "Now," he said, "you know it's not just a story."

it.h: Look for a physical reaction to fear.
