lessons.u: Unit 4: Voyages and Encounters (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: multiple accounts of the same event

it.q: What is the main focus of View 1 in "Two Views of 1492"?
ch: Columbus's daring voyage and its importance in world history
the daily life of the Taino
it.h: Read the title of View 1 and its details.

p.x: VIEW 1: A VOYAGE INTO THE UNKNOWN // On August 3, 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Palos, Spain, with three small ships: the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria. Columbus, an experienced sailor from Genoa, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean. The voyage was daring. For more than a month, the crews saw no land. Food spoiled, sailors grew frightened, and some talked of turning back. Columbus kept them going. On October 12, a lookout spotted land, an island in what is now the Bahamas. Columbus made four voyages across the Atlantic in all. His voyages opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas and began an exchange of plants and animals, as corn, potatoes and tomatoes traveled to Europe and horses and wheat came to the Americas. Many historians see his voyages as one of the turning points of world history. // VIEW 2: THE PEOPLE ON THE SHORE // When Columbus's ships arrived on October 12, 1492, the island was not empty. It was home to the Taino people, who called it Guanahani. The Taino lived in villages across the islands of the Caribbean. They farmed cassava and corn, fished from large canoes and traded among the islands. They greeted the strangers and offered gifts. Columbus, however, believed he had reached Asia and called the people "Indians." In his journal, he wrote that they would make good servants. Within a few years, Spanish settlers forced many Taino to work in mines and fields. Diseases the Europeans carried, such as smallpox, spread among people who had never been exposed to them. Within a few decades, the Taino population had dropped sharply. For many Native people today, 1492 marks the beginning of great loss, which is why some communities, including Los Angeles, now celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day in October.

it.q: What is the main focus of View 2 in "Two Views of 1492"?
ch: the Taino people and how the arrival of Europeans affected them
it.h: Read the title of View 2.

Both present it only as a loss.
View 1 focuses on the Taino, while View 2 focuses on Columbus.
it.h: Compare the last sentence of each view.

p.x: VIEW 1: A VOYAGE INTO THE UNKNOWN // On August 3, 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Palos, Spain, with three small ships: the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria. Columbus, an experienced sailor from Genoa, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean. The voyage was daring. For more than a month, the crews saw no land. Food spoiled, sailors grew frightened, and some talked of turning back. Columbus kept them going. On October 12, a lookout spotted land, an island in what is now the Bahamas. Columbus made four voyages across the Atlantic in all. His voyages opened lasting contact between Europe and the Americas and began an exchange of plants and animals, as corn, potatoes and tomatoes traveled to Europe and horses and wheat came to the Americas. Many historians see his voyages as one of the turning points of world history. // VIEW 2: THE PEOPLE ON THE SHORE // When Columbus's ships arrived on October 12, 1492, the island was not empty. It was home to the Taino people, who called it Guanahani. The Taino lived in villages across the islands of the Caribbean. They farmed cassava and corn, fished from large canoes and traded among the islands. They greeted the strangers and offered gifts. Columbus, however, believed he had reached Asia and called the people "Indians." In his journal, he wrote that they would make good servants. Within a few years, Spanish settlers forced many Taino to work in mines and fields. Diseases the Europeans carried, such as smallpox, spread among people who had never been exposed to them. Within a few decades, the Taino population had dropped sharply. For many Native people today, 1492 marks the beginning of great loss, which is why some communities, including Los Angeles, now celebrate Indigenous Peoples' Day in October.

it.ans: View 1 explains the courage of the voyage and the exchange of crops and animals, while View 2 shows that the island already had people, the Taino, who suffered forced labor and disease. Together they show both the achievement and the cost.
it.h: What would you miss if you read only one view?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Voyages and Encounters (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: correlative conjunctions and Latin roots

it.q: Which pair of words is a set of correlative conjunctions?
it.h: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs.

it.q: Which sentence uses correlative conjunctions correctly?
ch: The sailors could either turn back or keep sailing west.
The sailors could either turn back nor keep sailing west.
The sailors could neither turn back or keep sailing west.
The sailors could both turn back or keep sailing west.
it.h: "Either" goes with "or," and "neither" goes with "nor."

it.q: Which pair completes the sentence? "___ Kalani ___ Uncle Moku could see land."
it.h: The sentence means that no one could see land.

it.q: The Latin root "nav" means "ship." What does "navigate" mean?
ch: to steer or find the way, as a ship's crew does
it.h: Think about what a ship's crew must do.

it.q: The Latin root "mar" means "sea." Which word describes something that has to do with the sea?
it.h: Which word is used for sea animals?

it.q: Combine the sentences using "not only... but also": "The Taino farmed cassava. The Taino fished from large canoes."
it.ans: The Taino not only farmed cassava but also fished from large canoes.
it.h: Put "not only" before the first action and "but also" before the second.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Voyages and Encounters (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion: evaluating an explorer's choices with evidence

it.q: What does it mean to evaluate a historical choice?
ch: to judge whether it was wise or fair using evidence
to retell it without any judgment
it.h: Evaluating means making a judgment.

it.q: Which opinion statement about an explorer is clearest?
ch: The expedition's leader made a risky choice that cost many lives.
it.h: A clear opinion takes a position.

it.q: Which evidence best supports the opinion "The voyage was poorly planned"?
ch: The ships ran out of fresh food months before reaching land, and many sailors became sick.
The captain wrote in a journal.
it.h: Which evidence shows a planning problem?

it.q: Why should an opinion about explorers consider the Indigenous peoples the explorers met?
ch: Their experiences are part of the full story and affect whether a choice was fair.
it.h: A fair opinion looks at everyone affected.

it.q: Which linking phrase best introduces a counterargument?
it.h: A counterargument presents the other side.

it.q: Write a sentence that responds to this counterargument: "The explorer's voyage was worth the risk because it brought new maps and trade."
it.ans: Although the voyage produced new maps and trade, it also caused great harm to the people living in the lands the explorers reached, so the cost was too high.
it.h: Acknowledge the point, then explain your side.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Voyages and Encounters (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: life aboard a sailing ship in the 1500s

it.q: What is a voyage?
ch: a long journey, especially by sea
it.h: Voyages often lasted months.

it.q: Read: "Sailors ate hardtack, a hard, dry biscuit that would not spoil for months." Why was hardtack useful on long voyages?
ch: It was easy to grow on ships.
it.h: Look for the reason in the sentence.

it.q: Read: "Without fresh fruits and vegetables, many sailors developed scurvy." What caused scurvy?
ch: a lack of fresh fruits and vegetables
it.h: What were sailors missing?

it.q: Which tool helped sailors find their direction at sea?
it.h: Its needle points north.

it.q: Read: "The crew grew mutinous after months without sight of land." Using context, what does "mutinous" mean?
ch: ready to rebel against the leaders
it.h: How might a crew act after months of hardship?

it.q: Explain why long voyages in the 1500s were so dangerous. Give two reasons.
it.ans: Food often spoiled or ran out and the lack of fresh food caused scurvy, and storms and getting lost could wreck ships or leave crews without supplies.
it.h: Think about food, health and weather.

it.q: What is a word's origin?
ch: the language and history it came from
it.h: Dictionaries often show this in brackets.

it.q: The word "tomato" comes from "tomatl" in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztec people. What does this tell you?
ch: English borrowed the word from a language spoken in Mexico.
Tomatoes were first grown in England.
Nahuatl is a kind of food.
it.h: Borrowed words keep traces of their source.

it.q: Where in a dictionary entry would you most likely find a word's origin?
it.h: "Etymology" means word history.

it.q: The word "hurricane" came into English through Spanish from the Taino people of the Caribbean. Why might sailors have learned this word?
ch: They encountered powerful storms in the Caribbean and the people who named them.
it.h: Think about where sailors traveled.

it.q: Which word came into English from Nahuatl, through Spanish?
it.h: Think about a food made from cacao beans.

it.q: Explain why many English words come from other languages.
it.ans: As people traveled, traded and met other cultures, they borrowed words for new foods, animals, objects and ideas they had not known before.

it.q: Why does the crocodile invite the monkey to his home in "The Monkey and the Crocodile"?

He wants to show the monkey the river.

Every day he tossed sweet fruit down to a crocodile, and the two became friends. But the crocodile's wife grew jealous. "If that monkey eats such sweet fruit every day," she said, "his heart must be the sweetest thing in the world. Bring it to me." // The crocodile did not want to betray his friend, but he did as his wife asked. "Come to my home for dinner," he told the monkey. "Ride on my back across the river." // Halfway across, in the deepest water, the crocodile confessed. "I am sorry, friend. My wife wants to eat your heart." // The monkey's own heart pounded, but his face stayed calm. "Why didn't you tell me sooner?" he said. "I left my heart up in the rose-apple tree for safekeeping. Take me back, and I will fetch it for her." // The foolish crocodile turned around. The moment they reached the bank, the monkey leaped into the highest branches. "No one can take out a heart and leave it in a tree!" he called down. "Our friendship is over." // TALE 2: RABBIT AND THE BRIAR PATCH (an African American folktale, retold) // Fox had been trying to catch Rabbit for years, and one day he finally did. Fox grabbed Rabbit by the ears and grinned. "I've got you now," he said. "I'm going to roast you over a fire." // Rabbit thought fast. "Roast me, Fox, boil me, do anything you like," he begged, "but please, oh please, don't throw me into that briar patch!" // Fox looked at the thick tangle of thorny bushes beside the road. "Why not?" he asked. // "Those thorns would tear me to pieces!" Rabbit wailed. "Anything but the briar patch!" // Fox thought that sounded like the worst punishment of all. So he swung Rabbit by the ears and flung him deep into the briars. // For a moment, all was quiet. Then Fox heard laughter. lessons.u: Unit 5: Myths and Folktales Across Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how stories travel across cultures

it.q: What are two main ideas of "Tricksters Around the World"?
ch: Many cultures tell trickster tales, and these tales are popular because they entertain and teach lessons.
Spiders are clever, and rabbits are fast.
Coyote created fire, and crocodiles live in rivers.
Stories are short, and children like animals.
it.h: Look at the first and fifth paragraphs.

p.x: In almost every part of the world, people tell stories about a trickster: a clever, mischievous character who uses wit instead of strength. Tricksters break rules, fool powerful enemies and sometimes get tricked themselves. Although each culture's trickster is different, these characters share surprising similarities. // In West Africa, the Ashanti people of Ghana tell tales of Anansi, a spider who outsmarts animals far larger than himself. In one famous story, Anansi wins all the world's stories from the sky god by capturing creatures that seemed impossible to catch. When West Africans were forced across the Atlantic during the slave trade, they carried Anansi stories with them, and today Anansi tales are still told in Jamaica and other Caribbean islands. // In the American South, enslaved Africans and their descendants told stories about Brer Rabbit, a small, quick creature who escapes from stronger animals like Fox and Bear. Many scholars connect Brer Rabbit to the clever hare of African folktales. For people who were denied freedom and power, stories about a small animal who outwits the powerful carried a message of hope and resistance. // Many Native nations of western North America tell stories about Coyote. Coyote can be a creator who brings fire or helps shape the world, and he can also be a greedy fool whose tricks backfire. In Southeast Asia, children in Indonesia and Malaysia hear tales of Kancil, a tiny mouse deer who tricks crocodiles into lining up so he can hop across a river on their backs. // Why are tricksters so popular? One reason is that their stories are funny, and people everywhere enjoy a good laugh. Another is that tricksters often teach lessons, both by succeeding and by failing. When a trickster's greed or pride gets him into trouble, listeners learn what not to do. And when a small creature defeats a bully, listeners are reminded that brains can matter more than size. // These stories have lasted for hundreds of years because people kept telling them, from one generation to the next.

ch: West Africans forced across the Atlantic during the slave trade carried the stories with them.

p.x: In almost every part of the world, people tell stories about a trickster: a clever, mischievous character who uses wit instead of strength. lessons.u: Unit 5: Myths and Folktales Across Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: commas after introductory elements and Greek roots

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory word?
ch: Suddenly, the monkey leaped into the tree.
Suddenly the monkey, leaped into the tree.
Suddenly the monkey leaped, into the tree.
Suddenly the monkey leaped into, the tree.
it.h: Put the comma right after the introductory word.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory phrase?
ch: Halfway across the river, the crocodile confessed.
Halfway, across the river the crocodile confessed.
Halfway across the river the crocodile, confessed.
Halfway across, the river the crocodile confessed.
it.h: Find where the introductory phrase ends.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after an introductory clause?
ch: When Midas touched the bread, it turned to gold.
When Midas touched, the bread it turned to gold.
When Midas touched the bread it, turned to gold.
When, Midas touched the bread it turned to gold.
it.h: An introductory clause has a subject and a verb and comes before the main clause.

it.q: The Greek root "chron" means "time." What does "chronological order" mean?
ch: the order in which events happened in time
it.h: Think of "chron" as time.

it.q: The Greek root "bio" means "life," and "graph" means "write." What is a biography?
ch: a written account of a person's life
it.h: Combine the two root meanings.

it.q: Add a comma where it belongs and explain why: "After many years of telling the stories people wrote them down."
it.ans: "After many years of telling the stories, people wrote them down." The comma sets off the long introductory phrase from the main part of the sentence.
it.h: Where does the introduction end and the main idea begin?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Myths and Folktales Across Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: retelling a traditional tale in a new setting

it.q: When retelling a traditional tale in a new setting, what should a writer keep?
ch: the tale's main problem and lesson
it.h: The heart of the tale stays the same.

it.q: A writer moves "The Tortoise and the Hare" to a modern city. Which change fits best?
ch: The race becomes a bike race through busy streets.
The tortoise becomes the fastest racer from the start.
it.h: Change the setting but keep the problem.

it.q: Which detail best establishes a new setting for an old folktale?
ch: Neon signs flickered above the subway station where the clever fox sold newspapers.
it.h: Which sentence paints a specific new place?

it.q: Which sentence uses dialogue to show a trickster's personality?
ch: "Trust me," Raven grinned, "this shortcut will save you hours."
it.h: How does a trickster talk?

it.q: Which ending keeps the moral of "The Boy Who Cried Wolf" in a modern retelling?
ch: When the real fire alarm sounded, no one believed Leo's texts, because he had joked about it too many times.
Leo moved to a new city.
it.h: The original lesson is about lying.

it.q: Choose a folktale you know. Describe one way you would change the setting while keeping its lesson.
it.ans: I would set "The Ant and the Grasshopper" in a middle school, where the ant studies every night and the grasshopper plays video games until the night before a big test, keeping the lesson about preparing ahead.
it.h: Name the tale, the new setting and the lesson.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Myths and Folktales Across Cultures (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Trickster tales: comparing clever characters across cultures

it.q: What is a trickster in a folktale?
ch: a clever character who uses tricks to get what it wants
it.h: Think about Coyote, Anansi or Br'er Rabbit.

it.q: Trickster characters from different cultures often share which trait?
ch: They are smart but sometimes too sure of themselves.
They are always the biggest animal.
it.h: Think about why tricks sometimes backfire.

it.q: In one tale, a small rabbit outsmarts a strong lion. What message do such tales often share?
ch: Brains can be more powerful than size or strength.
it.h: How does the smaller animal win?

it.q: When comparing two trickster tales, which is the best question to ask?
ch: How do the tricksters' actions and their results compare?
it.h: Compare characters and outcomes.

it.q: A trickster tricks others all through a tale but is tricked at the end. What lesson does this suggest?
ch: People who trick others may be tricked themselves.
It is good to be greedy.
it.h: Think about what happens to the trickster.

it.q: Explain why trickster tales are found in many cultures.
it.ans: People everywhere enjoy stories about clever underdogs, and these tales teach lessons about wit, greed and pride in an entertaining way.
it.h: Think about what makes these stories fun and useful.

it.q: What law makes Mr. Hale angry in "The Stamp"?
ch: the Stamp Act, which taxed printed paper
it.h: Reread the first paragraphs.

p.x: Boston, 1765 // Eli Brooks had been an apprentice in Mr. Hale's print shop for two years, and in all that time he had never seen his master so angry. Mr. Hale slammed a newspaper onto the counter so hard that the type cases rattled. // "A tax on paper," he said. "On every newspaper, every pamphlet, every legal document, even every deck of playing cards! And not one person in Boston voted for it." // Eli wiped ink from his hands and read the headline. Parliament, far away in London, had passed a law called the Stamp Act. Starting in November, printed papers in the colonies would need a stamp from a British official, and the stamp cost money. // "Maybe it won't be so bad," Eli said carefully. "England did protect the colonies in the war against France. Wars cost money." // Mr. Hale's daughter, Abigail, who was setting type at the next table, looked up sharply. "That isn't the point, Eli. The point is who decides. We don't have a single representative in Parliament. If they can tax our paper without asking us, what will they tax next? Our tea? Our bread?" // Eli didn't answer. Abigail was only a year older than he was, but she read every newspaper that came through the shop, and she argued like a lawyer. // Over the next months, Boston boiled. Merchants agreed to stop buying British goods. Crowds marched through the streets shouting, "No taxation without representation!" One night, someone hanged a straw figure of the stamp collector from a tall elm tree. // When November came, Mr. Hale called Eli and Abigail to the press. "We will keep printing," he said quietly, "and we will not buy a single stamp." // Eli's stomach dropped. "But that's against the law." // "It is," said Mr. Hale. "And the law is wrong. Sometimes a person must choose." // Eli thought about it all night. In the morning, he walked to the shop, rolled up his sleeves and began inking the type. Abigail glanced at him and smiled. // In 1766, news arrived from London: Parliament had repealed the Stamp Act. Boston rang its church bells for hours. Eli rang the shop bell too, though he knew, as Abigail said, that this was not the end of the argument. It was only the beginning.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Colonial Life and the Road to Revolution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how authors use reasons and evidence

it.q: What is the main idea of "Common Sense: The Pamphlet That Changed Minds"?
ch: Thomas Paine's pamphlet used clear reasons to convince many colonists to support independence.
Kings should pass power to their children.
it.h: Read the first and last paragraphs.

p.t: Common Sense: The Pamphlet That Changed Minds
p.x: In January 1776, the American colonies had been fighting British soldiers for nine months, yet most colonists still did not want to break away from Great Britain completely. Many hoped the king would listen to their complaints and restore their rights. Then a pamphlet called Common Sense appeared in Philadelphia, and within months it had helped change the minds of thousands. // Its author, Thomas Paine, had arrived from England only about a year earlier. He wrote in plain, forceful language that ordinary people could understand, and he built his argument with a series of reasons. // First, Paine argued that it made no sense for a huge continent to be ruled by a small island across an ocean. He wrote: "Small islands not capable of protecting themselves are the proper objects for kingdoms to take under their care; but there is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island." // Second, Paine pointed to distance. Messages, laws and complaints had to travel about 3,000 miles across the Atlantic and back, a trip that could take months. A government so far away, he said, could never understand or respond to the colonies' needs. // Third, Paine attacked the idea of kings. He argued that passing power from parent to child was foolish, because a wise king might have a foolish son. People, he said, should choose their own leaders. // Fourth, Paine argued that independence would be good for business. Free of Britain, Americans could trade with any nation in the world instead of being dragged into Britain's wars with other countries. // Common Sense sold more than 100,000 copies in its first months, an enormous number at a time when the colonies had about 2.5 million people. It was read aloud in taverns and passed from hand to hand. In April 1776, General George Washington wrote that it was "working a powerful change" in the minds of many men. A few months later, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence.

it.q: Which of Paine's reasons does the quotation from Common Sense support?
ch: It made no sense for a continent to be ruled by a small island.
it.h: Which reason is stated right before the quotation?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Colonial Life and the Road to Revolution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: commas in a series, prefixes and suffixes

it.q: Which sentence about the Stamp Act uses commas correctly in a series?
ch: The tax covered newspapers, pamphlets, and playing cards.
The tax covered newspapers pamphlets, and playing cards.
The tax covered, newspapers, pamphlets and playing cards.
The tax covered newspapers, pamphlets and, playing cards.
it.h: Put a comma after each item in a series except the last.

it.q: Which sentence needs commas to separate items in a series?
ch: Eli inked the type set the paper and pulled the press.
it.h: Look for three or more actions in a row.

it.q: Which sentence about a protest uses commas correctly?
ch: Merchants, farmers, and printers protested the tax.
Merchants farmers, and printers protested the tax.
Merchants, farmers and, printers protested the tax.
Merchants, farmers, and printers, protested the tax.
it.h: Do not put a comma between the last item and the verb.

it.q: The suffix "-ment" turns a verb into a noun. What does "government" mean?
ch: the people and system that govern
it.h: Think "govern" plus "-ment."

it.q: The prefix "mis-" means "wrongly." What does "mistreat" mean?
it.h: Combine the prefix meaning with the base word.

it.q: Add commas to this sentence and explain the rule: "The grievances included unfair taxes soldiers in peacetime and limits on trade."
it.ans: "The grievances included unfair taxes, soldiers in peacetime, and limits on trade." Commas separate three or more items in a series. (The comma before "and" is optional in many styles.)
it.h: How many items are in the list?

it.q: What was a Loyalist?

it.q: What was a Patriot?
ch: a colonist who supported independence from Britain
a colonist who wanted to keep British rule

ch: Britain protected the colonies, and breaking away could lead to war and loss of trade.

it.h: Which phrase adds another reason?

it.q: According to "Langston Hughes: A Voice of Harlem," where did Hughes write "The Negro Speaks of Rivers"?
ch: on the back of an envelope while riding a train across the Mississippi River
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

p.t: Langston Hughes: A Voice of Harlem
p.x: In 1920, a teenager named Langston Hughes was riding a train across the Mississippi River on his way to visit his father in Mexico. As the sun set over the wide, muddy water, he thought about the rivers that had shaped the history of Black people: the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi. On the back of an envelope, he wrote a poem. It ended with a line that would be quoted for the next hundred years: "My soul has grown deep like the rivers." // "The Negro Speaks of Rivers" was published in 1921 in The Crisis, a magazine founded by the civil rights leader W. E. B. Du Bois. It was the beginning of an extraordinary career. // Hughes was born in Missouri in 1901 and was raised mostly by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas. She told him stories of the fight against slavery, and he spent hours in the library. Books, he later said, became a refuge for him. // In the 1920s, Hughes moved to Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City that had become a center of Black culture. Writers, painters and musicians filled its streets and clubs with new ideas. This creative explosion became known as the Harlem Renaissance. Hughes listened closely to the music around him, especially jazz and the blues, and he brought their rhythms into his poems. His first book of poetry, The Weary Blues, was published in 1926. // While many poets of his time wrote about elegant, faraway subjects, Hughes wrote about ordinary people: elevator operators, mothers, workers and children. He used everyday language so that anyone could read his work. He also wrote plays, stories, essays and books for young people. // Hughes died in 1967. Today, his poems are taught in schools across the country, and his home in Harlem has been honored as a landmark. His writing helped readers see the dignity, struggles and dreams of people whose voices had too often been ignored.

p.x: In 1920, a teenager named Langston Hughes was riding a train across the Mississippi River on his way to visit his father in Mexico. As the sun set over the wide, muddy water, he thought about the rivers that had shaped the history of Black people: the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi. On the back of an envelope, he wrote a poem. It ended with a line that would be quoted for the next hundred years: "My soul has grown deep like the rivers." // "The Negro Speaks of Rivers" was published in 1921 in The Crisis, a magazine founded by the civil rights leader W. E. B. Du Bois. It was the beginning of an extraordinary career. // Hughes was born in Missouri in 1901 and was raised mostly by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas. She told him stories of the fight against slavery, and he spent hours in the library. Books, he later said, became a refuge for him. // In the 1920s, Hughes moved to Harlem, a neighborhood in New York City that had become a center of Black culture. Writers, painters and musicians filled its streets and clubs with new ideas. This creative explosion became known as the Harlem Renaissance. Hughes listened closely to the music around him, especially jazz and the blues, and he brought their rhythms into his poems. His first book of poetry, The Weary Blues, was published in 1926. // While many poets of his time wrote about elegant, faraway subjects, Hughes wrote about ordinary people: elevator operators, mothers, workers and children. He used everyday language so that anyone could read his work. He also wrote plays, stories, essays and books for young people. // Hughes died in 1967. Today, his poems are taught in schools across the country, and his home in Harlem has been honored as a landmark. His writing helped readers see the dignity, struggles and dreams of people whose voices had too often been ignored.

it.q: According to the article, how was Hughes different from many poets of his time?
ch: He wrote about ordinary people in everyday language instead of elegant, faraway subjects.
He refused to publish his poems.
it.h: Reread the fifth paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Figurative Language (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: figurative language and commas with yes, no, tag questions and direct address

it.q: Which sentence contains hyperbole?
ch: I'm so hungry I could eat a whole mountain of tacos.
The tacos are like small boats.
it.h: Hyperbole is an extreme exaggeration.

it.q: Which sentence uses a metaphor?
ch: My little sister is a ball of energy.
My little sister is as energetic as a puppy.
My little sister has a lot of energy.
it.h: A metaphor says one thing is another, without "like" or "as."

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly with a person's name in direct address?
ch: Grandma, can you show me how to thread the needle?
Grandma can you, show me how to thread the needle?
Grandma can you show me, how to thread the needle?
Grandma can you show me how to thread, the needle?
it.h: Set off the name of the person being spoken to with a comma.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly with a tag question?
ch: You read that poem, didn't you?
You read that poem didn't, you?
You read, that poem didn't you?
You, read that poem didn't you?
it.h: Put the comma before the short question at the end.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after "no"?
ch: No, I haven't finished my haiku yet.
No I haven't, finished my haiku yet.
No I, haven't finished my haiku yet.
No I haven't finished my, haiku yet.
it.h: Put the comma right after "yes" or "no" at the start of a sentence.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses personification to describe the wind, and explain what human quality you gave it.
it.ans: "The wind whispered secrets through the trees." I gave the wind the human ability to whisper and share secrets.
it.h: Personification gives human qualities to something that is not human.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Figurative Language (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing with figurative language: crafting a poem and a descriptive scene

it.q: What is a simile?
ch: a word that imitates a sound
it.h: "Brave as a lion" is an example.

it.q: Which line is a metaphor?
ch: The classroom was a beehive of activity.
The classroom was as busy as a beehive.
it.h: A metaphor says one thing is another.

it.q: Which line uses personification?
ch: The old house groaned in the wind.
The old house was like a ghost.
The old house was near a lake.
it.h: Which object acts like a person?

it.q: Which line uses onomatopoeia?
ch: The rain went pitter-patter on the tin roof.
it.h: Which word imitates a sound?

it.q: Which revision makes this line more vivid? "The sun was hot."
ch: The sun pressed down like a heavy iron on the dusty road.
The sun was hot and bright.
it.h: Use a comparison and specific details.

it.q: Write one line of poetry about the ocean that uses a metaphor.
it.ans: The ocean is a restless giant, rolling over in its sleep.
it.h: Say the ocean IS something else.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Poetry and Figurative Language (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading a poem: speaker, imagery and structure in "Grandmother's Hands"

it.q: Who is the speaker of a poem?
it.h: The speaker may be different from the poet.

it.q: What is imagery?
ch: language that appeals to the senses to create pictures in the reader's mind
the number of lines in a poem
it.h: Images help you see, hear, smell, taste or feel.

it.q: Read: "Her laughter was a bowl of warm rice." What does this metaphor suggest about the laughter?
it.h: How does a bowl of warm rice make you feel?

it.q: How do stanzas help organize a poem?
ch: Each stanza can focus on one idea, moment or image.
Stanzas are only for long poems.
it.h: Think of stanzas like paragraphs.

it.q: A poem's last stanza repeats the first line with one word changed. What is the likely purpose?
ch: to show how the speaker's understanding has changed
it.h: Think about what the changed word might show.

it.q: Read: "The kitchen hummed with steam and stories." Explain what this line suggests about the kitchen.
it.ans: It suggests the kitchen is warm and busy, full of cooking and family members sharing stories, which makes it lively and welcoming.
it.h: Think about "hummed," "steam" and "stories."

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth and Space (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: setting, character and theme in stories about the sky

it.q: Why is Ines disappointed when she arrives at the star party in "The Rings of Saturn"?
it.h: Reread the second paragraph.

p.x: Ines had been waiting all year for the star party in Borrego Springs. Every spring, astronomers brought their telescopes to the desert, where the town kept its lights dim so the night sky stayed dark. Her grandfather had promised that this year she could see Saturn. // But when they arrived after sunset, a thin layer of clouds stretched across the sky like gauze. // "Of course," Ines groaned. "The one night that matters." // Grandpa Ramon unfolded two camping chairs. "The sky does not keep our calendar," he said. "We wait." // Around them, people were setting up telescopes of every size: little ones on tripods, a long white tube as big as a water heater, and one homemade telescope built from a cardboard tube and plywood. A woman in a red headlamp was adjusting it. "My father built this in 1978," she told Ines. "He ground the mirror himself, by hand. It took him a whole winter." // Ines couldn't believe that a telescope made of cardboard could work. She sat back down in her chair and stared at the blank gray sky. Time crawled. A coyote yipped somewhere far away. Grandpa told her the names of the constellations they would have seen if the clouds weren't there, tracing invisible shapes with his finger. // At ten-thirty, a cool breeze rose from the west. Slowly, the clouds frayed and drifted apart, and the stars came through, first one, then dozens, then so many that the sky looked dusted with sugar. A long, pale band stretched from one edge of the sky to the other. "The Milky Way," Grandpa whispered. "Our own galaxy, seen from the inside." // The woman in the red headlamp waved them over. "Saturn's up," she called. // Ines bent to the eyepiece of the cardboard telescope. For a moment she saw only black. Then, there it was: a tiny, perfect golden ball wrapped in a thin ring, floating in the dark like a toy someone had hung on a string. It was so small, and so far away, and so real. // She stepped back and looked at Grandpa, then at the woman, then at the cardboard tube. // "It works," she said, amazed. // "It waited a long time to show you," the woman said. "Some things are worth waiting for."

it.q: What does Grandpa Ramon mean when he says, "The sky does not keep our calendar"?
ch: Nature does not follow people's plans, so they must be patient.
They came on the wrong day.
it.h: What does he say right afterward?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth and Space (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: using information from more than one source

it.q: What is the main idea of "Why the Sun Looks So Bright"?
ch: The sun looks brighter than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.
The sun is the largest star in the universe.
it.h: Read the first sentence of the second paragraph.

p.t: Why the Sun Looks So Bright
p.x: On a clear day, the sun is so bright that you should never look directly at it. At night, the stars are just tiny points of light. You might think the sun must be a special kind of object. In fact, the sun is a star, just like the ones you see at night. // The sun looks so much bigger and brighter because it is so much closer to us. The sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. That sounds far, but the next closest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 25 trillion miles away, more than 250,000 times farther. Light from the sun reaches Earth in about eight minutes. Light from Proxima Centauri takes more than four years. // Distance changes how bright an object appears. Think about a flashlight. Up close, its beam can make you squint. Seen from across a football field at night, the same flashlight is only a small dot. The flashlight has not changed; only the distance has. In the same way, many stars that look dim to us are actually larger and brighter than the sun. They are simply much, much farther away. // FACT BOX: STARS COMPARED // The sun: about 93 million miles away; a medium-sized, yellowish star. // Proxima Centauri: the nearest star to the sun, about 4.2 light-years away; smaller and dimmer than the sun; too faint to see without a telescope. // Sirius: the brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light-years away; about twice as massive as the sun and about 25 times as bright. // Betelgeuse: a red supergiant star in the constellation Orion, hundreds of light-years away; so large that, if it took the sun's place, it would stretch far beyond the orbit of Mars. // A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, about 6 trillion miles.

it.q: Why does the author compare the sun to a flashlight?
ch: to show that distance changes how bright something appears
to show that the sun is small
it.h: What changes and what stays the same in the flashlight example?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth and Space (informative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: titles of works, reference materials and Greek roots

it.q: Which title should be written in quotation marks instead of italics or underlining?
ch: a poem titled Stars at Midnight
a book titled The Lost Comet
a magazine titled Space Kids Monthly
a movie titled Journey to Mars
it.h: Short works, such as poems, songs and articles, go in quotation marks.

it.q: When you type the title of a book in a report, how should you show it?
it.h: Long, whole works are typed in italics or handwritten with underlining.

it.q: The Greek root "astro" means "star," and "naut" means "sailor." What is an astronaut?
ch: a person who travels into space
it.h: Combine the two root meanings.

it.q: The Greek root "tele" means "far," and "scope" means "look at." What is a telescope used for?
it.h: Combine the two root meanings.

it.q: Which reference source would best tell you how to pronounce "Betelgeuse"?
it.h: Which source shows how words sound?

it.q: Explain how to write each title correctly in a typed report: a book called The Planets Up Close and a chapter in it called Rings of Ice.
it.ans: The book title is written in italics because a book is a long, whole work. The chapter title goes in quotation marks, "Rings of Ice," because a chapter is a short part of a larger work.
it.h: Think about which title names a whole work and which names a part.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth and Space (informative writing)
lessons.n: Writing an informative text using several sources about space

it.q: Why should a writer use several sources for an informative report?
ch: to gather more information and check that facts are accurate
so they can copy more text
because one source is never enough words
it.h: Sources can confirm each other.

it.q: Two sources give different distances from Earth to the moon. What should a writer do?
ch: check a third reliable source, such as a NASA website
it.h: Look for an expert source.

it.q: Which note correctly summarizes information in the writer's own words?
ch: Mars - red color from iron-rich dust - called "Red Planet"
"Mars is often called the Red Planet because of the iron oxide on its surface."
I want to go to Mars
it.h: Notes are short and paraphrased.

it.q: Which is the best way to organize a report comparing two planets?
ch: by features, such as size, temperature and moons, discussing both planets for each
by writing only about one planet
it.h: Comparison works best feature by feature.

it.q: Which sentence correctly names its source within a report about planets?
ch: According to NASA, Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system.
it.h: Name the source.

it.q: Write a sentence that combines these two facts from different sources: Source A, "Venus is about the same size as Earth." Source B, "Venus's thick clouds trap heat, making it the hottest planet."
it.ans: Although Venus is about the same size as Earth, its thick clouds trap heat, making it the hottest planet in the solar system.
it.h: Use a connecting word to join the ideas.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Earth and Space (informative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: why Earth has seasons

it.q: What is Earth's axis?
ch: an imaginary line through Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole
the path Earth travels around the sun
it.h: Earth spins around it.

it.q: What causes the seasons on Earth?
ch: the tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the sun
the sun getting bigger and smaller
it.h: Think about which half of Earth leans toward the sun.

it.q: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, what season is it there?
it.h: More direct sunlight means warmer weather.

it.q: When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, what season is it in the Southern Hemisphere?
it.h: The two hemispheres lean in opposite directions.

it.q: Read: "In summer, the sun's rays strike the ground more directly." What does "directly" mean here?
ch: straight on, at a steep angle
it.h: Think about shining a flashlight straight down.

it.q: A student says Earth has summer because it is closest to the sun then. Explain why this is incorrect.
it.ans: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis, not distance. In fact, Earth is closest to the sun in early January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
it.h: Think about when the Northern Hemisphere has winter.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Drama and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading literature: drama, scenes and characters' points of view

it.q: What is the conflict at the beginning of "The Group Project"?
ch: Maya and Amir disagree about how to present their water cycle project.
Maya is sick and cannot finish.
it.h: Read the narrator's first lines and the first few lines of dialogue.

p.x: CAST: MAYA; AMIR; MS. DELACROIX, their teacher; NARRATOR // SETTING: A fifth-grade classroom. Two desks are pushed together. On them lies a half-finished poster about the water cycle. // NARRATOR: It is Thursday afternoon. The water cycle projects are due tomorrow. Maya and Amir have been partners for two weeks, and for two weeks they have not agreed on anything. // (MAYA is carefully coloring a raindrop. AMIR bursts in, holding a shoebox.) // AMIR: (excited) Forget the poster! I built a model! Look, a real cloud made of cotton balls, and when you pull this string, glitter rain falls out! // MAYA: (without looking up) Ms. Delacroix said a poster. A poster has labels and arrows. A shoebox has glitter. // AMIR: (setting the box down with a thump) A poster is boring. Nobody remembers a poster. // MAYA: (finally looking up, frustrated) Nobody can read a shoebox! DELACROIX walks over.) // MS. DELACROIX: (calmly) I couldn't help overhearing. Maya, tell me what you think the project needs. // MAYA: (sighing) Clear information. lessons.u: Unit 9: Drama and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how theater works, then and now

it.q: According to "The Globe: A Theater for Everyone," when was the Globe Theatre first built?
it.h: Look in the second paragraph.

p.t: The Globe: A Theater for Everyone
p.x: More than four hundred years ago, in London, England, crowds packed into a round wooden building on the south bank of the River Thames. They came to see plays by William Shakespeare, who is now considered one of the greatest writers in the English language. The building was called the Globe Theatre. // The Globe was built in 1599 by Shakespeare's acting company. It had three levels of covered seating arranged in a circle around an open yard. The stage stuck out into the yard, so the audience surrounded the actors on three sides. There was no roof over the yard, so plays were performed in the afternoon, using daylight instead of stage lights. // The Globe was a theater for people of every class. Wealthy people paid more to sit in the covered galleries, where they stayed dry and could be seen by others. For just one penny, ordinary workers could stand in the yard right next to the stage. These standing audience members were called groundlings. They were known for being lively. They cheered heroes, booed villains and sometimes threw nutshells when they were bored. // Because there were few sets and no electric lights, Shakespeare used words to create the setting. A character might say that it was a dark, stormy night, and the audience would imagine it. In Shakespeare's time, women were not allowed to perform on the English stage, so young men and boys played the female characters. // In 1613, during a performance, a cannon fired as a special effect set the thatched roof on fire, and the Globe burned to the ground. No one was killed. The theater was rebuilt the next year, but it was closed in 1642, when the government shut down London's theaters. // Hundreds of years later, an American actor named Sam Wanamaker worked to rebuild the Globe. A new version opened in 1997, close to the original site. Today, audiences can once again stand in the yard as groundlings and watch Shakespeare's plays the way people did four centuries ago.

ch: The yard had no roof, so plays used daylight instead of stage lights.
Actors worked other jobs at night.
The groundlings went to sleep early.
it.h: Reread the second paragraph.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Drama and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: idioms, proverbs, homographs and dialect in drama

it.q: What does the idiom "break a leg" mean when said to an actor before a show?
it.h: Actors say it to each other before they go on stage.

it.q: What does the adage "Actions speak louder than words" mean?
ch: What people do shows more about them than what they say.
it.h: Compare actions and words.

it.q: "Amir got cold feet before his speech." What does "got cold feet" mean?
ch: became nervous and wanted to back out
it.h: How might someone feel right before a speech?

it.q: Which sentence uses "bow" to mean bending forward at the waist?
ch: The actors took a bow at the end of the play.
She tied a red bow in her hair.
He shot an arrow from his bow.
The violinist moved her bow across the strings.
it.h: Homographs are spelled the same but have different meanings.

it.q: Which word is an antonym of "reluctant"?
it.h: Reluctant means not wanting to do something.

it.q: In a play, a character from a small farm town says, "Y'all best come in 'fore the storm hits." Explain why a playwright might write the dialogue this way instead of "You should all come inside before the storm arrives."
it.ans: The playwright uses dialect, the way people speak in a certain region or group, to make the character sound real and to show where the character is from.
it.h: Think about what the words tell you about the character.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Drama and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Writing a scene for a play: dialogue, stage directions and conflict

it.q: How is a play script different from a story?
ch: It uses characters' names, dialogue and stage directions instead of a narrator.
it.h: Think about how a script looks on the page.

it.q: Which line is formatted correctly for a play script?
ch: MAYA: (slamming the door) I told you not to touch my project!
Maya slammed the door and yelled at him.
Maya: I told you not to touch my project! said Maya.
it.h: Character name, colon, stage directions in parentheses, then the words.

it.q: What is the purpose of stage directions?
ch: to tell actors how to move, speak or act
to tell the audience when to clap
it.h: They guide the actors.

it.q: Which stage direction best shows a character is nervous?
ch: (fidgeting with her sleeve and avoiding eye contact)
it.h: How does nervousness look?

it.q: What creates conflict in a scene?
ch: characters who want different things or face a problem
it.h: Conflict drives a play forward.

it.q: Write two lines of dialogue with stage directions that show two friends disagreeing about which game to play.
it.ans: LUIS: (crossing his arms) We played soccer yesterday. It's my turn to pick. / KEIKO: (rolling her eyes) Your turn means another hour of board games!
it.h: Show the disagreement through what they say and do.

lessons.u: Unit 9: Drama and Point of View (narrative writing)
lessons.n: Reading a drama: how scenes build conflict and resolution

it.q: How do scenes in a play work together?
ch: Each scene adds to the plot, building toward the climax and resolution.
Each scene is a separate story.
it.h: Think of scenes like chapters.

it.q: Why might a playwright end a scene at a tense moment?
ch: to make the audience eager to see what happens next
it.h: Think about cliffhangers.

it.q: Read: "(Lights dim. Two weeks later.)" What does this stage direction show?
it.h: Look for a time clue.

it.q: What is the resolution of a play?
ch: how the conflict is settled at the end
it.h: It comes after the climax.

it.q: Two characters in a play describe the same event differently. What does this show?
ch: One of them is not in the play.
it.h: Different people notice different things.

it.q: Explain how a stage direction can reveal something that a character does not say aloud.
it.ans: A stage direction like "(She hides the letter behind her back)" shows the audience a secret or feeling that the character keeps from others in the dialogue.
it.h: Think about actions versus words.

it.q: Why do the windows of the State House stay closed all summer in "The Summer of Closed Windows"?
ch: The delegates promised to keep their discussions secret.
The guards are afraid of flies.
it.h: Reread what Sarah's mother says.

p.x: This is a work of historical fiction. // Philadelphia, 1787 // All summer long, the windows of the State House stayed shut. Sarah Morris noticed it every afternoon as she carried pies from her mother's bakery past the brick building on Chestnut Street. It was the hottest summer anyone could remember. Horses drooped in the streets. Flies buzzed everywhere. Yet inside the State House, the windows were closed tight, and guards stood at the doors. // "Why do they keep them shut?" Sarah asked her mother. // "Secrecy," Mother said. "The delegates promised not to tell anyone what they say until they are finished. They're writing new rules for the whole country, and they don't want rumors flying before they agree." // The delegates often came into the bakery afterward, red-faced and wilted, wiping their foreheads with handkerchiefs. They never discussed their work. But one evening in July, two of them sat by the window, and their voices rose. // "It is simple fairness," said a tall man from Virginia. "A state with more people should have more votes in Congress." // "Fairness!" said a short man from Delaware. "Then the big states will swallow the small ones whole. Every state should have an equal vote, as we do now." // Sarah set down their tea and lingered, pretending to wipe the next table. It reminded her of her own brothers arguing over a single slice of cake: the older one said he deserved more because he was bigger, and the younger one said that halves were halves. // A few days later, the bakery was buzzing with a different mood. The two men came in together and even laughed. Sarah could not help herself. "Did someone win?" she asked. // The Delaware man smiled. "Nobody won, miss. Everybody gave a little. That's the trick of it." // In September, the windows finally opened, and the news spread through the city. The delegates had signed a new plan of government called the Constitution. People said that Dr. Benjamin Franklin, the oldest delegate, had told the others he used to wonder whether the sun painted on the back of George Washington's chair was rising or setting. Now, he said, he knew it was a rising sun. // That night, Sarah cut the last slice of cake exactly in half and handed one piece to each of her brothers. "Everybody gives a little," she said. They both stared at her. She just smiled.

it.q: What do the two delegates in the bakery disagree about?
ch: whether states with more people should have more votes in Congress
where to build the State House
it.h: Reread the conversation by the window.

it.q: What is the main idea of "Why a New Plan Was Needed"?
ch: The weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation led leaders to write the Constitution.
Rhode Island did not send delegates.
it.h: Which choice covers the whole article?

p.t: Why a New Plan Was Needed
p.x: After winning independence, the thirteen states needed a way to work together. Their first plan of government was called the Articles of Confederation, approved in 1781. The Articles created a very weak national government on purpose. Americans had just fought a war against a powerful king, and many feared that a strong central government might take away their rights. // But the weaknesses soon caused serious problems. First, Congress had no power to collect taxes. It could only ask the states for money, and the states often refused. Without money, the national government could not pay its debts or the soldiers who had fought in the Revolution. Second, Congress could not control trade between the states, so states taxed one another's goods and argued constantly. Third, each state had one vote in Congress, no matter its size, and important laws needed the approval of nine of the thirteen states. Changing the Articles required all thirteen to agree, which almost never happened. // In 1786 and 1787, a crisis showed how weak the government was. In Massachusetts, farmers who were losing their land because of debts and taxes rose up in a protest that became known as Shays' Rebellion. The national government had no army to stop it, and Massachusetts had to raise its own soldiers. Many leaders worried that the young nation might fall apart. // In May 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia. Rhode Island refused to send anyone. The delegates had been asked only to fix the Articles, but they soon decided to write an entirely new plan. George Washington was chosen to lead the meeting. James Madison of Virginia, who had studied governments throughout history, came with so many ideas that he is often called the "Father of the Constitution." // After four months of debate, on September 17, 1787, thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution. It created a stronger national government that could collect taxes, control trade and make laws, while still protecting the powers of the states and the rights of the people.

ch: They feared a strong central government might take away their rights, as the king had.
They had no money to build one.
They did not want a Congress at all.
it.h: Reread the first paragraph.

Many leaders worried that the young nation might fall apart. // In May 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia. Rhode Island refused to send anyone. The delegates had been asked only to fix the Articles, but they soon decided to write an entirely new plan. George Washington was chosen to lead the meeting. James Madison of Virginia, who had studied governments throughout history, came with so many ideas that he is often called the "Father of the Constitution." // After four months of debate, on September 17, 1787, thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution. It created a stronger national government that could collect taxes, control trade and make laws, while still protecting the powers of the states and the rights of the people.

it.q: How did Shays' Rebellion show the weakness of the national government?
ch: The national government had no army to stop the uprising, so Massachusetts had to raise its own soldiers.
The national government taxed the farmers.
it.h: Reread the third paragraph.

p.t: Why a New Plan Was Needed
p.x: After winning independence, the thirteen states needed a way to work together. Their first plan of government was called the Articles of Confederation, approved in 1781. The Articles created a very weak national government on purpose. Americans had just fought a war against a powerful king, and many feared that a strong central government might take away their rights. // But the weaknesses soon caused serious problems. First, Congress had no power to collect taxes. It could only ask the states for money, and the states often refused. Without money, the national government could not pay its debts or the soldiers who had fought in the Revolution. Second, Congress could not control trade between the states, so states taxed one another's goods and argued constantly. Third, each state had one vote in Congress, no matter its size, and important laws needed the approval of nine of the thirteen states. Changing the Articles required all thirteen to agree, which almost never happened. // In 1786 and 1787, a crisis showed how weak the government was. In Massachusetts, farmers who were losing their land because of debts and taxes rose up in a protest that became known as Shays' Rebellion. The national government had no army to stop it, and Massachusetts had to raise its own soldiers. Many leaders worried that the young nation might fall apart. // In May 1787, delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia. Rhode Island refused to send anyone. The delegates had been asked only to fix the Articles, but they soon decided to write an entirely new plan. George Washington was chosen to lead the meeting. James Madison of Virginia, who had studied governments throughout history, came with so many ideas that he is often called the "Father of the Constitution." // After four months of debate, on September 17, 1787, thirty-nine delegates signed the Constitution. It created a stronger national government that could collect taxes, control trade and make laws, while still protecting the powers of the states and the rights of the people.

it.q: How is "Why a New Plan Was Needed" mainly organized?
ch: as causes and effects, explaining problems with the Articles and how they led to the Constitution
as a story from Madison's point of view
as a comparison of two countries
it.h: Look for words such as "because," "so" and "showed."

it.ans: Congress could not collect taxes, so it could not pay its debts or the soldiers who fought in the Revolution. Congress also could not control trade between the states, so states taxed one another's goods and argued constantly.
it.h: Name each weakness, then its effect.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Building a New Nation: The Constitution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Word study and conventions: combining, expanding and reducing sentences, spelling and roots

it.q: Which sentence best combines these two sentences? "The delegates met in Philadelphia. They met in 1787."
ch: The delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787.
The delegates met in Philadelphia, they met in 1787.
In 1787 the delegates met and they met in Philadelphia.
it.h: Combine the ideas without repeating words.

it.q: Which sentence expands "Washington led the meeting" with the most useful detail?
ch: George Washington, a hero of the Revolution, led the meeting in Philadelphia.
Washington led the meeting, and he led it.
Washington really led the meeting a lot.
it.h: Look for added details that tell who, where or why.

it.q: Which revision best reduces this wordy sentence? "The delegates who were at the convention decided at that time to write a plan that was new."
ch: The delegates at the convention decided to write a new plan.
The delegates who were at the convention at that time decided to write a new plan that was new.
At the convention, the delegates, who were there, decided to write a plan.
it.h: Remove words that repeat ideas, but keep the meaning.

it.q: The Greek root "dem" means "people," and "cracy" means "rule" or "government." What is a democracy?
it.h: Combine the meanings of the two roots.

it.q: Which word meaning "the people and system that rule a country" is spelled correctly?
it.h: Listen for the "n" before "-ment."

it.q: Combine these sentences into one clear sentence: "The Senate has two senators from each state. The House has members based on population. Both are part of Congress."
it.ans: Congress includes the Senate, which has two senators from each state, and the House, which has members based on population.
it.h: Use "which" or "and" to join the ideas.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Building a New Nation: The Constitution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Writing an opinion: which right in the Bill of Rights matters most

it.q: What is the Bill of Rights?
ch: the first ten amendments to the Constitution
it.h: It was added to protect individual rights.

it.q: Which freedom is protected by the First Amendment?
ch: the right to a free car
the right to vote at age 12
it.h: The First Amendment protects expression.

it.q: Which opinion statement is clearest?
ch: Freedom of the press is the most important right because it keeps citizens informed.
The Bill of Rights has ten amendments.
it.h: Which statement takes a position and hints at a reason?

it.q: Which evidence best supports the opinion "Freedom of speech protects democracy"?
ch: When people can criticize leaders openly, problems can be discussed and fixed.
Speech is done with the mouth.
it.h: Connect speech to how a democracy works.

it.q: Which linking phrase best introduces a counterargument?
it.h: Which phrase signals another viewpoint?

it.q: Write a sentence explaining why the right to a fair trial is important.
it.ans: The right to a fair trial is important because it protects people from being punished unfairly without evidence and a chance to defend themselves.
it.h: Think about what could happen without it.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Building a New Nation: The Constitution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: three branches and checks and balances

it.q: Which branch of government makes the laws?
it.h: Congress is part of this branch.

it.q: Which branch carries out and enforces the laws?
it.h: The president leads this branch.

it.q: Which branch interprets laws and decides if they follow the Constitution?
it.h: The Supreme Court is part of this branch.

it.q: What is the purpose of checks and balances?
ch: to keep any one branch from becoming too powerful
to give the president all power
to let courts make every law
it.h: Each branch can limit the others.

it.q: Which is an example of a check?
ch: The president can veto, or reject, a bill passed by Congress.
The Supreme Court has nine justices.
The president lives in the White House.
it.h: Which action limits another branch?

it.q: Why did the writers of the Constitution divide power among three branches?
it.ans: They had lived under a king with too much power, so they divided power to protect people's rights and prevent any one person or group from ruling unfairly.
it.h: Think about their experience with the British king.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Building a New Nation: The Constitution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading a primary source: the Preamble to the Constitution

it.q: What is the Preamble?
ch: the introduction to the Constitution that states its purposes
it.h: "Pre-" means before.

it.q: What do the opening words "We the People" suggest?
ch: The government's power comes from the people.
The king gives the people power.
Only leaders wrote the Constitution for themselves.
it.h: Who is "we"?

it.q: In the Preamble, "establish Justice" means
ch: create a fair system of laws and courts
it.h: Justice means fairness.

it.q: Read: "insure domestic Tranquility." What does "domestic" mean here?
it.h: Think about the opposite of foreign.

it.q: "Posterity" in the Preamble most likely means
it.h: The framers wanted liberty for "ourselves and our Posterity."

it.q: Choose one goal from the Preamble and explain it in your own words.
it.ans: "Provide for the common defence" means the government should protect the country from attacks by other nations.
it.h: Restate the phrase with everyday words.

lessons.u: Unit 10: Building a New Nation: The Constitution (opinion writing)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: amending the Constitution and the Bill of Rights

it.q: What is an amendment?
ch: a change or addition to the Constitution
it.h: "Amend" means to change.

it.q: How many amendments are in the Bill of Rights?
it.h: It is a round number.

it.q: Why did some leaders refuse to support the Constitution until a bill of rights was promised?
ch: They feared a strong national government might take away individual rights.
They thought the Constitution was too short.
They wanted to stay part of Britain.
it.h: Think about what a bill of rights protects.

it.q: Why is it difficult to amend the Constitution?
ch: It requires approval from large majorities in Congress and the states.
Only the president can do it.
Any one citizen can change it.
it.h: The framers wanted changes to have wide support.

it.q: Read: "The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, protected women's right to vote." What does "ratified" mean?
it.h: An amendment becomes part of the Constitution when it is ratified.

it.q: Explain why the framers made it possible to amend the Constitution.
it.ans: They knew the country would change and that they could not predict every need, so they created a way to improve the Constitution over time.
it.h: Think about how the nation might change.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Finding Courage (narrative)
lessons.n: Narrator's point of view and how characters respond

it.q: Read: "I gripped the rail and told myself the bridge was perfectly safe." Which point of view is used?
it.h: Look at the pronoun the narrator uses to talk about himself or herself.

it.q: Read: "Jamal smiled at the crowd, but inside he was sure he would forget every line. Across the stage, Mei wondered why he looked so calm." What point of view is used?
it.h: Whose thoughts does the narrator share? Is it more than one character?

it.q: Read: "When the dog growled, Ana stepped in front of her little brother, even though her knees were shaking." What does Ana's response reveal about her?
ch: She protects others even when she is scared.
She is not afraid of dogs at all.
She wants her brother to be scared.
She does not notice the dog.
it.h: Think about the difference between what Ana feels and what Ana does.

it.q: A narrator says, "Everyone said the old Fenwick house was haunted, and I believed every word." How might this point of view affect the story?
ch: Readers see the house through the narrator's fears, which may not be accurate.
Readers learn every character's true thoughts.
Readers get only proven facts about the house.
The story cannot include any suspense.
it.h: Can a narrator's beliefs shape how events are described?

it.q: Read: "I told Grandpa I wasn't scared of the storm. Then the lights went out, and I was holding his hand before I knew it." Compare what the narrator says with what the narrator does. What does the difference show?
it.ans: The narrator says he or she is not scared but grabs Grandpa's hand when the lights go out. The difference shows the narrator is more afraid than he or she admits.
it.h: Compare the narrator's words with the narrator's actions.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Finding Courage (narrative)
lessons.n: Central idea and how it is developed

it.q: The central idea of an informational text is
ch: the most important point the whole text develops
the first fact in the text
the detail the author likes best
it.h: Think about the point that most of the paragraphs support.

it.q: Read: "Firefighters train for hundreds of hours. They practice in smoke-filled rooms, climb ladders in heavy gear and rehearse rescues until the steps feel automatic." What central idea do these details develop?
ch: Firefighters prepare carefully so they can act in emergencies.
it.h: What do all three examples have in common?

it.q: Which sentence would NOT belong in an objective summary of an article about mountain rescue teams?
ch: I think rescue workers are the coolest people alive.
Rescue teams search for lost or injured hikers.
Teams use dogs, helicopters and radios.
Volunteers train for months before joining a team.
it.h: An objective summary leaves out personal opinions.

it.q: An article about a swimmer who crossed a dangerous channel begins with her standing on a cold beach at dawn. What is the most likely purpose of this opening?
ch: to draw readers in and introduce the person the article is about
it.h: How does a scene at the beginning affect a reader?

it.q: Read: "Some people think courage means having no fear. In fact, many people who perform brave acts report feeling terrified. Courage is acting in spite of fear." What is the central idea, and which detail supports it?
it.ans: Central idea: courage means acting even when you are afraid. Support: many people who perform brave acts report feeling terrified.
it.h: Look for the sentence that sums up the point, then find the evidence behind it.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Finding Courage (narrative)
lessons.n: Prefixes, suffixes and context clues

it.q: The prefix "un-" in "unafraid" means
it.h: Try putting "not" in place of the prefix and read the word again.

it.q: What does "preview" mean?
it.h: The prefix "pre-" tells when something happens.

it.q: Read: "The trail was so treacherous that the guides roped every hiker together." What does "treacherous" most likely mean?
it.h: Why would guides need to rope hikers together?

it.q: Which word means "able to be reached"?
it.h: Which suffix means "able to be"?

it.q: The word "fearless" has a base word and a suffix. Name the suffix, tell what it means and explain the meaning of the whole word.
it.ans: The suffix is "-less," which means "without." Fearless means "without fear."
it.h: Split the word into two parts first.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Finding Courage (narrative)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: setting, dialogue, pacing and resolution

it.q: Which is the best opening for a narrative about a first day at a new school?
ch: My backpack felt like it was full of bricks as I stood outside Room 14, listening to laughter I was not part of.
This story is about my first day at a new school.
Schools are places where students learn.
I will now tell you what happened.
it.h: Which opening puts the reader inside a moment?

it.q: Which sentence punctuates dialogue correctly?
ch: "Wait for me," Lena called. "I'm almost there!"
"Wait for me" Lena called. "I'm almost there!"
Wait for me, Lena called, "I'm almost there!"
"Wait for me." Lena called "I'm almost there!"
it.h: Check where the quotation marks and commas go around the speaker tag.

it.q: A writer wants to slow down the most exciting moment of a story. Which strategy works best?
ch: adding sensory details and the character's thoughts during that moment
skipping ahead to the next day
summarizing the moment in one sentence
it.h: Pacing slows down when a writer spends more words on a moment.

it.q: Which transition best signals a shift in time?
it.h: Which phrase tells the reader when the next event happens?

it.q: Revise this sentence to show, not tell, that the character is nervous: "Marco was nervous before his piano recital."
it.ans: Marco wiped his damp palms on his pants for the third time and counted the keys again, his heart thumping. (Any revision that uses actions, body language or thoughts to show nervousness.)
it.h: What would nervousness look like or feel like in his body?

lessons.u: Collection 1: Finding Courage (narrative)
lessons.n: How a biography introduces and develops a person: Ruby Bridges

it.q: What does it mean for an author to "elaborate" on a person in a biography?
ch: to add details, examples and anecdotes that develop the reader's understanding
it.h: Elaborate means to develop in more detail.

it.q: An anecdote is
ch: a short account of a specific event that reveals something about a person
it.h: Anecdotes are small stories inside a larger text.

it.q: Why might an author open a biography with a dramatic scene instead of the person's birth?
ch: to engage readers and show right away why the person matters
it.h: Think about hooking a reader.

it.q: Read: "Each morning, she walked past the shouting crowd, her eyes straight ahead." What quality does this detail develop?
it.h: How does she respond to the crowd?

it.q: Which detail would best support the central idea that one person's actions influenced others?
ch: Years later, people who had shouted at her wrote to apologize.
it.h: Which detail shows an effect on other people?

it.q: Explain how quotations from a person can help develop a biography.
it.ans: Quotations let readers hear the person's own words and feelings, which shows their personality and point of view more vividly than the author's description alone.
it.h: Think about hearing someone speak for themselves.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
lessons.n: Theme and how a plot unfolds

it.q: A theme is
ch: a message about life that a story suggests
the place where a story happens
a list of the story's events
it.h: A theme is bigger than one character; it applies to life in general.

it.q: In a story, a boy ignores his grandmother's advice to bring water on a hike and becomes dizzy. Later he always packs extra water. Which theme fits?
ch: Learning from mistakes helps us make wiser choices.
it.h: What does the boy learn, and how could that apply to anyone?

it.q: Which event is most likely part of the rising action?
ch: A girl finds an injured fox and secretly tries to care for it in the barn.
The fox is released and runs into the woods.
The girl lives on a farm with her uncle.
Years later, the girl remembers the fox.
it.h: Rising action builds the conflict toward the climax.

it.q: Read: "Every time the stray dog came near, Omar shouted to scare it away. Then one night, the dog barked until Omar woke to find smoke in the kitchen." How is Omar most likely to respond next?
ch: He changes his attitude toward the dog.
He shouts at the dog again.
He moves to a new house.
it.h: Think about how a turning point changes a character.

it.q: Explain the difference between a story's topic and its theme. Use an animal story as your example.
it.ans: A topic is a word or phrase, such as "friendship with a horse." A theme is a complete message, such as "Caring for others can change us as much as it changes them."
it.h: A theme is written as a complete sentence.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
lessons.n: Text structure and central idea in informational texts

it.q: A text that explains why something happened and what resulted uses which structure?
it.h: Look for words like because, so and as a result.

it.q: Read: "Both dolphins and bats use echolocation. However, dolphins send sounds through water, while bats send them through air." Which structure is used?
it.h: Signal words like both, however and while point to a structure.

it.q: Read: "Honeybee colonies have been shrinking in many areas. In response, farmers are planting wildflower strips, and scientists are studying ways to keep hives healthy." Which structure is used?
it.h: Is something going wrong, and are people trying to fix it?

it.q: In an article about sea otters, a section is headed "Why Otters Need Kelp." What will this section most likely explain?
ch: how kelp forests help otters survive
the history of the fur trade
it.h: Headings preview the content of a section.

it.q: Read: "Sea otters eat sea urchins. When otters disappeared from some coasts, urchins multiplied and ate the kelp forests." Explain the cause-and-effect relationship.
it.ans: Because the otters disappeared, nothing kept the urchins in check, so the urchins multiplied and destroyed the kelp forests.
it.h: Find what happened first and what it led to.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
lessons.n: Pronoun case and intensive pronouns

it.q: Which pronoun is in the subjective case?
it.h: Subjective pronouns can be the subject of a sentence.

it.q: Choose the correct pronoun: "The ranger showed Maya and ___ the owl's nest."
it.h: Cover "Maya and." Would you say "showed I" or "showed me"?

it.q: Which sentence uses an intensive pronoun?
ch: The scientist herself counted every egg.
The scientist hurt herself on a rock.
it.h: An intensive pronoun adds emphasis and can be removed without changing the basic meaning.

it.q: Which pronoun correctly completes "Jorge and ___ volunteered at the animal shelter"?
it.h: The pronoun is part of the subject of the sentence.

it.q: Explain the difference between a reflexive and an intensive pronoun. Write an example sentence for each using "himself."
it.ans: A reflexive pronoun is needed because it receives the action: "Ravi taught himself to whistle." An intensive pronoun only adds emphasis and can be removed: "Ravi himself fed the goats."
it.h: Try deleting the pronoun. Does the sentence still make sense?

lessons.u: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
lessons.n: Writing an informative essay: thesis, organization and evidence

it.q: The thesis of an informative essay
ch: states the topic and the main points the essay will explain
tells a story about the writer
argues for one side of an issue
it.h: The thesis previews what the reader will learn.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis for an informative essay about service dogs?
ch: Service dogs help people with disabilities by guiding, alerting and assisting them with daily tasks.
Service dogs are the best dogs.
it.h: Look for a statement that names the topic and the main points.
