it.q: Which detail best supports the topic sentence "Elephants communicate in many ways"?
ch: Elephants make low rumbling sounds that other elephants can sense from far away.
Elephants are the largest land animals.
Elephants live in Africa and Asia.
it.h: Which detail is about communication?

it.q: Which transition best introduces an example?
it.h: Which phrase tells the reader that an example is coming?

it.q: Paraphrase this sentence in your own words: "Some monarch butterflies travel up to 3,000 miles each fall to reach their winter homes in Mexico."
it.ans: Every autumn, some monarchs make a very long trip, as far as about 3,000 miles, to spend the winter in Mexico.
it.h: Keep the facts, but change the words and the sentence structure.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Wild Partners (informative)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: kinds of symbiosis in nature

it.q: What is symbiosis?
ch: a close, long-term relationship between two different species
a group of the same species
it.h: "Sym-" means together and "bio" means life.

it.q: In mutualism,
it.h: "Mutual" means shared.

it.q: A tick feeds on a deer's blood. What kind of relationship is this?
it.h: One benefits, and one is harmed.

it.q: A barnacle attaches to a whale and gets carried to food, while the whale is mostly unaffected. This is an example of
it.h: One benefits; the other is neither helped nor harmed.

it.q: An article uses the headings "Mutualism," "Commensalism" and "Parasitism." What is its likely text structure?
it.h: The headings sort relationships into groups.

it.q: Explain why scientists might disagree about which type of symbiosis a relationship is.
it.ans: Effects can be hard to measure; a partner that seems unaffected might actually be helped or harmed in small ways, so the category may depend on new evidence.
it.h: Think about how hard it is to see every effect.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Word choice, tone and mood in literature

it.q: In literature, tone is
ch: the author's attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice
the time and place of a story
it.h: Think about how the words make the writing "sound."

it.q: Read: "The rocket roared upward, a pillar of fire splitting the sky." Which word best describes the tone?
it.h: How does the writer seem to feel about the launch?

it.q: Read: "The capsule drifted silently through the endless dark." What feeling does "endless dark" create?
it.h: Picture something with no end. How would it feel to be inside it?

it.q: Which word has the most positive connotation for describing an astronaut?
it.h: Which word suggests a good quality rather than a bad one?

it.q: Read: "The Moon hung over the desert like a cold coin." Explain what the comparison suggests about the Moon.
it.ans: It suggests the Moon looks round, pale and shiny like a coin, and the word "cold" makes it seem distant and unwelcoming.
it.h: What do a coin and the Moon have in common? What does "cold" add?

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Tracing and evaluating an argument

it.q: In an argument, a claim is
ch: the position the writer wants readers to accept
a fact that no one can argue with
it.h: The claim is what the writer is trying to prove.

it.q: Read: "Our school should start a rocketry club. Students who build model rockets practice measuring, graphing and testing ideas." Which sentence gives a reason?
ch: Students who build model rockets practice measuring, graphing and testing ideas.
Our school should start a rocketry club.
it.h: A reason explains why the claim should be accepted.

it.q: Which statement is a claim that is NOT supported?
ch: Space camp is the best summer activity in the world.
A survey of campers found that most said space camp taught them teamwork.
Campers at space camp build and launch model rockets.
Each space camp session lasts one week.
it.h: Which statement is a strong opinion with no evidence?

it.q: An author writes, "Some say space exploration costs too much. However, it has produced inventions we use every day." What is the author doing?
ch: stating a fact with no purpose
it.h: What does "Some say" introduce, and what does "However" signal?

it.q: Read: "Telescopes in space take clearer pictures than telescopes on the ground." Describe evidence that would best support this claim.
it.ans: Side-by-side images of the same object taken by a space telescope and a ground telescope, or an explanation from astronomers that Earth's air blurs and dims starlight.
it.h: What kind of proof would convince someone who doubts the claim?

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Greek and Latin roots and connotation

it.q: The Greek root "astro" means
it.h: Think of "astronaut" and "astronomy."

it.q: The Greek root "tele" means
it.h: A telescope helps you see things that are...?

it.q: The Latin root "vis" means "see." Which word means "able to be seen"?
it.h: Look for the suffix that means "able to be."

it.q: Which word has the most negative connotation?
it.h: Which word suggests taking risks in a foolish way?

it.q: The Greek root "graph" means "write" and "auto" means "self." Explain what "autograph" means and name another word with "graph."
it.ans: An autograph is a person's own signature, something written by oneself. Other words: photograph, biography, paragraph, graphic.
it.h: Put the meanings of the two roots together.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Writing an argument: claim, reasons, evidence and counterclaim

it.q: Which is a clear claim for an argument?
ch: Our city should build a public observatory.
Some people like to look at stars.
it.h: A claim takes a position that someone could disagree with.

it.q: Which evidence best supports the claim "Our school should add a space science elective"?
ch: Teachers at a nearby school reported that students in a space elective improved their science grades.
it.h: Evidence should be a fact or example that connects directly to the claim.

it.q: Which sentence introduces a counterclaim?
ch: Some people believe space programs cost too much money.
Space programs teach us about our own planet.
it.h: A counterclaim presents the other side.

it.q: Which is the best rebuttal to "Space exploration costs too much"?
ch: Space research has led to useful tools, such as weather satellites that help forecasters warn people about storms.
it.h: A strong rebuttal answers the other side with evidence, not insults.

it.q: Write a claim and one reason for this question: Should our school hold a stargazing night once a month?
it.ans: Claim: Our school should hold a monthly stargazing night. Reason: Observing the sky with telescopes helps students connect classroom science to the real world.
it.h: State your position clearly, then explain why.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Distinguishing supported and unsupported claims in an argument about space junk

it.q: What is a claim in an argument?
ch: a statement the author wants readers to accept
a fact no one disagrees with
it.h: Arguments are built around claims.

it.q: Which claim is supported by evidence?
ch: Space debris is a growing risk; the International Space Station has had to change course many times to avoid it.
Space debris is the worst problem ever.
it.h: Which claim includes proof?

it.q: Read: "Obviously, anyone who launches a satellite is careless." Why is this claim weak?
ch: It is an overgeneralization with no evidence.
it.h: Does it give any reasons?

it.q: Which source would provide the most credible evidence about space debris?
ch: a report from a space agency that tracks objects in orbit
a blog by an anonymous writer
it.h: Who actually tracks debris?

it.q: How does a writer strengthen an argument when addressing a counterclaim?
ch: by acknowledging it fairly and explaining with evidence why the claim still holds
by insulting people who hold it
it.h: Strong arguments respond to the other side.

it.q: Read: "Cleanup missions cost money, but losing a single weather satellite could cost far more." Is this claim supported? Explain what evidence would make it stronger.
it.ans: It is reasonable but not fully supported. It would be stronger with figures comparing the cost of a cleanup mission with the cost of replacing a weather satellite.
it.h: What numbers or facts would prove the comparison?

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Argument language: formal style, transitions and precise words

it.q: What is a formal style in argument writing?
it.h: Think about writing to a school board.

it.q: Which sentence uses formal style?
ch: Students would benefit from a longer lunch period.
Lunch is way too short, seriously.
it.h: Which sentence avoids slang?

it.q: Which transition best connects a claim to a reason?
it.h: Which word introduces "why"?

it.q: Which word for a person who will not give up has the most positive connotation?
it.h: Connotation is the feeling a word carries.

it.q: Which transition best introduces a counterclaim?
it.h: Which phrase signals another side?

it.q: Revise this informal sentence into formal style: "Homework on weekends is totally pointless and super annoying."
it.ans: Assigning homework on weekends may not be the most effective way to support learning.
it.h: Remove slang and exaggeration.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Beyond the Sky (argument)
lessons.n: Debating claims: speaking, listening and evaluating reasons

it.q: In a debate, what should a listener focus on?
ch: the speaker's claims, reasons and evidence
the length of the speech only
it.h: Listen for the argument's parts.

it.q: Which response to an opponent is most respectful and effective?
ch: "I understand your point about cost, but the evidence shows prevention saves money over time."
it.h: Address the idea, not the person.

it.q: A speaker says, "Everybody knows that's true." What is the problem with this reasoning?
ch: It offers no evidence and assumes agreement.
it.h: Does "everybody knows" prove anything?

it.q: Which presentation behavior helps a speaker's argument?
ch: making eye contact and speaking clearly
it.h: Delivery affects how well an argument is understood.

it.q: When taking notes during a debate, what is most useful to record?
ch: each claim and the evidence given for it
it.h: Notes help you evaluate later.

it.q: Explain the difference between a relevant and an irrelevant piece of evidence in a debate.
it.ans: Relevant evidence directly supports the claim being argued. Irrelevant evidence may be true but does not connect to the claim, so it does not help prove the point.
it.h: Ask whether the evidence connects to the claim.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How structure and key scenes develop a theme

it.q: The climax of a story is
ch: the turning point, when the conflict reaches its highest point
the ending after the conflict is solved
the time and place of the story
it.h: Think of the moment of greatest tension.

it.q: A story opens with a memory of a character's happy childhood before describing her family losing their home. Why might the author begin this way?
ch: to show what the character has lost, making the hardship feel stronger
to confuse the reader about the order of events
to explain how the story will end
it.h: How does knowing what came before change how you feel about the hard times?

it.q: Read: "Through the long winter, Abuelo's garden lay brown and frozen. But each night he studied his seed catalogs by lamplight." What does this detail suggest about Abuelo?
ch: He stays hopeful about the future.
He is planning to move away.
it.h: Why would someone study seed catalogs when nothing can grow?

it.q: Which statement is a theme, not a topic?
ch: Hardship can reveal a person's true strength.
it.h: A theme is a complete idea about life.

it.q: Explain how one scene can contribute to the theme of a whole story. Use this example: in a story about a struggling family, a boy gives his only coat to his younger sister during a snowstorm.
it.ans: The scene shows the boy putting his sister's needs ahead of his own, which develops a theme such as "Love means sacrifice, especially in hard times."
it.h: What does the boy's choice show about what matters in the story?

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How informational texts introduce and develop key events and people

it.q: In an informational text, an anecdote is
ch: a short account of a real event used to illustrate an idea
it.h: Think of a brief true story.

it.q: An article about a hospital during a hurricane begins by describing one nurse carrying a baby down nine flights of stairs. What does this anecdote mainly do?
ch: It introduces the topic in a personal, memorable way.
It proves that all nurses are strong.
it.h: Why might an author start with one person's experience?

it.q: Two accounts describe the same flood. One is a newspaper report with water levels and dates. The other is a farmer's diary entry. What would the diary most likely include that the report does not?
ch: personal feelings and details from one person's experience
official data from many river gauges
a list of every town affected
it.h: What would a person write in a private journal?

it.q: Which detail best elaborates on the idea "Many families struggled during the Great Depression"?
ch: Some families lost their homes and moved in with relatives to save money.
Cars were invented before the Depression.
it.h: Which detail gives an example of struggle?

it.q: Explain why an author might include both statistics and a personal story in an article about hard times.
it.ans: Statistics show how large the problem was, while a personal story helps readers connect emotionally and understand what it felt like for real people.
it.h: What does each kind of evidence do for the reader?

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Figurative language and word relationships

it.q: Personification gives
ch: human qualities to something that is not human
a comparison using like or as
a word that imitates a sound
it.h: Look for a non-human thing acting like a person.

it.q: Which sentence contains personification?
ch: The hungry wind clawed at the windows.
The wind was cold and strong.
The wind blew at forty miles per hour.
The windows were covered in dust.
it.h: Can wind really be hungry or have claws?

it.q: Read: "Her hope was a candle in a storm." What does this metaphor suggest?
ch: Her hope was small and fragile but still alive.
it.h: Think about what happens to a candle in a storm.

it.q: Which sentence is hyperbole?
ch: I've told you a million times to close the gate.
I told you twice to close the gate.
it.h: Hyperbole is an exaggeration that is not meant literally.

it.q: Write a sentence that uses personification to describe a drought. Explain what your personification suggests.
it.ans: "The sun stared down at the cracked fields without blinking." It suggests the sun is harsh and relentless, giving the land no relief.
it.h: Make the sun, the land or the dust act like a person.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis: thesis, evidence and commentary

it.q: A literary analysis essay mainly
ch: makes a claim about a text and supports it with evidence from the text
tells whether the writer found the story boring
it.h: Analysis explains how or why, not just what happens.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis for a literary analysis?
ch: The author uses the changing seasons to show how the main character's grief slowly turns into hope.
The story is about a girl and her grandmother.
The story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
it.h: A strong thesis makes a claim about how the author develops an idea.

it.q: Which sentence introduces a quotation correctly?
ch: When the storm ends, the narrator says, "The world felt washed clean."
"The world felt washed clean." This is when the storm ends.
The narrator says the world felt washed clean."
When the storm ends "the world felt washed clean" says the narrator.
it.h: Introduce the quotation with your own words and put quotation marks around the exact words.

it.q: After a quotation, commentary should
ch: explain how the evidence supports the claim
it.h: Ask yourself, "So what? How does this prove my point?"

it.q: Read this evidence: the main character saves half of his small lunch for his little brother every day. Write a sentence of commentary that connects this evidence to the theme "Love means sacrifice."
it.ans: By giving up part of his own small lunch every day, the character shows that he puts his brother's needs before his own, which reveals that love sometimes means sacrifice.
it.h: Explain what the action shows and link it to the theme.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading a poem: how structure develops a theme of resilience

it.q: How does a stanza break contribute to a poem?
ch: It can mark a shift in time, idea or mood.
it.h: Stanzas are like paragraphs.

it.q: A poem moves from winter imagery in its first stanza to spring imagery in its last. What might this structure suggest?
ch: that the poem has no theme
it.h: Think about what spring often symbolizes.

it.q: What is the effect of a repeated line, or refrain, in a poem?
it.h: Repetition draws attention.

it.q: Read: "The oak bends low but does not break." What does this line suggest about resilience?
ch: Strength can mean bending under pressure without giving up.
Breaking is a sign of strength.
it.h: Think about what it means to bend but not break.

it.q: What is a turn, or shift, in a poem?
ch: a point where the poem's tone or idea changes
it.h: Look for words like "but" or "yet."

it.q: Explain how a poet might use a short final line to emphasize an idea.
it.ans: A short final line stands out after longer lines, creating a pause and making its message feel strong and memorable.
it.h: Think about how a short line looks and sounds after long ones.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Getting Through Hard Times (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: the Civilian Conservation Corps in hard times

it.q: What was the Great Depression?
ch: a severe economic crisis in the 1930s when many people lost jobs
it.h: Many banks and businesses failed.

it.q: Read: "Unemployment rose sharply as factories closed." What does "unemployment" mean?
ch: the condition of not having a job
it.h: "Un-" means not.

it.q: How might a government program that hires people help during an economic crisis?
ch: It gives people income and can complete useful public projects.
it.h: Think about wages and work.

it.q: An article tells how a program began, what workers did and its lasting effects. What is its main structure?
ch: chronological order with cause and effect
it.h: Look at how events connect over time.

it.q: Which detail would best show a program's lasting impact?
ch: Trails and park buildings the workers built are still used today.
The program had a long name.
it.h: What remains years later?

it.q: Explain why a program that sent most of each worker's pay home might have helped families.
it.ans: Families who had lost income received money for food and rent, so the program supported not only the workers but their whole households.
it.h: Think about families with no income.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: A speaker's or narrator's point of view

it.q: The speaker of a poem is
ch: the voice that talks in the poem
it.h: The poet creates a voice; it may or may not be the poet.

it.q: Read these lines: "They say I'm too young to matter, / too small to be heard, / but a river begins as a single drop / and a song with a single word." What is the speaker's point of view?
ch: Young people's voices matter even if they start small.
Rivers are more important than songs.
The speaker is angry at rivers.
it.h: What does the speaker compare young voices to?

it.q: A poem says, "They say I'm too young to matter, / too small to be heard, / but a river begins as a single drop / and a song with a single word." What does "a river begins as a single drop" suggest?
ch: Big changes can grow from small beginnings.
The speaker lives near a river.
it.h: Think about how a river grows from its source.

it.q: A story is told by a narrator who believes her town's mayor is a villain. Later she learns the mayor was secretly helping. How does the narrator's point of view affect the reader?
ch: Readers share her mistaken belief until the truth is revealed.
Readers know the truth from the beginning.
The point of view makes the story completely factual.
it.h: Can readers know more than the narrator knows?

it.q: Explain why an author might tell a story about speaking up from the point of view of a shy character instead of a confident one.
it.ans: A shy character's thoughts show how hard it is to speak up, so readers feel the character's fear and understand the courage it takes, which makes the character's growth more meaningful.
it.h: Whose experience of speaking up would be more surprising or meaningful?

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Author's purpose, point of view and information in different formats

it.q: An author's purpose for writing an article that explains a city's new recycling law is most likely to
it.h: What do articles about laws usually do?

it.q: Read: "Skateparks are an absolute must for every town. Kids deserve safe places to ride." What is the author's point of view?
it.h: Which words show the author's opinion?

it.q: A report about a student-led park cleanup includes a bar graph showing the pounds of trash collected each month. What does the graph add?
ch: a clear picture of how the cleanup's results changed over time
the names of every student volunteer
it.h: What kind of information is easiest to see in a graph?

it.q: Which phrase reveals that an author has a positive view of a youth protest?
it.h: Look for a word with a strong positive connotation.

it.q: Explain the difference between an author's purpose and an author's point of view.
it.ans: Purpose is why the author writes (to inform, persuade or entertain). Point of view is the author's attitude or opinion about the topic, shown through word choice and the details the author includes.
it.h: One answers "Why write?" The other answers "How does the author feel about it?"

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Clear pronouns and punctuating extra information

it.q: A vague pronoun is one that
ch: does not clearly refer to a specific noun
it.h: Ask yourself: who or what does the pronoun mean?

it.q: Which sentence has a vague pronoun?
ch: When Maria talked to Kim, she seemed upset.
Maria seemed upset when she talked to Kim.
Maria and Kim talked about the vote.
Kim listened while Maria explained the vote.
it.h: Could the pronoun refer to more than one person?

it.q: Which sentence has an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?
ch: When students speak at meetings, you should prepare notes.
When students speak at meetings, they should prepare notes.
When you speak at meetings, you should prepare notes.
When I speak at meetings, I prepare notes.
it.h: Does the sentence switch from "students" to "you"?

it.q: Which sentence correctly uses commas to set off a nonrestrictive element?
ch: Ms. Ortiz, our class adviser, helped us write the petition.
Ms. Ortiz our class adviser, helped us write the petition.
Ms. Ortiz, our class adviser helped us write the petition.
Ms. Ortiz our class adviser helped, us write the petition.
it.h: Extra information in the middle of a sentence needs a comma on both sides.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence to fix the vague pronoun: "The students told the teachers that they needed more time."
it.ans: The students told the teachers, "We need more time." (Or: The students said the teachers needed more time. Any revision that makes clear who needed time.)
it.h: Decide who needed more time, then make it clear.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Research: questions, sources, notes and citations

it.q: A good research question for a short project is
ch: focused enough to answer with research but open enough to explore
so broad that whole books cover it
it.h: Think about a question you could answer in a short report.

it.q: Which research question is best for a short report?
ch: How did the 1899 newsboys' strike change the newsies' working conditions?
it.h: Look for a focused question that requires research to answer.

it.q: Which source is most likely to be credible for a report on a city's bike lanes?
it.h: Who has expert knowledge and no reason to sell something?

it.q: Which is the best way to take notes from a source?
ch: write notes in your own words and record the title, author and publisher or website
copy whole paragraphs without noting the source
write down only the website's colors
skip noting where the facts came from
it.h: You need to be able to find and credit the source later.

it.q: Explain the difference between quoting and paraphrasing. When might you choose each?
it.ans: Quoting uses the author's exact words in quotation marks; paraphrasing restates the idea in your own words. Quote when the exact wording is powerful or important; paraphrase to explain information more simply. Both need credit.
it.h: Think about exact words versus your own words.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how opinion pages and letters to the editor work

it.q: What is a letter to the editor?
ch: a short letter from a reader, published in a newspaper, giving an opinion
a news report written by a reporter
it.h: Readers write them to share views.

it.q: How is an opinion piece different from a news article?
ch: It argues a viewpoint, while a news article reports facts objectively.
it.h: Think about purpose.

it.q: Why do many newspapers ask letter writers to include their name and town?
ch: so readers know who is speaking and the paper can verify the writer
it.h: Think about trust and accountability.

it.q: Which element would make a letter to the editor most persuasive?
ch: a clear claim supported by a specific local example
a list of complaints with no reasons
it.h: Editors value clear, supported letters.

it.q: A news site places opinion articles in a section labeled "Opinion." Why is this labeling useful?
ch: It helps readers tell opinions apart from news reporting.
It shows the articles are false.
It means the articles are ads.
it.h: Readers need to know what kind of text they are reading.

it.q: Explain why reading opinion pieces from several writers can help you understand an issue.
it.ans: Different writers present different viewpoints and evidence, so reading several helps you see the whole issue and decide what you think.
it.h: Think about hearing more than one side.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Evaluating sources: credibility, purpose and bias

it.q: What does it mean for a source to be credible?
ch: believable and trustworthy, based on expertise and evidence
it.h: Credibility is about trust.

it.q: Which source is most credible for information about a disease?
it.h: Who are the experts?

it.q: What is bias?
ch: a strong preference that may make a source one-sided
it.h: Biased sources may leave out other views.

it.q: A website about the benefits of a sports drink is run by the company that sells it. What should a researcher consider?
ch: The company may be biased because it profits from sales.
The website must be completely objective.
it.h: Who benefits?

it.q: Why does the date of a source matter?
ch: Information can become outdated, especially in science and technology.
it.h: Think about how knowledge changes.

it.q: List two questions you should ask to decide whether a website is a reliable source.
it.ans: Who wrote or published this, and are they experts? When was it updated, and does it give evidence or cite sources?
it.h: Think about author, date, purpose and evidence.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Raising Your Voice (research)
lessons.n: Standard English in research writing: fixing common errors

it.q: What is standard English?
ch: the widely accepted grammar and usage expected in formal writing
it.h: It is expected in reports and essays.

it.q: Which sentence uses standard English?
ch: She and I gathered the sources.
Me and her gathered the sources.
Her and me gathered the sources.
She and me gathered the sources.
it.h: Use subject pronouns for subjects.

it.q: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?
ch: Each of the articles provides useful data.
Each of the articles provide useful data.
Each of the articles providing useful data.
Each of the articles have useful data.
it.h: "Each" is singular.

it.q: Which word, often used in research reports, is spelled correctly?
it.h: One c, two s.

it.q: Which revision corrects the error? "The researchers should of checked their data."
ch: The researchers should have checked their data.
The researchers should of check their data.
The researchers should checked their data.
The researchers should has checked their data.
it.h: "Should of" is a common error for "should have."

it.q: Correct the errors in this sentence: "Their going to there library to research they're topic."
it.ans: They're going to their library to research their topic.
it.h: Check each "their," "there" and "they're."

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Quest stories and the hero's journey

it.q: In a traditional quest story, the hero usually
ch: leaves home to reach a goal and faces challenges along the way
is always a king or queen
it.h: Think about what the word "quest" means.

it.q: A myth and a modern graphic novel both tell about a hero who defeats a monster. What is most likely different?
ch: the way the story is told, such as pictures and speech bubbles instead of narration
the idea that the hero faces a challenge
that there is a main character
it.h: Think about the form of each text, not the basic story elements.

it.q: Which is an example of a "trial" in a hero's journey?
ch: crossing a dangerous desert to reach a hidden spring
it.h: A trial tests the hero.

it.q: A poem and a story both describe a lost traveler finding home. How might the poem's form affect the reader's experience?
ch: Its line breaks, rhythm and images can create strong feeling in fewer words.
It is always divided into chapters.
it.h: What tools does a poet use that a storyteller might not?

it.q: Explain how a mentor character helps a hero in a quest story. Give an example from a story, movie or myth you know.
it.ans: A mentor gives the hero advice, training or a gift that helps on the journey, such as a wise teacher who trains a young hero before a battle.
it.h: Think of an older or wiser character who guides the hero.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Comparing two authors' accounts of the same events

it.q: When two authors write about the same event, they may
ch: emphasize different people, details or ideas
always use exactly the same facts and words
it.h: Think about what each author chooses to focus on.

it.q: A historian writes a biography of a mountain climber. The climber writes a memoir about the same climb. What might the memoir include that the biography does not?
ch: the climber's private thoughts and feelings during the climb
a list of the climber's awards
it.h: A memoir is written from the writer's own experience.

it.q: Two articles describe the Wright brothers' first airplane flights. One emphasizes their years of failed tests. The other emphasizes how slowly newspapers reported the news. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Each author shapes the story by choosing what to emphasize.
One of the articles must be false.
it.h: A different focus does not mean one account is false.

it.q: Which question best helps you compare two accounts of the same event?
ch: What details does each author include or leave out, and why?
Which author has the longer name?
Which account was printed in color?
it.h: Focus on the authors' choices.

it.q: Explain why reading two accounts of the same historical event can help you understand it better.
it.ans: Each author may focus on different people or details, so reading both gives a more complete picture, and comparing them helps you notice each author's point of view or gaps in the information.
it.h: What might one author leave out?

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Varying sentences, keeping a consistent style and using reference materials

it.q: A writer who wants to vary sentence patterns should
ch: combine some short sentences and begin sentences in different ways
make every sentence the same length
it.h: Variety keeps readers interested.

it.q: Which revision best combines these sentences: "The hero climbed the cliff. The cliff was icy. She did not slip."?
ch: The hero climbed the icy cliff without slipping.
The hero climbed. The cliff. It was icy.
The hero climbed the cliff, the cliff was icy, she did not slip.
Climbing, icy, the hero did not slip cliff.
it.h: Combine the details into one smooth sentence.

it.q: Which sentence would NOT fit the formal, serious tone of a report on ancient legends?
ch: Honestly, those old legends are kind of goofy.
Many cultures tell legends about great floods.
Legends often explain events in nature.
Some legends were passed down orally for centuries.
it.h: Which sentence sounds casual?

it.q: In a book about myths, a glossary is used to
ch: find the meanings of key words used in that book
find the page where a chapter begins
see a map of ancient Greece
it.h: Glossaries are usually at the back of informational books.

it.q: Rewrite this choppy passage using varied sentences: "The storm came. The ship rocked. The sailors were afraid. The captain stayed calm."
it.ans: As the storm came and the ship rocked, the sailors grew afraid, but the captain stayed calm.
it.h: Try starting with "As" or "When" and use a conjunction.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis that compares texts

it.q: In a compare-and-contrast essay, point-by-point organization
ch: discusses one point at a time, comparing both texts on each point
discusses only one of the texts
it.h: Each body paragraph covers one point for both texts.

it.q: Which thesis best compares two texts?
ch: Although a myth and a modern story tell of very different heroes, both show that true courage means putting others first.
I liked the myth better than the story.
The myth is old, and the story is new.
it.h: A strong comparison thesis names a meaningful similarity or difference.

it.q: Which transition shows contrast?
it.h: Contrast means difference.

it.q: Which revision step is most helpful after finishing a draft?
ch: rereading to check that each paragraph supports the thesis with evidence
adding a new topic at the end
it.h: Revision focuses on ideas and organization, not only small changes.

it.q: Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph that compares how two heroes respond to a challenge.
it.ans: While the first hero faces the storm with quiet patience, the second charges at danger with strength, showing two different kinds of courage.
it.h: Name both heroes and the point you are comparing.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading literature: archetypes in an original quest tale

it.q: What is an archetype?
ch: a character type, symbol or pattern that appears in stories across many cultures
the shortest story in a book
it.h: The wise mentor is one example.

it.q: Which character is an example of the mentor archetype?
ch: an old guide who gives the hero advice and a gift
a villain who blocks the road
a shopkeeper with no role in the plot
it.h: Mentors help heroes prepare.

it.q: In a quest story, what is the "call to adventure"?
ch: the event that pushes the hero to leave home and begin the journey
it.h: It starts the quest.

it.q: Which object often symbolizes guidance in quest stories?
it.h: What helps a traveler find the way?

it.q: Why do quest stories from different cultures share patterns?
ch: People everywhere tell stories about growth, challenge and returning changed.
They were all written in the same year.
They have the same characters' names.
it.h: Think about universal human experiences.

it.q: Name one archetype and describe how it usually functions in a quest story.
it.ans: The threshold guardian blocks the hero's path at the start of the journey and tests whether the hero is ready to continue.
it.h: Choose a character type like mentor, trickster or guardian.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Quests and Journeys (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: the voyages of the Hokule'a

it.q: What is wayfinding?
ch: navigating without instruments by reading stars, waves, wind and wildlife
it.h: Traditional navigators used nature.

it.q: Why might a navigator watch seabirds near the end of the day?
ch: Many seabirds fly back toward land in the evening, pointing the way to islands.
it.h: Where do birds go at night?

it.q: Read: "The voyage revived interest in traditional navigation, which had nearly been lost." What does "revived" mean?
it.h: "Re-" means again; "viv" relates to life.

it.q: An article about a voyage describes the people involved, the challenges and the results. Which structure helps show how events connect?
ch: cause and effect within a chronological account
it.h: Think about how actions led to outcomes.

it.q: What is a double-hulled voyaging canoe?
ch: a boat made of two hulls joined by a deck
it.h: "Double" means two.

it.q: Explain why a successful voyage using only traditional navigation might be important to a culture.
it.ans: It proves that ancestors had great skill and knowledge, restoring pride and keeping cultural traditions alive for future generations.
it.h: Think about history and identity.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
lessons.n: How setting, character and plot interact

it.q: Read: "In the drought-stricken town, water was rationed to one bucket a day, so when Rafael spilled his family's share, he could not bring himself to go home." How does the setting affect the plot?
ch: The water shortage turns a small accident into a serious conflict.
The setting has no effect on the events.
The setting explains what Rafael looks like.
it.h: Would spilling water matter as much in a place with plenty of it?

it.q: Read: "Because her family had just moved to a city where she knew no one, Aiko joined the first club that invited her, even though it was the chess club and she did not know how to play." What shapes Aiko's decision?
ch: her new setting and her loneliness
it.h: Look at the clause that begins with "Because."

it.q: How can a character's choice change the plot of a story?
ch: It can cause new events and conflicts.
it.h: Think about cause and effect.

it.q: Read: "The blizzard closed the only road out of town, trapping the two rival teams in the same small lodge." What is the most likely effect of this setting on the characters?
ch: It forces the rivals to interact and possibly settle their conflict.
It allows the teams to avoid each other.
It makes the teams forget the competition.
It has no effect on the characters.
it.h: What happens when rivals cannot get away from each other?

it.q: Choose a story, movie or show you know. Explain how one event changed a character or how a character's trait shaped an event.
it.ans: Any accurate example with a clear cause-and-effect link, such as: "Maya's stubbornness leads her to hike alone, which causes her to get lost; being lost teaches her to ask for help."
it.h: Use "because" or "so" to connect the character and the event.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
lessons.n: Central ideas and how people and events interact

it.q: The central idea of an informational text is best supported by
ch: key details found throughout the text
it.h: Look for an idea that many details develop.

it.q: Read: "After the levee broke, neighbors organized boat rescues. Their efforts inspired the city to create a volunteer emergency corps." How do the event and the individuals interact?
ch: The disaster led people to act, and their actions changed the city's plans.
The individuals caused the levee to break.
The event had no effect on people.
it.h: Trace what caused what.

it.q: Which detail best develops the idea that "one invention can change daily life"?
ch: After refrigerators became common, many families could store food for days instead of shopping daily.
it.h: Which detail shows a change in daily life?

it.q: Which is the best objective summary statement for an article about a scientist who found a new species after years of failure?
ch: After years of unsuccessful searches, a scientist discovered a new species.
This amazing scientist is my hero.
Scientists are boring until they find something.
I would never search that long.
it.h: Objective summaries leave out personal opinions.

it.q: Read: "When the town's factory closed, many workers lost their jobs. A former worker, Rosa Delgado, opened a training center that taught new skills. Within five years, a new business had moved into the old factory." Explain how the event and the individual influenced each other.
it.ans: The factory closing (event) led Rosa Delgado to open a training center (her response); the center helped workers gain skills and helped attract a new business, so her actions shaped later events.
it.h: Show the chain: event, response, result.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
lessons.n: Phrases and clauses

it.q: A clause
ch: contains a subject and a verb
it.h: Look for someone or something doing an action.

it.q: Which group of words is an independent clause?
it.h: An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence.

it.q: In "Before the sun rose, Malik packed his bag," what is "Before the sun rose"?
it.h: It has a subject and a verb, but can it stand alone?

it.q: Which group of words is a prepositional phrase?
it.h: A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and has no verb.

it.q: Write a sentence that contains one dependent clause and one independent clause. Label each.
it.ans: "When the bell rang (dependent clause), the students rushed outside (independent clause)."
it.h: Start with a word like when, because, although or if.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative: point of view, pacing and reflection

it.q: Which narrative technique shows what characters say to each other?
it.h: Think of quotation marks.

it.q: A writer wants readers to know only one character's thoughts. Which point of view should the writer use?
ch: first person or third person limited
it.h: Which points of view stay inside one character's mind?

it.q: Which sentence best uses a flashback?
ch: As I stared at the empty field, I remembered the day Dad first threw me a baseball, his laugh echoing across the grass.
it.h: A flashback interrupts the present to show an earlier event.

it.q: Which sentence uses the most precise verbs?
ch: The dog lunged, snapped and skidded across the tile.
The dog went fast and did things.
it.h: Look for verbs that create a clear picture.

it.q: Write a reflective final sentence for a narrative about a turning point when a character finally apologizes to a friend.
it.ans: "Walking home, I realized that saying 'I'm sorry' had cost me nothing but pride, and it had given me back my best friend."
it.h: Reflection shows what the narrator learned.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Turning Points (narrative)
lessons.n: A turning point in history: how people, ideas and events interact in the Wright brothers' story

it.q: In an informational text, what does it mean to analyze interactions between individuals and events?
ch: to explain how people influence events and how events shape people
it.h: Think about cause and effect in both directions.

it.q: Read: "After reading about a German glider pioneer's death in a crash, the brothers became determined to solve the problem of control." How did an event influence the individuals?
ch: The crash news pushed them to focus on controlling an aircraft.
They decided to stop studying flight.
it.h: What did they decide after the event?

it.q: Which detail would best support the central idea that careful testing led to success?
ch: They built a small wind tunnel and tested about two hundred wing shapes.
it.h: Which detail shows testing?

it.q: Why might an author call a single day a "turning point"?
ch: Events after it were fundamentally different because of what happened.
It was the longest day of the year.
it.h: A turning point changes direction.

it.q: An idea can also shape events. Which statement shows an idea influencing events?
ch: The brothers' belief that a pilot must be able to balance the craft, like a bicycle rider, shaped their design.
it.h: Look for a belief that guided action.

it.q: Explain how experiences from one job might prepare a person for a very different invention.
it.ans: Skills like building, repairing and testing machines in one job can transfer, giving the person tools and problem-solving habits to use on a new invention.
it.h: Think about skills that carry over.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
lessons.n: Poetry: form, structure and sound

it.q: In a poem, a stanza is
it.h: Stanzas are like paragraphs in poetry.

it.q: Which line contains alliteration?
ch: The wild wind whipped the willows.
The wind blew hard all night.
it.h: Look for repeated beginning consonant sounds.

it.q: Read: "Thunder grumbled over the hills." What does "grumbled" suggest?
ch: The thunder sounded low, rumbling and threatening.
it.h: What does a person sound like when he or she grumbles?

it.q: A poet repeats the line "And still the river rose" at the end of each stanza. What is the most likely effect?
ch: It builds tension and emphasizes the growing danger.
It shows the poet ran out of ideas.
it.h: Think about how a repeated line affects mood.

it.q: Explain how a poem's form, such as very short lines or a sonnet's structure, can affect its meaning. Give an example.
it.ans: Form shapes how readers experience a poem. Very short lines slow the reader and create emphasis or suspense, and a sonnet's final couplet can deliver a turn or conclusion.
it.h: Think about how line length or a rhyme pattern changes the way you read.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
lessons.n: Text structure and central ideas in informational texts

it.q: Which text structure explains a series of events in the order they happened?
it.h: Think about time.

it.q: Read: "Hurricanes form over warm ocean water. As warm, moist air rises, it cools and forms clouds, releasing heat that powers the storm." Which structure is used?
it.h: Look for how one thing leads to another.

it.q: Which signal words most often show a problem-and-solution structure?
ch: one way to solve, to address this
it.h: Which words point to fixing something?

it.q: An article about tornadoes has the sections "How Tornadoes Form," "Where They Strike" and "Staying Safe." How do these sections work together?
ch: They move from causes to locations to safety, building a full understanding of the topic.
They argue that tornadoes are not dangerous.
it.h: What does each heading add?

it.q: Explain why an author writing about a flood might use both chronological order and cause and effect.
it.ans: Chronological order shows how the flood unfolded over time, while cause and effect explains why it happened and what damage resulted; together they give a complete picture.
it.h: Think about "when" and "why."

lessons.u: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
lessons.n: Simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences

it.q: A compound sentence has
it.h: Look for clauses joined by and, but or so.

it.q: Which sentence is complex?
ch: When the wind shifted, the fire moved toward the town.
The wind shifted, and the fire moved.
The wind and the fire moved.
it.h: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

it.q: Which sentence is compound-complex?
ch: Because the river rose, the town flooded, and families moved to higher ground.
The river rose, and the town flooded.
Because the river rose, the town flooded.
it.h: Count the independent and the dependent clauses.

it.q: Which sentence is simple?
ch: Although it was late, thunder rolled, and we woke.
it.h: A simple sentence has one independent clause.

it.q: Combine these sentences into one complex sentence: "The tsunami warning sounded. Residents moved inland."
it.ans: When the tsunami warning sounded, residents moved inland. (Because or after also works.)
it.h: Use a word such as when, because or after.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
lessons.n: Writing an informative essay: thesis, definitions and organization

it.q: In an informative essay, the writer's purpose is to
ch: explain a topic using facts, definitions and examples
persuade readers to agree with an opinion
it.h: Informative writing informs.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis for an informative essay about wildfires?
ch: Wildfires are shaped by fuel, weather and terrain, and understanding these factors helps communities prepare.
it.h: A strong thesis previews the main points.

it.q: Which is the best way to define a technical term for readers?
ch: A fault is a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock move past each other.
Faults are things in the ground.
A fault is when you make a mistake.
it.h: Give a clear, accurate definition in context.

it.q: Which text feature would best help readers follow the earthquake safety steps Drop, Cover and Hold On?
it.h: Steps happen in order.

it.q: Write a topic sentence and one supporting fact for a body paragraph explaining how tsunamis form.
it.ans: Topic sentence: Most tsunamis begin with a sudden movement of the sea floor. Fact: When an undersea earthquake lifts or drops the sea floor, it pushes a huge amount of water and creates waves that spread outward.
it.h: The fact should explain the topic sentence.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Nature's Fury (informative)
lessons.n: Reading literature: how a storm setting shapes characters and plot

it.q: How can setting influence a story's plot?
ch: It can create obstacles and dangers that characters must face.
it.h: Think about a blizzard or a flood.

it.q: Read: "Snow erased the road ahead until the headlights lit only swirling white." What mood does this setting create?
it.h: How would you feel if you could not see the road?

it.q: How might a dangerous setting reveal a character's traits?
ch: It forces the character to act, showing courage, panic or resourcefulness.
It has no effect on characters.
it.h: Pressure reveals who people are.

it.q: Read: "Dad gripped the wheel so hard his knuckles turned white, but his voice stayed calm." What does this contrast reveal?
ch: Dad is afraid but trying to keep others calm.
Dad is angry at the car.
it.h: Compare his hands and his voice.

it.q: What does "whiteout" most likely mean in a story about a blizzard?
ch: a condition where snow makes it nearly impossible to see
it.h: Use the setting as a clue.

it.q: Explain how a story's setting could change a character's relationship with a sibling.
it.ans: Being stuck together in a dangerous setting might force siblings to rely on each other, ending an argument and bringing them closer.
it.h: Think about how danger changes priorities.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Contrasting characters' points of view

it.q: Dramatic irony occurs when
ch: the reader knows something a character does not
a story is told in first person
it.h: Think about who knows more.

it.q: Read: "Leo thought the abandoned mill was a perfect adventure. His sister, Rosa, saw only rotten boards and a 'No Trespassing' sign." How do their points of view differ?
ch: Leo sees excitement, while Rosa sees danger.
Rosa sees adventure, while Leo sees danger.
it.h: Compare what each character "sees."

it.q: Read: "Coach believed the team was ready for the tournament. The players, who had lost three practice games, were not so sure." What effect does the difference in points of view create?
ch: tension about whether the team will succeed
it.h: How do readers feel when characters disagree?

it.q: How can an author show a character's point of view?
ch: through the character's thoughts, words and actions
it.h: Think about all the ways readers get to know a character.

it.q: Write two sentences showing how two characters might view the same risk differently, such as trying out for a play.
it.ans: Marcus pictured himself bowing to a cheering crowd. His best friend, Dev, pictured himself forgetting every line in front of the whole school.
it.h: Give each character a different thought about the same event.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Evaluating an argument: sound reasoning and sufficient evidence

it.q: Evidence is sufficient when
ch: there is enough of it to convince a reasonable reader
it is only one personal story
it agrees with what the reader already thinks
it.h: Think about both the amount and the strength of the evidence.

it.q: Which evidence is most relevant to the claim "Bike helmets reduce head injuries"?
ch: hospital data showing fewer serious head injuries among riders who wore helmets
a survey showing most kids like blue helmets
a story about a bike race
it.h: Relevant evidence connects directly to the claim.

it.q: Read: "Every kid who skateboards ends up in the hospital." What is wrong with this claim?
ch: It is an overgeneralization that is not supported by evidence.
it.h: Watch for words like "every" and "always."

it.q: An author arguing for later school start times cites a study by a sleep scientist. How does this strengthen the argument?
it.h: Who is the source, and what kind of evidence is it?

it.q: Explain the difference between sound reasoning and faulty reasoning. Give an example of faulty reasoning.
it.ans: Sound reasoning logically connects evidence to a claim. Faulty reasoning makes leaps the evidence does not support, such as "My friend failed one test after staying up late, so everyone who stays up late fails tests."
it.h: Does the evidence really lead to the conclusion?

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Connotation, denotation and precise, concise language

it.q: A word's denotation is
it.h: Think "D" for dictionary.

it.q: Which word has the most negative connotation?
it.h: Which word suggests foolishness?

it.q: Which verb makes this sentence most precise? "The firefighter ___ into the burning building."
it.h: Which verb paints the clearest picture?

it.q: Which revision removes the wordiness from "Due to the fact that it was raining, we decided to make the decision to stay home"?
ch: Because it was raining, we decided to stay home.
Due to the fact that it was raining, we stayed home.
It was raining, so we made the decision to decide.
Because of rain, we made a decision to make.
it.h: Cut repeated or unnecessary words.

it.q: Explain how the connotations of "confident" and "arrogant" differ. Use each word in a sentence.
it.ans: Both describe believing in yourself, but "confident" is positive and "arrogant" is negative, suggesting too much pride. "The confident speaker smiled at the crowd." "The arrogant speaker ignored everyone's questions."
it.h: The words share a meaning, but how do they feel different?

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Writing an argument: claims, counterclaims and logical reasoning

it.q: In an argument, a counterclaim is
ch: an opposing view that the writer acknowledges
it.h: "Counter" means against.

it.q: Which claim is arguable?
ch: Middle schools should offer a rock-climbing elective.
it.h: An arguable claim is one that reasonable people could disagree with.

it.q: Which sentence acknowledges a counterclaim and responds to it?
ch: Although some parents worry about injuries, trained instructors and safety gear greatly reduce the risk.
it.h: Look for both sides in one sentence.

it.q: Which phrase best introduces evidence that supports a reason?
it.h: Evidence often follows a phrase that introduces an example.

it.q: Write a claim and two reasons for or against this question: Should middle schools offer tackle football?
it.ans: Example: Claim: Middle schools should offer flag football instead of tackle football. Reasons: Flag football teaches the same teamwork and skills, and it reduces the risk of head injuries for growing players.
it.h: Your reasons should explain why your claim is correct.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Evaluating an argument about taking academic risks

it.q: What makes reasoning "sound"?
ch: The reasons logically connect to the claim and are supported by evidence.
it.h: Sound reasoning holds together.

it.q: What does "sufficient evidence" mean?
ch: enough evidence to convincingly support a claim
it.h: Think about whether there is enough.

it.q: Read: "My cousin retook a test and did better, so retakes always improve learning." What is wrong with this reasoning?
it.h: Is one cousin enough?

it.q: Which evidence is most relevant to the claim "Allowing test retakes encourages students to learn from mistakes"?
ch: A study found students who reviewed errors before retakes scored higher on later exams.
it.h: Which connects directly to learning from mistakes?

it.q: How can an author's point of view affect an argument?
ch: It shapes which evidence the author chooses and emphasizes.
it.h: Authors select evidence that supports their view.

it.q: Explain the difference between a claim that is supported and one that is merely stated.
it.ans: A supported claim is backed by evidence such as data or examples; a merely stated claim gives no proof, so readers have no reason to accept it.
it.h: Look for evidence.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Spotting faulty reasoning: common logical fallacies

it.q: What is a logical fallacy?
ch: an error in reasoning that weakens an argument
it.h: Fallacies look convincing but are flawed.

it.q: "You can't trust Dana's idea about recycling; she's always late to class." What fallacy is this?
ch: attacking the person instead of the argument
it.h: Does being late affect the recycling idea?

it.q: "Either we ban all phones at school, or students will never learn anything." What fallacy is this?
ch: a false choice between only two extreme options
it.h: Are there really only two options?

it.q: "Everyone is buying these sneakers, so they must be the best." What fallacy is this?
it.h: Popularity does not prove quality.

it.q: "If we let students choose one book, soon they'll refuse to read anything assigned." What fallacy is this?
it.h: Does one step lead to an extreme without evidence?

it.q: Explain why recognizing fallacies helps you evaluate arguments.
it.ans: It lets you see when an argument relies on tricks instead of real evidence, so you are not persuaded by weak reasoning.
it.h: Think about being a careful reader.

lessons.u: Collection 3: Taking Risks (argument)
lessons.n: Listening to a speech: delineating claims and evaluating evidence

it.q: What does it mean to delineate a speaker's argument?
ch: to identify and describe the claim, reasons and evidence
it.h: Delineate means to outline clearly.

it.q: A speaker uses a personal story about a friend's injury to argue for bike helmets. What kind of support is this?
ch: an anecdote that appeals to emotion
it.h: A personal story is an anecdote.

it.q: Which question best helps evaluate a statistic in a speech?
ch: Where does the statistic come from, and is it current?
Does the speaker have a nice voice?
it.h: Check the source.

it.q: Why do speakers often repeat their main claim at the end?
ch: to help listeners remember the key point
it.h: Repetition helps memory.

it.q: A speaker says, "Studies show..." but never names the studies. How should a listener respond?
ch: Treat the evidence with caution until the source is verified.
it.h: Unnamed studies cannot be checked.

it.q: Explain the difference between an appeal to emotion and an appeal to logic, with an example of each.
it.ans: An appeal to emotion tries to make listeners feel something, like a sad story about a stray dog. An appeal to logic uses facts and reasoning, like data showing a shelter adopted out 40 percent more pets after a new program.
it.h: One targets feelings; the other targets reasoning.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Drama: structure, dialogue and stage directions

it.q: In a play, the dialogue is
it.h: Think about the lines the actors say.

it.q: A play is usually divided into
it.h: Which units are used in drama?

it.q: Read the stage direction "(MARISOL slams the door, then leans against it, smiling.)" What does it reveal?
ch: Marisol's actions show mixed or surprising feelings.
the time period of the play
it.h: Look at both of Marisol's actions.

it.q: How is reading a drama different from reading a short story?
ch: Readers learn about characters mainly through dialogue and stage directions rather than narration.
it.h: Who tells the story in a play?

it.q: Explain why a playwright might include a monologue, a long speech by one character.
it.ans: A monologue lets a character reveal private thoughts, feelings or background directly to the audience, which deepens the characterization or explains the conflict.
it.h: Think about what the audience learns when one character speaks at length.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: An author's point of view and how it differs from others'

it.q: An author's point of view is
ch: the author's position or attitude toward a topic
it.h: How does the author feel about the topic?

it.q: Which phrase most clearly reveals an author's point of view?
ch: "a rule that applies to grades 6 to 8"
it.h: Look for words with strong connotations.

it.q: An author writes, "Some educators argue that homework builds responsibility. While that may be true for older students, research on younger students shows little benefit." How does the author distinguish his or her position?
ch: by acknowledging another view and then presenting evidence against it
it.h: Look at the word "While" and what follows it.

it.q: Two articles about teen jobs give the same facts, but one calls part-time work "a valuable first step" and the other calls it "a distraction from school." What does this show?
ch: Authors with different points of view can present the same facts differently.
Facts have no effect on point of view.
it.h: Compare the word choices.

it.q: Explain why acknowledging opposing points of view can strengthen an author's argument.
it.ans: It shows the author is fair and has considered other views, which builds readers' trust, and it lets the author explain why his or her position is still stronger.
it.h: How does it affect a reader's trust?

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Figurative language and allusions

it.q: An allusion is
ch: a reference to a well-known person, place, story or event
a comparison using like or as
it.h: Allusions point to something readers are expected to recognize.

it.q: Read: "My little brother is a real Sherlock Holmes; he found my hidden candy in five minutes." What does the allusion suggest?
ch: The brother is very good at solving mysteries.
The brother wears a funny hat.
it.h: What is Sherlock Holmes known for?

it.q: Read: "Opening that box of old letters was like opening Pandora's box." What does this allusion suggest?
ch: Opening the box released many troubles.
The letters were written by a girl named Pandora.
it.h: In Greek mythology, what came out of Pandora's box?

it.q: Which sentence contains a metaphor?
ch: Adolescence is a bridge between childhood and adulthood.
Adolescence happens in the teen years.
it.h: A metaphor says one thing is another without using like or as.

it.q: Explain the meaning of "He met his Waterloo at the spelling bee." What does it allude to?
it.ans: It means he suffered a final, decisive defeat. It alludes to the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, where Napoleon was defeated.
it.h: Who was defeated at Waterloo?

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis: claims, quotations and commentary

it.q: A strong literary analysis thesis
ch: makes a specific claim about how an author develops a character or theme
gives a personal opinion of the text
it.h: Analysis explains how or why.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis about a play in which a boy learns to accept his sister's leaving for college?
ch: Through stage directions and dialogue, the playwright shows that growing up means finding new ways to stay connected to the people we love.
The play is about a brother and a sister.
it.h: Which thesis explains how the author develops a theme?

it.q: Which sentence cites evidence from a play most effectively?
ch: When the sister promises, "I'll call every Sunday," her words show her commitment to her brother.
The play says some stuff about calling.
I think she calls on Sunday.
it.h: Name the speaker, use quotation marks and explain the quote.

it.q: Which sentence is commentary rather than summary?
ch: The radio becomes a symbol of the siblings' bond, showing that love can outlast distance.
The sister gives her brother a radio.
The play takes place in August.
it.h: Commentary explains meaning.

it.q: Explain why literary analysis essays are usually written in the present tense. Give an example sentence.
it.ans: The literary present treats the events as happening whenever the text is read. Example: "When the brother turns on the radio, he begins to accept the change."
it.h: Think about how a story "happens" each time it is read.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading literature: how a coming-of-age story develops its theme

it.q: What is a coming-of-age story?
ch: a story about a young person growing in understanding or maturity
a story about very old people
it.h: The main character grows up in some way.

it.q: How does a theme usually develop over the course of a story?
ch: through the character's experiences, choices and changes
it.h: Track the character from beginning to end.

it.q: Read: "For years Lin had rolled her eyes at her father's stories. Tonight, she asked for one." What does this change suggest?
ch: Lin's attitude toward her father is maturing.
it.h: Compare "for years" with "tonight."

it.q: Which statement is an objective summary rather than an opinion?
ch: A boy takes over his family's food stand for a week and learns how hard his mother works.
The story is amazing and everyone should read it.
it.h: Objective summaries leave out personal opinions.

it.q: What is the purpose of a symbol in a coming-of-age story?
ch: to represent a larger idea, such as growing up or independence
it.h: Objects can stand for ideas.

it.q: Explain how a minor character can help develop a story's theme.
it.ans: A minor character can challenge or guide the main character, causing the change that reveals the theme, such as a neighbor whose advice teaches responsibility.
it.h: Think about mentors or rivals.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Growing Up (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading a poem: sound, form and meaning in a poem about growing up

it.q: What is free verse?
ch: poetry without a regular rhyme or meter
it.h: "Free" from fixed patterns.

it.q: What is alliteration?
ch: repetition of vowel sounds in the middle of words
a comparison using like or as
a word that imitates a sound
it.h: "Silent, sleepy streets"

it.q: How can line breaks affect a poem's meaning?
ch: They create pauses that emphasize certain words or ideas.
it.h: Where does a reader pause?

it.q: What is the effect of a poem shifting from past tense to present tense?
ch: It can show a change from memory to the speaker's current experience.
it.h: Think about time.

it.q: Read: "the door that once was a mountain / is only a door." What does this suggest about growing up?
ch: Things that seemed huge in childhood seem ordinary later.
it.h: Compare the "mountain" with "only a door."

it.q: Explain how repetition of a phrase across stanzas can show change.
it.ans: When a repeated phrase appears in a new context or with a small change, it highlights how the speaker or situation has changed over time.
it.h: Think about the same words in different moments.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Theme in science fiction

it.q: Science fiction often
ch: imagines how science or technology might change people's lives
explains how to repair a computer
it.h: Think about "what if" stories.

it.q: In a story, a boy's robot dog does everything perfectly, but he feels lonely until he adopts a real puppy that makes mistakes. Which theme fits?
ch: Imperfect, real relationships can matter more than perfect technology.
Technology is always better than nature.
it.h: What does the boy learn?

it.q: How is a theme usually developed over the course of a story?
ch: through the characters' changes, choices and key events
only through descriptions of the setting
it.h: Think of how events build meaning.

it.q: Which sentence is an objective summary of a story?
ch: A girl whose glasses answer every question learns to value her grandmother's stories during a shutdown.
This is the best story I have ever read.
The girl should have thrown away her glasses.
it.h: Leave out opinions.

it.q: Explain how a story's conflict can help develop its theme. Use an example about technology.
it.ans: The conflict forces a character to make choices that reveal the message. For example, a character who must choose between a video game tournament and a friend's birthday party learns that friendships matter more than winning.
it.h: How does the character's choice reveal the message?

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Comparing two authors' writing on the same topic

it.q: When two authors write about the same topic, a reader should compare
ch: only the length of each text
it.h: What parts make up an argument?

it.q: Two articles discuss electric scooters in cities. One cites accident data; the other cites reduced traffic. What does this show?
ch: The authors chose different evidence to support different emphases.
Both authors have the same purpose.
it.h: Think about what each author wants readers to notice.

it.q: Two authors describe the same survey, in which 60 percent of students wanted a longer lunch. One calls the result "a strong majority"; the other says "40 percent are satisfied." What does this show?
ch: Authors can interpret the same data differently.
it.h: Look at how each author describes the same numbers.

it.q: Which question best helps a reader evaluate two conflicting articles?
ch: Which article uses more credible and relevant evidence?
Which article has a longer title?
it.h: Focus on the quality of the evidence.

it.q: Explain why it is useful to read more than one source on a controversial topic.
it.ans: Different sources may present different evidence or interpretations. Comparing them helps you see the full picture, notice bias and form a well-informed opinion.
it.h: What might one source leave out?

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Placing modifiers and punctuating coordinate adjectives

it.q: A misplaced modifier is
ch: a word or phrase placed too far from the word it describes
a verb in the wrong tense
it.h: A modifier should sit next to the word it describes.

it.q: Which sentence has a misplaced modifier?
ch: We bought a laptop from the store with a cracked screen.
We bought a laptop with a cracked screen from the store.
From the store, we bought a laptop.
The laptop had a cracked screen.
it.h: Does the store have a cracked screen?

it.q: Which sentence has a dangling modifier?
ch: Scrolling through the app, the time flew by.
Scrolling through the app, Maya lost track of time.
The app was fun to scroll.
it.h: Who was scrolling? Is that person named?

it.q: Which sentence correctly uses a comma between coordinate adjectives?
ch: It was a long, boring video.
It was a long boring, video.
It was a, long boring video.
It was long, a boring video.
it.h: If you can switch the adjectives or put "and" between them, use a comma.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence to fix the dangling modifier: "While charging overnight, my alarm didn't go off."
it.ans: While my phone was charging overnight, the alarm didn't go off. (Any revision that names what was charging.)
it.h: Add who or what was charging.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Research: synthesizing credible sources and citing them

it.q: Synthesizing sources means
ch: combining information from several sources to answer a question
it.h: Think about putting pieces together.

it.q: Which source is most credible for research on how screen time affects sleep?
ch: an article in a peer-reviewed medical journal
it.h: Who checks the information carefully, and who might be biased?

it.q: A student's research question is "Is technology good?" How could it be improved?
ch: Narrow it to "How does using phones before bed affect middle schoolers' sleep?"
Make it broader: "What is everything about technology?"
it.h: A good research question is focused.

it.q: What is the best way to include a source's exact words in a report?
ch: put them in quotation marks and cite the source
change a few words and leave out the source
it.h: Exact words need quotation marks and credit.

it.q: Explain how you can tell whether a website is a reliable source.
it.ans: Check who wrote it and the author's expertise, whether it comes from a respected organization (a government agency, university or established news outlet), when it was published or updated, whether it cites evidence and whether it is trying to sell something.
it.h: Think about author, purpose, date and evidence.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how recommendation algorithms work

it.q: What is an algorithm?
ch: a set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task
it.h: A recipe is a simple example.

it.q: Why do apps recommend videos based on what you watched before?
ch: to predict what you will like and keep you watching
it.h: Think about the app's goal.

it.q: What is a "filter bubble"?
ch: a situation where you mostly see content that matches your existing interests or views
a soap bubble on a screen
it.h: Bubbles enclose things.

it.q: Read: "Engagement, such as likes, comments and time spent watching, is a key signal." What does "engagement" mean here?
ch: how much users interact with content
it.h: Look at the examples.

it.q: An article explains how algorithms work and then describes their benefits and drawbacks. What structure is used in the second part?
ch: compare and contrast, or advantages and disadvantages
it.h: Benefits versus drawbacks.

it.q: Name one benefit and one drawback of recommendation algorithms.
it.ans: Benefit: they help people quickly find content they enjoy. Drawback: they can keep people in filter bubbles or encourage spending too much time on screens.
it.h: Think about convenience and limits.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Media literacy: evaluating digital sources and spotting misinformation

it.q: What is misinformation?
ch: false or misleading information, whether shared on purpose or by mistake
it.h: "Mis-" means wrongly.

it.q: Which is the best first step when you see a shocking headline online?
ch: Read beyond the headline and check whether reliable sources report the same story.
Assume it is true because it has many likes.
it.h: Headlines can be misleading.

it.q: What does "lateral reading" mean?
ch: leaving a website to see what other sources say about it
reading a page from bottom to top
it.h: You go "across" to other sources.

it.q: A photo is shared with the caption "Flooding in our city today." How could you check it?
ch: do a reverse image search to see where and when the photo first appeared
it.h: Photos can be old or from somewhere else.

it.q: Which feature suggests a website may be satire, not real news?
ch: an "About" page explaining that the site publishes humor
it.h: Some sites are meant to be funny.

it.q: Explain why a post with thousands of shares is not necessarily true.
it.ans: Popularity does not prove accuracy; false information can spread quickly because it is surprising or emotional, so it must be checked with reliable sources.
it.h: Think about why false stories spread.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Living with Technology (research)
lessons.n: Quoting and citing sources correctly in research writing

it.q: When should a writer use a direct quotation?
ch: when the exact words are especially powerful or important
it.h: Quote sparingly.

it.q: Which sentence correctly integrates a quotation?
ch: According to the scientist, "Bees are essential to our food supply."
According to the scientist "Bees are essential to our food supply".
According to the scientist, Bees are essential to our food supply.
According to the scientist, "bees are essential to our food supply.
it.h: Check the comma and quotation marks.

it.q: What is a paraphrase?
ch: the author's idea restated in your own words and sentence structure
a summary of only the title
a quotation with one word changed
it.h: Change both words and structure.

it.q: Why must writers cite paraphrased ideas, not just quotations?
ch: The ideas still belong to the original author.
it.h: Credit goes with ideas, too.

it.q: What does an ellipsis (...) in a quotation show?
ch: that words have been left out
it.h: It marks an omission.

it.q: Paraphrase this sentence and add a citation phrase: "Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep each night to function at their best."
it.ans: Health experts explain that most teens function best with roughly eight to ten hours of sleep per night.
it.h: Use new wording and name the source type.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Historical fiction and historical accounts

it.q: Historical fiction is
ch: a made-up story set in a real time and place in the past
a true account written by a historian
a story with no real details
it.h: Think fiction plus history.

it.q: An author writes a novel about a boy working on the transcontinental railroad. Which detail is most likely invented?
ch: the boy's conversations with his best friend
the year the railroad was completed
it.h: What would no historical record contain?

it.q: Why might an author of historical fiction invent characters and details?
ch: to help readers connect emotionally with the people and the period
to make the history completely inaccurate
it.h: What can a story do that a history book cannot?

it.q: How can a reader check whether details in a historical novel are accurate?
ch: compare them with reliable historical sources
ask a character in the story
it.h: Fiction is not always fact.

it.q: Explain one way a historical novel and a history textbook might describe the same event differently.
it.ans: A textbook might give dates, causes and statistics, while a novel shows the event through one character's eyes, with feelings, dialogue and invented personal details.
it.h: Think about facts versus feelings.
