lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How individuals, events and ideas influence each other in history

it.q: Which question best helps you analyze how a person influenced events?
ch: What did this person do, and what changed because of it?
What was this person's favorite color?
Where did this person buy shoes?
it.h: Look for cause and effect.

it.q: Read: "After a drought destroyed their crops, many farmers moved west. Their arrival changed the economies of the towns they joined." How do the event and the people interact?
ch: The drought caused the farmers to move, and their move changed other towns.
it.h: Trace the chain of causes.

it.q: Which detail best shows an idea influencing people's actions?
ch: Inspired by speeches about equal rights, students organized peaceful protests.
The protest took place on a Tuesday.
it.h: Which detail shows an idea leading to action?

it.q: An article explains how a court ruling led a governor to sign a new law. What relationship does this show?
ch: One event led a person to take a new action.
it.h: Think about cause and effect between events and people.

it.q: Choose a historical figure you know. Explain one way that person was influenced by events and one way the person influenced events.
it.ans: Example: Cesar Chavez was shaped by the hard conditions he experienced as a farmworker, and he influenced events by organizing farmworkers and leading boycotts that improved working conditions.
it.h: Influence can go in both directions.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Greek and Latin roots, reference materials and concise language

it.q: The Latin root "jud" (as in "judge") relates to
it.h: Think of "judge" and "judicial."

it.q: "Segregate" comes from Latin words meaning "apart from the flock." What does "segregate" mean?
it.h: Think about the meaning of "apart."

it.q: The prefix "inter-" means "between." What does "interstate" mean?
it.h: Apply the meaning of the prefix.

it.q: Which revision is most concise? "In the year of 1947, the governor of the state signed a law that was new."
ch: In 1947, the governor signed a new law.
In the year of 1947, the state governor signed a new law that was new.
The governor in 1947 signed in that year a law.
In 1947 the governor of the state of California signed a law that was a new law.
it.h: Cut unnecessary and repeated words.

it.q: The Latin root "cred" means "believe." Explain the meanings of "credible" and "incredible," and name one more word with this root.
it.ans: "Credible" means believable; "incredible" means hard to believe or amazing. Other words: credit, credentials, creed.
it.h: Consider what the prefix "in-" adds.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis that compares fiction and history

it.q: When comparing historical fiction with a historical account, a writer should examine
ch: how the author of the fiction uses or changes historical facts
it.h: Ask how the story uses history.

it.q: Which thesis best compares a historical novel with a historical account?
ch: While the history article reports the facts of the 1906 earthquake, the novel uses one family's escape to show the fear and courage people felt.
Both texts are about an earthquake.
it.h: A strong comparison thesis explains how each text presents the topic.

it.q: Which transition best introduces a contrast between two texts?
it.h: Contrast shows difference.

it.q: Which evidence would best show that an author changed history?
ch: The novel says World War II ended in 1950, but historical records show it ended in 1945.
The novel has a sad ending.
The novel's main character is a girl.
it.h: Look for a factual difference.

it.q: Explain why an author of historical fiction might invent a character rather than write about a real person.
it.ans: An invented character gives the author freedom to create thoughts, dialogue and events while still showing what life was like, without misrepresenting a real person.
it.h: What freedom does an invented character allow?

lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading a historical account: Angel Island Immigration Station

it.q: What is an immigration station?
ch: a place where officials inspect people arriving in a country
it.h: Think about Ellis Island in New York.

it.q: What was the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882?
ch: a law that banned most Chinese laborers from immigrating to the United States
a law that welcomed all immigrants
it.h: "Exclusion" means keeping out.

it.q: Read: "Detainees waited weeks or months while officials questioned them." What does "detainees" mean?
ch: people held in custody or kept from leaving
it.h: "Detain" means to hold back.

it.q: How can laws shape individuals' lives, according to historical accounts?
ch: Laws can determine where people may live, work or travel, deeply affecting their experiences.
it.h: Think about immigration laws.

it.q: Why are poems carved into the walls of a building valuable to historians?
ch: They are firsthand evidence of the feelings and experiences of the people held there.
They show the building's age only.
it.h: Who wrote them, and why?

it.q: Explain how a single law could influence many individuals' lives over several decades.
it.ans: A law like the Chinese Exclusion Act stayed in effect for decades, so it shaped who could immigrate, separated families and affected generations of people and communities.
it.h: Think about long-term effects.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Fiction Meets History (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading historical fiction: how an author uses and alters history at Angel Island

it.q: How does historical fiction usually use history?
ch: It places invented characters and events in a real historical setting.
It has no connection to real events.
It is always set in the future.
it.h: Real setting, invented story.

it.q: Why might an author invent a character for a story about a real place?
ch: to help readers experience history through one person's thoughts and feelings
it.h: Fiction offers an inside view.

it.q: A novel set in 1920 has a character text a friend. What is the problem?
ch: It is an anachronism, something that does not belong in that time period.
it.h: Did phones text in 1920?

it.q: How can readers check the historical accuracy of a novel?
ch: by comparing it with reliable historical accounts
it.h: Use nonfiction sources.

it.q: An author's note explains that a character was based on several real people. What does this tell readers?
ch: The character is fictional but reflects real experiences.
The character is a real person.
it.h: Composite characters combine real lives.

it.q: Explain one way historical fiction can help readers understand history differently than a nonfiction account.
it.ans: Historical fiction shows events through a character's emotions and daily life, helping readers feel what the experience was like, while nonfiction focuses on facts and broad events.
it.h: Think about emotions versus facts.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How dialogue and incidents propel action and reveal character

it.q: Read: "'If you tell Coach, I'm off the team,' Marcus whispered. Jaylen looked at the broken window, then at his best friend." How does this dialogue propel the action?
ch: It forces Jaylen to make a difficult decision about loyalty and honesty.
it.h: What choice does Marcus's line create for Jaylen?

it.q: Which incident would most likely reveal a character's honesty?
ch: She returns extra change that a cashier gave her by mistake.
it.h: Look for an action that involves a moral choice.

it.q: Read: "'I'm fine,' Leah said, though her voice cracked." What does this line reveal?
ch: Leah is hiding her true feelings.
it.h: Compare what she says with how she says it.

it.q: What is a story's inciting incident?
ch: the event that sets the main conflict in motion
the time and place of the story
it.h: Think of the event that starts the trouble.

it.q: Explain how a single line of dialogue can provoke a character's decision. Give an example.
it.ans: Dialogue can present a challenge, threat or offer that forces a choice. For example, "Take it. No one will ever know" makes a character decide whether to steal.
it.h: Think of words that put pressure on a character.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Central ideas, connections and distinctions in informational texts

it.q: When an author draws a distinction between two ideas, the author
ch: shows that they are the same
it.h: To distinguish means to tell apart.

it.q: Read: "Like a coach, a good mentor offers encouragement. Unlike a coach, a mentor focuses on the whole person, not on winning." What does the author do?
ch: draws both a comparison and a distinction
it.h: Look for "like" and "unlike."

it.q: Which detail best develops the central idea "Small daily choices shape long-term health"?
ch: Studies show that regular brisk walking is linked to a lower risk of heart disease.
Walking shoes come in many colors.
it.h: Which detail connects a daily choice to a long-term result?

it.q: An author uses an analogy comparing a budget to a map. What is the purpose?
ch: to explain an unfamiliar idea by connecting it to something familiar
to tell a story about travel
it.h: Analogies make ideas clearer.

it.q: Write an objective summary of this paragraph: "Many students believe multitasking saves time. However, research suggests that switching between tasks reduces accuracy and increases the time needed to finish each task. Focusing on one task at a time is often more efficient."
it.ans: Although many students think multitasking saves time, research suggests that switching tasks lowers accuracy and slows work, so focusing on one task is usually more efficient.
it.h: Keep the central idea and key details; leave out opinions.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Verbals: gerunds, participles and infinitives

it.q: A gerund is
ch: a verb form ending in -ing that acts as a noun
a verb form that acts as an adjective
it.h: Gerunds name activities.

it.q: In "Swimming is Ana's favorite sport," what is "Swimming"?
it.h: It is the subject of the sentence.

it.q: In "The crying baby finally fell asleep," what is "crying"?
it.h: It describes a noun.

it.q: Which sentence contains an infinitive?
ch: Rafi wanted to tell the truth.
it.h: Look for "to" plus a verb.

it.q: Write three sentences about making a choice: one with a gerund, one with a participle and one with an infinitive. Label each.
it.ans: Gerund: "Deciding was the hardest part." Participle: "The worried student paced the hall." Infinitive: "She chose to speak up."
it.h: Gerund = noun, participle = adjective, infinitive = to plus a verb.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis of character and theme

it.q: A literary analysis essay about a character should explain
ch: how the author develops the character through actions, dialogue and choices
it.h: Focus on how the author does it.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis for an essay about a story in which a student reports a stolen answer key?
ch: Through the narrator's private struggle and public choice, the author shows that integrity often requires sacrificing comfort.
it.h: A strong thesis makes an arguable claim about how meaning is developed.

it.q: Which sentence best integrates a short quotation?
ch: The narrator's reply, "Just don't use it," shows his hesitation.
"Just don't use it." This is what he said.
Just don't use it, the narrator.
it.h: Blend the quotation into your own sentence.

it.q: Which sentence is analysis rather than summary?
ch: The narrator's refusal to name his friend reveals that he values fairness without wanting revenge.
The narrator goes to the teacher's room.
it.h: Analysis explains significance.

it.q: Write a sentence of commentary that explains how a character's choice reveals a theme, using this evidence: a girl returns a lost wallet full of cash even though her family is struggling.
it.ans: Her choice to return the wallet despite her family's need reveals that honesty is worth keeping even when it costs us.
it.h: Explain what the choice shows about the theme.

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading literature: how a single choice reveals character and develops theme

it.q: What is internal conflict?
ch: a struggle within a character's own mind
it.h: The struggle happens inside.

it.q: Read: "Ana's hand hovered over the send button for a full minute." What does this detail suggest?
ch: Ana is unsure about her decision.
Ana is sending a happy message.
it.h: Why would someone hesitate?

it.q: How can a character's decision propel the action of a story?
ch: It creates consequences that lead to new events.
It has no effect on events.
it.h: Choices cause effects.

it.q: Which detail reveals a character's values most clearly?
ch: He returned the extra money even though no one would have known.
it.h: Values show in choices.

it.q: Which is the best theme statement for a story about a girl who admits a mistake and loses a prize?
ch: Integrity can matter more than winning.
it.h: A theme is a complete idea about life.

it.q: Explain why authors often show a character's choice through actions and thoughts rather than stating the character's values directly.
it.ans: Showing lets readers infer values from evidence, which feels more real and engaging than being told, and it lets readers see the character's struggle.
it.h: Think about "show, don't tell."

lessons.u: Collection 1: Choices and Consequences (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how habits form and how they can change

it.q: What is a habit?
ch: a behavior repeated so often that it becomes nearly automatic
it.h: Think about brushing your teeth.

it.q: In the "habit loop" described by many researchers, what is a cue?
ch: a trigger that starts the behavior
it.h: Cues signal the brain to begin.

it.q: Read: "Every time Diego hears the bell, he checks his phone." In this example, what is the cue?
it.h: What triggers the action?

it.q: An article first explains a process, then compares two strategies for changing it. Which structures are used?
ch: sequence followed by compare and contrast
it.h: Look at both parts.

it.q: Why might replacing a habit work better than simply trying to stop it?
ch: Keeping the same cue and reward but swapping the routine is easier for the brain.
it.h: Think about what the brain still wants.

it.q: Describe one habit, and identify its cue, routine and reward.
it.ans: Cue: feeling bored after school. Routine: eating chips. Reward: a quick feeling of comfort and something to do.
it.h: Trigger, action, payoff.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Our Fragile Planet (informative)
lessons.n: Word choice, tone and comparisons in poetry

it.q: In poetry, tone is
ch: the speaker's attitude toward the subject
it.h: Think about the feeling behind the words.

it.q: Read: "The river, once a roaring giant, now whispers through the reeds." What change does the poet suggest?
ch: The river has become much smaller or weaker.
The river has moved to a new place.
it.h: Compare "roaring giant" with "whispers."

it.q: Which word gives the most hopeful tone to a line about a forest after a fire?
it.h: Which word suggests new life?

it.q: An analogy
ch: compares two things to explain a relationship between them
always compares a person to an animal
it.h: Analogies show how one relationship is like another.

it.q: Write a line of poetry about a melting glacier that uses a simile, and explain the effect of your comparison.
it.ans: "The glacier wept like a candle in a warm room." The simile suggests slow, steady melting and gives the ice a sense of sadness.
it.h: Choose a comparison that creates a feeling.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Our Fragile Planet (informative)
lessons.n: How paragraphs and sentences build a central idea

it.q: The topic sentence of a paragraph usually
it.h: It tells what the paragraph is about.

it.q: In a paragraph about coral reefs, a sentence reads: "For example, the Great Barrier Reef has lost large areas of coral during marine heat waves." What role does this sentence play?
ch: It gives an example that supports the paragraph's main point.
it.h: Notice the words "For example."

it.q: Which sentence would best connect a paragraph about the causes of air pollution to one about its health effects?
ch: These sources of pollution do more than dirty the sky; they also affect our bodies.
it.h: A transition links the previous idea to the next one.

it.q: Why might an author place a surprising statistic at the start of an article?
ch: to grab readers' attention and show why the topic matters
it.h: Think about hooking the reader.

it.q: Explain how a concluding sentence can strengthen a paragraph.
it.ans: It restates or extends the main point, ties the details together and can lead into the next paragraph, helping readers understand why the information matters.
it.h: Think about what the reader should remember.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Our Fragile Planet (informative)
lessons.n: Active and passive voice

it.q: In the active voice,
it.h: Who is doing the action?

it.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
ch: The beach was cleaned by volunteers.
it.h: Look for a form of "be" plus a past participle, often followed by "by."

it.q: Which revision changes "The turtle was rescued by the lifeguard" to active voice?
ch: The lifeguard was rescued by the turtle.
it.h: Make the doer of the action the subject.

it.q: When might a writer choose the passive voice?
ch: when the doer of the action is unknown or less important than the receiver
when the writer wants every sentence to be longer
when the writer is giving commands
when the writer is telling a joke
it.h: Think of "The window was broken" when no one knows who broke it.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence in the active voice: "Millions of tons of plastic are dumped into the ocean by people each year." Then explain which version is more effective in an argument about responsibility, and why.
it.ans: Active: "People dump millions of tons of plastic into the ocean each year." The active version is more effective for an argument about responsibility because it names people as the ones doing the action.
it.h: Who is doing the dumping?

lessons.u: Collection 2: Our Fragile Planet (informative)
lessons.n: Writing an informative essay with precise language and clear structure

it.q: Domain-specific vocabulary means
ch: words used in a particular subject, such as "ecosystem" or "biodiversity"
it.h: Think of science or history terms.

it.q: Which is the strongest thesis for an informative essay about ocean acidification?
ch: Ocean acidification, caused by the ocean absorbing carbon dioxide, threatens shellfish and coral reefs, but reducing emissions can slow it.
I think the ocean is sad.
it.h: A strong thesis previews causes, effects and solutions.

it.q: Which is the best way to organize an essay explaining how a wildfire affects an ecosystem over time?
ch: chronological order, from the fire to recovery years later
order of the writer's favorite facts
it.h: Think about time.

it.q: Which graphic would best help readers compare the amount of plastic recycled in five countries?
it.h: You are comparing amounts.

it.q: Write a sentence that defines "biodiversity" for the readers of an informative essay.
it.ans: Biodiversity is the variety of living things, including plants, animals and microorganisms, found in a particular place or on Earth as a whole.
it.h: Give a clear definition in context.

lessons.u: Collection 2: Our Fragile Planet (informative)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: kelp forests, sea otters and a fragile balance

it.q: What is a keystone species?
ch: a species that has a large effect on its ecosystem compared with its numbers
the largest animal in an ecosystem
a species found only in zoos
it.h: Like the keystone in an arch.

it.q: Read: "Sea otters eat sea urchins, which graze on kelp." What would likely happen if sea otters disappeared?
ch: Urchin numbers would rise and kelp could decline.
it.h: Follow the chain.

it.q: What is a trophic cascade?
ch: a chain of effects through a food web when one species changes
it.h: "Cascade" suggests effects flowing downward.

it.q: Read: "Urchin barrens, rocky areas stripped of kelp, now cover parts of the coast." What are urchin barrens?
ch: areas where urchins have eaten away the kelp
it.h: The definition follows the comma.

it.q: How does a paragraph that begins with a surprising statistic contribute to an article?
ch: It grabs attention and introduces the scale of the problem.
it.h: Think about hooks.

it.q: Explain why protecting one species can help an entire ecosystem.
it.ans: Species are connected in food webs, so protecting a keystone species like sea otters can keep other populations balanced and preserve habitats like kelp forests for many organisms.
it.h: Think about connections.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Theme and objective summary

it.q: An objective summary
ch: states the central ideas and key events without personal opinions
is written in the first person
it.h: Objective means without bias.

it.q: Which statement is a theme rather than a topic?
ch: Speaking up takes courage, but it can change unfair rules.
it.h: A theme is a complete idea.

it.q: How does a theme usually develop over the course of a story?
ch: through the conflict, the characters' choices and the ways they change
only through descriptions of the setting
it.h: Think about the whole story.

it.q: A story ends with a student who has been silent all year finally raising her hand. What does this final image most likely suggest?
ch: She has found the confidence to speak up.
it.h: Think about what the action represents.

it.q: Write a one-sentence theme statement for a story in which a boy writes to the city council about a dangerous intersection and a crosswalk is installed.
it.ans: One person's voice, used thoughtfully, can bring real change to a community.
it.h: State a message that applies beyond the story.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Delineating and evaluating an argument

it.q: To delineate an argument means to
ch: identify and describe its claim, reasons and evidence
it.h: Think "outline its parts."

it.q: An author arguing for more school libraries writes, "Libraries smell like old books, which is nice." What is the problem with this sentence?
ch: The evidence is irrelevant to the claim.
it.h: Does the detail show why libraries are needed?

it.q: Which evidence would best support the claim "Student voices should be included on school boards"?
ch: A district that added student board members reported that its policies on lunch and scheduling better reflected student needs.
Board meetings are held on Tuesdays.
it.h: Choose evidence that connects directly to the claim.

it.q: Which statement shows sound reasoning?
ch: Because a new crosswalk reduced accidents near one school, the city should study whether crosswalks would help near other schools.
Because one student liked the crosswalk, every city must build crosswalks.
Crosswalks are white, so they are safe.
If we build one crosswalk, soon all roads will close.
it.h: Does the conclusion follow carefully from the evidence?

it.q: Explain how an author's acknowledgment of conflicting evidence can make an argument more credible.
it.ans: It shows the author has considered all sides honestly and lets the author explain why the evidence still favors the claim, which builds readers' trust.
it.h: Think about trust.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Verb moods and avoiding shifts in mood

it.q: The indicative mood is used to
ch: express wishes or situations contrary to fact
it.h: Most ordinary statements use it.

it.q: Which sentence is in the imperative mood?
ch: If I were mayor, I would sign it.
it.h: Imperative sentences give commands.

it.q: Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
ch: If I were on the city council, I would vote for the new park.
If I was on the city council, I would vote for the new park.
If I am on the city council, I voted for the park.
If I be on the council, I vote.
it.h: Use "were" for wishes or situations that are not true.

it.q: Which sentence is in the conditional mood?
ch: If more students attended, the council might listen.
it.h: The conditional mood often uses would, could, might or should.

it.q: Write one sentence in each mood about speaking up: indicative, imperative, interrogative, conditional and subjunctive. Label each.
it.ans: Indicative: "Students spoke at the meeting." Imperative: "Write to your representative." Interrogative: "Will you speak at the meeting?" Conditional: "If we organized, we could change the rule." Subjunctive: "I wish the meeting were longer."
it.h: Use a statement, a command, a question, a condition and a wish.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Writing an argument: precise claims, opposing claims and cohesion

it.q: An effective argument distinguishes the writer's claim from
it.h: Strong arguments show awareness of other views.

it.q: Which claim is most precise?
ch: Our school should extend lunch from 30 to 45 minutes so students have time to eat and rest.
it.h: A precise claim is specific.

it.q: Which phrase best connects a reason to an opposing claim?
ch: While some argue that longer lunches reduce class time,
it.h: Look for words that link ideas.

it.q: Which evidence is most credible for an argument about student sleep?
ch: data from a national sleep research organization
it.h: Who has expert knowledge?

it.q: Write a claim and a reasonable opposing claim for this topic: Should students vote on school dress codes?
it.ans: Claim: Students should have a vote on dress codes because the rules directly affect them. Opposing claim: Some argue adults should decide because they must consider safety and district rules.
it.h: The opposing claim should be reasonable, not silly.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Analyzing a historical speech: Susan B. Anthony on the right to vote

it.q: What does it mean to analyze how a speaker responds to conflicting viewpoints?
ch: to examine how the speaker acknowledges and answers opposing arguments
it.h: Look for how opponents' ideas are handled.

it.q: Why would a speaker quote a founding document in an argument?
ch: to show that the speaker's claim is grounded in widely respected principles
it.h: Founding documents carry authority.

it.q: What is an indictment?
ch: a formal accusation of a crime
it.h: Think about courts.

it.q: Read: "It was we, the people; not we, the white male citizens." What technique does this use?
ch: contrast and repetition to emphasize who "the people" includes
it.h: Look at the repeated "we."

it.q: Why is this speech considered a primary source?
ch: It was delivered by a person directly involved in the events, at the time.
It was written by a modern historian.
it.h: Firsthand, from the time.

it.q: Explain why a speaker might begin by naming the accusation against her.
it.ans: Naming the accusation directly shows confidence and lets her immediately reframe it, arguing that what others call a crime was actually exercising her rights.
it.h: Think about controlling the framing.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Rhetorical devices in arguments: repetition, parallelism and rhetorical questions

it.q: What is parallelism?
ch: using the same grammatical structure for related ideas
it.h: "We came, we saw, we conquered."

it.q: What is a rhetorical question?
ch: a question asked for effect, not for an answer
a question with a numerical answer
it.h: The answer is implied.

it.q: Which sentence uses parallel structure?
ch: We will speak clearly, act boldly and listen carefully.
We will speak clearly, acting boldly and to listen carefully.
We will speak, boldly acting, listen.
Speaking clearly we will boldly and listening.
it.h: Check that each part has the same form.

it.q: What is the effect of repeating a phrase at the start of several sentences?
ch: It emphasizes the idea and creates rhythm.
it.h: Repetition draws attention.

it.q: What is an appeal to ethos?
ch: establishing the speaker's credibility and trustworthiness
it.h: Ethos relates to character.

it.q: Write a rhetorical question that could open a speech about protecting a local park.
it.ans: If we do not protect this park, where will our children play in twenty years?
it.h: Ask something whose answer seems obvious.

lessons.u: Collection 3: The Right to Be Heard (argument)
lessons.n: Presenting an argument and evaluating a speaker's evidence

it.q: What should a strong argument presentation include?
ch: a clear claim, relevant evidence, sound reasoning and a response to counterclaims
a long list of unrelated facts
it.h: Think about the parts of an argument.

it.q: Which delivery choice best supports credibility?
ch: speaking clearly, making eye contact and citing sources
reading quickly with no eye contact
it.h: Credibility comes from content and delivery.

it.q: When a speaker introduces irrelevant evidence, what should a listener do?
ch: Note that it does not support the claim.
Accept it because it is interesting.
Ignore the rest of the speech.
it.h: Relevance matters.

it.q: A speaker cites "a recent study" without naming it. Why is that a problem?
ch: It makes the speech too short.
it.h: Can you verify it?

it.q: Which visual would best support an argument that a crosswalk is needed?
ch: a chart showing near-collisions at the intersection over six months
it.h: Choose visuals that provide evidence.

it.q: Explain how a speaker can respond to a counterclaim without weakening their own argument.
it.ans: The speaker can acknowledge the counterclaim fairly, then use evidence and reasoning to show why their claim is still stronger, which makes them seem fair and credible.
it.h: Acknowledge, then refute.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
lessons.n: Dramatic irony, suspense and humor

it.q: Dramatic irony occurs when
ch: the audience knows something a character does not
a character says the opposite of what he or she means
an event turns out the opposite of what was expected
it.h: Think about who knows more.

it.q: In a play, the audience sees a villain pour poison into a cup, but the hero cheerfully reaches for it. What effect does this create?
it.h: How do you feel when you know danger is coming but a character does not?

it.q: In a comedy, a boy practices a romantic speech to the wrong person in the dark, while the audience knows who is really there. What effect is created?
it.h: Is the situation more scary or more funny?

it.q: Which kind of narrator makes dramatic irony easiest to create?
ch: a third-person omniscient narrator who shares information some characters lack
a first-person narrator who knows nothing
a narrator who never describes events
it.h: Who can reveal secrets to the reader?

it.q: Describe a moment from a movie, book or show in which you knew more than a character. Explain the effect it had on you.
it.ans: Example: In a mystery, viewers see the thief hide in a closet while the detective walks right past; this creates suspense because we want to warn the detective.
it.h: Did it make you nervous, or did it make you laugh?

lessons.u: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
lessons.n: Analyzing evidence and structure in texts about real mysteries

it.q: The strongest textual evidence is the evidence that
ch: most directly supports the analysis or inference
comes from any sentence in the text
it.h: Choose the quotation that proves your point best.

it.q: An article about a lost settlement presents three theories, each in its own paragraph, followed by an evaluation. What structure is used?
ch: a series of explanations followed by analysis
it.h: Look at how the paragraphs are arranged.

it.q: Which inference is best supported by the detail "The dinner plates were still on the table, half full"?
ch: The people had finished eating long before.
The house had been empty for years.
it.h: What would cause someone to leave food unfinished?

it.q: What is the role of a sentence such as "But the evidence does not support this theory"?
ch: It signals a shift from presenting an idea to challenging it.
it.h: Notice the word "But."

it.q: Explain why an author writing about an unsolved mystery might present several theories instead of only one.
it.ans: Presenting several theories gives readers a balanced view of the evidence, shows which explanations are stronger or weaker and lets readers draw their own conclusions.
it.h: Think about fairness and evidence.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
lessons.n: Punctuation for pauses, breaks and omissions

it.q: An ellipsis (...) can show
ch: that words were left out of a quotation or that a speaker pauses
it.h: Think about missing words or trailing off.

it.q: Which sentence uses an ellipsis to show a pause or hesitation?
ch: "I thought I heard... no, it's nothing."
it.h: Where does the speaker trail off?

it.q: A dash, typed here as two hyphens, is used in "The noise came from upstairs -- from the guest room." What does the dash do?
ch: It creates a break that emphasizes the added information.
It joins two words into one.
it.h: Dashes create a sharp break.

it.q: Which sentence uses a comma correctly before a contrasting phrase?
ch: The door was open, not closed.
The door was, open not closed.
The door, was open not closed.
The door was open not, closed.
it.h: Pause before the contrasting idea.

it.q: A quotation reads: "The captain wrote in the log that the weather was calm, the crew was healthy and the cargo was secure." Shorten it with an ellipsis so it keeps only the information about the cargo, without changing the meaning.
it.ans: "The captain wrote in the log that... the cargo was secure."
it.h: Remove the middle words and mark the omission.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
lessons.n: Writing a narrative that builds suspense

it.q: Foreshadowing is
ch: a hint about what will happen later
it.h: Think "a shadow of the future."

it.q: Which sentence best builds suspense?
ch: The footsteps stopped right outside my door.
it.h: Which sentence makes you want to know what happens next?

it.q: Which technique slows the pacing to build suspense?
ch: describing small sensory details moment by moment
summarizing several days in one sentence
it.h: Think slow motion.

it.q: Which point of view would let a writer create dramatic irony by showing readers things the main character does not know?
ch: first person, told by the main character
a diary written by the main character
it.h: The narrator must know more than the character.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence to build suspense with sensory details: "I went into the dark basement."
it.ans: Example: "I pressed my hand against the cold stair rail and eased down into the basement, where the air smelled of damp concrete and something shifted in the far corner."
it.h: Add sights, sounds, smells or feelings.

lessons.u: Collection 4: Into the Unknown (narrative)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: exploring the deep ocean

it.q: What is the Challenger Deep?
ch: the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, in the Mariana Trench
it.h: It is in the western Pacific.

it.q: Why is the deep ocean so difficult to explore?
ch: Crushing pressure, cold and complete darkness make it dangerous for people and machines.
it.h: Think about conditions miles down.

it.q: What is bioluminescence?
it.h: "Bio" means life; "lumin" means light.

it.q: Read: "Remotely operated vehicles, or ROVs, are controlled by pilots on ships." Why are ROVs useful?
ch: They can explore depths too dangerous for people.
it.h: No one needs to be inside.

it.q: How does a writer's choice to start with a comparison, such as "deeper than Mount Everest is tall," help readers?
ch: It helps them picture an enormous, unfamiliar distance.
it.h: Comparisons make big numbers concrete.

it.q: Explain why scientists might say we know more about the surface of the moon than about our own deep ocean.
it.ans: The deep ocean is dark, under extreme pressure and very hard to reach, so much of it has not been mapped or explored in detail, while the moon's surface can be photographed from space.
it.h: Think about how each is studied.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How modern stories draw on myths

it.q: An archetype is
ch: a character type, pattern or symbol that appears in stories across many cultures
it.h: Think of the "wise mentor" or the "hero's journey."

it.q: A modern novel features a girl who opens a forbidden box that releases troubles but also hope. Which myth does it draw on?
it.h: Which myth involves a box (or jar) and hope?

it.q: A story about a businessman whose greed turns everything he touches into money, until he cannot hug his daughter, draws on which myth?
it.h: Think of the golden touch.

it.q: When a modern author retells a myth, what is most often changed?
ch: the setting and details, while the core pattern or theme is kept
every event and the entire theme
it.h: What makes a retelling feel new?

it.q: Name a modern story, movie or show that draws on an old myth, fairy tale or traditional story, and explain one similarity and one difference.
it.ans: Example: A movie about a girl who disguises herself to take her father's place in the army draws on the legend of Mulan; both heroines hide their identity to protect family, but the movie adds humor and new characters.
it.h: Compare one pattern and one change.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How informational texts connect, compare and categorize ideas

it.q: When an author categorizes information, the author
ch: groups ideas or examples by shared features
it.h: Think of sorting.

it.q: An author compares the hero's journey to a map. What does this analogy suggest?
ch: The pattern guides storytellers from the beginning of a story to the end.
Maps are a kind of story.
it.h: What does a map do?

it.q: Which sentence would best serve as a topic sentence for a paragraph about trickster figures in folklore?
ch: Many cultures tell stories about clever tricksters who outwit stronger opponents.
it.h: Which sentence states a main idea that examples could support?

it.q: Why might an author include a paragraph about critics of a theory?
ch: to give a balanced view and show the theory's limits
it.h: Think about fairness.

it.q: Explain how a single paragraph can refine a key concept in an informational text. Give an example.
it.ans: A paragraph can add a definition, an example or a limitation that sharpens the reader's understanding. For example, after introducing the hero's journey, a paragraph listing its stages shows exactly what the pattern includes.
it.h: Think about adding precision.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Allusions, irony, puns and word origins

it.q: Verbal irony occurs when
ch: a speaker says the opposite of what he or she means
the audience knows more than a character
it.h: Think of sarcasm.

it.q: After the car breaks down in the rain, a passenger says, "Well, this is a lovely trip." What kind of irony is this?
it.h: Does the speaker really mean "lovely"?

it.q: Which sentence contains a pun?
ch: The baker quit because he couldn't make enough dough.
it.h: Look for a word with two meanings.

it.q: Read: "Her new job was a real Pandora's box." What does the allusion suggest?
ch: The job brought many unexpected problems.
The job came in a box.
it.h: What came out of Pandora's box?

it.q: The word "narcissistic" comes from the myth of Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection. Explain what "narcissistic" means and use it in a sentence.
it.ans: It means overly interested in oneself or one's appearance. "The narcissistic singer talked only about himself during the interview."
it.h: Think about Narcissus and his reflection.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Writing a literary analysis of a modern work and its source

it.q: When analyzing how a modern story draws on a myth, a writer should explain
ch: which elements are kept and which are changed, and why
only the plot of the myth
the design of the book cover
it.h: Think about similarities, differences and purpose.

it.q: Which thesis best analyzes a modern retelling of the Icarus myth?
ch: By moving the Icarus myth to a modern drone flight and adding forgiveness, the author turns a tale of punishment into a story about learning balance.
The story is like a myth.
it.h: A strong thesis explains how and why the story transforms its source.

it.q: Which sentence best uses evidence from both a myth and a modern story?
ch: Daedalus warns his son to avoid both the sun and the sea, just as the father in the modern story insists on the "middle path."
it.h: Connect specific details from both texts.

it.q: Which transition best signals that a modern author changed the source?
it.h: Which phrase shows a difference?

it.q: Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph explaining how a modern story changes the ending of the myth it draws on.
it.ans: Example: "Unlike the myth, which ends with Icarus drowning, the modern story ends with a father offering his daughter a second chance."
it.h: Name the change and its effect.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: How a modern story transforms a myth: Phaethon and the borrowed car

it.q: In the Greek myth, who was Phaethon?
ch: the son of the sun god, Helios, who tried to drive the sun's chariot
a hero who killed a monster
it.h: His father drove the sun across the sky.

it.q: What happened when Phaethon drove the sun chariot?
ch: He lost control, scorching the earth, and Zeus struck him down with a thunderbolt.
He gave it to his sister.
it.h: The horses were too strong for him.

it.q: When a modern author draws on a myth, what might change?
ch: the setting, characters and details, while the core pattern or theme stays recognizable
it.h: Modern stories often transform old patterns.

it.q: What theme is central to the Phaethon myth?
ch: Pride and insisting on power before you are ready can lead to disaster.
it.h: Why did he want to drive?

it.q: Why might a modern author retell a myth in a new setting?
ch: to show that its themes still apply to people today
it.h: Old stories carry lasting lessons.

it.q: Name one element a modern story might keep from a myth and one it might change, and explain why.
it.ans: It might keep the theme of pride leading to a fall, because that lesson still matters, but change the chariot to a car so modern readers connect with it.
it.h: Think about theme versus details.

lessons.u: Collection 5: Old Stories, New Forms (literary analysis)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: how one story appears in many cultures

it.q: What is a folktale variant?
ch: a version of a story told differently in a different culture or time
it.h: Variants share a core but differ in details.

it.q: Why do similar stories appear in cultures far apart?
ch: Shared human experiences, travel and trade can lead to similar stories.
They were all written in the same year.
it.h: Think about universal themes and contact.

it.q: Which detail would be a cultural variation in a Cinderella-type story?
ch: a golden slipper in one version and a fish that grants wishes in another
a kind heroine who is mistreated
a lost object that identifies her
it.h: Which element changes from culture to culture?

it.q: An article compares versions of a story and categorizes their shared elements. What structure is used?
it.h: Comparing and grouping.

it.q: Read: "Folklorists study how stories change as they travel." What is a folklorist?
ch: a scholar who studies traditional stories and customs
it.h: "Folk" plus "-lore."

it.q: Explain how comparing story variants can help readers understand different cultures.
it.ans: Differences in details, like the magical helper or the setting, reveal what each culture valued, believed or experienced.
it.h: Think about what changes reveal.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Theme in science fiction

it.q: Science fiction often explores
ch: how scientific or technological changes might affect people and society
it.h: Think "what if."

it.q: In a story, a scientist invents a pill that removes all fear, but people begin taking dangerous risks. Which theme fits?
ch: Removing a natural human feeling can have unexpected costs.
it.h: What happens after the invention?

it.q: How can a minor character help develop a story's theme?
ch: by challenging the main character or showing another side of the issue
only by appearing in the title
it.h: Think about different perspectives.

it.q: Which detail would most likely signal a theme about unintended consequences?
ch: After the new dam was built, the fish downstream began to disappear.
The dam took two years to build.
it.h: Look for a result nobody planned.

it.q: Write a theme statement for a story in which a teen creates an app that helps people find lost pets, but it is later used to track people without permission.
it.ans: Inventions can be used in ways their creators never intended, so creators must think ahead about how to prevent harm.
it.h: Think about what the inventor should learn.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Analyzing texts that present conflicting views

it.q: When two texts present conflicting information, readers should
ch: examine which facts each text uses and how each interprets them
assume the newer text is correct
it.h: Think about evidence and interpretation.

it.q: Two articles discuss the same wind farm. One says it "provides clean energy for 50,000 homes." The other says it "has disrupted bird migration routes." What best explains the difference?
ch: The authors emphasize different facts based on their concerns.
it.h: Can both facts be true?

it.q: Which is an example of a disagreement about interpretation rather than about facts?
ch: Both writers agree a new highway cut travel time by 10 minutes, but one calls it "progress" and the other "a small benefit for a large cost."
One says the highway is 5 miles long and the other says 50.
One says it opened in 2020 and the other says 2021.
Both say the highway is new.
it.h: Interpretation is about meaning, not the numbers themselves.

it.q: How can a reader check a fact that two sources disagree about?
ch: look for a third reliable source, such as an official report
trust whichever source agrees with you
it.h: Think about verification.

it.q: Explain why scientists might disagree about the same research results.
it.ans: They may interpret data differently, weigh risks and benefits differently, focus on different questions or hold different values about what matters most.
it.h: Think about interpretation and values.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Word meanings in science writing: roots, context and connotation

it.q: The Greek root "bio" means
it.h: Think of "biology."

it.q: "Gene" comes from a Greek root meaning "birth" or "origin." Which word means "the study of how traits are passed from parents to offspring"?
it.h: Which word shares the root "gen"?

it.q: Which phrase has the most negative connotation for describing a new technology?
it.h: Which phrase suggests harm?

it.q: The prefix "de-" can mean "remove" or "reverse." What does "de-extinction" mean?
ch: reversing extinction by bringing a species back
it.h: Combine the prefix with the base word.

it.q: Explain how a writer's choice between "genetically modified food" and "Frankenfood" could affect readers.
it.ans: "Genetically modified food" is a neutral, scientific term, while "Frankenfood" has a negative, frightening connotation that suggests something monstrous, which could make readers fearful or opposed.
it.h: Compare the feelings each term creates.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Research: focused questions, credible sources and citation

it.q: A short research project should
ch: answer a focused question and generate additional questions for further research
include every fact about a topic
it.h: Think focused, but open to more questions.

it.q: Which is the best research question for a short project on gene editing?
ch: What are the main benefits and risks of using gene editing to protect crops from disease?
it.h: Look for a focused, researchable question.

it.q: Which search terms would most likely find credible sources on cloud seeding?
it.h: Specific terms lead to specific sources.

it.q: A website about a new medicine was written by the company that sells it. What should a researcher consider?
ch: The source may be biased because the company profits from the medicine.
The source is always the most reliable.
it.h: Who benefits?

it.q: Explain how a researcher can avoid plagiarism when using a statistic from a source.
it.ans: Give credit by naming the source in the sentence or in a citation, use quotation marks for any exact words, and put other information in your own words.
it.h: Credit plus your own words.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Reading informational text: antibiotic resistance and scientific responsibility

it.q: What are antibiotics?
ch: medicines that kill or stop the growth of bacteria
medicines that cure viruses like colds
it.h: They target bacteria.

it.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
ch: when bacteria change so that antibiotics no longer work against them
when people become allergic to medicine
it.h: The bacteria resist the medicine.

it.q: Why does taking antibiotics for a cold not help?
ch: Colds are usually caused by viruses, and antibiotics do not work on viruses.
Colds are caused by bacteria that are too strong.
it.h: What causes colds?

it.q: Read: "Overuse accelerates resistance." What does "accelerates" mean?
it.h: Think about a car's accelerator.

it.q: Which evidence would best support the claim that antibiotic overuse in farm animals contributes to resistance?
ch: studies finding resistant bacteria are more common where antibiotics are heavily used in livestock
it.h: Look for research linking the two.

it.q: Explain why finishing a prescribed course of antibiotics, as directed by a doctor, is often recommended.
it.ans: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive to multiply, which can contribute to resistance, so following the doctor's directions helps clear the infection.
it.h: Think about which bacteria survive.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Analyzing two texts that disagree: delivery drones

it.q: When two texts disagree, where do they often differ?
ch: in how they interpret facts or which facts they emphasize
it.h: Same topic, different focus.

it.q: How can you tell whether two texts disagree on facts or on interpretation?
ch: Check whether they report different data or draw different conclusions from the same data.
it.h: Facts versus meaning.

it.q: An author who works for a drone company writes in favor of drone delivery. What should a reader consider?
ch: possible bias because the author may benefit from the claim
that the author must be wrong
that the article is automatically neutral
it.h: Who benefits?

it.q: Which question best helps compare two arguments?
ch: Which author provides more relevant and sufficient evidence?
Which author has a longer name?
Which was published on a Monday?
it.h: Focus on evidence.

it.q: Two texts agree that drones can deliver quickly but disagree about safety. Where is the conflict?
ch: in the interpretation of safety risks
in the definition of a drone
it.h: Locate the disagreement.

it.q: Explain why it is useful to read texts that disagree before forming an opinion on a new technology.
it.ans: Disagreeing texts reveal different benefits, risks and evidence, helping you weigh both sides and form a well-reasoned opinion.
it.h: Think about seeing the whole picture.

lessons.u: Collection 6: Science and Responsibility (research)
lessons.n: Synthesizing research: integrating quotations and paraphrases without plagiarism

it.q: What does it mean to synthesize sources?
ch: to combine information from several sources to support your own ideas
to list sources without using them
it.h: Synthesis blends ideas.

it.q: Which sentence synthesizes two sources?
ch: While a medical journal reports that resistance is rising, a health agency explains that reducing unnecessary prescriptions can slow it.
it.h: Which sentence connects ideas from both?

it.q: What is a signal phrase?
ch: words that introduce a quotation or paraphrase and name its source
it.h: "According to..." is one.

it.q: Which choice correctly uses brackets in a quotation?
ch: The researcher wrote, "[Antibiotics] remain essential to modern medicine."
The researcher wrote, "(Antibiotics) remain essential to modern medicine."
The researcher wrote, Antibiotics remain essential.
it.h: Brackets show words the writer added for clarity.

it.q: Why must a writer cite a paraphrase?
ch: The ideas still belong to the original author.
Citations make the paper look longer.
it.h: Credit follows ideas.

it.q: Paraphrase this sentence and add a signal phrase: "Hand washing is one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of infections."
it.ans: Public health experts explain that washing hands well is among the best ways to stop infections from spreading.
it.h: Change words and structure, and name the source type.

lessons.u: Literary terms and structure
lessons.n: Plot structure and types of conflict

it.q: In which part of a plot are the characters, setting and basic situation introduced?
it.h: Think about what a reader needs to know before the trouble begins.

it.q: A teenager must decide whether to report a friend who cheated. What kind of conflict is this mainly?
it.h: Is the struggle mainly inside the character's mind or against an outside force?

it.q: Which event would most likely be the climax of a story about a swimmer recovering from an injury?
ch: She dives in for the championship final, unsure whether her shoulder will hold.
She describes her town and her coach.
She celebrates with her family weeks later.
it.h: The climax is the point of greatest tension, where the outcome is decided.

it.q: A farmer fights to save her crops during a months-long drought. What kind of external conflict is this?
it.h: What force is working against the farmer?

it.q: Explain how the rising action of a story prepares readers for the climax.
it.ans: The rising action introduces complications that build tension and raise the stakes, so by the climax readers understand what the character could win or lose.
it.h: Think about what happens to the tension and the stakes as complications pile up.

lessons.u: Literary terms and structure
lessons.n: Pacing, flashback and foreshadowing

it.q: A hint or clue about what will happen later in a story is
it.h: The prefix "fore-" means before.

it.q: An author describes a ninety-second car crash across three pages but skips five years in one sentence. What is the author controlling?
it.h: Think about how fast or slow time moves for the reader.

it.q: Which sentence most clearly signals a flashback?
ch: Mina was seven the first time she saw the ocean, and she had screamed at the waves.
Mina will travel to the ocean next year.
Mina walks to the ocean every morning.
Mina likes the ocean more than lakes.
it.h: Which sentence moves to an earlier time than the main story?

it.q: Short sentences and sentence fragments during an action scene usually
ch: speed up the pace and increase tension
slow the story down for reflection
it.h: Read "He ran. A door. Locked." aloud. How does it feel?

it.q: Explain how foreshadowing can create suspense. Give an example of a foreshadowing detail.
it.ans: Foreshadowing hints at future trouble, so readers worry and keep reading to find out what happens. Example: a character notices a frayed rope before a climb.
it.h: What do readers feel when they suspect something bad is coming but do not know when?

lessons.u: Literary terms and structure
lessons.n: Figurative language and connotation

it.q: "Her words were daggers" is an example of
it.h: Is the comparison made with or without "like" or "as"?

it.q: Which word has the most negative connotation?
it.h: All four mean thin. Which one sounds like an insult?

it.q: "I've told you a million times to close the door" is
it.h: Is the speaker being exact or exaggerating?

it.q: "The deafening silence filled the room" contains
it.h: Look for two words that seem to contradict each other.

it.q: Explain the difference in connotation between "stubborn" and "determined" and how each could change a reader's view of a character.
it.ans: Both mean refusing to give up, but "stubborn" suggests being unreasonable while "determined" suggests admirable persistence, so the first makes a character seem difficult and the second makes her seem strong.
it.h: Which word would a character want to be called?

lessons.u: Literary terms and structure
lessons.n: Point of view, irony and suspense

it.q: A narrator who uses "I" and takes part in the events is
it.h: Look at the pronoun the narrator uses for himself or herself.

it.q: A third-person narrator who reveals the thoughts of every character is
it.h: "Omni" means all.

it.q: In a horror movie, viewers see the monster hide in the closet, but the character does not. This is
it.h: Who knows more, the audience or the character?

it.q: A character looks at a flooded kitchen and says, "Well, this is just perfect." This is
it.h: Does the speaker mean exactly what she says?

it.q: Explain how a limited point of view can create mystery for the reader.
it.ans: Because readers know only what one character knows or sees, information is hidden, and readers must guess along with that character.
it.h: What can a reader not know if the narrator stays inside only one character's head?

lessons.u: Literary terms and structure
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: The final part of a plot, where loose ends are tied up, is the
it.h: Think of the word "resolve."

it.q: "The old car groaned up the hill" is an example of
it.h: Can a car really groan?

it.q: Which structure would best create suspense in a mystery?
ch: revealing clues one at a time and delaying the answer
stating the solution in the first sentence
listing every character's secret at the start
it.h: What keeps a reader turning pages?

it.q: The feeling a reader gets from a text, such as dread or joy, is the
it.h: Tone belongs to the author; this belongs to the reader.

it.q: Choose one structural choice (flashback, foreshadowing, in medias res or a twist ending) and explain the effect it usually has on readers.
it.ans: In medias res drops readers into the action, creating immediate curiosity about how the characters got there.
it.h: Name the choice, then describe what the reader feels or wonders.

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Direct and indirect characterization

it.q: When an author directly states what a character is like, this is
it.h: Is the trait stated outright, or does the reader have to figure it out?

it.q: "Mrs. Liang counted the change twice and then counted it again." What trait does this suggest?
it.h: What kind of person checks something three times?

it.q: Which sentence shows indirect characterization through other characters' reactions?
ch: When Andre walked into the gym, the younger players stopped talking and straightened up.
it.h: Look for how others act around the character.

it.q: Which sentence is direct characterization?
ch: Kiana was impatient and quick to anger.
Kiana tapped her foot and checked the clock again.
Kiana's brother rolled his eyes when she complained.
it.h: Which sentence names the trait?

it.q: Write two sentences that reveal a character's nervousness through indirect characterization, without using the word "nervous."
it.ans: Elena rubbed her palms on her jeans and read the same line of her speech for the fifth time. When her name was called, she stood so fast her chair scraped the floor.
it.h: Show the trait through actions, speech or thoughts.

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Character motivation and interactions

it.q: A character's reason for acting is called
it.h: Ask, "Why does the character do this?"

it.q: A girl secretly visits her grandmother, even though her parents and grandmother are feuding, because she misses her. What is her motivation?
ch: a wish to anger her parents
it.h: What does she care about most in this situation?

it.q: Two brothers, one cautious and one reckless, must plan a hiking trip together. How is their contrast likely to affect the plot?
ch: Their differences create conflict and reveal each brother's traits.
It has no effect on the plot.
It makes them act exactly alike.
it.h: Think about what happens when opposites must make a decision together.

it.q: A character who opposes the protagonist is the
it.h: Think of the prefix "anti-," meaning against.

it.q: Explain how a conversation between two characters can reveal what each one wants.
it.ans: Dialogue shows what characters ask for, avoid or argue about, so readers can infer each one's goals and fears.
it.h: Think about what characters argue about or avoid saying.

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Developing a theme across a text

it.q: A theme is
ch: a message about life or human nature that a text conveys
the time and place of the story
it.h: A theme is usually a full sentence, not one word.

it.q: Which is the best theme statement for a story about a girl who hides her talent to fit in and later regrets it?
ch: Hiding who you are to win approval can cost you something valuable.
it.h: The best theme is a complete statement about life, not a summary.

it.q: Where do readers often find the strongest clues to a story's theme?
ch: in how the main character changes and what he or she learns
it.h: What lesson does the character learn?

it.q: Which detail would most likely help develop a theme about the cost of greed?
ch: A man who refused to share his water during a drought is left alone when his own well runs dry.
it.h: Which detail shows a consequence of a choice?

it.q: Explain why a story's title can be a clue to its theme. Give an example.
it.ans: Authors often choose titles that point to a central idea. A story titled "The Gift" might explore what it means to give or receive something meaningful.
it.h: Think about what a title emphasizes.

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Citing textual evidence and writing objective summaries

it.q: An objective summary should
ch: state the main events and ideas without personal opinions
it.h: "Objective" means without personal feelings.

it.q: Which sentence belongs in an objective summary?
ch: After an argument, the two friends agree to work together on the project.
I loved how the friends made up at the end.
The story is boring until the end.
The author should have made the ending happier.
it.h: Remove any sentence with an opinion.

it.q: Which phrase best introduces a quotation as evidence?
ch: The narrator reveals Mia's fear when she says,
In my opinion the quote is
it.h: Strong lead-ins connect the quotation to your point.

it.q: The strongest evidence for a claim about a character is evidence that is
ch: most directly connected to the claim
it.h: Does the quotation prove the exact point you are making?

it.q: Explain the difference between explicit evidence and evidence for an inference.
it.ans: Explicit evidence states something directly; evidence for an inference gives clues that a reader combines with reasoning to reach a conclusion that is not stated.
it.h: One is stated; one must be figured out.

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Foils and contrasting characters

it.q: A character whose traits contrast with another character's, making both clearer, is a
it.h: Think of how a dark background makes a bright color stand out.

it.q: In a story, a cautious older sister is paired with a daring younger sister. What is the most likely purpose of the pairing?
ch: to highlight each sister's traits through contrast
to confuse readers about who is who
to show that both sisters are identical
to remove conflict from the story
it.h: What do readers notice more clearly when two opposites stand side by side?

it.q: Read: "While Jordan rehearsed his speech twenty times, Malik wrote his on a napkin five minutes before class." What does this contrast reveal?
ch: Jordan is thorough and anxious, while Malik is relaxed or careless.
Malik is more nervous than Jordan.
Jordan does not care about the speech.
it.h: Compare how much effort each boy puts in.

it.q: A minor character makes the same mistake as the main character but never learns from it. How does this help develop theme?
ch: It shows what might have happened to the main character, emphasizing the lesson he learns.
It has no connection to theme.
it.h: Think of the minor character as a warning or a mirror.

it.q: Name a pair of contrasting characters from a book, film or show you know and explain what the contrast reveals.
it.ans: In many superhero stories, the hero uses power to protect others while the villain uses similar power for selfish goals; the contrast shows that character is defined by choices, not ability.
it.h: What does each character value?

lessons.u: Complex characters and theme
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: A character who does not change during a story is
it.h: Think of the opposite of a character who changes.

it.q: Which detail is the best evidence that a character feels guilty?
ch: He could not meet his sister's eyes when she thanked him.
it.h: Which action suggests an inner feeling?

it.q: Which sentence states a theme rather than summarizing plot?
ch: Courage sometimes means admitting you were wrong.
Marco admits he broke the window.
The window was broken in chapter 2.
it.h: A theme applies to life beyond this one story.

it.q: A character with many traits, including contradictions, is called
it.h: Think of a shape with depth.

it.q: Choose a character from a story or film you know and explain one motivation and one change.
it.ans: A character who wants to win at all costs (motivation) learns that friendship matters more (change) after hurting a teammate.
it.h: What does the character want, and how is the character different at the end?

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Central idea and author's purpose in nonfiction

it.q: The most important point an informational text makes is its
it.h: Every paragraph supports this one big point.

it.q: An article explains how wildfires spread and gives tips for preparing an evacuation kit. What is the author's main purpose?
ch: to inform readers and help them prepare
to entertain with a made-up story
to persuade readers to move away
it.h: What will readers be able to do after reading?

it.q: Which detail would best support the central idea "Sleep is essential for teen learning"?
ch: Research has linked getting enough sleep to better memory and attention.
Teens like to stay up late on weekends.
it.h: Which detail connects sleep to learning?

it.q: An author's point of view is
ch: the author's opinion or perspective on the topic
it.h: How does the author feel about the subject?

it.q: Explain how you can determine an author's point of view in an article that never says "I think."
it.ans: Look at word choice, which facts are included or left out, and how opposing views are described; these choices reveal the author's perspective.
it.h: Consider word choice and the evidence the author chooses.

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Ethos, pathos and logos in speeches

it.q: An appeal to the audience's emotions is
it.h: Think of the words "sympathy" and "empathy."

it.q: "As someone who has coached youth soccer for twenty years, I have seen what happens when kids burn out." This sentence mainly appeals to
it.h: Why does the speaker mention twenty years of coaching?

it.q: Which sentence appeals to logos?
ch: The program costs $40,000 a year but saves the district $90,000 in repairs.
Think of how proud our grandparents would be.
I have served this town for decades.
it.h: Look for numbers and reasoning.

it.q: Which sentence is the strongest use of pathos in a speech asking for animal shelter volunteers?
ch: Picture a shy puppy pressed against the bars, waiting for someone to say its name.
The shelter is open from 9 to 5.
it.h: Which sentence makes you feel something?

it.q: Explain why a speaker might use an emotional appeal and a logical appeal in the same speech.
it.ans: Logic shows the audience that the argument makes sense, while emotion makes them care enough to act; together they persuade more effectively.
it.h: Think about the difference between agreeing and acting.

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Rhetorical devices: repetition, parallelism and antithesis

it.q: Placing contrasting ideas side by side in a balanced sentence, as in "Some see a problem; we see a possibility," is
it.h: Look for two opposite ideas balanced against each other.

it.q: "We will build schools. We will build clinics. We will build hope." What device does this use?
it.h: Look at how each sentence begins.

it.q: Which sentence uses parallelism?
ch: The coach asked us to run faster, to pass sooner and to think smarter.
The coach asked us to run faster, passing sooner and smarter thinking.
The coach asked us running faster, to pass and thought smarter.
The coach asked for speed and that we think.
it.h: Are the grammatical forms the same in each part?

it.q: A speaker asks, "Is it fair that some students have to study in their cars?" This is
it.h: Does the speaker expect the audience to answer out loud?

it.q: Explain why speakers often use groups of three, as in Lincoln's "of the people, by the people, for the people."
it.ans: Three parallel parts create rhythm, sound complete and are easy to remember, which makes ideas more powerful.
it.h: Say the phrase aloud. Why does it stick?

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Evaluating claims, reasoning and evidence

it.q: A statement that can be proven true or false is a
it.h: Can you check it in a reliable source?

it.q: Which is relevant evidence for the claim "Later school start times help teens"?
ch: A study found that students at schools with later start times got more sleep on school nights.
it.h: Does the evidence connect directly to the claim?

it.q: An author claims all teens are addicted to phones and supports this with a survey of five students. What is the main weakness?
ch: The evidence is not sufficient to support such a broad claim.
it.h: Can five people represent all teens?

it.q: Which sentence contains a false statement that a careful reader should question?
ch: Since the Moon makes its own light, we can see it at night.
it.h: Does the Moon produce its own light?

it.q: Explain the difference between relevant evidence and sufficient evidence.
it.ans: Relevant evidence connects directly to the claim; sufficient evidence means there is enough of it, from credible sources, to convince a reasonable reader.
it.h: One is about connection; the other is about amount.

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Word choice and tone in nonfiction

it.q: The author's attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice, is the
it.h: It is like a speaker's tone of voice, but on the page.

it.q: Which word gives the most critical tone to "The council ___ the proposal"?
it.h: Which choice suggests the council acted unfairly or too fast?

it.q: A science article uses words such as "measured," "observed" and "estimated." What tone does this create?
it.h: How do scientists want to sound?

it.q: An article calls a new law "a bold step forward." Another calls the same law "a reckless gamble." What does this show?
ch: Word choice reveals each author's point of view.
Neither article has a point of view.
it.h: Compare the connotations of the two phrases.

it.q: Rewrite this sentence twice, once with a positive tone and once with a negative tone: "The city built a new parking garage downtown."
it.ans: Positive: The city finally opened a convenient new parking garage downtown. Negative: The city poured money into yet another concrete parking garage downtown.
it.h: Change only a few words and notice how the attitude shifts.

lessons.u: Rhetoric and informational text
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: A brief story used to illustrate a point in an argument is an
it.h: It is a short account of a real or imagined event.

it.q: An author describes a proposal as "wasteful" and "careless." What do these word choices reveal?
ch: the author's negative point of view
the author's support for the proposal
the author's lack of a claim
it.h: What connotations do these words carry?

it.q: Which is the best example of ethos in a speech about bike safety?
ch: As an emergency room nurse, I treat cyclists with head injuries every month.
People say many things about bikes.
it.h: Who is a trustworthy expert on injuries?

it.q: Which question best helps evaluate an author's evidence?
ch: Is the evidence from a credible source, and does it actually support the claim?
Does the author use big words?
it.h: Think about credibility and connection.

it.q: Explain how an author's purpose affects the evidence the author chooses.
it.ans: An author who wants to persuade chooses evidence that supports the claim and may leave out opposing evidence, while an author who wants to inform tries to present balanced facts.
it.h: Compare an article written to persuade with one written to inform.

lessons.u: Argument writing
lessons.n: Writing precise claims and reasons

it.q: In an argument essay, the claim is
ch: the writer's main position on the issue
it.h: It is the statement the whole essay tries to prove.

it.q: Which claim is most arguable?
ch: Cities should replace some parking lots with public parks.
it.h: Could a reasonable person disagree?

it.q: Which claim is most precise?
ch: Schools should offer free breakfast to every student because hungry students cannot focus.
Schools should do something about food.
it.h: Which claim states a specific position and a reason?

it.q: Which reason best supports the claim "Our school should start a community garden"?
ch: A garden would give science classes a place for hands-on experiments.
it.h: Which reason explains a benefit connected to the claim?

it.q: Revise this vague claim to make it precise and arguable: "Phones are bad."
it.ans: High schools should require students to store phones in lockers during class because phones distract from learning.
it.h: Name who should do what, and why.

lessons.u: Argument writing
lessons.n: Using evidence and commentary

it.q: The writer's explanation of how evidence supports a claim is called
it.h: It is the writer's own thinking after the evidence.

it.q: Which is the best paraphrase of "Regular physical activity can improve concentration and memory in adolescents"?
ch: Exercising often may help teens focus and remember better.
it.h: Keep the meaning, but use your own words and sentence structure.

it.q: Which source is most credible for an argument about water conservation in California?
ch: data from the state department of water resources
a post from an anonymous account
it.h: Which source has expertise and accountability?

it.q: Which sentence best integrates a quotation?
ch: According to the city report, the program "reduced litter by nearly half."
"Reduced litter by nearly half." The report.
Here is a quote "reduced litter by nearly half" from a report I found.
it.h: Introduce the source and blend the quotation into your sentence.

it.q: A student writes: "School gardens help students. A study found that students in garden programs ate more vegetables." Write one sentence of commentary that explains how the evidence supports the claim.
it.ans: This shows that gardens do more than teach science; by growing food themselves, students become more willing to eat healthy foods, which supports better health.
it.h: Explain why the evidence matters, not just what it says.

lessons.u: Argument writing
lessons.n: Counterclaims, rebuttals and transitions

it.q: An opposing argument that a writer acknowledges is a
it.h: "Counter" means against.

it.q: Which sentence best introduces a counterclaim?
ch: Some argue that a longer school day would exhaust students.
A longer school day is the best idea ever.
First, let me tell a story.
it.h: Look for language that presents the other side.

it.q: Which sentence is the strongest rebuttal to "Uniforms limit self-expression"?
ch: Students can still express themselves through their ideas, activities and accessories, while uniforms reduce pressure to buy expensive clothes.
it.h: A rebuttal answers the counterclaim with reasoning, not insults.

it.q: Which transition best introduces a contrasting idea?
it.h: Which word signals a turn in thought?

it.q: Explain why addressing a counterclaim can make an argument more persuasive.
it.ans: It shows the writer has considered other views fairly, builds credibility and answers readers' doubts before they can reject the claim.
it.h: Think about how readers who disagree will react.

lessons.u: Argument writing
lessons.n: Phrases, clauses and parallel structure

it.q: A group of words with a subject and a verb is a
it.h: Does the group of words contain both a subject and a verb?

it.q: Which sentence contains an independent clause and a dependent clause?
ch: Because the bus was late, we missed the first bell.
it.h: Look for a clause that starts with a word such as because, although or when.

it.q: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?
ch: The recipe needs three things: flour, sugar and eggs.
The recipe needs: flour, sugar and eggs.
The recipe: needs three things flour sugar.
it.h: A colon usually follows a complete sentence.

it.q: In "The student, a talented violinist, practiced daily," the words "a talented violinist" form
it.h: The phrase renames the noun right before it.

it.q: Combine these sentences using a dependent clause: "The storm knocked out power. Students finished the test by flashlight."
it.ans: Although the storm knocked out power, students finished the test by flashlight.
it.h: Try starting with a word such as although, when or because.

lessons.u: Argument writing
lessons.n: Writing strong introductions and conclusions

it.q: The sentence or two at the start of an essay meant to grab the reader's attention is the
it.h: Think of fishing.

it.q: Which is the most effective hook for an argument about banning single-use plastic bags?
ch: Every minute, people around the world throw away an enormous number of plastic bags, and many of them end up in rivers and oceans.
This essay is about plastic bags.
it.h: Which opening makes the reader want to keep reading?

it.q: In an argument introduction, the claim usually appears
ch: after the hook and background, near the end of the introduction
in the middle of a body paragraph
it.h: Introductions often move from general to specific.

it.q: Which conclusion strategy is most effective?
ch: explaining why the issue matters and what readers should do
