ch: Effectiveness depends on the audience the text was written for.
it.h: Were you the intended audience?

it.q: Explain why a rhetorical analysis should focus on the author's choices rather than on whether the reader agrees with the argument.
it.ans: Rhetorical analysis examines how a text works on its audience; a reader can recognize a well-crafted argument even when disagreeing with it, so personal agreement is a different question.
it.h: Separate "Do I agree?" from "How does it work?"

lessons.u: Rhetorical analysis of complex nonfiction
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: The speaker, audience, purpose and context of a text together make up the
it.h: Think of SOAPSTone.

it.q: Which tone word describes writing that mocks with bitterness?
it.h: It is close to sarcastic.

it.q: Which sentence uses a periodic structure?
ch: Though tired, hungry and far from home, she kept walking.
She kept walking, though tired, hungry and far from home.
it.h: Where does the main clause appear?

it.q: An argument that begins by acknowledging the audience's concerns and seeking common ground is
it.h: It is named after a psychologist who valued understanding.

it.q: Explain how timing (kairos) can affect the persuasiveness of a speech.
it.ans: A speech delivered at the right moment, such as just after an event that makes an issue urgent, catches the audience when they are most ready to listen and act.
it.h: Why does the moment matter?

lessons.u: Narrative and college writing
lessons.n: Narrative techniques: scene, dialogue and reflection

it.q: In a narrative, a moment shown in real time with action, dialogue and detail is a
it.h: It is like a scene in a film.

it.q: Which sentence uses dialogue to reveal character?
ch: "You can borrow it," Grandpa said, "but bring it back with a story."
it.h: Which sentence lets the character's voice show who he is?

it.q: Which sentence reflects on an experience rather than just reporting it?
ch: Only later did I understand that losing that election taught me how to listen.
I lost the election in October.
The election was held in the gym.
My opponent won by six votes.
it.h: Reflection explains meaning.

it.q: Which detail appeals to the sense of smell?
ch: The hallway still smelled of chalk and floor wax.
it.h: Which detail could you smell?

it.q: Explain why strong personal narratives balance scenes with reflection.
it.ans: Scenes make the experience vivid and let readers live it, while reflection explains what it meant and how the writer changed; without both, a narrative is either flat or lacks meaning.
it.h: What does each give the reader?

lessons.u: Narrative and college writing
lessons.n: Structuring a narrative: openings, turning points and endings

it.q: The moment in a narrative when the writer's understanding or situation changes is the
it.h: Something shifts here.

it.q: A narrative opens in the middle of a key moment and then flashes back to explain it. What structure is this?
ch: in medias res with a flashback
it.h: "In the middle of things."

it.q: Which opening most effectively creates curiosity?
ch: The day I accidentally set my chemistry teacher's notes on fire was also the day I decided to become a scientist.
I want to tell you about my life.
My name is Jordan and I am seventeen.
it.h: Which opening raises a question the reader wants answered?

it.q: Which ending best avoids a cliche?
ch: I still keep the burnt corner of those notes in my desk drawer, a reminder that mistakes can light the way.
And that is the end of my story.
In conclusion, I learned a lot.
it.h: Which ending uses a specific image instead of a stock phrase?

it.q: Explain why a narrative might end with an image rather than a direct statement of the lesson.
it.ans: An image lets readers feel the meaning themselves and stays in memory, while a stated lesson can seem preachy or obvious.
it.h: Think about "show, don't tell."

lessons.u: Narrative and college writing
lessons.n: Voice, precise language and sentence variety

it.q: The distinctive personality and style that comes through in a writer's words is
it.h: It sounds like a particular person.

it.q: Which sentence uses the most precise, vivid verb?
ch: The dog bolted across the yard.
The dog went across the yard.
The dog moved across the yard.
The dog did a run across the yard.
it.h: Which verb shows exactly how the dog moved?

it.q: Which revision varies sentence structure?
ch: Rain hammered the roof. Inside, by candlelight, we waited.
It rained. We waited. It was dark. We were inside.
It rained and we waited and it was dark and we were inside.
it.h: Look for different sentence lengths and openings.

it.q: Which phrase relies on a cliche and should be revised?
ch: my heart was beating a mile a minute
my pulse thudded in my ears
my hands left damp prints on the desk
I counted the ceiling tiles to stay calm
it.h: Which phrase have you heard many times before?

it.q: Revise this sentence to add precise detail and voice: "The room was messy."
it.ans: My brother's room looked like a laundry basket had exploded, with one sock dangling from the ceiling fan like a flag of surrender.
it.h: Use specific details and a comparison.

lessons.u: Narrative and college writing
lessons.n: Revising and adapting writing for purpose and audience

it.q: Writing that is suited to its task, purpose and audience is
it.h: Think about fitting the situation.

it.q: Which email greeting is most appropriate for a teacher you are asking for a recommendation?
it.h: Formal situations call for formal greetings.

it.q: Which subject line is most effective for an email requesting a job interview?
ch: Application for Summer Lifeguard Position - Maya Chen
it.h: Which subject line tells the reader exactly what the email is about?

it.q: When revising a draft, which question should a writer ask first?
ch: Does each part support my main purpose?
it.h: Big ideas before small details.

it.q: Explain the difference between global revision and local editing.
it.ans: Global revision changes big elements such as focus, organization and development; local editing corrects sentence-level issues such as grammar, punctuation and word choice.
it.h: Think of the whole essay versus individual sentences.

lessons.u: Narrative and college writing
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: In a narrative, the writer's thoughts about what an experience meant are called
it.h: The writer "looks back" on the event.

it.q: Which sentence shows rather than tells?
ch: My voice cracked on the first note, and I gripped the microphone stand.
it.h: Which sentence creates a picture?

it.q: Which detail would best slow the pace at a key moment?
ch: a close, sensory description of the seconds before the results were announced
a sentence skipping ahead a year
a list of every class the writer took
a summary of the whole summer
it.h: Detail stretches time.

it.q: Which revision is the most concise?
ch: I made the decision that I would go ahead and apologize.
I decided that I would be making an apology.
An apology was decided on by me.
it.h: Remove extra words.

it.q: Explain why a specific, small moment often makes a stronger personal essay than a broad summary of an achievement.
it.ans: A specific moment lets readers see the writer's character in action and feel the experience, while a broad summary sounds like a resume and reveals little about who the writer is.
it.h: Which shows more about who you are?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Senses and Science Tools
lessons.n: How do we find out about the world?

it.q: Which body part do you use to see?
it.h: Point to the part of your face you use to look at a picture.

it.q: Which body part do you use to smell a flower?
it.h: Pretend to sniff. What part of your face are you using?

it.q: Which body part helps you hear a bell?
it.h: Cover the sides of your head. Is the bell quieter now?

it.q: Which body part tells you the sand is bumpy?
it.h: Which part of your body touches the sand?

it.q: You taste a lemon. Which word tells how it tastes?
it.h: Think about the face people make when they eat a lemon.

it.q: Close your eyes and listen for one minute. Tell one sound you heard.
it.ans: Names a real sound, such as "I heard a car" or "I heard my friend talking."
it.h: Was it a loud sound or a quiet sound?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Senses and Science Tools
lessons.n: What can we learn with a magnifier and a scale?

it.q: Which tool makes a tiny bug look bigger?
it.h: This tool has a round glass part you look through.

it.q: Which tool helps you find which toy is heavier?
it.h: This tool has two sides that go up and down.

it.q: A balance scale has a rock on one side and a feather on the other. Which side goes down?
it.h: The heavier thing pulls its side down.

it.q: Leo looks at a leaf with a magnifier. What will he see better?
ch: the small lines on the leaf
it.h: A magnifier helps your eyes.

it.q: Draw what you see when you look at your fingertip with a magnifier.
it.ans: A drawing of a fingertip with curvy lines or swirls.
it.h: Look for lines and loops on your skin.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Senses and Science Tools
lessons.n: How can we sort and describe things?

it.q: Which word tells about the color of a banana?
it.h: Picture a banana. What color is its peel?

it.q: Which shape is a ball?
it.h: Can it roll all the way around?

it.q: Which one is smooth?
it.h: Smooth things have no bumps.

it.q: Kai sorts blocks into a big pile and a small pile. What is he sorting by?
it.h: Big and small are words about how much space something takes.

it.q: Which group has only things that are soft?
it.h: Check each thing in the group. Is every one soft?

it.q: Pick a toy. Tell two words that describe it.
it.ans: Two describing words, such as "red and bumpy" or "hard and round."

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Senses and Science Tools
lessons.n: How do we stay safe when we explore?

it.q: What do you wear to keep sand and water out of your eyes?
it.h: They fit over your eyes like big glasses.

it.q: You find a mystery berry on the playground. What should you do?
it.h: Some berries can make you sick.

it.q: How should you smell something new in science?
ch: wave the air to your nose
it.h: Use your hand like a fan.

it.q: A friend is holding a magnifier. What should you do?
it.h: Scientists take turns with tools.

it.q: Where should you look at a bee?
it.h: A bee can sting if it feels scared.

it.q: Tell one rule that keeps you safe when you explore outside.
it.ans: One safe rule, such as "Stay with a grown-up," "Do not taste things you find" or "Wash your hands after."
it.h: Think about what a teacher tells you before you go outside.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Senses and Science Tools
lessons.n: How can we measure how long and how much?

it.q: Which tool tells how long something is?
it.h: It is long and flat with lines and numbers.

it.q: Which tool holds water so you can see how much you have?
it.h: It has lines on the side and a spout for pouring.

it.q: A pencil is 4 blocks long. A crayon is 2 blocks long. Which is longer?
it.h: Which one needs more blocks?

it.q: Ana fills a big cup and a small cup with water. Which holds more?
it.h: Which cup has more room inside?

it.q: A shoe is as long as 5 paper clips in a row. How many paper clips long is the shoe?
it.h: Count the paper clips one by one.

it.q: Tell how you could find out which of two sticks is longer.
it.ans: Put them side by side with the ends lined up and see which one sticks out farther.
it.h: Line up the ends first.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Materials and How They Change
lessons.n: Which things float and which things sink?

it.q: A toy boat sits on top of the water. What is it doing?
it.h: Things that float stay on top of the water.

it.q: A rock drops to the bottom of a tub of water. What is it doing?
it.h: Did it stay on top or go down?

it.q: Which will most likely float?
it.h: Think about things you have seen bobbing on top of water.

it.q: Which will most likely sink?
it.h: Heavy metal things often go to the bottom.

it.q: Before testing, Ben says, "I think the crayon will sink." What is Ben doing?
it.h: He has not tried it yet. What do we call telling what we think will happen?

it.q: Pick one thing from the classroom. Tell if you think it will sink or float, and why.
it.ans: A prediction with a reason, such as "The block will float because it is wood and wood floats."
it.h: Is it heavy or light for its size? What is it made of?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Materials and How They Change
lessons.n: What happens to ice when it gets warm?

it.q: What does ice turn into when it melts?
it.h: Think about an ice cube in your cup at lunch.

it.q: Where will an ice cube melt fastest?
it.h: Melting needs warmth.

it.q: Liv puts a cup of water in the freezer overnight. What will she find in the morning?
it.h: The freezer is very cold.

it.q: What happens to a crayon left on a hot car seat?
it.h: Hot places can make some solid things soft.

it.q: Which feels cold?
it.h: Which one comes from cold winter weather?

it.q: Tell what happened to the ice cube we left on the table.
it.ans: It melted and turned into a puddle of water.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Materials and How They Change
lessons.n: What happens when we mix things?

it.q: Mix blue paint and yellow paint. What color do you get?
it.h: Think of the color of grass.

it.q: What happens to dry sand when you pour water on it?
ch: It gets wet and sticks together
it.h: Think about making a sandcastle.

it.q: You stir sugar into warm water. What happens to the sugar?
ch: It seems to disappear in the water
it.h: Look closely at the water after stirring. Can you still see the sugar?

it.q: Which makes mud?
it.h: What do you get when you step in a wet garden?

it.q: A wet paper towel is left in the sun. What happens later?
it.h: Where does water go when things dry in the sun?

it.q: Tell what happened when we mixed flour and water.
it.ans: It became sticky dough (or paste).

lessons.u: Unit 2: Materials and How They Change
lessons.n: What are things made of? Wood, metal, plastic and cloth

it.q: A table leg comes from a tree. What is it made of?
it.h: Trees are made of this material.

it.q: Your shirt is soft and bendy. What is it made of?
it.h: Socks and blankets are made of this too.

it.q: Which of these is made of metal?
it.h: Metal is hard, cold and often shiny.

it.q: Which is made of paper?
it.h: You can fold it and tear it.

it.q: A bucket is light, hard and bright red. It does not break when dropped. What is it made of?
it.h: Many toys are made of this.

it.q: Pick one thing in the room. Tell what it is made of.
it.ans: Names an object and its material, such as "The chair is wood" or "The spoon is metal."
it.h: Is it soft, hard, shiny or bendy?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Materials and How They Change
lessons.n: What happens when things get wet and dry?

it.q: Which soaks up spilled milk?
it.h: It is soft and full of tiny holes.

it.q: Which keeps you dry in the rain?
it.h: Water runs off it.

it.q: Pia drops a paper towel into water. What happens?
it.h: Paper towels drink up water.

it.q: A wet sponge sits in the sun all day. What happens?
it.h: The Sun warms the water and it goes into the air.

it.q: Which will dry fastest?
it.h: Where is it warm and airy?

it.q: Tell what happens to a sponge when you squeeze it after it gets wet.
it.ans: The water comes out.
it.h: Squeeze it over the sink. What drips?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Pushes, Pulls and Rolling
lessons.n: How can we make things move?

it.q: You move a swing away from you with your hands. Is that a push or a pull?
it.h: Does it go away from you or come toward you?

it.q: You open a door by moving it toward you. Is that a push or a pull?
it.h: Toward you is one kind of move. Away from you is the other.

it.q: Which is a pull?
ch: bumping a ball with your head
it.h: A pull brings something toward you.

it.q: A toy car is still on the floor. How can you make it move?
it.h: Things that are still need a push or a pull to start moving.

it.q: Which is a push?
it.h: A push moves something away from you.

it.q: Show me a push and a pull with a toy. Tell which is which.
it.ans: Pushes the toy away and says "push"; pulls it back and says "pull."

lessons.u: Unit 3: Pushes, Pulls and Rolling
lessons.n: How can we make a ball go farther?

it.q: You kick a ball very hard. What happens?
it.h: Think about a big kick on the playground.

it.q: Which push makes a toy car go farther?
it.h: Strong pushes give more go.

it.q: A ball rolls down a ramp. Which ramp makes it roll farther?
ch: a ramp lying on the floor
it.h: Try it. Does a taller ramp make the ball go faster?

it.q: Ty rolled a ball down a ramp and put a sticker where it stopped. Why did he use a sticker?
ch: to mark how far it went
it.h: How will Ty remember where the ball stopped?

it.q: A ball rolls toward a block. What happens when it hits the block?
it.h: Can a ball go through something hard?

it.q: Roll a ball softly and then roll it hard. Tell what was different.
it.ans: "When I rolled it hard, it went faster and farther."

lessons.u: Unit 3: Pushes, Pulls and Rolling
lessons.n: Which things roll and which things slide?

it.q: Which shape rolls?
it.h: Things with round sides can roll.

it.q: You put a block on a slide. What does it do?
ch: It stays at the top forever
it.h: A block has flat sides. Can flat sides roll?

it.q: Which will roll down a ramp?
it.h: Look for something round.

it.q: Which can roll and also stand still on its flat end?
it.h: A can is round on its side and flat on its ends.

it.q: Why do wagons have wheels?
it.h: Is it easier to drag a box or roll a wagon?

it.q: Find something in the room that rolls. Tell why it can roll.
it.ans: Names an object (ball, marker, cup on its side) and says it is round or has round sides.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Pushes, Pulls and Rolling
lessons.n: How do ramps change how things roll?

it.q: A ball sits on a flat floor. Will it roll by itself?
it.h: Does a ball on the floor move if nobody touches it?

it.q: A ball is put at the top of a slide. What does it do?
it.h: Things roll down a hill.

it.q: Which ramp makes a car go faster?
it.h: Think of a big slide and a little slide.

it.q: Sam makes his ramp taller. What happens to his car?
it.h: A taller ramp is steeper.

it.q: A toy car rolls off a ramp onto a rug. It stops fast. Why?
it.h: A bumpy floor slows things down.

it.q: Tell how you would make a toy car go farther off a ramp.
it.ans: Make the ramp higher (steeper) or let it roll onto a smooth floor.
it.h: Think about the height of the ramp.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Pushes, Pulls and Rolling
lessons.n: How do magnets push and pull?

it.q: What sticks to a magnet?
it.h: Magnets pull on some metal things.

it.q: What does a magnet hold on a fridge door?
it.h: Look at the front of a fridge at home.

it.q: Nico holds a magnet near a pile of things. Which one jumps to it?
it.h: Which one is made of metal?

it.q: A magnet is under a paper plate. A paper clip on top moves when the magnet moves. Why?
it.h: Magnets can pull through thin paper.

it.q: Two magnets push apart. What are they doing?
it.h: Hands out, away from each other.

it.q: Name one thing that sticks to a magnet and one thing that does not.
it.ans: Sticks: a paper clip, a nail or a metal lid. Does not: a crayon, a block or a paper.
it.h: Test things in the room. Do they jump to the magnet?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Living Things Grow and Change
lessons.n: How can we tell if something is alive?

it.q: Which is alive?
it.h: Living things eat, drink and grow.

it.q: Which is not alive?
it.h: Does it eat or grow?

it.q: How do we know a plant is alive?
it.h: Think about what happens to a plant over many days.

it.q: Which is alive: a real flower or a paper flower?
it.h: Which one would grow if you watered it?

it.q: Which group has only living things?
it.h: Check every one. Does each one grow and need food or water?

it.q: Name one living thing and one thing that is not alive in our classroom.
it.ans: Living: a person, a class plant or a pet. Not alive: a chair, a table, a crayon.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Living Things Grow and Change
lessons.n: What do plants and animals need to live?

it.q: What do plants need to grow?
it.h: What do we give our class plant?

it.q: What do all animals need?
it.h: What does a pet need every day?

it.q: Where does a fish live?
it.h: Fish have fins and swim.

it.q: Where does a bird keep its eggs?
ch: in a cave under the sea
it.h: Birds build this from twigs and grass.

it.q: Which helps a dog stay healthy?
ch: food, water and a safe place
it.h: Think about what you need too.

it.q: Tell two things people need to live.
it.ans: Two of: food, water, air, a home, sleep.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Living Things Grow and Change
lessons.n: How do plants grow and change?

it.q: What does a bean seed grow into?
it.h: Seeds grow into the same kind of plant they came from.

it.q: Which part of a plant grows down into the soil?
it.h: These look like little strings under the dirt.

it.q: What comes first?
it.h: What did we put in the soil on the first day?

it.q: Each week Pablo draws his plant. Why?
ch: to see how it grows and changes
it.h: How can drawings help him remember?

it.q: A sunflower plant was 2 blocks tall. Two weeks later it was 6 blocks tall. What happened?
it.h: Is 6 more or less than 2?

it.q: Tell what our seed looked like at first and what it looks like now.
it.ans: At first it was a small seed; now it has a stem, roots and leaves.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Living Things Grow and Change
lessons.n: How do animals and people grow and change?

it.q: A baby dog is called a
it.h: Think: puppy, kitten, chick. Which goes with a dog?

it.q: A baby cat is called a
it.h: Say "cat" and listen for the baby name.

it.q: What does a chick grow into?
it.h: Chicks hatch from chicken eggs.

it.q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
it.h: It makes a hard case, and something with wings comes out.

it.q: How are you different now than when you were a baby?
it.h: Look at a baby picture. Then look at yourself.

it.q: Name a baby animal and the grown-up it will become.
it.ans: For example: a puppy becomes a dog, a calf becomes a cow, a tadpole becomes a frog.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Living Things Grow and Change
lessons.n: Where do animals live and make their homes?

it.q: Where does a goldfish swim?
it.h: Fish swim.

it.q: What do many birds build to hold their eggs?
it.h: It is made of twigs and grass.

it.q: Where does a rabbit sleep?
ch: in a hole in the ground
it.h: Rabbits dig.

it.q: What does a spider make to catch food?
it.h: It is made of thin, sticky silk.

it.q: Which animal lives in a beehive?
it.h: Listen to the name.

it.q: Name one animal and tell where it lives.
it.ans: Names an animal and its home, such as "A bird lives in a nest" or "A frog lives in a pond."
it.h: Think of animals you see near school.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth and Sky
lessons.n: What are rocks, soil and sand like?

it.q: Which feels hard?
it.h: Squeeze it in your hand. Does it change shape?

it.q: Where do plants in a garden grow?
ch: in a cup of sand only
it.h: It is dark and crumbly, and worms live in it.

it.q: What is sand made of?
it.h: Look at sand with a magnifier. What do the tiny pieces look like?

it.q: Which lives in soil?
it.h: Dig in the garden. What wiggly animal might you find?

it.q: Nia sorts rocks into smooth rocks and bumpy rocks. What is she sorting by?
it.h: Smooth and bumpy are touch words.

it.q: Look at a rock with a magnifier. Tell two things you notice.
it.ans: Two observations, such as "It is gray and has sparkly spots" or "It is bumpy and heavy."

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth and Sky
lessons.n: What is the weather today?

it.q: What falls from clouds when it rains?
it.h: What makes puddles?

it.q: What do you wear on a rainy day?
it.h: What keeps you dry?

it.q: The trees are bending and leaves are flying. What is the weather?
it.h: What moves trees and leaves without anyone touching them?

it.q: Dark gray clouds fill the sky. What weather may come soon?
it.h: Rain clouds are often dark.

it.q: Which season is often cold and can be snowy in the mountains?
it.h: Think of the season with coats and hot cocoa.

it.q: Look outside. Tell what the weather is like today.
it.ans: Describes today's weather, such as "It is sunny and warm" or "It is cloudy."

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth and Sky
lessons.n: Why is the sky different in the day and at night?

it.q: What lights up the sky in the daytime?
it.h: It is big and bright, and you should never look right at it.

it.q: What can you often see in the sky at night?
it.h: Think of bedtime outside your window.

it.q: When do people usually sleep?
it.h: When is it dark outside?

it.q: Where is your shadow when the Sun is behind you?
it.h: Your body blocks the sunlight. The dark shape is on the other side.

it.q: The Moon does not always look round. What can it look like?
it.h: Look at the Moon on different nights.

it.q: Tell one thing you do in the day and one thing you do at night.
it.ans: Day: go to school, play outside. Night: sleep, look at the Moon.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth and Sky
lessons.n: How do we stay safe in storms and lightning?

it.q: What loud sound can you hear in a storm?
it.h: It rumbles and booms.

it.q: What is the bright flash in a storm?
it.h: It zigzags across the sky.

it.q: You are playing outside and hear thunder. What should you do?
it.h: When thunder roars, go indoors.

it.q: Where is safe in a thunderstorm?
it.h: A house or a school keeps you safe.

it.q: Dark clouds and wind come fast. What might be coming?
it.h: Storms often bring dark clouds.

it.q: Tell what you do when you hear thunder outside.
it.ans: Go inside a building with a grown-up and stay there until the storm is over.
it.h: Where is the safe place?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth and Sky
lessons.n: Where do we find water outside?

it.q: What fills up puddles?
it.h: What falls from clouds?

it.q: What is a big body of salty water called?
it.h: Waves and beaches are next to it.

it.q: Where does a river flow?
it.h: Rivers move and run along the ground.

it.q: Water on a cold mountain freezes. What does it become?
it.h: It is white and cold.

it.q: Where does rain go when it falls on soil?
it.h: Dig after a rain. Is the soil wet?

it.q: Name one place outside where you can find water.
it.ans: A puddle, pond, lake, river, ocean, rain or snow.
it.h: Think of a park, a beach or a rainy day.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: What makes things start moving and stop moving?

it.q: A ball is sitting still. What will make it start to roll?
it.h: Things that are still need a push or a pull to get going.

it.q: Which is a pull?
it.h: A pull moves something toward you.

it.q: A rolling ball hits a wall and stops. What stopped it?
it.h: The ball touched something hard. What did that hard thing do to it?

it.q: Which action is a push?
ch: picking up a toy toward you
it.h: Closing a door means moving it away from you.

it.q: A soccer goalie catches a ball. What did her hands do to the ball?
it.h: Was the ball still moving after she caught it?

it.q: Tell one way to make a toy car start moving and one way to make it stop.
it.ans: Start: push it or pull it. Stop: catch it, block it, or let it hit something.
it.h: What can your hands do? What could be in the car's way?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: What happens when we push harder or softer?

it.q: Which push makes a ball go farther?
it.h: Think about kicking a ball softly and then with all your might.

it.q: Ari gently pushes a toy car. It goes 2 blocks. Then he pushes it hard. What will most likely happen?
it.h: A harder push gives the car more speed.

it.q: To make a fair test of soft and hard pushes, Ari should use
ch: a big car one time and a tiny car the next
it.h: In a fair test, only the push changes.

it.q: A swing goes higher when you
it.h: Bigger pushes make bigger motion.

it.q: How can Ari tell how far the car went?
ch: put tape where it stopped and count blocks
it.h: Scientists measure and mark.

it.q: Tell what happened when you pushed the ball hard and when you pushed it softly.
it.ans: "The hard push made it roll far and fast. The soft push made it roll a little and slow."

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: How can we make a ball change direction?

it.q: A ball rolls toward you. You push it back. Which way does it go now?
ch: the other way, back where it came from
it.h: A push in a new direction can turn something around.

it.q: A ball is rolling right. A friend pushes it from the side. What happens?
ch: It goes faster the same way
it.h: Pushing from the side can make a ball turn.

it.q: In mini golf, why are there bumpers along the sides?
ch: to bounce the ball and change its direction
it.h: What happens when a ball hits the edge?

it.q: Which could you use to guide a marble around a corner?
it.h: The marble needs something to bump into and turn.

it.q: An engineer wants a ball to go into a cup at the end of a path. What should she do first?
ch: figure out the problem and where the ball needs to go
it.h: Engineers start by understanding the problem.

it.q: Tell how a wall can change the direction a ball moves.
it.ans: When the ball hits the wall, the wall pushes it, so it bounces back or goes a new way.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: What happens when moving things bump into each other?

it.q: A rolling ball hits a block. What happens to the block?
it.h: The ball gives the block a push.

it.q: A bowling ball rolls into the pins. What do the pins do?
it.h: The rolling ball pushes the pins.

it.q: A slow ball and a fast ball hit the same block. Which pushes the block farther?
it.h: A faster ball gives a bigger push.

it.q: A toy car bumps into a wall. What happens to the car?
it.h: The wall pushes back on the car.

it.q: A soccer ball hits a goal post. Which way does it go?
it.h: The post pushes the ball in a new direction.

it.q: Tell what happens when you roll a ball into a tower of blocks.
it.ans: The ball hits the blocks and pushes them, so the tower falls down.
it.h: Does the ball push the blocks?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: How do slopes and ramps change how fast things move?

it.q: A ball at the top of a ramp will
it.h: Things go down a slope by themselves.

it.q: Which hill would make a wagon go fastest?
it.h: Steeper means faster.

it.q: Maya lifts one end of her ramp higher. What happens to her toy car?
it.h: Higher makes the ramp steeper.

it.q: A car rolls down a ramp onto grass. It stops quickly. Why?
it.h: Think about how bumpy the grass is.

it.q: Leo put 2 books under his ramp. Then he added 3 more books. How many books are under the ramp now?
it.h: Count on from 2.

it.q: Tell how you could test if a taller ramp makes a car go farther.
it.ans: Roll the same car down a low ramp and a tall ramp and see which one goes farther.
it.h: Change only the height of the ramp.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Pushes and Pulls
lessons.n: How can we aim a push to hit a target?

it.q: You want a ball to go to the left. Which way do you push it?
it.h: A ball goes the way you push it.

it.q: Ty rolls a ball at a cup but it goes past on the right. What should he change?
it.h: Point the push more toward the cup.

it.q: Mia's ball stops before it gets to the pins. What should she do?
it.h: A bigger push makes it go farther.

it.q: In mini golf, the ball hits a wall and goes a new way. What changed its direction?
it.h: The wall pushes back on the ball.

it.q: Ava rolled 5 balls at a target. 3 hit it. How many missed?
it.h: Take 3 away from 5.

it.q: Tell how you would change your push if your ball went too far past the target.
it.ans: Push more gently (softer) so the ball does not go as far.
it.h: Strong or gentle?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Sunlight and Warmth
lessons.n: What does sunlight do to things outside?

it.q: Sunlight makes sand at the beach feel
it.h: Think about walking barefoot at the beach on a sunny day.

it.q: Where does sunlight come from?
it.h: Look up on a bright day (but never right at it).

it.q: Which feels hottest on a sunny afternoon?
ch: a black slide in the sun
a tree trunk in the shade
it.h: Things in the sun warm up. Dark things in the sun can get very hot.

it.q: A rock was in the sun all day. How does it feel?
it.h: What does sunlight do to things it shines on?

it.q: Why does a thermometer help us?
ch: It tells how warm or cool something is
It tells how long something is
It tells how heavy something is
it.h: A thermometer has numbers that go up when things get warmer.

it.q: Touch a sidewalk in the sun and in the shade. Tell what you notice.
it.ans: The sidewalk in the sun feels warm or hot; the sidewalk in the shade feels cooler.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Sunlight and Warmth
lessons.n: Why is it cooler in the shade?

it.q: Shade is made when something
it.h: Stand under a tree. What is above you?

it.q: Which spot is coolest on a hot day?
ch: in the middle of the field
on a metal slide in the sun
it.h: Find the spot where sunlight cannot reach.

it.q: Two cups of water start the same. One is in the sun and one is in the shade. After an hour, which is warmer?
it.h: Which cup got sunlight?

it.q: Dogs often lie under porches on hot days. Why?
it.h: Animals also look for cool places.

it.q: What could you use to make shade at a picnic?
it.h: What can you hold over your head to block the Sun?

it.q: Tell why it feels cooler under a tree.
it.ans: The tree's leaves block the sunlight, so less sunlight warms the ground and me.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Sunlight and Warmth
lessons.n: How can we build something to keep things cool?

it.q: What is the problem when a sandbox gets too hot to play in?
ch: too much sunlight warms the sand
it.h: What warms the sand?

it.q: Which would best keep a sandbox cooler?
ch: a black blanket on the sand in the sun
it.h: Find the choice that blocks sunlight.

it.q: Which material would make the best shade?
it.h: Sunlight passes through clear things.

it.q: Kai built a shade from paper. It blew away. What should he do?
ch: make it stronger and test again
it.h: Engineers fix problems and try again.

it.q: Before building, Mia drew her shade idea. What is her drawing called?
it.h: A drawing made before building shows the idea.

it.q: Draw a shade structure that would keep an ice cube cool outside. Tell what it is made of.
it.ans: A drawing of a roof or tent over the ice cube made of cardboard, cloth or wood that blocks sunlight.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Sunlight and Warmth
lessons.n: Which things get hottest in the sunlight?

it.q: What warms the sand at the beach?
it.h: Sand feels hot on sunny days.

it.q: A black shirt and a white shirt sit in the sun. Which gets warmer?
it.h: Dark colors take in more sunlight.

it.q: Which feels hottest on a sunny day?
it.h: Metal in the sun gets very hot.

it.q: Juan puts a rock in the sun and a rock in the shade. Later, which rock is warmer?
it.h: Which rock got sunlight?

it.q: Why should you check a slide before you go down on a hot day?
it.h: Touch it with your hand first.

it.q: Name one thing on the playground that gets hot in the sun.
it.ans: A metal slide, a black top, sand, a car seat or a dark bench.
it.h: Think of things you touch outside.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Sunlight and Warmth
lessons.n: How do people and animals stay cool on hot days?

it.q: Where do dogs go on a hot day?
it.h: Where is it cooler?

it.q: Which helps a person stay cool?
it.h: It makes shade for your face.

it.q: Why is a park bench under a tree cooler?
it.h: Leaves make shade.

it.q: Pigs roll in mud on hot days. How does this help them?
it.h: The wet mud is cool.

it.q: The class wants shade at recess. Which idea works?
ch: build a cover over a bench
add a metal roof that is hot to touch
it.h: Something that blocks the Sun.

it.q: Tell two ways you can stay cool on a very hot day.
it.ans: Stay in the shade, drink water, wear a hat or light clothes, or use a fan.
it.h: Think about shade and water.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather Watchers
lessons.n: How can we observe and record the weather?

it.q: Which word tells about weather?
it.h: Weather is what it is like outside.

it.q: Which tool tells how hot or cold the air is?
it.h: It has numbers and a line that goes up and down.

it.q: A wind sock is standing straight out. What is the weather?
it.h: What could push the wind sock?

it.q: Fog makes it
it.h: Fog is like a cloud near the ground.

it.q: Why do we color one weather box every day?
ch: to see what the weather was like over time
to make the chart pretty only
it.h: What can we learn by looking back at many days?

it.q: Tell what the weather is like today and how you know.
it.ans: "It is cloudy because I see gray clouds" or "It is sunny because the sky is bright and I see shadows."

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather Watchers
lessons.n: What patterns do we see in the weather?

it.q: Which season is usually warmest where we live?
it.h: When do people go swimming and to the beach most?

it.q: Our chart for the week shows sun, sun, cloud, sun, sun. Which weather happened most?
it.h: Count each kind of weather.

it.q: In many places, mornings are cooler and afternoons are warmer. Why?
ch: The Sun warms the land and air during the day
it.h: When has the Sun been shining longer?

it.q: In California, which season usually brings the most rain?
it.h: Most rain storms in California come in the colder months.

it.q: Which pattern is true about seasons?
it.h: Will summer come again next year?

it.q: Tell how the weather is different in summer and in winter.
it.ans: Summer is usually warm or hot and sunny; winter is cooler, with more rain (and snow in the mountains).

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather Watchers
lessons.n: How do weather forecasts help us stay safe?

it.q: A forecast tells
ch: what the weather will probably be
it.h: Forecasts are about weather that is coming.

it.q: The forecast says a big storm is coming. What should a family do?
ch: get ready and stay inside when it comes
it.h: Storms can be dangerous.

it.q: The forecast says it will be very hot tomorrow. What should you bring to school?
ch: a water bottle and a hat
it.h: How do you stay cool and safe in the heat?

it.q: You hear thunder while playing outside. What should you do?
ch: go inside a building right away
it.h: Thunder means lightning is near.

it.q: Which job helps people know about storms?
it.h: This person studies the weather and tells us what might happen.

it.q: Tell one thing your family can do to get ready for a big rainstorm.
it.ans: Bring things inside, have flashlights, stay home, wear rain gear, or clear drains.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather Watchers
lessons.n: What tools tell us about rain, wind and temperature?

it.q: Which tool tells how hot or cold it is?
it.h: It has numbers and a red line that goes up and down.

it.q: Which tool catches rain so we can see how much fell?
it.h: It is a tube or cup with lines on it.

it.q: A windsock is puffed out and flying straight. What is the weather?
it.h: Wind fills up the windsock.

it.q: The red line on the thermometer goes up. The air is getting
it.h: Up means more heat.

it.q: The rain gauge was empty in the morning. After a storm it is half full. What happened?
it.h: What fills a rain gauge?

it.q: Name one weather tool and tell what it shows.
it.ans: A thermometer shows how warm it is, a rain gauge shows how much rain fell, or a windsock shows wind.
it.h: Think of the tools in our weather station.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Weather Watchers
lessons.n: What are rain, snow, hail and fog?

it.q: Water falling from clouds in drops is
it.h: It makes puddles.

it.q: Soft white flakes falling on a cold day are
it.h: You can build a snowman with it.

it.q: Balls of ice falling in a storm are called
it.h: They bounce and can hurt.

it.q: A cloud is close to the ground and you cannot see far. What is it?
it.h: It is like a cloud you can walk in.

it.q: Hail is falling. What should you do?
it.h: Ice balls can hit you.

it.q: Tell what you like to do on a snowy day or a rainy day.
it.ans: Describes an activity, such as "build a snowman" or "jump in puddles with boots on."
it.h: What do you wear?

lessons.u: Unit 4: What Living Things Need
lessons.n: What do animals eat?

it.q: What does a rabbit eat?
it.h: Think of what a rabbit nibbles in a garden.

it.q: Which animal eats other animals?
it.h: Which one hunts?

it.q: What do all animals need to get from eating?
it.h: Animals cannot make their own food.

it.q: Which animal eats both plants and animals?
it.h: This animal eats berries and also catches fish.

it.q: A hummingbird drinks from flowers. What is it getting?
it.h: Flowers have a sweet liquid inside.

it.q: Name an animal and tell what it eats.
it.ans: Any correct pair, such as "a cat eats meat or fish" or "a cow eats grass."

lessons.u: Unit 4: What Living Things Need
lessons.n: What do plants need to live and grow?

it.q: What do plants need to live?
it.h: What do we give our class plant?

it.q: Do plants need to eat food like animals do?
ch: No, plants use light, air and water to make their own food
Yes, plants eat bugs every day
it.h: Plants have no mouths. How do they get food?

it.q: The class watered one bean plant and not the other. After a week, which looked healthier?
it.h: Which one got what plants need?

it.q: A plant was put in a closet with no light. What will most likely happen?
it.h: Plants need light.

it.q: Why do plant roots grow in soil?
it.h: Where is the water for the plant?

it.q: Tell two things a plant needs to grow.
it.ans: Water and light (also air and space or soil).

lessons.u: Unit 4: What Living Things Need
lessons.n: What do people and all living things need?

it.q: What do people need every day?
it.h: What would you need to stay alive on a camping trip?

it.q: Which need do all plants, animals and people share?
it.h: Think of something everything living needs.

it.q: Why do fish need water?
ch: They get air from the water to breathe
it.h: Fish breathe through gills in water.

it.q: Where do people get water?
ch: from a sink, fountain or bottle
it.h: Where do you get a drink at school?

it.q: Which is a pattern about living things?
it.h: Plants, animals and people: does each one need water?

it.q: Tell one thing you need that your pet or a farm animal also needs.
it.ans: Food, water, air or a safe place to live.

lessons.u: Unit 4: What Living Things Need
lessons.n: How do plants and animals get the water they need?

it.q: How does a plant drink water?
it.h: This part is under the soil.

it.q: Where do ducks get water?
it.h: Ducks swim and drink there.

it.q: A plant is not watered for many days. What happens?
it.h: Plants need water to stay strong.

it.q: Where does a deer find water in the forest?
it.h: Water that flows.

it.q: Why do people drink water every day?
ch: to grow taller in one day
it.h: Our bodies need water.

it.q: Tell how you take care of a class plant so it gets water.
it.ans: Water it a little every few days so the soil stays damp.
it.h: Feel the soil. Is it dry?

lessons.u: Unit 4: What Living Things Need
lessons.n: How do we care for a class pet and a class plant?

it.q: What does a class hamster need every day?
it.h: All animals need these.

it.q: What does a class plant need?
it.h: Put it by a window.

it.q: Where should the class fish tank go?
ch: on the floor where kids run
it.h: Too much heat is bad for fish.

it.q: The hamster's cage is messy. What should we do?
it.h: A clean home keeps animals healthy.

it.q: Our plant is leaning toward the window. Why?
it.h: What comes in the window?

it.q: Tell one job you could do to care for a class pet.
it.ans: Give food, give fresh water, clean the cage, or be gentle.
it.h: What does a pet need?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Living Things and Where They Live
lessons.n: Why do animals live where they live?

it.q: Where does a fish live?
ch: in a cave with no water
it.h: Fish need water to breathe.

it.q: Where does a squirrel make its home?
it.h: Squirrels climb.

it.q: Why does a deer live in a forest?
ch: The forest has plants to eat and places to hide
it.h: Think about what a deer needs.

it.q: Why do frogs live near ponds?
ch: They need water and catch insects there
it.h: Where do frogs lay eggs and find bugs?

it.q: Which animal lives in a desert where it is hot and dry?
it.h: Which animal is fine in heat and does not need much water?

it.q: Pick an animal. Tell where it lives and one thing it gets there.
it.ans: For example: "A bird lives in a tree. It gets a safe place for its nest."

lessons.u: Unit 5: Living Things and Where They Live
lessons.n: How do animals change the places they live?

it.q: Birds build nests out of
it.h: What can a bird find outside and carry with its beak?

it.q: A beaver chews trees and builds a dam in a stream. What happens?
ch: The water backs up and makes a pond
The trees grow back right away
it.h: A dam blocks water.

it.q: Prairie dogs dig tunnels. How do they change the land?
ch: They move dirt and make holes
it.h: What happens when you dig?

it.q: Why do squirrels bury acorns?
it.h: What will the squirrel eat in winter?

it.q: Ants build hills. Where do they get the dirt?
it.h: Ant hills are next to their tunnels.

it.q: Tell how one animal changes its home to get what it needs.
it.ans: Example: a bird builds a nest from twigs to keep its eggs safe; a beaver builds a dam to make a pond.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Living Things and Where They Live
lessons.n: How do plants and people change the places they live?

it.q: People cut down trees to
it.h: What are many houses made of?

it.q: Tree roots can crack a sidewalk. Why?
ch: Roots grow and push to find water
it.h: Roots grow and spread underground.

it.q: Why do farmers dig ditches near their fields?
it.h: What do crops need?

it.q: Dandelions grow in a crack in the sidewalk. How did the plant change its place?
ch: It made the crack bigger as it grew
it.h: Plants grow and push.

it.q: People build roads. How does this change the land?
ch: More grass grows on the road
it.h: What covers the ground where a road is?

it.q: Name one way people change the land to get what they need.
it.ans: Build houses or roads, plant farms or gardens, dig wells, build dams.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Living Things and Where They Live
lessons.n: Where do animals find shelter? Nests, burrows and dens

it.q: A hole that a rabbit digs to live in is a
it.h: It is under the ground.

it.q: A bear sleeps in a cave called a
it.h: It is a short word.

it.q: Why do animals need shelter?
it.h: Think about rain, cold and danger.

it.q: A woodpecker makes a hole in a tree. What is the hole for?
it.h: Some birds live inside trees.

it.q: Beavers build homes in water from
it.h: Beavers chew trees.

it.q: Name an animal and tell what its shelter is.
it.ans: Rabbit and burrow, bird and nest, bear and den, bee and hive, or beaver and lodge.
it.h: Where does it sleep?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Living Things and Where They Live
lessons.n: What lives in the desert, the forest and the ocean?

it.q: Which animal lives in the ocean?
it.h: It has eight arms and swims.

it.q: Which plant grows in a dry desert?
it.h: It stores water and has spines.

it.q: A forest has many trees. Which animal lives there?
it.h: It sleeps in trees.

it.q: Why can a fish not live in the desert?
it.h: What does a fish need to live?

it.q: A camel lives in the desert. What helps it?
ch: it can go a long time without water
it.h: Deserts are dry.

it.q: Name one animal that lives in the ocean and one that lives in a forest.
it.ans: Ocean: fish, whale, crab or octopus. Forest: deer, owl, bear or squirrel.
it.h: Think of water animals and tree animals.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.n: How do people change the land, water and air?

it.q: Which harms the ocean?
it.h: Where does beach trash go when the waves come?

it.q: Smoke from many cars makes the air
it.h: Think about the gray cloud that comes out of a car's tailpipe.

it.q: Why is a plastic bag in a pond a problem?
ch: Animals can eat it or get stuck in it
it.h: Animals sometimes think plastic is food.

it.q: People cut down a forest to build a mall. What happens to the forest animals?
it.h: Where did the animals live before?

it.q: Which uses up a lot of water?
it.h: Which one lets water run when no one needs it?

it.q: Tell one way people can make a place dirty or harm animals.
it.ans: Littering, dumping trash in water, cutting down trees or polluting the air.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.n: How can we make less trash?

it.q: Using something again is called
it.h: "Re" means again.

it.q: Which can go in the recycling bin?
it.h: Paper, cans and some plastic bottles can be made into new things.

it.q: Which makes less trash at lunch?
ch: a new plastic bottle every day
it.h: Which one can you use day after day?

it.q: Apple cores and leaves can be turned into rich soil. This is called
it.h: Worms help turn food scraps into soil.

it.q: Which is a way to reuse a jar?
it.h: Can the jar hold something new?

it.q: Tell one thing you can reuse at home or school.
it.ans: A jar, box, bag, bottle or paper used on both sides.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.n: How can we solve problems like engineers?

it.q: What do engineers do?
it.h: Engineers build tools and objects that help people.

it.q: The class has a problem: wind blows our recycling out of the bin. What is a good first step?
ch: watch what happens and ask questions
it.h: Engineers first understand the problem.

it.q: Which idea could keep recycling from blowing away?
ch: a bin with holes in the bottom
it.h: What could keep paper from flying out?

it.q: Before building, Tai draws his idea. Why?
ch: to plan and share his idea
it.h: A drawing helps others understand.

it.q: Two lid designs were tested. Lid 1 kept in 3 papers. Lid 2 kept in 9 papers. Which lid worked better?
it.h: Which kept more papers in the bin?

it.q: Tell or draw a way to keep birds from pulling trash out of a bin.
it.ans: A lid with a latch, a net over the top or a heavy cover.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.n: How can we save water and keep it clean?

it.q: What should you do while you brush your teeth?
it.h: Water runs away down the drain.

it.q: Which helps keep creeks clean?
it.h: Where does trash belong?

it.q: A faucet drips all day. What should a family do?
ch: put a cup under it forever
it.h: A leak wastes water.

it.q: Why should we not drop trash near a storm drain?
ch: rain carries it to the ocean
it.h: Storm drains lead to creeks and the ocean.

it.q: Which uses less water to water a garden?
ch: a watering can at the roots
a hose left on all day
it.h: Give water right where plants need it.

it.q: Tell one way you can save water at home.
it.ans: Turn off the tap while brushing, take shorter showers, fix leaks or use a cup.
it.h: Think of the sink and the bathtub.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.n: How can we help plants and animals near our school?

it.q: Which helps birds near school?
it.h: Birds need food.

it.q: What can we plant to give bees food?
it.h: Bees drink nectar.

it.q: Why should we stay on the path in a park?
it.h: Little plants can get crushed.

it.q: The class plants a tree. How does this help animals?
it.h: Think of nests and shade.

it.q: Which saves energy at school?
ch: turning off lights we are not using
it.h: Turn it off when you leave.

it.q: Tell one way your class could help animals near school.
it.ans: Plant flowers or trees, put up a bird feeder or birdbath, or pick up litter.
it.h: What do animals need?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Sound and Vibrations
lessons.n: What makes sound?

it.q: When something moves back and forth very fast, we say it
it.h: Pluck a rubber band and watch it shake.

it.q: Put your hand on your throat and hum. What do you feel?
it.h: Your voice comes from parts in your throat that shake.

it.q: Kofi plucks a guitar string. It makes a sound. What is the string doing?
it.h: Look closely at the string right after you pluck it.

it.q: A bell is ringing. Mira touches it and the sound stops. Why?
it.h: No vibration means no sound.

it.q: Which makes a louder sound?
ch: touching the drum with a feather
it.h: Bigger vibrations make louder sounds.

it.q: Tell how you can make a rubber band stretched over a box make a sound.
it.ans: Pluck or strum the rubber band so it vibrates; the vibration makes the sound.
it.h: What do you do with your finger?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Sound and Vibrations
lessons.n: Can sound make things move?

it.q: Rice is put on top of a drum. The drum is hit. What happens to the rice?
it.h: The drum skin shakes when hit.

it.q: A tuning fork is struck and touched to water. What happens?
it.h: A ringing tuning fork is vibrating.

it.q: A loud truck drives by and the windows rattle. What made them rattle?
it.h: Strong sounds can make things shake.

it.q: Paper is taped over a cup with salt on top. Someone sings loudly near it. The salt jumps. What does this show?
it.h: What moved the paper?

it.q: How can you tell a speaker is making sound if you cannot hear it?
ch: touch it and feel it vibrate
it.h: Sound is vibration.

it.q: Tell what happened to the rice on the drum and why.
it.ans: The rice jumped because the drum vibrated when it was hit.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Sound and Vibrations
lessons.n: How can we send a message with sound?

it.q: Which can send a message with sound?
it.h: Which one can you hear?

it.q: Two cups are tied with a tight string. Ana talks into one cup. How does Ben hear her?
ch: The string vibrates and carries the sound
it.h: The sound makes the cup and string vibrate.

it.q: The cup phone does not work when the string is loose. What should they do?
it.h: A loose string cannot carry the vibrations well.

it.q: Why does a fire truck use a loud siren?
ch: to warn people from far away
it.h: What does a siren tell people?

it.q: A school bell rings. What message does it send?
ch: It is time to change activities
it.h: What do you do when the bell rings?

it.q: Make up a drum code. Tell what one beat and two beats mean.
it.ans: For example: one beat means "come here" and two beats means "stop."

lessons.u: Unit 1: Sound and Vibrations
lessons.n: Why are some sounds high and some sounds low?

it.q: A mouse squeak is a
it.h: Is it squeaky like a whistle or deep like a drum?

it.q: A big drum makes a
it.h: Big drums go "boom."

it.q: Two rubber bands are on a box. One is thin and one is thick. Which makes the lower sound?
it.h: Thick and heavy things vibrate more slowly.

it.q: Jin pulls a rubber band tighter and plucks it. What happens to the sound?
it.h: Tighter bands vibrate faster.

it.q: Bottles hold different amounts of water. Tapping them makes different sounds. What is changing?
ch: how high or low the sound is
it.h: Listen for squeaky and deep sounds.

it.q: Tell how you could make a high sound and a low sound with rubber bands.
it.ans: Pluck a thin or tight rubber band for a high sound and a thick or loose rubber band for a low sound.
it.h: Try thick and thin bands.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Sound and Vibrations
lessons.n: How does sound travel through air, water and walls?

it.q: You hear a friend talk across the room. What carries the sound?
it.h: Sound moves through what is all around us.

it.q: Put your ear on a table. A friend taps the other end. What do you notice?
it.h: Sound can move through wood.

it.q: Whales call to each other. What does the sound travel through?
it.h: Whales live in the ocean.

it.q: You hear music from the room next door. How does it get to you?
it.h: Walls can vibrate.

it.q: A friend talks far away. Why is the sound quieter?
ch: sound gets weaker as it goes far
it.h: Think of yelling across a big field.

it.q: Tell one thing sound can travel through.
it.ans: Air, water, wood, walls, metal or a string.
it.h: Think of the table test.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: Can we see in the dark?

it.q: What do we need to see things?
it.h: What happens when someone turns off all the lights?

it.q: In a closed box with no light, can you see a toy inside?
ch: yes, if the toy is red
it.h: There is no light inside the box.

it.q: Which gives off its own light?
it.h: Which one makes light even in a dark room?

it.q: You shine a flashlight on a picture in a dark room. Why can you see the picture now?
ch: Light shines on it and comes to your eyes
The picture made its own light
it.h: Light lets you see things it shines on.

it.q: Cats can see well at night when there is a little light. Can they see in total darkness?
it.h: All eyes need some light.

it.q: Tell why you cannot see your bedroom toys when the lights are off and the curtains are closed.
it.ans: There is no light shining on the toys, and we can only see things when light shines on them.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: What happens when light hits different materials?

it.q: Light passes all the way through
it.h: Can you see through it?

it.q: Wax paper lets some light through. What kind of material is that?
it.h: Things look blurry through wax paper.

it.q: What forms behind a block when a flashlight shines on it?
it.h: The block stops the light.

it.q: What does a mirror do to light?
it.h: Shine a flashlight at a mirror. Where does the light go?

it.q: Which material blocks all light?
it.h: Which one can you not see through at all?

it.q: Shine a flashlight at wax paper, clear plastic and foil. Tell what happens with each one.
it.ans: Wax paper lets some light through; clear plastic lets almost all light through; foil blocks light and bounces some back.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: How can we send a message with light?

it.q: Which could send a message across a dark field?
it.h: What can be seen far away at night?

it.q: A traffic light turns red. What message does it send?
it.h: What do cars do at a red light?

it.q: How could a mirror help you send a light signal to a friend?
it.h: Mirrors bounce light.

it.q: Why do lighthouses shine bright lights?
it.h: Rocks near the shore can be dangerous for ships.

it.q: Ming wants to block a light signal to send "off." What can she use?
it.h: Which one stops light?

it.q: Make a flashlight code. Tell what one flash and two flashes mean.
it.ans: For example: one flash means "yes" and two flashes means "no."

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: Where does light come from?

it.q: What gives us light in the day?
it.h: It is a star.

it.q: Which of these glows with its own light when you switch it on?
it.h: Turn it on and it glows.

it.q: Which is a light source at night?
it.h: It shines when you push the button.

it.q: A mirror lights up a wall. Is the mirror a light source?
it.h: Does a mirror shine in a dark closet?

it.q: The Moon looks bright at night. Where does its light come from?
it.h: The Moon bounces light.

it.q: Name two things that make their own light.
it.ans: Two of: the Sun, a lamp, a flashlight, a candle flame, a fire, a TV screen or a firefly.
it.h: Think of things that glow in the dark.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: How do shadows change size and shape?

it.q: What do you need to make a shadow?
it.h: Something has to block the light.

it.q: Max moves his hand close to a flashlight. What happens to the shadow?
it.h: Close to the light blocks more light.

it.q: Max moves his hand far from the flashlight and close to the wall. The shadow gets
it.h: Now less light is blocked.

it.q: A shadow puppet looks like a bunny. What makes the shape?
it.h: Shadows have the outline of the object.

it.q: You turn off the flashlight. What happens to the shadow?
it.h: No light means no shadow.

it.q: Tell how you could make a shadow puppet look bigger on the wall.
it.ans: Move the puppet closer to the flashlight.
it.h: Try moving it near and far.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Light and Seeing
lessons.n: How do mirrors bounce light to help people?

it.q: When light hits a mirror, it
it.h: Shine a flashlight at a mirror and look at the wall.

it.q: Which helps a driver see cars behind the car?
it.h: It is on the side of the car.

it.q: A bike has a shiny red reflector. Why?
ch: car lights bounce off it so drivers see the bike
it.h: A reflector shines only when light hits it.

it.q: Sara wants to light up a dark corner with a flashlight that points the wrong way. What can she use?
it.h: What bounces light to a new place?

it.q: Which bounces the most light?
it.h: Smooth and shiny things bounce light best.

it.q: Tell one way people use mirrors in their lives.
it.ans: To see their face, to see behind a car, to look around a corner, or to bounce light into a dark place.
it.h: Think of the bathroom or a car.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plant and Animal Parts and Inventions
lessons.n: How do animal body parts help them survive?

it.q: Which part helps a fish swim?
it.h: Fish move these flat parts back and forth in water.

it.q: Which part does an eagle use to grab food?
it.h: Look at an eagle's feet.

it.q: A turtle pulls into its shell when a fox comes near. How does the shell help?
it.h: A shell is hard on the outside.

it.q: Why do ducks have webbed feet?
it.h: Webbed feet are like paddles.

it.q: Why do many birds have different beaks?
ch: Each beak shape helps get a certain food
it.h: A long thin beak and a thick strong beak help with different foods.

it.q: Pick an animal. Name one body part and tell how it helps the animal survive.
it.ans: Example: a giraffe's long neck helps it reach leaves high in trees; a porcupine's quills protect it.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plant and Animal Parts and Inventions
lessons.n: How do plant parts help plants survive?

it.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
it.h: These parts are under the ground.

it.q: Which part of a plant uses sunlight to make food?
it.h: These are usually green and flat to catch light.

it.q: Why do roses have thorns?
ch: to keep animals from eating them
it.h: What happens if you touch a thorn?

it.q: What does the stem do for a plant?
ch: holds it up and carries water
it.h: A stem is like a straw and a pole.

it.q: Why does a cactus have a thick, waxy stem?
it.h: Deserts get very little rain.

it.q: Tell how roots help a tree.
it.ans: Roots hold the tree in the ground and take in water from the soil.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plant and Animal Parts and Inventions
lessons.n: How can we copy plants and animals to solve problems?

it.q: Swim fins that people wear copy which animal part?
it.h: Which animal part pushes water?

it.q: A bike helmet protects your head. Which animal part is like a helmet?
it.h: Which hard outside part keeps an animal safe?

it.q: Hook-and-loop tape (like Velcro) was invented after a person studied
ch: burrs that stuck to a dog's fur
it.h: Some seeds have tiny hooks.

it.q: A winter coat keeps people warm like
it.h: What keeps animals warm in cold places?

it.q: A grabber tool with two arms that squeeze is most like
ch: a bird's beak picking up food
it.h: Which part pinches to pick things up?

it.q: Draw a tool that copies an animal part. Tell what problem it solves and which animal gave you the idea.
it.ans: Example: shoes with spikes for climbing, like a mountain goat's hooves, so you do not slip; or a coat with thick fur, like a bear.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plant and Animal Parts and Inventions
lessons.n: How do animals use their senses to survive?

it.q: Which part helps a cat feel its way in the dark?
it.h: They stick out from its face.

it.q: A dog finds food with its
it.h: Dogs sniff.

it.q: Why does an owl have big eyes?
it.h: Owls hunt in the dark.

it.q: A deer's ears turn toward a sound. How does this help?
it.h: Deer listen for animals that hunt them.

it.q: A snake flicks its tongue. What is it doing?
it.h: Snakes use their tongues to sense smells in the air.

it.q: Name an animal and a body part it uses to sense food or danger.
it.ans: Example: a rabbit uses its long ears to hear a fox coming.
it.h: Think of ears, eyes, noses or whiskers.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plant and Animal Parts and Inventions
lessons.n: How do colors and patterns help animals hide?

it.q: Hiding by matching the place around you is called
it.h: It is a long word that starts with "cam."

it.q: A green frog sits on a green leaf. Why is it hard to see?
it.h: Same color as the leaf.

it.q: A white rabbit lives where there is lots of snow. How does its color help?
it.h: What color is snow?

it.q: A brown moth rests on brown tree bark. Which animal will have a hard time finding it?
it.h: Birds eat moths.

it.q: Hunters and campers wear clothes with green and brown patches. What does this copy?
it.h: The clothes blend in with trees.

it.q: Tell why a crab on a sandy beach might be tan colored.
it.ans: Being tan helps it match the sand, so birds and other animals have a hard time seeing it.
it.h: What color is the sand?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Parents, Babies and Family Likeness
lessons.n: How do animal parents help their babies survive?

it.q: How do mother birds help their chicks?
it.h: Baby birds wait in the nest with open mouths.

it.q: A mother cat carries her kitten by the neck. Why?
ch: to move it to a safe place
it.h: Kittens are too small to walk far.

it.q: Why do emperor penguin parents keep their egg on their feet?
ch: to keep it warm off the icy ground
to hide it from the Sun
to make it hatch faster by kicking
it.h: The ice is very cold.

it.q: A mother elephant stands over her calf when a lion is near. What is she doing?
it.h: Elephants are big. The lion is dangerous.

it.q: Which baby animal drinks milk from its mother?
it.h: Mammal babies drink milk.

it.q: Name two ways animal parents help their babies.
it.ans: Two of: feed them, keep them warm, protect them from danger, teach them, carry them to safety.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Parents, Babies and Family Likeness
lessons.n: How do babies get help from their parents?

it.q: A baby bird is hungry. What does it do?
ch: chirps and opens its mouth wide
sleeps all day without a sound
it.h: How does a baby bird let its parent know?

it.q: A human baby cries. What might the baby need?
ch: food, a clean diaper or comfort
it.h: Babies cannot talk yet.

it.q: A lamb gets lost and bleats loudly. What happens?
ch: Its mother hears and comes to find it
The lamb grows up right away
The lamb turns into a goat
it.h: The sound is a call for help.

it.q: Ducklings follow their mother in a line. How does this help them?
it.h: Where is safest for a little duckling?

it.q: A puppy whines and moves close to its mother. What does it want?
it.h: Puppies cuddle to stay warm.

it.q: Tell one way a baby animal tells its parent it needs help, and what the parent does.
it.ans: Example: a baby bird chirps and the parent feeds it; a kitten mews and the mother cat comes to it.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Parents, Babies and Family Likeness
lessons.n: How are young plants and animals like their parents?

it.q: A baby dog grows up to be a
it.h: Babies grow into the same kind of animal as their parents.

it.q: How is a kitten like its mother?
ch: It has fur, whiskers and a tail
it.h: Look for parts that both have.

it.q: How is a puppy different from its parent?
it.h: Think about size.

it.q: An oak seed (acorn) grows into
it.h: Seeds grow into the same kind of plant.

it.q: Two puppies from the same mother have different spots. What does this show?
ch: Babies of the same parents can look a little different
it.h: Brothers and sisters can look different too.

it.q: Name one way a young plant is like its parent plant and one way it is different.
it.ans: Like: same leaf shape or flower color. Different: smaller, fewer leaves, shorter.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Parents, Babies and Family Likeness
lessons.n: How do animal groups protect their young?

it.q: A group of elephants that live together is a
it.h: Cows and horses also live in this kind of group.

it.q: A lion comes near. Adult musk oxen make a circle around their babies. Why?
it.h: The babies are in the middle.

it.q: Wolves in a pack bring food back to the pups. Who helps feed the pups?
it.h: A pack works together.

it.q: Baby fish swim in a big group called a school. How does this help?
ch: it is harder for a hunter to catch one
it.h: Many fish together can confuse a hunter.

it.q: Meerkats take turns standing tall and watching. What are they watching for?
it.h: One meerkat calls when a hawk comes.

it.q: Tell one way living in a group helps baby animals stay safe.
it.ans: Adults can watch for danger, protect the babies in the middle, or share food with them.
it.h: Think of elephants or wolves.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Parents, Babies and Family Likeness
lessons.n: Which baby belongs to which parent?

it.q: A baby cat is a
it.h: It meows.

it.q: A baby cow is a
it.h: It drinks milk and goes "moo."

it.q: A spotted dog has puppies. What will the puppies most likely have?
it.h: Puppies grow into dogs.

it.q: A tall sunflower makes seeds. What will grow from the seeds?
it.h: Seeds grow into the same kind of plant.

it.q: Three kittens have the same mother. One is black, one is orange and one is gray. What does this show?
ch: babies can look different from each other
it.h: Brothers and sisters can look different.

it.q: Tell one way a duckling is like its mother and one way it is different.
it.ans: Alike: both have a beak, webbed feet and feathers. Different: the duckling is smaller and fluffy.
it.h: Think about size and feathers.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky?

it.q: In the morning, the Sun rises in the
it.h: Look at the "east" sign on our wall.

it.q: In the evening, the Sun sets in the
it.h: The Sun goes down on the other side from where it rose.

it.q: When is the Sun highest in the sky?
it.h: Think about the middle of the day.

it.q: When is your shadow shortest?
it.h: When the Sun is high, shadows are short.

it.q: Which pattern can we predict?
ch: The Sun will rise again tomorrow morning
The Sun will rise in the west tomorrow
The Sun will stay still all day
The Sun will not set today
it.h: Does the Sun rise every single morning?

it.q: Tell where the Sun is in the morning, at noon and in the evening.
it.ans: Morning: low in the east. Noon: high in the sky. Evening: low in the west.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why does the Moon change its shape?

it.q: The Moon's shape looks different on different nights. This is a
it.h: The shapes change and then repeat.

it.q: About how long does it take the Moon to go through all its shapes and start again?
it.h: Think about our Moon calendar on the wall.

it.q: A full Moon looks like
it.h: "Full" means all of it.

it.q: Can you sometimes see the Moon in the daytime?
it.h: Have you ever seen a pale Moon in a blue sky?

it.q: Leo saw a full Moon tonight. What will he see in about one month?
it.h: The Moon's pattern repeats.

it.q: Draw three Moon shapes you might see in a month and name them.
it.ans: Drawings of a full Moon (circle), a half Moon and a crescent (thin curve), with labels.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: When can we see the stars?

it.q: When can we see most stars?
it.h: Stars are always there. When does the sky get dark?

it.q: Why can't we see stars in the daytime?
ch: The Sun is so bright it hides them
Stars go away during the day
it.h: Which star is very close and very bright?

it.q: Where would you see more stars?
ch: in the country far from city lights
it.h: Bright lights make dim stars hard to see.

it.q: Which is the closest star to Earth?
it.h: It lights our day.

it.q: Over a night, the stars seem to
it.h: The stars seem to move the same way the Sun does.

it.q: Tell one way the Sun and the stars at night are alike and one way they are different.
it.ans: Alike: both are stars and give off light. Different: the Sun is much closer, so it looks much bigger and brighter.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why do we have day and night?

it.q: When the Sun is up in our sky, it is
it.h: Light comes from the Sun.

it.q: When our side of Earth is away from the Sun, it is
it.h: No sunlight reaches us.

it.q: Earth spins all the way around one time each
it.h: Day and night happen once each time.

it.q: Which pattern happens every 24 hours?
it.h: Think of one whole day.

it.q: It is daytime here. On the other side of Earth it is
it.h: Only half of Earth faces the Sun at a time.

it.q: Tell why day and night keep happening.
it.ans: Earth spins, so our side faces the Sun (day) and then turns away from the Sun (night), again and again.
it.h: Spin a ball near a lamp.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: How do people use sky patterns to plan and find their way?

it.q: A full Moon comes back about every
it.h: Think of a Moon calendar.

it.q: Sailors long ago used a star that stays in the north to find their way. What is it called?
it.h: Its name tells the direction.

it.q: Farmers wake at sunrise to work in the fields. What pattern do they use?
it.h: The Sun comes up every day.

it.q: Why can people plan a night walk to see a full Moon?
it.h: Patterns help us predict.

it.q: The Sun sets in the west. Ana watches the sunset. Which way is she facing?
it.h: Look where the Sun goes down.

it.q: Tell one way people use a pattern in the sky.
it.ans: To tell time by the Sun, plan by the Moon's shapes, find directions with the North Star, or know when it will get dark.
it.h: Think of the Sun, Moon or stars.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: Why does it get dark earlier in winter?

it.q: Which season has the most hours of daylight?
it.h: Think of long summer evenings when it is still light after dinner.

it.q: Which season has the fewest hours of daylight?
it.h: When does it get dark before dinner?

it.q: In December, Liam sees it getting dark when he gets home from school. In June it is still light at bedtime. What does this show?
ch: There is more daylight in June than in December
There is more daylight in December
Daylight is the same all year
It never gets dark in June
it.h: Compare when it gets dark in each month.

it.q: From winter to summer, the days get
it.h: Each month after winter has a bit more daylight.

it.q: Which month has more daylight where we live?
it.h: Which one is in summer?

it.q: Tell how the amount of daylight changes from winter to summer.
it.ans: The days get longer: there are more hours of daylight in summer than in winter.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: How can we use data to compare daylight?

it.q: A chart shows: January 10 hours of daylight, June 14 hours. Which month has more daylight?
it.h: Which number is bigger?

it.q: March has 12 hours of daylight and December has 10 hours. How many more hours does March have?
it.h: Count up from 10 to 12.

it.q: A bar chart shows daylight bars getting taller from January to June. What does that mean?
it.h: A taller bar means more hours.

it.q: Which month most likely has about the same daylight as March?
it.h: Spring and fall are in between winter and summer.

it.q: The class recorded sunset times: October 6 o'clock, November 5 o'clock. What pattern do you see?
it.h: Is 5 o'clock earlier or later than 6 o'clock?

it.q: Tell how a chart of daylight hours helps us see a pattern.
it.ans: It shows the hours for each month side by side, so we can see that summer months have more daylight and winter months have less.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: How can we tell time with the Sun?

it.q: A tool that uses a shadow to tell time is a
it.h: "Sun" is part of its name.

it.q: Why can a shadow help tell time?
ch: Shadows move as the Sun moves across the sky
it.h: Remember our stick shadow from morning to afternoon.

it.q: Which day would a sundial not work well?
it.h: What does a sundial need to make a shadow?

it.q: Kim built a sundial but put it in the shade of a building. What is the problem?
ch: The stick cannot make a shadow from the Sun
it.h: A sundial needs sunlight to reach it.

it.q: Two sundials were tested. Sundial A had a tall stick and a clear shadow. Sundial B had a tiny stick and a hard-to-see shadow. Which works better?
it.h: Which shadow can you read easily?

it.q: Tell how you would build a simple sundial with a paper plate and a pencil.
it.ans: Push the pencil through the middle of the plate, put it in a sunny spot, and mark where the shadow points each hour.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: How do the seasons change what we wear and do?

it.q: Which season is usually the warmest?
it.h: School is out and people swim.

it.q: Which season comes after summer?
it.h: Leaves change color.

it.q: It is winter and it gets dark early. Which outdoor time is best for a walk?
it.h: When is there still daylight?

it.q: In summer the days are long. What can kids do after dinner?
it.h: The Sun sets late in summer.

it.q: Which clothes go best with a cold winter morning?
it.h: Winter mornings can be chilly.

it.q: Tell one thing you do in summer and one thing you do in winter.
it.ans: Summer: swim, go to the beach, play outside late. Winter: wear a coat, stay inside more, see the sunset early.
it.h: Think about the weather and the daylight.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: How do plants and animals change with the seasons?

it.q: In fall, many trees
it.h: Look at the ground under maple trees.

it.q: In spring, many plants
it.h: Spring brings green buds.

it.q: Some birds fly to warmer places in fall. Why?
it.h: Bugs and seeds are hard to find in cold places.

it.q: Some bears rest in a den for the winter. Why?
ch: there is little food in winter
it.h: Winter is hard for finding food.

it.q: A squirrel stores nuts in fall. Why?
it.h: Winter has fewer nuts.

it.q: Tell one way an animal gets ready for winter.
it.ans: Stores food, grows thicker fur, flies to a warmer place, or rests in a den.
it.h: Think of a squirrel or a bear.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Daylight Through the Year
lessons.n: Why is the noon Sun higher in summer than in winter?

it.q: At noon in summer, the Sun is
it.h: Summer noon shadows are short.

it.q: At noon in winter, the Sun is
it.h: Winter noon shadows are longer.

it.q: A flagpole's noon shadow is long in December and short in June. What changed?
it.h: A higher Sun makes a shorter shadow.

it.q: In which month would your noon shadow be longest?
it.h: When is the noon Sun lowest?

it.q: Mia's noon shadow was 3 steps long in June and 7 steps long in December. How many steps longer was it in December?
it.h: Count up from 3 to 7.

it.q: Tell how your noon shadow is different in summer and winter.
it.ans: In summer it is short because the Sun is high; in winter it is longer because the Sun is lower.
it.h: Think of where the Sun is at lunch.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.n: How can we describe and sort materials?

it.q: What is a property of a material?
ch: something you can observe about it, like color or hardness
it.h: Properties describe what a material is like.

it.q: Which word describes how a material feels?
it.h: Which word goes with touch?

it.q: Which material bends easily without breaking?
it.h: Bending without breaking is called flexible.

it.q: Which material soaks up water?
it.h: Soak up means water goes inside it.

it.q: Ivan sorted objects into two groups: "see-through" and "not see-through." Which goes in the see-through group?
it.h: Can you see your hand through it?

it.q: Pick two objects in the room. Describe two properties of each.
it.ans: Example: a pencil is hard and long; a sweater is soft and stretchy.
it.h: Think about color, shape, texture, hardness and whether it bends.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.n: What makes something a solid or a liquid?

it.q: Which is a solid?
it.h: A solid keeps its own shape.

it.q: Which is a liquid?
it.h: A liquid flows and can be poured.

it.q: You pour water from a tall glass into a bowl. What happens to its shape?
ch: It takes the shape of the bowl
It stays tall like the glass
