it.h: Liquids take the shape of their container.

it.q: Sand can be poured, but each grain keeps its shape. Is a grain of sand a solid or a liquid?
it.h: Look at one grain with a magnifier. Does it change shape?

it.q: Which is true about a wooden block?
ch: It keeps its shape in any container
It takes the shape of its container
it.h: Put a block in a cup and then in a bowl. Did it change?

it.q: Tell one way solids and liquids are different.
it.ans: A solid keeps its own shape; a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.n: Which material is best for the job?

it.q: Which material is best for a raincoat?
it.h: A raincoat must keep water out.

it.q: Why are cooking pots often made of metal?
ch: Metal lets heat pass through to cook food
it.h: Heat needs to get from the stove to the food.

it.q: Which material is best for a window?
it.h: A window should let light through.

it.q: The class tested 3 materials for wiping spills. Paper towel soaked up 10 drops, cloth 15 drops, and plastic 0 drops. Which is best for wiping spills?
it.h: The best one soaks up the most.

it.q: Why do we use rubber for the bottom of shoes?
ch: It grips the ground and bends
It is very hard and slippery
it.h: Think about running without slipping.

it.q: Tell which material you would use to build a doghouse and why.
it.ans: Wood, because it is strong, stiff and keeps rain out (or a similar reason).

lessons.u: Unit 1: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.n: Where do materials come from? Natural and human-made

it.q: Which material comes from trees?
it.h: Think of a log.

it.q: Wool comes from
it.h: It is an animal's thick coat.

it.q: Which material is made by people in factories?
it.h: You do not find it growing or lying on the ground in nature.

it.q: Glass is made by heating
it.h: The beach has lots of it.

it.q: Paper is made from
it.h: Paper and pencils start in the forest.

it.q: Name one natural material and one human-made material in your classroom.
it.ans: Natural: a wooden desk, a cotton shirt, a stone. Human-made: a plastic chair, a glass window, a nylon backpack.
it.h: Did it come straight from nature, or did people change it a lot?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.n: How can we test materials for strength and bendiness?

it.q: A material that bends without breaking is
it.h: Think of a rubber band.

it.q: A material that breaks into pieces easily is
it.h: Think of a cracker or a dry twig.

it.q: Kids hung pennies from strips of paper, cloth and plastic. The plastic held 30, cloth 22, paper 8. Which was strongest?
it.h: Which held the most pennies?

it.q: To make the penny test fair, the strips should be
ch: held by different people at different times
it.h: Change only the material.

it.q: A cloth strip held 22 pennies and a paper strip held 8. How many more pennies did cloth hold?
it.h: Subtract 8 from 22.

it.q: Tell which material you would choose for a jump rope and why.
it.ans: Nylon rope or rubber, because it is flexible and strong, so it bends without breaking.
it.h: A jump rope must bend a lot and not snap.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: Can we build something new from the same small pieces?

it.q: A house can be built from many small
it.h: Look at a brick wall. What is it made of?

it.q: Mia builds a tower with 20 blocks, takes it apart and builds a car with the same 20 blocks. What is true?
ch: The same pieces made a different object
it.h: Did she add or lose any blocks?

it.q: A wooden fence can be taken apart. What could you build from its boards?
it.h: The boards are still wood.

it.q: A necklace is taken apart into beads. What can you make with the same beads?
it.h: The beads can be put together in a new way.

it.q: Why do builders use small pieces like bricks instead of one giant rock?
ch: Small pieces can be put together into many shapes
it.h: Think about building shapes with blocks.

it.q: Tell how one set of building blocks can make two different things.
it.ans: The blocks can be arranged one way to make a tower and taken apart and arranged a different way to make a bridge or car.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: What happens when we heat things?

it.q: What happens to butter in a hot pan?
it.h: Think about pancakes cooking.

it.q: A cake batter is baked in the oven. Can you turn the cake back into batter?
it.h: Think about what happens to the batter in the oven.

it.q: A crayon melts in the sun. Then it is put in the shade and gets hard again. This change
it.h: Did the crayon go back to being solid?

it.q: Which change from heating cannot be undone?
it.h: Can toast become soft bread again?

it.q: Popcorn kernels are heated and pop. Can the popcorn change back into kernels?
it.h: Is the popcorn different now?

it.q: Name one change from heating that can be reversed and one that cannot.
it.ans: Can be reversed: melting chocolate, wax or ice. Cannot be reversed: cooking an egg, baking bread, toasting a marshmallow, burning wood.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: What happens when we cool things?

it.q: What happens to water in a freezer?
it.h: What do you find in ice cube trays?

it.q: Melted wax drips onto a cold table. What happens?
it.h: Cooling turns many liquids back into solids.

it.q: Juice is frozen into an ice pop. It melts on a hot day. Can it be frozen again?
it.h: Freezing and melting can go back and forth.

it.q: Which of these can be undone by cooling?
it.h: Which one only melted?

it.q: Liquid gelatin is put in the fridge. It turns into a wiggly solid. What caused the change?
it.h: Where did it go?

it.q: Tell how you could show that freezing water can be reversed.
it.ans: Freeze water into ice, then let the ice warm up and melt back into water.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: How do bending, cutting and folding change materials?

it.q: A sheet of paper is folded into a fan. Is it still paper?
it.h: Only its shape changed.

it.q: A wire is bent into a circle. What changed?
it.h: The wire is still metal.

it.q: Clay is rolled into a snake. Can it be made into a ball again?
it.h: Soft clay can be squished again.

it.q: Paper is cut into small pieces. Which is true?
it.h: Look at one small piece.

it.q: Which change can be undone easily?
it.h: Can you unfold it?

it.q: Tell how cutting paper and burning paper are different changes.
it.ans: Cut paper is still paper in smaller pieces. Burned paper becomes ash and smoke, so it is no longer paper and cannot change back.
it.h: Is it still paper afterward?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: How can we build strong structures from small pieces?

it.q: Which shape at the bottom helps a tower stand without tipping?
it.h: Think of a pyramid.

it.q: Kids built two block towers. Tower A had a wide bottom. Tower B had a narrow bottom. Which fell over first in the fan test?
it.h: Narrow bottoms tip more easily.

it.q: Bricks in a wall are laid so each brick sits across two bricks below. Why?
it.h: Each brick helps hold two others.

it.q: Which shape is often used in bridges because it is strong?
it.h: Look at the sides of many metal bridges.

it.q: A tower has 4 layers. Each layer has 6 blocks. How many blocks are in the tower?
it.h: Add 6 four times.

it.q: Tell how you would make a paper tower stronger.
it.ans: Roll paper into tubes, use triangles, make the bottom wide, and tape the pieces together.
it.h: Think about shape and the base.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Building With and Changing Materials
lessons.n: What happens when we mix materials with water?

it.q: Sugar stirred into warm water
it.h: You cannot see the sugar after stirring, but the water tastes sweet.

it.q: Sand stirred into water
it.h: Wait a minute and look at the bottom.

it.q: Salt water is left in a sunny dish until the water dries up. What is left?
it.h: Only the water goes into the air.

it.q: How could you get sand back out of sand and water?
it.h: A coffee filter lets water pass but not sand.

it.q: Which will not dissolve in water?
it.h: Which one will you still see in the cup?

it.q: Tell how you know sugar is still in the water after it dissolves.
it.ans: The water tastes sweet, and if the water dries up the sugar is left behind.
it.h: Use a sense other than sight, with a teacher's OK.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Seeds and Pollinators
lessons.n: Do plants need sunlight and water to grow?

it.q: In a fair test of whether plants need light, what should be different between the two plants?
ch: the size of the pot and the soil
it.h: Change only one thing.

it.q: Plant A got light and water. Plant B got water but was kept in a dark closet. After 2 weeks, B was pale and thin. What does this show?
ch: Plants need light to grow well
it.h: What was the only difference?

it.q: Why should both plants in a test be the same kind of plant?
it.h: If the plants were different kinds, what could cause a change?

it.q: Plant C got light but no water. What will most likely happen?
ch: It will wilt and dry out
it.h: What do roots take in from the soil?

it.q: How can you measure plant growth fairly?
ch: measure the height with a ruler each week
it.h: Scientists use tools and repeat measurements.

it.q: Plan a test to find out if a plant needs water. Tell what you will keep the same and what you will change.
it.ans: Use two same plants in the same light, soil and pots. Water one and do not water the other. Measure and observe both every few days.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Seeds and Pollinators
lessons.n: How do seeds travel to new places?

it.q: Why is it helpful for seeds to travel away from the parent plant?
ch: so they have space, light and water to grow
it.h: What would happen if all seeds dropped right under the parent?

it.q: A burr has tiny hooks. How does it travel?
ch: It sticks to an animal's fur
it.h: Have you ever found something stuck to your socks after a walk?

it.q: A bird eats a berry and flies away. How can this spread seeds?
ch: The seeds pass through the bird and are dropped somewhere new
The bird plants them with a shovel
it.h: Seeds inside berries can pass through an animal.

it.q: Dandelion seeds have fluffy tops. How do they travel?
ch: animals carry them in their mouths
it.h: Blow on a dandelion puff.

it.q: Why do squirrels help oak trees spread?
ch: They bury acorns and forget some
it.h: What happens to an acorn a squirrel never digs up?

it.q: Design a model of a seed that sticks to animal fur. Tell what materials you would use and how you would test it.
it.ans: A pom-pom or bean covered with hook-and-loop tape or tape; test by rubbing it on fake fur or a sock and see if it sticks and carries.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Seeds and Pollinators
lessons.n: How do animals help plants make seeds?

it.q: The yellow dust inside a flower is
it.h: Bees get covered in it.

it.q: A bee visits one flower, then another. What does it carry between them?
it.h: Look at the bee's fuzzy legs.

it.q: Why is pollination important to plants?
ch: It helps them make seeds and fruit
it.h: What grows after a flower is pollinated?

it.q: Which animal is a pollinator?
it.h: Which animal visits flowers to drink nectar?

it.q: Why do bees visit flowers?
ch: to get nectar and pollen for food
it.h: Bees make honey from what they collect.

it.q: Design a model of a bee's body that could carry pollen. Tell what material you would use and why.
it.ans: A pipe cleaner or cotton swab, because its fuzzy surface picks up powder (pollen) and can drop some on the next flower.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Seeds and Pollinators
lessons.n: What do seeds need to sprout?

it.q: When a seed starts to grow, it
it.h: A tiny root and shoot come out.

it.q: Kids put bean seeds on a wet paper towel and on a dry paper towel. Which seeds sprouted?
it.h: Seeds need water to start growing.

it.q: Which part comes out of a sprouting bean seed first?
it.h: It grows down.

it.q: Seeds in a warm room and seeds in a refrigerator got the same water. The warm seeds sprouted first. What does this show?
it.h: Compare the two places.

it.q: Kids planted 10 seeds. 7 sprouted. How many did not sprout?
it.h: Take 7 away from 10.

it.q: Plan a test to see if seeds need water to sprout.
it.ans: Put the same kind and number of seeds in two cups with the same soil and place. Water one cup and not the other. Check which seeds sprout.
it.h: Change only one thing.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Seeds and Pollinators
lessons.n: How can we measure and record plant growth?

it.q: Which tool measures how tall a plant is?
it.h: It has centimeters marked on it.

it.q: Where should you start the ruler when you measure a plant?
ch: at the top of the soil
at the bottom of the pot
it.h: Measure the part of the plant you can see.

it.q: A chart shows a plant at 2 cm on Monday, 4 cm on Wednesday and 6 cm on Friday. What pattern do you see?
it.h: Compare each number to the one before.

it.q: A plant was 5 cm tall. Two weeks later it was 13 cm tall. How many centimeters did it grow?
it.h: Subtract 5 from 13.

it.q: Why do scientists measure on the same day each week?
ch: so the data can be compared fairly
it.h: Fair tests keep things the same.

it.q: Tell why it helps to record plant height in a chart instead of remembering it.
it.ans: A chart keeps the numbers so we can compare them and see how much the plant grew over time.
it.h: Can you remember every number for a month?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Habitats and the Variety of Life
lessons.n: What lives in different habitats?

it.q: A habitat is
ch: the place where a plant or animal lives
it.h: Think "home."

it.q: Which animal lives in a desert?
it.h: Which one runs across hot, dry land?

it.q: Which living things would you find in a tide pool?
ch: sea stars, crabs and sea anemones
it.h: Tide pools are rocky pools at the ocean's edge.

it.q: Which plant grows in a California desert?
it.h: Which plant can live with very little rain?

it.q: Which animal lives in a pond?
it.h: Which animal swims and also sits on lily pads?

it.q: Name a habitat and two living things that live there.
it.ans: Example: an ocean, with fish and kelp; a forest, with deer and oak trees; a desert, with cactus and lizards.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Habitats and the Variety of Life
lessons.n: Why do different habitats have different living things?

it.q: A cactus can live in the desert because it
it.h: Deserts get very little rain.

it.q: Why can't a fish live in a desert?
ch: It is too hot for sand
It has no legs to dig
it.h: How does a fish breathe?

it.q: Why do many different animals live in a rainforest?
ch: There is lots of water, warmth and plants for food and shelter
it.h: More food and shelter can support more kinds of life.

it.q: Polar bears have thick fur. Which habitat fits them?
it.h: Thick fur keeps animals warm.

it.q: Which habitat would likely have the fewest kinds of plants?
it.h: Which place is coldest and has the least liquid water?

it.q: Explain why a frog lives near a pond and not in a dry desert.
it.ans: A frog needs water to keep its skin wet and to lay eggs, and it eats insects found near water.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Habitats and the Variety of Life
lessons.n: How can we count and compare living things in habitats?

it.q: A tool for counting what you see with marks is a
it.h: You make a line for each thing you see.

it.q: In the schoolyard, students saw 5 ants, 3 beetles and 2 worms. How many animals did they see?
it.h: Add all three numbers.

it.q: A chart shows: garden 12 kinds, blacktop 2 kinds, field 7 kinds. Which place has the most variety?
it.h: Variety means how many different kinds.

it.q: Why do scientists count living things in the same size area in each habitat?
it.h: A bigger area could have more things just because it is bigger.

it.q: Which is the best way to look for small animals under a log without harming them?
ch: lift it gently, look, and put it back
it.h: Scientists respect living things.

it.q: Tell how you would compare the living things in a garden and on the blacktop.
it.ans: Mark off the same size square in each place, look carefully, record each kind of living thing in a tally chart and compare the totals.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Habitats and the Variety of Life
lessons.n: How do living things in a habitat depend on each other?

it.q: Rabbits eat plants. What would happen to rabbits if all the plants were gone?
it.h: What do rabbits eat?

it.q: A bird builds a nest in an oak tree. How does the bird depend on the tree?
it.h: Where is the nest?

it.q: Bees get food from flowers. How do flowers depend on bees?
ch: bees carry pollen so flowers make seeds
it.h: Think of pollen.

it.q: Owls eat mice in a field. If there were fewer mice, what might happen to the owls?
it.h: Follow the food.

it.q: Squirrels bury acorns and forget some. How does this help oak trees?
ch: some acorns grow into new trees
it.h: An acorn is a seed.

it.q: Name a plant and an animal in a habitat and tell how one depends on the other.
it.ans: Example: a deer eats grass in a meadow, so the deer depends on grass for food.
it.h: Think of food or shelter.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Habitats and the Variety of Life
lessons.n: What lives in and around a creek?

it.q: A creek is a small stream of
it.h: It moves downhill.

it.q: Which animal lives in a creek?
it.h: It has claws and lives under rocks in water.

it.q: Dragonflies lay eggs in water. Where would you look for young dragonflies?
it.h: Where were the eggs laid?

it.q: Willow trees grow along creeks. Why?
ch: their roots get lots of water there
it.h: What is close by in a creek?

it.q: Which plant grows in the wet mud at the edge of a creek?
it.h: It has a fuzzy brown top.

it.q: Name two living things you might find at a creek and tell how the creek helps them.
it.ans: Frogs and crayfish; the creek gives them water, food like insects and places to hide under rocks.
it.h: Think of water, food and shelter.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: Which Earth changes happen fast and which happen slowly?

it.q: Which Earth event happens in just minutes?
ch: a river slowly changing its path
it.h: Which one can shake the ground all at once?

it.q: Which change takes a very long time?
it.h: Canyons are very deep. How long would it take water to carve that much rock?

it.q: Hot melted rock pours out of a mountain and cools into new land. What is this?
it.h: Think of lava.

it.q: A hillside slides down in one afternoon after heavy rain. This is
ch: a fast change called a landslide
a slow change called a canyon
it.h: It happened in one afternoon.

it.q: Sharp rocks on a mountain become smooth pebbles in a stream over many years. This change is
it.h: Many years means slow.

it.q: Name one Earth change that happens fast and one that happens slowly.
it.ans: Fast: earthquake, volcanic eruption, landslide or flood. Slow: a canyon being carved, rocks wearing down, a mountain wearing away.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: How do wind and water change the shape of the land?

it.q: When wind or water carries away soil and rock, it is called
it.h: The word starts with "e."

it.q: Water was poured on a sand hill in a tray. What happened to the sand?
ch: It washed down and made little channels
it.h: Moving water carries sand with it.

it.q: Strong wind blows across a dry desert. What can it move?
it.h: Have you seen sand blow at the beach?

it.q: Why does a river get muddy after a big storm?
ch: Rain washed soil into the river
it.h: Where did the soil come from?

it.q: Which land would erode fastest in a heavy rain?
ch: bare dirt on a steep hill
a flat lawn with thick grass
a rocky floor in a cave
a parking lot under a roof
it.h: Plant roots hold soil. Steep slopes make water run fast.

it.q: Describe what happened to our sand hill when we poured water on it.
it.ans: The water ran down the hill and carried sand to the bottom, making grooves and a pile of sand at the base.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: How can we protect land from wind and water?

it.q: Rows of trees planted to slow the wind are called
it.h: They "break" the wind.

it.q: Which helps keep a hillside from washing away?
it.h: What holds soil in place?

it.q: A house is near a river that floods. Which solution helps?
ch: building a wall of sandbags or a levee
it.h: What could block water?

it.q: Big rocks are placed along a beach cliff. Why?
ch: to take the force of waves so the cliff wears away slower
it.h: What will the waves hit first?

it.q: A fence of wooden slats is put on a beach. What does it do?
ch: slows the wind and catches blowing sand
it.h: Where does sand pile up when wind slows down?

it.q: Design a way to keep soil on a garden hill from washing away in rain. Tell how it works.
it.ans: Plant grass or shrubs whose roots hold soil, or build small steps (terraces) or a low wall that slows the water.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: How do people stay safe during earthquakes and floods?

it.q: In an earthquake, you should drop, cover and
it.h: Hold on to the table leg.

it.q: Where is a safe place to cover in a classroom earthquake?
ch: in the doorway of the hall
it.h: Something strong over your head.

it.q: Flood water is moving over a road. What should a family do?
ch: turn around and find another way
it.h: Moving water can sweep people and cars away.

it.q: Why do people tie tall bookshelves to the wall in California?
ch: so they do not fall in an earthquake
it.h: Earthquakes shake the ground fast.

it.q: A family packs water, food, a flashlight and a first aid kit. What is this?
it.h: It is ready for a disaster.

it.q: Tell what you do during an earthquake drill.
it.ans: Drop to the floor, cover my head under a sturdy desk, and hold on until the shaking stops.
it.h: Three words.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: How do ice, water and roots break rocks apart?

it.q: Breaking rock into smaller pieces is called
it.h: It starts with the word "weather."

it.q: Water gets into a crack in a rock and freezes. What happens?
ch: the ice pushes the crack wider
it.h: Water takes up more space when it freezes.

it.q: A tree root grows into a crack in a sidewalk. What can happen?
it.h: Growing roots push.

it.q: Rocks in a fast river bump into each other for many years. They become
it.h: Think of river pebbles.

it.q: Does weathering happen fast or slowly?
it.h: Old stone buildings show small changes over many years.

it.q: Tell how freezing water can break a rock.
it.ans: Water fills a crack, freezes into ice and gets bigger, pushing the crack wider. Over many freezes, the rock breaks apart.
it.h: Think about ice in a full bottle.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth Changes, Fast and Slow
lessons.n: How do volcanoes build new land?

it.q: Melted rock that comes out of a volcano is called
it.h: It is red-hot and glowing.

it.q: When lava cools, it becomes
it.h: Cool melted rock gets hard.

it.q: The islands of Hawaii were made by
it.h: Lava piled up from the ocean floor.

it.q: A volcano erupts and lava flows into the ocean. What can happen to the coast?
it.h: The lava cools into rock at the shore.

it.q: Can a volcano change the land in one day?
it.h: Lava can cover land in hours.

it.q: Tell how lava can make an island bigger.
it.ans: Lava flows to the edge of the island, cools and hardens into new rock, so the island grows.
it.h: What happens when lava cools?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
lessons.n: What shapes of land are on Earth?

it.q: A very tall, steep landform is a
it.h: Mount Whitney in California is one.

it.q: Low land between hills or mountains is a
it.h: Think of a "V" shape between two hills.

it.q: Land with water all around it is an
it.h: Catalina Island is off the coast of California.

it.q: Wide, flat land good for farming is a
it.h: California's Central Valley has very flat farmland.

it.q: Which is a body of water, not a landform?
it.h: Landforms are shapes of land. Which one is water?

it.q: Name two landforms and tell how they are different.
it.ans: A mountain is very tall and steep; a plain is flat and low.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
lessons.n: How can maps and models show land and water?

it.q: On most maps, water is shown with the color
it.h: Think of the color of a lake on a map.

it.q: The part of a map that tells what the symbols and colors mean is the
it.h: It "unlocks" the map.

it.q: A model is
ch: a small copy that shows how something looks or works
it.h: A toy globe is a model of Earth.

it.q: On a map key, a triangle means mountain. You see three triangles in a row. What do they show?
it.h: Look back at what one triangle means.

it.q: Which shows the whole Earth's land and water as a round model?
it.h: It spins on a stand.

it.q: Tell how a map key helps you read a map.
it.ans: The key tells what each color and symbol stands for, such as blue for water and triangles for mountains.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
lessons.n: Where is water found on Earth?

it.q: Where is most of Earth's water?
it.h: Look at how much blue is on a globe.

it.q: Ocean water is
it.h: Have you tasted seawater at the beach?

it.q: Water can be found on Earth as a solid. Where?
it.h: Solid water is ice.

it.q: Which is a body of fresh water?
it.h: Fresh water is not salty.

it.q: Snow on the Sierra Nevada melts in spring. Where does the water go?
it.h: Melted snow flows downhill.

it.q: Name two places water is found as a liquid and one place it is found as a solid.
it.ans: Liquid: oceans, rivers, lakes, ponds. Solid: glaciers, polar ice, snow on mountains.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
lessons.n: Where do rivers start and where do they go?

it.q: Water in a river flows
it.h: Water always runs down a slope.

it.q: Many rivers start high in the
it.h: Rain and melting snow fall there.

it.q: Where do many rivers end?
ch: in a lake or the ocean
in a cave in the sky
it.h: Follow the water down.

it.q: Snow melts on the Sierra Nevada in spring. What happens to the rivers below?
it.h: Melted snow is water.

it.q: On a map, a river is a
it.h: Water is often blue on maps.

it.q: Tell the path a raindrop might take from a mountain to the ocean.
it.ans: It falls on the mountain, runs into a stream, then a bigger river, and the river flows downhill to the ocean.
it.h: Start high and go low.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Land and Water on Earth
lessons.n: How do we use a compass rose and directions on a map?

it.q: The symbol that shows north, south, east and west on a map is a
it.h: It looks like a star with letters.

it.q: On most maps, north is at the
it.h: Look for the N.

it.q: On a map, the ocean is on the left side and north is at the top. Which way is the ocean?
it.h: Left is west when north is up.

it.q: A park is above the school on a map with north at the top. Which way is the park from the school?
it.h: Up is north.

it.q: Which helps you find how far apart two places are on a map?
it.h: It shows what one inch stands for.

it.q: Tell how to use a compass rose to find which direction a lake is from a town on a map.
it.ans: Find the town and the lake, look at the compass rose, and see whether the lake is toward N, S, E or W from the town.
it.h: Start at the town.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: How can we predict what the weather will be like?

it.q: Which tool measures how hot or cold the air is?
it.h: Think about which tool has a scale with degrees on it.

it.q: Which tool shows which direction the wind is blowing from?
it.h: This tool turns to point into the wind.

it.q: A class recorded the high temperature for 3 days: Monday 64°F, Tuesday 70°F, Wednesday 67°F. How many degrees warmer was Tuesday than Monday?
it.h: Subtract the smaller temperature from the larger one.

it.q: For 5 days in a row, clouds got thicker and darker each afternoon and then it rained. On day 6 the afternoon clouds are thick and dark again. What is the best prediction?
ch: It will snow for a week.
The sky will be clear all night.
The temperature will drop below freezing.
it.h: Look for a pattern that repeated before.

it.q: Which observation is about weather and not climate?
ch: It is windy and 58°F this morning.
Summers here are usually hot and dry.
This city gets about 15 inches of rain a year.
it.h: Weather is what is happening at one time and place.

it.q: Name two kinds of weather data a weather reporter collects. Tell what tool measures each one.
it.ans: Temperature, measured with a thermometer, and rainfall, measured with a rain gauge. (Wind direction with a wind vane or wind speed with an anemometer also count.)
it.h: Think about what you hear on a weather report.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: Why is it rainier in some seasons than others?

it.q: A table shows rainfall in Sacramento: January 4 inches, April 1 inch, July 0 inches, October 1 inch. Which season is the rainiest?
it.h: Find the month with the most inches, then name its season.

it.q: Using the same table (January 4 inches, April 1 inch, July 0 inches, October 1 inch), how many inches of rain fell in the four months altogether?
it.h: Add all four numbers.

it.q: Which kind of graph is best for comparing the rainfall in each month of the year?
ch: a bar graph with one bar for each month
a list of the days of the week
it.h: You want to compare amounts side by side.

it.q: In most of California, which season usually has the hottest temperatures?
it.h: Think about when school is out and days are longest.

it.q: The average high temperature in a town is 88°F in July and 55°F in January. How many degrees warmer is July?
it.h: Subtract 55 from 88.

it.q: A bar graph shows snowfall in a mountain town for each month. The bars are tall from December to March and zero from June to September. Describe the seasonal pattern.
it.ans: The town gets most of its snow in winter, from December to March. It gets no snow in summer, from June to September.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: Why are some places hot and others cold all year?

it.q: What is climate?
ch: the usual weather of a place over many years
it.h: Climate is about a long time, not one day.

it.q: Which place has a climate that is hot and very dry most of the year?
it.h: Which place gets very little rain?

it.q: A region is warm all year and gets rain almost every day. What kind of climate does it have?
it.h: Think about where it is both hot and wet.

it.q: Places near the poles, like northern Alaska, have cold climates. Which is true about these places?
ch: They are cold for most of the year.
They have no seasons at all.
They get the same weather as a desert.
it.h: Remember where the polar bears live.

it.q: City A gets 60 inches of rain a year. City B gets 8 inches a year. How many more inches does City A get?
it.h: Subtract to compare.

it.q: Describe the climate where you live. Use the words temperature and rain in your answer.
it.ans: Sample: Where I live, summers are hot and dry, and winters are cool with some rain. The temperature is warm most of the year.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: How do clouds help us read the weather?

it.q: Clouds are made of
ch: tiny drops of water or bits of ice
it.h: Clouds form when water vapor in the air cools.

it.q: Puffy white clouds with flat bottoms on a sunny afternoon are called cumulus clouds. What weather do they usually mean?
it.h: These are the "cotton ball" clouds of a nice day.

it.q: Very tall, dark clouds that tower high into the sky can bring
it.h: Thunder and lightning come from these giant clouds.

it.q: A flat gray layer of cloud covers the whole sky. Which weather is most likely?
it.h: Layer clouds are called stratus.

it.q: Thin, wispy clouds very high in the sky are called cirrus. What are they made of?
it.h: It is very cold high up in the sky.

it.q: Tell how watching the clouds can help you plan an afternoon picnic.
it.ans: If the clouds are small, puffy and white, the weather will probably stay nice. If tall, dark clouds are building, a storm may come, so plan to be indoors.
it.h: Think about which clouds bring storms.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: How do oceans and mountains shape a place's climate?

it.q: Places close to the ocean usually have
it.h: Ocean water warms up and cools down slowly.

it.q: A table shows July average highs: San Francisco 68°F, Sacramento 92°F. Which statement fits the data?
ch: The city by the ocean has cooler summers.
The inland city has cooler summers.
it.h: Compare the two numbers.

it.q: San Francisco's July average high is 68°F and Sacramento's is 92°F. How many degrees warmer is Sacramento?
it.h: Subtract 68 from 92.

it.q: Wet air from the ocean blows toward a tall mountain range. Which side of the mountains usually gets more rain?
it.h: The air drops much of its rain as it rises up the first side.

it.q: Why are mountain tops usually colder than valleys nearby?
ch: they are closer to the Sun
it.h: Think of snow on peaks in spring.

it.q: Explain why a beach town and a town 100 miles inland can have very different summer temperatures.
it.ans: The ocean warms and cools slowly, so it keeps the beach town cooler in summer. The inland town is far from the ocean, so it heats up more.
it.h: What is next to the beach town?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Weather Patterns and Climates
lessons.n: How do weather maps and symbols show a forecast?

it.q: On a weather map, a picture of a cloud with raindrops means
it.h: Look at what is falling from the cloud.

it.q: A weather map shows 85 next to Fresno and 64 next to San Diego. What do the numbers most likely show?
it.h: Which numbers make sense for a day's temperature?

it.q: The map shows Fresno at 85°F and San Diego at 64°F. How many degrees cooler is San Diego?
it.h: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

it.q: Why does a weather map have a key?
ch: to explain what the symbols and colors mean
it.h: Maps of all kinds use keys.

it.q: A 5-day forecast shows sun, sun, clouds, rain, rain. Which day is best for an outdoor field trip?
it.h: Look for the sunny symbols.

it.q: Design three simple symbols for a class weather map and tell what each means.
it.ans: Sample: a yellow circle for sunny, a cloud with lines for rain, and a cloud with swirls for windy.
it.h: Symbols should be easy to read quickly.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: What makes some kinds of weather dangerous?

it.q: Which is a weather-related hazard?
it.h: A hazard is something that can hurt people or damage things.

it.q: Heavy rain falls for three days on a town next to a river. Which hazard is most likely?
it.h: Where does all that rain water go?

it.q: A drought is a long time with
it.h: Think about what plants and farms would be missing.

it.q: Dry plants, hot temperatures and strong winds together make which hazard more likely in California?
it.h: Which hazard needs dry fuel to burn?

it.q: A town recorded 4 floods in the 1990s, 2 in the 2000s and 5 in the 2010s. How many floods is that in all?
it.h: Add the three numbers.

it.q: Choose one weather hazard. Describe one way it can harm people, animals or buildings.
it.ans: Sample: A hurricane brings very strong winds that can tear roofs off houses and knock down trees and power lines.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: How can we protect a home from floods and strong winds?

it.q: A house is built on tall posts near a river. What hazard does this design protect against?
it.h: Think about where water goes when the river rises.

it.q: What is the purpose of a levee, a high wall of earth along a river?
ch: to keep river water from spreading onto the land
to make the river flow faster uphill
to give fish a place to live
it.h: A levee is like a long, tall wall next to the water.

it.q: Which design helps a roof stay on a house during strong winds?
ch: metal straps that tie the roof to the walls
a roof painted a bright color
it.h: The roof needs to be held down tightly.

it.q: Which design reduces the danger of lightning hitting a tall building?
ch: a lightning rod connected to the ground
a fence around the parking lot
it.h: Lightning needs a safe path to the ground.

it.q: A town stacks sandbags along a river. Team A fills 45 bags and Team B fills 38 bags. How many sandbags do they fill in all?
it.h: Add the two teams' bags.

it.q: Describe one design that reduces damage from wildfire to a home.
it.ans: Sample: Clearing dry brush and dead plants away from the house so a fire has less fuel near the walls.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: How do engineers choose the best solution?

it.q: In engineering, criteria are
ch: the things a design must do to be successful
the limits on materials, time or money
the last step of a test
the people who use a design
it.h: Criteria answer "What counts as success?"

it.q: Which is a constraint?
ch: The design can cost no more than $20.
The design must keep water out.
it.h: A constraint is a limit.

it.q: A class must build a model shelter that stays dry in a rainstorm, using only paper, tape and foil. Which is a constraint?
ch: They can use only paper, tape and foil.
It must hold one toy figure.
It must survive the rainstorm test.
it.h: Which one limits what they can use?

it.q: Foil costs 3 cents per sheet. A team uses 8 sheets. How many cents do they spend on foil?
it.h: Multiply cost per sheet by number of sheets.

it.q: Why do engineers come up with several possible solutions before building one?
ch: so they can compare ideas and pick the one most likely to meet the criteria
because the first idea is always wrong
so they can use every material
so they do not have to test
it.h: Think about how having choices helps.

it.q: Your class must design a way to keep the school garden from drying out during a drought. Write one criterion and one constraint for the problem.
it.ans: Criterion: the plants must get enough water to stay alive. Constraint: we can only use water from the rain barrels, or we only have $30 to spend.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: How do engineers test and improve a design?

it.q: In a fair test, an engineer changes
ch: only one thing at a time
it.h: If you change many things, you cannot tell which one caused the result.

it.q: A team tests two model roofs in a wind test. To be fair, which must be the same for both roofs?
ch: the strength of the fan and the distance from the fan
it.h: Keep the test conditions the same so only the design is different.

it.q: A model house leaks water at the corners during a rain test. What should the team do next?
ch: find the failure point at the corners and improve that part
test a different house without fixing it
it.h: Look closely at where it failed.

it.q: A model shelter stayed dry for 4 minutes in the first test. After improvements it stayed dry for 11 minutes. How many minutes longer did it stay dry?
it.h: Subtract the first time from the second time.

it.q: Why do engineers test a design more than once?
ch: to make sure the results are reliable
it.h: What if the first test had a mistake?

it.q: Explain what a failure point is and why it helps engineers.
it.ans: A failure point is the part of a design that breaks or does not work during a test. Finding it shows engineers exactly what to improve.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: How can people stay safe from lightning?

it.q: Lightning is
ch: a giant electric spark in a storm
it.h: It is static electricity on a huge scale.

it.q: Why is standing under a lone tall tree dangerous in a thunderstorm?
it.h: Lightning usually hits the tallest thing around.

it.q: Which place is safest during a thunderstorm?
ch: inside a building with plumbing and wiring
under a picnic shelter with no walls
it.h: Find an enclosed building.

it.q: A lightning rod on a roof is connected by a thick wire to the ground. What does the wire do?
ch: carries the lightning safely into the ground
it.h: Follow the path from the rod to the ground.

it.q: Safety experts say to wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside. Why?
ch: lightning can still strike after the storm seems to pass
it takes 30 minutes to see the Sun
it.h: Storms can still be close when they seem over.

it.q: Describe what a family at the park should do when they hear thunder.
it.ans: Go into a building or a hard-topped car right away, stay away from trees and open fields, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going out.
it.h: When thunder roars, go indoors.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Weather Hazards and Engineering Solutions
lessons.n: How can towns design for extreme heat?

it.q: A heat wave is
ch: a period of very hot days
it.h: The word "heat" is a clue.

it.q: Why do many towns plant shade trees along streets?
ch: to make streets darker at night
it.h: Shade blocks sunlight.

it.q: A class put thermometers on a black roof sample and a white roof sample in the Sun. Black: 140°F. White: 95°F. Which conclusion fits?
ch: light-colored roofs stay cooler in sunlight
it.h: Compare the two temperatures.

it.q: The black roof sample was 140°F and the white sample was 95°F. How many degrees cooler was the white sample?
it.h: Subtract 95 from 140.

it.q: A town opens a library with air conditioning to anyone during heat waves. What is this called?
it.h: It is a place to cool off.

it.q: Name two ways a school could keep students safer on very hot days.
it.ans: Add shade structures or trees, give water breaks, move recess indoors during the hottest hours, or paint surfaces a light color.
it.h: Think of shade, water and timing.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: What makes an object start or stop moving?

it.q: A push or a pull is called a
it.h: It is the word scientists use for any push or pull.

it.q: A ball is sitting still on the grass. What is needed to make it move?
it.h: Objects at rest need a push or pull to start moving.

it.q: A wagon is rolling across the playground. Which force will make it stop?
ch: a pull or push in the opposite direction, like friction from the ground
a push in the same direction
it.h: To stop something, the force must act against the motion.

it.q: Which action is a pull?
it.h: A pull moves something toward you.

it.q: Ana pushes a toy car and it rolls 85 centimeters. Then she pushes it harder and it rolls 140 centimeters. How many centimeters farther did it roll after the harder push?
it.h: Subtract the shorter distance from the longer one.

it.q: Describe what happens to a soccer ball's motion when a player kicks it, and then when the goalie catches it.
it.ans: The kick is a force that makes the ball start moving. When the goalie catches it, the goalie's hands push against the ball and make it stop.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: What happens when forces are balanced or unbalanced?

it.q: When two forces are the same size and push in opposite directions, the forces are
it.h: Think of a tug of war where no one moves.

it.q: In a tug of war, Team Red pulls left with a force of 200 newtons and Team Blue pulls right with a force of 200 newtons. What happens to the rope?
it.h: Compare the two forces.

it.q: Team Red now pulls left with 250 newtons and Team Blue still pulls right with 200 newtons. Which way does the rope move?
it.h: The rope moves toward the bigger force.

it.q: Using the same tug of war (Team Red pulls 250 newtons, Team Blue pulls 200 newtons), how many newtons more does Team Red pull?
it.h: Find the difference between the two forces.

it.q: A book is resting on a table. Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up. What is true about these forces?
ch: They are balanced, so the book stays still.
They are unbalanced, so the book moves.
There are no forces on the book.
it.h: The book is not moving. What does that tell you?

it.q: Draw or describe a force diagram for a box that two children push from opposite sides, where one child pushes harder. Tell which way the box moves.
it.ans: Two arrows pointing toward each other from opposite sides of the box; the arrow for the harder push is longer. The box moves in the direction of the longer arrow, away from the child who pushes harder.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: How can we predict motion that repeats?

it.q: Which motion repeats in a pattern?
ch: a child swinging back and forth on a swing
a rock sitting on the ground
a leaf landing once on the grass
a ball resting in a box
it.h: Look for something that keeps going back and forth.

it.q: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string that swings back and forth. A class counts its swings: 10 swings in the first 10 seconds and 10 swings in the next 10 seconds. How many swings should it make in the next 10 seconds?
it.h: Use the pattern the class already saw.

it.q: A pendulum makes 12 swings every 10 seconds. How many swings will it make in 30 seconds?
it.h: 30 seconds is three groups of 10 seconds.

it.q: A ball is dropped and bounces. Each bounce is lower than the one before. Which prediction fits the pattern?
ch: The next bounce will be lower again.
The next bounce will be higher.
The ball will bounce forever at the same height.
it.h: What happened each time it bounced?

it.q: A seesaw goes up and down when two children take turns pushing off the ground. Why can you predict when one side will go up?
ch: The motion repeats in a regular pattern.
There is no force on it.
it.h: Think about what happens over and over.

it.q: A student times a swing. It goes forward and back 4 times every 10 seconds. Explain how the student can use this pattern to predict the number of swings in 20 seconds.
it.ans: The pattern shows 4 swings every 10 seconds. 20 seconds is two 10-second groups, so it should make about 4 + 4 = 8 swings.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: How does friction slow things down?

it.q: The force that acts when two surfaces rub against each other is
it.h: It is why a sliding book slows down.

it.q: Which surface has the most friction for a sliding block?
it.h: Rough surfaces grab more.

it.q: Why do people put sand on icy sidewalks?
ch: to add friction so people do not slip
it.h: Sand makes the surface rough.

it.q: Rubbing your hands together quickly makes them
it.h: Friction makes heat.

it.q: A block slid 12 cm on carpet and 47 cm on tile with the same push. How many more centimeters did it slide on tile?
it.h: Subtract 12 from 47.

it.q: Give one example where friction is helpful and one where people try to reduce friction.
it.ans: Helpful: shoe soles grip the ground so we do not slip. Reduced: oil on bike chains or wheels on a skateboard so things move easily.
it.h: Think of shoes and wheels.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: How does gravity pull things toward Earth?

it.q: The force that pulls objects down toward Earth is
it.h: It is why a dropped ball falls.

it.q: A ball is thrown straight up. Why does it come back down?
it.h: What force always pulls down?

it.q: A book rests on a desk and does not fall. Which is true?
ch: the desk pushes up as hard as gravity pulls down
there is no gravity on the book
it.h: Balanced forces mean no change in motion.

it.q: Water flows down a hill because of
it.h: Water flows from high places to low places.

it.q: Which way does gravity pull on people in California and in Australia?
it.h: Everyone on Earth is pulled toward the same center.

it.q: Describe what forces act on a skydiver after jumping from a plane.
it.ans: Gravity pulls the skydiver down. Air pushes up against the skydiver, and a parachute makes that air push much bigger so the skydiver falls slowly.
it.h: Think of one force down and one force up.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: How does an object's mass change how a push moves it?

it.q: Which needs a bigger push to start moving?
it.h: More stuff to move means more force needed.

it.q: The same push is given to a bowling ball and a soccer ball. Which rolls farther?
it.h: The soccer ball has less mass.

it.q: A class pushed a cart holding 1, 2 and 3 books with the same push. Distances: 90 cm, 60 cm, 35 cm. What pattern do you see?
it.h: Look at how the distance changes as books are added.

it.q: The cart with 1 book rolled 90 cm and with 3 books rolled 35 cm. How many centimeters farther did the 1-book cart roll?
it.h: Subtract 35 from 90.

it.q: Why is it harder to stop a heavy shopping cart than an empty one?
ch: it has more mass, so it needs more force to change its motion
it.h: Starting and stopping both need force.

it.q: Plan a test to find out whether mass changes how far a cart rolls after a push.
it.ans: Use the same cart, ramp or push each time, and change only the number of washers or books in the cart. Measure how far it rolls each time and compare.
it.h: Change only one thing.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
lessons.n: How do forces change motion in sports?

it.q: A batter hits a baseball. What does the bat give the ball?
it.h: The bat pushes the ball away.

it.q: A soccer goalie catches a fast ball. What does the goalie's force do?
it.h: The goalie's hands push against the ball's motion.

it.q: A basketball player bounces the ball. The floor pushes the ball
it.h: The ball comes back to the player's hand.

it.q: A tennis ball hits a racket and goes back the other way. What changed?
it.h: A force can change the way something moves.

it.q: In a tug of war, the rope moves toward Team A. Which is true?
ch: Team A pulls with more force
Team B pulls with more force
it.h: Unbalanced forces move the rope toward the stronger pull.

it.q: Describe two ways a force changes the motion of a ball in a soccer game.
it.ans: A kick starts the ball moving or makes it go faster, and a header or a block changes its direction or stops it.
it.h: Think about starting, stopping and turning.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: How can a magnet move something without touching it?

it.q: Which object will a magnet attract?
it.h: Magnets attract objects that contain iron, like steel.

it.q: A magnet pulls a paper clip toward it before they touch. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force can act without touching.
The paper clip is pushing itself.
it.h: Notice that there was a gap between them.

it.q: A student puts a sheet of paper between a magnet and a paper clip. The clip still moves toward the magnet. What can the student conclude?
ch: Magnetic force can pass through paper.
The paper clip is made of paper.
it.h: What happened even with the paper in the way?

it.q: Which is the best question to test with a magnet and a pile of objects?
ch: Which materials does a magnet attract?
it.h: A good science question can be answered by testing.

it.q: A class tested 12 objects. The magnet attracted 5 of them. How many objects were not attracted?
it.h: Subtract the attracted objects from the total.

it.q: Name two objects in your classroom a magnet would attract and two it would not. Tell what the attracted objects have in common.
it.ans: Attracted: a steel paper clip and a steel staple. Not attracted: a plastic ruler and a wooden pencil. The attracted objects contain iron or steel.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: Why do magnets sometimes push each other away?

it.q: The two ends of a bar magnet are called
it.h: They are labeled N and S.

it.q: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet?
it.h: Opposite poles behave differently from like poles.

it.q: What happens when two north poles are brought close together?
it.h: Poles that are the same push apart.

it.q: A magnet holds a paper clip when they are 1 cm apart but not when they are 5 cm apart. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force gets weaker as distance increases.
Magnetic force gets stronger with distance.
it.h: Compare what happened at the short and long distances.

it.q: A magnet attracted a paper clip from 4 cm away. A stronger magnet attracted it from 11 cm away. How many centimeters farther away did the stronger magnet work?
it.h: Subtract the distances.

it.q: Two ring magnets on a pencil float apart instead of touching. Explain why.
it.ans: The magnets are placed with the same poles facing each other, so they repel and push each other apart even though they are not touching.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: What makes a balloon stick to a wall?

it.q: When you rub a balloon on your hair, the balloon gets
it.h: This is called static electricity.

it.q: After a balloon is rubbed on hair, the hair stands up and moves toward the balloon. What does this show?
ch: Electric charges can attract without touching.
The hair is made of iron.
it.h: Was the balloon touching the hair when the hair moved?

it.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on a wool sweater. When they hang near each other, they push apart. Why?
ch: They have the same kind of charge, so they repel.
They have opposite charges, so they attract.
it.h: Like charges act like like poles.

it.q: Which is an example of static electricity?
ch: a shock when you touch a doorknob after walking on carpet
a ball rolling down a hill
it.h: Think of a tiny spark or a zap.

it.q: A charged balloon picked up 14 tiny bits of paper. After 5 minutes it could only pick up 6 bits. How many fewer bits did it pick up?
it.h: Subtract to compare.

it.q: How are static electricity and magnetism alike?
it.ans: Both can push or pull objects without touching them, and both can attract and repel.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: How can we use magnets to solve a problem?

it.q: Which everyday object uses a magnet to stay closed?
it.h: Think of a kitchen door that seals by itself.

it.q: A recycling center needs to separate steel cans from aluminum cans. Which design idea uses magnets?
ch: Pass the cans under a big magnet that lifts out the steel cans.
it.h: Which cans does a magnet attract?

it.q: A class wants to design a latch that keeps a cabinet door closed. Which is a criterion?
ch: The door must stay shut when a small child pulls gently.
It must be finished by Friday.
Only magnets and tape can be used.
it.h: A criterion tells what the design must do.

it.q: A magnet latch costs $4. The class needs latches for 6 cabinets. How many dollars will the latches cost?
it.h: Multiply the cost by the number of cabinets.

it.q: A student designs a game where a paper fish with a steel paper clip is picked up by a magnet on a string. Why does the game work?
ch: The magnet attracts the steel clip.
it.h: Which part of the fish does a magnet attract?

it.q: Describe a problem at home or school that a magnet could help solve, and explain how.
it.ans: Sample: Pins fall on the floor in the art room. A magnet on a stick could pick up the steel pins quickly without anyone touching the sharp points.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: How is lightning like a giant static spark?

it.q: A small shock from a doorknob after walking on carpet is caused by
it.h: Electric charges built up on your body.

it.q: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice and water bump into each other. What builds up?
it.h: Rubbing and bumping can separate charges, like rubbing a balloon.

it.q: How is lightning like a static shock from a doorknob?
ch: both are sparks from built-up electric charge
it.h: Both happen when charge jumps across a gap.

it.q: Why do we hear thunder after lightning?
ch: lightning heats the air so fast it makes a loud boom
it.h: Very fast heating makes air expand suddenly.

it.q: You see lightning and then hear thunder a few seconds later. Why does the sound come later?
ch: light travels much faster than sound
it.h: Light reaches you almost instantly.

it.q: Explain one way a static shock from a doorknob and a lightning strike are alike and one way they are different.
it.ans: Alike: both are sparks that happen when built-up electric charge jumps across a gap. Different: lightning is huge, powerful and dangerous, while a doorknob shock is tiny.
it.h: Think about size and danger.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: How does electricity make an electromagnet?

it.q: An electromagnet is made by wrapping wire around an iron nail and
ch: connecting the wire to a battery
it.h: It needs electric current to work.

it.q: What happens to an electromagnet when the battery is disconnected?
ch: it stops attracting most of the paper clips
it.h: No current, no magnet.

it.q: A class wrapped 10, 20 and 30 turns of wire around the same nail with the same battery. It picked up 4, 9 and 15 clips. What pattern does the data show?
ch: more turns picked up more clips
more turns picked up fewer clips
it.h: Compare turns with clips.

it.q: With 10 turns the electromagnet held 4 clips and with 30 turns it held 15. How many more clips did 30 turns hold?
it.h: Subtract 4 from 15.

it.q: Why are electromagnets useful in a scrap yard crane?
ch: they can be turned on to lift steel and off to drop it
it.h: Think about letting go of the load.

it.q: Name one way an electromagnet is different from a fridge magnet.
it.ans: An electromagnet works only when electric current flows, so it can be turned on and off; a fridge magnet is always magnetic.
it.h: Can you switch a fridge magnet off?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
lessons.n: How does a compass use magnetism to find north?

it.q: The needle of a compass is a
it.h: It turns because of magnetic force.

it.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
ch: Earth acts like a giant magnet
it is heavier on one end
it.h: Earth has magnetic poles too.

it.q: A student brings a bar magnet near a compass. What happens?
ch: the needle turns toward or away from the magnet
it.h: The magnet's force acts on the magnetic needle.

it.q: Hikers use a compass in a forest. Why?
ch: to find direction when they cannot see landmarks
it.h: A compass shows north.

it.q: A hiker walks 350 meters north and then 275 meters more north. How many meters north did the hiker walk in all?
it.h: Add the two distances.

it.q: Explain why you should keep a compass away from magnets when using it to find north.
it.ans: A nearby magnet pulls on the compass needle and makes it point the wrong way, so the hiker could get lost.
it.h: What force moves the needle?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: Do all living things have the same life cycle?

it.q: Which shows the stages of a butterfly's life cycle in order?
it.h: Start with the stage that hatches.

it.q: What do all life cycles have in common?
it.h: Think about what happens to every living thing.

it.q: A young frog that lives in water and breathes with gills is called a
it.h: This stage has a tail and no legs at first.

it.q: Which is a stage in the life cycle of a bean plant?
it.h: Which word describes a young plant that just sprouted?

it.q: A monarch egg hatched after 4 days. The caterpillar ate and grew for 14 days. Then it was a chrysalis for 10 days. How many days passed from egg to adult?
it.h: Add all three stages.

it.q: Draw or describe a model of a plant's life cycle. Label at least four stages.
it.ans: A circle with arrows: seed, seedling (sprout), adult plant, flower, fruit with new seeds, and back to seed.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: Why do offspring look like their parents?

it.q: A trait passed from parents to offspring is called
it.h: "Inherit" means to get something from your parents.

it.q: Which is an inherited trait in a dog?
ch: knowing how to sit on command
it.h: Which one was the dog born with?

it.q: Two black cats have a litter of kittens. Some kittens are black and one is gray. What does this show?
ch: Offspring can vary even though they inherit traits from their parents.
Kittens never look like their parents.
it.h: Variation means differences among members of a group.

it.q: A litter of 7 puppies has 4 puppies with spots. How many puppies do not have spots?
it.h: Subtract the spotted puppies from the total.

it.q: Which trait of a sunflower is inherited from the parent plants?
ch: a broken stem from the wind
a tag a gardener tied on it
a bite taken by a rabbit
it.h: Which trait comes from the plant's parents and not from something that happened to it?

it.q: Describe two traits you could observe to show that a baby rabbit is related to its parents.
it.ans: Sample: The shape of its long ears and the color of its fur are similar to its parents' traits.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: Can the environment change an organism's traits?

it.q: Two plants grew from seeds of the same parent. One grew in a sunny window and is tall and green. One grew in a dark closet and is short and pale. What caused the difference?
ch: the environment, because of the amount of light
it.h: The seeds came from the same parent. What was different?

it.q: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the food they eat. A flamingo in a zoo is given food without these pigments. What will most likely happen?
ch: Its new feathers will be paler.
it.h: The color comes from the food.

it.q: Which trait is caused by the environment?
ch: strong arm muscles from swimming every day
the shape of a person's nose
it.h: Which one changed because of something the person did?

it.q: A plant in rich soil grew 32 cm. A plant from the same seed packet in poor soil grew 19 cm. How many centimeters taller was the plant in rich soil?
it.h: Subtract the heights.

it.q: A dog inherits a body built for running fast. Its owner never lets it exercise, so it becomes slow and out of shape. What does this show?
ch: Traits can be affected by both inheritance and the environment.
Running speed has nothing to do with the body.
The dog did not inherit any traits.
Exercise changes a dog's fur color.
it.h: Think about what the dog was born with and what happened to it.

it.q: Give one example of a trait in a plant that can be changed by the environment, and explain how.
it.ans: Sample: A plant's height can change. If it gets less water or light than it needs, it grows shorter than it would in good conditions.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: How do flowering plants make new seeds?

it.q: Which plant part makes seeds?
it.h: After a flower fades, a fruit often forms.

it.q: Moving pollen from one flower to another is called
it.h: Bees and hummingbirds help with this.

it.q: After a flower is pollinated, what grows to hold the seeds?
it.h: Think of an apple or a tomato.

it.q: Which list shows a flowering plant's life cycle in order?
ch: seed, seedling, adult plant, flower, fruit with seeds
it.h: Start with what you plant.

it.q: A pumpkin plant had 14 flowers. 5 of them became pumpkins. How many flowers did not become pumpkins?
it.h: Subtract 5 from 14.

it.q: Explain how a bee helps an apple tree make apples.
it.ans: The bee carries pollen from flower to flower. Pollinated flowers can then grow into apples that hold seeds.
it.h: What does the bee carry?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: How much do traits vary in a group of the same kind?

it.q: Differences in a trait among organisms of the same kind are called
it.h: No two are exactly alike.

it.q: Students measured the length of 6 bean pods from one plant: 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 11 cm. Which statement fits?
ch: the pods are from different plants
it.h: Look at the numbers.

it.q: The longest pod was 11 cm and the shortest was 8 cm. How many centimeters longer was the longest pod?
it.h: Subtract 8 from 11.

it.q: Which pod length was most common in the data 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 11 cm?
it.h: Count how many times each length appears.

it.q: Which graph would best show how many students have each hand span length?
it.h: Bars can show counts for each length.

it.q: Name two traits you could measure to study variation in a group of classmates.
it.ans: Hand span, height, arm length or foot length.
it.h: Choose traits you can measure with a ruler.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
lessons.n: How long do different living things live? Comparing life spans

it.q: The length of time a living thing usually lives is its
it.h: It is measured from birth to death.

it.q: A chart shows life spans: house mouse about 2 years, dog about 12 years, horse about 28 years. Which lives longest?
it.h: Find the biggest number.

it.q: Using the chart (dog about 12 years, horse about 28 years), about how many more years does a horse live than a dog?
it.h: Subtract 12 from 28.

it.q: Some bristlecone pine trees in California are more than 4,000 years old. What does this show?
ch: some organisms have very long life spans
trees do not have life cycles
it.h: Compare 4,000 years to a dog's life.

it.q: Which is true about all life cycles, long or short?
ch: they include birth, growth, reproduction and death
it.h: Think of what every organism does.

it.q: Explain why a plant with a short life span can still keep its kind going for many years.
it.ans: It makes seeds before it dies, and the seeds grow into new plants that make more seeds, so the cycle keeps going.
it.h: What does it make before it dies?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: Why do some animals live in groups?

it.q: A large group of fish swimming together is called a
it.h: It is the same word as a place where you learn.

it.q: How does living in a pack help wolves?
ch: They can hunt large animals together.
They can fly to find food.
it.h: Think about what is hard for one wolf to do alone.

it.q: In a beehive, some bees collect food, some care for young and some guard the hive. What is the benefit?
ch: Dividing the jobs helps the whole group survive.
Each bee has to do everything.
It keeps the bees from making honey.
it.h: What happens when everyone has a job?

it.q: Emperor penguins huddle close together in the Antarctic winter. Why?
ch: to share body heat and stay warm
it.h: Antarctica is extremely cold.

it.q: A herd has 23 adult elephants and 9 young elephants. How many elephants are in the herd?
it.h: Add the adults and the young.

it.q: Name one animal that lives in a group and describe one way the group helps it survive.
it.ans: Sample: Meerkats live in groups. While some meerkats look for food, one stands guard and warns the others when a predator comes.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: How do an animal's traits help it survive?

it.q: Fur, feathers or color that helps an animal blend in with its surroundings is called
it.h: It helps an animal hide.

it.q: A white rabbit and a brown rabbit live in a snowy field. Which one is more likely to be seen by a fox?
it.h: Which color stands out against the snow?

it.q: Some male birds have brighter feathers than others of the same kind. How can this trait help them?
ch: Bright feathers can help them attract mates and reproduce.
Bright feathers help them hide from all predators.
Bright feathers make them fly slower.
it.h: Survival also means having offspring.

it.q: A scientist put 20 green and 20 brown paper "beetles" on green grass. Birds found 15 brown beetles and 4 green beetles. How many beetles did the birds find in all?
it.h: Add the brown and green beetles found.

it.q: Using the same beetle data (20 green and 20 brown paper beetles were put on green grass, and birds found 15 brown and 4 green), which trait was an advantage on green grass?
it.h: Which color was found less often?

it.q: Explain how a cactus's spines are a trait that helps it survive.
it.ans: The spines protect the cactus from animals that might eat it for its water and food.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: What happens when a habitat changes?

it.q: A habitat is
ch: the place where an organism lives and gets what it needs
a stage in a life cycle
it.h: It is an organism's home.

it.q: Which animal can survive well in a hot, dry desert?
ch: a camel that can go a long time without drinking
a polar bear with thick fur
a fish that breathes with gills
a seal that hunts in icy water
it.h: Which animal has traits for little water and high heat?

it.q: A pond dries up during a long drought. Which organisms will have the hardest time surviving?
ch: birds that can fly to a new pond
deer that can walk to a river
it.h: Which organisms cannot leave the water?

it.q: A wetland had 64 frogs before it was drained to build a road. Afterward, scientists counted 15 frogs. How many fewer frogs were there?
it.h: Subtract the new count from the old count.

it.q: A forest is cut down and the land becomes a grassy field. Which animal is most likely to do well in the new habitat?
ch: a woodpecker that nests in trees
a squirrel that stores nuts in trees
it.h: Which animal needs grass instead of trees?

it.q: Explain why some organisms survive well in a habitat, some survive less well and some cannot survive at all.
it.ans: Each organism has traits that fit certain conditions. If the habitat gives it what it needs, it survives well. If it gets only some of what it needs, it survives less well. If its needs are not met, it cannot survive there.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: What can fossils tell us about the past?

it.q: A fossil is
ch: the remains or traces of a living thing from long ago
it.h: Fossils can be bones, shells, footprints or imprints.

it.q: A fossil of a fern is found in a place that is now very cold and icy. What does this suggest?
ch: The place was once warmer and wetter.
The fossil is from the future.
it.h: Ferns need warm, moist places to grow.

it.q: Fossils of fish and seashells are found in rock on a dry hilltop. What can you infer?
ch: The area was once covered by water.
Birds dropped the fish there last week.
it.h: Where do fish and shells live?

it.q: The La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles hold fossils of mammoths, saber-toothed cats and dire wolves. What do these fossils tell us?
ch: Animals that no longer live there once lived in that area.
Those animals still live in Los Angeles today.
The animals are only made-up stories.
it.h: Are mammoths alive in Los Angeles now?

it.q: A museum has 27 mammoth bones and 19 saber-toothed cat bones on display. How many bones are on display in all?
it.h: Add the two numbers.

it.q: Explain how a dinosaur footprint fossil can give information even though it is not a bone.
it.ans: The footprint shows the size and shape of the dinosaur's foot, how many toes it had and that it walked over soft mud in that place.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: How do plants and animals survive in the desert?

it.q: A desert gets
it.h: Deserts are dry.

it.q: A cactus has a thick stem. How does this help it survive in the desert?
it.h: Rain does not come often.

it.q: Many desert animals sleep in burrows during the day and come out at night. Why?
ch: to avoid the hottest part of the day
it.h: Nights in the desert are cooler.

it.q: A jackrabbit has very large ears with many blood vessels. How do they help in the desert?
ch: they help it lose heat and stay cool
it.h: Big ears give off heat.

it.q: Which plant would survive least well in the Mojave Desert?
ch: a fern that needs wet shade
it.h: Which one needs a lot of water?

it.q: Choose a desert plant or animal and explain how one of its traits helps it survive.
it.ans: Sample: a cactus has spines instead of wide leaves, so it loses less water and animals do not eat it.
it.h: Think about water and heat.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
lessons.n: How do animals survive cold winters?

it.q: Some birds fly to warmer places for the winter. This is called
it.h: Think of geese flying south.

it.q: Some animals spend the winter in a deep, inactive sleep-like state with a slow heartbeat. This is
it.h: Some ground squirrels do this.

it.q: An arctic fox grows a thick white coat in winter. How does this help?
ch: it keeps it warm and helps it hide in snow
it.h: Think of warmth and color.

it.q: Why do many animals eat a lot in the fall?
ch: to store fat for winter when food is scarce
it.h: Winter has less food.

it.q: Honeybees stay in the hive and cluster together in winter. How does this help?
it.h: Many bodies close together stay warmer.

it.q: Name two ways animals survive cold winters and give an example of each.
it.ans: Migration: many geese fly to warmer places. Hibernation: some bats and ground squirrels go into a deep sleep-like state. Other ways: growing thick fur or storing food.
it.h: Leave, sleep or adapt.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
lessons.n: Why does a faster object have more energy?

it.q: An object that is moving has
it.h: Anything that moves has a kind of energy.

it.q: Two identical balls roll across the floor. Ball A rolls faster than Ball B. Which has more energy of motion?
it.h: Compare their speeds.

it.q: A class rolled a marble down a ramp from different heights and timed it over 1 meter of floor. Higher starting points made the marble move faster. Why?
ch: Starting higher gave the marble more energy, so it moved faster.
it.h: Think about what the height gave the marble before it was released.

it.q: A marble rolled 1 meter in 4 seconds from a low ramp and 1 meter in 2 seconds from a high ramp. How many seconds faster was the high-ramp roll?
it.h: Subtract the times.

it.q: A soccer ball is kicked softly and then kicked hard. Evidence that the hard kick gave it more energy is that it
ch: moved faster and knocked over more cones
it.h: What can a faster ball do that a slower ball cannot?

it.q: Explain how you could tell which of two rolling toy cars has more energy without touching them.
it.ans: Measure or compare their speeds. The faster car has more energy. I could also see which car pushes a cup farther when it hits it.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
lessons.n: What happens to energy when objects collide?

it.q: When two objects run into each other, it is called a
it.h: Think of bumper cars.

it.q: A rolling marble hits a still marble. The first marble slows down and the second marble starts moving. What happened?
ch: Energy moved from the first marble to the second marble.
The second marble made new energy.
it.h: Where did the second marble get its energy?

it.q: A moving toy car crashes into a block, and you hear a loud bang. Into what forms did some of the car's energy change?
ch: sound and heat, plus motion of the block
it.h: What did you hear and what moved?

it.q: A cart moving at 60 cm per second hits a wall and bounces back at 25 cm per second. How many centimeters per second slower is it moving after the collision?
it.h: Subtract the speed after from the speed before.

it.q: In a game of pool, a cue ball hits another ball. Which question asks about energy changes in this collision?
ch: How does the speed of the cue ball change after it hits the other ball?
What color is the cue ball?
How old is the pool table?
it.h: Energy changes show up as changes in speed.

it.q: Describe what happens to the energy in a collision between a rolling ball and a row of dominoes.
it.ans: The ball's energy of motion moves to the first domino, which falls and transfers energy to the next one. Some energy also becomes sound and a little heat.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
lessons.n: Where does the energy go after a crash?

it.q: When you clap your hands, the energy of your moving hands changes partly into
it.h: What do you hear?

it.q: Rubbing your hands together quickly makes them feel warm. What does this show?
ch: Motion energy can change into heat.
it.h: Notice the warmth.

it.q: A falling apple hits the ground and stops. Where did most of its energy go?
ch: into sound, heat and moving the ground a tiny bit
it.h: Energy is never destroyed. Think about what you would hear and feel.

it.q: A car's bumper is tested in a crash. At 10 km per hour, a sensor records 15 units of sound. At 30 km per hour, it records 48 units. How many more units of sound were recorded at 30 km per hour?
it.h: Subtract the smaller reading.

it.q: Why do helmets have foam inside?
ch: The foam takes in some of the energy of a collision so less reaches your head.
Foam adds energy to a crash.
it.h: Think about what foam does when it is squeezed.

it.q: A car brakes and stops. Explain where the car's energy of motion goes.
it.ans: The brakes rub against the wheels, and friction changes the energy of motion into heat. A little energy also becomes sound.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
lessons.n: Measuring and comparing speed with distance and time

it.q: Speed tells
ch: how far something moves in a certain amount of time
it.h: Think about a race. What two things do you measure?

it.q: A toy car rolled 120 cm in 4 seconds. How many centimeters did it roll each second?
it.h: Divide the distance by the time.

it.q: Three runners raced 50 meters. Ana took 10 seconds, Ben took 8 seconds and Chloe took 12 seconds. Who was fastest?
ch: They all had the same speed.
it.h: For the same distance, the fastest runner needs the least time.

it.q: A snail crawled 6 cm in 3 minutes. How many centimeters did it crawl each minute?
it.h: Share the 6 cm equally among the 3 minutes.

it.q: Two carts rolled for 5 seconds. Cart A went 100 cm and Cart B went 60 cm. Which statement is true?
ch: Cart A was faster and had more energy of motion.
Both carts had the same speed.
Cart B had more energy of motion.
it.h: The time was the same. Which cart moved farther?

it.q: Explain how you would find out which of two paper airplanes flies faster. Name the two things you would measure.
it.ans: Throw each plane the same way and measure how far it flies and how long it takes with a meter tape and a stopwatch. Compare distance divided by time (or compare the times over the same distance). Repeat a few trials for each plane.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
lessons.n: Collisions in sports: balls, bats and helmets

it.q: When a swinging bat hits a baseball, energy moves
ch: from the bat to the ball
from the ball to the bat only
from the ground to the ball
it.h: Which object was moving first?

it.q: A soccer player kicks a still ball, and right after the kick the ball is moving fast. What gave the ball its energy of motion?
it.h: In a collision, a moving object can pass energy to the object it hits.

it.q: When a baseball lands in a glove, you hear a loud pop. What does the sound show?
ch: Some of the ball's energy changed into sound.
it.h: Sound is a form of energy. Where did it come from?

it.q: A tennis ball hit by a racket swung slowly flew 8 meters. When the racket was swung fast, the ball flew 21 meters. How many meters farther did it fly?
it.h: Subtract the shorter distance from the longer one.

it.q: Why does a bike helmet have a foam layer inside?
ch: The foam squishes and takes in energy, so less energy reaches the head.
The foam makes the helmet heavier.
The foam makes the rider faster.
The foam keeps the head cold.
it.h: Think about what happens to the foam when the helmet hits something.

it.q: Explain why a hockey puck that is hit hard slides farther across the ice than a puck that is hit gently.
it.ans: A hard hit gives the puck more energy, so it moves faster. A faster puck has more energy of motion, so it can slide farther before rubbing on the ice slows it to a stop.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: How does energy travel from place to place?

it.q: Sunlight warms a sidewalk. Which form of energy traveled from the Sun to the sidewalk?
it.h: What travels from the Sun to Earth through space?
