it.q: A metal spoon is placed in a cup of hot soup. Soon the handle feels hot. What happened?
ch: Heat moved from the soup through the spoon.
Cold moved from the spoon into the soup.
The spoon made its own heat.
it.h: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.

it.q: You hit a drum and a nearby paper scrap on a second drum jumps. What does this show?
ch: Sound carries energy from place to place.
it.h: Something made the paper move without touching it.

it.q: A cup of cocoa was 80°C. After 15 minutes it was 52°C. How many degrees did it cool?
it.h: Subtract the ending temperature from the starting temperature.

it.q: Which is an example of energy moving by electric current?
ch: a wire carrying energy from a battery to a bulb
a ball rolling down a hill
it.h: Electric current moves through wires.

it.q: Give two examples from your home of energy moving from one place to another. Name the form of energy in each.
it.ans: Sample: Heat moves from a stove burner to a pot. Light moves from a lamp to my book so I can read. Electricity moves through a cord to a TV.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: How does electricity move through a circuit?

it.q: A complete path that electricity can flow through is called a
it.h: The path must have no gaps.

it.q: Which material is a good conductor of electricity?
it.h: Conductors let electricity flow easily. Most metals are conductors.

it.q: A bulb is connected to a battery with two wires, but one wire is not touching the battery. What happens?
ch: The bulb does not light because the circuit is open.
it.h: Is there a complete loop?

it.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic or rubber?
ch: These insulators keep electricity from flowing where it should not.
They make the wire conduct better.
it.h: Insulators block the flow of electricity.

it.q: A class tested 14 objects in a circuit. The bulb lit for 6 objects. How many objects did not light the bulb?
it.h: Subtract the objects that lit the bulb from the total.

it.q: Draw or describe a simple circuit that lights a bulb. Explain why it works.
it.ans: A battery, two wires and a bulb connected in a loop from one end of the battery, through the bulb and back to the other end. It works because the closed loop lets electric current carry energy from the battery to the bulb.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: How can we change energy from one form to another?

it.q: A solar panel changes
it.h: Solar panels work in sunlight.

it.q: An electric fan changes electrical energy mostly into
it.h: What do the blades do?

it.q: A speaker changes electrical energy into
it.h: What do you hear from a speaker?

it.q: A flashlight battery stores energy. When the flashlight is on, the energy changes into
it.h: An old-style bulb gets hot after it has been on a while.

it.q: A small motor lifted a paper clip 40 cm with 1 battery and 95 cm with 2 batteries. How many centimeters higher did it lift the clip with 2 batteries?
it.h: Subtract the heights.

it.q: Name a device in your home and describe the energy change it makes.
it.ans: Sample: A toaster changes electrical energy into heat that browns the bread.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: How do engineers design and improve an energy device?

it.q: A class must build a solar oven that warms a cracker to at least 40°C using a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap. The temperature goal is a
it.h: It describes what success looks like.

it.q: A class must build a solar oven using only a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap. The rule "only a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap" is a
it.h: It limits the materials.

it.q: Why would a team line its solar oven with foil?
ch: Foil reflects more sunlight into the oven.
it.h: Think about what shiny surfaces do with light.

it.q: The team's oven heated from 22°C to 47°C. How many degrees did the temperature rise?
it.h: Subtract the starting temperature from the ending temperature.

it.q: A solar oven test was done on a sunny day, and the improved oven was tested on a cloudy day. What is wrong with comparing these results?
ch: The weather changed, so the test was not fair.
Ovens work better on cloudy days.
The oven should be tested at night.
it.h: What else changed besides the design?

it.q: List two criteria and one constraint for a device that changes motion into sound, such as an alarm that rings when a door opens.
it.ans: Criteria: it must make a sound loud enough to hear across the room; it must make sound every time the door opens. Constraint: it must cost less than $5, or it must use only materials from the classroom.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: Conductors, insulators, and series and parallel circuits

it.q: In a series circuit, the parts are connected
ch: one after another in a single loop
it.h: "Series" means one after another, like a line of train cars.

it.q: In a parallel circuit, each bulb
ch: has its own path to the battery
shares one single path with every other bulb
it.h: Picture a road that splits into several lanes.

it.q: Two bulbs are in a series circuit. One bulb burns out. What happens to the other bulb?
ch: It goes out too, because the only path is broken.
it.h: Is there still a complete loop for the current?

it.q: The lights in a house are wired in parallel. Why is this useful?
ch: One light can be turned off while the others stay on.
All the lights must be on at the same time.
It makes every bulb burn out together.
it.h: Think about turning off one lamp in your home.

it.q: A student tested 20 objects to see if they conduct electricity. 9 were conductors. How many were insulators?
A student adds a second bulb to a series circuit that has one battery. What happens to the brightness?
ch: Both bulbs glow dimmer than one bulb did alone.
it.h: The same battery now pushes current through two bulbs in one path.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: Static electricity, lightning and electrical safety

it.q: Rubbing a balloon on your hair can make your hair stand up and reach toward the balloon. This is caused by
it.h: Rubbing moves tiny electric charges from one material to another.

it.q: After a balloon is rubbed on a wool sweater, it sticks to a wall. What does this show?
ch: Rubbing moved electric charges, and the charged balloon is pulled toward the wall.
Air pushed the balloon against the wall.
it.h: What did the rubbing change about the balloon?

it.q: Lightning is
ch: a giant spark of static electricity between clouds or between a cloud and the ground
it.h: Think about the small spark you sometimes feel after walking on carpet.

it.q: Light travels much faster than sound. A rule of thumb is that every 3 seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder means the lightning is about 1 kilometer away. A student counts 9 seconds. About how many kilometers away is the lightning?
it.h: How many groups of 3 seconds are in 9 seconds?

it.q: Why should you never use a hair dryer near a bathtub full of water?
ch: Tap water conducts electricity, so you could get a dangerous shock.
Water makes the hair dryer cold.
Hair dryers do not work indoors.
The water turns into steam right away.
it.h: Is tap water a conductor or an insulator?

it.q: Explain why you see a lightning flash before you hear the thunder.
it.ans: Light travels much faster than sound. The light reaches your eyes almost instantly, but the sound of thunder takes longer to travel the same distance.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
lessons.n: Electric current at work: electromagnets and motors

it.q: A wire coiled around an iron nail and connected to a battery becomes
it.h: Electric current flowing in a coil of wire can make a magnet.

it.q: A student disconnects the wire of an electromagnet from the battery, and the paper clips fall off the nail. Why?
ch: Without current, the nail stops acting as a strong magnet.
it.h: What was flowing through the coil before the wire was disconnected?

it.q: An electromagnet with 10 coils of wire picked up 4 paper clips. With 30 coils, it picked up 13 paper clips. How many more clips did it pick up with 30 coils?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number of clips from the larger number.

it.q: The electric motor in a toy car changes
it.h: What does the toy car do when the motor runs?

it.q: Why do scrap yards use electromagnets on cranes instead of ordinary magnets?
ch: An electromagnet can be switched off to drop the metal.
it.h: Think about how the crane lets go of a load of scrap metal.

it.q: Plan a fair test to find out whether the number of coils changes the strength of an electromagnet.
it.ans: Use the same nail, battery and kind of wire each time. Change only the number of coils, such as 10, 20 and 30. Count how many paper clips each one picks up, and repeat each test 3 times.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
lessons.n: Where does the energy we use come from?

it.q: A natural resource is
ch: something from nature that people use
something made only in a factory
it.h: It comes from Earth, not from people.

it.q: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels because they formed from
ch: remains of living things from millions of years ago
it.h: Think about what "fossil" means.

it.q: How does a power plant that burns natural gas make electricity?
ch: Burning the gas makes heat that boils water into steam, and the steam spins a generator.
The gas glows like a bulb.
The gas freezes and makes current.
it.h: Follow the energy from burning to spinning.

it.q: Which natural resource is used to make electricity at a hydroelectric dam?
it.h: "Hydro" means water.

it.q: A town gets its electricity from three sources: 45 percent natural gas, 35 percent solar and the rest from wind. What percent comes from wind?
it.h: All the parts add up to 100 percent.

it.q: Choose one energy source and explain where its energy originally comes from.
it.ans: Sample: Wind energy comes from moving air. The Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, which makes air move as wind.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
lessons.n: Which energy resources will run out?

it.q: A renewable resource is one that
ch: can be replaced naturally in a short time
will be used up and never replaced
it.h: "Renew" means to make new again.

it.q: Which is a nonrenewable energy resource?
it.h: Which takes millions of years to form?

it.q: Why will we eventually run out of oil if we keep using it?
ch: It takes millions of years to form, much longer than we use it.
Oil is made by the Sun each day.
it.h: Compare how fast it forms with how fast we use it.

it.q: A school used 1,200 units of electricity in March and 950 units in April after turning off unused lights. How many units did the school save?
it.h: Subtract April from March.

it.q: Which list has only renewable resources?
it.h: Check each item in the list.

it.q: Sort these into renewable and nonrenewable: wind, coal, sunlight, natural gas. Explain one of your choices.
it.ans: Renewable: wind and sunlight. Nonrenewable: coal and natural gas. Coal is nonrenewable because it took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
lessons.n: How does using energy affect the environment?

it.q: Burning fossil fuels in cars and power plants can
it.h: Think about the exhaust from a car.

it.q: Coal is often dug out of large mines. Which is an effect on the environment?
it.h: What happens to the land when a large mine is dug?

it.q: A dam on a river makes electricity but blocks salmon from swimming upstream. How could engineers reduce this problem?
ch: build a fish ladder that lets salmon pass the dam
it.h: The fish need a path around the dam.

it.q: A family switched 10 old light bulbs to LED bulbs. Each LED saves 50 units of electricity a year. How many units does the family save each year?
it.h: Multiply the number of bulbs by the savings per bulb.

it.q: Which choice reduces the amount of fuel people use?
ch: walking or biking for short trips
running the heater with windows open
it.h: Which choice uses no fuel?

it.q: Describe one way your class could use less energy at school and explain how it helps the environment.
it.ans: Sample: Turn off computers and lights when we leave the room. Using less electricity means power plants burn less fuel, which means less air pollution.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
lessons.n: How fossil fuels formed and how we get them

it.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel that is a black rock dug from mines?
it.h: It is burned in some power plants and is solid, not a liquid or gas.

it.q: Most coal formed from
ch: plants in ancient swamps that were buried and pressed for millions of years
it.h: Coal sometimes has prints of leaves and ferns in it.

it.q: How do people usually get oil out of the ground?
it.h: Oil is a liquid deep underground.

it.q: A train car carries 20 tons of coal. A power plant burns 140 tons of coal in a day. How many train cars of coal does the plant need each day?
it.h: How many 20s are in 140?

it.q: The energy stored in coal first came from
ch: the Sun, captured by ancient plants
it.h: Plants use sunlight to make their food.

it.q: Describe the steps that turned ancient swamp plants into coal.
it.ans: The plants died and fell into swamp water. Layers of mud and sand buried them. Over millions of years, the weight of the layers and heat underground pressed the plant remains into coal.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
lessons.n: Choosing an energy plan for a California town

it.q: Solar panels make electricity only when sunlight reaches them. What could a town add so it still has solar power at night?
ch: large batteries that store extra electricity made during the day
more panels facing away from the Sun
nothing, because solar panels work best in the dark
it.h: How could energy made in the day be saved for later?

it.q: Geothermal power plants use heat from inside Earth. Which kind of place would be best for one?
ch: a place with hot springs and hot rock close to the surface
a flat place with cold rock deep down
it.h: Geothermal means "Earth heat."

it.q: A town needs 1,000 units of electricity a day. Its solar panels make 450 units and its wind turbines make 300 units. How many more units does the town need?
it.h: Add what is made, then subtract that from what is needed.

it.q: Which is a constraint for a town's energy plan?
ch: The town can spend no more than $2 million.
The plan should make little pollution.
The plan should make enough electricity.
The plan should work in all seasons.
it.h: A constraint is a limit the plan must stay within.

it.q: A town on a windy hilltop wants clean energy that does not burn fuel. Which resource fits best?
it.h: Which resource is renewable and plentiful on a windy hill?

it.q: Give one benefit and one problem of using wind turbines to power a town.
it.ans: Benefit: wind is renewable and turbines make no air pollution while they run. Problem: the wind does not always blow, so the town needs another source or batteries; turbines also need open space and can harm birds.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: How do waves move?

it.q: The height of a wave from its resting position to its top is its
it.h: Think "how tall."

it.q: The distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next wave is the
it.h: Measure from one peak to the next peak.

it.q: A cork floats on a pond. Waves pass by. What does the cork mostly do?
ch: bobs up and down in about the same place
travels all the way across the pond with the waves
it.h: Waves carry energy, not the water itself very far.

it.q: Ocean waves with a very large amplitude crash on the beach. What can they do that small waves cannot?
ch: move larger rocks and wear away more sand
it.h: A bigger amplitude means more energy.

it.q: A wave model drawn on paper has peaks at 0 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm and 18 cm. What is its wavelength in centimeters?
it.h: Find the distance between any two peaks next to each other.

it.q: Draw or describe two waves: one with a large amplitude and short wavelength, and one with a small amplitude and long wavelength.
it.ans: Wave 1 has tall peaks that are close together. Wave 2 has short, low peaks that are far apart.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: What makes a sound loud or high?

it.q: Sound is caused by
it.h: Touch your throat while you hum.

it.q: A drum is hit gently and then hard. The hard hit makes a louder sound because the sound wave has a
it.h: Loudness is connected to the size of the vibration.

it.q: A short guitar string makes a higher sound than a long string. In sound waves, a higher pitch has a
it.h: Higher pitch means faster vibrations and waves closer together.

it.q: Rice on a drum jumps more when the drum is hit harder. What does this show?
ch: Louder sound waves carry more energy.
it.h: Compare how much the rice moved.

it.q: A sound meter read 45 units for a whisper and 70 units for a shout. How many units louder was the shout?
it.h: Subtract the whisper reading.

it.q: Explain how you could make a rubber band make a higher sound and a louder sound.
it.ans: Stretch it tighter or make it shorter for a higher pitch. Pluck it harder for a louder sound with a bigger amplitude.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: How do we see things?

it.q: We see an object when light
ch: reflects off the object and enters our eyes
comes out of our eyes and hits the object
is absorbed completely by the object
it.h: Light has to reach your eyes.

it.q: In a completely dark room with no light at all, can you see a red ball?
ch: No, because no light reflects from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you look hard enough.
Only if the ball is big.
it.h: What does seeing need?

it.q: A mirror reflects light very well. Why can you see your face in it?
ch: Light reflects off your face, then off the mirror, into your eyes.
The mirror makes its own light.
Your eyes send light to the mirror.
The mirror absorbs all the light.
it.h: Trace the light's path.

it.q: A light beam travels 30 cm from a flashlight to a mirror and 45 cm from the mirror to a student's eye. How far does the light travel in all, in centimeters?
it.h: Add both parts of the path.

it.q: Which object reflects the least light?
it.h: Dark colors absorb more light.

it.q: Draw or describe a model that shows how you see a book on your desk while a lamp is on.
it.ans: Arrows go from the lamp to the book, then from the book to my eye. Light from the lamp reflects off the book and enters my eye, and my brain makes sense of it.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: How can we send messages using patterns?

it.q: A pattern of long and short signals used to send letters is a
it.h: Morse code is one example.

it.q: Two students send a message across the field by flashing a flashlight: one flash means "yes" and two flashes mean "no." What is being used to carry the information?
it.h: What did they flash?

it.q: Drums in some places were used long ago to send messages between villages. Why did this work?
ch: Patterns of drumbeats could travel as sound over a distance.
it.h: How does sound get from one village to another?

it.q: In a code, each letter uses 3 light flashes. How many flashes are needed for a 4-letter word?
it.h: Multiply flashes per letter by the number of letters.

it.q: A code uses 1 = on and 0 = off. Which pattern means on, off, on?
it.h: Write 1 for on and 0 for off, in order.

it.q: Design a simple code using claps to send the words "stop," "go" and "wait" to a teammate. Explain how your teammate would know which word you mean.
it.ans: Sample: 1 clap = go, 2 claps = stop, 3 claps = wait. My teammate counts the claps, and each number stands for a different word.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Mirrors and periscopes: modeling how light reflects

it.q: When light hits a smooth, shiny mirror, it
it.h: What do you see when you look into a mirror?

it.q: A narrow flashlight beam hits a mirror at a slant. How does the beam leave the mirror?
ch: It bounces off at the same angle on the other side.
It always goes straight back to the flashlight.
it.h: Think of a ball bouncing off a wall at a slant.

it.q: A periscope uses two mirrors to let you see over a wall. What does light do inside it?
ch: It reflects off one mirror, then off the other, and into your eye.
It is made by the mirrors.
It passes straight through both mirrors.
It travels from your eye out to the object.
it.h: Trace the light from the object to your eye.

it.q: You see a friend's face in a mirror. Which path did the light take?
ch: from a lamp, off your friend's face, off the mirror and into your eyes
from your eyes to the mirror and then to your friend
from the mirror to the lamp
it.h: Light must reach your eyes for you to see.

it.q: A flashlight beam hit a mirror at an angle of 30 degrees from a line pointing straight out of the mirror. At what angle from that line did the beam bounce off?
it.h: The angle going in matches the angle going out.

it.q: Explain why you can see yourself clearly in a mirror but not in a sheet of black paper.
it.ans: A mirror is smooth and shiny, so it reflects light in an even pattern back to your eyes and makes a clear image. Black paper absorbs most of the light, so very little reflects and no image forms.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Waves that move things: water waves and earthquake waves

it.q: A wave is
ch: a repeating motion that carries energy from place to place
a piece of matter that travels across the ocean
it.h: Think about what a wave can do to things it reaches.

it.q: A rope is tied to a doorknob with a ribbon tied in its middle. A student shakes the free end up and down. The ribbon moves up and down but does not travel toward the door. What does this show?
ch: The wave carries energy along the rope while the rope itself mostly moves up and down in place.
The rope moves to the door.
Waves carry objects to the end of the rope.
it.h: Watch the ribbon, not the wave.

it.q: Earthquakes send waves through the ground. Why can these waves damage buildings far from where the earthquake started?
ch: The waves carry energy that shakes the ground and the buildings.
The waves carry rocks to the buildings.
The waves are made of water.
The waves only shake the place where they start.
it.h: What does a wave carry as it travels?

it.q: Ocean waves reached a beach every 6 seconds. How many waves arrived in 1 minute (60 seconds)?
it.h: How many groups of 6 are in 60?

it.q: Two water waves pass the same dock. Wave A is 2 meters tall and Wave B is 0.5 meters tall. Which wave can push a boat harder?
ch: Wave A, because a larger amplitude carries more energy
Wave B, because it is smaller
Neither wave can push a boat
it.h: Which wave has the larger amplitude?

it.q: Describe how you could use a spring toy (a slinky) to show that a wave can make an object move.
it.ans: Stretch the slinky on the floor and set a paper cup at the far end. Send a wave pulse down the slinky. When the wave reaches the cup, it knocks the cup over, showing the wave carried energy that moved an object.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: How do plant structures help plants survive?

it.q: Which plant structure takes in water and minerals from the soil?
it.h: This part grows underground.

it.q: Where does a plant make most of its food using sunlight?
it.h: These parts are usually flat and green.

it.q: A rose bush has sharp thorns on its stems. What is the function of the thorns?
ch: They protect the plant from animals that might eat it.
They help the plant drink water.
it.h: Think about what an animal would feel if it bit the stem.

it.q: Bright, sweet-smelling flowers help a plant
ch: attract pollinators so it can make seeds
it.h: Bees and butterflies visit flowers.

it.q: A class measured a sunflower stem. In week 1 it was 18 cm tall, and in week 4 it was 75 cm tall. How many centimeters did it grow?
it.h: Subtract to find the change.

it.q: Choose one plant structure and explain how it helps the plant survive, grow or reproduce.
it.ans: Sample: The stem holds the plant up toward sunlight and carries water from the roots to the leaves.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: How do animal body parts help them survive?

it.q: A turtle's hard shell is an external structure that helps it
it.h: Think about what a turtle does when it is in danger.

it.q: An eagle has sharp, curved talons. What is their function?
ch: building a nest out of mud
it.h: Talons are the eagle's claws.

it.q: A duck has webbed feet. How do they help the duck?
ch: They push water to help it swim.
They keep it cool in the desert.
it.h: Think about where ducks spend time.

it.q: A porcupine is covered in sharp quills. Which statement is the best argument about this structure?
ch: The quills help the porcupine survive by keeping predators away.
The quills help the porcupine fly.
The quills help it see better.
The quills help it smell food.
it.h: What would happen to an animal that tried to bite it?

it.q: A hummingbird's beak is 2 cm long. A woodpecker's beak is 5 cm long. How many centimeters longer is the woodpecker's beak?
it.h: Subtract the lengths.

it.q: Describe an external structure of an animal that lives in a cold place and explain how it helps the animal survive.
it.ans: Sample: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. The fur traps heat and the fat keeps the bear warm in icy water and snow.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: What structures inside the body help animals survive?

it.q: Which internal organ pumps blood through the body?
it.h: You can feel it beat in your chest.

it.q: Which internal structures take in oxygen from the air?
it.h: They fill up when you breathe in.

it.q: A fish lives underwater. Which structure lets it get oxygen from water?
it.h: Look at the slits on the sides of a fish's head.

it.q: Many birds have hollow bones. How does this help them?
ch: Their light bones make flying easier.
Their bones make them heavier for diving.
it.h: Think about what flying requires.

it.q: A student counted her heartbeats for 15 seconds while resting: 21 beats. After jumping jacks, she counted 33 beats in 15 seconds. How many more beats did she count after exercise?
it.h: Subtract the resting count.

it.q: Explain how the skeleton and muscles work together to help an animal move.
it.ans: The skeleton is a frame of bones that supports the body. Muscles attach to the bones and pull on them, which makes the body parts move.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: How do animals sense and respond to their surroundings?

it.q: Which body part sends information from the senses to be processed?
it.h: The brain is the body's control center.

it.q: You touch a hot pan and quickly pull your hand away. In what order does this happen?
ch: skin senses heat -> nerves send a message -> muscles move the hand
muscles move -> skin senses heat -> brain forgets
brain moves the pan -> skin cools
eyes see the pan -> stomach responds
it.h: Start with the sense organ.

it.q: Owls hunt mice at night in dim light. Which senses most help them?
it.h: Think about how to find a mouse in the dark.

it.q: Bats send out high-pitched sounds and listen for the echoes. What does this help them do?
ch: find insects and avoid objects in the dark
it.h: The echoes bounce off things.

it.q: A student's reaction time was tested by catching a falling ruler. Trial 1: 18 cm. Trial 2: 14 cm. Trial 3: 13 cm. What was the average distance in centimeters? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
it.h: Add 18, 14 and 13, then divide by 3.

it.q: Describe how a dog uses its senses to find a hidden treat. Name the sense, the sense organ and how the brain responds.
it.ans: The dog smells the treat with its nose. Nerves send the smell information to the brain, which recognizes food and tells the dog's legs to move toward it.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: Structures for growth and reproduction in plants and animals

it.q: The part of a flowering plant that makes seeds is the
it.h: Seeds form after pollen reaches this part.

it.q: A maple seed has a thin wing that makes it spin as it falls. How does this structure help the plant reproduce?
ch: The wind can carry the seed away from the parent tree.
It helps the seed make food.
It protects the seed from rain.
it.h: Where would new trees grow if every seed dropped straight down?

it.q: A bird egg has a hard shell. What is the function of the shell?
ch: It protects the growing chick inside.
It makes food for the parent bird.
it.h: Think about what could happen to the chick without a shell.

it.q: Burrs are seeds covered with tiny hooks. How do the hooks help the plant?
ch: They catch on animal fur, so the seeds are carried to new places.
They make the seeds grow faster.
it.h: What happens when a dog runs through a patch of burrs?

it.q: A sunflower head had 1,200 seeds. Birds ate 450 of them. How many seeds were left?
Choose a fruit, such as an apple or a berry. Explain how the fruit helps the plant's seeds reach new places.
it.ans: Animals eat the sweet fruit, and the seeds pass through their bodies and are dropped far from the parent plant, where new plants can grow.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
lessons.n: Eyes, ears and brains: how animals process information

it.q: Light enters the eye through a small opening called the
it.h: It looks like a black dot in the middle of the colored part of the eye.

it.q: In bright sunlight, your pupils get smaller. How does this help you?
ch: Less light gets in, which protects the inside of the eye.
Your eyes make their own light.
it.h: Think about what a smaller opening does to the amount of light.

it.q: Sound makes the eardrum vibrate. What happens next?
ch: Nerves carry signals to the brain, which figures out what the sound is.
The sound travels to the stomach.
it.h: Which organ makes sense of information from the senses?

it.q: Rabbits have eyes on the sides of their heads. How does this help them survive?
ch: They can see a wide area around them and spot predators.
it.h: Rabbits are often hunted by other animals.

it.q: In a test, a cat heard a sound 12 times and turned toward it 9 times. How many times did it not turn toward the sound?
Explain how a dog learns to run to the kitchen when it hears its food bag rattle. Use the words senses, brain and memory.
it.ans: The dog's ears sense the rattle, and nerves send signals to its brain. The brain remembers that this sound came before food in the past, so the dog responds by running to the kitchen.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: What can rock layers tell us about the past?

it.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is usually
it.h: Layers pile up over time, like a stack of newspapers.

it.q: A layer of rock contains fossils of seashells and coral. What environment did that layer most likely form in?
it.h: Where do seashells and coral live?

it.q: A cliff has a bottom layer with fish fossils, a middle layer with fern fossils and a top layer with no fossils of water animals. Which story fits the layers?
ch: The area was underwater first, then later became land with plants.
The area was always a dry desert.
The area was land first and then the ocean.
The fossils were all buried at the same time.
it.h: Read the layers from bottom (oldest) to top (newest).

it.q: A layer of sediment builds up about 2 cm every 100 years. About how many centimeters would build up in 500 years?
it.h: 500 years is five groups of 100 years.

it.q: Which type of rock forms from layers of sand, mud and shells pressed together over a long time?
it.h: "Sediment" means bits of sand, mud and shells.

it.q: Explain how scientists can tell the order in which rock layers formed.
it.ans: New layers are laid down on top of older layers, so in undisturbed rock the bottom layer formed first and the top layer formed last.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: How do water, wind, ice and plants change the land?

it.q: The breaking of rock into smaller pieces is called
it.h: "Weather" is in the word, but it means breaking down.

it.q: The moving of rock and soil from one place to another is called
it.h: This step carries pieces away.

it.q: A class poured water over a sand hill model. With a small cup, little sand moved. With a big pitcher poured faster, a deep channel formed. What does this show?
ch: Faster, larger amounts of water cause more erosion.
Small cups cause the most erosion.
it.h: Compare the amount and speed of the water.

it.q: A tree's roots grow into a crack in a rock and make the crack wider. This is an example of
it.h: The roots are breaking the rock.

it.q: A riverbank wore away 15 cm in one year and 23 cm the next year after a big flood. How many centimeters did it wear away in both years?
it.h: Add the two years.

it.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes. Explain how this can break the rock.
it.ans: Water expands when it freezes into ice. The ice pushes on the sides of the crack and makes it bigger, and after many freezes and thaws the rock breaks apart.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Why are earthquakes and volcanoes found where they are?

it.q: A map of earthquakes around the world shows that most earthquakes
ch: happen in long bands, often near the edges of continents and oceans
it.h: Look for lines and patterns on the map.

it.q: The "Ring of Fire" is a band of volcanoes and earthquakes around which ocean?
it.h: California is on the edge of this ocean.

it.q: A map shows that many tall mountain ranges, volcanoes and earthquakes are found in the same areas. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: The same forces inside Earth cause all three.
it.h: Why would they be found together?

it.q: A list shows 48 earthquakes in one month in California and 9 in Nevada. How many more were in California?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number.

it.q: Which California landform is a volcano?
it.h: It is a tall, cone-shaped mountain in northern California.

it.q: Describe what a map of volcanoes and earthquakes tells us about where they happen.
it.ans: They are not spread out evenly. Most happen in bands along the edges of the giant plates of Earth's surface, such as around the Pacific Ocean.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: How can we reduce damage from natural hazards?

it.q: Which is a natural hazard caused by Earth processes?
ch: a power outage from a broken cable
it.h: It happens because of forces inside Earth.

it.q: Which design helps a building stay standing during an earthquake?
ch: a flexible frame and pads under the base that let the ground move beneath it
walls that are not attached to the foundation
it.h: Buildings that can sway a little are less likely to break.

it.q: A community near the ocean worries about tsunamis after earthquakes. Which solution helps most?
ch: warning sirens and marked routes to higher ground
building homes closer to the beach
it.h: What helps people get out of danger quickly?

it.q: A model building on a shake table stayed standing for 8 seconds. After adding cross braces, it stayed standing for 25 seconds. How many seconds longer did it last?
it.h: Subtract the times.

it.q: Why do scientists place instruments around active volcanoes?
ch: to detect warning signs and alert people before an eruption
it.h: Watching for changes helps people prepare.

it.q: Name two solutions that reduce damage from landslides and explain one of them.
it.ans: Building retaining walls and planting trees on slopes. A retaining wall holds back soil and rocks so they do not slide onto roads or homes.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Using maps to find patterns in mountains, volcanoes and ocean trenches

it.q: A map that shows high and low places on land and under the ocean helps scientists find
it.h: What does a map of landforms show?

it.q: A map shows many volcanoes in a ring around the edges of the Pacific Ocean. What is this ring called?
it.h: The name describes a circle of erupting volcanoes.

it.q: A map of the ocean floor shows a long chain of underwater mountains running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. What does this show?
ch: Mountain chains are found under the ocean too.
The ocean floor is flat everywhere.
it.h: Is the ocean floor flat or bumpy on this map?

it.q: The deepest spot in the ocean is about 11 kilometers deep. The tallest mountain on land is about 9 kilometers high. About how many kilometers greater is the depth of the deepest spot than the height of the tallest mountain?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

it.q: Which feature is often found near a deep ocean trench along the edge of a continent?
ch: a chain of volcanoes and tall mountains
a wide, flat plain with no hills
it.h: Trenches form where Earth's plates push together.

it.q: Describe how you could use a world map to find a pattern in where volcanoes are.
it.ans: Mark each volcano on the map with a dot. Then look for places where the dots line up or cluster, such as around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, and compare them with maps of earthquakes and mountains.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Fossils as clues to past environments

it.q: A fossil is
ch: the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock
any rock with a pretty color
a plant that is alive today
a crystal that grows in caves
it.h: Fossils tell about life from the past.

it.q: A dinosaur footprint is preserved in rock. What can this trace fossil tell scientists?
ch: how big the animal was and how it walked
it.h: What can you learn from a footprint in mud today?

it.q: A rock layer with fossils is 30 cm thick. It formed at about 1 cm every 1,000 years. About how many years did the layer take to form?
it.h: Multiply the thickness by the years for each centimeter.

it.q: In a cliff, a lower layer has fossil corals and a higher layer has fossil land plants. What does this suggest?
ch: The area changed from a shallow sea to land.
The area changed from land to sea.
Corals and land plants lived together.
it.h: Where do corals live? Where do land plants live?

it.q: Fossils of ferns and tree trunks are found in rock in a very cold, icy place where no trees grow today. What does this suggest?
ch: The climate there was once much warmer.
The fossils were carried there by people.
it.h: What do ferns and trees need to grow?

it.q: Explain how a fern leaf that fell into mud long ago could become a fossil.
it.ans: The leaf was buried quickly in mud. More layers of mud and sand piled on top. Over a very long time, the mud hardened into rock and kept the shape of the leaf.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Testing erosion with a stream table

it.q: A stream table is a tilted tray of sand with water poured in at the top end. What does it model?
ch: a river wearing away and moving land
it.h: Watch where the water flows and what it carries.

it.q: A student wants to test whether the amount of water changes how much sand is carried away. What should stay the same in every trial?
ch: the slope of the tray and the kind of sand
it.h: In a fair test, only one thing changes.

it.q: In a stream table, 1 cup of water carried away 40 g of sand and 2 cups carried away 85 g. How many more grams did 2 cups carry away?
it.h: Subtract the two amounts.

it.q: A tray covered with grass loses much less soil than a bare tray when the same water is poured on. Why?
ch: Grass roots hold the soil in place.
it.h: What is under the grass, in the soil?

it.q: In a stream table, where does the carried sand pile up?
ch: at the low end, where the water slows down and spreads out
at the top of the tray
in the air above the tray
it.h: Moving water drops sand when it slows down.

it.q: Plan a stream table test to find out whether faster-flowing water causes more erosion.
it.ans: Use the same tray, slope and sand. Pour the same amount of water slowly in one trial and quickly in another. Collect and weigh the sand that washes to the bottom each time, and repeat each trial 3 times.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: Is air made of anything?

it.q: All matter is made of tiny particles that are
ch: big enough to see with our eyes
it.h: Even air is made of particles.

it.q: A basketball is weighed flat, then pumped full of air and weighed again. It is heavier the second time. What does this show?
ch: Air has mass because it is made of particles.
The pump added rubber to the ball.
it.h: What was added to the ball?

it.q: A cup is turned upside down and pushed straight down into a tub of water. A paper towel stuck in the bottom of the cup stays dry. Why?
ch: Air trapped in the cup takes up space and keeps the water out.
it.h: What fills the cup before it goes in the water?

it.q: A deflated ball weighed 410 grams. After pumping in air, it weighed 418 grams. What was the mass of the air pumped in, in grams?
it.h: Subtract the empty weight from the full weight.

it.q: In a model of a gas, how are the particles arranged?
ch: far apart and moving freely in all directions
it.h: Think about how a gas spreads to fill a balloon.

it.q: You smell popcorn from across the room even though you cannot see anything in the air. Use a particle model to explain why.
it.ans: Tiny particles from the popcorn move through the air and spread out across the room. They are too small to see, but when they reach my nose I can smell them.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: Where does sugar go when it dissolves?

it.q: When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar
ch: breaks into particles too small to see that spread through the water
it.h: Can you still taste it?

it.q: A student stirs salt into water until she can no longer see it. How can she prove the salt is still there?
ch: Let the water evaporate and look for salt crystals left behind.
Shine a flashlight on the water.
it.h: What happens if the water goes away?

it.q: A puddle disappears on a sunny day. Where did the water go?
ch: Its particles moved into the air as water vapor.
It was destroyed by the Sun.
it.h: The water particles are still somewhere.

it.q: 200 g of water and 15 g of sugar were mixed. The sugar dissolved. What was the total mass of the sugar water in grams?
it.h: Matter is not lost when it dissolves.

it.q: Food coloring is dropped into hot water and cold water. It spreads faster in hot water. What is the best explanation?
ch: Particles move faster in hot water.
it.h: Temperature affects how fast particles move.

it.q: Draw or describe a particle model of sugar before and after dissolving in water.
it.ans: Before: a sugar crystal is a tight cluster of sugar particles next to water particles. After: the sugar particles are spread out evenly among the water particles, too small to see.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: How can we identify a material by its properties?

it.q: A property is
ch: a characteristic used to describe or identify a material
it.h: Color and hardness are examples.

it.q: Which property could help you tell aluminum foil from plastic wrap?
ch: Aluminum conducts electricity and plastic does not.
it.h: Think of a test with a battery and a bulb.

it.q: A student has two white powders, salt and baking soda. Which test could help identify them?
ch: Add vinegar: baking soda fizzes and salt does not.
it.h: Look for a test where they act differently.

it.q: A mineral scratches glass, but glass cannot scratch it. What property is being tested?
it.h: Which one is harder?

it.q: A metal cube has a mass of 81 grams and a volume of 30 cubic centimeters. A different cube made of the same metal has a volume of 10 cubic centimeters. What is its mass in grams?
it.h: The volume is one third as much, so the mass is one third as much.

it.q: You find a shiny gray object. Describe two tests you could do to find out whether it is steel.
it.ans: Test it with a magnet; steel is attracted to magnets. Test it in a circuit; steel conducts electricity and will light a bulb.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: Evaporation, condensation and smells: evidence for invisible particles

it.q: Wet footprints on a hot sidewalk fade away in a few minutes. What happened to the water?
ch: Its tiny particles moved into the air as water vapor.
The water soaked into the Sun.
The water became part of the sidewalk forever.
it.h: Matter does not vanish. It can change to a form we cannot see.

it.q: Someone opens a jar of peanut butter across the room, and soon you can smell it. Which model explains this?
ch: Tiny particles from the peanut butter spread through the air to your nose.
The smell is a kind of light.
Your nose moved to the jar.
it.h: Smells reach you even though you cannot see anything traveling.

it.q: Drops of water form on the outside of a cold glass of juice on a warm day. Where did the water come from?
ch: Water vapor particles in the air cooled and condensed on the glass.
The ice melted through the glass.
it.h: The water is on the outside, and the glass is sealed.

it.q: A dish held 50 mL of water. After 3 days in a sunny window, 14 mL was left. How many milliliters evaporated?
it.h: Subtract what was left from what you started with.

it.q: A wet towel dries faster outside on a hot, windy day than inside a cool room. Why?
ch: Warmer, moving air helps water particles leave the towel faster.
Wind adds water to the towel.
it.h: Think about what heat does to how fast particles move.

it.q: Use a particle model to explain why a wet chalkboard drawing disappears as it dries.
it.ans: The water is made of particles too small to see. As they gain energy, they leave the board one by one and spread out in the air as water vapor, so the water seems to disappear even though it still exists.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: Mystery powders: identifying substances with property tests

it.q: A characteristic that can be used to identify a substance, such as color, hardness or whether it dissolves, is a
it.h: Scientists use these to tell substances apart.

it.q: Two white powders look the same. Which test would help tell them apart?
ch: Add a few drops of vinegar to each and watch for fizzing.
Look at the color of each.
Weigh two equal spoonfuls of each.
it.h: Choose a test that would give different results for different substances.

it.q: A white powder dissolves in water, does not fizz with vinegar and tastes sweet in a safe kitchen test. Which substance is it most likely?
it.h: Which of these dissolves and is sweet?

it.q: A student tested 4 powders with water, vinegar and iodine. How many tests did she do in all?
it.h: Each powder gets each of the three tests.

it.q: Why must a scientist use a clean spoon for each powder?
ch: to keep the powders from mixing, which would change the results
to make the test go faster
it.h: What could happen if bits of one powder got into another?

it.q: Explain why you should never identify an unknown substance in a lab by tasting it.
it.ans: Unknown substances might be harmful or poisonous. Scientists use safe tests such as looking, dissolving in water and mixing with vinegar instead.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Matter Is Made of Particles
lessons.n: Solids, liquids and gases: squeezing, spreading and expanding

it.q: In which state of matter are particles spread farthest apart?
ch: they are the same in all states
it.h: Think about which state fills any container.

it.q: A student pushes the plunger of a sealed syringe full of water and it barely moves. With a syringe full of air, the plunger moves in a lot. What does this show?
ch: Gas particles have space between them, but liquid particles are close together.
Water particles are bigger than the syringe.
it.h: Which one has more empty space to squeeze?

it.q: A balloon is moved from a warm room into a freezer and it shrinks. Which particle model explains this?
ch: The cold gas particles move slower and push less on the balloon.
it.h: How does temperature affect the speed of particles?

it.q: A balloon measured 60 cm around in a warm room and 52 cm around after an hour in a freezer. How many centimeters smaller was it?
it.h: Subtract the two measurements.

it.q: A solid block of ice keeps its shape, but melted ice takes the shape of its cup. Why?
ch: Particles in a solid are locked in place, while particles in a liquid can slide past each other.
it.h: Picture how the particles can move in each state.

it.q: Draw or describe particle models of water as ice, liquid water and water vapor.
it.ans: Ice: particles packed tightly in a neat pattern, only vibrating. Liquid water: particles close together but able to slide past each other. Water vapor: particles far apart and moving quickly in all directions.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: Does matter disappear when it melts or freezes?

it.q: When ice melts into water in a sealed container, its mass
it.h: The particles are rearranged, not lost.

it.q: A sealed jar of water weighed 350 g. After it was frozen, it still weighed 350 g. Which statement explains this?
ch: Freezing changes how the particles are arranged but not how many there are.
it.h: Did any particles leave the jar?

it.q: A chocolate bar with a mass of 45 g melts in a sealed bag. What is its mass after melting, in grams?
it.h: Melting is a change of state.

it.q: A pot of soup is boiled without a lid for 20 minutes. It has less mass afterward. Why?
ch: Water particles escaped into the air as steam.
it.h: Was the container sealed?

it.q: Which graph would best show that mass stays the same as ice melts in a sealed bag?
ch: a line graph of mass over time that stays flat
a bar graph of different colors of ice
a pie chart of water and air
it.h: You want to show mass at many times.

it.q: Explain why melting butter in a covered pan is a good way to test whether mass changes when a substance is heated.
it.ans: Covering the pan keeps any particles from escaping, so if the mass is the same before and after, it shows melting does not change the total mass.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: When does mixing make a new substance?

it.q: Which is evidence that a new substance has formed?
ch: gas bubbles form when two liquids are mixed
sand is stirred into water and sinks
it.h: Look for something new that was not there before.

it.q: Milk and vinegar are mixed. Soft white clumps form that were not there before. What does this show?
it.h: Is the solid something new?

it.q: Salt and pepper are mixed. You can still pick out the pepper and the salt grains. Is this a new substance?
ch: No, it is a mixture and each part keeps its properties.
Yes, it is a new substance.
it.h: Can you separate them again?

it.q: An iron nail left outside gets reddish-brown and flaky. What happened?
ch: The iron reacted with water and air to form rust, a new substance.
it.h: Rust is not the same as iron.

it.q: A class mixed four pairs of substances. Two pairs made gas, one pair changed color and one pair made no change. How many pairs showed evidence of a new substance?
it.h: Count the pairs that showed gas or a color change.

it.q: List three kinds of observations that can show a new substance has formed when two substances are mixed.
it.ans: A gas forms (bubbles or fizzing), the color changes, a new solid appears, there is a new smell, or the temperature changes.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: Where does the mass go when a gas is made?

it.q: Baking soda and vinegar are mixed in an open cup. The cup's total mass goes down. Why?
ch: A gas formed and escaped into the air.
it.h: Where do the bubbles go?

it.q: Baking soda and vinegar are mixed inside a sealed plastic bag. What happens to the total mass?
it.h: Can the gas leave the bag?

it.q: Before mixing in a sealed bag, the baking soda, vinegar and bag had a total mass of 160 g. What should the total mass be after the fizzing stops, in grams?
it.h: Nothing could get in or out.

it.q: In an open cup, the total mass was 160 g before mixing and 154 g after. How many grams of gas escaped?
it.h: Subtract the after mass from the before mass.

it.q: Which statement is always true when substances react in a closed container?
ch: The total mass before equals the total mass after.
New particles are created from nothing.
it.h: Particles are rearranged, not made or destroyed.

it.q: Explain why scientists use a closed container to study whether mass changes in a reaction.
it.ans: A closed container keeps gases from escaping or air from entering, so all the particles are measured before and after, giving an accurate comparison.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: How can we test a design fairly and improve it?

it.q: In a fair test, the one thing you change on purpose is the
it.h: Everything else stays the same.

it.q: A team tests how much water makes a fizzing tablet rocket fly highest. Which should stay the same in every trial?
ch: the size of the tablet and the type of canister
it.h: Only the amount of water should change.

it.q: In one trial, the canister lid was not snapped on tightly and the rocket did not fly. What should the team do?
ch: Count it as a failure point, fix the lid and repeat the trial.
Report it as the best result.
Change the amount of water and the tablet size at once.
it.h: A failure shows what part needs improvement.

it.q: The rocket flew 120 cm, 135 cm and 126 cm in three trials. What is the average height in centimeters?
it.h: Add the three heights and divide by 3.

it.q: Why do scientists repeat trials?
ch: to check that results are reliable
it.h: One trial might have a mistake.

it.q: Name one variable you would change and two variables you would keep the same to test which amount of baking soda makes a balloon inflate most.
it.ans: Change: the amount of baking soda. Keep the same: the amount of vinegar and the size of the bottle and balloon.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: Graphing mass data to show matter is conserved

it.q: Conservation of matter means that in a sealed container, the total mass
ch: stays the same during a change
it.h: Matter cannot be created or destroyed.

it.q: A student graphs the mass of a sealed bag every minute while ice melts inside. Which graph shape should she get?
ch: a line that goes up steeply
a line that drops to zero
it.h: Does the mass change in a sealed bag?

it.q: A sealed jar of water and an antacid tablet had a mass of 250 g before the tablet fizzed. What should the mass be after the fizzing stops?
it.h: Nothing entered or left the jar.

it.q: In a graph of mass over time, which axis usually shows time?
it.h: Time goes along the bottom of most graphs.

it.q: A student recorded the mass of a melting chocolate bar in a sealed bag at 0, 5, 10 and 15 minutes. How many data points will be on her graph?
it.h: Count the times she measured.

it.q: A graph of an open cup of fizzing vinegar and baking soda shows the mass going down over 5 minutes. Explain what the graph shows and why.
it.ans: The mass went down because the reaction made carbon dioxide gas that escaped into the air from the open cup. The matter was not destroyed; it left the cup as a gas.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: Physical and chemical changes in the kitchen

it.q: A change in which no new substance forms, such as melting butter, is a
it.h: Melted butter is still butter.

it.q: Which kitchen change makes a new substance?
ch: toasting bread until it turns brown
it.h: Look for a change you cannot easily undo, with a new color or smell.

it.q: An egg is cooked and changes from runny and clear to firm and white. What kind of change is this?
ch: chemical, because a new substance with new properties formed
physical, because it can be undone
it.h: Can you turn a cooked egg back into a raw egg?

it.q: A cook melts 250 g of chocolate in a bowl. What is the mass of the melted chocolate in grams?
it.h: Melting is a change of state.

it.q: Bread dough rises because yeast makes bubbles of gas. What does the gas show?
it.h: Gas bubbles that come from mixing are a sign of what kind of change?

it.q: Name one physical change and one chemical change you might see when making pancakes. Explain how you know each one.
it.ans: Physical: butter melting in the pan; it is still butter and can harden again. Chemical: the batter cooking into a pancake that is brown and firm, with new smells; it cannot change back into batter.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mixing, Reactions and Conservation of Matter
lessons.n: Separating mixtures: filters, magnets and evaporation

it.q: A combination of substances that keep their own properties is a
it.h: In trail mix, the nuts are still nuts.

it.q: Which tool would best separate sand from water?
ch: a filter, such as a coffee filter
it.h: Which tool lets liquid through but catches solid bits?

it.q: How could you get salt back from salt water?
ch: Let the water evaporate, leaving the salt behind.
Freeze it and pick out the salt.
it.h: Dissolved salt passes through filters. What happens when water leaves as a gas?

it.q: A mixture contains iron filings, sand and salt. What is the best first step?
ch: Use a magnet to pull out the iron filings.
it.h: Which material has a property the others do not have?

it.q: A mixture of sand and iron filings has a mass of 80 g. A magnet removes 35 g of iron. What is the mass of the sand in grams?
it.h: The total mass is the sum of its parts.

it.q: Explain why being able to separate a mixture shows that no new substance was made.
it.ans: Each part keeps its own properties in a mixture, so it can be separated by those properties (size, magnetism, dissolving). If a new substance formed, the original materials would be gone and could not be separated this simple way.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: Where do plants get the materials to grow?

it.q: Plants get most of the materials they use to build their bodies from
it.h: Soil gives only a small amount of minerals.

it.q: Which gas from the air do plants take in to make food?
it.h: Animals breathe this gas out.

it.q: A scientist in the 1600s planted a small willow tree in a pot of soil and gave it only water for 5 years. The tree gained about 74 kg, but the soil lost only about 0.06 kg. What does this evidence suggest?
ch: Most of the tree's mass did not come from the soil.
Trees lose mass as they grow.
Soil gains mass when trees grow.
it.h: Compare how much the tree gained with how much the soil lost.

it.q: A bean plant grew from a 1 g seed to a 46 g plant. The soil in its pot lost less than 1 g. About how many grams did the plant gain?
it.h: Subtract the seed's mass from the plant's mass.

it.q: Lettuce can be grown with its roots in water with a few added nutrients and no soil at all. What does this show?
ch: Plants do not need soil to get most of their building materials.
Soil is the only source of plant food.
it.h: Where did the lettuce's mass come from if there was no soil?

it.q: Your friend says, "A big tree is made mostly of soil." Explain why this is not correct.
it.ans: Plants build their bodies mostly from carbon dioxide from the air and water. Soil only gives small amounts of minerals. Experiments show the soil around a growing plant loses very little mass.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: How do plants capture energy from the Sun?

it.q: Plants use energy from
it.h: Leaves face toward this.

it.q: When a plant makes food, energy from sunlight is stored in
it.h: Food is a way to store energy.

it.q: A plant is kept in a dark closet for two weeks. Its leaves turn yellow and it stops growing. What is the best explanation?
ch: Without light, it cannot make the food it needs for energy.
Plants grow faster in the dark.
it.h: What does the plant need light for?

it.q: A class gave plants different hours of light each day. 4 hours: grew 3 cm. 8 hours: grew 7 cm. 12 hours: grew 11 cm. How many more centimeters did the 12-hour plant grow than the 4-hour plant?
it.h: Subtract to compare.

it.q: Which model shows how energy moves into a plant's food?
it.h: Start with where the energy comes from.

it.q: Describe what goes into a leaf and what comes out when a plant makes food.
it.ans: In: carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots and light energy from the Sun. Out: sugar that stores energy for the plant and oxygen that goes into the air.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: Where does the energy in our food come from?

it.q: Animals get the energy they need from
it.h: Think about why you get hungry.

it.q: A cow eats grass. A person drinks the cow's milk. Where did the energy in the milk originally come from?
it.h: Trace the energy back step by step.

it.q: Your body uses energy from food to
it.h: What do you do all day that needs energy?

it.q: An apple has about 95 Calories of energy. A banana has about 105 Calories. How many Calories are in both?
it.h: Add the two amounts.

it.q: Which chain correctly traces energy to a hawk?
it.h: Arrows show where the energy goes.

it.q: Trace the energy in a bowl of rice back to the Sun.
it.ans: The Sun's light energy was captured by the rice plant's leaves and stored in sugar and starch in the rice grains. When I eat the rice, my body uses that stored energy.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: A tree's mass from air: a famous experiment from the 1600s

it.q: In the 1600s, a scientist planted a small willow tree in a pot of soil and gave it only rainwater for 5 years. The tree gained about 164 pounds, but the soil lost only about 2 ounces. What does this show?
ch: The tree's mass did not come mainly from the soil.
Trees do not grow in pots.
it.h: Compare how much the tree gained with how much the soil lost.

it.q: The scientist thought the tree's mass came from water. Today we know that much of a plant's mass comes from
ch: carbon dioxide from the air, along with water
it.h: What gas do plants take in through their leaves?

it.q: A small tree weighed 5 pounds when planted and 169 pounds after 5 years. How many pounds did it gain?
it.h: Subtract the starting weight from the ending weight.

it.q: Why was it important that the pot of soil was covered and weighed at the start and end?
ch: so the scientist could tell how much the soil changed
to make the tree grow faster
it.h: What measurement did the scientist need to compare?

it.q: A pot of soil weighed 200 pounds at the start of a growing test and 199 pounds 14 ounces at the end. How many ounces did it lose? (1 pound = 16 ounces)
it.h: 200 pounds is 199 pounds and 16 ounces.

it.q: Explain why a plant can gain a lot of mass even though the soil barely changes.
it.ans: Plants make their food from carbon dioxide in the air and water, using energy from sunlight. Those materials become the plant's body, so very little mass comes from the soil.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: Testing what plants need: light, water and air

it.q: A part of an experiment that is changed on purpose is the
it.h: Only one thing should change in a fair test.

it.q: A student wants to test whether plants need light. Which setup is best?
ch: two identical plants with the same water and soil, one in light and one in a dark box
one plant in light with water and one in the dark without water
it.h: Change just one thing.

it.q: Four seedlings were grown in the dark for 2 weeks. They grew 6 cm, 8 cm, 7 cm and 7 cm. What was the average growth in centimeters?
it.h: Add the four numbers and divide by 4.

it.q: Seedlings grown in the dark are tall, thin and pale yellow. Seedlings in light are shorter, thick and green. What does this show?
ch: Plants need light to stay healthy and make food.
it.h: Which seedlings look healthy?

it.q: A leaf is coated on both sides with petroleum jelly so air cannot get in. After a week it turns yellow. What does this suggest?
ch: Leaves need to take in gas from the air.
it.h: Leaves have tiny openings for gases.

it.q: Plan a fair test to find out whether a plant needs water to grow.
it.ans: Use two identical plants in the same soil, light and temperature. Water one plant regularly and give the other none. Measure height and observe color every few days for two weeks.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Plants, Food and Energy from the Sun
lessons.n: How animals use the energy in food: moving, growing and staying warm

it.q: Unlike plants, animals cannot make their own food, so they get energy by
it.h: Animals cannot make their own food like plants.

it.q: A hummingbird eats nectar many times a day. Why does it need so much food?
ch: Its fast wing beats use a lot of energy.
It is storing food for plants.
it.h: Moving fast takes energy.

it.q: Which body activity uses energy from food?
ch: all of these: moving, growing, and keeping body temperature steady
it.h: Even resting animals use energy.

it.q: A student ate a 150 Calorie apple and a 350 Calorie sandwich. How many Calories in all?
it.h: Add the two amounts.

it.q: Why do many animals eat more food in the fall before winter?
ch: to store energy as body fat for the cold months
because food has less energy in fall
it.h: Food may be hard to find in winter.

it.q: Trace the energy in a hamburger back to the Sun.
it.ans: The Sun's light energy was used by grass to make food. A cow ate the grass and stored some of that energy in its body. When I eat a hamburger made from beef, I get energy that first came from the Sun.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: Who eats whom in an ecosystem?

it.q: An organism that makes its own food using sunlight is a
it.h: Plants and algae are examples.

it.q: In a food chain, an arrow points from
ch: the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it
it.h: The arrow shows the direction the energy and matter move.

it.q: In the food chain kelp -> sea urchin -> sea otter, which organism is a consumer that eats a producer?
it.h: Which animal eats the kelp?

it.q: Which organism is a producer in a California oak woodland?
it.h: Which one makes its own food?

it.q: A food web shows 4 producers, 7 herbivores and 3 predators. How many organisms are in the web?
it.h: Add all three groups.

it.q: Write a food chain with at least four organisms from one ecosystem and label the producer and consumers.
it.ans: Sample: grass (producer) -> grasshopper (consumer) -> lizard (consumer) -> hawk (consumer).

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: What happens to dead plants and animals?

it.q: Organisms that break down dead plants and animals are
it.h: Mushrooms and many bacteria do this job.

it.q: Which organism is a decomposer?
ch: a mushroom growing on a fallen log
it.h: Which one feeds on dead material?

it.q: What do decomposers return to the soil?
it.h: Think about why compost helps gardens.

it.q: A class weighed a pile of fruit scraps in a compost bin. Week 1: 800 g. Week 4: 350 g. How many grams were broken down?
it.h: Subtract the later mass from the earlier mass.

it.q: A log in a forest gets soft and crumbly over several years. What is causing this?
ch: fungi, bacteria and insects breaking it down
it.h: Look for living things on and in the log.

it.q: Explain why a forest floor does not pile up higher and higher with dead leaves every year.
it.ans: Decomposers like fungi, bacteria and worms break the leaves down into nutrients that go back into the soil, so the leaves do not keep piling up.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: How does matter move through an ecosystem?

it.q: Which statement best describes how matter moves in an ecosystem?
ch: It cycles between organisms and the environment again and again.
It is used once and disappears.
It comes only from the Sun.
It stays inside the producer forever.
it.h: Think about where nutrients go after something dies.

it.q: A plant takes in carbon dioxide and water. A rabbit eats the plant. The rabbit dies and decomposers break it down. Where does the matter go?
ch: back into the soil and air, where plants can use it again
it.h: Follow the matter all the way around.

it.q: Which part of an ecosystem is NOT living but is part of the matter cycle?
it.h: The environment is part of the cycle.

it.q: In a sealed jar ecosystem, a student put 6 water plants and 3 snails. Two weeks later she counted 8 plants and 5 snails. How many more organisms were in the jar?
it.h: Add each count, then compare totals.

it.q: Animals breathe out carbon dioxide. How does this connect them to plants?
ch: Plants take in the carbon dioxide to make food.
Plants breathe out carbon dioxide too and never use it.
Animals and plants do not connect.
it.h: Which gas do plants use?

it.q: Draw or describe a model that shows how matter moves among a plant, an animal, a decomposer and the environment.
it.ans: Plant takes carbon dioxide and water from the environment -> animal eats the plant -> animal's wastes and body go to decomposers -> decomposers return nutrients and carbon dioxide to soil and air -> plant uses them again.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: Changes to an ecosystem: invasive species and food web balance

it.q: A living thing brought to a new place where it spreads and harms the ecosystem is called
it.h: It "invades" a place where it did not live before.

it.q: In a food web, rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits. If all the foxes are removed, what will most likely happen first?
ch: The grass will grow taller right away.
it.h: What stops the rabbit population from growing?

it.q: An invasive plant grows so thickly in a stream that native plants get no light. How could this affect animals?
ch: Animals that eat the native plants may lose their food.
All the animals will get more food.
it.h: Follow the food web from the plants to the animals.

it.q: A lake had 400 native fish. After an invasive fish arrived, there were 250 native fish. How many fewer native fish were there?
it.h: Subtract the new number from the old number.

it.q: Why do invasive species often grow so fast in a new place?
ch: They may have no natural predators there.
it.h: What usually keeps a population in balance?

it.q: Explain how removing one organism from a food web can affect several other organisms.
it.ans: Every organism is connected. If a predator is removed, its prey may increase and eat more producers, so producers decrease and other animals that eat those producers lose food.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: Modeling a closed bottle ecosystem

it.q: A closed bottle ecosystem contains water, soil, plants, snails and tiny decomposers. What must come in from outside for it to keep working?
it.h: Matter stays inside a sealed bottle, but something must enter.

it.q: In a sealed bottle ecosystem, what do the snails provide for the plants?
ch: carbon dioxide and waste that decomposers turn into nutrients
it.h: Think about what animals give off.

it.q: What do the plants provide for the snails?
it.h: Plants make food and release a gas.

it.q: A sealed bottle ecosystem had 6 snails and 4 water plants. How many organisms that you can see were in the bottle?
it.h: Add the snails and plants.

it.q: A dead leaf in the bottle slowly breaks down. Which organisms are doing this?
ch: decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
it.h: Who recycles dead matter?

it.q: Explain how matter can cycle for months in a sealed bottle ecosystem.
it.ans: Plants use carbon dioxide, water and nutrients to make food and oxygen. Snails eat plants and use oxygen, giving off carbon dioxide and waste. Decomposers break down waste and dead parts into nutrients that plants reuse.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystems, Food Webs and Decomposers
lessons.n: Energy pyramids: why there are fewer predators than prey

it.q: In an energy pyramid, which level is at the bottom?
it.h: Which organisms capture energy from the Sun?

it.q: Most energy an animal takes in from food is
ch: used for living, such as moving and staying warm, or given off as heat
passed on to its predator completely
it.h: Animals are busy using energy all day.

it.q: Why does a food chain rarely have more than four or five levels?
ch: Too little energy is left to support more levels.
it.h: Energy gets smaller at each step.

it.q: Grass in a field stores 10,000 units of energy. Only about one tenth passes to the grasshoppers that eat it. About how many units reach the grasshoppers?
it.h: Divide by 10.

it.q: In a pond pyramid, algae are at the bottom, small fish in the middle and herons at the top. Which group has the most total energy?
it.h: The bottom of the pyramid is widest.

it.q: Explain why a large field might support thousands of grasshoppers but only a few hawks.
it.ans: Energy decreases at each level because most is used by each organism for living. Grass supports many grasshoppers, which support fewer birds or snakes, so only a little energy is left to support a few hawks.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Systems and Water
lessons.n: How do Earth's systems work together?

it.q: Earth's system made of rock, soil and sediment is the
it.h: "Geo" means Earth or ground.

it.q: The layer of gases that surrounds Earth is the
it.h: It is the air.

it.q: Ocean waves crash against a cliff and wear it away over many years. Which two systems are interacting?
it.h: Waves are water; cliffs are rock.

it.q: Plant roots grow into cracks in rock and break it apart. Which two systems are interacting?
it.h: Roots are part of a living thing.

it.q: A volcano released ash that blocked some sunlight. The average temperature in a nearby region was 18°C the year before and 16.5°C the year after. How many degrees cooler was it?
it.h: Subtract the two temperatures.

it.q: Describe one example of the atmosphere affecting the geosphere.
it.ans: Sample: Wind blows sand against rocks in the desert and slowly wears them into new shapes.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Systems and Water
lessons.n: How does water move around Earth?

it.q: When liquid water changes into water vapor, it is called
it.h: Think about a puddle drying up.

it.q: When water vapor cools and forms tiny drops in clouds, it is called
it.h: Think of drops forming on a cold glass.

it.q: What provides the energy that drives the water cycle?
it.h: What warms the water so it evaporates?

it.q: Rain falls on a hill and flows over the ground into a creek. This water is called
it.h: It runs off the surface.

it.q: A rain gauge collected 18 mm on Monday, 25 mm on Tuesday and 9 mm on Wednesday. How many millimeters fell in all?
it.h: Add the three amounts.

it.q: Describe the path a drop of water could take from the ocean to a mountain and back to the ocean.
it.ans: It evaporates from the ocean into the atmosphere, condenses into a cloud, falls as snow on a mountain, melts in spring, flows down a river and returns to the ocean.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Systems and Water
lessons.n: Where is Earth's water?

it.q: About how much of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
it.h: The oceans hold almost all of it.

it.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water found?
ch: frozen in glaciers and ice caps
it.h: Think of Antarctica and Greenland.

it.q: A pie graph of Earth's water shows a huge slice for oceans and a tiny slice for fresh water. What does this tell us?
ch: Fresh water is a small part of Earth's water, so it is precious.
There is plenty of fresh water everywhere.
it.h: Compare the size of the slices.

it.q: If Earth's water were 100 cups, about 97 cups would be salt water. About how many cups would be fresh water?
it.h: Subtract 97 from 100.

it.q: Which is the largest source of fresh water that is liquid?
it.h: Much of it is stored underground.

it.q: Explain why people cannot simply drink ocean water even though Earth has so much water.
it.ans: Ocean water is salty, and drinking it would make people sick. Removing the salt takes a lot of energy and money, so people mostly rely on the small amount of fresh water.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Systems and Water
lessons.n: How can communities protect Earth's resources?

it.q: Which action helps save water at home?
ch: running the hose while washing a car
it.h: Which choice stops waste?

it.q: Fertilizer from farms washes into a river during rain. Which problem could this cause?
ch: algae grows too fast and harms fish
it.h: Fertilizer helps plants grow, even in water.

it.q: A school wants to reduce the trash it sends to the landfill. Which solution helps most?
ch: composting food scraps and recycling paper
it.h: Find ways to reuse or recycle matter.

it.q: A leaky faucet wastes 15 liters of water a day. How many liters does it waste in a week?
it.h: A week has 7 days.

it.q: A city plants native plants that need little water instead of grass lawns. How does this help?
it.h: Native plants are used to the local climate.

it.q: Describe one way people's activities harm Earth's land, water or air, and one way a community can reduce that harm.
it.ans: Sample: Trash washes from streets into storm drains and then into the ocean. A community can put screens on storm drains and hold beach and street cleanups.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Systems and Water
lessons.n: Systems in action: wildfires, floods and landslides

it.q: Which Earth system includes all living things?
it.h: "Bio" means life.

it.q: A wildfire burns a forest and sends smoke into the sky. Which two systems are interacting when the smoke rises?
it.h: What burned, and where did the smoke go?

it.q: After a wildfire, heavy rain falls on the burned hillside and mud slides downhill. Why is a landslide more likely after a fire?
ch: Plant roots that held the soil were burned.
it.h: What normally holds soil on a slope?

it.q: A hillside lost 2 cm of soil a year before a fire and 14 cm the year after. How many times as much soil was lost after the fire?
it.h: Divide the larger number by the smaller.

it.q: A river floods and spreads mud over farm fields. Which systems interact?
it.h: Water carried soil.

it.q: Describe how a flood can affect all four Earth systems.
it.ans: Hydrosphere: river water rises. Geosphere: water moves soil and rock. Biosphere: plants and animals are harmed or habitats change. Atmosphere: storms bring the rain that causes the flood, and water evaporates back afterward.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why do things fall down everywhere on Earth?

it.q: The force that pulls objects toward Earth's center is
it.h: It is why a dropped apple falls.

it.q: A child in California and a child in Australia each drop a ball. Which way do the balls fall?
ch: toward the center of Earth for both
up for the child in Australia
it.h: "Down" always means toward Earth's center.

it.q: Which observation is evidence that gravity pulls things down?
ch: Rain falls from clouds to the ground.
A balloon floats in a breeze.
it.h: Look for something that moves toward the ground.

it.q: A ball was dropped from a balcony 3 times. It took 1.2, 1.3 and 1.1 seconds to hit the ground. What was the average time in seconds?
it.h: Add the times and divide by 3.
