it.q: A model shows people standing all around a globe with arrows. Which arrows show gravity correctly?
ch: arrows pointing from each person toward the globe's center
arrows pointing to the top of the page
arrows pointing away from the globe
arrows pointing to the North Pole
it.h: Gravity pulls toward the center from every side.

it.q: Explain why people at the bottom of a globe do not fall off Earth.
it.ans: Gravity pulls everything toward Earth's center, so "down" for every person is toward the middle of Earth, no matter where they stand.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why is the Sun so much brighter than other stars?

it.q: The Sun is
it.h: It makes its own light.

it.q: Why does the Sun look much bigger and brighter than the stars we see at night?
ch: It is much closer to Earth.
It is the biggest star in the universe.
It is the only star that makes light.
Other stars are tiny and dim up close.
it.h: How does distance change how bright a light looks?

it.q: Two identical flashlights are turned on. One is 2 meters away and one is 20 meters away. Which looks brighter?
it.h: This models how distance affects brightness.

it.q: A light meter read 400 units at 1 meter from a lamp and 25 units at 4 meters. How many units dimmer was it at 4 meters?
it.h: Subtract the readings.

it.q: Compared with other stars, the Sun is
it.h: Many stars are much bigger than the Sun.

it.q: Explain why stars that are much bigger and brighter than the Sun look like tiny points of light.
it.ans: They are extremely far away compared with the Sun, so their light spreads out over a huge distance and looks dim and small from Earth.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why do shadows change during the day?

it.q: Day and night happen because
it.h: Earth spins once about every 24 hours.

it.q: In the morning the Sun is in the east. Which way does a flagpole's shadow point?
it.h: Shadows point away from the light.

it.q: When is a shadow outside usually the shortest?
ch: around midday, when the Sun is highest
it.h: The higher the light, the shorter the shadow.

it.q: A stick's shadow was 140 cm at 8 a.m. and 35 cm at noon. How many centimeters shorter was it at noon?
it.h: Subtract the noon length from the morning length.

it.q: The Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west each day. Why?
ch: Earth rotates from west to east.
The Sun orbits Earth each day.
it.h: Think about a merry-go-round: the scenery seems to move the opposite way.

it.q: Describe how the length of a tree's shadow changes from morning to afternoon.
it.ans: In the morning the shadow is long and points west. It gets shorter until about midday, then grows longer again in the afternoon, pointing east.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Why do we see different stars in different seasons?

it.q: How long does it take Earth to orbit the Sun once?
it.h: One orbit is one year.

it.q: A group of stars that forms a pattern people have named is a
it.h: Orion is an example.

it.q: Why can we see stars only at night?
ch: During the day, sunlight is so bright that it hides the stars' light.
Stars turn off in the day.
Stars move under Earth in the day.
Clouds always hide stars in the day.
it.h: The stars are still there in the daytime.

it.q: Orion is easy to see on winter evenings but not on summer evenings. Why?
ch: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different parts of space in different seasons.
Orion only shines in cold weather.
The Moon blocks Orion all summer.
it.h: Think about which way the night side of Earth faces.

it.q: A class counted visible stars in one constellation on four nights: 7, 9, 8 and 8. What was the average?
it.h: Add the counts and divide by 4.

it.q: Explain why the stars seem to move across the sky during one night.
it.ans: Earth rotates on its axis, so stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west during the night, just like the Sun appears to move during the day.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Daylight hours through the year

it.q: In California, the days with the most hours of daylight come in
ch: they are the same all year
it.h: Think about when it stays light late in the evening.

it.q: A student recorded daylight in her town: December, about 10 hours; March, about 12 hours; June, about 14 hours; September, about 12 hours. What pattern does this show?
ch: Daylight is longest in June, shortest in December, and repeats each year.
Daylight is the same every month.
Daylight gets shorter every month forever.
it.h: Look at the highest and lowest numbers.

it.q: Sunrise was at 6:00 a.m. and sunset was at 8:00 p.m. How many hours of daylight were there?
it.h: Count from 6 a.m. to noon, then from noon to 8 p.m.

it.q: In winter, the noon Sun is lower in the sky than in summer. How does this affect noon shadows?
ch: There are no shadows in winter.
Shadows are the same all year.
it.h: A low light source makes long shadows.

it.q: A town had 14 hours of daylight in June and 10 hours in December. How many more hours of daylight were there in June?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Describe how you would collect data to show that the amount of daylight changes during the year.
it.ans: Record the sunrise and sunset times once a week or once a month for a whole year, calculate the hours of daylight each time, and make a line graph of daylight hours by month.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Gravity, Stars and Patterns in the Sky
lessons.n: Weight, mass and gravity on Earth and the Moon

it.q: The force of gravity pulling on an object is its
it.h: A bathroom scale measures this pull.

it.q: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. What happens to her mass?
it.h: Mass is the amount of matter. Does she lose any matter?

it.q: The Moon's gravity is about one sixth as strong as Earth's. What happens to the astronaut's weight on the Moon?
ch: It is about one sixth of her Earth weight.
It is six times her Earth weight.
it.h: Weight depends on the pull of gravity.

it.q: A backpack weighs 60 newtons on Earth. The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of Earth's. About how much would it weigh on the Moon in newtons?
it.h: Divide by 6.

it.q: A ball is dropped on Earth and on the Moon. On both, which way does it fall?
ch: toward the center of that world
it.h: Gravity pulls objects toward the center of the large body.

it.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight.
it.ans: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, so it changes on worlds with different gravity.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: Is it alive? Looking for cells

it.q: What do all living things have in common?
ch: They are made of one or more cells
They can all move from place to place
They all have leaves or roots
They are all large enough to see
it.h: Think about the smallest unit that every living thing is built from.

it.q: A student puts a drop of pond water under a microscope and sees tiny moving things that each have a cell membrane, take in food and divide. What can the student conclude?
ch: The tiny things are single-celled living organisms
The tiny things are dust floating in water
The tiny things are bubbles of air
The tiny things are rocks that move with currents
it.h: Which characteristics of life are described?

it.q: A microscope has a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
it.h: Total magnification is found by multiplying the two lens powers.

it.q: A cork slice and a slice of onion skin both show many small box-like units under a microscope. Which statement does this evidence support?
ch: Cork is made of atoms you can see
Cells are only found in animals

it.q: Kenji says a rock is alive because it can grow larger when minerals build up on it. Use the idea of cells to explain why a rock is not a living thing.
it.ans: A rock is not made of cells. Living things are made of one or more cells that use energy, grow and reproduce. Minerals piling up on a rock is not cell growth.
it.h: What would you see if you looked at a rock under a microscope?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: Inside a cell: parts with jobs

it.q: Which cell part controls the cell's activities and contains its genetic material (DNA)?
it.h: Think of the cell's "control center."

it.q: Which cell part controls what enters and leaves the cell?
Muscle cells use a lot of energy. Which cell part would you expect to find in large numbers in muscle cells?
it.h: Which part releases energy from food?

it.q: A model compares a cell to a school. Which pairing is the best match?
ch: the nucleus is like the principal's office
the cell membrane is like the cafeteria
the mitochondria are like the library shelves
the cytoplasm is like the front gate

it.q: A cell's membrane is damaged so that it can no longer control what enters and leaves. Predict one problem the cell would have.
it.ans: Harmful substances could enter, or water and needed materials could leak out, so the cell could not keep the conditions it needs to stay alive.
it.h: Think about what the membrane normally keeps in and keeps out.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: Plant cells and animal cells

it.q: Which part is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
it.h: Which part captures light to make food?

it.q: Which pair of parts do BOTH plant and animal cells have?
Under a microscope, a cell has a rigid boundary, many green structures and one large water-filled sac. Which kind of cell is it most likely?
ch: a leaf cell from a plant
it.h: Look for the parts that only plant cells have.

it.q: Why can a plant stand upright without a skeleton?
ch: Cell walls and water-filled vacuoles make plant cells stiff
Plant cells have bones inside them
The nucleus holds the plant up

it.q: Make a T-chart comparison in words: list two parts found in both plant and animal cells and two parts found only in plant cells.
it.ans: Both: nucleus, cell membrane (also cytoplasm, mitochondria). Plant only: cell wall, chloroplasts (also a large central vacuole).

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: Cells working as a system

it.q: In a cell, the nucleus sends instructions, the mitochondria supply energy and the membrane controls what goes in and out. Why is a cell called a system?
ch: Its parts interact to carry out the functions of life
It is the largest structure in the body
it.h: A system is a group of parts that work together.

it.q: A single-celled organism such as an amoeba must do everything to stay alive with just one cell. Which job must that one cell do?
ch: take in food and get rid of wastes

it.q: A nerve cell is long and thin with branches. How does this shape help it do its job?
ch: It can carry signals over long distances to other cells
It can store large amounts of water
It can make the cell wall stronger
it.h: Think about what nerve cells do in the body.

it.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 1 bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 1 hour?
it.h: Count the divisions in 60 minutes: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then...

it.q: Explain why many different kinds of cells are found in a multicellular organism like a person.
it.ans: Different cells have different structures that fit different jobs, such as muscle cells for movement, nerve cells for signals and red blood cells for carrying oxygen.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: The cell membrane: diffusion and osmosis

it.q: The movement of particles from an area where they are crowded to an area where they are less crowded is
it.h: Think about how a smell spreads through a room.

it.q: The cell membrane lets oxygen and water pass through but keeps many larger molecules out. Which word describes the membrane?
it.h: The membrane "selects" what can pass.

it.q: A raw egg with its shell dissolved away is placed in corn syrup overnight and shrinks. Corn syrup has very little water. What happened?
ch: Water moved out of the egg toward the syrup, where there was less water.
it.h: Water moves across a membrane toward the side with less water and more dissolved material.

it.q: A potato slice had a mass of 10.0 g. After an hour in salt water, its mass was 8.6 g. How many grams did it lose?
it.h: Subtract the final mass from the starting mass.

it.q: Oxygen is more crowded in the blood than inside a working muscle cell. Which way does oxygen diffuse?
ch: from the blood into the muscle cell
from the cell into the blood
only when the cell is dividing
it.h: Particles spread from crowded to less crowded areas.

it.q: Explain why wilted celery becomes firm again when its cut end is placed in fresh water.
it.ans: The celery cells have less water than the fresh water around them, so water moves into the cells by osmosis. The cells swell and press against their cell walls, making the stalk firm.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life
lessons.n: Single-celled organisms: one cell does it all

it.q: A paramecium, an amoeba and a bacterium are all made of just one cell. Organisms like these are called
it.h: "Uni" means one.

it.q: A paramecium is a single-celled organism covered with tiny hairs that beat back and forth. What is the job of these hairs?
ch: to help it move and sweep in food
it.h: What does a paramecium need to do to survive?

it.q: Bacteria cells do not have a nucleus. Where is their genetic material?
it.h: The genetic material still has to be inside the cell.

it.q: A bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes. Starting with 1 bacterium, how many will there be after 1 hour?
it.h: Double it three times: 20, 40 and 60 minutes.

it.q: Some single-celled algae, like euglena, have chloroplasts. What can they do that an amoeba cannot?
ch: make their own food using light
it.h: What do chloroplasts do?

it.q: A single cell in your body depends on other cells, but a single-celled organism can live on its own. Explain why.
it.ans: A single-celled organism must carry out all life functions itself, such as getting food, getting rid of waste, moving and reproducing. Cells in a multicellular body are specialized for one job and depend on other cells for the rest.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Body as a System
lessons.n: From cells to organ systems

it.q: A group of similar cells that work together to do one job is called
it.h: This level is just one step bigger than a cell.

it.q: The heart is made of muscle tissue, nerve tissue and connective tissue working together. What level of organization is the heart?
Which list is in order from simplest to most complex?
ch: muscle cell, muscle tissue, heart, circulatory system
heart, muscle cell, circulatory system, muscle tissue
circulatory system, heart, muscle tissue, muscle cell
muscle tissue, muscle cell, heart, circulatory system
it.h: Start with the smallest living unit.

it.q: The stomach, small intestine and liver work together to break down food. Together they are part of the
Explain how a single muscle cell is connected to the whole human body using the levels of organization.
it.ans: Muscle cells form muscle tissue, muscle tissue forms organs such as muscles or the heart, those organs make up organ systems such as the muscular system, and the systems together make the organism.
it.h: Name each level from cell to organism.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Body as a System
lessons.n: Moving oxygen and nutrients

it.q: Which organ system carries oxygen and nutrients to cells all over the body?
it.h: This system includes the heart and blood vessels.

it.q: In the lungs, oxygen moves from tiny air sacs into the blood. Which two systems are interacting?
The small intestine absorbs nutrients from digested food. Where do the nutrients go next?
ch: into the blood, which carries them to cells
into the lungs to be breathed out
into the bones to be stored as calcium only
into the stomach to be digested again

it.q: A student counted 18 breaths in 1 minute while resting. At this rate, how many breaths would the student take in 15 minutes?
it.h: Multiply the breaths per minute by the number of minutes.

it.q: Trace the path of oxygen from the air into a muscle cell in your leg.
it.ans: Air enters the nose or mouth, travels down the trachea to the lungs, oxygen passes into blood in the air sacs, the heart pumps the blood through blood vessels to the leg, and oxygen moves from the blood into the muscle cell.
it.h: Start at the nose and name each stop along the way.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Body as a System
lessons.n: Sensing and responding

it.q: Which organ system receives information from the senses and sends signals to muscles?
it.h: This system includes the brain, spinal cord and nerves.

it.q: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away before you even feel pain. Why does this happen so fast?
ch: Sensory nerves send a signal through the spinal cord, which signals muscles right away
Your skin moves your hand by itself
Your blood carries the message to your hand

it.q: Sense receptors in your eyes respond to light. What do they do with that information?
ch: send it as nerve signals to the brain
store it in the eye forever

it.q: Students measured reaction times by catching a falling ruler. Five trials gave 0.22, 0.20, 0.25, 0.21 and 0.22 seconds. What is the mean reaction time in seconds?
it.h: Add all five times, then divide by 5.

it.q: Explain how the nervous, muscular and skeletal systems work together when you kick a ball.
it.ans: Eyes sense the ball and send signals to the brain; the brain sends signals through nerves to leg muscles; muscles contract and pull on bones, which move the leg to kick.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Body as a System
lessons.n: Systems working together during exercise

it.q: When you run, your muscle cells need more oxygen. Which change helps deliver it?
ch: Your heart beats faster and you breathe faster
it.h: Think about which two systems bring oxygen to cells.

it.q: A student's heart rate was 70 beats per minute at rest and 140 beats per minute after running. What was the percent increase?
it.h: Find the increase, divide by the starting value and multiply by 100.

it.q: Why do you sweat during exercise?
ch: Sweat evaporating from your skin helps cool your body
Sweat adds oxygen to your blood

it.q: After exercise, a student's heart rate slowly returned to normal over 5 minutes. What does this show?
ch: Body systems adjust to keep conditions inside the body stable

it.q: Describe two systems that change during exercise and explain why each change helps the body.
it.ans: Respiratory: breathing speeds up to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Circulatory: heart rate rises to deliver oxygen and nutrients to working muscles faster.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Body as a System
lessons.n: Defending the body: skin, immune and circulatory systems together

it.q: The body's first line of defense against germs is the
it.h: It covers your whole body.

it.q: White blood cells travel through the blood to an infected cut. Which two systems are working together?
ch: the immune system and the circulatory system
it.h: Which system carries the white blood cells?

it.q: A cut becomes red, warm and swollen. What is happening?
ch: More blood flows to the area, bringing white blood cells to fight germs.
The skin is turning into muscle.
The nerves are making new blood.
it.h: Think about why extra blood would help.

it.q: A normal white blood cell count is about 7,000 per drop-sized sample. During an infection it rose to 15,000. How many more white blood cells were counted?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: How does a vaccine help protect the body?
ch: It trains the immune system to recognize a germ so it can respond faster later.
It makes the heart beat faster.
it.h: The immune system can remember germs.

it.q: Explain how the respiratory system and immune system work together to keep germs out of the lungs.
it.ans: The airways are lined with sticky mucus and tiny hairs that trap dust and germs and move them up and out. Coughing and sneezing force them out, and white blood cells attack germs that get through.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Two ways to make offspring

it.q: Reproduction that needs only one parent is called
it.h: "A-" can mean "without." Without what kind of partner?

it.q: A strawberry plant sends out a runner that grows into a new plant. How do the genes of the new plant compare with the parent's?
ch: They are identical to the parent's genes
Half come from each of two parents
The new plant has no genes

it.q: In sexual reproduction, where do an offspring's genes come from?
ch: half from each of two parents
it.h: Two parents each give one sex cell.

it.q: Two black rabbits have a litter. Some babies are black and one is brown. Which type of reproduction best explains this variation?
ch: sexual reproduction, which mixes genes from two parents
asexual reproduction, which copies one parent

it.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction for an organism.
it.ans: Advantage: it is fast and needs only one parent, so a population can grow quickly. Disadvantage: offspring are all genetically alike, so a disease or change in the environment could harm all of them.
it.h: Think about speed and about variety among offspring.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Animal behaviors that help reproduction

it.q: A male peacock spreads its colorful tail in front of a female. This behavior most likely helps it
Emperor penguin fathers hold an egg on their feet for about two months in the Antarctic winter. How does this behavior help the species reproduce?
ch: It keeps the egg warm so the chick can develop and hatch
It helps the father find food
It teaches the egg to swim
It keeps predators away from the ocean
it.h: What would happen to an egg left on the ice?

it.q: Some songbirds sing loudly in spring. Scientists found males that sang more song types mated earlier. Which conclusion fits?
Wolves in a pack bring food back to the den for pups. What is the main benefit to the pack?
ch: More pups survive to become adults

it.q: Describe one animal behavior that increases the chance that offspring will survive, and explain how it helps.
it.ans: Example: a mother bear guards her cubs and teaches them to find food, which protects them from predators and helps them survive until they can live alone.
it.h: Think of protecting, feeding or teaching young.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Plant structures for reproduction

it.q: What part of a flowering plant makes seeds?
Bright red, tube-shaped flowers that make lots of nectar are often visited by hummingbirds. How do these flower traits help the plant?
ch: They attract hummingbirds that carry pollen to other flowers
They protect the plant from frost
They help the roots take in water
They make the leaves grow larger
it.h: What does a hummingbird carry from flower to flower?

it.q: Burdock seeds have tiny hooks that stick to animal fur. What does this structure help the plant do?
ch: spread its seeds to new places

it.q: Maple seeds have wing-like parts that spin as they fall. Why does this help the maple tree?
ch: The wind carries seeds farther from the parent tree

it.q: Explain why a plant that grows a sweet fruit around its seeds might have its seeds spread farther than a plant with plain, dry seeds.
it.ans: Animals eat the sweet fruit and carry the seeds away; the seeds pass through or are dropped in new places, sometimes far from the parent plant, where they can grow without competing with it.
it.h: Who eats fruit, and where do they go afterward?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Genes and environment shape growth

it.q: Two cuttings from the same plant have identical genes. One grows in sunlight and becomes tall; the other grows in shade and stays short. What caused the difference?
it.h: The genes are identical, so what was different?

it.q: A Great Dane puppy and a Chihuahua puppy eat the same food and get the same care. The Great Dane grows much larger. What best explains the difference?
A plant grew from 12 cm to 30 cm in 6 weeks. What was its average growth rate in cm per week?
it.h: Find the total growth, then divide by the number of weeks.

it.q: Which is an environmental factor that can affect how large an animal grows?
ch: the amount of food it eats

it.q: Plan a simple investigation to test whether fertilizer affects the growth of bean plants. Name the variable you change, the variable you measure and two things you keep the same.
it.ans: Change: amount of fertilizer (none versus some). Measure: plant height after 3 weeks. Keep the same: type of bean, amount of water, light, pot size and soil.
it.h: Only one thing should be different between the groups.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Predicting offspring traits with Punnett squares

it.q: In sexual reproduction, each parent passes on
ch: one of its two copies (alleles) of each gene
only the genes for eye color
it.h: Offspring get half of their genetic information from each parent.

it.q: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant over white (p). A plant with Pp has which flower color?
it.h: A dominant allele shows its trait when at least one copy is present.

it.q: Two Pp pea plants are crossed. Which offspring allele pairs are possible?
it.h: Fill in a 2 by 2 Punnett square with P and p from each parent.

it.q: In a Punnett square for Pp x Pp, how many of the 4 boxes show pp?
it.h: Each parent gives P or p.

it.q: Why do offspring of sexual reproduction look different from their siblings?
ch: Each gets a different combination of alleles from the parents.
Only the mother's genes are used.
it.h: Think about the many possible combinations.

it.q: Explain why two purple-flowered pea plants can have a white-flowered offspring.
it.ans: Both parents could be Pp. Each can pass on the recessive p allele, and an offspring that gets p from both parents (pp) has white flowers.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Drought, fertilizer and crowding: environmental effects on plant growth

it.q: A factor such as water, light, temperature or nutrients that affects how an organism grows is
it.h: It comes from the organism's surroundings.

it.q: Corn plants with identical genes are grown in two fields. One field gets rain and the other has a drought. The rainy field's plants grow taller. What caused the difference?
it.h: The genes were the same.

it.q: Bean plants given fertilizer grew to 32 cm. Plants with no fertilizer grew to 24 cm. How many centimeters taller were the fertilized plants?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Radish seeds were planted 1 cm apart in one tray and 5 cm apart in another. The crowded radishes were smaller. Which explanation fits best?
ch: Crowded plants competed for light, water and nutrients.
it.h: What do neighboring plants share?

it.q: Hydrangea flowers can be pink or blue depending on the soil chemistry. What does this show?
ch: The environment can affect a plant's traits.
All hydrangeas are the same color.
it.h: Same plant type, different soil.

it.q: Plan an investigation to test whether the amount of fertilizer affects tomato plant growth.
it.ans: Use plants of the same variety and size, the same pots, soil, light and water. Give groups different amounts of fertilizer (0, 5 and 10 g per week). Measure height and count tomatoes weekly for 6 weeks, with several plants per group.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Growing Up and Passing On - Reproduction and Growth
lessons.n: Food, temperature and space: environmental effects on animal growth

it.q: A young trout grows in a stream. Which of these is an environmental factor that can change how fast it grows?
it.h: Environmental factors come from outside the organism.

it.q: Goldfish kept in a small, crowded tank stay small, but the same kind of goldfish in a large pond grow much larger. What does this show?
ch: Space and resources in the environment affect growth.
Small tanks change fish into a new species.
Goldfish size is set only by genes.
it.h: What is different between the tank and the pond?

it.q: Tadpoles in 25 °C water turned into frogs in 40 days. Tadpoles in 15 °C water took 70 days. How many more days did the cooler tadpoles take?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Children today in many countries are taller on average than children 150 years ago. Which explanation is best supported?
ch: Better nutrition and health care in the environment.
Children's genes changed completely in 150 years.
it.h: Genes change very slowly in a population.

it.q: Two puppies from the same litter are given different diets. The well-fed puppy grows larger. What caused the difference?
it.h: They have the same parents.

it.q: Give one genetic factor and one environmental factor that affect how tall a person grows.
it.ans: Genetic: the height genes inherited from parents. Environmental: nutrition (enough protein and other nutrients), sleep, or health during childhood.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Temperature, thermal energy and moving particles

it.q: Temperature is a measure of
ch: the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance
the total mass of a substance
how much space a substance takes up
it.h: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. What is moving in a substance?

it.q: A cup of tea and a bathtub of water are both at 40 °C. Which has more thermal energy?
ch: the bathtub, because it has many more particles
the tea, because it is smaller
they have the same thermal energy
it.h: Thermal energy depends on the total energy of all the particles.

it.q: When you rub your hands together quickly, they get warm. What is happening to energy?
ch: The kinetic energy of your moving hands is transferred into thermal energy
Your hands are creating new energy

it.q: How do the particles in hot soup compare to the particles in cold soup?
A skateboard rolling across the playground slows down and stops. Explain where its kinetic energy went.
it.ans: Friction between the wheels, the bearings and the ground transferred the skateboard's kinetic energy into thermal energy (and a little sound), warming the wheels and ground slightly. The energy was transferred, not destroyed.
it.h: Energy is not destroyed. What happens when surfaces rub?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: How heat moves: conduction, convection and radiation

it.q: Heat transfer through direct contact between objects is
it.h: Think of touching a hot pan.

it.q: In a pot of water on a stove, warm water rises and cooler water sinks, forming a loop. This is
You feel warmth on your face from a campfire even though you are not touching it and the air between you is cool. Which type of transfer is this?
In which direction does thermal energy move between a cold can of juice and your warm hand?
ch: from your hand to the can
from the can to your hand
it.h: Energy always flows from warmer to cooler.

it.q: Explain why a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot faster than a wooden spoon.
it.ans: Metal is a good conductor, so thermal energy moves quickly from the hot soup through the metal; wood is an insulator, so energy moves through it slowly.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Mass, material and temperature change

it.q: A student heats 100 g of water and 300 g of water on identical burners for 2 minutes. Which will have the larger temperature increase?
it.h: The same energy is spread over fewer particles in the smaller mass.

it.q: Equal masses of sand and water sit in the same sunlight for 30 minutes. The sand warms 12 °C and the water warms 4 °C. What does this show?
ch: Different materials change temperature by different amounts with the same energy
Sand has more mass than water
The sunlight was stronger on the sand

it.q: Equal masses of sand and water sat in the same sunlight for 30 minutes. The sand warmed 12 °C and the water warmed 4 °C. How many times larger was the sand's temperature increase?
it.h: Divide the sand's change by the water's change.

it.q: Which question can be answered by heating different masses of the same liquid for the same time and measuring the temperature change?
ch: How does mass affect temperature change?

it.q: Identify the independent variable, dependent variable and two controlled variables in this investigation: Students added the same amount of heat to 50 g, 100 g and 150 g of cooking oil and recorded the temperature increase.
it.ans: Independent: mass of oil. Dependent: temperature increase. Controlled: type of liquid (oil), amount of heat added, starting temperature, container type.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Design challenge: control the flow of heat

it.q: A team must design a lunch box that keeps food cold for 4 hours, costs less than $5 and fits in a backpack. What are the cost and size limits called?
it.h: Constraints are limits; criteria describe what success looks like.

it.q: Which material would be best for the inside lining of a cooler?
ch: foam, because it is an insulator
aluminum foil only, because it conducts heat

it.q: A shiny, reflective cover is placed over a car windshield on a sunny day. How does it keep the car cooler?
ch: It reflects radiation from the Sun
It conducts heat into the car

it.q: Design A kept an ice cube frozen for 96 minutes and Design B for 72 minutes. How many minutes longer did Design A work?
it.h: Subtract the shorter time from the longer time.

it.q: Name one criterion and one constraint for a device that keeps a cup of soup hot for a school field trip.
it.ans: Criterion: keeps soup above 60 °C for 3 hours. Constraint: must cost under $10, be safe for students and fit in a backpack.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Thermal equilibrium: heat flows until temperatures match

it.q: An ice cube is held in a warm hand. In which direction does thermal energy flow?
ch: from the hand into the ice
from the ice into the hand
it.h: Compare the temperatures of the hand and the ice.

it.q: A hot metal spoon is placed in a cup of room-temperature water. What happens over time?
ch: The spoon cools and the water warms until they reach the same temperature.
it.h: Energy flows until there is no temperature difference.

it.q: Equal masses of water at 80 °C and 20 °C are mixed in an insulated cup. What temperature will the mixture reach in °C?
it.h: With equal masses, the final temperature is halfway between.

it.q: When the temperatures of two touching objects become equal, they have reached
it.h: "Equilibrium" means balanced.

it.q: A can of juice from the refrigerator sits on a table. Why does it warm up?
ch: Thermal energy moves from the warmer air and table into the can.
it.h: Which way does thermal energy flow?

it.q: Explain, using particles, what happens when a hot rock is dropped into a bucket of cold water.
it.ans: The rock's fast-moving particles collide with the slower water particles and transfer kinetic energy. The rock's particles slow down (cooling) and the water's speed up (warming) until both have the same average kinetic energy and temperature.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Cooling by evaporation: sweat, clay pot coolers and swamp coolers

it.q: When a liquid evaporates from a surface, the surface
it.h: Think about how you feel stepping out of a pool on a windy day.

it.q: Why does sweating help cool your body?
ch: Evaporating sweat takes thermal energy away from the skin.
Sweat is cold when it is made.
it.h: Particles need energy to escape as a gas.

it.q: A clay pot cooler is a small clay pot inside a larger one with wet sand between them. Why does food inside stay cool?
ch: Water evaporating from the outer pot removes thermal energy.
it.h: What is happening to the water in the sand?

it.q: A wet thermometer read 24 °C and a dry thermometer read 31 °C in the same breeze. How many degrees cooler was the wet thermometer?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Evaporative coolers work better in dry Sacramento summers than in humid places. Why?
ch: Water evaporates faster when the air is dry.
it.h: Humid air already holds lots of water vapor.

it.q: Explain, using particles, why evaporation cools the liquid that is left behind.
it.ans: The fastest-moving particles have enough energy to escape as a gas. When they leave, the particles left behind have a lower average kinetic energy, so the liquid's temperature drops.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Thermal Energy - Keeping Things Hot and Cold
lessons.n: Graphing warming and cooling data

it.q: On a graph of temperature over time, a steep line shows
it.h: Steep means the line goes up or down quickly.

it.q: A cooling graph for a cup of tea drops fast at first, then levels off near room temperature. Why does it level off?
ch: The tea nears room temperature, so less thermal energy flows out.
The tea runs out of particles.
The room heats up to boiling.
it.h: Energy flow depends on the temperature difference.

it.q: Tea cooled from 80 °C to 60 °C in the first 10 minutes. What was the average cooling rate in degrees per minute?
it.h: Divide the temperature change by the time.

it.q: Which variable belongs on the horizontal axis of a cooling graph?
it.h: The variable that is not affected by the others goes on the x-axis.

it.q: A beaker of water warmed from 20 °C to 44 °C in 8 minutes on a hot plate. What was the average warming rate in degrees per minute?
it.h: Find the change, then divide by the minutes.

it.q: Describe what a graph would look like for 50 g and 200 g of water heated on the same hot plate, and explain why.
it.ans: Both lines rise, but the 50 g line is steeper. The same energy input spread through less mass raises the average kinetic energy of the particles faster.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: The water cycle runs on sunlight and gravity

it.q: What provides the energy that drives evaporation in the water cycle?
it.h: What warms ocean and lake water every day?

it.q: Water vapor high in the air cools and forms tiny droplets that make a cloud. This process is
Which force pulls rain and snow down from clouds and makes rivers flow downhill to the ocean?
In the Sierra Nevada, snow melts in spring and the water flows into reservoirs. Which water cycle processes are involved?
ch: melting and runoff pulled by gravity
it.h: Think about what happens to snow as it warms, and which way water flows.

it.q: Describe the path of one water molecule that evaporates from the Pacific Ocean and ends up in a California river.
it.ans: Sunlight warms ocean water so the molecule evaporates; it rises and cools, condensing into a cloud; winds carry the cloud over land; it falls as rain or snow; gravity pulls it downhill as runoff or melted snow into a river.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: Air pressure, humidity and clouds

it.q: The amount of water vapor in the air is called
A cold glass of lemonade on a summer day gets water droplets on the outside. Where does the water come from?
ch: water vapor in the air condenses on the cold glass
the ice melts through the glass
the Sun makes water on the glass
it.h: What happens to water vapor when it touches something cold?

it.q: Weather reports show falling air pressure. Which weather is most likely coming?
ch: colder clear skies with no clouds
a heat wave with no wind

it.q: Air at a certain temperature can hold 20 grams of water vapor per cubic meter. It now holds 15 grams. What is the relative humidity in percent?
it.h: Divide the amount held by the most it can hold, then multiply by 100.

it.q: Explain why clouds often form when warm, moist air rises up the side of a mountain.
it.ans: As the air rises it expands and cools; cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so the vapor condenses into droplets that form clouds.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: Air masses meet: fronts and storms

it.q: A large body of air with similar temperature and humidity throughout is called
An air mass that forms over the North Pacific Ocean would most likely be
it.h: Think about where it formed: ocean or land, north or south?

it.q: When a cold air mass pushes into a warm air mass, the warm air is forced upward quickly. What weather often results?
ch: thunderstorms and heavy rain, followed by cooler weather

it.q: Which weather change usually happens after a cold front passes?
ch: the temperature drops and skies clear
it becomes foggy for a week

it.q: Compare the weather usually caused by a cold front and by a warm front.
it.ans: A cold front moves fast and pushes warm air up steeply, causing short, heavy storms and then cooler, clearer weather. A warm front moves slowly as warm air rises gently over cold air, causing longer periods of light rain or drizzle and warmer weather afterward.
it.h: Think about how steeply the warm air is pushed upward.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: Forecasting with data

it.q: Why do meteorologists collect weather data from many locations at the same time?
ch: to track how air masses and fronts are moving
to measure only their own city
it.h: Air masses move across large areas.

it.q: Which tool measures wind speed?
A town west of yours had storms yesterday. Weather in most of the United States usually moves from west to east. What might you predict?
ch: storms may reach your town soon
storms will move away to the west
your town will have snow in July

it.q: A storm moved 360 km in 12 hours. What was its average speed in km per hour?
it.h: Speed equals distance divided by time.

it.q: A forecast says "70% chance of rain." Explain what this means and why forecasts use probability.
it.ans: It means rain is likely but not certain in the area; forecasts use probability because the atmosphere is complex and scientists can only estimate how air masses will move and interact.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: Severe weather: thunderstorms, tornadoes and hurricanes

it.q: A large, rotating tropical storm with winds of at least 119 km per hour is a
it.h: It forms over warm oceans.

it.q: Thunderstorms often form when
ch: warm, moist air rises quickly and its water vapor condenses into tall clouds
the air is perfectly still and dry
it.h: Rising air cools and its water vapor forms clouds.

it.q: Why do hurricanes weaken after they move over land?
ch: They lose their supply of warm, moist ocean air.
it.h: What gives a hurricane its energy?

it.q: A hurricane's winds were 150 km per hour over the ocean and 90 km per hour a day after landfall. By how many km per hour did the wind speed drop?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Tornadoes in the central United States often form where
ch: warm, moist air from the south meets cold, dry air from the north
two warm air masses stay still
it.h: Fronts between very different air masses cause storms.

it.q: Explain how energy from the Sun ends up powering a hurricane.
it.ans: Sunlight warms tropical ocean water. Warm water evaporates into the air. When the moist air rises and the water vapor condenses into clouds, it releases thermal energy that warms the air and keeps it rising, powering the storm.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth System Interactions Cause Weather
lessons.n: Land and sea breezes: local winds from uneven heating

it.q: Wind is caused mainly by
ch: differences in air pressure from uneven heating
it.h: Air moves from high pressure to low pressure.

it.q: On a sunny afternoon, land heats faster than the ocean. Which way does the breeze usually blow at the beach?
ch: from the ocean toward the land
from the land toward the ocean
it.h: Warm air over land rises; what replaces it?

it.q: At night, land cools faster than water. Which breeze forms?
ch: a land breeze blowing toward the ocean
a sea breeze blowing toward the land
it.h: Now the air over the water is warmer.

it.q: At 2 p.m., the beach sand was 38 °C and the ocean water was 18 °C. What was the temperature difference?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Why does warm air over the land rise?
ch: It is less dense than the cooler air around it.
It is pulled by the Moon.
it.h: Warm air particles spread farther apart.

it.q: Explain why San Francisco often has cool afternoon breezes in summer while inland valleys are hot.
it.ans: The inland land heats up a lot, warming the air so it rises and lowers the pressure. Cooler, denser air over the cold Pacific Ocean flows inland to replace it, bringing cool breezes (and often fog) to the coast.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: Weather or climate? Unequal heating of Earth

it.q: Climate is
ch: the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years
the amount of rain in one storm
it.h: Think long term, not one day.

it.q: Why is the equator warmer than the poles on average?
ch: Sunlight strikes the equator more directly, so energy is concentrated on a smaller area
The equator is closer to the Sun
The poles have no sunlight all year

it.q: A flashlight shines straight down on graph paper and lights 20 squares. Tilted, the same light covers 40 squares. What does this model show?
ch: Light at a low angle is spread over a larger area, so each square gets less energy
The flashlight made more light when tilted
it.h: The same amount of light is shared by more squares.

it.q: A flashlight shining straight down lights 20 squares of graph paper; tilted, the same light covers 40 squares. How many times less light does each square get when tilted?
A student says, "It is raining today in Seattle, so Seattle has a rainy climate." Explain why one day of weather is not enough to describe climate.
it.ans: Climate is based on long-term averages, usually 30 years or more. One rainy day is weather; to describe the climate you need many years of data on temperature and precipitation.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: Global winds and Earth's rotation

it.q: Near the equator, warm air rises. What happens as this air rises and cools?
ch: Water vapor condenses and causes heavy rain
it.h: Rising air cools. What happens to vapor in cool air?

it.q: Air that rose at the equator sinks back down near 30° north and south latitude. Sinking air is dry. Which kind of region is common near 30° latitude?
The turning of winds caused by Earth's rotation is called
In the Northern Hemisphere, Earth's rotation causes moving air to curve
it.h: Picture yourself facing the direction the wind is moving.

it.q: Describe how unequal heating and Earth's rotation together create global wind patterns.
it.ans: Unequal heating makes air rise at the equator and sink at other latitudes, setting up large convection loops; Earth's rotation curves these winds, producing belts such as the trade winds and westerlies.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: Ocean currents carry energy around the planet

it.q: Large streams of moving water in the ocean are called
The Gulf Stream carries warm water from near the equator north across the Atlantic. How does it affect Western Europe?
ch: It helps give Western Europe milder winters than other places at the same latitude
It makes Western Europe a desert
It has no effect on climate

it.q: The California Current flows south along the West Coast, bringing cold water from the north. How does it affect coastal California summers?
ch: They are cooler and often foggy
it.h: Air over cold water gets cooled.

it.q: What two main factors drive surface ocean currents?
Explain how an ocean current can move thermal energy from one part of Earth to another.
it.ans: Water warmed near the equator flows toward higher latitudes, carrying thermal energy with it; it releases heat to the air there, warming nearby land. Cold currents carry cold water toward the equator.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: Mountains, oceans and California's climates

it.q: Moist air from the Pacific rises over the Sierra Nevada and drops rain and snow on the western slopes. What happens on the eastern side?
ch: The air sinks, warms and is dry, creating a rain shadow
It snows more than the west side
it.h: The air already lost much of its water on the way up.

it.q: Death Valley, east of the Sierra Nevada, is one of the driest places in North America. Which factor best explains this?
ch: It is in a rain shadow of mountains
It is next to the ocean
It is at the North Pole
It gets air that is rising and cooling

it.q: As you climb a tall mountain, the air temperature usually
ch: goes up and down randomly every meter

it.q: Air temperature drops about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 meters of elevation gain. If it is 20 °C at sea level, what is the temperature at 2,000 meters?
it.h: Find the total drop for 2,000 meters first.

it.q: Explain why inland cities like Fresno have hotter summers than coastal cities like Santa Cruz.
it.ans: Coastal cities are cooled by the nearby ocean and cold current, which change temperature slowly; inland cities are far from the ocean's influence, so land heats up more in summer sunlight.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: Reading climate graphs: comparing cities

it.q: A climate graph usually shows a place's
it.h: Climate is the pattern over many years.

it.q: A climate graph shows a city with about the same temperature all year and heavy rain every month. Which climate is it most likely?
it.h: Warm all year and wet all year.

it.q: San Diego's climate graph shows mild temperatures, wet winters and almost no summer rain. This pattern is called
it.h: California shares this climate with lands around a famous sea.

it.q: A city's average temperature is 25 °C in July and 9 °C in January. What is the annual temperature range in °C?
it.h: Subtract the coldest month from the warmest.

it.q: Two cities are at the same latitude. City A is on the coast and has a temperature range of 8 °C. City B is far inland and has a range of 25 °C. What explains the difference?
ch: The ocean moderates temperatures near the coast.
City B is closer to the equator.
it.h: Water heats and cools slowly.

it.q: Describe what you would look for on two climate graphs to decide which city has a wetter winter.
it.ans: Compare the precipitation bars for the winter months (December to February in the Northern Hemisphere). The city with taller bars in those months has a wetter winter.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Causes and Effects of Regional Climates
lessons.n: El Nino and La Nina: when ocean patterns shift

it.q: El Nino is a pattern in which surface water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean becomes
it.h: El Nino brings unusually warm water.

it.q: During a normal year, trade winds blow warm surface water westward across the tropical Pacific. During El Nino, these winds
ch: weaken, so warm water spreads back east
it.h: Weaker winds cannot hold the warm water in the west.

it.q: La Nina is the opposite of El Nino. During La Nina, the eastern tropical Pacific surface water is
it.h: La Nina means the opposite pattern.

it.q: Normal surface water off Peru in December is 22 °C. During a strong El Nino it measured 26.5 °C. How many degrees above normal was it?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: How can a change in ocean temperature far away change weather in California?
ch: Ocean temperatures change where air rises and storms form, which shifts storm paths.
Ocean water flows into California rivers.
it.h: Warm water heats the air above it.

it.q: Explain how El Nino shows that the ocean and atmosphere interact to affect climate.
it.ans: When trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east. The warm ocean heats the air above it, causing more rising air and storms in new places. These changes in the atmosphere then shift rain and temperature patterns in many regions.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: The greenhouse effect

it.q: Which gas released by burning fossil fuels is a major greenhouse gas?
How do greenhouse gases warm Earth?
ch: They absorb heat given off by Earth's surface and send some back toward the ground
They block all sunlight from reaching Earth
it.h: Sunlight warms the ground; the ground gives off heat. What happens to that heat?

it.q: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth's average temperature would be far below freezing. What does this tell us?
ch: Some greenhouse effect is natural and needed for life
Earth gets no energy from the Sun
Greenhouse gases are made only by people

it.q: A model has two jars in sunlight. One jar has extra carbon dioxide added. After 30 minutes it is 2 °C warmer. What does this model suggest?
ch: More carbon dioxide can trap more heat
The sunlight was stronger on one jar
it.h: What was the only difference between the jars?

it.q: Explain the difference between the natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by humans.
it.ans: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Human activities like burning fossil fuels add extra greenhouse gases, which trap more heat and raise global temperatures.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: Reading the evidence: temperature and carbon dioxide

it.q: Measurements at Mauna Loa, Hawaii show carbon dioxide rising from about 315 parts per million (ppm) in 1958 to about 420 ppm in 2023. What is the trend?
Carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa was about 315 ppm in 1958 and about 420 ppm in 2023. By how many ppm did carbon dioxide increase?
it.h: Subtract the earlier value from the later value.

it.q: Global average temperature has risen about 1 °C since the late 1800s. Why do scientists use averages from thousands of stations?
ch: One place's weather varies a lot, so many stations show the global trend

it.q: Scientists compare a graph of rising carbon dioxide with a graph of rising global temperature. What kind of relationship do the graphs show?
ch: both increase over the same time period

it.q: A student says, "It snowed a lot this winter, so global warming is not real." Use the difference between weather and climate to respond.
it.ans: One snowy winter is weather in one place. Global warming is a long-term rise in Earth's average temperature measured over decades around the world, so one cold season does not disprove it.
it.h: Is one season in one place weather or climate?

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: Effects on Earth's systems and living things

it.q: As the ocean warms, water expands and land ice melts. What is the effect on sea level?
Warmer winters mean more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow in the Sierra Nevada. Why is this a problem for California's water supply?
ch: Less snowpack stores water for the dry summer months
Rain is not made of water
Snow is too heavy for reservoirs
it.h: When does snowpack release its water?

it.q: Corals turn white and can die when ocean water stays too warm. What happens to fish that depend on coral reefs?
ch: Their food and shelter decrease, so their populations may decline
They begin to live on land

it.q: From 1900 to 2020, global sea level rose about 24 cm. What was the average rise in cm per decade?
it.h: How many decades are in 120 years?

it.q: Describe one way warming temperatures can affect a plant or animal species and explain why.
it.ans: Example: pikas living high in the Sierra Nevada need cool temperatures; as it warms they must move higher up mountains, and when there is no higher place, their habitat shrinks and populations can drop.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: Designing solutions to reduce human impacts

it.q: Which choice would most reduce the carbon dioxide released when a school uses electricity?
ch: installing solar panels on the roof

it.q: A city wants to cut car emissions. Which plan addresses the cause most directly?
ch: adding safe bike lanes and frequent electric buses
it.h: Which option means fewer gasoline-burning cars on the road?

it.q: A school's electricity bill shows 50,000 kilowatt-hours used per year. Solar panels produce 30,000 kilowatt-hours. What percent of the school's electricity do they supply?
When evaluating designs to reduce food waste in a cafeteria, why is a decision matrix helpful?
ch: It compares each design against the same criteria in a fair way
It picks a design at random
It makes every design score the same

it.q: Describe one criterion and one constraint for a plan to reduce the carbon dioxide produced by students' trips to school.
it.ans: Criterion: reduce car trips by at least 20 percent. Constraint: must be safe for students, cost little and work for families who live far away.
it.h: Criteria describe success; constraints describe limits.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: Carbon footprints: where greenhouse gases come from

it.q: The total amount of greenhouse gases released by a person's activities is their
it.h: It is a measure of impact, like a footprint left behind.

it.q: Which activity usually adds carbon dioxide to the air?
it.h: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide.

it.q: A car releases about 0.2 kg of carbon dioxide per kilometer. How many kilograms does it release on a 50 km trip?
it.h: Multiply the distance by the amount per kilometer.

it.q: Electricity from a coal power plant has a larger carbon footprint than electricity from solar panels because
it.h: Think about which source burns fuel.

it.q: Why does wasting food add to greenhouse gases?
ch: Energy was used to grow, move and store it, and rotting food in landfills releases methane.
it.h: Consider the whole path of food from farm to trash.

it.q: List two changes a family could make to shrink its carbon footprint and explain why each helps.
it.ans: Walk, bike or take the bus instead of driving short trips, which burns less gasoline. Use efficient LED bulbs or turn off unused devices, so less electricity is generated from fossil fuels.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Global Warming and Its Effects on Living Systems
lessons.n: Natural or human causes? Weighing the evidence for warming

it.q: Which is a natural factor that can change Earth's temperature?
ch: changes in the Sun's energy output
it.h: Natural factors are not caused by people.

it.q: After the large eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991, global temperatures dropped for about one to two years. Why?
ch: Particles in the upper atmosphere reflected some sunlight back to space.
The volcano added heat to the oceans.
it.h: Volcanic particles can block some sunlight.

it.q: Measurements show the Sun's energy reaching Earth has stayed about the same since the 1950s while global temperatures have risen. What does this suggest?
ch: Changes in the Sun do not explain recent warming.
The Sun is the cause of recent warming.
it.h: If one factor stays the same while temperature rises, can it be the cause?

it.q: Carbon dioxide in the air was about 280 parts per million (ppm) before the 1800s and about 420 ppm recently. By how many ppm did it increase?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Scientists ask, "Which factor changed in the same way as global temperature over the past century?" Why is this a good question?
ch: Comparing patterns helps identify likely causes.
It proves only one answer is possible.
it.h: A cause usually changes along with its effect.

it.q: Name one natural factor and one human factor that can change global temperature, and tell which one matches recent warming better.
it.ans: Natural: changes in the Sun or volcanic eruptions. Human: burning fossil fuels, which adds carbon dioxide. Rising carbon dioxide matches recent warming better, since the Sun's output has stayed steady and volcanoes cause only short cooling.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Everything is made of atoms

it.q: What is the smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element?
it.h: Elements are made of only one kind of this particle.

it.q: A water molecule (H2O) is made of
Which is a pure element?
it.h: An element is made of only one kind of atom.

it.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of carbon dioxide, CO2?
Explain the difference between an atom and a molecule, using oxygen gas (O2) as an example.
it.ans: An atom is a single particle of an element, like one oxygen atom (O). A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together; O2 is a molecule made of two oxygen atoms.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Molecules and extended structures

it.q: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine atoms arranged in a repeating cube pattern that continues in all directions. This is an example of
it.h: Does the pattern stop at a few atoms, or repeat?

it.q: A diamond is made only of carbon atoms, each bonded to four others in a repeating network. What does this tell you about diamond?
ch: It is an extended structure made of one element
It is a compound of many elements

it.q: Which is made of individual small molecules rather than an extended structure?
In table salt (NaCl), sodium and chlorine atoms are present in a 1 to 1 ratio. A tiny salt crystal has 5,000 sodium atoms. How many chlorine atoms does it have?
it.h: Equal numbers of each.

it.q: Graphite (pencil lead) and diamond are both made only of carbon. Explain how they can have such different properties.
it.ans: Their carbon atoms are arranged differently. In diamond each atom bonds to four others in a strong 3D network, making it hard; in graphite atoms form flat layers that slide over each other, making it soft.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Particles in motion: solids, liquids and gases

it.q: In which state of matter are particles packed tightly and only vibrate in place?
How do particles in a liquid move?
ch: They stay close together but slide past one another
They are locked in fixed positions
They are far apart and move freely in all directions

it.q: A balloon is put in a freezer and shrinks. Which explanation is best?
ch: The gas particles slow down and hit the balloon less often and less hard
it.h: How does temperature affect particle speed?

it.q: A gas takes up 30 mL in a syringe at 20 °C. When warmed, it takes up 33 mL. By how many mL did the volume increase?
Use particle motion to explain why you can smell soup cooking from across a room.
it.ans: The warm soup's particles move fast; some escape as gas and spread out, moving freely and mixing with air particles until they reach your nose.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Adding and removing thermal energy: changes of state

it.q: The change from a liquid to a gas is
As ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature stays at 0 °C even though heat is added. Where does the energy go?
ch: It breaks the particles out of their fixed positions
it.h: Think about what changes when a solid becomes a liquid.

it.q: When water vapor in the air touches a cold window and forms droplets, thermal energy is
ch: removed from the water vapor, so its particles slow down and come together

it.q: Heating data for water: 0 min, -10 °C; 2 min, 0 °C; 6 min, 0 °C; 10 min, 40 °C. For how many minutes did the temperature stay at 0 °C?
it.h: Find when the temperature first reached 0 °C and when it began rising again.

it.q: Explain what happens to the particles of water as a pot is heated from room temperature until it boils.
it.ans: The particles gain energy and move faster, raising the temperature; at 100 °C (at sea level) they have enough energy to break away from the liquid and become gas, forming bubbles of water vapor.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Pure substances and mixtures at the particle level

it.q: A sample made of only one kind of atom or one kind of molecule is a
it.h: "Pure" means only one kind of particle.

it.q: A particle diagram shows only identical H2O molecules. What does it represent?
it.h: Are all the particles the same?

it.q: A particle diagram shows O2 molecules and N2 molecules spread out and mixed but not bonded to each other. What is it?
ch: a mixture of two elements, like air
it.h: The two kinds of molecules are not joined together.

it.q: A drawing of air shows 100 molecules: 78 are N2, 21 are O2 and the rest are argon atoms. How many argon atoms are shown?
it.h: Subtract the nitrogen and oxygen molecules from 100.

it.q: Salt water can be separated by boiling off the water. Water cannot be separated into hydrogen and oxygen by boiling. What does this show?
ch: Salt water is a mixture; water is a compound.
it.h: Mixtures are separated by physical processes; compounds need chemical reactions.

it.q: Draw or describe particle diagrams for pure water and for salt water.
it.ans: Pure water: many identical H2O molecules, each with one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms. Salt water: the same water molecules with sodium and chlorine particles spread among them, not bonded to the water.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Melting points, boiling points and pressure

it.q: The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid is its
it.h: The word tells you what happens.

it.q: Each pure substance has its own melting point. How does this help scientists?
ch: It can be used to identify an unknown substance.
It depends on the size of the sample.
it.h: A property that is always the same for a substance can identify it.

it.q: Water boils at about 100 °C at sea level but at about 90 °C high in the mountains. Why?
ch: Lower air pressure makes it easier for water particles to escape as gas.
it.h: Less air is pushing down on the water's surface.

it.q: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level and at about 93 °C in a mountain town. How many degrees lower is the boiling point in the town?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: A pressure cooker raises the pressure inside the pot. What happens to the boiling point of the water?
ch: It goes up, so food cooks at a higher temperature.
The water cannot boil at all.
it.h: Higher pressure makes it harder for particles to escape.

it.q: Explain, using particles, why a substance stays at its melting point while it is melting even though heat is still being added.
it.ans: The added energy is used to break particles free from their fixed positions in the solid, not to make them move faster. The average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, stays the same until all the solid has melted.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Atoms, Molecules and States of Matter
lessons.n: Counting atoms in chemical formulas

it.q: In the formula H2O, the small number 2 tells you
it.h: A subscript applies to the element just before it.

it.q: How many atoms in all are in one molecule of carbon dioxide, CO2?
it.h: Add 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.

it.q: Glucose has the formula C6H12O6. How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule?
it.h: Look at the number after H.

it.q: Which formula shows a molecule with 1 nitrogen atom and 3 hydrogen atoms?
it.h: Write the symbol, then the number of atoms as a subscript.

it.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of methane, CH4?
it.h: 1 carbon plus 4 hydrogen.

it.q: Explain the difference between 2H and H2.
it.ans: 2H means two separate hydrogen atoms. H2 means one molecule made of two hydrogen atoms bonded together.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Properties identify substances

it.q: Which is a characteristic property that can help identify a pure substance?
it.h: It stays the same no matter how much of the substance you have.

it.q: A metal block has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 cubic centimeters. What is its density in g per cubic centimeter?
it.h: Density equals mass divided by volume.

it.q: A reference table lists densities: aluminum 2.7, iron 7.9, copper 9.0 and gold 19.3 g per cubic centimeter. A metal block has a density of 2.7 g per cubic centimeter. It is most likely
Two clear liquids look the same. Which test would best tell them apart?
ch: measure the boiling point of each
compare how much is in each cup
look at the shape of each cup

it.q: A student says a large piece of iron has a greater density than a small nail made of the same iron. Explain why this is wrong.
it.ans: Density is a characteristic property; the large piece has more mass but also more volume in the same ratio, so its density is the same as the nail's.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Evidence of a chemical reaction

it.q: Which observation is the best evidence that a chemical reaction happened?
ch: A new substance with different properties formed
it.h: In a chemical reaction, new substances form.

it.q: When vinegar and baking soda are mixed, bubbles form and the mixture gets colder. Which of these is evidence of a chemical reaction?
ch: both the gas forming and the temperature change
only that the mixture is wet
only that the cup is plastic

it.q: Which is a physical change, not a chemical change?
Two clear solutions are mixed and a cloudy yellow solid forms. What is the solid called?
ch: a mixture of the same substances

it.q: A student melts chocolate and says a chemical reaction happened because it changed from solid to liquid. Explain why this is not a chemical reaction.
it.ans: Melting is a physical change; the chocolate is still the same substance with the same properties and it can harden again. No new substance formed.
it.h: Did a new substance form?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Atoms rearrange; mass is conserved

it.q: In a chemical reaction, what happens to atoms?
ch: They rearrange to form new substances, but none are created or destroyed
it.h: Count atoms on both sides of a reaction.

it.q: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 makes 2H2O, how many hydrogen atoms are on the reactant side?
it.h: 2H2 means two molecules, each with 2 hydrogen atoms.

it.q: Steel wool is burned on a balance in an open dish and its mass increases. Which explanation is best?
ch: Oxygen atoms from the air combined with the iron
New atoms were created by the flame

it.q: 30 g of reactants react in a sealed container. What is the total mass of the products in g?
Vinegar and baking soda react in an open cup and the mass goes down. Explain why this does not break the law of conservation of mass.
it.ans: One product is carbon dioxide gas, which escaped into the air and was not weighed. If the reaction were sealed, the total mass would stay the same.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Synthetic materials from natural resources

it.q: A material that people make through chemical reactions, instead of finding in nature, is called
Most plastics are made from which natural resource?
it.h: Think about fossil fuels.

it.q: Nylon, used in jackets and ropes, is made by chemical reactions that join small molecules into long chains. Why do engineers make materials like nylon?
ch: to get useful properties, such as strength and light weight, that natural materials may lack
because natural materials do not exist
to make materials that break easily

it.q: Glass is made by melting sand with other minerals at high temperature. Glass is an example of
ch: a material made from a natural resource
a material found already made in nature

it.q: Choose one synthetic material. Name the natural resource it comes from and describe one effect its use has on society.
it.ans: Example: plastic comes from petroleum; it makes lightweight, cheap packaging and medical supplies, but plastic waste pollutes oceans and harms wildlife.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Design challenge: chemical heat and cold packs

it.q: A process that releases thermal energy and makes its surroundings warmer is
A cold pack feels cold when squeezed because the process inside
ch: absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings
it.h: Energy moves from your hand into the pack.

it.q: A team designs a hand warmer for hikers. Which is a criterion?
ch: It stays above 40 °C for at least 1 hour
it.h: A criterion says how well the design must work.

it.q: A hand warmer started at 20 °C and reached 52 °C. What was the temperature increase in °C?
Explain how a team could use test data to improve a cold pack design.
it.ans: Measure how cold each version gets and how long it stays cold, compare results to the criteria, keep the features that worked best, change one thing at a time and test again.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Balancing simple chemical equations

it.q: In a chemical equation, the substances on the left side of the arrow are the
it.h: They react to make something new.

it.q: Why must a chemical equation be balanced?
ch: Atoms are not created or destroyed, so each kind must be the same on both sides.
it.h: Think about conservation of mass.

it.q: In the equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many hydrogen atoms are on the left side?
it.h: 2 molecules each with 2 hydrogen atoms.

it.q: In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many oxygen atoms are on the right side?
it.h: Each water molecule has 1 oxygen atom, and there are 2 water molecules.

it.q: Which equation is balanced?
it.h: Count C, H and O on each side.

it.q: Explain why the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants in a closed system.
it.ans: The same atoms are present before and after; they are only rearranged into new molecules. Since each atom keeps its mass, the total mass stays the same.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Chemical Reactions - New Substances from Old
lessons.n: Combustion: burning as a chemical reaction

it.q: Burning a fuel in oxygen is a chemical reaction called
it.h: Campfires and car engines both use it.

it.q: When natural gas (methane) burns completely, what are the products?
it.h: The carbon and hydrogen atoms combine with oxygen.

it.q: A candle in a closed jar goes out after a short time. Why?
ch: The flame used up much of the oxygen it needs.
it.h: What does combustion need besides fuel?

it.q: A candle had a mass of 40 g before burning and 32 g after an hour. How many grams of wax reacted?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Where does the mass of a burning candle go?
ch: Into gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapor that escape into the air
It is destroyed by the flame
it.h: Mass is conserved.

it.q: Name three signs that a burning log is going through a chemical reaction.
it.ans: It gives off heat and light, it produces smoke and gases, and it turns into ash with new properties that cannot change back into wood.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: Where does a tree's mass come from?

it.q: In the 1600s, Jan van Helmont grew a 2 kg willow tree in a pot of soil for 5 years, giving it only water. The tree gained about 74 kg, but the soil lost only about 0.06 kg. What does this show?
ch: Most of the tree's mass did not come from the soil
Trees are made mostly of soil
it.h: Compare the mass the tree gained with the mass the soil lost.

it.q: Which two raw materials do plants use to make sugar in photosynthesis?
Where does the carbon in a plant's sugar come from?
In van Helmont's experiment, the tree grew from 2 kg to 76 kg. How many kg did it gain?
A student says plants get their food from the soil. Use evidence and the idea of photosynthesis to explain why this is not correct.
it.ans: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, using carbon dioxide from the air and water to build sugar with light energy. Experiments like van Helmont's show soil mass barely changes as a plant grows, so most of the plant's mass comes from the air and water.
it.h: What did the soil data show?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: Light energy becomes food energy

it.q: Where does the energy stored in sugar made by plants come from?
An aquatic plant in water releases bubbles of oxygen in light. Students count bubbles at different light levels. What are they measuring?
it.h: Oxygen is a product of which process?

it.q: An aquatic plant made 12 bubbles per minute with the lamp 10 cm away and 4 bubbles per minute with the lamp 40 cm away. How many times faster was bubbling at 10 cm?
Students count oxygen bubbles from an aquatic plant with a lamp placed 10, 20, 30 and 40 cm away. What is the independent variable?
Predict what would happen to the bubble count if the lamp were turned off, and explain why.
it.ans: The bubbling would slow and stop because without light energy the plant cannot carry out photosynthesis, so it stops producing oxygen.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: Cellular respiration releases energy

it.q: In which cell part does cellular respiration mainly happen?
Which is the word equation for cellular respiration?
ch: sugar + oxygen makes carbon dioxide + water + energy
carbon dioxide + water makes sugar + oxygen
it.h: It is close to the reverse of photosynthesis.

it.q: Do plants carry out cellular respiration?
ch: Yes, plant cells use respiration to release energy from the sugar they make
Only at night, never in the day

it.q: When food is digested, large molecules are broken into smaller ones. What happens to the atoms?
ch: They are rearranged into new molecules the body can use

it.q: Explain why you breathe faster when you exercise, using cellular respiration.
it.ans: Muscles need more energy, so their cells carry out more respiration, which uses more oxygen and makes more carbon dioxide; breathing faster brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: The cycle between photosynthesis and respiration

it.q: How are photosynthesis and cellular respiration related?
ch: The products of one are the reactants of the other
it.h: Compare the inputs and outputs of each.

it.q: Bromothymol blue turns yellow when carbon dioxide is added and back to blue when it is removed. A yellow tube with an aquatic plant is placed in light. After a few hours it turns blue. What happened?
ch: The plant used carbon dioxide in photosynthesis

it.q: In a sealed jar with a plant in light, carbon dioxide fell from 800 ppm to 500 ppm in 2 hours. What was the mean rate of change in ppm per hour?
A sealed jar with a green plant is moved from light into the dark. What will happen to the carbon dioxide in the jar?
ch: It will increase because the plant only respires
It will stay exactly the same

it.q: Describe the path of a carbon atom from the air, into a plant, into a rabbit that eats the plant and back into the air.
it.ans: Carbon dioxide from the air is used in photosynthesis to make sugar in the plant; the rabbit eats the plant and digests the sugar; the rabbit's cells use the sugar in respiration and release the carbon as carbon dioxide when it breathes out.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: Building a body: food molecules rebuilt for growth

it.q: Digestion breaks large food molecules into
ch: smaller molecules that cells can absorb and use
it.h: Cells cannot absorb a whole piece of food.

it.q: Proteins in food are broken into amino acids. What do body cells do with amino acids?
ch: They rebuild them into the proteins the body needs, like muscle.
They store them as bone only.
it.h: Think of taking apart a building to build a different one.

it.q: Where does the matter in a growing teenager's new muscle come from?
ch: molecules from the food the teenager eats
it.h: Matter for growth must come from somewhere.
