it.q: A student ate 60 g of protein in one day: 25 g at lunch, 20 g at dinner and the rest at breakfast. How many grams at breakfast?
it.h: Subtract the lunch and dinner amounts from the total.

it.q: Starch from bread is broken into glucose. What are two things cells can do with glucose?
ch: release energy in respiration or build it into stored molecules
turn it into protein without nitrogen
turn it into atoms of gold
it.h: Glucose is a source of energy and building material.

it.q: Explain how a hamburger can become part of the muscle in a person's arm.
it.ans: Digestion breaks the proteins in the meat into amino acids. Blood carries the amino acids to muscle cells, which link them together in new orders to build the proteins that make muscle.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Matter and Energy in Organisms
lessons.n: Measuring photosynthesis and respiration with indicators

it.q: Bromothymol blue (BTB) is an indicator that turns from blue to yellow when
ch: carbon dioxide is added to the water
it.h: Breathing out through a straw into BTB turns it yellow.

it.q: A student breathes into blue BTB until it turns yellow. Then she puts a water plant in it under a lamp. After a few hours the BTB is blue again. What happened?
ch: The plant used carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.
it.h: Which process takes carbon dioxide out of the water?

it.q: The same setup with yellow BTB and a water plant is kept in the dark. The BTB stays yellow. Why?
ch: Without light the plant cannot photosynthesize, but it still respires.
Plants make carbon dioxide only in light.
it.h: Respiration happens all the time, photosynthesis only in light.

it.q: Small spinach leaf disks were placed in a solution under a lamp. As they made oxygen, they floated. After 10 minutes, 8 of 10 disks floated. What percent floated?
it.h: Divide by 10 and multiply by 100.

it.q: In the leaf disk test, why do the disks float?
ch: Oxygen made by photosynthesis collects in the disks.
it.h: Which gas does photosynthesis release?

it.q: Design a test with BTB to show that light is needed for a plant to use carbon dioxide.
it.ans: Make two identical tubes of yellow BTB (carbon dioxide added), each with a same-size water plant. Put one in light and one in the dark. After several hours, the tube in light turns blue (carbon dioxide used) and the dark tube stays yellow.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Resources limit populations

it.q: A group of the same species living in the same area is a
Which is a limiting factor for a population of deer?
ch: the length of the deer's name
it.h: A limiting factor is a resource that keeps a population from growing without end.

it.q: After a very rainy year, a desert's plants grow well and the rabbit population increases. What is the best explanation?
ch: More water led to more plant food for rabbits
Rain makes rabbits reproduce without food

it.q: A rabbit population grew from 200 to 260 in one year. What was the percent increase?
it.h: Find the increase, divide by the starting number and multiply by 100.

it.q: Explain what happens to a population when it grows larger than its food supply can support.
it.ans: Individuals compete for limited food; some starve, reproduce less or move away, so the population decreases until it matches what the resources can support.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Patterns of interactions

it.q: An interaction in which both species benefit is
Yucca moths carry pollen between yucca flowers and lay eggs in the flowers; the caterpillars eat some of the seeds. Both species depend on each other to reproduce. What kind of relationship is this?
A tick feeds on a deer's blood, and the deer is harmed. This is
it.h: One benefits and one is harmed, but is not usually killed right away.

it.q: Coyotes and hawks both hunt ground squirrels in the same field. What is the relationship between the coyotes and hawks?
Give an example of predation and explain how the predator and prey populations can affect each other.
it.ans: Example: owls eat mice. When mice are plentiful, owls have more food and their numbers grow; more owls eat more mice, so mice decrease; then owls have less food and decrease, allowing mice to increase again.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Food webs and the flow of energy

it.q: In a food web, arrows point from
ch: the organism eaten to the organism that eats it
the eater to the organism eaten
it.h: Arrows show the direction energy moves.

it.q: In a kelp forest, sea otters eat sea urchins and sea urchins eat kelp. If sea otters disappeared, what would most likely happen?
ch: Urchins would increase and kelp would decrease

it.q: Which organisms get energy by eating producers?
Producers in a meadow store 10,000 units of energy. If about 10 percent passes to each next level, how many units reach the primary consumers?
it.h: Find 10 percent of 10,000.

it.q: Explain why most of the energy at one level of a food chain does not pass to the next level.
it.ans: Organisms use most of the energy they take in for life processes like moving and staying warm, releasing it as heat, and some parts are not eaten or digested, so only about 10 percent is stored in their bodies for the next level.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Decomposers and the cycling of matter

it.q: Organisms that break down dead matter and wastes, such as fungi and bacteria, are
Why are decomposers important to producers?
ch: They return nutrients from dead matter to the soil
They produce oxygen at night only

it.q: Which statement about matter in an ecosystem is correct?
ch: Atoms are recycled between living and nonliving parts
Matter is used up and disappears

it.q: A compost pile had a mass of 60 kg. After 6 months, decomposers had reduced it to 24 kg. By what percent did the mass decrease?
it.h: Find the decrease first.

it.q: Trace the path of a nitrogen or carbon atom from a dead leaf back into a living plant.
it.ans: Decomposers break down the dead leaf; they release carbon dioxide into the air and nutrients like nitrogen into the soil; a plant takes in the carbon dioxide through its leaves or the nitrogen through its roots and uses it to build new tissue.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Biomagnification: toxins move up food chains

it.q: When a toxin builds up to higher concentrations at each level of a food chain, it is called
it.h: "Magnify" means make larger.

it.q: Why do top predators often have the highest levels of a toxin like mercury?
ch: They eat many smaller animals, and the toxin stays in their bodies and builds up.
it.h: Each animal eats many organisms from the level below.

it.q: The pesticide DDT was used widely in the mid-1900s. Bald eagles and brown pelicans that ate contaminated fish laid eggs with thin shells. What happened to their populations?
ch: They dropped because many eggs broke before hatching.
it.h: Thin shells break easily.

it.q: Water in a lake had 0.001 units of a toxin. Tiny algae had 1,000 times that amount. How many units were in the algae?
it.h: Multiply.

it.q: After DDT was banned in the United States in 1972, bald eagle populations recovered. What does this suggest?
ch: Removing the toxin from the food web helped the predators recover.
it.h: Compare before and after the ban.

it.q: Explain why it is safer to eat small fish such as sardines than large predator fish such as swordfish, in terms of mercury.
it.ans: Mercury builds up as it moves up the food chain. Small fish are low on the chain and have little mercury, while large predator fish eat many smaller fish over long lives and collect much more.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ecosystem Interactions and Energy Flow
lessons.n: Same patterns, different places: interactions across California ecosystems

it.q: Interactions such as predation, competition and mutualism that show up in many different ecosystems are called
it.h: The same kinds of relationships repeat from place to place.

it.q: In the Mojave Desert, coyotes hunt jackrabbits. In a kelp forest, sea otters hunt sea urchins. What pattern do these share?
it.h: In each pair, one animal eats the other.

it.q: In a grassland, ground squirrels and pocket gophers both eat the same grasses. In a tide pool, two kinds of snails eat the same algae. What pattern do these share?
it.h: What happens when two species need the same food?

it.q: A desert had 240 jackrabbits and 12 coyotes. How many jackrabbits were there for each coyote?
it.h: Divide.

it.q: In the ocean, clownfish shelter among sea anemone tentacles and chase off fish that eat anemones. In an oak woodland, scrub jays bury acorns to eat later, and the forgotten ones grow into new oaks. Which pattern do both show?
it.h: Do both benefit?

it.q: Give one example of predation and one of competition from two different ecosystems, and explain why scientists say these patterns repeat.
it.ans: Predation: hawks eating mice in a grassland; competition: two kinds of fish eating the same insects in a stream. The same kinds of interactions happen everywhere because all organisms need food, space and other limited resources.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Materials, the Rock Cycle and Resources
lessons.n: Inside Earth: layers and internal heat

it.q: Which is Earth's thinnest layer?
Which layer of Earth is liquid metal, mostly iron and nickel?
it.h: There are two core layers; one is solid and one flows.

it.q: Where does most of the energy that melts rock deep inside Earth come from?
ch: heat from Earth's interior, including the breakdown of radioactive elements

it.q: Earth's radius is about 6,400 km. The crust under a continent is about 40 km thick. What percent of Earth's radius is that crust?
it.h: Divide 40 by 6,400 and multiply by 100.

it.q: Scientists cannot drill to Earth's core. Explain how they know about Earth's layers.
it.ans: They study how earthquake waves travel through Earth: waves change speed and direction at layer boundaries, and some waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Materials, the Rock Cycle and Resources
lessons.n: The rock cycle

it.q: Rock that forms when magma or lava cools and hardens is
Granite in Yosemite has large crystals. What does this tell you about how it formed?
ch: It cooled slowly from magma deep underground
It cooled quickly from lava on the surface
It formed from layers of sand
it.h: Crystals have more time to grow when cooling is slow.

it.q: Limestone is changed into marble by heat and pressure deep underground. Marble is
Which process forms sedimentary rock?
ch: sediments are deposited, compacted and cemented
rock is heated and squeezed without melting

it.q: Describe one path a piece of igneous rock could take to become sedimentary rock.
it.ans: The igneous rock is weathered into small pieces; water carries the sediment to a lake or ocean where it settles in layers; over time the layers are buried, compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock.
it.h: Think: break, move, settle, press.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Materials, the Rock Cycle and Resources
lessons.n: Shaping the surface: weathering, erosion and deposition

it.q: The breaking down of rock into smaller pieces is
Water seeps into a crack in a rock, freezes and expands, widening the crack. This is an example of
Which force moves sediment downhill in landslides and helps rivers carry sediment to the ocean?
it.h: What pulls everything toward Earth's center?

it.q: A river carries sediment that builds a delta 4 cm higher each year. How many cm higher will it be after 25 years?
Explain how the Sun provides energy for weathering and erosion.
it.ans: The Sun drives the water cycle and winds; water and wind break rocks and carry sediment, and the Sun's heating and cooling of rocks can crack them.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Materials, the Rock Cycle and Resources
lessons.n: Why resources are where they are

it.q: Gold in California's Sierra Nevada foothills formed in quartz veins when hot water rich in minerals flowed through cracks in rock and cooled. Why is gold found there but not everywhere?
ch: Past geologic processes concentrated it only in certain places
Gold falls evenly from the sky
Gold grows in soil each year

it.q: Fossil fuels such as oil and natural gas formed from
ch: remains of ancient organisms buried and heated over millions of years
it.h: Think about what "fossil" means.

it.q: Groundwater is stored in layers of rock and sediment with many connected spaces. What are these layers called?
An oil field held 600 million barrels. 450 million barrels have been pumped out. What percent of the oil remains?
Explain why mineral resources and fossil fuels are called nonrenewable.
it.ans: They form over thousands to millions of years through geologic processes, much more slowly than people use them, so once used they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Earth's Materials, the Rock Cycle and Resources
lessons.n: Identifying minerals by their properties

it.q: A naturally formed, nonliving solid with a definite chemical makeup and a crystal structure is a
it.h: Rocks are made of these.

it.q: On the Mohs scale, talc has a hardness of 1 and diamond 10. A mineral that scratches glass (about 5.5) but is scratched by quartz (7) has a hardness of about
it.h: It is harder than glass but softer than quartz.

it.q: The color of a mineral's powder when rubbed on a white tile is its
it.h: The powder leaves a line.

it.q: A mineral sample has a mass of 52 g and a volume of 20 cubic centimeters. What is its density in grams per cubic centimeter?
it.h: Density equals mass divided by volume.

it.q: Why is color alone a poor way to identify many minerals?
ch: The same mineral can come in different colors because of small impurities.
All minerals are the same color.
it.h: Quartz can be clear, pink or purple.

it.q: Explain how minerals form when hot water rich in dissolved minerals cools inside cracks in rock.
it.ans: As the water cools, it cannot hold as many dissolved materials, so mineral particles come out of solution and arrange into crystals that fill the cracks, forming veins.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Evidence that continents move

it.q: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, are found only in southern Africa and eastern South America. What is the best explanation?
ch: The two continents were once joined
Mesosaurus swam across the Atlantic Ocean
The fossils were carried by wind
it.h: Could a freshwater animal cross a salty ocean?

it.q: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. This observation supports the idea that
ch: the continents were once connected and have moved apart
the continents were always in the same place

it.q: Rock layers of the same type and age are found in mountains in eastern North America and in Scotland. What does this suggest?
ch: The mountains formed together before the continents separated
Scotland was formed from North American soil
Mountains are always the same age

it.q: The Atlantic Ocean widens about 2.5 cm per year. How many cm would it widen in 1,000 years?
it.h: Multiply the rate by the time.

it.q: Fossils of tropical plants have been found in rocks in Antarctica. Explain what this suggests about Antarctica's past.
it.ans: Antarctica was once in a warmer place closer to the equator, and plate motion has slowly carried it to the South Pole.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Plate boundaries build and break the land

it.q: At which type of plate boundary do plates move apart?
The Himalayas formed and are still rising where the Indian Plate pushes into the Eurasian Plate. What kind of boundary is this?
The San Andreas Fault, where the Pacific Plate slides past the North American Plate, is
it.h: Do the plates move apart, together or side by side?

it.q: Where an ocean plate meets a continental plate, the denser ocean plate sinks beneath it. Which features commonly form there?
ch: deep ocean trenches and volcanic mountains

it.q: The Cascade volcanoes, including Mount St. Helens in Washington and Mount Shasta in Northern California, form a line near the coast. Explain how plate motion causes them.
it.ans: A small ocean plate sinks beneath the North American Plate; as it sinks, rock melts into magma, which rises to form a chain of volcanoes parallel to the boundary.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Changes fast and slow, large and small

it.q: Which change to Earth's surface happens in seconds to minutes?
Which change takes millions of years?
it.h: Think about which processes add up slowly over a long time.

it.q: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon about 1,800 m deep in about 6 million years. What is the average rate of cutting in mm per year? (1 m = 1,000 mm)
A small stream carries sand downhill every day. Over millions of years, how could this affect a mountain?
ch: It can wear the mountain down and build up sediment in valleys
It makes the mountain grow taller
It turns the mountain into lava

it.q: Give one example of a geoscience process that changes Earth's surface quickly and one that changes it slowly, and explain how both can shape the same landscape.
it.ans: Quickly: a landslide or volcanic eruption. Slowly: plate motion lifting mountains or river erosion carving canyons. A mountain can be pushed up slowly by plates, worn down slowly by rivers and changed suddenly by landslides.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Forecasting and reducing harm from natural hazards

it.q: Scientists cannot predict the exact day of an earthquake. What can they forecast?
ch: which areas are likely to have strong earthquakes in coming decades
the exact hour of the next earthquake

it.q: California's earthquake early warning system detects the first waves of a quake and sends alerts. How does this help people?
ch: It gives seconds of warning to drop, cover and hold on and to slow trains
It tells the exact date of future quakes
it.h: Seconds can matter.

it.q: Which design choice best reduces earthquake damage to buildings?
ch: flexible frames and bases that absorb shaking
tall glass towers on soft soil

it.q: An earthquake happened 120 km from a city. The first waves travel about 6 km per second and the damaging waves about 4 km per second. How many seconds after the first waves do the damaging waves arrive?
it.h: Find each wave's travel time, then subtract.

it.q: Explain why scientists monitor volcanoes for small earthquakes, ground swelling and gas releases.
it.ans: These signs show magma moving underground; when they increase, scientists can warn people that an eruption may be coming so they can evacuate.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Seafloor spreading and magnetic stripes

it.q: The process in which new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away on both sides is
it.h: The seafloor "spreads" out from the ridge.

it.q: Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times. When lava cools at a ridge, iron-rich minerals line up with the field. What pattern does this make?
ch: matching stripes of normal and reversed magnetism on both sides of the ridge
it.h: New rock forms on both sides and moves outward.

it.q: Why are the magnetic stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge a mirror image of the stripes on the other side?
ch: The rock formed at the ridge at the same time and then moved apart in both directions.
Magnets attract each other across the ridge.
it.h: Think of a conveyor belt moving two directions from the center.

it.q: Seafloor rock 150 km from a ridge is 5 million years old. How many kilometers per million years has the seafloor moved?
it.h: Divide the distance by the age.

it.q: Ocean floor sediments are thin near ridges and thicker far from them. What does this support?
ch: Rock near the ridge is younger, so less sediment has settled on it.
Sediment falls only far from ridges.
Ocean currents are faster at ridges.
it.h: Sediment builds up over time.

it.q: Explain how magnetic stripes give evidence that the seafloor is moving.
it.ans: Rock forming at the ridge records the direction of Earth's magnetic field. The same pattern of stripes appears on both sides, getting older with distance, which shows the new rock formed at the ridge and then moved away in both directions.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Plate Tectonics and Natural Hazards
lessons.n: Earthquake waves and seismographs: measuring and locating quakes

it.q: An instrument that records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake is a
it.h: "Seismo" refers to earthquakes.

it.q: Two kinds of earthquake waves are P waves and S waves. P waves are faster. At a station far from an earthquake, which wave arrives first?
it.h: The faster wave wins the race.

it.q: The longer the time between the arrival of P waves and S waves at a station, the
it.h: The waves spread farther apart the longer they travel.

it.q: P waves arrived at a station at 10:02:10 and S waves at 10:02:40. How many seconds apart did they arrive?
it.h: Subtract the times.

it.q: Why do scientists need data from at least three stations to find an earthquake's location?
ch: Each station gives a distance, and three circles cross at one point.
One station shows the exact location.
it.h: One distance gives a circle of possible places.

it.q: Explain why earthquake early warning systems in California can alert people before strong shaking arrives.
it.ans: Sensors detect the faster but weaker P waves near the earthquake. Computers send warnings electronically, which travel much faster than the slower, stronger S and surface waves, giving people seconds to take cover.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Sustaining Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
lessons.n: Disturbances change ecosystems

it.q: After a wildfire in California chaparral, many shrubs sprout from their roots and some seeds sprout only after fire. What does this show?
ch: Some organisms are adapted to recover after fire
it.h: Think about what happens in the months after the fire.

it.q: A long drought dries up a pond. Which population is most likely to decrease first?
ch: frogs that need water to lay eggs
lizards that live in dry places

it.q: Which is an example of a physical change to an ecosystem?
ch: a flood that moves soil and rocks
a disease in a bird species

it.q: After a fire, a hillside had 2 plant species. Five years later it had 18 species. How many species were added?
it.h: Subtract the starting number from the later number.

it.q: Explain how a change to one part of an ecosystem, such as less rain, can affect populations at several levels of a food web.
it.ans: Less rain means fewer plants grow; herbivores that eat those plants have less food and decrease; predators that eat the herbivores then have less food and may decrease too.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Sustaining Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
lessons.n: Biodiversity and ecosystem health

it.q: The variety of species in an area is called
Which ecosystem would most likely be most stable when a disease kills one plant species?
it.h: What happens if the only food source disappears?

it.q: Biodiversity can be measured by counting
ch: the number of different species in an area

it.q: In a sample, students counted 5 species of insects with 40, 30, 20, 6 and 4 individuals. What percent of all insects were the most common species?
it.h: Find the total first.

it.q: Explain why scientists are concerned when biodiversity decreases in an ecosystem.
it.ans: Lower biodiversity makes food webs simpler and less stable, so a disturbance can harm more of the ecosystem, and people lose benefits such as food, medicines and clean water.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Sustaining Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
lessons.n: Ecosystem services: what nature does for us

it.q: Wetlands slow down floodwater and filter pollutants. These benefits to people are called
California's almond orchards rely on bees to make almonds. Which ecosystem service do bees provide?
Forests on mountain slopes help prevent landslides because
ch: tree roots hold soil in place
trees cause more rain to run off
it.h: What keeps soil from sliding away?

it.q: A wetland reduced the amount of nitrogen pollution in water from 20 mg per liter to 5 mg per liter. What percent of the pollution was removed?
Describe one ecosystem service provided by a California ecosystem and explain how people benefit.
it.ans: Example: forests in the Sierra Nevada store water in soil and snow shade and release it slowly into rivers, supplying drinking water and reducing floods for cities downstream.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Sustaining Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
lessons.n: Designing solutions to protect biodiversity

it.q: Mountain lions near Los Angeles are blocked by freeways from finding mates and food. Which solution most directly addresses the problem?
ch: a wildlife bridge over the freeway planted with native plants

it.q: Engineers build fish ladders beside dams. What problem do they solve?
ch: They let fish swim upstream past the dam to spawn
They keep all fish out of the river

it.q: A team designs a way to reduce trash in a creek. Which is a constraint?
ch: The solution must cost less than $5,000
The solution must remove 80 percent of the trash
The solution must keep fish safe
The solution must catch plastic bottles
it.h: A constraint is a limit, such as cost, time or materials.

it.q: A trash net caught 72 kg of trash in 6 weeks. What was the mean amount caught per week in kg?
Name one criterion and one constraint for a solution that protects nesting birds on a busy beach.
it.ans: Criterion: increase the number of chicks that survive by 50 percent. Constraint: the beach must stay open to visitors and the plan must cost little to maintain.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Sustaining Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
lessons.n: Pollinators in decline: an ecosystem service at risk

it.q: Animals such as bees, butterflies, bats and hummingbirds that move pollen between flowers are
it.h: They help plants make seeds.

it.q: California grows most of the world's almonds, and almond trees need bees for pollination. What would happen to almond harvests if bee populations fell sharply?
it.h: No pollination means no nuts.

it.q: Which human activity can harm pollinator populations?
ch: heavy pesticide use and loss of wildflower habitat
it.h: Pollinators need food and safe places to live.

it.q: A field with hedgerows of wildflowers had 48 bee visits per hour. A field without them had 18. How many more visits per hour did the hedgerow field have?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Monarch butterfly caterpillars eat only milkweed. Why would removing milkweed along roadsides harm monarchs?
ch: Caterpillars would lose their only food.
it.h: Follow the food the caterpillars need.

it.q: Explain why pollination is called an ecosystem service.
it.ans: Pollinators provide a benefit to people for free: they help plants make fruits, seeds and nuts we eat, and they support wild plants that other animals depend on.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Describing motion: speed and velocity

it.q: Speed is calculated by dividing
it.h: Think of units such as meters per second.

it.q: A cyclist rides 1,200 meters in 240 seconds. What is her average speed in meters per second?
it.h: Divide distance by time.

it.q: Two runners both run at 6 m/s, one north and one south. Which statement is true?
ch: They have the same speed but different velocities

it.q: A train travels at 80 km per hour for 3.5 hours. How far does it travel in km?
A distance-time graph for a toy car is a straight line rising from 0 to 10 meters over 5 seconds, then a flat line from 5 to 8 seconds. Describe the car's motion.
it.ans: The car moved at a constant speed of 2 m/s for the first 5 seconds, then stopped and stayed at 10 meters from 5 to 8 seconds.
it.h: What does a flat line on a distance-time graph mean?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Net force, mass and changes in motion

it.q: Two students push a box from opposite sides. One pushes with 30 N to the right and the other with 30 N to the left. What happens?
ch: The forces are balanced, so the box's motion does not change
it.h: Add forces in the same direction; subtract forces in opposite directions.

it.q: A sled is pulled with 50 N forward while friction pushes back with 20 N. What is the net force in newtons?
The same push is given to an empty shopping cart and a full shopping cart. Which accelerates more?
ch: the empty cart, because it has less mass
the full cart, because it has more mass

it.q: Using F = m x a, what force in newtons is needed to accelerate a 4 kg ball at 3 meters per second each second?
Plan an investigation to show how the mass of a cart affects its acceleration when the same force pulls it.
it.ans: Pull carts of different masses (add weights) with the same force, such as the same falling weight or spring scale reading; measure the time to travel a set distance or use a motion sensor; keep the track and force the same; repeat trials and compare accelerations.
it.h: Change only the mass. What must stay the same?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Newton's third law: action and reaction

it.q: Newton's third law says that when one object pushes on another, the second object
ch: pushes back with an equal force in the opposite direction
pushes back with a smaller force

it.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water. What pushes the swimmer forward?
ch: the water pushing forward on the swimmer
it.h: Look for the pair of forces between the swimmer and the water.

it.q: A rocket pushes hot gases downward out of its engine. Why does the rocket go up?
ch: The gases push up on the rocket with an equal and opposite force
The gases pull the rocket by gravity
The air below lifts the rocket like a hand

it.q: A 50 kg student on skates pushes a wall with 100 N. With what force in newtons does the wall push back on the student?
A small car and a large truck collide head-on. Compare the forces each exerts on the other and explain why the small car is affected more.
it.ans: By Newton's third law the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. The car has less mass, so the same force gives it a much larger change in motion, which is why its passengers feel a bigger jolt.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Design challenge: safer collisions

it.q: Why do car airbags reduce injuries in a crash?
ch: They make the passenger stop over a longer time, lowering the force on the body
They make the car stop faster
it.h: Spreading a stop over more time lowers the force.

it.q: A team must design a bumper that protects a toy car carrying an egg in a crash. Which is a constraint?
ch: Use only cardboard, tape and straws
The car must hit the wall at full speed
The bumper must absorb the impact

it.q: Crumple zones in cars are designed to
ch: crush and absorb energy during a collision

it.q: Three bumper designs were tested 4 times each. Design A protected the egg in 3 tests, B in 4 tests and C in 1 test. What percent of tests did Design A pass?
Explain how Newton's third law applies when a car hits a wall during a crash test.
it.ans: The car pushes on the wall and the wall pushes back on the car with an equal and opposite force; this force stops the car, so designs focus on reducing how suddenly that force acts on passengers.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Momentum: mass times velocity

it.q: An object's momentum equals its
it.h: Both how heavy and how fast matter.

it.q: A 2 kg ball rolls at 3 m/s. What is its momentum in kg x m/s?
it.h: Multiply mass by velocity.

it.q: A bicycle and a truck move at the same velocity. Which has more momentum?
ch: the truck, because it has more mass
it.h: Velocity is the same, so compare masses.

it.q: A 50 kg skater has a momentum of 200 kg x m/s. What is her velocity in m/s?
it.h: Divide momentum by mass.

it.q: In a collision between two carts with no outside forces, the total momentum of the two carts
it.h: Momentum lost by one cart is gained by the other.

it.q: Explain why it is harder to stop a loaded shopping cart than an empty one moving at the same speed.
it.ans: The loaded cart has more mass, so it has more momentum. A larger force (or the same force for a longer time) is needed to change its momentum to zero.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Bouncing and sticking: comparing collisions

it.q: In a collision where two objects stick together and move as one, the objects
it.h: Think of two train cars coupling.

it.q: A rubber ball and a clay ball of the same mass hit a wall at the same speed. The rubber ball bounces back; the clay ball sticks. Which pushes harder on the wall?
ch: the rubber ball, because its velocity changes more
it.h: Bouncing back means a bigger change in velocity.

it.q: A 3 kg cart moving at 2 m/s sticks to a still 1 kg cart. What is their combined speed in m/s?
it.h: Momentum before = 6. Divide by the total mass of 4 kg.

it.q: In car crash tests, a car that crumples instead of bouncing off the wall is safer for passengers. Why?
ch: Crumpling stretches out the collision time, reducing the force on passengers.
it.h: The same change in momentum over more time needs less force.

it.q: Two identical carts move toward each other at the same speed and stick together. What happens?
ch: They stop, because their momenta cancel.
it.h: Momentum has direction.

it.q: Describe how a bumper on a bumper car is designed to reduce the force on riders during a collision.
it.ans: The soft rubber bumper squishes during the hit, increasing the time over which the cars change speed. Since the change in momentum is the same, a longer time means a smaller force on the riders.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Forces, Motion and Collisions
lessons.n: Investigating friction: surfaces, weight and sliding

it.q: Friction is a force that
ch: acts against the motion of surfaces sliding past each other
it.h: It is why a sliding book slows down.

it.q: A block is pulled across sandpaper and then across smooth glass with a spring scale. Which surface needs more force at a steady speed?
ch: sandpaper, because it has more friction
it.h: Rougher surfaces grip more.

it.q: A spring scale read 6 N while pulling a block at steady speed on carpet. What was the force of friction in newtons?
it.h: At a steady speed, the forces are balanced.

it.q: Adding a second identical block on top of the first increases the friction force. Why?
ch: The blocks press harder against the surface.
it.h: Think about how hard the surfaces are pushed together.

it.q: Why do cars need more distance to stop on icy roads?
ch: Ice gives less friction between tires and road.
Ice adds mass to the car.
it.h: Which force slows the car?

it.q: Plan an investigation to test how surface type affects friction.
it.ans: Pull the same block with a spring scale at a steady speed across wood, carpet, sandpaper and plastic. Keep the block's mass and pulling direction the same. Record the force for 3 trials on each surface and compare the averages.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed

it.q: The energy an object has because it is moving is
A bowling ball and a tennis ball roll at the same speed. Which has more kinetic energy?
ch: the bowling ball, because it has more mass
the tennis ball, because it is smaller
they have the same kinetic energy

it.q: Kinetic energy = 1/2 x mass x speed x speed. What is the kinetic energy in joules of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s?
it.h: Square the speed first: 3 x 3 = 9.

it.q: A graph of kinetic energy against mass (speed held constant) is a straight line through zero. What does this show?
ch: Kinetic energy is proportional to mass
Kinetic energy does not depend on mass

it.q: Explain why a car moving at 60 km per hour is much more dangerous in a crash than the same car at 30 km per hour.
it.ans: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed makes the car's kinetic energy four times larger; more energy must be transferred in the crash, causing more damage.
it.h: What happens to kinetic energy when speed doubles?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Potential energy and the distance between objects

it.q: Energy stored because of an object's position or shape is
A book is lifted from the floor to a high shelf. What happens to the gravitational potential energy of the Earth-book system?
ch: It increases because the book is farther from Earth
it.h: Lifting against gravity stores energy.

it.q: Two magnets that repel are pushed closer together. What happens to the potential energy stored between them?
Gravitational potential energy = mass x 9.8 x height. What is the potential energy in joules of a 2 kg rock on a 5 m ledge?
Explain why stretching a rubber band farther stores more energy, and what happens to that energy when you let go.
it.ans: Stretching changes the band's shape and increases the distance it is pulled, storing more elastic potential energy; when released, the stored energy changes into kinetic energy as the band snaps back.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Energy changes form

it.q: A roller coaster car is at the top of the first hill. Where is its kinetic energy greatest?
ch: at the bottom of the hill
at the top of the hill
it.h: Where is the car moving fastest?

it.q: A swinging pendulum moves fastest at the bottom of its swing. Which energy change happens as it swings down?
ch: potential energy changes to kinetic energy
kinetic energy changes to potential energy

it.q: A pendulum's swings slowly get smaller and it stops. Where did the energy go?
ch: It was transferred to the air and the pivot as thermal energy and sound
It went back into the string

it.q: A 2 kg ball is dropped and has 40 J of potential energy at the top. Ignoring air resistance, how much kinetic energy in joules does it have just before hitting the ground?
Describe the energy changes when you throw a ball straight up and it falls back to your hand.
it.ans: At first the ball has kinetic energy; as it rises, kinetic energy changes into gravitational potential energy until it stops at the top; as it falls, potential energy changes back into kinetic energy. Some energy is lost to air as heat.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Energy in an asteroid impact

it.q: An asteroid that struck near Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula about 66 million years ago is linked to the extinction of the dinosaurs. Why did it release so much energy?
ch: It had enormous mass and very high speed
it.h: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed.

it.q: Two asteroids have the same mass. Asteroid A moves twice as fast as Asteroid B. How does A's kinetic energy compare?
A 1,000 kg meteorite moves at 20,000 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules (KE = 1/2 x m x v x v)?
When a meteorite hits the ground, where does its kinetic energy go?
it.ans: It is transferred into heat, sound, light and the work of digging a crater and throwing rock and dust into the air.

it.q: As an asteroid falls toward Earth, the Earth-asteroid system's potential energy

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Braking distance and speed: graphing kinetic energy

it.q: The distance a car travels after the brakes are applied until it stops is its
it.h: It depends on how much kinetic energy the brakes must remove.

it.q: Test data for one car: 10 m/s, braking distance 8 m; 20 m/s, 32 m; 30 m/s, 72 m. What happens to braking distance when speed doubles?
ch: It becomes about four times as long.
it.h: Compare 10 m/s with 20 m/s.

it.q: A car's braking distance is 8 m at 10 m/s, 32 m at 20 m/s and 72 m at 30 m/s. Following the pattern, what is it at 40 m/s in meters?
it.h: Braking distance grows with the square of speed: 8 x 4 x 4.

it.q: Why does braking distance grow faster than speed?
ch: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, and brakes must remove all of it.
Brakes get weaker at high speed.
it.h: KE = 1/2 x m x v x v.

it.q: A graph of braking distance (y-axis) against speed (x-axis) would be
it.h: The distance quadruples when speed doubles.

it.q: Explain why school zones set speed limits around 25 miles per hour instead of 40.
it.ans: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so a car at 40 has more than twice the kinetic energy of one at 25. Lower speed means shorter braking distance and less energy in a crash.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Energy of Motion and Position
lessons.n: Useful and wasted energy: efficiency in devices

it.q: The percent of input energy that a device turns into useful output is its
it.h: A perfect device would be 100 percent.

it.q: An old incandescent bulb gets very hot. What does this show?
ch: Much of its electrical energy becomes thermal energy instead of light.
it.h: Is heat the useful output for a light bulb?

it.q: A motor uses 200 J of electrical energy and does 150 J of useful work lifting a load. What is its efficiency as a percent?
it.h: Divide useful output by input, then multiply by 100.

it.q: Where does the "wasted" energy in a car engine go?
ch: mostly into thermal energy of the engine and surroundings
it.h: Energy is conserved; it changes form.

it.q: An LED bulb gives the same light as an incandescent bulb but uses 9 W instead of 60 W. How many watts does it save?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Explain why no device can be 100 percent efficient, using the idea of conservation of energy.
it.ans: Energy is never destroyed, but in every real device some input energy changes into forms that are not useful, mostly thermal energy from friction and electrical resistance. So the useful output is always less than the input.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Fields: forces without touching

it.q: A force that acts on an object without touching it is a
A paper clip jumps toward a magnet held 1 cm above it. What does this show?
ch: The magnet's field exerts a force on the clip without touching it
The clip is pushed by air
The magnet must touch the clip to pull it
The clip has its own gravity only

it.q: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet form curved lines from pole to pole. What do the lines show?
ch: the shape of the magnetic field
it.h: Filings line up with an invisible region around the magnet.

it.q: A paper clip moved toward a magnet from 4 cm away, but not from 6 cm away. How many cm closer did it have to be?
Plan a simple investigation to show that a magnetic field can pass through materials.
it.ans: Place sheets of paper, plastic, cardboard and other materials between a magnet and a paper clip; count how many sheets the force passes through before the clip no longer moves; keep the magnet and distance the same.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Electric forces and charges

it.q: Two balloons are both rubbed with wool and get the same type of charge. What happens when they are brought close?
it.h: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

it.q: A charged comb picks up small bits of paper. As the comb is moved farther away, the force
Which change would make the electric force between two charged objects stronger?
ch: increasing the amount of charge on them

it.q: A charged rod lifted 12 bits of paper from 1 cm away and 3 bits from 2 cm away. How many times more bits did it lift at 1 cm?
Explain why your hair sticks to a sweater you just pulled off.
it.ans: Rubbing moved electrons, giving the hair and sweater opposite charges; opposite charges attract, so the hair is pulled toward the sweater.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Magnetic forces and electromagnets

it.q: The north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another. What happens?
Wire is coiled around an iron nail and connected to a battery. The nail picks up paper clips. What is this device?
An electromagnet with 10 coils picked up 4 clips, 20 coils picked up 8 clips and 30 coils picked up 12 clips. How many clips would 40 coils likely pick up?
it.h: Look for how many clips are added for every 10 coils.

it.q: Which change would make an electromagnet weaker?
Explain one advantage of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet for a junkyard crane.
it.ans: An electromagnet can be turned on to lift scrap metal and turned off to drop it, and its strength can be changed by adjusting the current.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Gravity depends on mass and distance

it.q: Gravity is a force that
ch: always attracts objects with mass toward each other

it.q: Why do you weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
ch: The Moon has less mass, so its gravitational pull is weaker
You have less mass on the Moon
The Moon is closer to the Sun
it.h: Your mass stays the same everywhere; what changes is the strength of the gravitational pull on you.

it.q: Weight = mass x gravity. On the Moon, gravity is 1.6 newtons per kg. What does a 50 kg astronaut weigh on the Moon in newtons?
Which pair has the greatest gravitational attraction?
ch: a pencil and a paper clip

it.q: Explain why you do not feel the gravitational pull between you and a nearby classmate.
it.ans: All objects with mass attract, but people have very small masses compared with planets, so the force between you is far too small to notice.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Generators: making electric current with magnets

it.q: Moving a magnet into and out of a coil of wire makes an electric current in the wire. This is
it.h: The current is "induced" by the moving magnet.

it.q: A student holds a magnet still inside a coil connected to a meter. What does the meter show?
ch: no current, because the magnet is not moving
current only if the coil is plastic
it.h: Induction needs change or motion.

it.q: Which change would make a bigger current in a generator?
it.h: Think about how quickly the magnetic field changes in the coil.

it.q: A coil with 100 loops made a peak current reading of 4 units. With 300 loops and the same motion, the reading was 12 units. How many times bigger was the reading?
it.h: Divide 12 by 4.

it.q: In a hydroelectric dam, falling water spins a turbine attached to a generator. What energy change happens in the generator?
it.h: The generator is spinning.

it.q: Explain how a generator and a motor are similar and how they are different.
it.ans: Both use magnets and coils of wire. A generator changes motion (kinetic energy) into electrical energy by moving coils and magnets past each other. A motor does the opposite, using electric current in coils to create magnetic forces that make motion.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Electric motors and speakers: electromagnets at work

it.q: An electric motor uses magnetic forces to change
it.h: A motor makes things spin.

it.q: Inside a motor, a coil of wire carrying current sits between magnets. Why does the coil spin?
ch: Magnetic forces push and pull on the coil's magnetic field.
The wire is lighter than air.
it.h: A current-carrying coil acts like a magnet.

it.q: Which change would make a small motor spin faster?
ch: increasing the current through the coil
it.h: More current makes a stronger electromagnet.

it.q: A motor spun at 900 rotations per minute with 1 battery and 1,750 with 2 batteries. How many more rotations per minute did it spin with 2 batteries?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: A speaker has a coil attached to a paper cone near a magnet. A changing current makes the coil move back and forth. What does the cone make?
it.h: A vibrating cone pushes on air.

it.q: Explain why reversing the battery in a simple motor makes it spin the other way.
it.ans: Reversing the battery reverses the direction of current in the coil, which flips the poles of the coil's magnetic field. The magnetic forces now push in the opposite direction, so the motor spins the other way.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Forces at a Distance - Electric, Magnetic and Gravitational Fields
lessons.n: Earth's magnetic field: compasses, auroras and protection

it.q: A compass needle points north because
ch: it lines up with Earth's magnetic field
it is pulled by the North Star
gravity is stronger at the North Pole
it.h: The needle is a small magnet.

it.q: Scientists think Earth's magnetic field is produced by
ch: movement of molten iron in Earth's outer core
it.h: Moving electric charges in metal can make a magnetic field.

it.q: A compass is placed near a bar magnet instead of on its own. What happens?
ch: The needle turns toward the magnet's field.
The needle points to the Sun.
it.h: A nearby magnet's field can be stronger than Earth's.

it.q: A compass was carried 3 m away from a magnet in steps of 1 m. The needle turned 60 degrees at 1 m, 20 degrees at 2 m and 5 degrees at 3 m. How many degrees less did it turn at 3 m than at 1 m?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Auroras (northern and southern lights) are usually seen near the poles. Why?
ch: Earth's magnetic field guides charged particles from the Sun toward the poles.
The poles are closer to the Sun.
it.h: Field lines curve in near the poles.

it.q: Explain how iron filings around a bar magnet give evidence that a magnetic field exists even though it cannot be seen.
it.ans: The filings line up in curved patterns from pole to pole without being touched. Something must be pushing on them at a distance, which is evidence of a field that exerts forces around the magnet.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: Moon phases and eclipses

it.q: Why does the Moon appear to change shape during the month?
ch: As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half
Earth's shadow covers parts of it
it.h: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

it.q: During a new moon, where is the Moon located?
ch: on the far side of Earth from the Sun
at the same distance as the Sun

it.q: A lunar eclipse happens when
ch: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Moon is between the Sun and Earth
the Sun is between Earth and the Moon

it.q: The Moon's cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. Using 29.5 days, how many days pass from a full moon to the next new moon?
it.h: Full moon to new moon is half the cycle.

it.q: Explain why we do not have a solar eclipse every month at new moon.
it.ans: The Moon's orbit is tilted slightly compared with Earth's orbit around the Sun, so most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line between Earth and the Sun and its shadow misses Earth.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: Why Earth has seasons

it.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
ch: the tilt of Earth's axis as Earth orbits the Sun
Earth's changing distance from the Sun
the Sun getting hotter in summer
the Moon blocking sunlight in winter
it.h: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

it.q: In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. What season is it in California?
In June, what season is it in Australia?
On the summer solstice, Sacramento gets about 15 hours of daylight; on the winter solstice, about 9.5 hours. How many more hours of daylight are there in summer?
Explain two ways the tilt of Earth's axis makes summer warmer than winter.
it.ans: In summer, sunlight hits more directly, so its energy is concentrated on a smaller area; days are also longer, so the ground receives sunlight for more hours.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: Gravity holds the solar system and galaxy together

it.q: What force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
If the Sun's gravity suddenly stopped, what would Earth do?
ch: move off in a straight line into space
it.h: Without a force pulling it inward, a moving object keeps going straight.

it.q: The Milky Way is a galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars that orbit its center. What keeps the stars together?
Mercury takes 88 days to orbit the Sun, and Earth takes 365 days. About how many Mercury orbits happen in one Earth year? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
Explain how gravity and an object's forward motion together produce an orbit.
it.ans: Gravity pulls the planet toward the Sun, while the planet's forward motion carries it sideways; the combination makes it curve around the Sun in a path that keeps falling around it.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: The scale of the solar system

it.q: The average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km, is called
Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun. How many million km is that? (1 AU = 150 million km)
it.h: Multiply 5.2 by 150.

it.q: Jupiter's diameter is about 143,000 km and Earth's is about 12,700 km. About how many Earths would fit across Jupiter?
A model uses 1 cm for each AU. Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun. How many cm from the model Sun should Neptune be placed?
Explain why it is hard to make a model of the solar system with both planet sizes and distances to the same scale.
it.ans: The distances are enormous compared with the sizes; if planets were large enough to see, the model would need to be kilometers long, and if it fit in a room, the planets would be tiny specks.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: Tides: the Moon's and Sun's gravity on the oceans

it.q: The regular rise and fall of ocean water levels along a coast is called the
it.h: Most coasts have high and low ones twice a day.

it.q: What mainly causes tides on Earth?
ch: the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth and its oceans
it.h: Which nearby object pulls on Earth strongly?

it.q: Most coasts have two high tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes. Why two?
ch: Ocean water bulges on the side facing the Moon and the opposite side.
The Moon orbits twice a day.
it.h: There are two bulges, and Earth rotates through both.

it.q: On most coasts, one high tide follows another about every 12 hours and 25 minutes. How many minutes is that in all?
it.h: Change 12 hours into minutes, then add 25.

it.q: Spring tides, with the highest high tides and lowest low tides, happen when
ch: the Sun, Earth and Moon line up at new and full moon
the Moon is at first quarter
it.h: Two pulls in a line add together.

it.q: Explain why the Moon affects tides more than the Sun, even though the Sun has much more mass.
it.ans: The Moon is much closer to Earth. Tides depend on the difference in gravity's pull across Earth, and that difference is larger for the close Moon than for the distant Sun.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Earth, the Moon and the Solar System
lessons.n: Asteroids, comets and meteors: small bodies of the solar system

it.q: Most asteroids in our solar system orbit the Sun in a belt between
it.h: It lies between the inner and outer planets.

it.q: A comet is mostly made of
it.h: Comets are sometimes called "dirty snowballs."

it.q: Why does a comet grow a glowing tail when it gets close to the Sun?
ch: Sunlight heats its ice, releasing gas and dust that the Sun's energy pushes away.
It is pulled apart by Earth.
it.h: What happens to ice when it warms?

it.q: A comet orbits the Sun once every 70 years. It was last near Earth in 1990. In what year will it next be near Earth?
it.h: Add 70 to 1990.

it.q: What keeps asteroids and comets in orbit around the Sun?
it.h: The same force holds the planets in orbit.

it.q: Explain the difference between a meteoroid, a meteor and a meteorite.
it.ans: A meteoroid is a small rock or bit of dust in space. A meteor is the streak of light when it burns through Earth's atmosphere. A meteorite is a piece that survives and lands on the ground.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Wave properties and energy

it.q: The height of a wave from its rest position to its crest is its
The distance from one crest to the next crest is the
it.h: Picture measuring along the wave from one high point to the next.

it.q: Wave speed = frequency x wavelength. A wave has a frequency of 4 waves per second (4 Hz) and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed in m/s?
Two ocean waves have the same wavelength. Wave A is 1 m tall and Wave B is 3 m tall. Which carries more energy?
ch: Wave B, because it has a larger amplitude
Wave A, because it is smaller

it.q: Explain what a wave carries from one place to another and what it does not carry. Give an example.
it.ans: A wave carries energy, not matter. In an ocean wave, a floating ball bobs up and down in about the same place while the energy moves toward the shore.
it.h: Watch a cork floating as waves pass.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Sound waves

it.q: Why can't sound travel through outer space?
ch: Sound needs a medium, such as air, to travel through
it.h: Sound is a vibration of particles.

it.q: A guitar string vibrates faster when it is tightened. How does this change the sound?
Sound travels about 340 m/s in air. How far does sound travel in 3 seconds in meters?
A louder sound has
Explain why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
it.ans: Light travels much faster than sound; the light reaches you almost instantly, while sound in air travels about 340 m/s, so it arrives later.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Light: reflect, absorb, transmit

it.q: A red apple looks red in white light because it
ch: reflects red light and absorbs other colors
it.h: The color you see is the light that bounces to your eye.

it.q: Light passes easily through a clear window. This is
A straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. What causes this?
ch: Light refracts (bends) as it changes speed passing from water to air

it.q: Which material would most likely absorb the most sunlight and get hottest?
Describe what happens to light when it hits a mirror, a black piece of paper and a glass window.
it.ans: The mirror reflects almost all light; the black paper absorbs most light and warms up; the glass window transmits most light through it.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Digital signals carry information

it.q: A digital signal sends information as
ch: a series of on and off pulses, like 1s and 0s

it.q: Why are digital signals often more reliable than analog signals?
ch: Small amounts of noise do not change whether a pulse is read as 1 or 0
it.h: Think about how easily a 1 or 0 can be read even with a little static.

it.q: Each character in a text message uses 8 bits. How many bits does a 15-character message use?
Which uses waves to carry digital information?
Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of digital signals.
it.ans: Advantage: they can be copied, stored and sent many times without losing quality. Disadvantage: they need devices to encode and decode them, and if too many bits are lost the message can drop out completely.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: The electromagnetic spectrum: radio waves to gamma rays

it.q: Visible light, radio waves, microwaves and X-rays are all
it.h: They can all travel through empty space.

it.q: Which list orders electromagnetic waves from longest to shortest wavelength?
ch: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
it.h: Radio waves are the longest.

it.q: Why do people wear sunscreen?
ch: to block ultraviolet waves from the Sun that can damage skin
it.h: Sunburn is caused by waves just beyond violet light.

it.q: All electromagnetic waves travel about 300,000 km each second in space. How many seconds would a radio signal take to reach the Moon, about 384,000 km away? Round to one decimal place.
it.h: Divide the distance by the speed.

it.q: Thermal cameras can "see" warm animals in the dark. Which waves do they detect?
it.h: Warm objects give off these waves.

it.q: Give two examples of how people use electromagnetic waves to carry information.
it.ans: Radio and TV broadcasts use radio waves; cell phones and Wi-Fi use microwaves and radio waves; fiber-optic cables use pulses of light or infrared.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Waves, Light and Information
lessons.n: Lenses: how refraction forms images in eyes and cameras

it.q: A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together is a
it.h: "Converging" lenses bulge out.

it.q: A magnifying glass makes a bug look bigger. How does it work?
ch: Its convex lens bends light rays from the bug before they reach your eye.
It reflects light like a mirror.
it.h: Light bends as it passes through curved glass.

it.q: In the human eye, which part focuses light onto the retina?
it.h: Like a camera, the eye has a lens.

it.q: A camera lens forms a sharp image when the sensor is 50 mm behind it. If the sensor is moved to 48 mm, by how many millimeters is it out of position?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: A person who is nearsighted sees close objects clearly but distant objects blurry. Which lens corrects this?
ch: a concave lens that spreads light rays slightly
it.h: The eye focuses distant light too early, in front of the retina.

it.q: Explain why a straw in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface.
it.ans: Light from the straw changes speed and bends (refracts) as it passes from water into air, so it reaches our eyes from a different direction than it left the straw, making the straw look broken or bent.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
lessons.n: Reading rock layers and geologic time

it.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is usually
it.h: Layers pile up one on top of another over time.

it.q: A layer of volcanic ash lies between Layer A (below) and Layer B (above). What can you say about the ash?
ch: It is younger than Layer A and older than Layer B
It is older than both layers
It is younger than both layers

it.q: A crack (fault) cuts through Layers 1, 2 and 3 but not Layer 4 on top. When did the fault form?
ch: after Layers 1 to 3 formed and before Layer 4
at the same time as Layer 4

it.q: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. Non-avian dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago. How many million years did Earth exist before that extinction?
it.h: 4.6 billion = 4,600 million.

it.q: A fossil of a sea animal is found in a layer below a layer with land plant fossils. What does this suggest about how the area changed?
it.ans: The area was once covered by sea, and later it became land where plants grew, because lower layers formed earlier than upper layers.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
lessons.n: Patterns in the fossil record

it.q: Fossils show that many species that once lived are no longer alive today. This is evidence of
In older rock layers, fossils of living things tend to be simpler; in younger layers, more types of complex organisms appear. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: Life on Earth has changed over time
it.h: Compare what you find at the bottom with what you find near the top.

it.q: A rock layer from about 252 million years ago records a mass extinction. If a sample had 200 species of sea animals before it and 20 after it, what percent of the species disappeared?
Fossils of the same kind of organism found in many layers show small changes in shape over time. What does this show?
ch: Species can change gradually over many generations

it.q: Explain why the fossil record is incomplete.
it.ans: Most organisms decay before they are fossilized; fossils form only under special conditions like quick burial in sediment, and many fossils are destroyed by erosion or are never found.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
lessons.n: Similar structures, shared ancestors

it.q: A human arm, a cat's front leg, a whale's flipper and a bat's wing all have the same set of bones in the same order. What does this suggest?
ch: These animals share a common ancestor
They all use their limbs in the same way
it.h: Similar structure is evidence of relationship, even if the jobs differ.

it.q: Structures that have similar bones but different functions in related species are called
A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are both used for flying but are built very differently. What does this suggest?
ch: They evolved separately and are not evidence of close relationship
They come from the same ancestor recently

it.q: A modern horse has 1 toe per foot. A fossil ancestor from about 50 million years ago had 4 toes on each front foot. How many fewer front toes per foot does the modern horse have?
Explain how a whale's tiny hip bones are evidence that its ancestors lived on land.
it.ans: Hip bones attach legs in land mammals; whales have small, unused hip bones, which suggests they inherited them from ancestors that walked on land with hind legs.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
lessons.n: Clues from embryos

it.q: Early embryos of fish, chickens, pigs and humans all have a tail and pouches in the throat region. What does this similarity suggest?
ch: These animals share a common ancestor
They live in the same habitat

it.q: As embryos develop, they become more different from each other. Which explanation fits?
ch: Different genes switch on as each species develops its own features
it.h: Similar early stages, different later stages.

it.q: A study compared 12 early embryo features in a chicken and a turtle. They shared 9 features. What percent did they share?
Which observation from embryos would best support that two species are closely related?
ch: Their embryos look alike for a long time during development

it.q: Explain why comparing embryos can show relationships that are hard to see in adult animals.
it.ans: Many shared features appear only early in development and later change or disappear, so embryos can reveal similarities, such as tails or throat pouches, that are hidden in adults.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Earth's History and Evidence of Common Ancestry
lessons.n: Dating rocks: index fossils and radioactive half-life

it.q: A fossil of an organism that lived over a wide area for a short time, used to match rock layers by age, is
it.h: It works like a time stamp.

it.q: Placing rock layers in order from oldest to youngest without knowing exact ages is
it.h: "Relative" means compared with each other.

it.q: A radioactive element's half-life is the time it takes for
ch: half of its atoms to change into another element
all of its atoms to disappear
twice as many atoms to form
it.h: "Half" is the key word.

it.q: A radioactive element has a half-life of 1 million years. A rock starts with 800 atoms of it. How many remain after 2 million years?
it.h: Halve it twice.

it.q: The same index fossil is found in a layer in Utah and a layer in Wales. What can scientists conclude?
ch: The layers are about the same age.
The layers are in the same place.
The fossil was moved by people.
The layers formed at very different times.
it.h: Index fossils lived for a short time.

it.q: Explain the difference between relative dating and absolute (numerical) dating.
it.ans: Relative dating puts rock layers and fossils in order (older or younger) using principles like superposition. Absolute dating finds an age in years, usually by measuring how much of a radioactive element has decayed.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Family Histories (2.1)
