it.h: Voters fill it out.

it.q: Why is voting secret?
ch: so people can choose freely without being pressured
so leaders can pick for you
it.h: Would you want someone telling you how to vote?

it.q: In 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women in the United States the right to
it.h: Before 1920, women could not vote in national elections in most states.

it.q: In a class election, Paolo gets 9 votes, Mei gets 12 votes and Sami gets 5 votes. How many more votes does Mei get than Paolo?
it.h: Subtract Paolo's votes from Mei's votes.

it.q: Tell why it is important for grown-up citizens to vote.
it.ans: Voting lets people choose leaders who will listen to them and make good laws.
it.h: Who chooses the leaders?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Government, Laws and Getting Along (2.3)
lessons.n: Taxes Pay for Public Services

it.q: A tax is
ch: money people pay to the government
it.h: Governments need money to pay for things everyone uses.

it.q: Which is a public service paid for by taxes?
it.h: Public means for everyone in the community.

it.q: Which workers are often paid with tax money?
it.h: Who works for the city or state?

it.q: A city collects taxes to fix potholes. Who benefits?
it.h: Who drives, rides and walks on streets?

it.q: A town gets 900 dollars in taxes. It spends 500 dollars on the library and the rest on the park. How many dollars go to the park?
it.h: Subtract the library money from the total.

it.q: Name two public services in your community.
it.ans: The public library and the fire department.
it.h: Think about places and workers that help everyone.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Government, Laws and Getting Along (2.3)
lessons.n: How Other Countries Govern

it.q: The leader of Canada's government is the
it.h: Canada uses a different title than the United States.

it.q: Mexico, like the United States, has a president and a group that makes laws called a
it.h: Mexico's lawmakers have the same name as ours.

it.q: The United Kingdom has a king, but laws are made by
ch: the President of the United States
it.h: The United Kingdom's lawmaking group meets in London.

it.q: How are many countries' governments alike?
ch: they make laws, carry out laws and settle disagreements
they all have the same leader
it.h: Think about the three jobs of government.

it.q: Mexico, Canada and the United States are the 3 largest countries in North America. A class studies their governments and 2 more countries. How many countries do they study?
it.h: Add the 3 countries and 2 more.

it.q: Tell one way the government of Canada or Mexico is like the government of the United States.
it.ans: Mexico has a president and a congress, just like the United States.
it.h: Think about leaders and lawmakers.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: From Farm to Market

it.q: Food that is picked from the fields is
it.h: Harvest time is when crops are ready.

it.q: The Salinas Valley grows a lot of lettuce. After it is picked, how does it usually get to stores far away?
it.h: Big vehicles on highways carry boxes of food.

it.q: Put the steps in order for strawberries.
it.h: First a plant must grow.

it.q: At a packing house, workers
it.h: Packing gets food ready to ship.

it.q: A farm worker picks 8 boxes of grapes in the morning and 7 boxes in the afternoon. How many boxes does she pick?
it.h: Add the morning and afternoon boxes.

it.q: Name two workers who help food get from a farm to your table.
it.ans: A farm worker picks it, and a truck driver brings it to the store.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: Producers and Consumers

it.q: A producer is a person who
ch: makes or grows goods or gives services
it.h: Produce means make.

it.q: A consumer is a person who
ch: buys and uses goods and services
it.h: Consume means use.

it.q: A baker makes bread and buys flour from a mill. The baker is
ch: both a producer and a consumer
it.h: Does the baker make things and also buy things?

it.q: Which is a service?
it.h: A service is work done for you.

it.q: Tell about a time you were a consumer.
it.ans: I bought a book at the book fair.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: Scarcity and Making Choices

it.q: Scarcity means
ch: there is not enough of something for everyone who wants it
there is too much of everything
it.h: Scarce means hard to get because there is not much.

it.q: During a drought, there is less water. What might farmers do?
ch: plant fewer crops or use water carefully
it.h: When something is scarce, people must choose carefully.

it.q: Jia has 5 dollars. She can buy a book or a puzzle, each 5 dollars. If she buys the book, what does she give up?
it.h: She can only choose one.

it.q: Why can't people have everything they want?
it.h: Limited means there is only so much.

it.q: Leo has 10 dollars. A soccer ball costs 7 dollars. How many dollars will he have left if he buys it?
it.h: Subtract the price from the money he has.

it.q: Tell about a time you had to choose between two things you wanted.
it.ans: I wanted a toy and a game, but I only had enough money for one, so I chose the game.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: Specialization: Each Worker Does One Job

it.q: Specialization means
ch: each worker focuses on one kind of job
it.h: Special means one particular thing.

it.q: In a bike factory, one worker puts on wheels, another adds seats and another paints. Why work this way?
ch: each worker gets fast and skilled at one step
it.h: What happens when you practice the same thing many times?

it.q: A dentist, a plumber and a baker each specialize. How do they get the other things they need?
ch: they earn money and buy goods and services from others
it.h: Can a dentist bake all her own bread and fix her own pipes?

it.q: Which is an example of specialization?
ch: a farmer who grows only strawberries
a family that makes every single thing it uses
a child who tries a new sport each day
it.h: Look for someone who focuses on one thing.

it.q: Working alone, Ken makes 3 sandwiches in 10 minutes. With specialization, a team of 3 makes 15 sandwiches in 10 minutes. How many more sandwiches does the team make than 3 people working alone like Ken?
it.h: Three people like Ken would make 3 + 3 + 3 sandwiches.

it.q: Tell what job you would like to specialize in and what you would need to buy from others.
it.ans: I would be a baker. I would need to buy clothes, a car and doctor visits from other workers.
it.h: Think about all the things you could not make yourself.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: Earning, Spending and Saving: Making a Budget

it.q: Income is
it.h: You earn income by working.

it.q: A budget is
ch: a plan for how to spend and save money
it.h: A budget helps you plan.

it.q: Aiyana earns 8 dollars. She saves 3 dollars and spends the rest. How many dollars does she spend?
it.h: Take the saved money away from what she earned.

it.q: Which is the best plan for money in a budget?
ch: pay for needs first, then save, then spend on wants
it.h: Which things must come first?

it.q: A bank pays you a little extra money for keeping your savings there. This extra money is called
it.h: It makes your savings grow.

it.q: Make a simple budget for 10 dollars. Tell how much you would save and spend.
it.ans: I would save 4 dollars, spend 5 dollars on lunch and give 1 dollar to a food drive.
it.h: Make sure your amounts add up to 10 dollars.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Producers, Consumers and Choices (2.4)
lessons.n: Trade Near and Far: Imports and Exports

it.q: An export is a good that is
ch: sent to another country to sell
made at home and never sold
it.h: Ex- means out.

it.q: An import is a good that is
it.h: Im- means in.

it.q: California grows many almonds and sells them to countries around the world. These almonds are
it.h: Are the almonds going out of the country or coming in?

it.q: Most bananas sold in California grocery stores are grown in Central and South America. For the United States, these bananas are
it.h: Are the bananas coming into the country or going out?

it.q: Big ships carry goods in and out of the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Oakland. Why are ports important?
it.h: What do ships carry?

it.q: Look at a label on something you own. Tell where it was made and if it was an import.
it.ans: My shoes say they were made in Vietnam, so they were imported.
it.h: Labels often say "Made in" a place.

lessons.u: Unit 6: People Who Make a Difference (2.5)
lessons.n: Heroes Who Worked for Fairness

it.q: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta worked to help
ch: farm workers get fair pay and safe conditions
it.h: They worked with people who pick crops in California fields.

it.q: In 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks would not give up her seat on a bus. She was standing up for
it.h: The law then was unfair to Black riders.

it.q: Ruby Bridges was 6 years old in 1960 when she became the first Black student at her New Orleans elementary school. She showed
it.h: Many people shouted at her, but she kept going to school.

it.q: Dolores Huerta helped make the words "Si, se puede" famous. In English this means
it.h: It is a message of hope.

it.q: Name one hero who worked for fairness and tell what they did.
it.ans: Rosa Parks would not give up her bus seat and helped start the fight to end unfair bus laws.

lessons.u: Unit 6: People Who Make a Difference (2.5)
lessons.n: Scientists, Inventors and Explorers

it.q: George Washington Carver studied plants and found many uses for
it.h: He helped farmers in the South grow crops that are good for the soil.

it.q: Marie Curie was a scientist who won the Nobel Prize two times. She was the first woman to
it.h: The Nobel Prize is a famous award for great work.

it.q: In 1983, Sally Ride, who grew up in California, became the first American woman to
it.h: She flew on a space shuttle.

it.q: Ellen Ochoa, born in Los Angeles, became the first Hispanic woman to go to space in 1993. She showed
it.h: She studied for many years to become an astronaut.

it.q: Sally Ride went to space in 1983. Ellen Ochoa went to space in 1993. How many years apart were their first flights?
it.h: Count by tens from 1983.

it.q: Name a scientist or explorer and tell how their work helped others.
it.ans: George Washington Carver taught farmers how to keep soil healthy by planting peanuts.

lessons.u: Unit 6: People Who Make a Difference (2.5)
lessons.n: Character and Everyday Heroes

it.q: A hero is someone who
ch: helps others and does what is right, even when it is hard
it.h: Heroes can be famous or people in your own community.

it.q: Helen Keller could not see or hear after an illness when she was a baby. In 1903 she wrote: "The most important day I remember in all my life is the one on which my teacher, Anne Mansfield Sullivan, came to me." Why was that day important?
ch: her teacher helped her learn to communicate
she moved to a new house
it.h: Anne Sullivan spelled words into Helen's hand.

it.q: In a book from 1903, a writer said: "The most important day I remember in all my life is the one on which my teacher, Anne Mansfield Sullivan, came to me." Who wrote these words?
it.h: The writer says "my teacher."

it.q: In 1947, Jackie Robinson, who grew up in Pasadena, became the first Black player in modern Major League Baseball. He showed
it.h: Some people treated him badly, but he kept playing well.

it.q: Name an everyday hero in your community and tell what makes them a hero.
it.ans: My neighbor is a nurse who takes care of sick people at night.

lessons.u: Unit 6: People Who Make a Difference (2.5)
lessons.n: Heroes of Health and Nature

it.q: Clara Barton was a nurse who cared for hurt soldiers during the Civil War. In 1881 she started the
it.h: This group still helps people after disasters today.

it.q: Polio was a disease that made many children very sick. Jonas Salk created a
it.h: A vaccine helps the body fight a disease before you get sick.

it.q: Rachel Carson wrote a book in 1962 warning that some chemicals sprayed on crops were harming birds and other animals. She showed
ch: courage to speak up for nature
it.h: People did not all agree with her, but she spoke up anyway.

it.q: What do Clara Barton and Jonas Salk have in common?
ch: they helped people stay healthy or get well
it.h: Think about nurses and vaccines.

it.q: Clara Barton started the American Red Cross in 1881. How many years ago was that from {year}?
it.h: Subtract 1881 from this year.

it.q: Name one of these heroes and tell how their work still helps people today.
it.ans: Jonas Salk. His polio vaccine keeps children from getting polio.
it.h: Think about the Red Cross, vaccines or protecting animals.

lessons.u: Unit 6: People Who Make a Difference (2.5)
lessons.n: California Heroes Who Built Fair Communities

it.q: Biddy Mason was born enslaved. In 1856 a court in Los Angeles said she was free. Later she
ch: bought land and helped people in need
it.h: She used her money and land to help her community.

it.q: Wong Kim Ark was born in San Francisco to Chinese parents. In 1898 the Supreme Court said he was a U.S. citizen because
ch: he was born in the United States
it.h: Where was he born?

it.q: In the 1940s, a court case helped end school segregation in California for Mexican American children. The family who brought the case was the
it.h: Sylvia Mendez's family went to court so she could attend her neighborhood school.

it.q: What do Biddy Mason, Wong Kim Ark and the Mendez family have in common?
ch: they stood up for fair treatment
it.h: Think about fairness.

it.q: Biddy Mason won her freedom in 1856. Wong Kim Ark's case was decided in 1898. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract 1856 from 1898.

it.q: Tell why going to court can be a peaceful way to work for fairness.
it.ans: People can ask judges to decide fairly instead of fighting.
it.h: Who decides what laws mean?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: Map tools

it.q: Which part of a map tells what the symbols mean?
it.h: Look for the box that shows each small picture and what it stands for.

it.q: On a compass rose, which direction is opposite of north?
it.h: Picture the four arrows. Which one points the other way from north?

it.q: A map scale shows that 1 inch stands for 10 miles. Two towns are 3 inches apart on the map. How many miles apart are the towns?
it.h: Each inch is 10 miles. Count by 10s three times.

it.q: A map grid has letters across the top and numbers down the side. The library is in the box under C and beside 4. What is its location?
it.h: Give the letter first, then the number.

it.q: How is a globe different from a flat map?
ch: A globe is round like the Earth, so it shows shapes and sizes most correctly.
A globe shows only one city.
A globe is always smaller than a map.

it.q: You want to walk from your school to a park. Name two map tools that would help you and tell how each one helps.
it.ans: A compass rose tells which direction to walk, and a scale tells how far it is. A map key shows symbols such as the park.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: Landforms and bodies of water

it.q: Which is a landform?
it.h: A landform is a shape of the land, not water.

it.q: A low area of land between hills or mountains is a
it.h: Think of a long, low place where a river might flow.

it.q: Which body of water is along California's western coast?
it.h: California's coast faces the ocean that lies between North America and Asia.

it.q: A desert is a place that
Land with water on three sides is a
it.h: Think of San Francisco, which sits on land surrounded by water on most sides.

it.q: Name two physical features in or near your community. Tell one way people use each one.
it.ans: For example: a river gives water for farms and drinking; hills are used for hiking and grazing cattle.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: People use and change the land

it.q: A natural resource is
ch: something in nature that people use, such as water or soil
something people make in a factory
a law made by the city
it.h: Think of things that come from the Earth, not from a store.

it.q: Which is a human feature?
ch: a lake made by a glacier
it.h: Human features are things that people build.

it.q: People build a dam across a river. What usually forms behind the dam?
it.h: A dam holds water back. Where does the water go?

it.q: Why do many people live in valleys and along the coast instead of high in the mountains?
ch: The land is flatter and easier to build on, farm and travel through.
Mountains have no water at all.

it.q: A city built a dam in 1923. A student visited the reservoir in 2023. How many years after the dam was built did the student visit?
it.h: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.

it.q: People cut down a forest to build houses. Tell one good effect and one problem this change might cause.
it.ans: Good: more homes for families. Problem: animals lose their homes, and soil may wash away without tree roots.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: California's regions: coast, valley, mountains and desert

it.q: A region is
ch: an area with features that make it different from other areas
it.h: Think about how the coast is different from the desert.

it.q: Which region of California has cool, foggy summers and beaches?
it.h: Fog often comes in from the ocean.

it.q: Which region has hot, dry summers, flat land and many farms?
it.h: Farms need flat land and water.

it.q: Joshua trees and cactus grow in which region?
it.h: These plants can live with very little rain.

it.q: Snow in the Sierra Nevada melts in spring. Which region uses much of this water to grow crops?
it.h: Rivers carry melted snow down the mountains to flat farmland.

it.q: Choose two California regions. Compare the land and one way people earn a living in each.
it.ans: The coast has beaches and harbors, so many people fish or work in tourism. The Central Valley is flat with rich soil, so many people farm.
it.h: Think about landforms, weather and jobs.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: Weather, climate and natural hazards

it.q: Climate is
ch: the usual weather of a place over many years
it.h: Weather can change each day. Climate is the pattern.

it.q: California sits on many faults, like the San Andreas Fault. Which natural hazard happens when the ground moves along a fault?
it.h: Faults are cracks in the Earth's crust.

it.q: During hot, dry, windy weather, which hazard is a big danger in California hills and forests?
it.h: Dry plants burn easily.

it.q: A drought is
ch: a long time with much less rain than normal
it.h: Think about dry reservoirs and brown lawns.

it.q: Why do California schools hold "drop, cover and hold on" drills?
ch: to practice staying safe during an earthquake
to practice for a fire in the ocean
to get ready for a parade
it.h: What should you do if the ground shakes?

it.q: Name one natural hazard in your region and two ways people prepare for it.
it.ans: Earthquakes. Families keep water and flashlights in an emergency kit, and schools practice drop, cover and hold on.
it.h: Think about supplies, drills and building rules.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Our Local Region: Land, Water and Maps (3.1)
lessons.n: Reading tables, graphs and charts about our region

it.q: A bar graph is used to
ch: compare amounts using bars of different lengths
list the steps of a law
it.h: Longer bars mean bigger amounts.

it.q: A table shows the number of farms in a county: 1950, 400 farms; 2000, 250 farms. How many fewer farms were there in 2000?
it.h: Subtract the newer number from the older number.

it.q: A bar graph shows crops grown in a county: almonds 50 farms, grapes 30 farms, tomatoes 20 farms. Which crop is grown on the most farms?
it.h: Find the longest bar.

it.q: A line graph shows a town's population: 2,000 in 1980, 3,500 in 2000 and 6,000 in 2020. How much did the population grow from 2000 to 2020?
it.h: Subtract the 2000 number from the 2020 number.

it.q: A pie chart shows how land in a county is used: half is farms, one fourth is towns and one fourth is parks. Which use covers the most land?
it.h: Half is bigger than one fourth.

it.q: Explain why a graph can be easier to read than a long list of numbers.
it.ans: A graph shows the numbers as pictures or bars, so you can quickly see which is biggest and how things change.
it.h: Think about how fast you can compare bars.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: Living with the land long ago

it.q: For thousands of years before Spanish explorers came, California was home to
it.h: Think about how many different groups lived in California's many regions.

it.q: Which food was important to many California Indian nations?
it.h: Think of the nuts that fall from oak trees.

it.q: Acorns taste bitter. How did many California Indian families make them safe and good to eat?
ch: They ground them into flour and rinsed the flour with water many times.
They ate them raw right off the tree.
They fed them only to animals.
They traded them away to explorers.
it.h: Water was used to wash away the bitter taste.

it.q: The Chumash lived along the coast near Santa Barbara. What did they build to travel on the ocean?
it.h: Think about what you need to travel on water.

it.q: People who lived near marshes and lakes used tall tule reeds to make
Explain why California Indian nations in different regions built different kinds of homes.
it.ans: Each nation used materials found in its own environment, such as redwood planks in the north, tule reeds near marshes and brush in dry areas.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: Customs, stories and trade

it.q: Stories passed from elders to children by speaking, not writing, are called
it.h: "Oral" has to do with the mouth and speaking.

it.q: The Pomo people are famous for making beautiful
it.h: These were woven from plants and some were so tight they held water.

it.q: The Chumash made beads from shells and used them in trade. What did the beads work like?
it.h: Think about what people use today to buy and sell.

it.q: A coast nation traded dried fish to a mountain nation for obsidian. Why did they trade?
ch: Each had something the other did not have nearby.
Fish and obsidian were the same thing.
They wanted to get rid of their own goods.
it.h: Think about what resources each region has.

it.q: Coyote is a character in many California Indian stories. What do stories like these often do?
ch: teach lessons and explain the world
tell the news of the day

it.q: Why do people pass down stories, songs and dances from one generation to the next?
it.ans: To teach lessons, share history and beliefs, and keep the culture and language alive.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: When newcomers arrived

it.q: Spanish soldiers and priests began building missions in California in
it.h: The first mission was in San Diego, the same year as the Portola expedition.

it.q: How did diseases brought by newcomers affect California Indians?
ch: Many people died because they had no protection against the new diseases.
The diseases only made animals sick.
it.h: New germs can be very dangerous to people who never met them before.

it.q: Newcomers brought cattle and horses that ate the grasses and seeds where Indians gathered food. What was one effect?
ch: It was harder for Indian families to gather the food they needed.

it.q: Historians estimate about 300,000 California Indians lived in California before 1769 and about 30,000 by 1870. How many fewer people is that?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

it.q: Why might a California Indian and a Spanish priest describe the same mission very differently?
ch: They had different goals and different experiences of mission life.
One of them was not there.
it.h: Think about what each person wanted and what each person lived through.

it.q: Describe one way life changed for a California Indian nation after newcomers arrived.
it.ans: Many were moved to missions and had to work and follow new rules, and they lost land where they gathered food.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: California Indian nations today

it.q: Today, California is home to
ch: tribes that live only in museums
it.h: California Indian nations are living communities today.

it.q: Many tribes are led by an elected group of leaders called a
it.h: Members vote to choose these leaders.

it.q: What does it mean that a tribe is a sovereign nation?
ch: It has the right to govern itself and make many of its own laws.
It must follow only Spanish laws.
it.h: Sovereign means having the power to rule yourself.

it.q: A tribe teaches its language to children in after-school classes. Why?
ch: to keep the language alive for the future
it.h: What could happen to a language if no children learn it?

it.q: Some tribes write a tribal constitution. What is it?
ch: a plan of government that lists the tribe's rules and how leaders are chosen

it.q: Name two ways California Indian nations keep their cultures alive today.
it.ans: Teaching their languages, holding ceremonies and dances, making baskets and other arts, telling stories, and running tribal governments.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: Mapping California Indian nations and their regions

it.q: Long ago, California Indian nations lived
it.h: Think about coast, valley, mountain and desert peoples.

ch: shellfish, fish and tule reeds from the bay
it.h: Look at where they lived on the map.

ch: coast and nearby valleys and hills
it.h: San Diego and Los Angeles are both near the ocean.

it.q: The Mojave people lived along the Colorado River in the desert. Why was the river so important to them?
ch: it gave water for drinking and for farming its banks
it.h: What does the desert lack?

it.q: The Yokuts lived in the San Joaquin Valley. Which landform was their home?
it.h: Valleys are low, flat land.

it.q: Choose one California Indian nation. Tell where it lived and how its region shaped its way of life.
it.ans: The Yurok lived along the Klamath River in the north. They fished for salmon and built plank houses from redwood.
it.h: Think about land, water, plants and animals.

lessons.u: Unit 2: American Indian Nations of Our Region (3.2)
lessons.n: How we learn about California Indian history

it.q: An archaeologist is a scientist who
ch: studies objects people left behind long ago
it.h: They dig carefully to find old tools and remains of villages.

it.q: Which is an artifact from a California Indian village long ago?
ch: a stone mortar used to grind acorns
it.h: An artifact was made and used by people of that time.

it.q: A tribal elder shares a story her grandfather told her about their village. This is an
it.h: Oral means spoken.

it.q: Why is it important to learn from California Indian people today about their own history?
ch: they know their own traditions, languages and point of view
they do not know their history
it.h: Who knows a culture best?

ch: California Indian nations lived and named places here first
no one lived near the lake
it.h: Think about who was here first.

it.q: Name two kinds of sources you could use to learn about a California Indian nation and tell what each could show.
it.ans: A basket in a museum could show their weaving skills. An interview with a tribal member could show how traditions continue today.
it.h: Think about objects, stories and people.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)

it.q: Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo sailed into San Diego Bay in 1542. He was exploring for

it.q: Many California cities have Spanish names, such as San Diego and Los Angeles. Why?
ch: Spanish settlers named places during the mission period.
The names come from the Gold Rush.
it.h: Think about who settled California after 1769.

it.q: A pueblo was a
Los Angeles was founded as a pueblo in 1781. How many years old was the city in 1981?
it.h: Subtract 1781 from 1981.

it.q: Name the four kinds of Spanish and Mexican settlements in California and tell the purpose of one of them.
it.ans: Missions, presidios, pueblos and ranchos. A presidio was a fort where soldiers protected Spain's land.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: Newcomers keep coming

it.q: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in
it.h: The miners who came the next year were called forty-niners.

it.q: Why did thousands of people from around the world come to California in 1849?
it.h: Think about what was found at Sutter's Mill.

it.q: Many Chinese immigrants came to California during the Gold Rush. Which is a contribution they made?
ch: They helped build the railroad and started businesses and farms.
They wrote the Declaration of Independence.

it.q: The transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869. How did it change California?
ch: People and goods could travel between California and the East much faster.
It only carried mail to Mexico.
it.h: Before the railroad, the trip across the country took months by wagon or ship.

it.q: Before the railroad, a wagon trip to California took about 5 months. After 1869, the train trip took about 1 week. A month is about 4 weeks. About how many weeks shorter was the train trip?
it.h: Change 5 months into weeks first, then subtract 1 week.

it.q: Why do people still move to California today? Give two reasons.
it.ans: For jobs, to be with family, for schools, to find safety, or for the climate.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: How our community changed over time

it.q: A primary source is
ch: something made or written by a person who was there at the time
a book written much later by someone who was not there
a map drawn by a student today
it.h: "Primary" means first. Think of first-hand.

it.q: Which is a primary source about a town in 1910?
ch: a letter written by a person living there in 1910
it.h: Which one was made in 1910?

it.q: A timeline starts at 1850 and has a mark every 25 years. What year is the third mark after 1850?
it.h: Add 25 three times.

it.q: An old photo shows horses and wagons on Main Street. A new photo shows cars and a bus on the same street. What changed?
The same church building stands in a photo from 1900 and in a photo from today. This is an example of
ch: continuity, something that stayed the same
it.h: Continuity means continuing without change.

it.q: Name two kinds of primary sources you could use to learn how your community has changed.
it.ans: Old photographs, letters, newspapers, maps, diaries or an oral history interview with an older resident.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: Mexican California and the Californios

it.q: Mexico became independent from Spain in
it.h: This was about 50 years after the first mission.

it.q: Spanish-speaking people who lived in California when it belonged to Mexico were often called
it.h: The name comes from the word California.

it.q: After 1834, the Mexican government closed the missions and gave much of their land to
it.h: Ranchos were huge cattle ranches.

it.q: Vaqueros on the ranchos were skilled at
it.h: Vaca means cow in Spanish.

it.q: California was part of Mexico from 1821 to 1848. How many years was that?
it.h: Subtract 1821 from 1848.

it.q: Describe life on a rancho in Mexican California.
it.ans: Families raised cattle on huge areas of land. Vaqueros herded the cattle, and hides and tallow were traded to ships for goods.
it.h: Think about cattle, horses, trade and work.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: California becomes a state

it.q: California became the 31st state of the United States in
it.h: It happened two years after gold was discovered.

it.q: After the war between the United States and Mexico, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) gave California to
it.h: Which country did California join?

it.q: In 1846, a group of American settlers in Sonoma raised a flag with a bear and a star. This event is called the
it.h: Today's state flag still has a bear and a star on it.

it.q: Why did California's population grow so fast just before statehood?
ch: the Gold Rush brought thousands of people
it.h: What was found at Sutter's Mill in 1848?

it.q: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed in 1848. California became a state in 1850. How many years apart are these events?
it.h: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.

it.q: Put these events in order and explain how one led to the next: statehood, Gold Rush, Mexico gives up California.
it.ans: Mexico gave up California in 1848, the Gold Rush brought many people in 1848 and 1849, and with so many people, California became a state in 1850.
it.h: Think about the years 1848, 1849 and 1850.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: Farming, water and growth in the 1900s

it.q: In the early 1900s, many farms in Southern California grew
it.h: These citrus fruits appeared on many crate labels.

it.q: In the 1930s, many families left the dry, dusty Great Plains, called the Dust Bowl, and came to California to
it.h: Their farms back home had dried up.

it.q: During the Bracero Program, from 1942 to 1964, many workers from Mexico came to California to
it.h: Brazo means arm in Spanish. The workers worked with their hands.

it.q: Why did California build dams, canals and aqueducts in the 1900s?
ch: to move water to farms and growing cities
it.h: Most rain and snow fall in the north, but many people live in the south.

it.q: The Bracero Program lasted from 1942 to 1964. How many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract 1942 from 1964.

it.q: Explain how water projects helped California's communities grow.
it.ans: Canals and aqueducts carried water to dry places, so farms could grow crops and cities could have enough water for more people.
it.h: Think about deserts and dry valleys.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Settlement and Change in Our Community (3.3)
lessons.n: Timelines, decades and points of view

it.q: A decade is
it.h: Dec- means ten.

it.q: A century is
it.h: A cent is one hundredth of a dollar.

it.q: A timeline starts in 1800 and has a mark every 10 years. How many marks are there from 1800 to 1850, counting both ends?
it.h: List them: 1800, 1810, and so on.

it.q: Which event belongs in the 1840s?
ch: gold is found at Sutter's Mill
it.h: The 1840s are the years 1840 to 1849.

it.q: A point of view is
ch: how a person sees and thinks about an event
it.h: Two people can see the same event differently.

it.q: Make a short timeline of three events in California history and tell why their order matters.
it.ans: 1769 first mission, 1848 gold found, 1869 railroad finished. The order shows how each wave of newcomers came after the one before.
it.h: Pick events with years you know.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: Why we have rules and laws

it.q: A law is
ch: a rule made by a government that everyone must follow
it.h: Think of rules for a whole city, state or country.

it.q: Why do we have a law that says cars must stop at red lights?
ch: to keep drivers and walkers safe
it.h: What could happen if no one stopped?

it.q: What is a consequence for a driver who breaks a speeding law?
Which is a rule at school, not a law of the state?
ch: Raise your hand before you speak in class.
it.h: Which one only applies in a classroom?

it.q: A park has a rule: "Dogs must be on a leash." Who does this rule help?
ch: dog owners, other visitors and the dogs themselves
it.h: Think about everyone who visits the park, not just one group.

it.q: Think of a rule at your school. Explain why it is important and what might happen without it.
it.ans: For example, "Walk in the halls" keeps students from running into each other and getting hurt.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: Being a good citizen

it.q: A citizen is
ch: a member of a community or country
a person who never follows rules
only a person who owns land
it.h: You are a citizen of your school, city and country.

it.q: Which is a responsibility of a good citizen?
Adults who are citizens can choose leaders by
it.h: On election day, people mark a ballot.

it.q: Students pick up trash at a beach. This shows
it.h: Who benefits when a beach is clean?

it.q: Public virtue means
ch: caring about the common good of everyone, not just yourself
it.h: "Public" means everyone in the community.

it.q: Describe one way a third grader can be a good citizen in class and one way in the community.
it.ans: In class: take turns, follow rules and help classmates. In the community: recycle, pick up litter or help a neighbor.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: American symbols, landmarks and documents

it.q: The U.S. flag has 50 stars. What do the stars stand for?
it.h: How many states are in the United States?

it.q: The 13 stripes on the U.S. flag stand for
it.h: The country started with 13.

it.q: The bald eagle was chosen as a national symbol. What does it stand for?
it.h: Think about how an eagle flies high and free.

it.q: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France. In 1883 Emma Lazarus wrote a poem about it that says, "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." What does the statue mean to many immigrants?
ch: a welcome to a land of freedom
it.h: Think about the words "breathe free."

it.q: Which is a symbol of California?
ch: the California grizzly bear on the state flag
it.h: Look at the California state flag. What animal is on it?

it.q: Choose one American symbol or landmark. Tell what it is and what it stands for.
it.ans: The Statue of Liberty is a statue in New York Harbor; it stands for freedom and welcomes immigrants.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: Heroes who took risks for freedom

it.q: Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery and then went back many times to lead others to freedom on the
it.h: It was not a real train. It was a secret network of people and hiding places.

it.q: Abraham Lincoln was President during the Civil War. In 1863 he said the nation should have "government of the people, by the people, for the people." What did he mean?
ch: The government should belong to and serve all the people.
The government should be run by a king.
it.h: Look at who the word "people" refers to.

it.q: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became a famous speaker and writer. What did he work for?
ch: an end to slavery and equal rights
it.h: He spoke and wrote against something he had lived through.

it.q: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta worked to
ch: win fair pay and safe conditions for farm workers
it.h: Think of the people who pick fruits and vegetables in California's fields.

it.q: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led people to work for civil rights using
it.h: He believed in change without fighting.

it.q: Choose a hero who took a risk for freedom. Describe the risk and what the person accomplished.
it.ans: Harriet Tubman risked capture to lead enslaved people to freedom on the Underground Railroad; Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat, which helped end unfair bus laws.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: Our rights in the Bill of Rights

it.q: The Bill of Rights is
ch: the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution
a list of things to buy
it.h: An amendment is a change or addition.

it.q: The First Amendment (1791) says, "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press." What does this protect?
ch: people's right to speak and print their ideas
it.h: Abridging means cutting short or limiting.

it.q: Freedom of religion means people can
ch: never go to a place of worship
it.h: The government does not choose your religion.

it.q: Which is an example of freedom of the press?
ch: a newspaper writes that the mayor made a mistake
a student reads a library book
a family moves to a new city
it.h: The press means newspapers and other news.

it.q: The Constitution was written in 1787 and the Bill of Rights was added in 1791. How many years later was the Bill of Rights added?
it.h: Subtract 1787 from 1791.

it.q: Choose one right in the Bill of Rights. Explain why it is important.
it.ans: Freedom of speech is important because people can share ideas and tell leaders when they disagree without being punished.
it.h: Think about speech, religion, the press or a fair trial.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Rules, Laws and Good Citizens (3.4)
lessons.n: Citizens take action to solve community problems

it.q: A petition is
ch: a written request signed by many people asking for a change
it.h: People sign their names to show they agree.

it.q: Students notice there is no recycling at their school. What is a good first step?
ch: gather facts and talk to the principal
it.h: Who can make a change at school?

it.q: Neighbors want a park cleaned up. Which action shows citizens working together?
ch: they hold a volunteer clean-up day
it.h: Many hands make light work.

it.q: Why do people speak at public meetings of a city council?
ch: to share their ideas so leaders can hear them
it.h: Leaders work for the people.

it.q: Students collect 128 signatures on a petition. They need 200. How many more signatures do they need?
it.h: Subtract what they have from what they need.

it.q: Name a problem in your community and two steps citizens could take to help solve it.
it.ans: Litter at the beach. Citizens could organize a clean-up day and write to the city asking for more trash cans.
it.h: Think about learning, speaking and volunteering.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: The three branches of government

it.q: The branch of government that makes laws is the
it.h: "Legislate" means to make laws.

it.q: The branch that carries out laws is the
it.h: The President, governor and mayor lead this branch.

it.q: The branch that decides what laws mean and whether they were broken is the
it.h: Judges work in this branch.

it.q: Why is the government split into three branches?
ch: so no one branch has too much power
so laws take longer to read
so one person can make all the decisions
it.h: Think about what could happen if one person had all the power.

it.q: The President leads which branch of the U.S. government?
Name the three branches of government and the job of each.
it.ans: Legislative makes laws; executive carries out laws; judicial decides what laws mean and settles disputes in courts.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: Local government: city and county

it.q: Who leads the executive branch of many city governments?
it.h: Think of the leader of a city.

it.q: A city council is like which branch of government?
ch: legislative, because it makes city laws
executive, because it runs the army
it.h: What does a city council vote on?

it.q: Which service is usually provided by a city government?
California is divided into 58
it.h: Each one has a board of supervisors.

it.q: A city council has 7 members. A new law needs a majority, more than half of the votes. What is the smallest number of votes needed to pass the law?
it.h: Half of 7 is 3 and a half. The next whole number above that is the answer.

it.q: Name two services your city or county provides and tell how each helps people.
it.ans: Police keep people safe; libraries lend books; parks give places to play; trash pickup keeps streets clean.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: State, tribal and national government

it.q: The capital of California is
it.h: The governor and the state legislature work in this city on a river.

it.q: The leader of California's executive branch is the
it.h: Each state has one.

it.q: California's legislature has two parts, the Senate and the
it.h: It starts with the letter A.

it.q: Which job belongs to the national, or federal, government?
ch: printing money and protecting the whole country

it.q: A sovereign tribal nation in California works with the United States government
it.h: Sovereign nations deal with each other as governments.

it.q: Give one example of a job for each level of government: local, state and national.
it.ans: Local: run parks and police. State: run state highways and set rules for schools. National: protect the country and print money.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: How a bill becomes a law in California

it.q: A bill is
ch: a written idea for a new law
a law that is already passed
it.h: A bill is the first step toward a law.

it.q: In California, a bill must pass the Assembly and the
it.h: California's legislature has two houses.

it.q: After both houses pass a bill, it goes to the governor. If the governor signs it, it
it.h: The governor leads the executive branch.

it.q: If the governor vetoes a bill, the legislature can still make it a law if
ch: two-thirds of each house vote to override the veto
it.h: Override means to overrule. It takes a large vote.

it.q: The State Assembly has 80 members. A bill needs more than half to pass. What is the smallest number of votes needed?
it.h: Half of 80 is 40. More than half is one more.

it.q: List the steps a bill takes to become a California law.
it.ans: A member writes the bill, the Assembly and the Senate each vote, and the governor signs it or vetoes it.
it.h: Think: idea, vote, vote, sign.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: Checks and balances

it.q: Checks and balances means
ch: each branch of government can limit the power of the other branches
it.h: Each branch can "check" the others.

it.q: The President vetoes a bill passed by Congress. Which branch is checking which?
ch: the executive is checking the legislative
the judicial is checking the executive
the legislative is checking the judicial
it.h: The President leads the executive branch.

it.q: Congress overrides a President's veto with a two-thirds vote. What does this show?
ch: the legislative branch can check the executive branch
the President can never be checked
it.h: Who voted, and whose action did they overrule?

it.q: The Constitution (1787) says, "All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress." What does this mean?
ch: Congress has the power to make laws
it.h: Legislative means lawmaking.

it.q: The U.S. House has 435 members. A veto override needs two-thirds of the members voting. If all 435 vote, two-thirds is 290. How many members could vote no and the override still pass?
it.h: Subtract 290 from 435.

it.q: Give one example of how one branch checks another and explain why this matters.
it.ans: The President can veto a law from Congress. This matters because it keeps Congress from passing laws without anyone else agreeing.
it.h: Think about vetoes, overrides and courts.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: Courts, judges and juries

it.q: A judge is a person who
ch: leads a court and makes sure trials are fair
it.h: Judges work in courtrooms.

it.q: A jury is
ch: a group of citizens who listen to a trial and decide what happened
it.h: Adult citizens can be called to serve.

it.q: In California, a jury in a serious criminal trial has
it.h: It is the same number as months in a year.

it.q: Why is serving on a jury called a responsibility of citizens?
ch: courts need ordinary citizens to help decide cases fairly
it is a way to earn a lot of money
it.h: Who helps make trials fair?

it.q: A court has 3 trials each day. How many trials does it hold in 5 days?
it.h: Multiply trials per day by days.

it.q: Explain why it is important for a judge to be fair to both sides in a trial.
it.ans: Everyone has the right to a fair trial, so a judge must listen to both sides and follow the law, not personal feelings.
it.h: Think about what fair means.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Our Governments: Local, State, Tribal and National (3.4)
lessons.n: Elections and representatives

it.q: A representative is
ch: a person elected to speak and act for a group of people
a judge who is not elected
it.h: Represent means to stand for others.

it.q: California has many members in the U.S. House of Representatives because
ch: it has a very large population
it is next to the ocean
it.h: States with more people get more representatives.

it.q: Each state, large or small, has how many U.S. senators?
it.h: Every state has the same number in the Senate.

it.q: A district is
ch: an area whose voters elect one representative
it.h: A state is divided into many of these for elections.

it.q: California has 52 members in the U.S. House and 2 U.S. senators. How many members of Congress does California have in all?
it.h: Add the House members and the senators.

it.q: Explain why we elect representatives instead of having every citizen vote on every law.
it.ans: There are millions of people and thousands of decisions, so we choose representatives to study the issues and vote for us.
it.h: Think about how many people live in California.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Goods, services and resources

it.q: Which is a good?
it.h: A good is something you can touch and hold.

it.q: Which is a service?
it.h: A service is work someone does for you.

it.q: A farmer uses soil and water to grow tomatoes. Soil and water are
it.h: These come from nature.

it.q: A baker's oven is a capital resource. What is a capital resource?
ch: a tool, machine or building used to make goods or services
it.h: Think of things people make so they can make other things.

it.q: The workers at a restaurant are
Choose a local business. Name one natural resource, one human resource and one capital resource it uses.
it.ans: A pizza shop uses wheat and tomatoes (natural), cooks and servers (human), and ovens and the building (capital).

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Made here, made far away

it.q: Trade means
it.h: Think about what happens when you swap something with a friend.

it.q: California farms grow many of the country's almonds. Where are these almonds sold?
ch: in California, across the United States and in other countries
it.h: Think about how many people in the world eat almonds.

it.q: Bananas need a hot, wet climate all year. Most bananas sold in California are grown
ch: in other countries with tropical climates
it.h: Does California have a hot, wet climate all year long?

it.q: A label on a shirt says "Made in Vietnam." What does this tell you?
ch: The shirt was made in another country and shipped here.
The shirt was made in your town.
The shirt is not for sale.
The shirt was made in California.
it.h: The label tells where the shirt was produced.

it.q: Why do cities like Los Angeles and Oakland have large ports?
ch: Ships bring goods from other countries and carry California goods away.

it.q: Name one good made or grown in your region and one good made far away. Explain why your community trades for goods.
it.ans: Strawberries are grown nearby; phones are made in other countries. We trade because no place can make everything it needs.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Making economic choices

ch: not having enough of something to meet all wants
it.h: When there is not enough to go around.

ch: the game she did not buy
it.h: Opportunity cost is the best thing you give up.

it.q: A benefit is
ch: something good you get from a choice
it.h: Think of the word "beneficial," which means helpful.

it.q: Jamal has $15. He buys a kite for $9. How much money does he have left?
it.h: Subtract what he spent from what he had.

it.q: Why do people have to make choices about how to spend money?
ch: People have more wants than money.
Stores make everyone buy the same things.

it.q: Describe a choice you made. Tell what you chose and what you gave up.
it.ans: I chose to play soccer after school, so I gave up going to art club. My opportunity cost was art club.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Jobs, work and human capital

it.q: Human capital is
ch: the skills and knowledge a person has
it.h: Think of what you learn in school that helps you later.

it.q: How does learning to read and do math help you in the future?
ch: It builds skills you can use in many jobs.
It does not help at all.
It only helps you in third grade.
it.h: What skills do most jobs need?

it.q: Specialization means
ch: doing one kind of job and becoming very good at it
it.h: A baker bakes and a plumber fixes pipes.

it.q: A nurse trained for years to learn how to care for patients. What did the training increase?
A worker earns $15 each hour. How much does the worker earn in 8 hours?
it.h: Multiply the pay for one hour by the number of hours.

it.q: Name a job you might like in the future. Tell two skills you are learning now that would help you do it.
it.ans: A scientist: reading to learn facts, math to measure, and working with a team in class.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Entrepreneurs and local businesses

ch: the money a business has left after paying its costs
it.h: Profit = money earned minus money spent.

ch: miners and other workers who needed tough pants

ch: immigrants started businesses that are still known today
it.h: Many newcomers sold goods to miners instead of digging for gold.

it.q: An entrepreneur opens a bakery. Which is a cost of running the business?
it.h: A cost is money the business must pay out.

it.h: Subtract the costs from the money earned.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Our Local Economy (3.5)
lessons.n: Supply, demand and prices at the market

it.q: Supply is
ch: how much of a good is available to sell
how much people want to buy
it.h: Think about how many strawberries are on the farm stand.

it.q: Demand is
ch: how much of a good people want to buy
the cost to make a good
it.h: Think about how many shoppers want strawberries.

ch: it will stay exactly the same
it.h: When something is scarce, buyers may pay more.

it.q: At the end of the day, a farm stand still has many peaches left. What might the farmer do?
ch: lower the price so people buy them
it.h: How can the farmer get people to buy more?

it.q: Strawberries cost 4 dollars a basket in June. In winter they cost 7 dollars a basket. How much more do they cost in winter?
it.h: Subtract the June price from the winter price.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)

east and west of the prime meridian

it.h: California is north of the equator and west of the prime meridian.

it.q: Sacramento is at about 38 degrees north, 121 degrees west. Los Angeles is at about 34 degrees north, 118 degrees west. Which city is farther north?
it.h: A bigger north latitude number means farther north.

it.q: California's border with Oregon is at 42 degrees north latitude. San Diego is at about 33 degrees north. How many degrees of latitude apart are they?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number from the larger one.

it.q: Explain the difference between relative location and absolute location. Give an example of each for your school.
it.ans: Relative location describes a place compared to other places, like "next to the park." Absolute location is an exact spot using latitude and longitude or an address.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)
lessons.n: California's regions

it.q: California's four main natural regions are
ch: the coast, the mountains, the Central Valley and the desert
the north, south, east and west
the plains, prairies, swamps and tundra
the islands, lakes, rivers and bays
it.h: Think of where the ocean is, where the high peaks are, the long flat middle and the dry southeast.

it.q: Which mountain range runs along much of California's eastern side?
it.h: Its name means "snowy mountain range" in Spanish.

it.q: Death Valley, in the desert region, has the lowest point in North America. It is about how far below sea level?
it.h: Mount Whitney is about 14,500 feet high, and it is not in a valley.

it.q: The Central Valley lies between which two mountain ranges?
ch: the Coast Ranges and the Sierra Nevada
the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada

it.q: The two main rivers of the Central Valley are the
it.h: One shares its name with the state capital.

it.q: Choose two California regions. Describe the climate of each and one way people use the land there.
it.ans: Coast: mild, foggy climate; ports and fishing. Desert: hot and dry; solar energy and resorts, with water brought in for farms.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)
lessons.n: How geography shapes California communities

it.q: A mountain pass is
ch: a low place where people can cross a mountain range
a river at the bottom of a canyon
a road that goes around a desert
it.h: Travelers look for the easiest way through the mountains.

it.q: Why did San Francisco grow into a major port city?
ch: It sits on a large, protected bay where ships can dock.
It is in the middle of a desert.
it.h: Think about what ships need.

it.q: Sacramento grew where the Sacramento and American Rivers meet. Why was this a good place for a town in the 1840s and 1850s?
ch: Boats could carry people and goods on the rivers.
It was on top of the Sierra Nevada.
it.h: Before trains and cars, rivers were like highways.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 inch = 50 miles. Sacramento and San Francisco are about 1 and a half inches apart. About how many miles apart are they?
it.h: One inch is 50 miles, and half an inch is 25 miles.

it.q: Population density means
ch: how many people live in an area

it.q: Compare a farm town in the Central Valley with a large coastal city. Give two differences in land use or transportation.
it.ans: The farm town has fields, orchards and trucks on country roads; the coastal city has tall buildings, a port, freeways and public transit, and many more people.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)
lessons.n: Earthquakes, wildfires, floods and droughts: California's natural hazards

it.q: Most earthquakes in California happen along cracks in the Earth's crust called
it.h: The San Andreas is the most famous one in California.

it.q: Along the San Andreas Fault, two huge pieces of the Earth's crust
it.h: An earthquake happens when stuck rock suddenly moves.

it.q: Dry summers and strong autumn winds, such as the Santa Ana winds, raise the danger of
it.h: Think about what dry brush and strong wind do to a small flame.

it.q: A drought is
ch: a long period with much less rain or snow than normal
it.h: The opposite of a very wet year.

it.q: A town gets about 18 inches of rain in a normal year. During a drought year it got 7 inches. How many inches less rain fell in the drought year?
it.h: Subtract the drought amount from the normal amount.

it.q: Name one natural hazard in California and describe one way families or communities prepare for it.
it.ans: Earthquakes: families make an emergency kit with water, food and a flashlight and practice "drop, cover and hold on," and buildings are built to resist shaking. (Wildfire: clearing brush near homes; flood: levees.)

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)
lessons.n: Natural resources and how Californians use them

it.q: A natural resource is
ch: something from nature that people use
a product made in a factory
it.h: Think of water, soil, trees and minerals.

it.q: The tall forests of northwestern California have long been an important source of
it.h: Redwoods and firs grow there.

it.q: Oil fields in the southern San Joaquin Valley near Bakersfield provide
it.h: Think about what is pumped from deep underground there.

it.q: Which renewable resource do large power plants in California's sunny deserts use to make electricity?
it.h: Renewable resources do not run out.

it.q: A sawmill cut 450 logs in one week. It cut the same number on each of 5 workdays. How many logs did it cut each day?
it.h: Divide the total by the number of days.

it.q: Explain the difference between a renewable and a nonrenewable resource. Give a California example of each.
it.ans: A renewable resource can be replaced by nature, like sunlight, wind or replanted trees. A nonrenewable resource cannot be replaced in our lifetime, like oil or gold.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Geography of California (4.1)
lessons.n: Reading California maps: scale, symbols and map types

it.q: The box on a map that explains what its symbols and colors mean is the
it.h: It is sometimes called the key.

it.q: Which kind of map would best show where the Sierra Nevada is high and the Central Valley is low?
it.h: Look for a map that shows landforms with colors or shading.

it.q: A political map of California would best show
it.h: Political maps show lines that people drew.

it.q: On a map, the compass rose shows
ch: directions such as north, south, east and west
how many people live in a city

it.q: A map scale shows 1 inch = 20 miles. Two towns are 6 inches apart on the map. How many miles apart are they?
it.h: Multiply the number of inches by the miles in each inch.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The First Peoples of California (4.2)
lessons.n: Many nations in many regions

it.q: Before 1769, about how many people lived in what is now California?
it.h: Historians estimate California had one of the largest populations north of Mexico.

it.q: California Indian nations spoke
ch: many different languages, some as different as English and Chinese
it.h: Mountains, deserts and rivers separated many groups for thousands of years.

it.q: The Yurok and Hupa lived along rivers in the northwest forests. Which resources shaped their lives most?
it.h: Think about what is found in northwestern rivers and forests.

it.q: The Mojave people lived along the Colorado River. Unlike most California Indians, they
ch: planted crops such as corn, beans and squash in soil left by river floods

it.q: The Yokuts lived in the San Joaquin Valley near lakes and marshes. Which material would they use most for houses and mats?
it.h: Think about what grows thickly in marshes.

it.q: Why did California Indian nations in the desert, valley, mountains and coast develop different ways of life?
it.ans: Each region had different climate, plants, animals and water, so each nation adapted its food, shelter and tools to what was there.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The First Peoples of California (4.2)
lessons.n: Food, trade and caring for the land

it.q: An economy based on hunting animals and gathering wild plants is called a
it.h: The name describes what people did to get food.

it.q: Acorns were a main food for many nations. Why did families store acorns in granaries?
ch: to have food through the winter and in years with few acorns
it.h: Oak trees do not make the same number of acorns every year.

it.q: Many nations set small controlled fires on the land. What was one result?
ch: new grass and plants grew, and more animals came to feed
it.h: Fire clears old brush so new growth can come up.

it.q: The Chumash made money from small shells. Inland nations wanted these beads. What did the beads allow?
A trader carried 240 shell beads. She traded 75 for obsidian and 90 for deer hides. How many beads were left?
it.h: Add the beads she traded, then subtract from 240.

it.q: Explain how trade connected California Indian nations in different regions. Give one example of goods traded.
it.ans: Trails linked the coast, valleys, mountains and deserts. Coast nations traded shell beads and dried fish for obsidian, furs, pine nuts or salt from inland nations.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The First Peoples of California (4.2)
lessons.n: Family, government and beliefs

it.q: Most California Indian villages were led by
ch: a headman or chief, often with advice from elders
a king who ruled all of California
it.h: Villages were small and governed themselves.

it.q: Many nations, such as the Miwok and Maidu, built large roundhouses. What were they used for?
it.h: Think about a building where the whole village could meet.

it.q: Why are oral traditions important sources for learning about California Indian history?
ch: They pass down knowledge, history and beliefs from elders through generations.
They are always about other countries.
They were made up last year.
it.h: Many nations did not use writing, so knowledge was shared by speaking.

it.q: Which describes the role of a healer in many California Indian communities?
ch: a respected person who used plants, songs and prayer to care for the sick

it.q: A basket is decorated with a pattern that has a special meaning to the weaver's family. What can historians learn from it?
ch: about the skills, art and beliefs of the people who made it
it.h: Objects can tell us about the people who made and used them.

it.q: Name two ceremonies or traditions of California Indian nations and explain why they mattered to the community.
it.ans: Acorn and salmon ceremonies gave thanks for food; dances and songs marked seasons and brought people together; storytelling taught lessons.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The First Peoples of California (4.2)
lessons.n: Homes, tools and baskets: California Indian technology

it.q: Many California Indian families pounded acorns into flour using
it.h: One is a bowl or hollow in stone, and the other is a heavy stone held in the hand.

it.q: Raw acorns taste bitter. Before cooking, people poured water through the acorn flour many times. Why?
ch: to wash out the bitter acid
it.h: Think about what rinsing does to something that tastes bad.

it.q: The Yurok and Hupa of the northwest forests built rectangular houses from
it.h: Huge trees grew in their homeland.

it.q: Pomo basket makers are famous for baskets that were
ch: woven so tightly they could hold water
it.h: A very tight weave leaves no gaps.

it.q: A fish weir is a fence of poles built across a stream. What was it used for?
Choose one tool or object made by California Indians. Describe what it was made from and how it helped people live.
it.ans: A cooking basket woven from plant fibers: hot stones were dropped into acorn mush inside it to cook the food, so families could cook without metal pots.
it.h: Think about the materials that came from the land nearby.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The First Peoples of California (4.2)
lessons.n: California Indian nations today

it.q: California Indian nations today
ch: still live in California and keep their cultures, languages and governments
it.h: Think about tribal governments and ceremonies that continue now.

it.q: California has more than 100 tribes that the U.S. government formally recognizes. What does federal recognition mean?
ch: The United States deals with the tribe as a nation with its own government.
The tribe must move to another state.
The tribe follows no laws at all.
it.h: Recognition is about a government-to-government relationship.

it.q: Many tribes run language classes for children and adults. Why is this important?
ch: Some languages have few speakers left, and classes help keep them alive.
It is required to drive a car.
it.h: What happens to a language if no young people learn it?

it.q: In 1851 and 1852, U.S. officials signed 18 treaties with California Indian groups that promised them land. What happened next?
ch: The U.S. Senate refused to approve the treaties, so the promised land was never set aside.

it.q: The 18 treaties were rejected in 1852 and kept secret until 1905. For how many years were they kept secret?
it.h: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.

it.q: Name two ways California Indian nations keep their cultures strong today.
it.ans: Teaching their languages, holding ceremonies and dances, weaving baskets, sharing oral histories, and running tribal museums and cultural centers.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: Explorers sail the Pacific coast

it.q: In 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo led the first European expedition to explore the coast of what is now California. He sailed for
it.h: This country already ruled Mexico, which it called New Spain.

it.q: Why did Spanish ships sailing north along California have a hard time?
ch: Strong winds and the ocean current flowed from the north, against them.
There was no wind at all.
it.h: Think about which way the wind and water pushed the ships.

it.q: English explorer Francis Drake landed on the California coast in 1579. What did this worry Spain about?
ch: that other countries might claim the land
that the Russians would build railroads

it.q: Vitus Bering sailed for Russia and explored the waters near Alaska in the 1700s. Why did this matter to Spain?
ch: Spain feared Russia would move south into California.
Spain wanted to trade with Russia.
it.h: Spain wanted to protect its claim to the land north of Mexico.

it.q: Cabrillo explored California in 1542. Sebastian Vizcaino mapped Monterey Bay in 1602. How many years apart were these voyages?
it.h: Subtract 1542 from 1602.

it.q: Explain why Spain waited more than 200 years after Cabrillo's voyage to settle Alta California.
it.ans: California was far from Mexico, sailing north was hard because of winds and currents, and Spain was busy elsewhere. Spain acted only when Russia and England seemed to threaten its claim.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: Soldiers, missionaries and settlers arrive

it.q: In 1769, Gaspar de Portola and Father Junipero Serra led an expedition that founded the first mission and presidio at
it.h: It is the southernmost of the California missions.

it.q: Father Juan Crespi traveled with Portola and kept a
it.h: Crespi's writing is a primary source historians still read.

it.q: In 1775-1776, Juan Bautista de Anza led about 240 settlers over land from Mexico to found a settlement at
Spain built three kinds of settlements to hold California. Which list is correct?
it.h: One was for religion, one for soldiers and one for farming towns.

it.q: Why did Spain need pueblos?
ch: to grow food for the soldiers in the presidios
it.h: Soldiers and priests needed food. Who would grow it?

it.q: Describe the job of each group in Spanish California: soldiers, missionaries and pueblo settlers.
it.ans: Soldiers guarded presidios and the land; missionaries tried to convert California Indians to Christianity and ran the missions; settlers farmed and raised animals in pueblos to supply food.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: Life and change in the missions

it.q: How many missions did the Franciscans build in Alta California?
it.h: The first was in 1769 and the last in 1823.

it.q: The missions were built about a day's walk apart along a road called
it.h: Its name means "the royal road."

it.q: How did the missions change California's economy?
ch: from hunting and gathering to farming and raising cattle and sheep
it.h: Think about the crops and animals the missions brought.

it.q: California Indians who were baptized and lived at the missions were called
The first mission was founded in 1769 and the last in 1823. How many years did it take to build all the missions?
it.h: Subtract the first year from the last year.

it.q: Describe two kinds of work California Indians did at the missions.
it.ans: They farmed wheat and corn, herded cattle and sheep, made adobe bricks and buildings, wove cloth, made candles and soap, and cooked.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: Resistance and survival: California Indians in the mission era

it.q: When neophytes left a mission without permission, what did the padres often do?
ch: sent soldiers to bring them back
it.h: The missions depended on Indian workers.

it.q: In November 1775, Kumeyaay fighters attacked and burned Mission San Diego. Which was one reason?
ch: anger at soldiers' mistreatment and the loss of land and freedom
a wish to join the United States
it.h: Think about how the mission and presidio changed Kumeyaay life.

it.q: In 1824, Chumash people rose up at Missions Santa Ines, La Purisima and Santa Barbara. At La Purisima they
ch: held the mission for about a month
it.h: The revolt was not ended in a single day.

it.q: Estanislao, a Yokuts man who had lived at Mission San Jose, led a revolt in 1828 and 1829. Which California places are named for him?
ch: the Stanislaus River and Stanislaus County
it.h: Say his name out loud and listen for it in a place name.

it.q: The Kumeyaay attack on Mission San Diego was in 1775, and the Chumash revolt was in 1824. How many years apart were they?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Resistance did not always mean fighting. Describe one quieter way California Indians resisted or survived mission life.
it.ans: Running away, secretly keeping their own languages, songs and beliefs, working slowly or refusing work, or teaching traditional skills to their children.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: The legacy of the missions: place names, buildings and memory

it.q: Many California cities have Spanish names from the mission era, such as
ch: San Luis Obispo and Santa Clara
it.h: San and Santa mean "saint" in Spanish.

it.q: Many California schools and train stations have red tile roofs, arches and thick plastered walls. This building style copies
it.h: Picture an old mission church.

it.q: The missions brought grapes, olives, figs and citrus to California. Which statement shows the legacy of this?
ch: These crops became an important part of California farming.
it.h: Think of California's vineyards and orchards today.

it.q: Many missions fell into ruin after secularization. Why were many of them restored in the 1900s?
ch: People wanted to preserve them as historic places and attract visitors.
They were needed for gold mining.

it.q: Mission Santa Barbara was founded in 1786. How many years ago was that from {year}?
it.h: Subtract 1786 from this year.

it.q: Name two ways the mission era still shows up in California today.
it.ans: Spanish place names, mission buildings that are now churches and museums, bells marking El Camino Real, mission-style architecture, and crops such as grapes and olives.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Exploration and the Mission Period (4.2)
lessons.n: Timelines and maps of Spanish California, 1542-1823

it.q: A timeline shows events
it.h: Look at the years.

it.q: Which event came first?
ch: Cabrillo sails along the California coast
the founding of Mission San Diego
it.h: Find the earliest year: 1542, 1769, 1781 or 1821.

it.q: A map of the missions shows Mission San Diego at the southern end of the chain. Which mission was the farthest north?
ch: Mission San Francisco Solano in Sonoma
it.h: The last mission was founded north of San Francisco Bay in 1823.

it.q: The presidio of San Francisco was founded in 1776. What else happened that same year on the other side of the continent?
ch: The Declaration of Independence was signed.

it.q: The Spanish founded Mission San Diego in 1769 and the pueblo of Los Angeles in 1781. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract the earlier year from the later year.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: Mexico wins independence

it.q: Mexico won its independence from Spain in
it.h: The war for independence began in 1810 and ended eleven years later.

it.q: After Mexico won independence, Alta California became
it.h: Think about which country now ruled the land that Spain had claimed.

it.q: Secularization of the missions meant
ch: mission lands were taken from the church and given to the government to divide
the missions were moved to Spain
it.h: "Secular" means not religious.

it.q: Mexico's law said much of the mission land should go to the California Indians who worked it. What actually happened to most of it?
ch: It was given as land grants to Californios and other settlers.
All of it went to the Indians.

it.q: Mexico began secularizing the missions in 1834. How many years after the founding of the first mission in 1769 was that?
it.h: Subtract 1769 from 1834.

it.q: Explain one way life changed in Alta California after Mexico won independence.
it.ans: Mexico ended the mission system, divided mission land into ranchos, opened trade with foreign ships, and Californios gained more power.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: Life on the ranchos

it.q: A rancho was
ch: a large land grant used mainly for raising cattle
it.h: Think of huge open grasslands and herds.

it.q: Cattle hides were called "California bank notes" because
it.h: How did people pay for goods when there was little money?

it.q: Most of the work on the ranchos was done by
ch: California Indian workers, including many skilled vaqueros
it.h: Many of these workers had learned ranching at the missions.

it.q: Tallow is
ch: fat from cattle used to make candles and soap
it.h: Think about what ranchers could make from every part of a cow.

it.q: Ships from Boston sailed to California to buy hides. What did the ships bring to trade?
it.h: California had few factories. What goods would people there want?

it.q: Describe a day on a rancho for the ranchero's family and for an Indian vaquero.
it.ans: The ranchero family managed the land, hosted guests and oversaw the herds; the vaquero rode long hours herding, roping and branding cattle, often for food and shelter instead of wages.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: Newcomers and new trails

it.q: In 1812, Russian fur traders built a settlement on the northern California coast called
it.h: Its name comes from an old word for Russia.

it.q: John Sutter, a Swiss immigrant, built a fort and trading post in the Sacramento Valley in
it.h: It was a stopping place for overland travelers in the 1840s.

it.q: In 1841, the Bidwell-Bartleson Party became one of the first groups of American settlers to
ch: travel by wagon over land to California
it.h: They crossed the Great Basin and the Sierra Nevada.

it.q: James Beckwourth, an African American mountain man and trail guide, is remembered for
ch: finding a pass through the Sierra Nevada that wagons could use
it.h: Mountain men knew routes through rough country.

it.q: The Donner Party was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846-1847. What lesson did it teach other travelers?
ch: Leave early enough to cross the mountains before winter.
it.h: Think about what the weather is like in the mountains in winter.

it.q: Compare two ways newcomers traveled to California in the 1840s. Give one danger of each.
it.ans: By wagon over land: deserts, mountains, snow and running out of food. By ship around South America: storms, disease and a very long trip of many months.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: The Bear Flag Revolt and the Mexican-American War

it.q: In June 1846, American settlers in Sonoma declared California independent and raised a flag with a grizzly bear. This was the
it.h: The flag gives the event its name.

it.q: During the revolt, settlers took Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo prisoner. Who was he?
ch: a leading Californio and Mexican army general
it.h: He lived in Sonoma and was one of the most powerful Californios.

it.q: The Bear Flag Republic began June 14, 1846, and ended when the U.S. flag was raised in Sonoma on July 9, 1846. How many days did it last?
it.h: Count the days left in June after the 14th, then add the days in July.

it.q: The Mexican-American War was fought between the United States and Mexico from
