it.h: It began the same year as the Bear Flag Revolt and ended with a treaty in 1848.

it.q: At the Battle of San Pasqual in December 1846, Californio soldiers on horseback with lances
ch: defeated U.S. troops led by Stephen Kearny
it.h: The Californios were skilled riders who knew the land.

it.q: Why did many Californios oppose the Bear Flag Revolt?
it.ans: It was an attack on their country by newcomers who took their leaders prisoner and threatened their land and way of life.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: Californios after the war: the Land Act of 1851 and losing the ranchos

it.q: The Land Act of 1851 required Californio landowners to
ch: prove to a U.S. board that their land grants were legal
give their land to the railroad
it.h: The United States wanted proof of who owned which land.

it.q: Many Mexican land grants used hand-drawn maps called diseños that marked borders with landmarks such as a tree, a creek or a pile of rocks. Why did this cause problems in U.S. courts?
ch: Landmarks could change or disappear, so the borders were hard to prove.
The maps were written in English.
The maps showed where gold was.
Courts did not allow any maps.
it.h: What can happen to a tree or a creek over many years?

it.q: Squatters are people who
ch: settle on land they do not own
it.h: Many newcomers believed the open land was free to take.

it.q: Proving a land claim often took many years. How did many Californios pay their lawyers?
ch: by giving them part of their land

it.q: A ranchero owned 48,000 acres. He gave one fourth of his land to his lawyers. How many acres did he give away?
it.h: Divide by 4.

it.q: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo promised to protect Mexican property. Explain how the Land Act of 1851 still made it hard for Californios to keep their land.
it.ans: Owners had to prove their titles in a new legal system, in English, using old maps with landmarks; cases took years, lawyers took land as payment, and squatters moved onto ranchos in the meantime.
it.h: Think about time, money, language and maps.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
lessons.n: Ports and trade in Mexican California: Monterey and Yerba Buena

it.q: Under Mexico, foreign ships trading in Alta California were supposed to stop first at the customs house in
it.h: It was the capital of Mexican California for most of the period.

it.q: A customs house collected
ch: taxes on goods brought in by ships
it.h: Ships paid a fee on the goods they carried in.

it.q: The small village of Yerba Buena on San Francisco Bay was renamed in 1847. What is it called today?
it.h: The bay already had this name.

it.q: Ships from Boston brought cloth, shoes, tools and furniture to California. What did Californios usually give in return?
A ship paid a tax of $3 for every $10 of goods it brought in. It brought $1,000 of goods. How much tax did it pay?
it.h: How many groups of $10 are in $1,000?

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
lessons.n: Gold is discovered

it.q: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill on the American River in January of
it.h: The people who rushed in the next year were named for that next year.

it.q: Who found the first flakes of gold at Sutter's Mill?
it.h: He was building a sawmill for Sutter.

it.q: Henry Bigler, a worker at the mill, wrote in his diary on January 24, 1848: "This day some kind of mettle was found in the tail race that looks like goald." Why is this diary a primary source?
ch: It was written by a person who was there when it happened.
it.h: Think about who wrote it and when.

it.q: People who came to California for gold in 1849 were called
A ship from New York sailed about 13,000 miles around South America to San Francisco. Another route through Panama was about 5,000 miles. How many miles shorter was the Panama route?
it.h: Subtract the shorter route from the longer one.

it.q: Name two routes the forty-niners used to reach California and one hardship of each.
it.ans: Overland by wagon: deserts, mountains, disease and lack of water. Around South America by ship: storms, seasickness and a trip of five to eight months. Across Panama: jungle diseases like malaria.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
lessons.n: Life in the gold fields

it.q: A shallow metal pan used to wash gravel and find gold is a
it.h: The name of the tool is in the answer.

it.q: Miners from Sonora, Mexico, and from Chile were often skilled because
ch: many had mined gold and silver at home
it.h: Think about the mining history of Mexico and South America.

it.q: In 1850, California passed a Foreign Miners' Tax of $20 a month. Who did it hurt most?
ch: miners from Mexico, Chile and other parts of Latin America
miners born in the United States
it.h: The tax was only for miners who were not U.S. citizens.

it.q: A miner paid the $20 Foreign Miners' Tax every month for 6 months. How much did he pay?
it.h: Multiply the monthly tax by the number of months.

it.q: Hydraulic mining sprayed water through big hoses to wash away hillsides. What was one effect?
ch: Mud and gravel filled rivers and flooded farms downstream.

it.q: Describe a day in the life of a gold miner in 1850. Include work, food and living conditions.
it.ans: Miners worked from dawn digging and washing gravel in cold streams, lived in tents or cabins, ate beans, bread and salted meat bought at high prices, and often got sick.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
lessons.n: Boomtowns and businesses

it.q: A town that grows very quickly is a
it.h: Think of a sudden loud "boom."

it.q: Which group often made more money than the miners?
ch: merchants who sold supplies to miners
it.h: Every miner needed food, tools and clothes.

it.q: Levi Strauss came to San Francisco in 1853 and sold cloth and goods. He later became famous for
ch: sturdy work pants called blue jeans
it.h: Miners needed clothes that would not tear while they worked.

it.q: Biddy Mason was brought to California as an enslaved woman. In 1856 she
ch: went to court in Los Angeles and won freedom for herself and her family
it.h: California's constitution did not allow slavery.

it.q: When the gold ran out, many mining towns were abandoned and became
it.h: Think about what a town becomes when everyone leaves.

it.q: Explain why Sacramento and San Francisco grew so fast during the Gold Rush.
it.ans: San Francisco had a harbor where ships brought people and supplies; Sacramento was on rivers near the gold fields. Both became trade and supply centers for miners.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
lessons.n: Becoming the 31st state

it.q: California became a state on September 9 of
it.h: It was two years after gold was found.

it.q: In 1849, delegates met at Colton Hall in Monterey to write
it.h: A state needs a plan of government before it can join the union.

it.q: California's 1849 constitution was printed in two languages. Which ones?
it.h: Think about who lived in California at the time.

it.q: The 1849 constitution said: "Neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated in this State." What did this mean?
ch: California would be a free state.

it.q: California became the 31st state in 1850. In what year did it celebrate 150 years of statehood?
it.h: Add 150 to the year of statehood.

it.q: Explain why California became a state so quickly after the Gold Rush began.
it.ans: The Gold Rush brought so many people that California needed a government, courts and laws to keep order and protect property, so leaders wrote a constitution and asked to join the union.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
lessons.n: Claims, courts and justice in Gold Rush California

it.q: In the gold fields, a piece of ground that a miner had the right to dig was called a
it.h: Miners marked a spot to show it was theirs.

it.q: Miners in many areas met and wrote their own rules about claims. Why?
ch: There were few courts or sheriffs, so miners needed a way to settle arguments.
The governor ordered every camp to write a constitution.
They wanted to stop all mining.
it.h: People poured into the gold fields faster than government could arrive.

it.q: Claim jumping meant
ch: leaving a claim to go home
it.h: What would it mean to "jump" into someone else's spot?

it.q: In 1851 and 1856, groups called vigilance committees took control of justice in San Francisco. Why do many historians criticize them?
ch: They punished and even hanged people without fair trials.
it.h: Think about what a fair trial gives a person who is accused.

it.q: A mining camp's rule allowed each miner a claim 100 feet long. Four miners marked their claims side by side. How many feet long were their claims all together?
it.h: Multiply.

it.q: Why is it dangerous for a group of people to punish others without courts or trials?
it.ans: Innocent people can be hurt, accused people cannot defend themselves, and anger or prejudice can decide the outcome instead of evidence and law.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
lessons.n: Connecting California to the nation

it.q: The Pony Express carried mail on horseback between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento starting in
it.h: It began about ten years after statehood.

it.q: The Pony Express ended in October 1861. What replaced it?
it.h: This invention sent messages over wires in minutes.

it.q: The Pony Express route was about 1,900 miles. Riders took about 10 days. About how many miles did the mail travel each day?
it.h: Divide the miles by the number of days.

it.q: Why did Californians want faster mail and travel to the East?
ch: California was far from the rest of the country, and news took weeks or months to arrive.
They wanted to stop all trade.
They wanted to move back to Mexico.

it.q: Stagecoaches of the Overland Mail Company carried mail and passengers to California beginning in 1858. About how long did the trip take?
it.h: Stagecoaches were faster than wagon trains but much slower than trains.

it.q: Explain why the Pony Express lasted less than two years but is still remembered.
it.ans: The telegraph made it unnecessary in 1861. It is remembered because it was fast for its time and showed how much Californians wanted to be connected to the nation.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
lessons.n: Building the transcontinental railroad

it.q: The Central Pacific Railroad began building east from
it.h: The capital city on the river was the starting point.

it.q: Most of the workers who built the Central Pacific through the Sierra Nevada were
it.h: The railroad hired thousands of workers who had come from Guangdong.

it.q: The Central Pacific and the Union Pacific met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on
it.h: This happened 21 years after gold was found.

it.q: Why was building through the Sierra Nevada so dangerous?
ch: Workers blasted tunnels through granite and faced avalanches and deep snow.
The land was flat and dry.
it.h: Think about what it takes to put a railroad through mountains.

it.q: The four businessmen who led the Central Pacific, including Leland Stanford, were called
Describe two contributions of Chinese workers to the transcontinental railroad.
it.ans: They cleared land, blasted tunnels through granite, laid track and worked through snow and danger. Without them the Central Pacific could not have crossed the Sierra Nevada.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
lessons.n: Newcomers from many lands

it.q: An immigrant is a person who
ch: moves to a new country to live
it.h: "Im-" means into. An immigrant moves into a new country.

it.q: Which group came to California in large numbers from Japan beginning in the 1880s?
ch: Japanese immigrants who worked on farms
it.h: The answer names the country in the question.

it.q: In 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act. What did it do?
ch: It stopped most Chinese workers from coming to the United States.
It gave land to Chinese families.
it.h: "Exclude" means to keep out.

it.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act said that "the coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities." What was the point of view of the people who wrote it?
ch: They saw Chinese workers as a threat and wanted to keep them out.
They wanted to build more railroads.
it.h: Read the word "endangers" closely.

it.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed in 1882 and ended in 1943. How many years did it last?
Name two immigrant groups who came to California between 1850 and 1900 and tell one contribution of each.
it.ans: Chinese immigrants built railroads, levees and farms; Irish immigrants worked on railroads and in cities; Italians started farms and vineyards; Japanese immigrants became important farmers.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
lessons.n: Towns and cities grow

it.q: The Southern Pacific Railroad connected Los Angeles to San Francisco in
it.h: It was seven years after the transcontinental railroad was finished.

it.q: In the 1880s, two railroads competed and ticket prices to Los Angeles fell very low. What happened next?
ch: Thousands of people moved to Southern California in a land boom.
it.h: Think about what people do when a trip becomes cheap.

it.q: Los Angeles had about 100,000 people in 1900 and about 1,200,000 in 1930. How many more people is that?
it.h: Subtract the 1900 population from the 1930 population.

it.q: Refrigerated railroad cars, used in the late 1880s, let farmers
ch: ship fresh oranges and other fruit across the country
it.h: Cold keeps fruit fresh on a long trip.

it.q: Oil was discovered in Los Angeles in 1892. How did this change the city?
ch: Oil wells and new jobs helped the city grow.

it.q: Explain how railroads helped towns in the Central Valley and Southern California grow.
it.ans: Railroads carried crops to markets, brought new settlers and goods, and towns grew up around train stations.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
lessons.n: Farming becomes big business: wheat, irrigation and farm workers

it.q: In the 1870s and 1880s, huge farms in the Central Valley grew so much of which crop that ships carried it to Europe?
it.h: It is ground into flour for bread.

it.q: Giant harvesting machines on the wheat farms were pulled by teams of
it.h: This was before gasoline tractors were common.

it.q: In the 1860s and 1870s, Chinese workers built levees and drained marshes in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. What was the result?
ch: The Delta turned into a desert.
Gold was found in the levees.
it.h: Levees keep water out of the land behind them.

it.q: Over time, many farmers switched from wheat to fruit and vegetables. Which was one reason?
ch: Irrigation made fruit possible, and fruit earned more money per acre.
it.h: Think about what changed when water could reach the fields.

it.q: A wheat farm harvested 25 bushels per acre on 400 acres. How many bushels did it harvest?
it.h: Multiply bushels per acre by the number of acres.

it.q: Explain how irrigation changed farming in California.
it.ans: Irrigation brought river and well water to dry land, so farmers could grow fruit, nuts and vegetables in summer and on land that was too dry before, and farms became more valuable.
it.h: Most of California gets little or no rain in summer.

lessons.u: Unit 7: California in the Twentieth Century (4.4)
lessons.n: Water for a growing state

it.q: An aqueduct is
ch: a large channel or pipe that carries water a long distance
a dam that makes electricity only
it.h: "Aqua" means water.

it.q: Most of California's rain and snow falls in the north, but many people live in the south. What problem does this cause?
ch: Water must be moved from the north and east to the dry south.
The south has too much water.
it.h: Think about where the water is and where the people are.

it.q: The Los Angeles Aqueduct carried water about 233 miles from the Owens Valley. A worker walked 25 miles of it in one day. How many miles were left?
it.h: Subtract the miles walked from the total.

it.q: When the Los Angeles Aqueduct opened in 1913, its builder William Mulholland said, "There it is. Take it." What was he talking about?
ch: the water arriving for Los Angeles

it.q: Shasta Dam, finished in 1945, was part of a large federal plan to store water for Central Valley farms called the
it.h: The answer names the valley it served.

it.q: Explain one benefit and one cost of building dams and aqueducts in California.
it.ans: Benefit: water for cities and farms and electricity. Cost: valleys flooded, rivers and lakes dried up, fish and wildlife harmed, and farmers in places like the Owens Valley lost their water.

lessons.u: Unit 7: California in the Twentieth Century (4.4)
lessons.n: Hard times and war

it.q: The Great Depression, which began in 1929, was a time when
ch: many people lost jobs, money and homes
it.h: "Depression" means a time when things go down.

it.q: During the 1930s, dust storms and drought drove many farm families from Oklahoma and nearby states to California. This was called the
it.h: Dry, blowing soil gave this time its name.

it.q: Photographer Dorothea Lange took pictures of migrant families in California in the 1930s. Why are her photos important?
ch: They show the hardships of families during the Depression.
it.h: Photos are primary sources. What do they let us see?

it.q: In 1942, during World War II, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast, most of them U.S. citizens, to
ch: leave their homes and live in guarded camps
it.h: One of these camps, Manzanar, was in the Owens Valley.

it.q: The Bracero Program brought workers from Mexico to work on U.S. farms from 1942 to 1964. How many years did it last?
Explain why many Dust Bowl families had a hard life even after they reached California.
it.ans: Jobs were few and paid little, families lived in camps or tents, and some Californians did not welcome them.

lessons.u: Unit 7: California in the Twentieth Century (4.4)
lessons.n: New industries and a Pacific economy

it.q: The movie industry grew in which part of Los Angeles in the 1910s?
it.h: The famous sign is in the hills above it.

it.q: Why did filmmakers move to Southern California?
ch: sunny weather all year and many kinds of scenery nearby
it.h: Early movies needed lots of natural light.

it.q: The area around San Jose and Palo Alto became known for computer chips and technology. Its nickname is
it.h: The material used to make computer chips gives the area its nickname.

it.q: Aircraft and aerospace factories grew in Southern California during and after World War II. Why?
ch: The government needed planes, and the mild weather allowed year-round flying and testing.
it.h: Think about what a war needs and what the weather allows.

it.q: The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach handle goods from Asia. If one ship carries 8,000 containers and 5 ships arrive, how many containers arrive?
Name two industries that grew in California in the 1900s and explain one reason each grew there.
it.ans: Movies grew because of sunshine and scenery; aerospace grew because of wartime contracts and weather; technology grew because of universities and inventors near San Jose; agriculture grew because of irrigation.

lessons.u: Unit 7: California in the Twentieth Century (4.4)
lessons.n: Schools, culture and civil rights

it.q: The University of California was founded in
it.h: It began the year before the transcontinental railroad was finished.

it.q: In 1947, a court ruled in Mendez v. Westminster that Mexican American children in Orange County
ch: could not be forced into separate schools
it.h: Sylvia Mendez's family went to court so she could attend the same school as other children.

it.q: In 1965, Filipino American farm workers led by Larry Itliong began a grape strike in Delano. Who joined them?
ch: Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta and Mexican American farm workers

it.q: John Steinbeck wrote novels about farm workers and life in the Salinas Valley. Ansel Adams took photographs of
it.h: His black-and-white pictures helped people value national parks.

it.q: California women won the right to vote in state elections in
it.h: It was nine years before the 19th Amendment gave women the vote nationwide in 1920.

it.q: Explain why the Mendez v. Westminster case was important.
it.ans: It ended school segregation of Mexican American children in California and helped lead to the end of segregated schools in the whole country.

lessons.u: Unit 7: California in the Twentieth Century (4.4)
lessons.n: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire

it.q: The great San Francisco earthquake struck early in the morning on April 18 of
it.h: It happened in the early twentieth century.

it.q: The shaking lasted less than a minute. What caused most of the destruction afterward?
ch: fires that burned for about three days
a tsunami that covered the city
it.h: Broken gas lines and fallen stoves started something that spread fast.

it.q: Firefighters had trouble stopping the fires. Which was a main reason?
ch: The earthquake broke many water pipes.
The fires were too small to find.
Firefighters were away at the Gold Rush.
it.h: What do firefighters need from the pipes under the street?

it.q: Hundreds of thousands of people lost their homes. Where did many of them stay?
ch: in tents and camps in parks such as Golden Gate Park

it.q: About 400,000 people lived in San Francisco in 1906. Suppose 225,000 of them lost their homes. How many people did not lose their homes?
it.h: Subtract.

it.q: Writer Jack London described the disaster in a magazine in 1906. Explain why an eyewitness account like his is a useful source, and one reason to read it carefully.
it.ans: It describes what the writer actually saw and felt, but it shows only one person's view and may include strong feelings or details he did not check.
it.h: Think about what a single eyewitness can and cannot see.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: The U.S. Constitution and the federal government

it.q: The U.S. Constitution is
ch: the written plan for the national government and the highest law of the land
a law made by California only
it.h: Every other law in the country must agree with it.

it.q: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, which protect people's rights, are called the
it.h: Think of a list, or "bill," of rights.

it.q: The Preamble to the U.S. Constitution (1787) begins "We the People of the United States." What idea does this show?
ch: The government's power comes from the people.
A king gives the people their rights.
it.h: Look at who is speaking in the first three words.

it.q: Which power belongs only to the federal government?
ch: printing money and making treaties with other countries
running public schools in each town

it.q: Federalism means
ch: power is shared between the national government and the state governments
cities make all laws for the country
it.h: "Federal" and "state" each have their own jobs.

it.q: Explain why the writers of the U.S. Constitution divided power among three branches.
it.ans: They wanted to keep any one person or group from having too much power, so each branch can check the others.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: California's state government

it.q: The leader of California's executive branch is the
it.h: Each state elects one.

it.q: California's legislature meets in the state capitol in
it.h: It has been the capital since 1854.

it.q: California's legislature has two houses. They are the
The State Assembly has 80 members and the State Senate has 40. How many more members does the Assembly have?
it.h: Subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

it.q: When the governor rejects a bill passed by the legislature, it is called a
it.h: This Latin word means "I forbid."

it.q: Describe how a bill becomes a California state law.
it.ans: A member of the legislature writes a bill; it must pass both the Assembly and the Senate; then the governor signs it into law or vetoes it. The legislature can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: Local, tribal and special governments

it.q: California is divided into 58
it.h: Each one is led by a board of supervisors.

it.q: A city government is usually led by
ch: a mayor and a city council
it.h: Think of the leaders who make decisions for your city or town.

it.q: A school district is a kind of local government that
ch: runs public schools in an area
it.h: The name tells you what it is in charge of.

it.q: Rancherias and reservations in California are lands where
ch: federally recognized tribes govern their own communities
missions are still run by priests
it.h: Tribes are sovereign nations with their own governments.

it.q: A county board of supervisors has 5 members. A plan needs a majority of votes to pass. What is the smallest number of votes needed?
Name three kinds of local government in California and one job of each.
it.ans: City: police and parks. County: elections, public health and the sheriff. School district: runs public schools. Water district: delivers water.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: Citizens in action: voting and ballot propositions

it.q: In California, a U.S. citizen can vote in elections starting at age
it.h: It is the same age for voting in every state.

it.q: Before voting for the first time, a citizen must
it.h: Your name has to be on the list of voters.

it.q: On a California ballot, a proposition is
ch: a law or change to the state constitution that voters decide
it.h: Voters say yes or no to it.

it.q: To put an initiative on the ballot, supporters must first
ch: collect signatures from many registered voters
it.h: The idea has to show it has enough support before everyone votes.

it.q: A proposition received 6,000,000 yes votes and 4,500,000 no votes. How many more yes votes than no votes did it get?
it.h: Subtract the no votes from the yes votes.

it.q: Explain why voting is called both a right and a responsibility.
it.ans: It is a right because the law protects citizens' power to choose leaders and laws; it is a responsibility because democracy works only if citizens take part and make informed choices.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: Rights and responsibilities of citizens

it.q: A person can become a U.S. citizen by being born in the United States or through
it.h: Immigrants study, pass a test and take an oath.

it.q: Which is a responsibility of citizens, not a right?
ch: serving on a jury when called
it.h: A responsibility is something you do for the community.

it.q: Article I of California's constitution is called the Declaration of Rights. What does it do?
ch: lists rights the state government must protect
it.h: Compare it with the Bill of Rights in the U.S. Constitution.

it.q: Paying taxes is a responsibility. What do taxes pay for?
ch: public services such as schools, roads, parks and firefighters

it.q: A city collects $500,000 in taxes and spends 2/5 of it on schools. How many dollars go to schools?
it.h: Find one fifth first, then multiply by 2.

it.q: Name one right and one responsibility of a citizen. Explain how they are connected.
it.ans: Right: freedom of speech. Responsibility: respect others' rights and stay informed. Using free speech responsibly means listening to others and sharing accurate information.
it.h: Think about how one person's rights affect other people.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: Checks and balances in California's government

it.q: The idea that each branch of government can limit the power of the other branches is called
it.h: No branch should get too much power.

it.q: If the governor vetoes a bill, the legislature can still make it a law if
ch: two-thirds of the members of each house vote to override the veto
it.h: Overriding a veto takes more than a simple majority.

it.q: Which branch of California's government decides whether a law follows the state constitution?
it.h: This branch includes the courts.

it.q: The governor appoints judges to the California Supreme Court. Later, voters decide whether each justice keeps the job. What is this an example of?
ch: voters checking the power of the governor and the courts

it.q: The State Assembly has 80 members. How many votes are needed for two-thirds of the Assembly to override a veto? Round up to a whole number of members.
it.h: Find 2/3 of 80, then round up.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Government in California (4.5)
lessons.n: Paying for government: taxes, budgets and public services

it.q: A budget is
ch: a plan for how money will be collected and spent
it.h: Families and governments both make one.

it.q: When you buy a toy at a store in California, you usually pay an extra amount for the state and local government. This is a
it.h: It is added at the time of a sale.

it.q: Property taxes on homes and land help pay mostly for
ch: local services such as schools, counties and cities
it.h: Property is in a community, so the tax helps that community.

it.q: The governor of California proposes a state budget each January. Who must then pass it?
A town's budget is $900,000. It spends $360,000 on police and fire. How much is left for everything else?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 1: American Indian Nations of North America (5.1)
lessons.n: The desert Southwest and the Pacific Northwest

it.q: The Ancestral Puebloans built cliff dwellings at places such as
it.h: This site is in southwestern Colorado and its name means "green table" in Spanish.

it.q: Pueblo peoples built homes of adobe and stone. Why were these materials a good choice in the desert?
ch: Thick earth and stone walls stayed cool in the day and warm at night, and few trees grew there.
They were the only materials in the world.
They were easy to carry from place to place.
it.h: Think about desert temperatures and what materials are found there.

it.q: How did Pueblo farmers grow corn, beans and squash in a dry land?
ch: They collected rain and used ditches and dams to water their fields.

it.q: Nations of the Pacific Northwest, such as the Tlingit and Haida, depended most on
ch: salmon from rivers and the sea, and cedar trees
it.h: The region is rainy, with thick forests and many rivers.

it.q: A potlatch was a ceremony in the Pacific Northwest where a host
ch: gave away gifts to show wealth and honor guests
it.h: Think of a big feast where the host is generous.

it.q: Explain how the environment of the Pacific Northwest let people live in large, permanent villages without farming.
it.ans: Rivers full of salmon, a rich sea and forests of cedar gave plenty of food and materials all year, so people did not need to move or farm.

lessons.u: Unit 1: American Indian Nations of North America (5.1)
lessons.n: The Great Plains

it.q: The nations of the Great Plains, such as the Lakota and Cheyenne, depended most on the
it.h: Huge herds of this animal roamed the grasslands.

it.q: Plains peoples who followed the buffalo herds lived in tipis. Why?
ch: Tipis could be taken down and moved quickly.
Tipis were the largest houses in the world.
it.h: Think about a home for people who traveled often.

it.q: Horses were brought to the Americas by the Spanish. How did horses change Plains life in the 1700s?
ch: Hunting buffalo and moving camp became much faster and easier.
Horses made people farm in one place.

it.q: Which use of the buffalo is correct?
ch: hides for tipis and clothing, and bones for tools
it.h: Plains peoples used almost every part of the animal.

it.q: A Lakota band of 240 people moved camp. Each tipi held about 8 people. How many tipis did they need?
it.h: Divide the number of people by the people in each tipi.

it.q: Explain why many Plains nations moved during the year instead of living in one village.
it.ans: They followed the buffalo herds, which moved with the seasons and the grass, because the buffalo gave them food, clothing and shelter.

lessons.u: Unit 1: American Indian Nations of North America (5.1)
lessons.n: The Eastern Woodlands and the Mississippian cities

it.q: Corn, beans and squash, grown together by many Eastern Woodlands nations, were called the
it.h: The plants were thought of as a family that helped one another grow.

it.q: The Haudenosaunee, also called the Iroquois, lived in long bark-covered houses called
it.h: The name describes the shape of the house.

it.q: Five Haudenosaunee nations joined together in a league under the Great Law of Peace. Why?
ch: to end fighting among themselves and make decisions together
it.h: Unity can bring peace.

it.q: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was a large city built by Mississippian people around 1000 to 1200. What is it famous for?
ch: huge earthen mounds, including one about 100 feet tall
it.h: These people were sometimes called the Mound Builders.

it.q: Woodlands nations used the forests for
ch: deer, wood for homes and canoes, and nuts and berries

it.q: Explain how the Three Sisters helped each other grow and fed the people.
it.ans: Corn gave beans a pole to climb, beans added nutrients to the soil, and squash leaves shaded the ground and kept in water. Together they gave a healthy diet.

lessons.u: Unit 1: American Indian Nations of North America (5.1)
lessons.n: The Arctic and the Great Basin: living in harsh lands

it.q: The Inuit and other Arctic peoples lived in a land of
ch: long, freezing winters with few trees
it.h: Picture the far north near the Arctic Ocean.

it.q: Because few trees grow in the Arctic, Inuit families made many tools and boat frames from
ch: bone, antler, driftwood and animal skins
it.h: Think about what the animals and the sea gave them.

it.q: Some Inuit families built domed winter shelters from blocks of packed snow. Why did snow work as a building material?
ch: Packed snow traps air and holds in warmth.
it.h: Air pockets act like a blanket.

it.q: The Great Basin, between the Sierra Nevada and the Rocky Mountains, has little rain. Many Shoshone and Paiute families gathered which important food each fall?
it.h: It comes from a short, tough pine tree.

it.q: Choose the Arctic or the Great Basin. Explain how people adapted to the climate there.
it.ans: Great Basin: families moved with the seasons to gather pine nuts, seeds and roots, hunted rabbits and small animals, and built light brush shelters they could leave behind.
it.h: Think about food, shelter and moving with the seasons.

lessons.u: Unit 1: American Indian Nations of North America (5.1)
lessons.n: Comparing American Indian regions with maps and artifacts

it.q: A map of North America divided into areas where nations lived in similar ways is called a
it.h: The areas show groups with similar ways of life.

it.q: A map shows the Pacific Northwest, the Southwest, the Great Plains and the Eastern Woodlands. Which region would most likely have plank houses?
it.h: Which region had the tallest forests near the sea?

it.q: An artifact is
ch: an object made and used by people long ago
a law passed by a council
it.h: Archaeologists dig them up.

it.q: Why did nations in different regions build such different homes?
ch: Each used the materials and fit the climate of its own region.
One leader ruled all of them.
They did not know about other homes.
They wanted to look different only.

it.q: Choose two regions. Name one food each region depended on and explain how geography made that food possible.
it.ans: Plains: buffalo, because huge herds grazed on the grasslands. Pacific Northwest: salmon, because rivers full of fish flowed into the ocean.
it.h: Think about land, water and climate.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
lessons.n: Why Europeans explored

it.q: In the 1400s, many Europeans wanted a sea route to Asia mainly to
ch: trade for spices, silk and other valuable goods
find a place to farm wheat
it.h: These goods were rare and costly in Europe.

it.q: After 1453, the Ottoman Empire controlled the land routes between Europe and Asia. How did this affect European traders?
ch: Asian goods became harder to get and more expensive, so they looked for sea routes.
it.h: Think about what happens when someone else controls the road you need.

it.q: Historians often sum up the reasons for exploration as "God, gold and glory." Which is an example of "glory"?
ch: an explorer wanting fame for his country and himself
it.h: Glory is about honor and fame.

it.q: A caravel was
ch: a small, fast ship with sails that could sail against the wind
it.h: Portuguese sailors used this ship to explore the coast of Africa.

it.q: An astrolabe helped sailors find their latitude by
ch: measuring the angle of the sun or stars above the horizon
showing the depth of the ocean

it.q: Explain why kings and queens sponsored, or paid for, voyages of exploration.
it.ans: They hoped to gain wealth from trade and gold, claim new land, spread their religion and win power and glory over rival countries.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
lessons.n: Spain in the Americas

it.q: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west for
it.h: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella paid for his voyage.

it.q: Columbus thought he had reached
ch: islands near Asia, which he called the Indies
a new continent he named America
it.h: This is why he called the people he met "Indians."

it.q: The Taino people met Columbus in the Caribbean. What happened to them in the years that followed?
ch: Many died from disease, war and forced labor under Spanish rule.

it.q: In 1521, Hernan Cortes and his soldiers, with thousands of Indigenous allies, conquered the capital of the
it.h: Its capital, Tenochtitlan, is now Mexico City.

it.q: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition left Spain in 1519 with about 270 sailors. In 1522, only 18 returned on the ship Victoria. About how many sailors did not return on that ship?
it.h: Subtract the sailors who returned from those who left.

it.q: Explain why Spanish conquistadors were able to defeat large empires like the Aztec and Inca.
it.ans: They had steel weapons, guns and horses, they made alliances with Indigenous peoples who opposed those empires, and European diseases like smallpox killed huge numbers of people.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
lessons.n: France, England and the Netherlands in North America

it.q: In 1497, John Cabot explored the coast of Newfoundland and claimed land for
it.h: He was born in Italy, but his voyage was paid for by King Henry VII.

it.q: Many explorers searched for a Northwest Passage. What was it?
ch: a hoped-for water route through North America to Asia
it.h: The name gives a direction and a kind of path.

it.q: Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s. Which country did he sail for?
it.h: Quebec, a city on this river, still speaks this country's language.

it.q: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. It became the center of
ch: New France and its fur trade
it.h: Beaver furs were very valuable in Europe.

it.q: Henry Hudson explored the Hudson River for the Dutch in 1609. Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. How many years apart are these events?
Compare the goals of French and Spanish explorers in North America.
it.ans: Spanish explorers searched mostly for gold and to conquer and convert people; French explorers mostly sought furs, trade with American Indians and a route to Asia.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
lessons.n: Atlantic trade and the Columbian Exchange

it.q: The Columbian Exchange was
ch: the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world
a treaty between Spain and Portugal
a trade of gold for spices only
it.h: It is named after Columbus because it began after his voyages.

it.q: Which crops first came from the Americas and spread to Europe, Africa and Asia?
it.h: Think of foods first grown by Indigenous farmers in the Americas.

it.q: Which animals came from Europe to the Americas?
The triangular trade linked which three areas?
it.h: Picture three sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

it.q: The Middle Passage was
ch: the voyage that carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas
a road through the Rocky Mountains
it.h: It was the middle side of the triangular trade.

it.q: Describe one positive and one negative effect of the Columbian Exchange.
it.ans: Positive: new foods like potatoes and corn helped feed people around the world. Negative: diseases like smallpox killed millions of American Indians, and the slave trade forced millions of Africans across the ocean.

lessons.u: Unit 2: The Age of Exploration (5.2)
lessons.n: Mapping the voyages: explorers' routes and timelines

it.q: On a map of the voyages, Columbus's 1492 route goes
ch: west across the Atlantic Ocean from Spain
south along the coast of Africa to India
it.h: He wanted to reach Asia by sailing west.

it.q: Vasco da Gama's route to India went
ch: south around the tip of Africa and across the Indian Ocean
west across the Atlantic to Mexico
it.h: Portugal looked for a route around Africa.

it.q: On a map, Magellan's expedition passed from the Atlantic to the Pacific through a narrow strait near
ch: the southern tip of South America
it.h: The strait still carries his name.

it.q: On a timeline, which explorer comes first?
it.h: Find the smallest year.

it.q: Columbus's first voyage was in 1492 and Champlain founded Quebec in 1608. How many years apart are these events?
it.h: Subtract the smaller year from the larger year.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
lessons.n: Jamestown and the Southern Colonies

it.q: The first permanent English settlement in North America was founded in 1607 at
it.h: It was named after King James I.

it.q: Jamestown was paid for by the Virginia Company. What did the company's investors most hope for?
ch: to make a profit from gold, trade or crops
it.h: A company exists to earn money for the people who invest in it.

it.q: Captain John Smith told the Jamestown settlers in 1608 that "he that will not worke shall not eate." Why did he make this rule?
ch: Many settlers were not working, and the colony was running out of food.
The settlers had too much food.
He wanted them to go home.

it.q: Which crop saved Jamestown's economy after John Rolfe began growing it for sale around 1612?
it.h: It was sold in England and smoked in pipes.

it.q: About 500 people lived in Jamestown in the fall of 1609. Only about 60 were alive in the spring of 1610. About how many people died during this "starving time"?
it.h: Subtract the survivors from the starting number.

it.q: Explain why the Powhatan people were important to the survival of Jamestown, and why relations grew tense.
it.ans: The Powhatan traded corn and food that kept settlers alive. Relations grew tense as settlers took more land for tobacco and fought over food and land.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
lessons.n: The New England Colonies

it.q: The Pilgrims sailed to North America in 1620 on the
it.h: The ship's name is also the name of a spring flower.

it.q: Why did the Pilgrims leave England?
ch: to worship in their own way, separate from the Church of England
it.h: Think about religious freedom.

it.q: In the Mayflower Compact (1620), the Pilgrims agreed to "covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic." What does this show?
ch: They agreed to make fair laws and govern themselves.
They agreed to obey only the king.
They agreed to return to England.
it.h: A "civil body politic" is a group that governs itself.

it.q: Tisquantum, also called Squanto, was a Wampanoag man who
ch: helped the Pilgrims plant corn and fish

it.q: The Mayflower carried 102 passengers. About half died during the first winter. About how many passengers survived?
it.h: Find half of 102.

it.q: Explain why the Wampanoag leader Massasoit made an agreement with the Pilgrims in 1621.
it.ans: Disease had weakened the Wampanoag, and Massasoit hoped an alliance with the English would help protect his people from rival nations and bring trade.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
lessons.n: The Middle Colonies

it.q: In 1664, England took over the Dutch colony of New Netherland and renamed it
it.h: It was named after the king's brother, the Duke of York.

it.q: William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681. He was a member of which religious group?
it.h: This group believed in peace and equality.

it.q: Penn called his colony a "holy experiment." What did he mean?
ch: a colony where people of different religions could live together in peace
a colony with one official church
it.h: Think about what Quakers believed about people of other faiths.

it.q: The Middle Colonies were called the "breadbasket colonies" because they
ch: grew large amounts of wheat and other grains
it.h: Bread is made from grain.

it.q: William Penn made treaties and paid for land with which American Indian nation?
Explain why the Middle Colonies were more diverse than New England.
it.ans: They offered religious tolerance and good farmland, so settlers came from the Netherlands, Germany, Sweden, Scotland, Ireland and other places, along with many religious groups.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
lessons.n: Comparing the colonial regions

it.q: Which region had the coldest winters and rockiest soil?
it.h: It is the farthest north.

it.q: Which region relied most on plantation crops grown by enslaved people?
it.h: Think of tobacco, rice and indigo.

it.q: A colonist works in a shipyard building ships from local timber. Which region does the colonist most likely live in?
it.h: Which region had thick forests and many harbors?

it.q: Why did most colonial towns grow along the Atlantic coast and rivers?
ch: Ships could carry people and goods to trade with England and other colonies.
The inland mountains had better soil.
Rivers were too dangerous to use.

it.q: A map shows that Boston is about 300 miles from Philadelphia and Philadelphia is about 200 miles from Williamsburg, Virginia. How many miles is the trip from Boston to Philadelphia to Williamsburg?
it.h: Add the two distances.

it.q: Choose two colonial regions. Compare their climate and how people earned a living.
it.ans: New England had cold winters and rocky soil, so people fished, built ships and traded. The Southern Colonies had a warm climate and rich soil, so planters grew tobacco and rice with enslaved labor.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Founding the Thirteen Colonies (5.4)
lessons.n: Families, children and schools in the early colonies

it.q: Many colonial children learned to read using a wooden paddle with a printed lesson on it called a
it.h: It was covered with a thin, clear layer of animal horn.

it.q: In 1647, Massachusetts passed a law that towns with 50 families must hire a teacher. Why did Puritans care so much about reading?
ch: They wanted everyone to be able to read the Bible.
They wanted children to read newspapers only.
Reading was needed to farm tobacco.
it.h: Think about the Puritans' religious goals.

it.q: An apprentice was
ch: a young person who lived with and learned a trade from a skilled worker
it.h: A boy might learn to be a printer or blacksmith this way.

it.q: In the Southern Colonies, farms and plantations were far apart. How were many wealthy planters' children taught?
ch: by tutors at home or at schools in England

it.q: Describe one way colonial childhood was different from childhood today.
it.ans: Many colonial children worked long hours on farms or as apprentices, had few years of school, and learned from hornbooks instead of many books.
it.h: Think about work, school and chores.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Self-government and the colonial economy

it.q: In a New England town meeting,
ch: local men gathered to discuss and vote on town matters
the king chose the town's leaders
it.h: Think of neighbors meeting in one room to decide together.

it.q: Most colonies had an elected assembly. What did these assemblies do?
ch: made local laws and decided on colonial taxes
it.h: Colonists elected representatives to make decisions for the colony.

it.q: Under mercantilism, colonies existed mainly to
ch: send raw materials to England and buy English goods
make all of their own products
it.h: The home country wanted to grow rich from its colonies.

it.q: The Navigation Acts required colonists to ship many goods only on English ships to English ports. Why did England pass them?
ch: so England would earn the profits from colonial trade
to help the colonists trade with Spain
it.h: Under mercantilism, who should benefit most from trade?

it.q: In 1735, a jury in New York found printer John Peter Zenger not guilty after he printed articles criticizing the governor. This case helped establish
ch: the right to a free education

it.q: Explain how English colonists gained experience in self-government before the American Revolution.
it.ans: They elected assemblies like the House of Burgesses, held town meetings, wrote agreements like the Mayflower Compact and made many local laws, because England was far away.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Religion and the Great Awakening

it.q: The First Great Awakening was
ch: a religious revival that spread through the colonies in the 1730s and 1740s
it.h: "Awakening" suggests people's faith being stirred up.

it.q: George Whitefield, a preacher from England, drew huge crowds during the Great Awakening by
ch: preaching outdoors with powerful, emotional sermons
it.h: Many churches were too small for his crowds.

it.q: Jonathan Edwards was a leader of the Great Awakening who preached in
it.h: He lived in New England.

it.q: The Great Awakening encouraged people to think they could decide on their own faith instead of following church leaders. How did this later affect colonists?
ch: It helped them question authority, including the king.
It made them obey the king more.
it.h: If you can question church leaders, whom else might you question?

it.q: Which group came to Pennsylvania from Germany seeking religious freedom?
ch: many German Protestant groups, such as the Mennonites

it.q: Explain why the colonies had so many different religions by the 1700s.
it.ans: People from many countries came seeking religious freedom, and colonies like Rhode Island, Pennsylvania and Maryland allowed different faiths.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Slavery in the colonies

it.q: Slavery in the English colonies began after enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia in
it.h: It was the same year the House of Burgesses first met.

it.q: Slave codes were
ch: laws that controlled enslaved people and took away their rights
it.h: "Code" here means a set of laws.

it.q: Where did slavery become most widespread in the colonies?
ch: in the Spanish missions of California
it.h: Which region grew cash crops on huge farms?

it.q: Enslaved families kept their cultures alive by
ch: sharing songs, stories, foods and traditions from Africa
it.h: Think about what families pass down to children.

it.q: In 1688, Quakers in Germantown, Pennsylvania, wrote one of the first protests against slavery. What was their main argument?
ch: People should treat others the way they want to be treated.
Slaves should be paid more by the king.

it.q: Describe two ways enslaved Africans resisted slavery.
it.ans: Running away, working slowly, breaking tools, learning to read in secret, keeping African traditions, and armed rebellions such as the Stono Rebellion.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Cooperation and conflict with American Indians

it.q: French traders and many American Indian nations cooperated mainly through the
it.h: Beaver pelts were in great demand in Europe.

it.q: King Philip's War (1675-1676) was a conflict in New England led by the Wampanoag leader
ch: Metacom, called King Philip by the English
it.h: His father was Massasoit, who had made peace with the Pilgrims.

it.q: Why did conflicts often break out between colonists and American Indian nations?
ch: Colonists kept taking more land for farms and settlements.
American Indians wanted to move to Europe.
They had nothing in common to fight over.
it.h: Think about what colonists needed for their growing farms and towns.

it.q: The French and Indian War (1754-1763) was fought between
ch: Great Britain and France, along with their American Indian allies
it.h: Its name in America comes from Britain's enemies in the war.

it.q: The French and Indian War began in 1754 and ended in 1763. How many years did it last?
Give one example of cooperation and one example of conflict between colonists and American Indians.
it.ans: Cooperation: the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims and the French traded furs with many nations. Conflict: the Pequot War, King Philip's War or the Powhatan wars over land.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Benjamin Franklin and new ideas in the colonies

it.q: Benjamin Franklin worked as a
it.h: He started as an apprentice in his brother's print shop.

it.q: Poor Richard's Almanack, which Franklin published starting in 1732, gave readers
ch: weather predictions, calendars and wise sayings
it.h: Farmers liked it for its calendar and advice.

it.q: Franklin's almanac said, "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise." What value does this saying teach?
it.h: Think about the habits it recommends.

it.q: In Philadelphia, Franklin helped start a lending library and a volunteer fire company. What do these show about him?
ch: He believed citizens could work together to improve their community.

it.q: Name one of Franklin's inventions or projects and explain how it helped people.
it.ans: The lightning rod protected buildings from fires caused by lightning; the lending library let ordinary people borrow books they could not afford.
it.h: Think of something that made life safer or easier.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Colonial Life, Cooperation and Conflict (5.3, 5.4)
lessons.n: Spanish and French colonies beside the English

it.q: St. Augustine, founded by Spain in Florida in 1565, is the oldest
ch: continuously settled city founded by Europeans in the United States
it.h: It was founded decades before Jamestown.

it.q: France founded New Orleans in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi River. Why was this location important?
ch: It controlled river trade going in and out of the middle of the continent.
It was on top of a mountain.
It was near the Pacific Ocean.
it.h: Think about the river as a highway.

it.q: Spain built missions and presidios in Florida, New Mexico and Texas. What were its main goals?
ch: to spread Christianity and protect its claims from rivals
it.h: Compare them with the missions in California.

it.q: Santa Fe was founded around 1610 as the capital of Spain's colony of New Mexico. Which present-day city is it?
St. Augustine was founded in 1565 and Jamestown in 1607. How many years older is St. Augustine?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: New taxes and colonial protests

it.q: The Stamp Act of 1765 taxed
ch: newspapers, legal papers and other printed items
it.h: Each paper needed an official stamp showing the tax was paid.

it.q: Colonists protested with the slogan "No taxation without representation." What did they mean?
ch: Parliament should not tax them because they had no elected members in it.
They wanted to pay taxes only to France.
They did not want any government at all.
it.h: Did the colonists elect anyone to Parliament?

it.q: Britain said the colonists should help pay for the French and Indian War and for soldiers protecting them. This was
ch: the British point of view about the new taxes
the American Indian point of view

it.q: A boycott is
ch: refusing to buy certain goods to protest
it.h: Colonists stopped buying British goods to put pressure on merchants.

it.q: The Daughters of Liberty helped the boycotts by
ch: spinning their own cloth instead of buying British cloth
it.h: If you refuse to buy British cloth, how do you get clothes?

it.q: Explain why Britain began taxing the colonies after 1763.
it.ans: Britain had a large debt from the French and Indian War and needed money to pay for soldiers in America, so Parliament decided the colonists should help pay.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: The crisis grows

it.q: On December 16, 1773, colonists dressed as Mohawk Indians dumped British tea into Boston Harbor. This was the
it.h: The event is named after the drink.

it.q: At the Boston Tea Party, colonists dumped 342 chests of tea from 3 ships. If each ship carried the same number of chests, how many chests came from each ship?
it.h: Divide the total chests by the number of ships.

it.q: Parliament punished Boston in 1774 by closing its harbor and limiting town meetings. Colonists called these laws the
it.h: Colonists thought these laws were too harsh to tolerate.

it.q: Committees of Correspondence, started in Boston in 1772,
ch: shared news and plans among towns and colonies by letter

it.q: The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in 1774 to
ch: decide how the colonies should respond to the Intolerable Acts
it.h: The Intolerable Acts had just been passed that year.

it.q: Explain why the Intolerable Acts made other colonies support Massachusetts.
it.ans: Colonists feared Britain could take away their rights and self-government too, so they sent supplies to Boston and united against the acts.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: Declaring independence

it.q: In January 1776, Thomas Paine published a pamphlet that urged independence, called
it.h: Paine argued that independence was simply sensible.

it.q: Thomas Paine wrote in Common Sense (1776): "There is something very absurd, in supposing a continent to be perpetually governed by an island." What was his argument?
ch: It made no sense for small, faraway Britain to rule all of America forever.
it.h: Which is the continent and which is the island?

it.q: The main writer of the Declaration of Independence was
The Declaration of Independence was adopted by the Continental Congress on
it.h: Americans celebrate this date every summer.

it.q: The Declaration says governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed." What does this mean?
ch: A government's power should come from the people's agreement.
Kings get their power from God alone.
People must always obey the government.
it.h: "Consent" means permission or agreement.

it.q: Name the three parts of the Declaration of Independence and tell what each does.
it.ans: A statement of beliefs about rights and government; a list of complaints (grievances) against the king; and a declaration that the colonies are free and independent states.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: Patriots, Loyalists and leaders

it.q: Colonists who supported independence were called
it.h: They loved their country, America.

it.q: Colonists who stayed loyal to the king were called
it.h: The answer comes from the word "loyal."

it.q: Patrick Henry told the Virginia convention in 1775, "Give me liberty, or give me death!" What did he mean?
ch: Freedom was worth risking his life for.
He wanted to stay loyal to the king.
it.h: Which did he value more, freedom or safety?

it.q: King George III believed the colonists
ch: should obey Parliament and pay their share of taxes
it.h: He was the ruler of Great Britain.

it.q: Why did many enslaved African Americans join the British side when Lord Dunmore offered freedom in 1775?
ch: The British promised freedom to those who escaped Patriot owners and fought for Britain.
They wanted to pay British taxes.

it.q: Explain why some colonists became Loyalists.
it.ans: Some were government officials or merchants who depended on trade with Britain, some felt loyalty to the king, and some feared war and disorder.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: Bunker Hill and the siege of Boston

it.q: The Battle of Bunker Hill in June 1775 was mostly fought on nearby
it.h: The battle is named for the hill the colonists first planned to fortify.

it.q: At Bunker Hill the British finally took the hill after several attacks. Why did the colonists still feel encouraged?
ch: They showed they could stand up to the British army and caused heavy British losses.
They won the war that day.
it.h: Compare the number of soldiers each side lost.

it.q: In May 1775, Ethan Allen and Benedict Arnold captured Fort Ticonderoga in New York. What valuable supplies did the Patriots gain there?
it.h: Washington later needed heavy guns to threaten Boston.

it.q: In the winter of 1775-1776, Henry Knox moved the cannons from Ticonderoga about 300 miles to Boston using
ch: sleds pulled by oxen and horses over snow

it.q: The British lost about 1,050 soldiers killed and wounded at Bunker Hill, and the Americans lost about 450. How many more soldiers did the British lose?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 5: The Road to Revolution (5.5)
lessons.n: Cause and effect: from the French and Indian War to independence

it.q: A cause is
it.h: An effect is what happens because of it.

it.q: Britain owed a large debt after the French and Indian War. What was one effect?
ch: Parliament passed new taxes on the colonists.
it.h: Britain needed money.

it.q: Colonists boycotted British goods after the Stamp Act. What was one effect?
ch: Merchants in Britain lost money and Parliament repealed the act.
Britain raised the tax higher right away.
The colonies declared independence that year.
it.h: Who was hurt when colonists stopped buying?

it.q: Which event was a cause of the Intolerable Acts?
Choose one event between 1763 and 1776 and explain one cause and one effect.
it.ans: Boston Tea Party: caused by the Tea Act and anger over taxes without representation; effect: Parliament passed the Intolerable Acts and closed Boston Harbor.
it.h: Ask: why did it happen, and what happened next?

lessons.u: Unit 6: The American Revolution (5.6)
lessons.n: Battles and turning points

it.q: The British army at the start of the war was
ch: larger, better trained and better supplied than the Continental Army
it.h: Britain had one of the strongest armies and navies in the world.

it.q: On the night of December 25, 1776, George Washington led his troops across the Delaware River and won a surprise victory at
it.h: The battle was in New Jersey the morning after Christmas.

it.q: Thomas Paine wrote in The American Crisis (December 1776): "These are the times that try men's souls." Why did he write this?
ch: to encourage discouraged soldiers and Patriots to keep fighting

it.q: The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 is called a turning point because
ch: it convinced France to join the war on the American side
it.h: Think about what happened in 1778 because of this win.

it.q: The Continental Army camped at Valley Forge in the winter of 1777-1778. About 12,000 soldiers arrived, and about 2,000 died of disease, cold and hunger. About how many survived?
it.h: Subtract the soldiers who died from those who arrived.

it.q: Name two advantages the Patriots had in the war, even though the British army was stronger.
it.ans: They fought on familiar land, defended their homes, had a strong leader in George Washington, used hit-and-run tactics, and later had help from France. Britain had to send troops and supplies across an ocean.

lessons.u: Unit 6: The American Revolution (5.6)
lessons.n: Help from other nations and individuals

it.q: Benjamin Franklin went to France during the war to
ch: win French money, supplies and an alliance
it.h: He was a famous and well-liked American in Paris.

it.q: The Marquis de Lafayette was
ch: a young French nobleman who became a general in the Continental Army
it.h: He volunteered and became a close friend of Washington.

it.q: Baron Friedrich von Steuben came from Prussia and helped the Continental Army by
ch: training soldiers to march and fight as a disciplined army
paying all of the army's bills

it.q: Tadeusz Kosciuszko, an engineer from Poland, helped the Patriots by
ch: designing forts and defenses, including those at Saratoga and West Point
being King of Poland in America
it.h: Engineers design and build structures.

it.q: Bernardo de Galvez, the Spanish governor of Louisiana, helped the American cause by
ch: capturing British forts along the Gulf of Mexico
it.h: Louisiana bordered the Gulf of Mexico, where Britain had forts.

it.q: Explain why help from France was so important to the American victory.
it.ans: France sent money, soldiers, weapons and a navy. The French navy trapped the British at Yorktown, which led to the surrender of Cornwallis's army.

lessons.u: Unit 6: The American Revolution (5.6)
lessons.n: Women, African Americans and families in the war

it.q: Abigail Adams wrote to her husband John in 1776, asking him to "Remember the Ladies." What was she asking for?
ch: that the new laws give women more rights
that he buy her new clothes
it.h: John Adams was helping make laws for a new nation.

it.q: Phillis Wheatley was brought from Africa as an enslaved child and became
ch: the first published African American woman poet
it.h: Her book of poems was published in 1773.

it.q: Women helped during the war by
ch: running farms and businesses, making supplies, nursing soldiers and sometimes fighting

it.h: Count the months from October to January.

They wanted to be ruled by France.

it.h: All means every single one.

it.q: Explain two weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation.
it.ans: Congress could not collect taxes, could not regulate trade between states, had no national army or courts, had no President to enforce laws, and needed all 13 states to change the Articles.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

it.h: Its name comes from the document they wrote.

it.h: Fathers help create something. What did Madison create and record?

one house based only on population

Explain why large states and small states disagreed about representation in Congress.
it.ans: Large states wanted representation based on population, giving them more votes. Small states wanted equal votes for every state so they would not be outvoted.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

it.q: The Preamble says the Constitution was written "in Order to form a more perfect Union, establish Justice, insure domestic Tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general Welfare, and secure the Blessings of Liberty." What is the Preamble's purpose?
ch: to state the goals of the government
it.h: The Preamble is the introduction that says why the Constitution was written.

the national government has no power
it.h: "Federal" means national. Who else has power besides the nation?

it.q: Which branch of government includes the Supreme Court?
Give two examples of checks and balances in the Constitution.
it.ans: The President can veto bills; Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote; the Senate approves judges; the Supreme Court can rule that a law is unconstitutional; Congress can remove a President through impeachment.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

ch: it did not include a bill of rights to protect people's freedoms
it made the national government too weak

ch: convince people to ratify the Constitution
describe the French and Indian War
it.h: They were printed in New York newspapers in 1787 and 1788.

Compare the views of the Federalists and the Anti-Federalists.
it.ans: Federalists wanted a strong national government to hold the union together. Anti-Federalists feared it would take away states' power and people's rights, and they demanded a bill of rights.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

it.h: Multiply.

a law passed by a city

gave women the right to vote

lessons.u: Unit 7: Creating the Constitution (5.7)

it.h: Think about what makes a trial fair.

it.h: Look for the word "cruel."

it.q: The Tenth Amendment says powers not given to the national government are reserved to

it.h: Divide.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The New Nation Moves West (5.8, 5.9, 5.3)
lessons.n: Roads, rivers, canals and trails

it.h: These large, flat rafts floated downstream with the current.

ch: Shipping goods between the Midwest and New York City became much cheaper and faster.
It closed New York City's port.

it.q: The Erie Canal was about 363 miles long. A canal boat traveled about 60 miles a day. About how many full days did it take to go 360 miles?
it.h: Divide 360 by 60.

they were sent by the king

ch: cross the western mountains before winter snow

it.q: Compare two ways people traveled west between 1790 and 1850.
it.ans: Flatboats were cheap but went only downstream; steamboats could go upstream; canals like the Erie Canal moved goods cheaply; wagons on roads and trails could go overland but were slow and hard.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The New Nation Moves West (5.8, 5.9, 5.3)

ch: find a water route to the Pacific and learn about the land, plants, animals and peoples

building a fort in St. Louis

Describe two things the Lewis and Clark expedition accomplished.
it.ans: They mapped a route to the Pacific, described hundreds of plants and animals, met and traded with many American Indian nations, and strengthened U.S. claims to the Oregon Country.

lessons.u: Unit 8: The New Nation Moves West (5.8, 5.9, 5.3)

it.h: Divide 4,000 by 16,000 and simplify.

it.q: Explain why the Cherokee are an example of a nation that resisted removal by peaceful means.
it.ans: They had a written language, a newspaper, a constitution and elected leaders like John Ross, and they took their case to the U.S. Supreme Court instead of fighting.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution (6.1)

it.h: The word comes from "art" (skill) and "fact" (made).

it.q: Archaeologists find stone blades, animal bones with cut marks and ash from a fire pit in a cave. What is the best conclusion?
ch: People once used the cave to make tools, cut meat and cook
The cave was used as a farm
People built a city inside the cave
it.h: Each object is a clue. What were people doing with blades, bones and fire?

it.h: Both dates are BCE, so subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

a textbook chapter written last year
a museum website about cave art
a documentary film about the Stone Age
it.h: A primary source was made by people at the time being studied.

it.q: Explain why archaeologists must be careful to record exactly where each artifact was found before removing it.
it.ans: The location and layer tell when the object was used and what it was used with. Once an artifact is moved, that information is lost, so recording it helps scientists understand how people lived.
it.h: What could the position of an object tell you that the object alone cannot?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution (6.1)
lessons.n: Hunter-gatherers and the use of fire and tools

it.q: Paleolithic people who moved from place to place to hunt animals and gather plants are called
it.h: These people did not live in one place all year.

it.q: Why did hunter-gatherers usually live in small groups?
ch: A small area could only feed a few people with wild food
They did not like large families
They had too many crops to share
it.h: Think about how much wild food one area can provide.

it.q: Which was the most important result of learning to control fire?
ch: People could cook food, stay warm and live in colder places
it.h: Think of three ways fire helps people survive.

it.q: Why did hunter-gatherer groups often move with the seasons?
ch: They followed animal herds and ripening plants
They had to pay taxes in different places
They were escaping floods every week

it.q: A group of hunter-gatherers walks 12 kilometers a day for 5 days to reach a winter camp. How many kilometers do they travel?
it.h: Multiply the distance each day by the number of days.

it.q: Describe how men and women in a hunter-gatherer group may have divided work, and explain why sharing work helped the group survive.
it.ans: Many groups divided tasks such as hunting large animals, gathering plants, making tools, caring for children and preparing food. Dividing work let the group do many jobs at once, so everyone was fed and protected.
it.h: List jobs a group needed done every day.

lessons.u: Unit 1: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution (6.1)
lessons.n: The Agricultural Revolution

it.q: The change from hunting and gathering to farming and herding is called the
it.h: Neolithic means New Stone Age, when farming began.

it.q: Taming plants and animals so they can be raised by people is called
it.h: Think of the word "domestic," which means having to do with the home.

it.q: Farming first began more than 10,000 years ago in
ch: the Fertile Crescent of Southwest Asia
it.h: Look for a region of river valleys between Egypt and Mesopotamia.

it.q: What did farming allow people to do that hunting and gathering did not?
ch: Stay in one place and build permanent villages
it.h: Farmers have to tend their fields all season.

it.q: A Neolithic village grew from 150 people to 600 people. How many times larger was the village?
it.h: Divide the new number by the old number.

it.q: Explain why many historians call the beginning of farming a "revolution."
it.ans: It changed nearly every part of life. People settled down, populations grew, villages formed, and people began to own land, store food and do new kinds of work.
it.h: A revolution is a very big change. What changed?

it.q: Why did the first civilizations develop in river valleys?
ch: Rivers provided water and fertile soil for growing extra food
Rivers protected people from all enemies
Mountains in river valleys made farming easy
it.h: What do farmers need most?

it.q: Which list shows the correct order of events?
ch: domesticating plants, building villages, growing cities
growing cities, building villages, domesticating plants
building villages, growing cities, domesticating plants
growing cities, domesticating plants, building villages
it.h: People had to settle down before villages could grow into cities.

it.q: Which job would be found in an early city but NOT in a hunter-gatherer band?
ch: a scribe who kept written records
a person who made stone tools
a person who cared for children

it.h: First change kilometers to meters.

it.ans: With extra food, some people became priests, rulers, merchants or craftspeople instead of farmers. People who controlled land, food or trade gained more wealth and power, creating classes.
it.h: Who controls the extra food?

lessons.u: Unit 1: Early Humans and the Agricultural Revolution (6.1)

it.q: Most scientists agree that modern humans (Homo sapiens) first appeared in

ch: a land bridge often called Beringia

lessons.u: Unit 2: Mesopotamia (6.2)

it.h: Mesopotamia had plenty of river mud.

it.h: They were known as fierce warriors.

it.q: To control conquered lands, Assyrian kings often
ch: forced conquered peoples to move and placed governors over provinces
let every city rule itself freely
it.h: Moving peoples made rebellion harder.

it.q: After Assyria fell, the Chaldeans built the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Its most famous king was
it.h: He rebuilt Babylon in the 500s BCE.

it.q: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon was decorated with
ch: blue glazed bricks showing lions, bulls and dragons

it.q: Assyria's capital Nineveh fell in 612 BCE, and Babylon fell to Persia in 539 BCE. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: The Nile River and Egyptian farming

it.q: Ancient Egypt grew up along which river?
it.h: It is one of the longest rivers in the world.

it.q: The Nile flows from south to north. This means Upper Egypt was in the
it.h: "Upper" means upstream, closer to where the river begins.

it.q: The fan-shaped area of rich land where the Nile meets the Mediterranean Sea is called the
it.h: It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.

it.q: What happened each year when the Nile flooded?
ch: It left a layer of dark, fertile silt on the fields
It washed all the soil into the sea
It turned the river into a desert
it.h: Egyptians called their land Kemet, the "black land."

it.q: A map shows the Nile with a scale of 1 centimeter = 200 kilometers. The river measures about 33 centimeters on the map. About how long is the Nile in kilometers?
it.h: Multiply 33 by 200.

it.q: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about 440 BCE, called Egypt "the gift of the river" (adapted translation). Explain what he meant.
it.ans: Without the Nile, Egypt would be desert. The river's floods brought water and rich soil for farming, and the river was used for travel and trade, so Egypt's whole civilization depended on it.
it.h: What would Egypt be like without the Nile?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: Pharaohs, government and religion

it.q: The rulers of ancient Egypt were called
it.h: The word first meant "great house."

it.q: About 3100 BCE, a king named Menes (also called Narmer) is said to have
ch: united Upper and Lower Egypt into one kingdom
it.h: The pharaoh's double crown showed this event.

it.q: Egyptians believed their pharaoh was
ch: a god-king who kept order in the land
it.h: Religion and government were joined in Egypt.

it.q: Why did Egyptians mummify the dead?
ch: They believed the body was needed in the afterlife
it.h: Think about what Egyptians believed happened after death.

it.q: Egyptian history is divided into the Old Kingdom (about 2686 to 2181 BCE), Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. About how many years did the Old Kingdom last?
it.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

it.q: Describe the Egyptian social pyramid from top to bottom.
it.ans: Pharaoh at the top; then priests and nobles; then scribes and government officials; then artisans and merchants; then farmers, the largest group; enslaved people at the bottom.
it.h: Who had the most power, and which group had the most people?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: Writing, pyramids and achievements

it.q: Egyptian writing that used picture symbols is called
it.h: The word means "sacred carvings."

it.q: Egyptians made a paper-like writing material from
it.h: Our word "paper" comes from its name.

it.q: The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, helped scholars read hieroglyphics because it
ch: had the same text in hieroglyphics, another Egyptian script and Greek
was a dictionary of every language
it.h: Scholars could already read one of the scripts on it.

it.q: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as
ch: a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu
it.h: Old Kingdom pyramids were royal burial places.

it.q: The Great Pyramid was built about 2560 BCE. The Rosetta Stone was carved in 196 BCE. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Both dates are BCE. Subtract.

it.q: Archaeologists found villages near the pyramids with bakeries, workers' tombs and bones of cattle. What does this evidence suggest about who built the pyramids?
it.ans: It suggests the pyramids were built by organized teams of paid and fed workers, including farmers who worked during the flood season, who lived nearby, ate well and were buried with honor.
it.h: Would people bury and feed workers they did not value?

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: The kingdom of Kush

it.q: The kingdom of Kush was located
ch: south of Egypt along the Nile, in Nubia
