it.h: Find the land past the cataracts upstream from Egypt.

it.q: Kush was rich in
ch: gold, ivory, ebony and other trade goods
it.h: These goods came from Africa south of Egypt.

it.q: In the 700s BCE, Kushite kings such as Piye
ch: conquered Egypt and ruled it as pharaohs
it.h: Kush and Egypt traded places as the stronger power.

it.q: The later Kushite capital of Meroe became famous for
it.h: Archaeologists found huge piles of slag there.

it.q: Meroe had more than 200 pyramids, and Egypt has about 120. Using these numbers, how many more pyramids did Meroe have than Egypt?
it.h: Use 200 for Meroe and subtract.

it.q: Explain how Egypt and Kush influenced each other.
it.ans: They traded goods such as gold and grain, fought for control of the Nile, and shared culture: Kushites built pyramids, worshipped some Egyptian gods and used hieroglyphics, and later ruled Egypt as pharaohs.
it.h: Think about trade, war and culture.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: Daily life and trade along the Nile

it.q: Most ancient Egyptians worked as
it.h: Think about what the Nile's soil was used for.

it.q: During the flood season, when farmers could not work their fields, many of them
ch: worked on building projects for the pharaoh
went to school to become priests
it.h: Fields were underwater for months.

it.q: Egypt had few tall trees. From which region along the eastern Mediterranean did Egyptians import cedar wood?
ch: Lebanon, through ports such as Byblos
it.h: The cedar tree is a symbol of this place today.

it.q: Compared with women in many ancient societies, Egyptian women
ch: could own property and take part in business and legal matters
were never allowed to leave home

it.q: An Egyptian worker was paid 10 loaves of bread and 2 jugs of beer each day. How many loaves did he get in a 30-day month?
it.h: Multiply.

lessons.u: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)
lessons.n: The New Kingdom: Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Egypt's empire

it.q: During the New Kingdom, Egypt was strongest because it
ch: built a large empire with a powerful army
it.h: Pharaohs led armies north and south.

it.q: The pharaoh Akhenaten changed Egyptian religion by
ch: worshipping mainly one god, the sun disk Aten
it.h: His name includes the god's name.

it.q: After Akhenaten died, the young pharaoh Tutankhamun
ch: brought back the worship of the traditional gods
it.h: Many people had disliked the change.

it.q: Why is Tutankhamun so famous today when he was a minor pharaoh?
ch: His tomb was found in 1922 with most of its treasures still inside.

it.q: Tutankhamun's tomb was opened in 1922. How many years ago was that from {year}?
it.h: Subtract 1922 from this year.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ancient Israel (6.3)
lessons.n: Origins and beliefs of the Hebrews

it.q: The ancient Hebrews, later called Israelites and Jews, were among the first people to practice
ch: monotheism, the belief in one God
polytheism, the belief in many gods
it.h: Mono means one.

it.q: According to the Hebrew Bible, the founder of the Hebrew people who left Mesopotamia for Canaan was
it.h: Jewish tradition traces the people back to this figure.

it.q: A covenant is
ch: a sacred promise or agreement, which the Hebrews believed they had with God
a written law code from Babylon
it.h: Think of a promise between two sides.

it.q: Canaan, the land where the Hebrews settled, was located
ch: along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea
it.h: Today this area includes Israel, Lebanon and nearby lands.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 100 kilometers. The route from Ur to Canaan through the Fertile Crescent measures about 16 centimeters. About how many kilometers is the route?
it.h: Multiply the map distance by the scale.

it.q: Read this verse from the Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 6:4, King James Version, 1611): "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." What central belief does this verse express, and why was it unusual in the ancient world?
it.ans: It expresses monotheism, the belief in one God. It was unusual because most ancient peoples, such as the Egyptians and Mesopotamians, worshipped many gods.
it.h: Count how many gods the verse names.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ancient Israel (6.3)
lessons.n: Moses, the Exodus and the Ten Commandments

it.q: According to the Hebrew Bible, the leader who led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt was
it.h: The story is told in the book of Exodus.

it.q: The Exodus is
ch: the story of the Israelites' departure from slavery in Egypt
it.h: Exodus means "going out."

it.q: According to the Bible, Moses received the Ten Commandments at
it.h: It is a mountain in the desert between Egypt and Canaan.

it.q: The Jewish festival of Passover remembers
it.h: It is still celebrated each spring.

it.q: In the Jewish way of counting, the Hebrew Bible has 24 books. The first 5 make up the Torah. How many books of the Hebrew Bible are not part of the Torah?
it.h: Subtract the books of the Torah from the total.

it.q: Read these commandments (Exodus 20:13-15, King James Version, 1611): "Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal." Explain how rules like these could help a community live together.
it.ans: They protect people's lives, families and property. If everyone follows them, people can trust one another and live in peace.
it.h: What would a community be like if people broke these rules?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ancient Israel (6.3)
lessons.n: Kings, prophets and the Temple

it.q: The first king of the Israelites, according to the Hebrew Bible, was
it.h: He was followed by David.

it.q: King David is remembered for
ch: making Jerusalem the capital and uniting the tribes
it.h: Jerusalem is sometimes called the City of David.

it.q: King Solomon is known for
ch: his wisdom and for building the First Temple in Jerusalem
leading the Israelites out of Egypt
it.h: The Temple became the center of worship.

it.q: After Solomon died, about 930 BCE, the kingdom split into
ch: Israel in the north and Judah in the south
it.h: The southern kingdom gave the Jews their name.

it.q: Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE. Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 587 BCE. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

it.q: The prophet Micah taught (Micah 6:8, King James Version, 1611): "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" What did the prophets teach people to value?
it.ans: They taught that God wants justice, kindness and humility, so how people treat others matters as much as religious ceremonies.
it.h: Find the three things the verse lists.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ancient Israel (6.3)
lessons.n: Exile, return and the Jewish diaspora

it.q: The Babylonian Exile was the time when
ch: many people of Judah were forced to live in Babylon
it.h: It began after Babylon conquered Jerusalem.

it.q: The scattering of Jews to many lands outside their homeland is called the
it.h: The word comes from a Greek word meaning "scattering."

it.q: In 539 BCE, the Persian king Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon and
ch: allowed the exiles to return to Judah and rebuild the Temple
it.h: Cyrus was known for allowing conquered peoples to keep their religions.

it.q: How did Jews keep their religion during the exile without the Temple?
ch: They gathered to study and pray, read scripture and kept traditions such as the Sabbath
it.h: What can people practice anywhere?

it.q: Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 587 BCE. The Second Temple was completed about 516 BCE. About how many years later was it completed?
it.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

it.q: Explain how the Diaspora helped spread Jewish ideas to other parts of the world.
it.ans: As Jews settled in many lands across the Mediterranean and Middle East, they brought their beliefs, scriptures and laws, and their neighbors learned about monotheism and Jewish ethics.
it.h: Think about what people carry with them when they move.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ancient Israel (6.3)
lessons.n: Ruth, Naomi, Deborah and lasting Jewish teachings

it.q: In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth is remembered for her loyalty to her mother-in-law
it.h: Ruth refused to leave her after both of their husbands died.

it.q: Ruth says to Naomi (Ruth 1:16, King James Version, 1611): "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." What value does this show?
it.h: Think about what Ruth is promising.

it.q: Ruth was a Moabite, not an Israelite, yet the Bible names her as an ancestor of King David. What message might readers take from this?
ch: People from outside a community can be welcomed and honored.
it.h: Think about how Ruth was treated.

it.q: According to the Book of Judges, Deborah was
ch: a prophet and judge who led Israel

it.q: The Book of Ruth has 4 chapters, and the Book of Judges has 21 chapters. How many chapters is that in all?
it.h: Add.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Geography and the rise of city-states

it.q: Greece is a peninsula. This means it is
ch: land surrounded by water on three sides
an island in the middle of the ocean
it.h: Look at a map: water lies to the east, west and south of Greece.

it.q: A Greek city-state was called a
it.h: Our words "politics" and "police" come from this word.

it.q: Why did ancient Greece develop as many separate city-states instead of one kingdom?
ch: Mountains and seas divided the land into small, isolated areas
Greek people spoke many different languages
it.h: Think about how hard it was to travel over mountains.

it.q: Because Greece had little good farmland, many Greeks
ch: became sailors and traders and founded colonies around the Mediterranean
moved to Egypt to become pharaohs
it.h: The sea was all around them.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 25 kilometers. Athens and Sparta are about 6 centimeters apart in a straight line. About how many kilometers apart are they?
it.h: Multiply 6 by 25.

it.q: Explain how the sea shaped the economy and culture of ancient Greece.
it.ans: Greeks traded olive oil, wine and pottery by sea for grain and metals, founded colonies, and spread their culture and borrowed ideas such as the alphabet from other peoples.
it.h: Think about trade, travel and ideas.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Athens, Sparta and democracy

it.q: Democracy comes from Greek words meaning
it.h: Demos means people; kratos means power or rule.

it.q: Athens is known for developing
it.h: Citizens met in an assembly to vote.

it.q: In Athenian direct democracy,
ch: citizens voted on laws themselves in the assembly
a king made all the laws
it.h: Direct means without representatives.

it.q: Who could NOT vote in Athens?
it.h: Citizenship in Athens was limited.

it.q: Historians estimate that Athens had about 30,000 adult male citizens and a total population of about 300,000. What fraction of the population were adult male citizens? Write it as a fraction in lowest terms.
it.h: Divide 30,000 by 300,000 and simplify.

it.q: Describe life for boys in Sparta and explain why Sparta trained them this way.
it.ans: Boys left home at about age 7 to train as soldiers, living in barracks with strict discipline. Sparta needed a powerful army to control the large number of helots (unfree workers) and to defend the city.
it.h: What did Sparta fear, and what did it value most?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: The Persian Wars, the Peloponnesian War and Alexander

it.q: The Persian Wars were fought between
ch: the Greek city-states and the Persian Empire
it.h: Persia was a huge empire to the east.

it.q: At the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE,
ch: the Athenians defeated a larger Persian army
it.h: The modern marathon race is named after this battle.

it.q: The Peloponnesian War (431 to 404 BCE) was fought between
ch: Athens and its allies and Sparta and its allies
it.h: The two most powerful Greek city-states became rivals.

it.q: What was one effect of the Peloponnesian War?
ch: The Greek city-states were weakened, making it easier for Macedonia to conquer them
it.h: Long wars use up soldiers, money and food.

it.q: The Peloponnesian War lasted from 431 BCE to 404 BCE. How many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

it.q: Explain why the Greek victory in the Persian Wars was important for Athens.
it.ans: The victory kept Greece independent and gave Athens confidence and wealth. Athens led an alliance, built a strong navy, and entered a golden age of democracy, art and building such as the Parthenon.
it.h: What did Athens do after the threat was gone?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Greek religion, literature, philosophy and science

it.q: The ancient Greeks believed their many gods lived on
it.h: Zeus was the king of these gods.

it.q: Homer's epic poems about the Trojan War and its hero's journey home are the
it.h: Odysseus is the hero of one of them.

it.q: Greek myths were stories that
ch: explained nature and taught values through gods and heroes
it.h: Many myths explain why things happen in the world.

it.q: Socrates taught by
ch: asking questions that made people examine their beliefs
it.h: This teaching method is still named after him.

it.q: Socrates died in 399 BCE. Aristotle was born in 384 BCE. How many years after Socrates' death was Aristotle born?
it.h: For BCE dates, subtract the smaller number from the larger.

it.q: Aesop's fables, such as "The Tortoise and the Hare," end with a lesson. Explain why the Greeks used short stories like these to teach values.
it.ans: Short stories with animal characters were easy to remember and retell, and the lesson (such as "slow and steady wins the race") taught people how to behave.
it.h: What makes a lesson easy to remember?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Greek art, architecture and theater

it.q: The three main styles of Greek columns are
it.h: One is plain, one has scrolls and one has carved leaves.

it.q: Greek theater began as part of festivals honoring the god
it.h: He was the god of wine and celebration.

it.q: A tragedy was a play that
ch: showed the suffering and downfall of a main character
it.h: Think of the meaning of "tragic."

it.q: Greek theaters were built into hillsides in a half-circle. Why?
ch: so large audiences could see and hear the actors
because the Greeks disliked flat land

it.q: The theater at Epidaurus could seat about 14,000 people. If it was three-quarters full, about how many people were watching?
it.h: Find one quarter first.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Family, women, children and slavery in ancient Greece

it.q: The Greek word oikos referred to
ch: the household, including family members, enslaved people and property
it.h: The word is the root of the English word economy.

it.q: In Athens, most women from citizen families
ch: stayed mostly at home, managing the household
it.h: Athenian democracy was limited to men.

it.q: Enslaved people in Athens were often
ch: prisoners of war or people bought from other lands
it.h: Wars and trade supplied enslaved people.

it.q: In Sparta, enslaved people called helots
ch: farmed the land so Spartan men could train as soldiers

it.q: A historian estimates that an Athenian household had 6 free family members and 2 enslaved workers. What fraction of the household was enslaved? Write in lowest terms.
it.h: Find the total first.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Ancient Greece (6.4)
lessons.n: Pericles and the Golden Age of Athens

it.q: Pericles was
ch: an Athenian leader during the Golden Age in the 400s BCE
it.h: Athens built the Parthenon while he led.

it.q: After the Persian Wars, many city-states joined the Delian League. What was its purpose?
ch: to defend Greece against Persia together
it.h: The Persians might return.

it.q: Athens moved the League's treasury from the island of Delos to Athens and used some of the money for its own buildings. How did other members react?
ch: Many resented Athens, which seemed to be building an empire.
They thanked Athens and gave more.
it.h: Think about whose money it was.

it.q: Pericles began paying citizens who served on juries and in public offices. Why did this matter?
ch: Poorer citizens could afford to take part in government.

it.q: Pericles led Athens from about 461 BCE until his death in 429 BCE. About how many years was that?
it.h: For BCE dates, subtract the smaller number from the larger.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: Geography and the Indus Valley civilization

it.q: The landmass that includes India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal is called a
it.h: It is a large part of a continent, set apart by mountains.

it.q: The highest mountains in the world, which form India's northern border, are the
it.h: Mount Everest is in this range.

it.q: Monsoons are
ch: seasonal winds that bring heavy summer rains
it.h: Farmers in India depended on them for water.

it.q: The early civilization in the Indus River valley built cities such as
it.h: Both cities are in present-day Pakistan.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 50 kilometers. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are about 13 centimeters apart. About how many kilometers apart are they?
it.h: Multiply 13 by 50.

it.q: Explain how monsoons could both help and hurt farmers in ancient India.
it.ans: Monsoon rains watered crops and filled rivers. But if the rains came late or were weak, crops failed, and if they were too heavy, floods destroyed fields and villages.
it.h: Think about too little rain and too much rain.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: Vedic society and the beliefs of Hinduism

it.q: The oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, composed in Sanskrit, are the
it.h: Their name means "knowledge."

it.q: In Vedic society, people were divided into four main social groups called
it.h: These groups became the basis of the caste system.

it.q: Which list shows the four varnas from the highest to lowest rank in Vedic society?
it.h: Priests were at the top.

it.q: The Hindu belief that the soul is reborn into a new body after death is called
it.h: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

it.q: The Rig Veda contains about 1,000 hymns divided into 10 books. If each book had the same number of hymns, how many hymns would each book have?
it.h: Divide 1,000 by 10.

it.q: Explain what the Hindu ideas of dharma and karma mean and how they are connected.
it.ans: Dharma is a person's duty according to their place in life. Karma is the idea that a person's actions bring results in this life or future lives. Fulfilling one's dharma brings good karma and a better rebirth.
it.h: One idea is about duty; the other is about the results of actions.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: Siddhartha Gautama and Buddhism

it.q: The founder of Buddhism was
it.h: He was a prince who gave up his wealth.

it.q: The title "Buddha" means
it.h: Think about what he reached under the tree.

it.q: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man and a dead man. Why did these sights trouble him?
ch: They showed him that all people suffer, even the rich
He had never seen anyone working
He wanted to become a soldier
He was afraid of the monsoon
it.h: What do old age, sickness and death have in common?

it.q: The Buddha taught the Middle Way, which means
ch: avoiding both too much luxury and too much self-denial
living only in the middle of cities
eating only one meal a day
it.h: He had tried both extremes.

it.q: The Buddha's teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. How many teachings are in these two lists combined?
it.h: Add 4 and 8.

it.q: Read this verse from the Dhammapada, a collection of Buddhist teachings (translated by F. Max Muller, 1881): "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Explain this teaching in your own words.
it.ans: Answering hate with more hate only keeps it going. Hatred ends only when people respond with love and kindness.
it.h: What happens when two people keep hurting each other?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: The Maurya and Gupta empires

it.q: The first great empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent was the
it.h: It was founded by Chandragupta Maurya about 321 BCE.

it.q: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga, the emperor Ashoka
ch: became a Buddhist and promised to rule through peace and kindness
it.h: He was horrified by the deaths in the war.

it.q: Ashoka spread his ideas by
ch: carving edicts on rocks and pillars across his empire
it.h: Some of these stone carvings still stand today.

it.q: The Gupta Empire is known as a golden age because of
ch: great achievements in mathematics, science, art and literature
it.h: Golden age means a time of peace and great accomplishment.

it.q: Ashoka ruled from about 268 BCE to about 232 BCE. About how many years did he rule?
it.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

it.q: Ashoka's edicts (adapted translation) say that he felt deep sorrow over the many people killed and taken away in the Kalinga war. How did this change the way he ruled?
it.ans: He turned to Buddhism, gave up wars of conquest, and promoted nonviolence, respect for all religions, care for the sick and kindness to people and animals.
it.h: What did he do differently after the war?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: The Ramayana, the Mahabharata and Indian storytelling

it.q: The Ramayana tells the story of Prince Rama, his wife Sita and
ch: his rescue of Sita from the demon king Ravana
it.h: Rama's ally Hanuman helps him.

it.q: Hanuman, a hero of the Ramayana, is
ch: a loyal monkey leader who helps Rama
it.h: He is famous for his strength and devotion.

it.q: The Bhagavad Gita, part of the Mahabharata, is a conversation between Prince Arjuna and
it.h: Arjuna's charioteer turns out to be a god.

it.q: The Panchatantra is a collection of
ch: animal fables that teach lessons about wisdom and behavior

it.q: The Mahabharata is often said to have about 100,000 verses, and the Ramayana about 24,000. About how many more verses does the Mahabharata have?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Ancient India (6.5)
lessons.n: Trade routes and the spread of Indian ideas

it.q: Seasonal monsoon winds helped sailors cross the Indian Ocean because they
ch: blew in one direction for part of the year and the opposite direction later
it.h: Sailors timed their trips with the winds.

it.q: Which goods from India were wanted in the Roman Empire?
ch: pepper, spices, cotton cloth and precious stones
it.h: Think of spices still used in cooking today.

it.q: Archaeologists have found many Roman coins in southern India. What do they show?
ch: Rome traded with India and paid for goods with gold and silver.
The coins were made in India.
it.h: Coins travel with trade.

it.q: Buddhism spread from India to China mainly along
ch: the Silk Road and sea routes

it.q: A ship sailed 2,800 kilometers from India to Arabia at 140 kilometers a day. How many days did the trip take?
it.h: Divide.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: Geography and the Shang and Zhou dynasties

it.q: Chinese civilization began along the
it.h: The river is named for the color of the soil it carries.

it.q: A dynasty is
ch: a series of rulers from the same family
it.h: The Shang, Zhou and Han are examples.

it.q: The Huang He was called "China's Sorrow" because
ch: its floods often destroyed villages and killed many people
no one could farm near it
it.h: The river brought both rich soil and disaster.

it.q: How did deserts, mountains and the Pacific Ocean affect ancient China?
ch: They isolated China, so it developed its own culture with less outside contact
They made China part of Mesopotamia
They connected China closely to Greece
it.h: Look at what lies on each side of China.

it.q: The Shang dynasty lasted from about 1600 BCE to 1046 BCE. About how many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract 1046 from 1600.

it.q: Shang kings asked questions about the future by carving them on animal bones or turtle shells and heating them until they cracked. What can historians learn from these oracle bones?
it.ans: They contain the earliest Chinese writing and show what Shang rulers worried about, such as harvests, weather, wars and illness, and how they tried to learn the will of their ancestors and gods.
it.h: Think about the writing on the bones and the questions it asks.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism

it.q: Confucius was a teacher who lived from about 551 to 479 BCE. His sayings were collected in the
it.h: His students wrote down his teachings.

it.q: Confucius taught that society would be orderly if
ch: people respected their roles in five key relationships, such as ruler and subject and parent and child
it.h: Think about family and duty.

it.q: Filial piety means
ch: respect and care for one's parents and ancestors
it.h: Filial refers to sons and daughters.

it.q: Daoism, linked to the teacher Laozi, teaches people to
ch: live simply and in harmony with nature and the Dao (the Way)
follow strict laws with harsh punishments
it.h: The Dao means "the Way."

it.q: The Warring States period lasted from 475 BCE to 221 BCE. How many years was that?
it.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger.

it.q: Confucius said (Analects, translated by James Legge, 1861): "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Explain this teaching and give an example of following it.
it.ans: Treat other people the way you want to be treated. For example, if you do not want people to make fun of you, do not make fun of others.
it.h: Think of a time someone treated you in a way you did not like.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: The Qin dynasty unifies China

it.q: The ruler who unified China in 221 BCE and called himself the First Emperor was
it.h: The name China may come from his dynasty's name.

it.q: Qin Shi Huangdi ruled using the ideas of
it.h: He used strict laws and harsh punishments.

it.q: To unify China, the First Emperor standardized
it.h: Standardize means to make the same everywhere.

it.q: Why did Qin Shi Huangdi connect and extend earlier walls into a long wall in the north?
ch: to defend China against attacks by nomadic peoples
to keep the Huang He from flooding
to mark the border with India
to hold back the Pacific Ocean
it.h: Who lived to the north of China?

it.q: Qin Shi Huangdi unified China in 221 BCE and died in 210 BCE. How many years did he rule all of China?
it.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

it.q: Explain why having one standard system of writing helped unify China.
it.ans: People in different regions spoke different languages, but with one writing system officials could send orders, collect taxes and keep records everywhere, and people could share ideas.
it.h: How would officials communicate with distant regions?

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: The Han dynasty and the Silk Road

it.q: The dynasty that ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE is the
it.h: Many Chinese people still call themselves by this dynasty's name.

it.q: Han emperors made Confucianism the official belief of the government and
ch: began choosing some officials by examinations on Confucian learning
it.h: Officials needed to know Confucius' teachings.

it.q: Which invention of the Han dynasty changed how people recorded information?
ch: the printing press with movable metal type
it.h: Before this, Chinese people wrote on bamboo strips and silk.

it.q: The Silk Road was
ch: a network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean
a single paved road in Rome
a wall built by the Han
it.h: It was named for China's most famous export.

it.q: The Silk Road stretched about 6,400 kilometers. A caravan traveled about 32 kilometers a day. About how many days would it take to travel the whole route without stopping?
it.h: Divide the total distance by the distance each day.

it.q: Explain how the Silk Road spread both goods and ideas.
it.ans: Merchants carried silk, paper and other goods west and brought horses, glass and new foods east. Along the way, ideas and religions such as Buddhism spread into China.
it.h: Traders carried more than things to sell.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: Family, farming and daily life in ancient China

it.q: Most people in ancient China were
it.h: China's huge population needed food.

it.q: In northern China, farmers grew mainly millet and wheat. In the warmer, wetter south, they grew mainly
it.h: This crop grows in flooded fields.

it.q: Honoring and remembering family members who have died is called
it.h: Families kept shrines at home for this.

it.q: In a traditional Chinese family shaped by Confucian ideas, who usually had the most authority?
ch: the oldest male, such as the father or grandfather

it.q: A farm family grew 1,500 kilograms of rice and paid 1/5 of it as tax. How many kilograms did they pay?
it.h: Divide by 5.

lessons.u: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
lessons.n: The Great Wall and the northern frontier

it.q: The walls on China's northern border were built mainly to defend against
ch: nomadic peoples from the northern steppes
it.h: These peoples rode horses across the grasslands.

it.q: During the Qin and Han dynasties, the main nomadic group threatening China was the
it.h: Han emperors fought and also made treaties with them.

it.q: Early sections of the wall were made of
it.h: Use materials that were nearby.

it.q: Most of the brick and stone Great Wall that tourists visit today was built much later, during the
A team of workers built 15 meters of wall a week. How many meters could it build in 52 weeks?
it.h: Multiply.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Geography, founding and the Roman Republic

it.q: Rome was built on seven hills beside the
it.h: This river runs through central Italy to the sea.

it.q: According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE by
it.h: The legend says he and his twin brother were raised by a wolf.

it.q: Why was Rome's location on the Italian peninsula an advantage?
ch: It was near the center of the Mediterranean, good for trade and expansion
It was far from any sea
it.h: Look at where Italy sits in the Mediterranean.

it.q: A republic is a government in which
ch: citizens elect leaders to make decisions for them
all citizens vote on every law directly
it.h: The Romans set one up after overthrowing their last king in 509 BCE.

it.q: Rome was founded in 753 BCE, according to legend, and became a republic in 509 BCE. How many years passed between these dates?
it.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

it.q: Explain why the Romans divided power among two consuls who served for only one year.
it.ans: After living under kings, Romans did not want one person to hold too much power. Two consuls could check each other, and short terms kept leaders from becoming tyrants.
it.h: What were the Romans afraid of?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Expansion and the end of the Republic

it.q: The Punic Wars were fought between Rome and
it.h: This city was in North Africa.

it.q: The Carthaginian general Hannibal is famous for
ch: leading an army with elephants across the Alps into Italy
it.h: He surprised Rome by coming over the mountains.

it.q: What was one result of the Punic Wars?
ch: Rome destroyed Carthage and gained control of the western Mediterranean
it.h: The third war ended in 146 BCE.

it.q: Why did conquest cause problems for the Roman Republic?
ch: Wealth went to a few, many small farmers lost their land, and generals gained armies loyal to them
Rome ran out of land to farm
The Senate gave all power to the plebeians
it.h: Think about who gained and who lost from the wars.

it.q: The Punic Wars lasted from 264 BCE to 146 BCE. How many years passed from the start of the first war to the end of the third?
it.h: Subtract 146 from 264.

it.q: Explain why Julius Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon River with his army in 49 BCE was a turning point.
it.ans: Roman law forbade a general from bringing his army into Italy. By crossing, Caesar started a civil war against the Senate, which he won, gaining power that helped end the Republic.
it.h: What did crossing the river with an army mean under Roman law?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: The Roman Empire and the Pax Romana

it.q: The Pax Romana was
ch: about 200 years of relative peace and prosperity in the Roman Empire
a war between Rome and Carthage
it.h: Pax is the Latin word for peace.

it.q: The historian Suetonius (about 121 CE) wrote that Augustus boasted he had found Rome built of brick and left it built of marble. What does this show?
ch: Augustus carried out great building projects
Augustus did not care about buildings
it.h: Marble buildings were grander than brick ones.

it.q: Roman aqueducts were built to
ch: carry fresh water from far away into cities
it.h: Aqua means water.

it.q: Latin, the language of the Romans, developed into
ch: Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian
it.h: These are called Romance languages.

it.q: The Pax Romana lasted from 27 BCE to 180 CE. Counting the BCE years and the CE years separately and adding them, about how many years did it last?
it.h: Add 27 and 180.

it.q: Explain how Roman roads helped hold the empire together.
it.ans: Roads let armies move quickly to defend the borders, let officials and messengers travel, and helped merchants trade, which connected distant provinces to Rome.
it.h: Who and what traveled on the roads?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Christianity and the decline of the Western Empire

it.q: Christianity began in the eastern Mediterranean with the teachings of
it.h: He lived in Judea, which was under Roman rule.

it.q: The Christian Bible's New Testament records Jesus as teaching (Matthew 22:39, King James Version, 1611), "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." This teaching also appears in
it.h: Christianity grew out of Judaism.

it.q: The apostle Paul helped spread Christianity by
ch: traveling around the eastern Mediterranean and writing letters to early Christian communities
it.h: Many of his letters are part of the New Testament.

it.q: Why were early Christians sometimes persecuted by Roman officials?
ch: They refused to worship the Roman gods and the emperor
They refused to pay for roads
it.h: Romans saw worship of the emperor as a sign of loyalty.

it.q: Christianity became legal in the Roman Empire with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, and it became the official religion in 380 CE. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract 313 from 380.

it.q: Explain how Roman roads and the use of a common language helped Christianity spread.
it.ans: Missionaries such as Paul traveled easily on Roman roads and sea routes, and they could preach and write in Greek or Latin, which people across the empire understood.
it.h: How did people and ideas move across the empire?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Daily life in ancient Rome

it.q: In a Roman family, the oldest male, who had great power over the household, was called the
it.h: The Latin word pater means father.

it.q: Most poorer people in the city of Rome lived in crowded apartment buildings called
it.h: The word means islands, because the buildings filled whole blocks.

it.q: Public baths were important in Roman cities because they
ch: were places to bathe, exercise and meet friends
it.h: Few homes had their own running water.

it.q: Wealthy Romans often lived in large houses with an open courtyard and also owned country estates called
An apartment building in Rome had 5 floors with 6 apartments on each floor. How many apartments did it have?
it.h: Multiply.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Roman citizenship, law and the provinces

it.q: A province was
ch: a conquered territory ruled by a Roman governor
it.h: Rome divided its empire into these regions.

it.q: Roman citizens had special rights, such as
ch: the right to a trial and to appeal to higher courts
the right to never pay taxes
the right to own the Senate
it.h: Citizenship protected people in legal cases.

it.q: Over time, Rome gave citizenship to more people in conquered lands. Why?
ch: It won their loyalty and tied them to Rome.
It made them pay no taxes.
it.h: Think about how people feel when they are included.

it.q: In 212 CE, Emperor Caracalla gave citizenship to
ch: nearly all free people in the empire

it.q: A Roman governor collected 900,000 coins in taxes and sent 2/3 of it to Rome. How many coins went to Rome?
it.h: Find one third first.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
lessons.n: Pompeii: a Roman town frozen in time

it.q: In 79 CE, the city of Pompeii was buried by the eruption of
it.h: The volcano stands near the Bay of Naples.

it.q: Pompeii was buried under several meters of volcanic ash and rock. Why does this help archaeologists today?
ch: The ash preserved buildings, objects and paintings almost as they were.
The ash turned everything to gold.
The ash made it easy to rebuild.
it.h: Think about what covering something can protect.

it.q: Pliny the Younger saw the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters about it to the historian Tacitus. What kind of source are these letters?
it.h: He was an eyewitness.

it.q: Pliny described the cloud from the volcano as shaped like a tall pine tree spreading at the top. Why is his description useful to scientists?
ch: It helps them understand how this kind of eruption behaves.
It proves the volcano is in Greece.
It gives the price of bread.

it.q: Pompeii was buried in 79 CE. How many years ago was that from {year}?
it.h: Subtract 79 from this year.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
lessons.n: Why the Western Roman Empire fell

it.q: In which year is the Western Roman Empire usually said to have fallen?
it.h: A Germanic leader removed the last emperor in the West.

it.q: Between 235 and 284 CE, Rome had more than 20 emperors, and many were killed. This is an example of which kind of problem?
it.h: Think about what it means when leaders change very often.

it.q: To pay soldiers, emperors put less silver in coins, so prices rose sharply. Rising prices are called
it.h: The same coin bought less and less.

it.q: Why did Rome begin hiring Germanic soldiers called mercenaries?
ch: Fewer Romans were willing to join the army
it.h: Mercenaries are soldiers who fight for pay, not for their homeland.

it.q: Rome had more than 20 emperors between 235 CE and 284 CE. How many years is that period?
it.h: Subtract 235 from 284.

it.q: Explain why the size of the Roman Empire made it hard to defend.
it.ans: The borders were thousands of kilometers long, so the army was spread thin, troops took a long time to reach trouble spots, and defending them cost huge amounts of money.
it.h: Think about the length of the borders and the cost of soldiers.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
lessons.n: The legacy of Rome

it.q: The language of the Western Roman Empire was
it.h: It was still used by scholars and the Church for centuries.

it.q: After 476 CE, the lands of the Western Empire were divided into
it.h: The peoples who invaded set up their own kingdoms.

it.q: Which institution helped keep Roman learning alive in Western Europe after Rome fell?
ch: the Christian Church, whose monks copied old books
it.h: Monasteries had libraries.

it.q: The Roman Empire's borders reached as far north as
it.h: Hadrian's Wall was built there.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 250 kilometers. The Roman Empire's border along the Rhine and Danube rivers measures about 16 centimeters. About how many kilometers long was that border?
it.h: Multiply 16 by 250.

it.q: Name two parts of Roman culture that survived after the fall of the Western Empire and explain how they still affect us.
it.ans: Latin became the basis of Romance languages and many English words; Roman law shaped legal systems; Roman architecture with arches and domes; the Christian Church that grew in the empire.
it.h: Think about language, law, buildings and religion.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
lessons.n: The Byzantine Empire and Justinian

it.q: The capital of the Byzantine Empire was
it.h: It is now the city of Istanbul in Turkey.

it.q: Why was Constantinople's location valuable?
ch: It controlled trade routes between Europe and Asia and was easy to defend by water
It was in the middle of a desert
It was far from any trade route
It was on the Atlantic coast
it.h: The city sits on a strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.

it.q: Justinian is known for
ch: organizing Roman laws into one code and rebuilding the Hagia Sophia
it.h: His code later influenced many European legal systems.

it.q: The main language of the Byzantine Empire was
it.h: The eastern Mediterranean had long been influenced by Greece.

it.q: Justinian ruled from 527 CE to 565 CE. How many years did he rule?
it.h: Subtract 527 from 565.

it.q: During a riot in 532 CE, the historian Procopius reports that Empress Theodora refused to flee, saying (translated by H. B. Dewing, 1914) "royalty is a good burial-shroud." What did she mean, and why was her decision important?
it.ans: She meant it was better to die as a ruler than to run away. Her courage convinced Justinian to stay; the riot was crushed, and he kept his throne.
it.h: A shroud is a cloth used to wrap the dead.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
lessons.n: The Eastern Orthodox Church and the fall of Constantinople

it.q: The branch of Christianity that developed in the Byzantine Empire is the
it.h: Its leader was the patriarch of Constantinople.

it.q: Icons are
ch: religious images of Jesus, Mary and the saints
it.h: Some Byzantines argued about whether they should be used in worship.

it.q: In 1054, the Christian Church split into the Roman Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church. This split is called the
it.h: Schism means a split.

it.q: Which was one disagreement between the Church in Rome and the Church in Constantinople?
ch: whether the pope had authority over all Christians
it.h: The patriarch did not accept the pope as the leader of all Christians.

it.q: The Great Schism happened in 1054. Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract 1054 from 1453.

it.q: Compare the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches in leader, language and location.
it.ans: Catholic: led by the pope in Rome, used Latin, strongest in Western Europe. Orthodox: led by patriarchs, especially in Constantinople, used Greek, strongest in the Byzantine Empire and Eastern Europe.
it.h: Make a chart with three rows.

lessons.u: Unit 1: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire (7.1)
lessons.n: Daily life, trade and art in Byzantine Constantinople

it.q: The Hippodrome in Constantinople was a huge arena used mainly for
it.h: Fans cheered for teams called the Blues and the Greens.

it.q: Byzantine artists decorated churches with pictures made from small pieces of colored glass and stone. These are called
it.h: The church of San Vitale in Ravenna has famous ones of Justinian and Theodora.

it.q: According to the historian Procopius, about 552 CE monks smuggled silkworm eggs from Asia to Constantinople. Why was this important?
ch: The Byzantines could make their own silk instead of buying it all from China.
It caused the fall of Rome.
it.h: Silk was one of the most valuable goods of the time.

it.q: Byzantine sailors defended Constantinople with "Greek fire." What was it?
ch: a burning liquid that kept burning even on water

it.q: A Byzantine silk merchant bought 40 bolts of silk for 6 solidi each and sold them for 9 solidi each. How many solidi of profit did he make?
it.h: Find the profit on one bolt first.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: Arabia and the beginnings of Islam

it.q: Islam began in the early 600s CE on the
it.h: This large peninsula lies between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

it.q: Much of Arabia is desert. Where could people settle and farm?
ch: at oases, where underground water reaches the surface
it.h: Think of a green spot in the desert.

it.q: Many Arabs were Bedouins. Bedouins were
ch: nomadic herders who moved with their camels, sheep and goats
it.h: They moved to find water and grazing land.

it.q: Before Islam, Mecca was important because it was
ch: a center of trade and the site of the Kaaba, a shrine visited by pilgrims
the capital of the Roman Empire
the home of the Byzantine emperor
it.h: Caravans and pilgrims both came to the city.

it.q: A camel caravan travels about 40 kilometers a day. How many days does it take to cross 480 kilometers of desert?
it.h: Divide the distance by the distance per day.

it.q: Explain how Arabia's location helped Mecca become a trade center.
it.ans: Arabia lies between Africa, Asia and Europe, and caravan routes carrying spices, incense and other goods between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean passed through Mecca.
it.h: Look at which continents and seas surround Arabia.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: Beliefs and practices of Islam

it.q: The holy book of Islam is the
it.h: Muslims believe it contains God's revelations to Muhammad.

it.q: The Arabic word for God, used by Muslims, is
it.h: Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use the same word.

it.q: The Five Pillars of Islam are
ch: five basic duties of Muslim life
it.h: Pillars hold up a building.

it.q: Which list names three of the Five Pillars?
ch: declaring faith, daily prayer and charity
pilgrimage to Rome, prayer and fasting
it.h: The others are fasting during Ramadan and the pilgrimage to Mecca.

it.q: Muslims are expected to pray 5 times each day. How many prayers is that in one week?
it.h: Multiply 5 by 7.

it.q: Explain how Islam is connected to Judaism and Christianity.
it.ans: All three are monotheistic and trace their roots to Abraham. Muslims honor many of the same prophets, including Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and call Jews and Christians "People of the Book."
it.h: Think about belief in one God and shared prophets.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: The spread of Islam and the caliphates

it.q: A leader of the Muslim community after Muhammad was called a
it.h: The word means successor.

it.q: Muslims disagreed about who should lead after Muhammad. This led to the division between
it.h: One group believed leaders should come from Muhammad's family through Ali.

it.q: Within about 100 years of Muhammad's death, Muslim rule stretched from
ch: Spain in the west to the Indus River in the east
it.h: Look at a map showing the empire around 750 CE.

it.q: The Umayyad caliphs made their capital in
it.h: This city is in present-day Syria.

it.q: Muhammad died in 632 CE. Muslim armies entered Spain in 711 CE. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract 632 from 711.

it.q: Give two reasons Muslim rule spread so quickly.
it.ans: The Byzantine and Persian empires were weakened by long wars with each other; Muslim armies were united and skilled; many conquered people were allowed to keep their religion and customs; trade and the Arabic language connected the lands.
it.h: Think about the strength of the Muslims and the weakness of their neighbors.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: Trade and achievements of the Muslim world

it.q: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad was
ch: a center where scholars translated and studied books from many cultures
a royal palace for the caliph
it.h: Scholars there translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic.

it.q: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book that gave its name to
it.h: Part of his book's title was "al-jabr."

it.q: The doctor Ibn Sina wrote a medical encyclopedia that was
ch: used in European universities for centuries
lost right after he wrote it
it.h: In Latin it was called the Canon of Medicine.

it.q: Muslim scholars helped spread the numerals 0 to 9 from India to
it.h: Europeans called them Arabic numerals.

it.q: Ibn Battuta traveled for about 29 years, from 1325 to 1354. If he traveled about 4,000 kilometers each year, about how many kilometers did he travel in all?
it.h: Multiply 29 by 4,000.

it.q: Explain why Muslim scholars' translations of Greek works were important for later Europe.
it.ans: They preserved and added to the works of Greek thinkers such as Aristotle. Later, these works were translated into Latin, and European scholars used them, which helped lead to the Renaissance.
it.h: What might have happened to these books otherwise?

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: Al-Andalus: Muslim Spain and Cordoba

it.q: In 711 CE, Muslim forces from North Africa crossed into Spain. The Muslim-ruled lands of the Iberian Peninsula were called
it.h: The name lives on in the Spanish region of Andalusia.

it.q: The name Gibraltar comes from the Arabic Jabal Tariq. What does it honor?
ch: Tariq ibn Ziyad, the commander who led forces across the strait
it.h: Jabal means mountain.

it.q: In 756 CE, Abd al-Rahman, a survivor of the Umayyad family, set up a new state with its capital at
it.h: The Abbasids had overthrown his family in the east.

it.q: The scholar Ibn Rushd (Averroes), born in Cordoba in 1126, is famous for
ch: writing commentaries on Aristotle that later influenced European scholars

it.q: Muslim forces entered Spain in 711, and the last Muslim kingdom, Granada, fell in 1492. How many years is that?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 2: Islam in the Middle Ages (7.2)
lessons.n: Cities, architecture and daily life in the Muslim world

it.q: The tall tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given, is a
it.h: The muezzin calls Muslims to prayer from it.

it.q: Inside a mosque, a niche in the wall called the mihrab shows
ch: the direction of Mecca for prayer
it.h: Muslims face Mecca when they pray.

it.q: Islamic religious buildings are often decorated with geometric patterns, flowing plant designs and Arabic calligraphy rather than pictures of people. Why?
ch: Many Muslims believed religious art should avoid images of people and animals.
it.h: Think about beliefs about worship and images.

it.q: A covered market in a Muslim city, with many shops grouped by trade, is often called a
A merchant in a souk sold 45 rugs at 12 dinars each. How many dinars did he receive?
it.h: Multiply.

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: Reunification under the Sui and Tang

it.q: After more than 350 years of division, China was reunified in 589 CE by the
it.h: This short dynasty came just before the Tang.

it.q: The Grand Canal, built mainly under the Sui, connected
ch: the Huang He in the north with the Chang Jiang (Yangtze) in the south
it.h: It linked the two great river systems.

it.q: Why was the Grand Canal so important?
ch: It let rice and other goods from the south be shipped north to the capital and armies
It was used only for festivals
It brought water to the Gobi Desert
it.h: The south grew more food; the government was in the north.

it.q: During the Tang dynasty, the government expanded the civil service examinations so that
ch: more officials were chosen for their knowledge of Confucian texts
it.h: Exams tested what officials had studied.

it.q: The Tang dynasty ruled from 618 to 907 CE. How many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract 618 from 907.

it.q: Explain why the Sui dynasty fell quickly even though it reunified China.
it.ans: It forced millions of people to work on huge projects such as the Grand Canal and fought costly wars, which made people angry and led to rebellions.
it.h: Think about the costs of its great projects.

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: The Song dynasty: trade, cities and inventions

it.q: The Song dynasty ruled China from
it.h: It came after a time of division following the Tang.

it.q: A fast-ripening rice from Southeast Asia helped Song farmers
ch: grow two crops a year, so food supplies and population grew
it.h: More harvests mean more food.

it.q: Which Chinese invention made long ocean voyages safer?
it.h: It always points north and south.

it.q: Paper money developed in Song China because
ch: carrying heavy strings of metal coins was difficult for merchants
there was no metal in China
it.h: Think about trade involving large amounts of money.

it.q: Bi Sheng developed movable type in the 1040s. Johannes Gutenberg developed his movable-type printing press in Europe about 1450. Using 1045 for Bi Sheng, about how many years earlier was Bi Sheng's invention?
it.h: Subtract 1045 from 1450.

it.q: Explain how improvements in farming led to the growth of cities and trade in Song China.
it.ans: New rice and better farming produced more food, so fewer people had to farm. The population grew, people moved to cities, and merchants traded surplus goods, helped by canals and paper money.
it.h: Follow the chain from food to people to cities.

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: The Mongols and the Yuan dynasty

it.q: The Mongols were
ch: nomadic herders from the grasslands north of China
it.h: They lived on the steppe and were expert riders.

it.q: The leader who united the Mongols and began their conquests in the early 1200s was
it.h: His title means "universal ruler."

it.q: Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai Khan conquered China and founded the
it.h: It was the first time all of China was ruled by foreigners.

it.q: Why were Mongol armies so successful?
ch: They were skilled horse archers who moved fast and were very well organized
They had the largest navy in the world
it.h: Think about their life on horseback.

it.q: The Yuan dynasty ruled China from 1271 to 1368. How many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract 1271 from 1368.

it.q: Explain how the Mongol Empire made travel and trade across Asia easier.
it.ans: The Mongols controlled lands from China to Eastern Europe, kept the Silk Road safe, and set up relay stations, so merchants, travelers and ideas could move across the continent.
it.h: What happens when one empire controls an entire trade route?

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zheng He

it.q: In 1368 a rebellion drove out the Mongols and founded the
it.h: Its name means "brilliant."

it.q: The Forbidden City in Beijing was
ch: the huge palace complex of the Ming emperors
it.h: Ordinary people could not enter.

it.q: Zheng He was a Ming admiral who
ch: led seven great voyages to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa
it.h: His fleets sailed between 1405 and 1433.

it.q: Ming emperors rebuilt and strengthened the Great Wall to
ch: protect China from attacks from the north
it.h: The Mongols and other northern peoples were still a threat.

it.q: Zheng He's voyages took place from 1405 to 1433. How many years passed from the first voyage to the last?
it.h: Subtract 1405 from 1433.

it.q: Explain the purpose of Zheng He's voyages.
it.ans: They showed the power and wealth of the Ming, collected tribute from foreign rulers, encouraged trade and brought back gifts such as giraffes and rare goods.
it.h: Think about showing power and gaining tribute.

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: China's neighbors: Korea, Vietnam and the spread of Chinese culture

it.q: Korea and Vietnam both borrowed from China
ch: Confucian ideas, Chinese characters and Buddhism
it.h: Think of China's ideas about government, writing and religion.

it.q: The English name "Korea" comes from the Goryeo dynasty, which ruled from 918 to 1392. Goryeo potters became famous for
it.h: Its color is like jade.

it.q: In the 1400s, King Sejong of Korea introduced Hangul. What was it?
ch: a simple alphabet for writing the Korean language
it.h: Chinese characters were very hard for ordinary people to learn.

it.q: Vietnam was ruled by China for about a thousand years. In 939 CE, Vietnam
Goryeo ruled Korea from 918 to 1392. How many years did the dynasty last?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 3: China in the Middle Ages (7.3)
lessons.n: Sea trade and the ports of medieval China

it.q: Large Chinese wooden sailing ships of this period are often called
it.h: They had sails made of mats stiffened with bamboo.

it.q: Chinese ships were divided inside by walls into watertight compartments. Why was this useful?
ch: If one part was damaged, water would not flood the whole ship.
It made ships faster on land.
it.h: Think about what happens when a ship's hull gets a hole.

it.q: The southern port of Quanzhou, called Zayton by foreign visitors, was famous for
ch: trade with merchants from India, Arabia and Southeast Asia
it.h: Marco Polo described it as a great port.

it.q: Which goods did China export most by sea?
A ship carried 12,000 porcelain bowls packed in crates of 50. How many crates were there?
it.h: Divide.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
lessons.n: Geography and the trans-Saharan trade

it.q: The largest hot desert in the world, which covers much of northern Africa, is the
it.h: Its name comes from the Arabic word for desert.

it.q: The strip of dry grassland just south of the Sahara is called the
it.h: Its name means "shore" or "edge" in Arabic.

it.q: The major river of West Africa that helped trade and farming is the
it.h: It curves through Mali.

it.q: Which animal made regular trade across the Sahara possible?
it.h: It can travel many days without water.

it.q: A caravan crosses about 1,500 kilometers of the Sahara at about 30 kilometers a day. How many days does the crossing take?
it.h: Divide 1,500 by 30.

it.q: Explain why salt was so valuable in West Africa that it was sometimes traded for gold.
it.ans: People in the hot south needed salt to stay healthy and to preserve food, but there was little salt there. Salt came from mines in the Sahara, so it was scarce and in great demand.
it.h: Think about where salt came from and why people needed it.

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
lessons.n: The empire of Ghana

it.q: The empire of Ghana was located
ch: in West Africa, between the Senegal and Niger rivers
in the same place as the modern country of Ghana
in North Africa on the Mediterranean
it.h: The modern country took the name but is farther south and east.

it.q: Ghana's kings grew rich mainly by
ch: taxing gold and salt that passed through their lands
it.h: Every load of goods paid a tax.

it.q: The king of Ghana controlled the supply of gold nuggets, while gold dust could be traded. Why?
ch: to keep gold scarce so its value stayed high
to give gold away for free
it.h: What happens to the price of something when there is too much of it?

it.q: Ghana's capital, Koumbi Saleh, had two towns: one for the king and one for
ch: Muslim merchants, which had several mosques
it.h: Muslim traders from North Africa lived there.

it.q: The Arab geographer al-Bakri wrote in 1068 that the king of Ghana collected 1 gold dinar for each donkey-load of salt brought into the country. How many dinars would the king collect on 240 donkey-loads?
it.h: One dinar for each load.

it.q: Al-Bakri never visited Ghana himself; he wrote in Spain using reports from travelers. How should a historian use his description?
it.ans: It is valuable because it is one of the few written sources about Ghana, but it is secondhand, so historians should compare it with archaeology and oral traditions.
it.h: Is it a firsthand or secondhand account?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
lessons.n: Mali and Mansa Musa

it.q: The founder of the empire of Mali, remembered in a famous epic, was
it.h: Griots still tell the story of his life.

it.q: The title "mansa" in Mali meant
it.h: Mansa Musa was the most famous one.

it.q: Mali grew larger and richer than Ghana partly because it
ch: controlled more gold fields and trade cities along the Niger River
it.h: Look at the cities of Timbuktu and Gao on the river.

it.q: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 is famous because he
ch: brought so much gold that he spent and gave away enough in Cairo to lower its value there
it.h: Too much gold in one place lowers its value.

it.q: Mansa Musa ruled from about 1312 to about 1337. About how many years did he rule?
it.h: Subtract 1312 from 1337.

it.q: Explain why Mansa Musa's pilgrimage made Mali famous in North Africa, Southwest Asia and Europe.
it.ans: His huge caravan and generous spending of gold in Cairo and Mecca were reported by writers, and his image appeared on European maps, showing the world that Mali was rich and powerful.
it.h: Who saw or heard about his journey?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
lessons.n: Islam, learning and oral tradition

it.q: Storytellers in West Africa who preserve history through spoken words and music are called
it.h: They memorized long histories and family lines.

it.q: Islam spread to West Africa mainly through
ch: Muslim traders who crossed the Sahara
it.h: Trade routes also carried ideas.

it.q: Timbuktu became famous as
ch: a center of Islamic learning with mosques, scholars and thousands of manuscripts
it.h: Scholars came to study there.

it.q: Many rulers of Mali became Muslims, while many ordinary people
ch: kept their traditional religious beliefs or blended them with Islam
it.h: Religious change often happened first among rulers and merchants.

it.q: The Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu was built in 1327. How many years ago was that from {year}?
it.h: Subtract 1327 from {year}.

it.q: Explain why oral tradition is an important source for West African history.
it.ans: Much history was passed down by griots rather than written, so oral traditions preserve stories, family lines, laws and values, such as the Epic of Sundiata, that would otherwise be lost.
it.h: How was history kept if few people wrote it down?

lessons.u: Unit 4: Ghana, Mali and West Africa (7.4)
lessons.n: Songhai: the last great West African empire

it.q: The Songhai Empire had its capital at
it.h: The capital was on the river, east of Timbuktu.

it.q: Sunni Ali, who ruled Songhai from 1464 to 1492, is remembered for
ch: conquering Timbuktu and Djenne and building a large empire
making a pilgrimage with tons of gold
it.h: He was a powerful military leader.

it.q: Askia Muhammad, who ruled from 1493, made Songhai a center of Islamic learning and
it.h: Like Mansa Musa before him, he traveled to a holy city.

it.q: In 1591, an army from Morocco defeated Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi. Which advantage did the Moroccans have?
Sunni Ali ruled from 1464 to 1492, and Askia Muhammad ruled from 1493 to 1528. How many more years did Askia Muhammad rule?
it.h: Find each length first.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
lessons.n: Geography and early influences from China and Korea

it.q: Japan is an archipelago, which means it is
it.h: Japan has four main islands and thousands of smaller ones.

it.q: The largest island of Japan is
it.h: Tokyo and Kyoto are on this island.

it.q: Most of Japan's land is mountainous. How did this affect where people lived?
ch: Most people lived and farmed on narrow coastal plains and in river valleys
People could not farm at all
it.h: Where is flat land found?

it.q: Japan is close to Korea and China. How did this location affect early Japan?
ch: It allowed Japan to borrow ideas such as Buddhism, writing and government from China and Korea
It made Japan part of China
It kept Japan from all contact
It caused Japan to conquer China
it.h: The sea was narrow enough to cross but wide enough to protect.

it.q: A map scale shows 1 centimeter = 50 kilometers. The narrowest crossing between Japan and Korea measures about 4 centimeters. About how many kilometers is it?
it.h: Multiply 4 by 50.

it.q: Explain how the sea both connected and protected Japan.
it.ans: Japan was close enough for envoys, monks and traders to bring ideas from Korea and China, but the sea made invasion difficult, so Japan could choose what to borrow and keep its own culture.
it.h: Think about both ideas and armies crossing the sea.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
lessons.n: The Heian court

it.q: In 794 CE the imperial capital moved to Heian-kyo, a city now called
it.h: It was the capital for more than 1,000 years.

it.q: The Heian period is known for
ch: the refined art, poetry and manners of the emperor's court
it.h: Nobles at court valued beauty and elegance.

it.q: The Tale of Genji, often called one of the world's first novels, was written by
it.h: She was a lady at the Heian court.

it.q: Why were women at the Heian court able to write many famous works?
ch: They often wrote in kana, the Japanese script, and had time and education at court
They were the only people who could read Chinese
Men were not allowed to write
it.h: Men at court usually wrote in Chinese; women often wrote in Japanese.

it.q: The Heian period lasted from 794 to 1185. How many years did it last?
it.h: Subtract 794 from 1185.

it.q: The Pillow Book by Sei Shonagon lists things she found beautiful or annoying at court. Why is it a valuable primary source?
it.ans: It gives a firsthand, personal view of daily life, manners and values at the Heian court, written by someone who lived there.
it.h: Who wrote it, and when?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
lessons.n: Shoguns, daimyo and samurai

it.q: The supreme military ruler of Japan, who held real power while the emperor remained a figurehead, was the
it.h: Minamoto Yoritomo received this title in 1192.

it.q: Professional warriors who served lords in feudal Japan were the
it.h: Their name means "those who serve."

it.q: Daimyo were
ch: powerful landowning lords who had samurai armies
it.h: They ruled their own lands under the shogun.

it.q: Bushido, the samurai code, stressed
it.h: Bushido means "the way of the warrior."

it.q: Minamoto Yoritomo became shogun in 1192. The Mongols invaded Japan in 1274. How many years later was the first Mongol invasion?
it.h: Subtract 1192 from 1274.

it.q: Describe the structure of feudal Japanese society from top to bottom.
it.ans: The emperor at the top had little real power; the shogun held military power; daimyo ruled lands; samurai served the daimyo; peasants farmed, then artisans and merchants, who were ranked lowest even if wealthy.
it.h: Think about who had the title and who had the power.

lessons.u: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
lessons.n: Religion, arts and the samurai way of life

it.q: The form of Buddhism that stresses meditation and self-discipline and appealed to many samurai is
it.h: Its name comes from a word meaning meditation.

it.q: Why did Zen appeal to samurai?
ch: Its focus on discipline, calm and concentration helped them in training and battle
It required them to give up fighting
it.h: What does a warrior need in battle?

it.q: Pure Land Buddhism became popular with ordinary people because it taught that
ch: anyone could reach paradise through faith in the Amida Buddha
meditation required years in a monastery
it.h: It offered a simple path to salvation.

it.q: The Japanese tea ceremony is
ch: a quiet ritual of preparing and serving tea that reflects Zen values of simplicity and calm
a festival for the emperor's birthday
it.h: Every movement is done carefully and simply.

it.q: A traditional haiku poem has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables. How many syllables does it have in all?
it.h: Add the three numbers.

it.q: Explain how Shinto and Buddhism existed side by side in Japan.
it.ans: Many people honored the kami at Shinto shrines for life events and nature, and followed Buddhist teachings about suffering and the afterlife; some shrines and temples were even built together.
it.h: Did people have to choose only one?

lessons.u: Unit 5: Medieval Japan (7.5)
lessons.n: Unifying Japan: Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu

it.q: The time of near-constant war among daimyo in Japan from the late 1400s to the late 1500s is called the
it.h: Lords fought each other for land and power.

it.q: Portuguese traders who reached Japan in 1543 brought
it.h: These weapons changed Japanese warfare.

it.q: Oda Nobunaga used soldiers with guns firing in turns at the Battle of Nagashino in 1575. What does this show?
ch: He adopted new technology to defeat his rivals.
it.h: Think about why taking turns firing would help.

it.q: Toyotomi Hideyoshi ordered a "sword hunt" in 1588. What did it do?
Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, and his family ruled until 1867. How many years did the Tokugawa shogunate last?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: Geography and the early Middle Ages

it.q: The period in Europe from about 500 to 1500 CE is called the
it.h: It comes between ancient times and modern times.

it.q: Which geographic feature helped trade in medieval Europe?
ch: many navigable rivers and seas close to most land
it.h: Look at the rivers such as the Rhine and Danube on a map.

it.q: After Rome fell, which group brought Christianity to many peoples in Northern Europe?
ch: missionaries, including monks sent by the pope
it.h: Ireland and England were reached by these religious travelers.

it.q: The Frankish king crowned emperor by the pope on Christmas Day in 800 CE was
it.h: His name means "Charles the Great."

it.q: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800 CE and died in 814 CE. How many years did he rule as emperor?
it.h: Subtract 800 from 814.

it.q: Explain why the pope crowning Charlemagne in 800 was important.
it.ans: It joined the power of the Church with the power of a Christian king, showed the pope's authority to crown rulers and created the idea of a new Western empire after Rome.
it.h: Think about Church power and royal power together.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: Feudalism and the manor

it.q: Feudalism was a system in which
ch: lords gave land to vassals in exchange for loyalty and military service
it.h: Land was traded for service.

it.q: A piece of land granted by a lord to a vassal was called a
it.h: The word is related to "feudal."

it.q: Serfs were
ch: peasants bound to the land who worked for the lord and could not leave without permission
it.h: They were not enslaved, but they were not free either.

it.q: A manor was
ch: a lord's estate with fields, a village, a mill and a church that produced most of what people needed
a city with walls and merchants
it.h: Manors were nearly self-sufficient.

it.q: A serf had to work 3 days a week in the lord's fields. How many days is that in 12 weeks?
it.h: Multiply 3 by 12.

it.q: Explain how feudalism provided protection in a time of invasions.
it.ans: Kings could not defend every area, so they gave land to lords, who gave land to knights; knights defended the lord's land and peasants, and peasants farmed in exchange for protection.
it.h: Who protected whom, and what did each group give?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: Church and kings: power, law and the Magna Carta

it.q: The leader of the Roman Catholic Church is the
it.h: He lived in Rome.

it.q: Excommunication meant
ch: being cut off from the Church and its sacraments
it.h: Medieval people believed this could cost them their salvation.

it.q: In 1077, Emperor Henry IV stood in the snow at Canossa to ask Pope Gregory VII for forgiveness. What does this show?
ch: The pope had great power, even over emperors
it.h: Who had to ask whom for forgiveness?

it.q: The Magna Carta, signed by King John of England in 1215,
ch: limited the power of the king and protected certain rights of nobles and free men
it.h: Nobles forced the king to agree.

it.q: The Magna Carta was signed in 1215. The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787. How many years apart were these documents?
it.h: Subtract 1215 from 1787.

it.q: The Magna Carta (1215, adapted translation) says that no free man shall be imprisoned or have his property taken "except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land." Explain why this idea was important.
it.ans: It meant even the king had to follow the law and could not punish people without a fair legal process, which became the basis for ideas such as trial by jury and due process.
it.h: Who else besides ordinary people had to follow the law?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: The Crusades and the Reconquista

it.q: The Crusades were a series of
ch: military expeditions by European Christians to win control of the Holy Land
it.h: They began in 1096.

it.q: In 1095, Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade to
ch: take control of Jerusalem and help the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks
it.h: The Byzantine emperor had asked for help.

it.q: Jerusalem is a holy city to
it.h: Think about the three religions that trace their roots to Abraham.

it.q: Salah al-Din (Saladin) is remembered for
ch: retaking Jerusalem in 1187 for the Muslims
it.h: He was a Muslim leader of Egypt and Syria.

it.q: The First Crusade began in 1096. The last Crusader stronghold, Acre, fell in 1291. How many years passed?
it.h: Subtract 1096 from 1291.

it.q: Explain one way the Crusades affected trade in Europe.
it.ans: Crusaders and merchants brought back goods such as spices, sugar and silk, which increased demand for trade with the eastern Mediterranean and helped Italian cities such as Venice and Genoa grow rich.
it.h: What did crusaders bring home?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: The late Middle Ages: plague, war and learning

it.q: The Black Death, which struck Europe beginning in 1347, was
ch: a deadly plague that killed about one-third or more of Europe's people
a war between England and France
it.h: It spread along trade routes.

it.q: The Black Death spread mainly through
ch: fleas on rats and from person to person along trade routes
it.h: Ships and caravans carried more than goods.

it.q: The Hundred Years' War was fought between
it.h: It lasted from 1337 to 1453.

it.q: Joan of Arc is remembered for
ch: leading French troops to important victories against the English
it.h: She was a young peasant woman who said she was guided by saints.

it.q: Before the Black Death, Europe had about 75 million people. About one-third died. About how many million people died?
it.h: Divide 75 by 3.

it.q: Explain how the Black Death weakened the feudal system.
it.ans: So many peasants died that workers were scarce, so survivors could demand wages or leave the manor, which weakened lords' control over serfs.
it.h: What happens to the value of work when there are fewer workers?

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: Towns, trade and guilds revive in medieval Europe

it.q: A guild was
ch: an association of merchants or craftspeople in a town
it.h: Bakers, weavers and goldsmiths each had one.

it.q: A young person learning a craft from a master usually started as
it.h: Next came journeyman, then master.

it.q: The three-field system and new tools like the heavy plow helped farmers grow more food. What was one effect?
it.h: More food can feed more people.

it.q: Towns often bought a charter from their lord or king. What did a charter give a town?
ch: rights to govern itself and hold markets

it.q: A medieval town had 3,000 people in 1100 and 4 times as many in 1300. How many people lived there in 1300?
it.h: Multiply.

lessons.u: Unit 6: Medieval Europe (7.6)
lessons.n: Women in medieval Europe: nuns, queens, workers and writers

it.q: Hildegard of Bingen (1098-1179) was
ch: an abbess who wrote music and works on religion, medicine and nature
it.h: She led a community of nuns in Germany.

it.q: Why did some medieval women choose to become nuns?
ch: Convents offered education, a religious life and some independence.
it.h: Few other places taught women to read and write.

it.q: Eleanor of Aquitaine was unusual because she
ch: was queen of France and later queen of England and held great lands and influence
it.h: She married two kings.

it.q: Most peasant women in medieval Europe
ch: worked in the fields and ran households, spinning, cooking and caring for animals

it.q: Hildegard of Bingen was born in 1098 and died in 1179. How old was she when she died?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Maya, Aztec and Inca (7.7)
lessons.n: The Maya

it.q: The Maya civilization developed in southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and the
ch: Valley of Mexico lake region only
it.h: This peninsula juts north into the Gulf of Mexico.

it.q: The Maya were organized into
ch: many independent city-states, each ruled by a king
one empire ruled from a single capital
it.h: Tikal, Copan and Palenque each had its own ruler.

it.q: Maya farmers cleared rainforest and grew mostly
it.h: These three crops are sometimes called the "three sisters."

it.q: The Maya developed a writing system that used
ch: glyphs, symbols standing for words and sounds
it.h: Many are carved on stone monuments.

it.q: The Maya used a number system based on 20. In this system, the second place stands for groups of 20. A number written as 3 in the second place and 5 in the first place equals 3 x 20 + 5. What is this number?
it.h: Multiply 3 by 20, then add 5.

it.q: Explain why Maya priests and rulers valued their calendars so highly.
it.ans: Calendars told them when to plant and harvest and when to hold religious ceremonies, and knowledge of the calendar gave priests and kings authority.
it.h: Think about farming and religion.

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Maya, Aztec and Inca (7.7)
lessons.n: The Aztec Empire

it.q: The Aztecs founded their capital, Tenochtitlan, in 1325 on an island in
it.h: Mexico City is built on the same site today.

it.q: Chinampas were
ch: floating gardens built in the lake for farming
it.h: Farmers piled mud and plants on reed mats in shallow water.

it.q: How did the Aztecs connect their island city to the mainland?
ch: They built raised roads called causeways
They built tunnels under the lake
it.h: These roads crossed the water.

it.q: The Aztec Empire grew rich by
ch: collecting tribute such as food, cloth and gold from conquered peoples
it.h: Conquered city-states had to pay regularly.

it.q: Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325. Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract 1325 from 1519.

it.q: Explain how the Aztecs changed their environment to support a large city.
it.ans: They built chinampas to farm in the lake, causeways to reach the mainland, aqueducts to bring fresh water and canals for canoes, which fed and served a huge population.
it.h: Think about food, water and travel.

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Maya, Aztec and Inca (7.7)
lessons.n: The Inca Empire

it.q: The Inca Empire stretched along the
it.h: These mountains run along the west coast of South America.

it.q: The capital of the Inca Empire was
it.h: It is in present-day Peru.

it.q: Inca farmers grew crops on steep mountainsides by building
ch: terraces, flat steps cut into the hillsides
it.h: Look for stair-step fields.

it.q: Instead of writing, the Inca kept records using
ch: quipus, knotted strings of different colors
it.h: The knots could stand for numbers.

it.q: Pachacuti began expanding the Inca Empire in 1438. The Spanish captured the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532. How many years passed?
it.h: Subtract 1438 from 1532.

it.q: Explain how the Inca governed such a long, mountainous empire.
it.ans: They built a vast road system with rope bridges and relay runners, kept records on quipus, required everyone to speak Quechua, appointed officials and collected labor as a tax, all under the emperor in Cusco.
it.h: Think about roads, records, language and officials.

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Maya, Aztec and Inca (7.7)
