lessons.n: The Spanish conquest

it.q: The Spanish conquistador who conquered the Aztec Empire was
it.h: He landed on the coast of Mexico in 1519.

it.q: The Spanish conquistador who conquered the Inca Empire was
it.h: He captured Atahualpa in 1532.

it.q: Which disease, brought by Europeans, killed huge numbers of Native peoples who had no immunity to it?
it.h: It spread through Tenochtitlan in 1520.

it.q: Cortes defeated the Aztecs partly because thousands of warriors from groups such as the Tlaxcalans
ch: joined him as allies against the Aztecs
it.h: Many peoples resented paying tribute to the Aztecs.

it.q: Cortes arrived in Mexico in 1519, and Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532. How many years after the fall of Tenochtitlan did Pizarro capture Atahualpa?
it.h: Subtract 1521 from 1532.

it.q: Explain how a civil war helped the Spanish conquer the Inca.
it.ans: Two brothers, Atahualpa and Huascar, had fought for the throne, which divided and weakened the empire just as Pizarro arrived, making it easier for a small Spanish force to capture Atahualpa.
it.h: What was happening inside the Inca Empire when the Spanish arrived?

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Maya, Aztec and Inca (7.7)
lessons.n: Schools, markets and daily life in the Aztec, Maya and Inca worlds

it.q: In Aztec society, boys from noble families attended a school called the calmecac, while commoner boys attended
it.h: Commoner boys trained mainly to be warriors.

it.q: The huge market at Tlatelolco, next to Tenochtitlan, sold food, cloth, tools and animals. What did people often use as money there?

ch: caring for wounded soldiers and later founding the American Red Cross
it.h: She was called the "Angel of the Battlefield."

it.q: The Union and the Confederacy both used a draft, which means
ch: requiring men to serve in the military
it.h: Not enough men volunteered.

it.q: The New York City draft riots of 1863 broke out partly because
ch: wealthy men could pay to avoid the draft, and rioters attacked African Americans
it.h: Many working people resented the $300 exemption.

it.q: About 620,000 soldiers died in the Civil War. If about two-thirds died from disease, about how many died from disease?
it.h: Multiply 620,000 by 2, then divide by 3, and round to the nearest whole number.

it.q: Explain how the war changed life for women in the North and South.
it.ans: Women ran farms, businesses and plantations, worked in factories and government offices, served as nurses, raised money and supplies, and some served as spies, gaining new responsibilities and confidence.
it.h: Who did the work when men left to fight?

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Civil War (8.10)
lessons.n: The war in the West and at sea

it.q: In February 1862, Ulysses S. Grant captured Forts Henry and Donelson in Tennessee and became known for demanding
it.h: He did not accept any conditions from the Confederates.

it.q: In March 1862, the ironclad ships USS Monitor and CSS Virginia fought at Hampton Roads, Virginia. Why was this battle important?
ch: It showed that wooden warships would soon be outdated.
It was fought on the Mississippi.
it.h: Think about iron versus wood.

it.q: In April 1862, Union Admiral David Farragut captured
it.h: It was the South's largest city, near the mouth of the Mississippi.

it.q: The Battle of Shiloh in Tennessee (April 1862) shocked Americans mainly because of
About 23,000 soldiers were killed, wounded or missing at Shiloh. If about 13,000 were Union, about how many were Confederate?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Unit 7: The Civil War (8.10)
lessons.n: Leaders at war: Lincoln, Davis, Grant and Lee

it.q: Before the war, Robert E. Lee was offered a high command in the U.S. Army but chose to
ch: resign and serve Virginia and the Confederacy
it.h: His home state seceded in April 1861.

it.q: Lee wrote in April 1861, "Save in defense of my native State, I never desire again to draw my sword." What does this show about his reason for joining the Confederacy?
ch: His loyalty to Virginia came before his loyalty to the Union.
He wanted to invade the North.
He wanted to retire to Europe.
it.h: Look at the words "native State."

it.q: Jefferson Davis had trouble getting Confederate states to send troops and money. Why?
ch: Many states insisted on their own rights and resisted a strong central government.
it.h: The Confederacy was founded on states' rights.

it.q: Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus in some areas during the war. What did this allow?
ch: holding suspected enemies without bringing them quickly before a judge

it.q: Lee resigned from the U.S. Army in April 1861 and surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865. How many years apart were these events?
it.h: Subtract the years.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Rebuilding the Union: plans and amendments

it.q: The period after the Civil War when the nation rebuilt the South and decided the rights of freed people is called
it.h: It lasted from 1865 to 1877.

it.q: The Thirteenth Amendment (1865)
ch: abolished slavery in the United States
it.h: It applied everywhere, unlike the Emancipation Proclamation.

it.q: The Fourteenth Amendment (1868)
ch: made all persons born in the U.S. citizens and guaranteed equal protection of the laws
it.h: Think of citizenship and equal protection.

it.q: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) said the right to vote could not be denied because of
ch: race, color or previous condition of servitude
it.h: It protected the voting rights of Black men.

it.q: The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in 1865 and the Fifteenth in 1870. How many years apart were they?
it.h: Subtract 1865 from 1870.

it.q: Explain how Radical Republicans' plan for Reconstruction differed from President Andrew Johnson's plan.
it.ans: Johnson wanted to readmit Southern states quickly with few demands and did little to protect freed people. Radical Republicans wanted to punish Confederate leaders, protect the rights of freed people, put the South under military rule and require states to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment.
it.h: Which side cared more about the rights of freed people?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Freedom, setbacks and the end of Reconstruction

it.q: In 1870, Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first African American to serve in the
it.h: He filled a seat once held by Jefferson Davis.

it.q: Sharecropping was a system in which
ch: farmers worked land owned by others in exchange for a share of the crop, often trapping them in debt
it.h: Many freed people had no land or money.

it.q: The Ku Klux Klan used violence and threats to
ch: stop African Americans from voting and exercising their rights
it.h: It was a terrorist group formed after the war.

it.q: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction when
ch: federal troops were removed from the South in exchange for Rutherford B. Hayes becoming president
it.h: It settled a disputed presidential election.

it.q: More than 1,500 African Americans held public office during Reconstruction. If 16 of them served in Congress, how many held other offices? Use 1,500 as the total.
it.h: Subtract 16 from 1,500.

it.q: Explain how sharecropping kept many freed people poor.
it.ans: Sharecroppers had to buy seed, tools and food on credit, often at high prices from landowners, and after giving up a share of the crop they rarely earned enough to pay their debts, so they were trapped on the land.
it.h: Follow the money from planting to harvest.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Railroads, industry and big business

it.q: The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 at
it.h: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met there.

it.q: Thousands of workers from China built much of the
ch: Central Pacific line through the Sierra Nevada
Union Pacific line across Nebraska only
it.h: The Central Pacific started in Sacramento.

it.q: Andrew Carnegie built his fortune in the
it.h: Steel was needed for rails, bridges and skyscrapers.

it.q: John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil Company became a monopoly, which means it
ch: controlled nearly all of an industry, limiting competition
it.h: Mono means one.

it.q: The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869. The U.S. had about 35,000 miles of track in 1865 and about 193,000 miles in 1900. How many miles were added?
it.h: Subtract 35,000 from 193,000.

it.q: Explain how the transcontinental railroad changed the West.
it.ans: It cut the trip from coast to coast from months to about a week, brought settlers, towns, farms and ranches to the West, linked Western goods to Eastern markets, and sped the loss of American Indian lands and buffalo herds.
it.h: Think about travel time, settlement and American Indian nations.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Immigrants, workers and cities

it.q: Most immigrants arriving in New York after 1892 passed through the immigration station at
it.h: It is near the Statue of Liberty.

it.q: Many immigrants arriving on the West Coast, especially from China, were processed and often detained at
ch: Angel Island in San Francisco Bay
it.h: The station opened in 1910.

it.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882
ch: banned most Chinese immigration to the United States
it.h: It was the first federal law to bar immigrants by nationality.

it.q: Tenements were
ch: crowded, poorly built apartment buildings where many city workers lived
it.h: Jacob Riis photographed them.

it.q: Between 1880 and 1920, more than 20 million immigrants came to the United States. On average, about how many came each year over those 40 years?
it.h: Divide 20 million by 40.

it.q: Emma Lazarus's poem "The New Colossus" (1883), placed on the Statue of Liberty, says, "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." Compare this welcome with the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.
it.ans: The poem welcomed poor immigrants seeking freedom, but just a year earlier the Chinese Exclusion Act barred Chinese immigrants, showing that America's welcome was not extended equally to all groups.
it.h: Look at the dates and who was welcomed.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: The West after the Civil War

it.q: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered settlers
ch: 160 acres of public land if they farmed it for five years
it.h: Many settlers moved to the Great Plains.

it.q: Why did the destruction of the buffalo herds devastate Plains nations such as the Lakota?
ch: They depended on buffalo for food, clothing, shelter and tools
Buffalo were only for trade with Europe
They were farmers who ate only corn
it.h: Think of everything the buffalo provided.

it.q: At the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876,
ch: Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated Custer's cavalry
the U.S. Army defeated the Lakota
it.h: Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse were leaders there.

it.q: The Dawes Act of 1887 tried to
ch: divide reservation land into individual plots and make American Indians give up their cultures
it.h: Much reservation land was lost as a result.

it.q: Under the Homestead Act, a family received 160 acres. How many acres would 25 families receive?
it.h: Multiply 160 by 25.

it.q: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce said when he surrendered in 1877, "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever." What does this statement show about the experience of American Indian nations in this period?
it.ans: It shows the exhaustion and grief of nations forced from their homelands after long resistance against the U.S. Army, losing land, people and freedom.
it.h: Why would a leader say he would fight no more?

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Farmers organize: the Grange and the Populists

it.q: The Grange, founded in 1867, was an organization of
it.h: It began as a social and educational group.

it.q: Farmers in the late 1800s were angry at railroads mainly because
ch: railroads charged high rates to ship crops
railroads refused to cross the Plains
railroads were run by the government
it.h: Farmers needed trains to get crops to market.

it.q: The Populist Party of the 1890s called for
ch: government regulation of railroads, a graduated income tax and more money in circulation
it.h: Many of these ideas later became law.

it.q: Many farmers wanted the government to coin silver as well as gold. Why?
ch: More money in circulation could raise crop prices and make debts easier to pay.

it.q: A farmer sold 1,000 bushels of wheat for 60 cents a bushel. The railroad charged 25 cents a bushel to ship it. How many dollars did the farmer keep after shipping?
it.h: Find the money left per bushel first, then convert cents to dollars.

lessons.u: Unit 8: Reconstruction and the Industrial Age (8.11, 8.12)
lessons.n: Responding to Jim Crow: Wells, Washington and Du Bois

it.q: Ida B. Wells, a journalist from Memphis, became famous for
ch: investigating and speaking out against lynching
it.h: She published Southern Horrors in 1892.

it.q: Booker T. Washington, founder of the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama (1881), urged African Americans to focus first on
ch: job skills, education and economic progress
it.h: He believed economic strength would lead to rights.

it.q: W. E. B. Du Bois disagreed with Washington and argued that African Americans should
ch: demand full civil and political rights now
it.h: Du Bois earned a doctorate from Harvard.

it.q: In The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Du Bois wrote, "The problem of the Twentieth Century is the problem of the color-line." What did he mean?
ch: Racial division would be the central problem facing the nation.

it.q: Washington gave his Atlanta speech in 1895 and Du Bois published The Souls of Black Folk in 1903. How many years apart are these events?
it.h: Subtract.

lessons.u: Geography and Earth's regions
lessons.n: Maps, projections and geographic tools

it.q: Lines of latitude measure distance
ch: north or south of the equator
east or west of the prime meridian

it.h: It was set at an observatory near London.

it.h: Each inch on the map stands for the same number of miles.

it.q: Which tool layers data such as roads, rivers and population on digital maps so they can be compared?
it.h: Think of a computer system built for maps and data.

it.q: A thematic map differs from a general reference map because it
ch: shows one topic, such as rainfall or population density
it.h: "Thematic" comes from "theme."

it.q: A student says the Mercator map proves Greenland is about the same size as Africa. Explain the student's mistake.
it.ans: The Mercator projection stretches land far from the equator. Greenland is near the North Pole, so it looks huge, but Africa is actually about 14 times larger in area.
it.h: Where is Greenland, and what does Mercator do to land in that area?

lessons.u: Geography and Earth's regions
lessons.n: Landforms, plate tectonics and physical processes

it.q: Earth's outer shell is broken into large moving pieces called
it.h: These pieces move a few centimeters a year.

it.q: The Himalayas formed mainly where
ch: the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate
a hot spot formed in the Pacific
it.h: The highest mountains form where two continents push together.

it.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is a boundary where
ch: two plates slide past each other
one plate dives under another and makes volcanoes
two plates pull apart under the ocean
it.h: The Pacific plate and the North American plate move side by side.

it.q: Weathering and erosion differ because
ch: weathering breaks rock down, while erosion moves the pieces away
weathering moves rock, while erosion breaks it
it.h: One process breaks; the other carries.

it.q: A river drops sediment where it enters the sea and builds a fan-shaped landform called a
it.h: The Nile and the Mississippi both end in one.

it.q: Explain why so many earthquakes and volcanoes happen around the edges of the Pacific Ocean.
it.ans: Many plates meet around the Pacific. Where ocean plates sink under other plates, the movement causes earthquakes and melting rock rises to form volcanoes.
it.h: What is happening to the plates at the edges of the Pacific?

lessons.u: Geography and Earth's regions
lessons.n: Climate zones, climate controls and biomes

it.q: Weather is the condition of the air on a given day, while climate is
ch: the usual pattern of weather over many years
it.h: Climate is about the long run.

it.q: In general, places near the equator are warmer because they
ch: receive more direct sunlight all year
it.h: Think about the angle of the sun's rays, not distance.

it.q: The side of a mountain range facing away from moist ocean winds is often dry. This is called
it.h: Air drops its moisture as it rises over the mountains.

it.q: The cold California Current offshore helps keep summers along much of the California coast
it.h: Cold water cools the air above it.

it.q: Which biome has permanently frozen subsoil and very short summers?
it.h: The frozen layer is called permafrost.

it.q: Explain how elevation affects climate, using an example.
it.ans: Air gets colder as elevation rises, so high places are cooler than low places at the same latitude; for example, Sierra Nevada peaks get snow while the Central Valley stays warm.
it.h: Compare a mountaintop with a valley nearby.

lessons.u: Geography and Earth's regions
lessons.n: Regions, human characteristics and current events

it.q: A functional region is organized around a central point, such as
ch: the area served by an airport hub
it.h: Functional regions are tied together by movement or service.

it.q: A perceptual (vernacular) region is based on
ch: people's shared ideas and feelings about a place
it.h: Its borders exist mostly in people's minds.

it.q: The five themes of geography are location, place, region, movement and
it.h: This theme is about how people and nature affect each other.

it.q: Which is a human characteristic of a place?
it.h: Human characteristics are made by people.

it.q: A drought hits a farming region that grows much of a country's rice. Which effect is most likely?
ch: rice prices rise across the country
it.h: Think about supply.

it.q: Name a current event and explain how a physical characteristic of the place affects it.
it.ans: For example, California wildfires are linked to dry summers, strong seasonal winds and dense dry vegetation.
it.h: Pick a flood, fire, drought, storm or trade story, then look at climate or landforms.

lessons.u: Geography and Earth's regions
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which pair correctly matches a landform with how it formed?
ch: a delta - sediment dropped at a river mouth
a canyon - lava cooling in the sea
a plateau - waves piling up sand
it.h: Which process actually builds land where a river meets the sea?

it.q: Which line of longitude is on the opposite side of the globe from the prime meridian?
it.h: Halfway around a circle is how many degrees?

it.q: Rice paddies cut into hillsides as terraces are an example of
ch: people changing the environment to farm
it.h: Who built the terraces?

it.q: Which climate control helps explain why London has milder winters than many places at the same latitude in Canada?
it.h: Look at the ocean near Britain.

it.q: Choose two of the five themes of geography and apply each one to your city.
it.ans: For example, location: about 34 degrees N, 118 degrees W; movement: freeways and a port move people and goods in and out.
it.h: The themes are location, place, region, movement and human-environment interaction.

lessons.u: Population and migration
lessons.n: Population distribution, density and growth

it.q: A country has 50 million people and an area of 250,000 square kilometers. What is its population density in people per square kilometer?
it.h: Divide the number of people by the area.

it.q: Most of the world's people live in
it.h: Look at where most of Earth's land is.

it.q: Which areas tend to have low population density?
ch: deserts, high mountains and polar regions
it.h: Where is it hardest to grow food and find water?

it.q: The birth rate minus the death rate, not counting migration, is the
it.h: It shows growth from births and deaths alone.

it.q: In the demographic transition model, death rates fall before birth rates fall. What happens to population during that stage?
it.h: Compare births and deaths during that stage.

it.q: Explain why Egypt's population is concentrated in a small part of the country.
it.ans: Most Egyptians live along the Nile River and in its delta because the rest of the country is desert; the river provides water and fertile farmland.
it.h: Picture a map of Egypt. Where is the water?

lessons.u: Population and migration
lessons.n: Population, resources and the environment

it.q: Thomas Malthus wrote in 1798: "Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio." What did he predict?
ch: population would outgrow the food supply unless something checked it
food would always grow faster than population
population would stop growing on its own
it.h: "Subsistence" means food and the basic needs of life.

it.q: The Green Revolution of the mid-1900s raised food production in many countries through
it.h: Think of new farming science.

it.q: Carrying capacity is
ch: the largest population an environment can support over time
the weight a truck can carry
the number of cities in a region
it.h: It is about the limits of resources.

it.q: World population grew from about 1 billion around 1800 to about 8 billion by the 2020s without the worldwide famine Malthus predicted. Which best explains this?
it.h: What changed about how food is grown?

it.q: World population was about 1 billion around 1800 and about 8 billion in 2022. About how many times larger was it in 2022?
it.h: Divide the later number by the earlier one.

it.q: Explain how rapid population growth can strain water supplies in a dry region.
it.ans: More people need more water for homes, farms and industry; if rain and rivers do not increase, groundwater and reservoirs are used up faster, leading to shortages and conflict over water.
it.h: Supply stays about the same; what happens to demand?

lessons.u: Population and migration
lessons.n: Push and pull factors in historical migrations

it.q: The Irish famine of the 1840s pushed many Irish people to emigrate because
ch: a potato disease destroyed the main food crop and caused mass hunger
it.h: What happened to the crop most families depended on?

it.q: From 1892 to 1954 the main U.S. immigration station in New York Harbor was
it.h: It is near the Statue of Liberty.

it.q: Angel Island, in San Francisco Bay, was an immigration station where many immigrants from
ch: China were detained and questioned, sometimes for weeks or months
it.h: It operated while the Chinese Exclusion Act was law.

it.q: Emma Lazarus wrote in "The New Colossus" (1883), a poem later placed at the Statue of Liberty: "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." Which idea does the poem express?
ch: the United States as a refuge for people seeking freedom and a better life
the United States closing its doors
it.h: Who is the statue speaking to in these lines?

it.q: Which was a pull factor for people who came to California in 1849?
ch: news of gold discovered in the Sierra Nevada foothills
it.h: A pull factor is about the destination.

it.q: Distinguish between voluntary and forced migration, giving one historical example of each.
it.ans: Voluntary migration is chosen, such as Europeans moving to U.S. cities for factory jobs around 1900. Forced migration is not chosen, such as the transatlantic slave trade or the Trail of Tears.
it.h: Who made the decision to move?

lessons.u: Population and migration
lessons.n: Urbanization and megacities

it.q: A city with more than 10 million people is often called a
it.h: "Mega" means very large.

it.q: Suburbs are
ch: residential communities on the edges of cities
it.h: Think of where many commuters live.

it.q: Which helped cause rapid urbanization in Britain in the 1800s?
ch: factory jobs in growing industrial cities
a law forcing people out of cities
it.h: Why would rural people move to Manchester or Birmingham?

it.q: Informal settlements, sometimes called shantytowns, often form when
ch: cities grow faster than affordable housing and services can be built
it.h: Compare how fast people arrive with how fast homes are built.

it.q: A city grew from 4 million people to 6 million people. What was the percent increase?
it.h: Find the change, divide by the starting number, then multiply by 100.

it.q: Describe one benefit and one problem caused by rapid urbanization.
it.ans: Benefit: more jobs, schools and hospitals close together. Problem: traffic, pollution, high housing costs or overcrowded informal settlements.
it.h: Think about both opportunities and pressures.

lessons.u: Population and migration

it.h: They hoped to find farm work in the West.

the state paid for the move

it.h: Think of Little Saigon in Orange County.

it.q: A graph shows California's population rose from about 7 million in 1940 to about 16 million in 1960. Which best explains this growth?
ch: wartime and postwar jobs drew migrants from other states
it.h: What happened in the 1940s and 1950s?

it.q: Explain the difference between a refugee and an economic migrant.
it.ans: A refugee is forced to flee their country because of war, violence or persecution; an economic migrant chooses to move mainly to find work or a better income.
it.h: Think about whether the person is in danger at home.

lessons.u: Population and migration

it.q: A population pyramid with a narrow base and wide middle and top suggests

ch: a family moving from a farm in Iowa to Chicago
a family moving from Mexico to Texas
a student studying abroad for a semester
it.h: Internal means within one country.

it.q: A town grew from 20,000 to 25,000 people. What was the percent increase?

it.h: One factor works at the starting point; the other at the destination.

lessons.u: Culture and globalization

it.q: A language family is
ch: a group of languages that developed from a common ancestor

it.q: Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese all developed from
it.h: These are the Romance languages, named after Rome.

it.q: A lingua franca is
ch: a common language used between speakers of different native languages

ch: Spanish colonial history in the region
a link between Spanish and Chinese
it.h: Who named many places in California before 1848?

it.ans: Religion can be seen in places of worship, holidays, food customs and architecture; for example, mission churches in California or temples and mosques in many cities.
it.h: What buildings, holidays or customs could you see?

lessons.u: Culture and globalization

only gold from Europe to Asia

lessons.u: Culture and globalization

lessons.u: Culture and globalization
lessons.n: Cultural landscapes, heritage and endangered languages

it.q: A cultural landscape is
ch: an area shaped by the activities and beliefs of the people who live there

it.q: UNESCO World Heritage Sites are
ch: places recognized for outstanding cultural or natural value to humanity
national parks owned by the United Nations

it.q: An endangered language is one that
ch: fewer and fewer children are learning, so it may stop being spoken
it.h: What happens when children stop learning a language?

it.q: Rice terraces, a mosque's minaret and a Chinatown gate are all examples of
it.h: Who made each of these?

it.q: A city plans to tear down a historic neighborhood to build a highway, and residents object. Which argument uses the idea of cultural heritage?
ch: the neighborhood's buildings and businesses hold the community's history and identity
it.h: Which argument is about history and identity?

it.q: Describe a feature of your community's cultural landscape and what it reveals about the people who built it.
it.ans: For example, a mission church shows Spanish colonial history and Catholic faith; a Japanese garden or a Sikh gurdwara shows the culture of communities that settled there.
it.h: Think of a building, sign, garden, mural or street name.

lessons.u: Culture and globalization
lessons.n: Evaluating sources about global issues

it.q: A primary source is
ch: a firsthand record created at the time of an event
it.h: Who created it, and when?

it.q: Lateral reading means
ch: checking what other reliable sources say about a website or author
reading a page from top to bottom
it.h: You leave the page to check it.

it.q: Which question best helps judge a source's bias?
ch: Who created it, and what did they want readers to think?
it.h: Think about purpose.

it.q: A report on a soda tax was paid for by a soda company. A careful reader should
ch: check whether independent sources reach the same conclusions
trust it fully because it has charts
reject every fact in it automatically
it.h: Funding is a reason to check, not proof of error.

it.q: Two sources disagree about how many people a flood affected. Which step is best?
ch: compare both with a third independent source such as official records and note how each counted
it.h: How can you test which is closer to the truth?

it.q: Explain the difference between a primary and a secondary source, with an example of each about globalization.
it.ans: A primary source comes from the time, such as a factory worker's interview or a trade agreement; a secondary source analyzes later, such as a textbook chapter on world trade.
it.h: Ask who made it and when.

lessons.u: Culture and globalization
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which is the best example of globalization?
ch: a smartphone designed in California and assembled in Asia
a farmer selling vegetables at a local market
it.h: Look for connections across countries.

it.q: Which source would give the best firsthand view of travel on the Silk Road?
ch: a merchant's travel account written at the time
it.h: Firsthand means from someone who was there.

it.q: Which statement about culture is accurate?
ch: cultures change over time through contact and new ideas
it.h: Think of how your community's culture has changed.

it.q: English spread to many parts of the world mainly through
ch: British colonization and later American media and business
it.h: Think about empire and modern media.

it.q: Explain how a local tradition might change when it meets global culture.
it.ans: It may blend in new elements, such as new foods, music or technology, while keeping its core meaning; or it may fade if young people adopt global trends instead.
it.h: Think about blending and loss.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Identity, race and ethnicity

it.q: Ethnicity usually refers to
ch: a shared culture, such as language, ancestry, traditions or religion
it.h: Think about shared heritage.

it.q: Social scientists describe race as "socially constructed." This means
ch: racial categories were created and changed by societies over time rather than fixed by biology
race has no effect on people's lives
it.h: "Constructed" means built by people.

it.q: The U.S. Census has changed its racial and ethnic categories many times. What does this suggest?
ch: ideas about race and ethnicity change over time
the categories are fixed by science
it.h: If the categories were fixed, would they need to change?

it.q: Intersectionality describes how
ch: different parts of identity, such as race, gender and class, combine to shape a person's experiences
all people have the same experiences
it.h: "Intersect" means to cross or overlap.

it.q: A family speaks Tagalog at home and English at school and celebrates both Filipino and American holidays. This best shows that
ch: identity can include several cultures at once
language has nothing to do with identity
it.h: Can a person belong to more than one culture?

it.q: Describe two factors that shape a person's identity and explain how each one does.
it.ans: For example, family passes down language and traditions, and community and history shape how people see themselves and how others treat them.
it.h: Think of family, language, religion, place and history.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Asian American and Pacific Islander histories: exclusion and resistance

it.q: In the 1860s thousands of Chinese workers built much of
ch: the western section of the first transcontinental railroad
it.h: The Central Pacific Railroad built east from California.

it.q: In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898), the Supreme Court ruled that
ch: a man born in the U.S. to Chinese immigrant parents was a U.S. citizen
Chinese immigrants could never live in the U.S.
the Chinese Exclusion Act was unconstitutional
it.h: Think of the Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship clause.

it.q: Poems carved into the walls of the Angel Island Immigration Station by detained Chinese immigrants are valuable sources because they
ch: record the immigrants' own feelings about detention
it.h: Whose voices do they preserve?

it.q: The Civil Liberties Act of 1988
ch: formally apologized and paid redress to surviving Japanese Americans who had been incarcerated
it.h: "Redress" means making up for a wrong.

it.q: Filipino farm workers led by Larry Itliong began the 1965 Delano grape strike, and Mexican American workers led by Cesar Chavez soon joined them. This shows that
ch: different ethnic groups cooperated in the farm labor movement
the strike had one leader only
it.h: Who started the strike, and who joined?

it.q: Explain how the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 reflected attitudes of its time and affected Chinese American communities.
it.ans: It reflected racial prejudice and fears that Chinese workers took jobs and lowered wages. It kept most new Chinese immigrants out, separated families and left mostly male communities that shrank for decades.
it.h: Think about why it was passed and who it hurt.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: African American and Native American histories of resistance

it.q: Frederick Douglass said in an 1852 speech: "This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn." What was his main point?
ch: the nation celebrated freedom while millions of people were still enslaved
it.h: What was true for millions of Black Americans in 1852?

it.q: The Dawes Act of 1887
ch: divided many reservations into individual plots, and Native nations lost much of their land
ended the reservation system with full sovereignty
it.h: The land not given to individuals was opened to settlers.

it.q: Federal Indian boarding schools such as the Carlisle Indian Industrial School (founded 1879) tried to
ch: replace Native languages and cultures with Euro-American ways
train Native leaders for tribal governments
it.h: Children were often punished for speaking their own languages.

it.q: The Indian Citizenship Act of 1924
ch: granted U.S. citizenship to Native Americans born in the United States
it.h: The name of the act tells you.

it.q: Nez Perce leader Chief Joseph is recorded as saying in 1877: "I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever." What does this source reveal?
ch: the exhaustion and loss his people suffered in war with the U.S. Army
it.h: What feelings do his words express?

it.q: Explain how Native nations have resisted efforts to erase their cultures, giving one example.
it.ans: For example, through language revitalization programs, the 1969 occupation of Alcatraz, legal fights for treaty rights and building tribal colleges and governments.
it.h: Think of language, land, law and protest.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Chicana/o and Latina/o histories and movements

it.q: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the U.S.-Mexican War and
ch: transferred a large territory, including California, to the United States
it.h: Think about which land changed hands in 1848.

it.q: In 1968, thousands of Mexican American students in East Los Angeles walked out of their high schools to protest
it.h: The walkouts are also called "blowouts."

it.q: Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the farm workers union, is known for the slogan
it.h: It means "Yes, it can be done."

it.q: In Mendez v. Westminster, Mexican American families went to court because their children were
ch: sent to separate schools from white children
it.h: The case was about segregation.

it.q: Mendez v. Westminster (1947) came seven years before Brown v. Board of Education (1954). Why do historians see Mendez as important to Brown?
ch: it was an earlier legal challenge to school segregation, and Thurgood Marshall helped write a brief supporting the families
it was decided by the Supreme Court
it ended segregation in every state
it.h: Think about lawyers and arguments that carried forward.

it.q: Explain why the Delano grape boycott asked people across the country to stop buying grapes.
it.ans: Strikers alone could be replaced, but a national boycott cut growers' sales and pressured them to sign contracts with better wages and conditions.
it.h: How could shoppers far away help farm workers?

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander histories

it.q: In 1893 the Hawaiian Kingdom's government, led by Queen Liliuokalani, was overthrown by
ch: a group of mostly American businessmen, with support from U.S. Marines
a vote of the Hawaiian people
it.h: Sugar planters and businessmen wanted closer ties with the United States.

it.q: The United States annexed Hawaii in
it.h: It was the same year as the Spanish-American War.

it.q: Queen Liliuokalani gave up her authority in 1893 "under protest," saying she yielded to the force of the United States to avoid loss of life. What does her protest show?
ch: she did not accept the overthrow as lawful
she wanted to move to the mainland
it.h: Why would someone write a formal protest?

it.q: In 1976 the voyaging canoe Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using traditional navigation by stars, waves and wind. Why was the voyage important?
ch: it showed the skill of ancient Polynesian navigators and renewed pride in Hawaiian culture
it was the first trip by airplane
it proved Hawaii was settled from Europe
it opened a shipping route for sugar
it.h: Some people had doubted that Polynesians settled the Pacific on purpose.

it.q: After the 1890s, Hawaiian-language schools declined when English became the required language of instruction. Which later effort was a response to this loss?
ch: Hawaiian-language immersion schools starting in the 1980s
it.h: Look for an effort to bring the language back.

it.q: Explain why many Native Hawaiians view the 1893 overthrow differently from the way U.S. officials described annexation at the time.
it.ans: Many Native Hawaiians see it as the illegal takeover of an independent kingdom against the will of its people and queen; U.S. supporters at the time described annexation as natural growth that brought stability and trade.
it.h: Compare the view of the queen's supporters with the view of the annexation's supporters.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Oral history and community research

it.q: An oral history is
ch: a recorded interview about a person's memories and experiences
it.h: "Oral" means spoken.

it.q: Before recording an oral history interview, a researcher should
ch: explain the project and get the person's permission
it.h: Think about respect and consent.

it.q: Which is the best open-ended interview question?
ch: "What do you remember about your first year in California?"
it.h: Open-ended questions cannot be answered with one word.

it.q: Because memory can change over time, historians
ch: compare oral histories with documents and other accounts
it.h: How do historians check any source?

it.q: A student's grandfather remembers a 1970 farm workers march as "huge." A newspaper from that day estimates the crowd at a few hundred. What should she do?
ch: report both accounts and consider why they might differ
it.h: Different sources can see the same event differently.

it.q: Write two interview questions you would ask an elder about your community's history, and explain why each is useful.
it.ans: For example, "Why did your family come here?" reveals push and pull factors; "How has the neighborhood changed?" shows change over time.
it.h: Ask open-ended questions about reasons and change.

lessons.u: Ethnic studies: identity, history and movements
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which pair correctly matches a movement with one of its goals?
ch: United Farm Workers - better pay and conditions for farm workers
the Alcatraz occupation - higher grape prices
the East Los Angeles walkouts - a new freeway
it.h: Think about who each group represented.

it.q: Which event came first?
it.h: Put the dates in order: 1882, 1942, 1947, 1965.

it.q: Fred Korematsu's 1944 conviction for refusing the exclusion order was
ch: overturned by a federal court in 1983
it.h: New evidence came to light decades later.

it.q: Which best describes ethnic studies as a field?
ch: it studies the histories, cultures and contributions of racial and ethnic groups, often from their own perspectives
it studies only one country's government
it studies only rocks and minerals
it.h: Think about what this whole unit has covered.

it.q: Choose two movements from this unit and explain one strategy they shared.
it.ans: For example, the UFW and the civil rights movement both used nonviolent protest and boycotts to win public support and pressure decision makers.
it.h: Think of boycotts, marches, lawsuits or strikes.

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: Reason and rights: the ideas of the Enlightenment

it.q: The Scientific Revolution influenced Enlightenment thinkers because it showed that
ch: reason and observation could explain the natural world, so perhaps society too
it.h: If nature follows laws people can discover, what about government?

it.q: Thomas Hobbes argued in "Leviathan" (1651) that without government life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." What kind of government did he favor?
ch: a strong ruler with great power to keep order
it.h: If life without government is that bad, how much power should government have?

it.q: The idea of a social contract holds that
ch: people agree to form a government to protect their rights and well-being
kings receive power directly from God
businesses sign deals with the state
it.h: A contract is an agreement between parties.

it.q: Voltaire is best known for defending
ch: freedom of speech and religious toleration
it.h: He often criticized the church and censorship.

it.q: Mary Wollstonecraft argued in "A Vindication of the Rights of Woman" (1792) that
ch: women should receive the same education as men so they could reason for themselves
rights belong only to property owners
it.h: Look at the title of her book.

it.q: Compare Hobbes's and Locke's views of human nature and government.
it.ans: Hobbes thought people were selfish and needed a strong ruler to keep order; Locke thought people had natural rights and that government should protect them, and could be replaced if it did not.
it.h: What did each think people are like without government?

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: The English Civil War and the Glorious Revolution

it.q: The English Civil War (1642-1651) was mainly a conflict between
it.h: Who was fighting over power inside England?

it.q: After the civil war, Charles I was
it.h: The war ended badly for the king.

it.q: In 1688 Parliament invited William and Mary to take the throne after James II fled. Why is this called the "Glorious" Revolution?
ch: power changed hands with little bloodshed
it.h: Compare it with the civil war forty years earlier.

it.q: The English Bill of Rights (1689) declared "that excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed; nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted." Which U.S. document repeats this idea?
ch: the Eighth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution
it.h: Look for "cruel and unusual" in the U.S. Bill of Rights.

it.q: John Locke published his "Two Treatises of Government" in 1689. How did the Glorious Revolution relate to his ideas?
ch: it showed a people replacing a ruler and limiting royal power, which his theory defended
it gave the king absolute power, as he wanted
it.h: Locke defended the right to replace a ruler who abuses power.

it.q: Explain how the Glorious Revolution changed the balance of power between the English monarch and Parliament.
it.ans: The monarch had to accept the Bill of Rights, could not suspend laws or raise taxes or an army in peacetime without Parliament, and Parliament became the stronger branch, creating a constitutional monarchy.
it.h: Think about who controlled taxes and laws afterward.

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: The American Revolution as a world event

it.q: Thomas Paine wrote in "Common Sense" (1776): "Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil." Which idea does this express?
ch: government should be limited and serve the people
it.h: What does "necessary evil" say about how much government we want?

it.q: The Declaration of Independence (1776) states that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed." Which Enlightenment idea is this?
ch: popular sovereignty and the social contract
it.h: Where does the power come from?

it.q: France helped the American colonies win independence mainly by
ch: sending money, troops and a navy
it.h: Think of the French fleet at Yorktown in 1781.

it.q: The war cost France a great deal of money. Which later event did this debt help cause?
it.h: France's government was nearly bankrupt by 1788.

it.q: The Declaration of Independence said "all men are created equal," yet slavery remained legal in the new nation. How did this contradiction matter later?
ch: abolitionists and others used the Declaration's words to demand freedom and equal rights
it was removed from the Declaration
it.h: Think about how later movements quoted the Declaration.

it.q: Explain why the American Revolution inspired people in Europe and Latin America.
it.ans: It showed that colonists could defeat a powerful empire and set up a republic based on natural rights and consent of the governed, proving Enlightenment ideas could work in practice.
it.h: What did the American victory prove was possible?

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: The French Revolution: causes and radical phases

it.q: Before 1789, French society was divided into three estates. The Third Estate was
ch: the large majority of commoners, from peasants to wealthy merchants
it.h: About 97 percent of the people belonged to it.

it.q: Abbe Sieyes wrote in 1789: "What is the Third Estate? Everything. What has it been until now in the political order? Nothing. What does it ask? To become something." What was his main argument?
ch: the commoners made up the nation but had no real political power
the Third Estate should pay no taxes at all
it.h: Compare "Everything" and "Nothing."

it.q: The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789
ch: became a symbol of the people rising against royal tyranny
it.h: The Bastille was a royal fortress and prison.

it.q: The Reign of Terror (1793-1794) was
ch: a period when the revolutionary government executed thousands of people it called enemies
it.h: The guillotine was used often.

it.q: France's government was nearly bankrupt in 1788, bread prices were high and Enlightenment ideas were spreading. Which conclusion is best?
ch: economic crisis and new political ideas together helped cause the revolution
the revolution had one simple cause
it.h: Look for an answer that combines causes.

it.q: Explain how the French Revolution became more radical between 1789 and 1794.
it.ans: It began with a constitutional monarchy and declaration of rights, then war and fear of counterrevolution led to the end of the monarchy, the king's execution in 1793 and the Reign of Terror under Robespierre.
it.h: Trace the steps from reform to the Terror.

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: Napoleon and the spread of revolutionary ideas

it.q: Napoleon Bonaparte took power in France in 1799 through
ch: a coup that ended the government called the Directory
an election by all of Europe
it.h: A coup is a sudden seizure of power.

it.q: The Napoleonic Code (1804)
ch: created one set of laws for France, including equality before the law for men
restored the privileges of the nobility
gave women equal rights with men
it.h: Think about which revolutionary ideas it kept.

it.q: Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804. Why do historians say this both kept and betrayed the revolution?
ch: he kept legal equality and merit, but ruled as an autocrat without real democracy
he gave all power to the people
it.h: Look for an answer with two sides.

it.q: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812
ch: failed disastrously, destroying most of his army
ended the war in a quick victory
it.h: Think about the Russian winter and the long retreat.

it.q: Napoleon's armies spread ideas of legal equality and nationalism across Europe. Why did this backfire on him?
ch: conquered peoples developed their own nationalism and resisted French rule
it.h: If people feel loyal to their own nation, how do they feel about foreign rulers?

it.q: Evaluate whether Napoleon was a champion or an enemy of the French Revolution's ideals.
it.ans: A strong answer weighs his legal code, equality before the law and careers based on merit against his censorship, dictatorship, wars and restoration of slavery in French colonies in 1802.
it.h: List things that matched the ideals and things that did not.

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: Revolutions in Haiti and Latin America

it.q: Before its revolution, Saint-Domingue (Haiti) was
ch: a French colony whose sugar plantations relied on enslaved Africans
a Spanish colony of free farmers
it.h: It was one of the richest colonies in the world.

it.q: Toussaint Louverture was
ch: a formerly enslaved man who became the leading general of the Haitian Revolution
it.h: He organized and led the revolutionary army.

it.q: Haiti declared independence in
it.h: It was the same year Napoleon became emperor.

it.q: Simon Bolivar is remembered as
ch: a leader of independence movements in northern South America
a leader of the Haitian Revolution
it.h: The country Bolivia is named for him.

it.q: Creoles, people of European descent born in the Americas, led many Latin American independence movements. Which was a major cause?
ch: they resented that Spanish-born officials held the top positions
it.h: Who held power in the colonies, and who was left out?

it.q: Explain how the French Revolution and the Haitian Revolution influenced each other.
it.ans: The French declaration of rights inspired enslaved and free Black people in Saint-Domingue to demand freedom; the uprising pushed France to abolish slavery in 1794, and Haiti later defeated Napoleon's attempt to restore control.
it.h: Ideas moved in both directions across the Atlantic.

lessons.u: Enlightenment and democratic revolutions
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which events are in the correct order?
ch: Glorious Revolution, American Revolution, French Revolution, Haitian independence
French Revolution, Glorious Revolution, American Revolution, Haitian independence
American Revolution, Glorious Revolution, Haitian independence, French Revolution
Haitian independence, French Revolution, American Revolution, Glorious Revolution
it.h: Use the dates 1688, 1776, 1789 and 1804.

it.q: Which thinker is matched with the correct idea?
ch: Rousseau - the general will and popular sovereignty
it.h: Which choice matches a thinker with an idea he actually supported?

it.q: All four democratic revolutions in this unit shared which idea?
ch: government power should come from the people or be limited by law
it.h: Find the common thread.

it.q: Which is a primary source about the French Revolution?
ch: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789)
it.h: Primary sources come from the time.

it.q: Choose one revolution and explain one way it fulfilled and one way it fell short of its own ideals.
it.ans: For example, the American Revolution created a republic based on consent but kept slavery and denied women the vote.
it.h: Compare its words with who actually gained rights.

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: Why industrialization began in Britain

it.q: The Agricultural Revolution in Britain helped start the Industrial Revolution because
ch: new farming methods produced more food with fewer workers, freeing people for factory work
it.h: If farms need fewer workers, where can the others go?

it.q: The enclosure movement in Britain
ch: fenced off common lands into private farms, pushing many rural people to seek work in towns
it.h: What happened to people who used to farm the common land?

it.q: Britain had large deposits of coal and iron. Why did this matter?
ch: coal fueled steam engines and iron built machines and railways
coal was used only for heating homes
iron was used only for coins
it.h: Think of what machines and engines need.

it.q: Which invention sped up the spinning of thread in the British textile industry?
it.h: Textiles were the first industry to use factories.

it.q: Britain had capital from trade, colonies that supplied raw materials and markets, and a stable government that protected property. What do these facts suggest?
ch: several conditions together made Britain a likely place for industrialization to start
it.h: Look for the answer that combines factors.

it.q: Explain how James Watt's improvements to the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s changed industry.
it.ans: His more efficient engine used less coal and could power machines anywhere, so factories no longer had to be built beside rivers, and steam later powered trains and ships.
it.h: Before steam, many factories needed water wheels.

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: Factory life, reform and new economic ideas

it.q: In early British textile mills, children often
ch: worked long hours for low pay in dangerous conditions
it.h: Factory owners hired children because they could pay them less.

it.q: The Factory Act of 1833 in Britain
ch: limited the working hours of children in textile mills
it.h: Reformers wanted to protect the youngest workers.

it.q: Adam Smith argued in "The Wealth of Nations" (1776) for
ch: laissez-faire, letting markets work with little government interference
it.h: "Laissez-faire" is French for "let do."

it.q: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote in "The Communist Manifesto" (1848): "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." What did they mean?
ch: history is driven by conflict between groups such as workers and owners
it.h: Think about workers and factory owners.

it.q: A factory owner in 1840 says low wages keep goods cheap for everyone. A mill worker says low wages leave her family hungry. Which statement best describes these perspectives?
ch: each is shaped by the person's position in the industrial economy
it.h: Where each person stands affects what they see.

it.q: Explain how labor unions tried to improve conditions for industrial workers.
it.ans: Workers joined together to bargain with owners as a group, using strikes and negotiation to win higher pay, shorter hours and safer workplaces.
it.h: What power do workers have together that they lack alone?

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: Industrialization spreads: Germany, the United States and Japan

it.q: The Bessemer process, developed in the 1850s,
ch: made it cheaper to produce large amounts of steel
it.h: Steel became the material of railroads and skyscrapers.

it.q: The "Second Industrial Revolution" in the late 1800s was based on
it.h: Think of new industries after 1870.

it.q: After Germany unified in 1871, it became an industrial power partly because of
ch: rich coal deposits, railroads and strong science and engineering
it.h: The Ruhr region was full of coal.

it.q: During the Meiji era, which began in 1868, the Japanese government
ch: sent students abroad and built railroads, factories and a modern army
it.h: Japan wanted to avoid being colonized like its neighbors.

it.q: The United States had huge natural resources, a fast-growing population and many immigrants by 1900. How did immigration support industrial growth?
ch: immigrants provided much of the labor for factories, mines and railroads
it.h: Who worked in the new factories?

it.q: Explain why Japan's leaders chose to industrialize rapidly after 1868.
it.ans: After seeing Western powers force unequal treaties on Japan and China, they believed modern industry and a strong military were needed to protect Japan's independence.
it.h: Think about what had happened to China.

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: The scramble for Africa and African resistance

it.q: By 1914 the only African countries not under European control were
it.h: One defeated an Italian army; the other was founded by formerly enslaved Americans.

it.q: At the Battle of Adwa in 1896
ch: Ethiopian forces defeated an Italian army and kept Ethiopia independent
Italy gained all of East Africa
it.h: Ethiopia's emperor Menelik II led the army.

it.q: The Maxim gun and the drug quinine helped Europeans conquer Africa because
ch: the gun gave overwhelming firepower and quinine protected against malaria
they were gifts to African rulers
it.h: One is a weapon, the other a medicine.

it.q: Rudyard Kipling's poem "The White Man's Burden" (1899) urged Americans to colonize the Philippines and described colonized peoples as "Half devil and half child." What attitude does this reveal?
ch: a racist belief that colonizers had a duty to rule people they saw as inferior
it.h: What does the phrase say about how he viewed colonized peoples?

it.q: Under King Leopold II, the Congo Free State forced people to collect rubber and punished them brutally. Missionaries and journalists published reports and photographs. What was the result?
ch: international outrage led Belgium's government to take over the colony in 1908
it.h: What can public pressure do?

it.q: Explain how the borders drawn by European powers in Africa caused later problems.
it.ans: Borders often split ethnic groups or combined rivals in one colony without regard to local history, contributing to conflicts after independence.
it.h: Who drew the lines, and did they consult Africans?

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: Imperialism in Asia and the Pacific

it.q: The Opium War (1839-1842) began when
ch: China tried to stop British merchants from selling opium in China
it.h: Britain wanted to keep selling the drug.

it.q: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) forced China to
ch: give Hong Kong to Britain and open more ports to trade
it.h: Treaties after a defeat usually favor the winner.

it.q: After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British government
ch: took direct control of India from the British East India Company
it.h: This period of rule is called the British Raj.

it.q: A sphere of influence is
ch: an area where a foreign power has special trading or political rights
it.h: China was divided into several of these.

it.q: Siam (today Thailand) was the only Southeast Asian kingdom not colonized. Which helps explain this?
ch: its rulers modernized and balanced British and French interests against each other
it was too far from Europe for anyone to reach
it.h: It sat between British and French colonies.

it.q: Explain how the Boxer Rebellion (1900) reflected Chinese anger at foreign influence.
it.ans: The Boxers attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians, blaming foreign powers for China's humiliation, unequal treaties and economic problems; foreign armies crushed the uprising.
it.h: Who were the Boxers' targets?

lessons.u: Industrialization and imperialism
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which pair correctly matches a cause with an effect?
ch: need for raw materials - competition for colonies
enclosure - more people living on farms
the Factory Act - longer hours for children
it.h: Check each pair carefully.

it.q: Which statement about industrialization and imperialism is accurate?
ch: factories needed raw materials and markets, which encouraged empire building
industry had no link to colonies
it.h: What did factories need from abroad?

it.q: Which country industrialized first?
it.h: Think about where the spinning jenny and Watt's engine came from.

it.q: Which group would most likely have criticized imperialism around 1900?
it.h: Who lost the most under colonial rule?

it.q: Explain one long-term effect of imperialism that can still be seen today.
it.ans: For example, borders drawn by colonizers, European languages spoken in former colonies or economies built around exporting raw materials.
it.h: Think of borders, languages and economies.

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: Causes of World War I

it.q: By 1914 Europe was divided into two alliances: the Triple Entente of France, Russia and Britain, and the
ch: Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy
Axis of Japan, Italy and Germany
it.h: Germany was the leading power in this group.

it.q: Militarism before World War I meant
ch: glorifying military power and building up armies and navies
it.h: Britain and Germany raced to build battleships.

it.q: Nationalism in the Balkans contributed to the war because
ch: Slavic peoples, backed by Serbia, wanted to break free of Austria-Hungary
everyone in the Balkans supported Austria-Hungary
the Balkans had no ethnic groups
it.h: The assassin of Franz Ferdinand was a Bosnian Serb nationalist.

it.q: Germany's Schlieffen Plan called for
ch: quickly defeating France through Belgium before turning to fight Russia
it.h: Germany feared a two-front war.

it.q: Germany's invasion of neutral Belgium in August 1914 brought which country into the war?
it.h: This country had promised to protect Belgium's neutrality.

it.q: Explain how the alliance system turned a conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia into a world war.
it.ans: When Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia mobilized to defend Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary and declared war on Russia and France, and Britain joined when Germany invaded Belgium.
it.h: Trace each country's promise to another.

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: Total war: fighting World War I

it.q: Total war means
ch: a nation uses all its people, industry and resources for the war effort
it.h: Factories, farms and civilians all took part.

it.q: The Battle of the Somme in 1916 is remembered for
ch: enormous casualties for small gains of ground
the first use of atomic weapons
it.h: Over a million men were killed or wounded.

it.q: Wilfred Owen, a British soldier, wrote a poem about a gas attack, published in 1920, that ends by calling "Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori" (It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country) "The old Lie." What is his view?
ch: the glory of war is a lie told to young people
it.h: Why would he call this saying a lie?

it.q: Which new weapon first used widely in World War I caused terrible injuries and panic in the trenches?
it.h: Soldiers carried masks against it.

it.q: Women in Britain worked in munitions factories during the war, and in 1918 many British women over 30 won the vote. What connection can be drawn?
ch: women's war work strengthened the case for their right to vote
the war ended women's suffrage campaigns
it.h: What did their work prove to the public?

it.q: Explain why the Western Front became a stalemate.
it.ans: Machine guns, artillery and barbed wire made attacks across open ground deadly, so both sides dug long lines of trenches and neither could break through.
it.h: Think of what defenders had that attackers could not overcome.

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: Revolution in Russia and the peace settlements

it.q: In March 1917 (February in Russia's old calendar), Tsar Nicholas II gave up the throne because
ch: war losses, food shortages and strikes turned the people and army against him
he wanted to retire to France
it.h: Think of the effects of war on Russia's people.

it.q: The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, won support with the slogan
it.h: What did tired soldiers and hungry peasants want?

it.q: President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918) called for "a general association of nations" to guarantee "political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike." Which organization came from this idea?
it.h: It was created after the war to keep peace.

it.q: The U.S. Senate refused to approve the Treaty of Versailles mainly because many senators
ch: feared the League of Nations would pull the U.S. into future wars
wanted to join the war again
it.h: Think about the debate over joining the League.

it.q: Wilson's Fourteen Points called for self-determination, but at the 1919 peace conference most colonies in Africa and Asia did not gain independence. How did many colonized peoples react?
ch: they were disappointed, and nationalist movements grew stronger
it.h: What happens when a promise is not kept?

it.q: Explain how World War I helped cause the Russian Revolution.
it.ans: Huge losses, food and fuel shortages and the tsar's poor leadership led to strikes and mutinies, the tsar's fall in 1917 and the Bolshevik seizure of power later that year.
it.h: Connect the war at the front to life at home.

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: The rise of totalitarian states

it.q: Fascism, as practiced by Benito Mussolini in Italy, emphasized
ch: extreme nationalism, a single all-powerful leader and suppression of opposition
it.h: Mussolini's party used violence against opponents.

it.q: Joseph Stalin's Five-Year Plans, beginning in 1928, aimed to
ch: rapidly build heavy industry under state control
it.h: Steel, coal and machinery were the targets.

it.q: Stalin's forced collectivization of farms
ch: combined private farms into state-controlled collective farms and contributed to famines that killed millions
it.h: Peasants who resisted were punished.

it.q: The Great Depression helped Hitler gain support in Germany because
ch: mass unemployment and fear made many Germans desperate for strong leadership
it.h: How do hard times affect voters?

it.q: Hitler became chancellor of Germany legally in January 1933, then quickly ended democracy. What does this show?
ch: democratic institutions can be dismantled from within by leaders who gain power legally
dictators always take power by invasion
it.h: How did he get into office, and what did he do next?

it.q: Explain how totalitarian regimes in the 1930s used schools and youth groups to control society.
it.ans: They taught loyalty to the leader and party ideology, rewrote textbooks and enrolled young people in groups such as the Hitler Youth to shape beliefs and report on others.
it.h: Why target young people?

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: The road to World War II and the course of the war

it.q: At the Munich Conference in 1938, Britain and France
ch: allowed Germany to take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia to avoid war
it.h: This policy is called appeasement.

it.q: In August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union surprised the world by
it.h: It secretly divided Eastern Europe between them.

it.q: World War II in Europe began when
it.h: Britain and France had promised to defend this country.

it.q: The Battle of Stalingrad (1942-1943) was a turning point because
ch: the Soviet Union defeated a large German army and began pushing west
it.h: After it, the Germans were mostly retreating in the east.

it.q: Britain and France let Germany remilitarize the Rhineland in 1936 and annex Austria in 1938. What lesson did many leaders draw after the war?
ch: giving in to an aggressor's demands can encourage more aggression
it.h: What did Hitler do after each success?

it.q: Explain why the Battle of Midway in 1942 was a turning point in the Pacific.
it.ans: The U.S. Navy sank four Japanese aircraft carriers, ending Japan's ability to expand and letting the U.S. go on the offensive.
it.h: What did Japan lose that it could not replace quickly?

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: The Holocaust, war crimes and a new world order

it.q: Kristallnacht, in November 1938, was
ch: a night of violent attacks on Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany
it.h: The name means "Night of Broken Glass."

it.q: At the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, Nazi officials
ch: coordinated plans for the systematic murder of Europe's Jews
it.h: They called it the "Final Solution."

it.q: Besides Jews, the Nazis persecuted and murdered
ch: Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others
it.h: The Nazis targeted many groups they labeled inferior or enemies.

it.q: The Nuremberg trials (1945-1946) were important because
ch: Nazi leaders were tried for crimes against humanity, establishing that following orders is no excuse
it.h: What principle did the trials set about individual responsibility?

it.q: Some Germans and others hid Jews at great risk, while many people stayed silent. What does this show about the Holocaust?
ch: individuals made choices, and some chose to resist even under a brutal regime
it.h: Think about rescuers.

it.q: Explain why the United Nations was created in 1945 and how it differed from the League of Nations.
it.ans: It was created to prevent another world war and promote cooperation; unlike the League, it included the United States and the Soviet Union and had a Security Council with power to authorize action.
it.h: Which great powers stayed out of the League?

lessons.u: World Wars and totalitarianism
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which events are in the correct order?
ch: assassination of Franz Ferdinand, Treaty of Versailles, Munich Conference, invasion of Poland
Munich Conference, Treaty of Versailles, invasion of Poland, assassination of Franz Ferdinand
Treaty of Versailles, assassination of Franz Ferdinand, invasion of Poland, Munich Conference
invasion of Poland, Munich Conference, Treaty of Versailles, assassination of Franz Ferdinand
it.h: Use the years 1914, 1919, 1938 and 1939.

it.q: Which pair correctly matches a leader with a country?
it.h: Check each leader carefully.

it.q: Which policy did Britain and France follow toward Hitler in the 1930s?
it.h: It means giving in to demands to avoid war.

it.q: Which is a primary source about World War I?
ch: a soldier's letter home from the trenches in 1916
it.h: Primary sources come from people at the time.

it.q: Explain one way World War I helped lead to World War II.
it.ans: For example, the harsh Treaty of Versailles left Germans angry and poor, which Hitler used to gain support.
it.h: Think about the treaty and its effects.

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: Origins of the Cold War

it.q: At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union
ch: planned the postwar division of Germany and discussed the future of Eastern Europe
it.h: The war in Europe was almost over.

it.q: After World War II, the Soviet Union set up communist governments in
ch: Poland, Hungary and other Eastern European nations
it.h: These were countries the Soviet army had occupied.

it.q: The "Iron Curtain" was a phrase used in 1946 by Winston Churchill to describe
ch: the division between communist Eastern Europe and the democratic West
it.h: It was not a real curtain.

it.q: The Truman Doctrine (1947) promised U.S. support to
ch: free peoples resisting communist takeover, starting with Greece and Turkey
it.h: It is an early example of containment.

it.q: The Soviet Union had been invaded from the west twice in about 30 years. How might this explain its actions in Eastern Europe after 1945?
ch: it wanted friendly governments as a buffer zone against future attack
it wanted to give those nations independence
it.h: Consider the Soviet perspective on security.

it.q: Explain how the Berlin Airlift (1948-1949) showed the conflict between the superpowers.
it.ans: When the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, the U.S. and Britain flew in food and fuel for months instead of fighting, showing their determination to resist without starting a war; the Soviets lifted the blockade.
it.h: What did each side do, and why didn't they fight directly?

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: Proxy wars, the arms race and the nonaligned world

it.q: A proxy war is
ch: a conflict in which rival powers support opposing sides instead of fighting each other directly
it.h: "Proxy" means someone acting for another.

it.q: The Korean War began in 1950 when
it.h: The invader was backed by the Soviet Union.

it.q: The Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957
ch: was the first artificial satellite and started the space race
it.h: The U.S. feared it was falling behind in technology.

it.q: The idea of mutually assured destruction (MAD) held that
ch: neither superpower would start a nuclear war because both would be destroyed
nuclear war could be won easily
only one side had nuclear weapons
it.h: Why would no one dare to strike first?

it.q: The Soviet Union fought a long war in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989, while the U.S. armed Afghan fighters. Which term best describes this conflict?
it.h: Who was fighting directly, and who was supplying weapons?

it.q: Explain why many newly independent nations joined the Non-Aligned Movement.
it.ans: They wanted to avoid being pulled into the superpower rivalry, keep their independence and focus on their own development; many had just escaped colonial rule.
it.h: Why would a new nation avoid choosing a side?

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: Decolonization in Asia and the Middle East

it.q: India and Pakistan became independent in 1947 when British India was
ch: partitioned, causing mass migration and deadly violence
it.h: The division was largely along religious lines.

it.q: Gandhi's Salt March in 1930 protested
ch: the British monopoly and tax on salt
it.h: Marchers walked to the sea to make their own salt.

it.q: Indonesia won independence in 1949 from
it.h: It had been called the Dutch East Indies.

it.q: The French were defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, which
it.h: Vietnam was then divided into North and South.

it.q: In 1948 the State of Israel was declared, and in the war that followed hundreds of thousands of Palestinian Arabs fled or were driven from their homes. Why do Israelis and Palestinians often describe 1948 so differently?
ch: for many Israelis it marks independence and survival, while for many Palestinians it marks loss and displacement
both sides describe it the same way
it.h: Consider what the year meant to each people.

it.q: Explain why the partition of India in 1947 led to violence.
it.ans: Drawing new borders quickly along religious lines left millions on the "wrong" side; as Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs fled in both directions, communal violence killed hundreds of thousands or more.
it.h: What happens when borders are drawn quickly through mixed communities?

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: Decolonization in Africa and the end of apartheid

it.q: In 1957 Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became
ch: one of the first African colonies to win independence after World War II
it.h: It was formerly called the Gold Coast.

it.q: Seventeen African nations gained independence in 1960, which became known as
it.h: Most were former French colonies.

it.q: Algeria won independence from France in 1962 after
ch: a long and violent war that began in 1954
a peaceful vote with no conflict
it.h: France had many settlers in Algeria and fought to keep it.

it.q: Apartheid in South Africa (1948 to the early 1990s) was
ch: a system of laws enforcing racial segregation and white minority rule
it.h: The word means "apartness" in Afrikaans.

it.q: Nelson Mandela was imprisoned for 27 years and was released in 1990. In 1994 he was elected president in South Africa's first election open to all races. What does this show?
ch: sustained resistance and international pressure helped end apartheid
apartheid ended because of one election only
it.h: What happened between his arrest and his election?

it.q: Explain one challenge many African nations faced after independence.
it.ans: For example, colonial borders that grouped rival groups together, economies built to export raw materials, few trained officials, and Cold War interference contributed to conflict and instability.
it.h: Think of borders, economies and outside pressure.

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: The end of the Cold War and a globalized world

it.q: Mikhail Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika meant
ch: more openness and restructuring of the Soviet economy
it.h: Glasnost means openness.

it.q: In Poland in 1980, workers formed the independent trade union
it.h: It was led by Lech Walesa.

it.q: Germany was reunified in
it.h: It was one year after the Berlin Wall fell.

it.q: Beginning in 1978, China under Deng Xiaoping
ch: introduced market reforms while the Communist Party kept political control
it.h: China opened to foreign investment.

it.q: In 1989 communist governments fell across Eastern Europe, mostly without war. Which helps explain this?
ch: Gorbachev did not send the Soviet army to keep them in power
the leaders asked to be removed
it.h: What had the Soviets done in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968?

it.q: Explain one way globalization after the Cold War changed the world economy.
it.ans: For example, former communist countries joined world trade, the World Trade Organization was created in 1995, supply chains spread across countries and the internet sped up trade and communication.
it.h: Think of trade, technology and new markets.

lessons.u: The Cold War and the modern world
lessons.n: Unit review

it.q: Which pair correctly matches a Cold War event with its year?
it.h: Check each date carefully.

it.q: Which is an example of containment?
ch: U.S. aid to Greece and Turkey in 1947
it.h: Containment was a U.S. policy to stop the spread of communism.

it.q: Which nation gained independence first?
it.h: Use the years 1947, 1957, 1962 and 1963.

it.q: Which statement about the Cold War is accurate?
ch: the superpowers competed through alliances, aid, arms and proxy wars
the U.S. and USSR fought a direct world war
it.h: Think of Korea, Vietnam and the space race.

it.q: Explain how decolonization and the Cold War affected each other.
it.ans: Superpowers competed for influence in newly independent nations, sometimes backing sides in their conflicts, while many new nations tried to stay nonaligned.
it.h: Think about where proxy wars happened.

lessons.u: Progressive Era and World War I
lessons.n: Immigration, cities and the new industrial economy

it.q: Around 1900, most "new immigrants" to the United States came from
ch: Southern and Eastern Europe, such as Italy, Poland and Russia
it.h: Earlier immigrants had come mostly from Britain, Ireland and Germany.

it.q: Jacob Riis began "How the Other Half Lives" (1890) with the saying that "one half of the world does not know how the other half lives." What did his book and photographs show?
